companyDescription: The Walt Disney Company is a global entertainment conglomerate that operates streaming services including Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN+, as well as theme parks, film studios, and television networks.
companyLongDescription: The Walt Disney Company is one of the world's largest media and entertainment corporations, with operations spanning streaming video (Disney+, Hulu, ESPN+), theatrical films, television networks (ABC, ESPN), theme parks, and consumer products. Founded in 1923, Disney operates across multiple continents and serves hundreds of millions of consumers annually. The company collects extensive personal information from its streaming service subscribers to enable targeted advertising and content personalization.
caseDescription: Disney failed to provide clear and conspicuous opt-out mechanisms for the sale and sharing of consumer personal information on its streaming services (Disney+, Hulu, ESPN+), and failed to implement consumer-friendly opt-out processes as required by the California Consumer Privacy Act. The company also failed to properly handle opt-out requests and provide adequate notice regarding cross-context behavioral advertising using third-party data.
violationSummary: Disney improperly disclosed and shared personal information obtained from third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising without adequate opt-out mechanisms or clear notices, constituting a disclosure violation under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Disney failed to provide clear and conspicuous opt-out mechanisms for the sale and sharing of consumer personal information on Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN+.
whyTheyWereWrong: 100 million Disney+ and Hulu subscribers had their personal data sold or shared with third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising without easy ways to stop it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disney's opt-out mechanisms were clear and easy to use for consumers wishing to stop the sale and sharing of their personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disney buried opt-out links, required unnecessary scrolling and steps, used hidden menu icons, and made the process confusing—deliberately obstructing consumers' statutory right to opt out.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disney provided meaningful notice to consumers about cross-context behavioral advertising using third-party data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disney failed to provide clear notice about its collection and use of third-party data for tracking consumers across the internet and targeting them with behavioral advertising.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disney promptly honored consumer opt-out requests and stopped selling and sharing their personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disney failed to implement proper systems to process opt-out requests across its streaming services and did not reliably stop selling and sharing consumer data after opt-out.

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA requires clear and conspicuous notice to consumers regarding sale or sharing of personal information and cross-context behavioral advertising
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney failed to provide clear notice regarding cross-context behavioral advertising using third-party personal information
violations: Disney failed to provide clear notice regarding cross-context behavioral advertising using third-party personal information
Disney failed to provide adequate notice of the right to opt-out of sale or sharing of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA requires consumer-friendly, easy-to-execute opt-out mechanisms for sale or sharing of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney's opt-out process was not consumer-friendly or easy to execute
violations: Disney's opt-out process was not consumer-friendly or easy to execute
Disney failed to implement minimal-step opt-out procedures
Disney failed to properly implement account-wide opt-out choices across all Disney streaming services

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA requires compliance with consumer opt-out requests and notification to third parties
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney failed to properly effectuate consumer opt-out choices
violations: Disney failed to properly effectuate consumer opt-out choices
Disney failed to notify third parties to whom personal information was sold or shared of consumer opt-out requests

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA prohibits sale or sharing of personal information of children (under 13) and minors (13-15) without affirmative authorization
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney continued to sell or share personal information of children and minors without proper parental/minor authorization
violations: Disney continued to sell or share personal information of children and minors without proper parental/minor authorization

outcome: Disney is ordered to implement consumer-friendly opt-out mechanisms across all Disney streaming services within required timeframes, provide clear notices regarding cross-context behavioral advertising and sale/sharing of personal information, ensure opt-out choices are effectuated account-wide, cease selling or sharing information of children and minors without authorization, implement a three-year compliance monitoring program, and pay $2,750,000 to the California Attorney General's Office. The company must provide compliance updates every 60 days until full compliance is achieved, and annual reports for three years thereafter documenting monitoring results.
companyNow: Disney remains a dominant global media and entertainment corporation, though its streaming services face intensifying competition and regulatory scrutiny over data practices across multiple jurisdictions.
dataType: Personal information including unique identifiers, behavioral data, cross-context activity data
legalBasisViolated: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 et seq.

companyDescription: Disney is a major media and entertainment conglomerate that owns and operates streaming services including Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN+, generating significant revenue through advertising and data monetization.
companyLongDescription: The Walt Disney Company is a global entertainment corporation that operates multiple streaming platforms (Disney+, Hulu, ESPN+) requiring consumer accounts and login credentials. Disney leverages its extensive database of consumer device associations and viewing behavior to build a profitable targeted advertising business, combining internal data with third-party ad-tech partners and data brokers to create detailed consumer profiles for cross-device and cross-service ad targeting.
caseDescription: Disney implemented fragmented opt-out mechanisms that failed to honor consumers' requests to prevent the sale and sharing of their personal information for targeted advertising. Consumers had to opt out separately on each device and service, even though Disney could link devices to accounts for advertising purposes. Disney also failed to honor opt-out preference signals like Global Privacy Control and misled consumers by labeling incomplete opt-out tools as functional opt-out mechanisms.
violationSummary: Disney disclosed and shared consumers' personal information with third-party ad-tech partners despite receiving opt-out directives. The core violation involves the improper dissemination of data when consumers explicitly requested it be restricted, despite Disney's technical ability to implement comprehensive opt-outs.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Disney implemented fragmented opt-out mechanisms across multiple services and devices that failed to honor consumers' requests to prevent sale.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' personal data continued to be sold to ad-tech partners and used for targeted advertising across devices even after opting out.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disney's opt-out mechanisms were functional and allowed consumers to prevent sale and sharing of their data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Opt-out requests were only partially honored—webform opt-outs stopped Disney's direct advertising but not third-party sharing; toggle/GPC opt-outs only affected the specific service and device used, not across the consumer's linked account and devices.

claimsVsReality.claim: Technical and vendor limitations prevented Disney from implementing device-linked opt-outs.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disney successfully linked devices for advertising targeting purposes, proving the technical capability existed; Disney simply chose not to apply the same device-linking infrastructure to honor opt-out requests.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disney honored opt-out preference signals like Global Privacy Control.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disney accepted GPC signals but only implemented them for the specific service and device where the signal originated, not across all devices and services linked to the consumer's account.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers could fully opt-out through one simple method.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumers with Disney bundle accounts accessing three services across three devices had to complete opt-out actions up to ten times, and some connected TV apps had no in-app opt-out mechanism at all.

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.120(a) – Consumer Right to Opt-Out: Consumers have the right to opt-out of the sale or sharing of their personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney continued to share consumers' data with third-party ad-tech partners despite receiving opt-out requests through its webform
violations: Disney continued to share consumers' data with third-party ad-tech partners despite receiving opt-out requests through its webform
Disney only honored opt-out requests for its own advertising platform, not for third-party ad-tech partners
Disney required consumers to opt-out separately on each device and service, rather than implementing account-level opt-outs

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.135(a) – Methods for Opt-Out: Businesses must provide consumers with methods to submit opt-out requests
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney failed to provide easy-to-use opt-out methods that required minimal steps
violations: Disney failed to provide easy-to-use opt-out methods that required minimal steps
Disney required consumers to complete up to ten separate opt-out actions across devices and services
Disney did not provide in-app opt-out mechanisms for connected TV streaming apps, instead directing consumers to webforms that had no practical effect

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.135(e) – Opt-Out Preference Signals: Businesses must treat opt-out preference signals as valid requests for known consumers
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney failed to honor Global Privacy Control (GPC) signals as comprehensive opt-out requests
violations: Disney failed to honor Global Privacy Control (GPC) signals as comprehensive opt-out requests
Disney only partially implemented opt-out preference signals on specific services and devices

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 – Unfair Competition: Unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent acts or practices constitute unfair competition
regulatoryFindings.description: Disney engaged in deceptive practices by labeling incomplete opt-out tools as functional opt-out mechanisms
violations: Disney engaged in deceptive practices by labeling incomplete opt-out tools as functional opt-out mechanisms
Disney misrepresented compliance with opt-out preference signals when it failed to honor them comprehensively
Disney's conduct constituted fraud by creating the appearance of CCPA compliance while failing to honor consumer privacy rights

outcome: The complaint seeks injunctive relief to prevent future CCPA violations, civil penalties of $2,663 per violation or $7,988 per intentional violation or violation involving minors' data under CCPA, civil penalties of $2,500 per Business and Professions Code § 17200 violation, disgorgement of profits obtained through unfair competition, restoration of money and property obtained through unfair competition, and recovery of costs. The case has been filed and awaits adjudication by the Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles.
companyNow: Disney remains one of the largest media and entertainment companies in the world, operating streaming services and traditional media properties globally. The company continues to face regulatory scrutiny over data privacy practices as streaming services become increasingly central to its business model.
dataType: Device identifiers, device type, IP addresses, streaming behavior, browsing history, income, household size, predicted interests, personal information of minor consumers

companyDescription: Xponential Fitness is a franchisor operating numerous fitness studio brands including Club Pilates, Stretch Lab, Pure Barre, and Yoga Six across the United States.
companyLongDescription: Xponential Fitness, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Irvine, California that operates and franchises some of the largest fitness-studio brands in the United States. The company sells franchise opportunities to prospective franchisees who invest significant capital to open branded fitness studios. Xponential controls multiple franchise entities and brand portfolios across the fitness industry. The company was accused of systematically deceiving franchisees through incomplete and inaccurate disclosure documents required under federal franchising law.
caseDescription: Xponential, a fitness franchise operator, violated the FTC Act and Franchise Rule by failing to provide Franchise Disclosure Documents (FDDs) at least 14 days before prospective franchisees signed binding agreements and by materially misrepresenting or omitting critical information in its FDDs. The company falsely claimed studios typically took six months to open when franchisees actually required over twelve months; failed to disclose information about founder Anthony Geisler's fraudulent practices; omitted material litigation and bankruptcy information; and withheld names of terminated franchisees.
violationSummary: Xponential knowingly distorted and misrepresented material facts in its FDDs, including timeframes for opening studios, financial performance data, and backgrounds of key officers, causing prospective franchisees to make decisions based on false information.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Xponential failed to provide Franchise Disclosure Documents 14 days before franchisees signed binding agreements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective franchisees were deceived into investing hundreds of thousands of dollars based on false claims that studios typically open in six months when they actually require over twelve.

claimsVsReality.claim: The typical length of time to open a studio is six months.
claimsVsReality.reality: Franchisees actually required over twelve months on average to open studios, during which they incurred substantial ongoing costs like rent and payroll.

claimsVsReality.claim: Founder Anthony Geisler had no relevant legal issues affecting the franchise opportunity.
claimsVsReality.reality: Geisler was held liable for fraudulent, unfair, and deceptive practices while serving as a controlling officer and manager of Xponential, information withheld from prospective franchisees for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Complete and accurate franchisee reference lists were provided in disclosure documents.
claimsVsReality.reality: Xponential omitted names and contact information for numerous franchisees whose studios had been terminated, canceled, not renewed, or ceased business in the most recent fiscal year.

claimsVsReality.claim: Xponential had no material legal actions or compliance issues.
claimsVsReality.reality: Xponential failed to disclose numerous relevant legal actions involving the company or its officers, as well as the bankruptcy of its former Vice President of Franchise Development.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5 prohibits unfair or deceptive practices in commerce
regulatoryFindings.description: Misrepresented typical timeframe to open studios as six months when SEC filings showed over twelve months average
violations: Misrepresented typical timeframe to open studios as six months when SEC filings showed over twelve months average
Failed to disclose founder's prior involvement in fraudulent practices
Omitted material litigation and legal actions involving company officers
Withheld names of terminated franchisees as required

regulatoryFindings.act: Franchise Rule requires provision of FDD at least 14 calendar days before signing and mandates 23 items of material information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to furnish FDD 14 days before some prospective franchisees signed binding agreements
violations: Failed to furnish FDD 14 days before some prospective franchisees signed binding agreements
Omitted or misrepresented material facts regarding officer backgrounds, litigation history, and franchisee experience data
Failed to disclose bankruptcy information on company executives
Misrepresented financial performance and operational timelines

outcome: FTC filed complaint and consent agreement in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. Xponential is prohibited from misrepresenting material facts in connection with franchise sales, required to comply with the Franchise Rule, and ordered to pay $17 million in consumer redress to franchisees injured by the alleged misconduct.
companyNow: As of 2026, Xponential Fitness faces a $17 million FTC settlement and is subject to strict compliance orders regarding franchise disclosures and prohibited from misrepresenting material facts to franchisees.
dataType: Business and financial information, personal contact information of franchisees and former franchisees, officer/management backgrounds

companyDescription: WPATH (World Professional Association for Transgender Health) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit membership organization that promotes evidence-based care, education, and research in transgender health through professional standards, educational programs, and publications.
companyLongDescription: WPATH is an international nonprofit professional association with regional affiliates in Europe and the United States. The organization publishes the International Journal of Transgender Health, hosts educational events and symposia, provides certification programs through its Global Education Institute, and develops and updates the Standards of Care—a consensus document on the psychiatric, psychological, medical, and surgical management of transgender and gender-diverse people. WPATH's membership includes healthcare professionals and academics working across different jurisdictions and regulatory environments.
caseDescription: The FTC issued a Civil Investigative Demand (CID) to WPATH, a nonprofit professional organization, to investigate whether WPATH or others have made false or unsubstantiated representations or engaged in unfair practices in marketing pediatric gender dysphoria treatments (PGDT) to consumers. WPATH petitioned to quash the CID arguing lack of FTC jurisdiction over nonprofits, First Amendment violations including retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, and that the CID was overbroad and unduly burdensome. The FTC denied WPATH's petition, finding it had investigatory authority over any legal entity and that WPATH's First Amendment claims lacked merit.
violationSummary: The investigation focuses on whether WPATH or others disseminated false or unsubstantiated claims about PGDT safety and efficacy, potentially deceiving consumers. This falls under disclosure of misleading information affecting commerce.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: WPATH, a nonprofit professional association for transgender health, petitioned the FTC to quash a Civil Investigative Demand (CID) seeking information about pediatric gender dysphoria treatments.
whyTheyWereWrong: WPATH's petition failed because the FTC has authority to investigate any legal entity to determine jurisdiction.

claimsVsReality.claim: WPATH argued the FTC lacks jurisdiction over nonprofits and cannot serve a CID on WPATH.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC has clear statutory authority under Section 20 of the FTC Act to serve a CID on any legal entity, including nonprofits, to investigate whether they fall within the Commission's enforcement jurisdiction.

claimsVsReality.claim: WPATH claimed it is a 'true' nonprofit operating solely for charitable purposes without profit motives.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC rejected WPATH's self-characterization and asserted authority to conduct fact-intensive inquiry into WPATH's actual operations, including financial relationships with pharmaceutical companies, device manufacturers, and clinicians.

claimsVsReality.claim: WPATH argued the CID was overly broad, unduly burdensome, and sought irrelevant information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CID specifications were reasonably relevant to investigating whether WPATH made false or unsubstantiated representations about pediatric gender dysphoria treatments affecting consumers.

claimsVsReality.claim: WPATH raised First Amendment concerns about the investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC's investigation into factual representations about medical treatments and business practices is not barred by First Amendment protections.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 20 – Authority to issue CID to any 'person' (legal entity) in investigating potential unfair or deceptive practices
regulatoryFindings.description: WPATH claimed FTC lacked authority to issue CID to nonprofit organizations; FTC found Section 20 plainly authorizes CID service on any legal entity regardless of nonprofit status
violations: WPATH claimed FTC lacked authority to issue CID to nonprofit organizations; FTC found Section 20 plainly authorizes CID service on any legal entity regardless of nonprofit status

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5 and 12 – Prohibition on false, unsubstantiated, or unfair representations in commerce
regulatoryFindings.description: Investigation into whether WPATH made or assisted others in making false or unsubstantiated claims about PGDT safety, efficacy, and necessity for minors with gender dysphoria
violations: Investigation into whether WPATH made or assisted others in making false or unsubstantiated claims about PGDT safety, efficacy, and necessity for minors with gender dysphoria

regulatoryFindings.act: First Amendment – Protection against retaliation for protected speech and viewpoint discrimination
regulatoryFindings.description: WPATH alleged CID was retaliatory in response to its advocacy positions on gender-affirming care; FTC found no causal link between WPATH's speech and CID issuance, no extraordinary circumstances constituting retaliation, and no chilling effect
violations: WPATH alleged CID was retaliatory in response to its advocacy positions on gender-affirming care; FTC found no causal link between WPATH's speech and CID issuance, no extraordinary circumstances constituting retaliation, and no chilling effect

outcome: WPATH's petition to quash the CID was denied. The FTC affirmed the CID's validity and necessity to investigate potential deceptive practices related to PGDT marketing and advertising. WPATH was ordered to comply fully with the CID no later than 60 days after the court's decision on WPATH's Motion for Preliminary Injunction in its collateral federal court challenge, or at such other date as FTC staff determines.
companyNow: WPATH continues to operate as a professional membership organization, though it has reportedly discontinued certain education and mentorship programs following the FTC's Civil Investigative Demand.
dataType: Member information, communications, donor information, organizational records, medical research data, financial statements
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts or practices)
FTC Act Section 20 (civil investigative demand authority)

companyDescription: The Endocrine Society is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit medical organization dedicated to advancing excellence in endocrinology through scientific discovery, medical practice, and education.
companyLongDescription: Founded in 1918, the Endocrine Society is the world's largest organization devoted to the study of hormones and clinical endocrinology practice. The organization serves over 18,000 members globally and publishes peer-reviewed journals, clinical practice guidelines, and position statements on endocrine disorders. The society advances its charitable mission through scientific research, educational forums, and professional development programs for endocrinologists and related specialists.
caseDescription: The FTC issued a Civil Investigative Demand to Endocrine Society, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit medical organization, to investigate whether Endocrine Society or other parties made false or unsubstantiated representations about Pediatric Gender Dysphoria Treatments (PGDT) in violation of FTC Act Sections 5 and 12. Endocrine Society challenged the CID on multiple grounds including jurisdictional limits, overbreadth, and First Amendment concerns, but the Commission denied the petition and ordered full compliance.
violationSummary: While the document does not allege a privacy breach per se, it investigates whether Endocrine Society's medical guidance and statements to consumers and healthcare providers regarding PGDT lack adequate substantiation for safety and efficacy claims. This falls under Information Processing – Insecurity because it involves the potential inadequate handling of sensitive health information through unsubstantiated claims to consumers about medical interventions affecting minors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Endocrine Society published clinical practice guidelines and position statements on pediatric gender dysphoria treatments that the FTC investigated for potential false or unsubstantiated.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents and minors may have relied on the organization's medical guidance to make irreversible treatment decisions without full understanding of risks, safety data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Endocrine Society claimed it is a 'true' charitable nonprofit organization exempt from FTC enforcement jurisdiction because it is organized as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit with tax-exempt status since 1918.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC determined it has investigatory jurisdiction over the organization under Section 20 of the FTC Act regardless of nonprofit status, and must conduct a fact-intensive inquiry into how Endocrine Society actually operates, including examination of financial relationships with pharmaceutical companies and medical device manufacturers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Endocrine Society argued the CID exceeds the Commission's authority and violates the First and Fourth Amendments.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC Commission denied all of Endocrine Society's challenges to the CID, affirming its authority to issue compulsory process to investigate whether the organization made false or unsubstantiated representations about pediatric gender dysphoria treatments.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5 prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged making or assisting others in making false or unsubstantiated representations concerning PGDT marketing and advertising
violations: Alleged making or assisting others in making false or unsubstantiated representations concerning PGDT marketing and advertising

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 12 prohibits false advertising of food, drugs, devices, and cosmetics
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged dissemination of unsubstantiated claims about safety and efficacy of PGDT treatments
violations: Alleged dissemination of unsubstantiated claims about safety and efficacy of PGDT treatments

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 20 authorizes Commission to issue Civil Investigative Demands to any 'person' (defined broadly to include nonprofit legal entities) for information relevant to unfair or deceptive practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Endocrine Society challenged the FTC's authority to issue CID to a nonprofit organization, but the Commission reaffirmed that Section 20 applies to all legal entities regardless of nonprofit status
violations: Endocrine Society challenged the FTC's authority to issue CID to a nonprofit organization, but the Commission reaffirmed that Section 20 applies to all legal entities regardless of nonprofit status

outcome: The FTC Commission denied Endocrine Society's petition to quash the CID in its entirety. Endocrine Society is ordered to comply in full with the Civil Investigative Demand no later than 60 days after the Court's decision on Endocrine Society's Motion for Preliminary Injunction in Endocrine Society v. FTC, No. 1:26-cv-512 (D.D.C. filed Feb. 17, 2026), or at such other date and time as FTC staff determines. The Commission rejected all of Endocrine Society's arguments regarding lack of FTC jurisdiction over nonprofits, unreasonable relevance, overbreadth, undue burden, and First Amendment violations. The investigation remains open pending Endocrine Society's compliance and further FTC evaluation of whether enforcement action is warranted.
companyNow: The Endocrine Society continues to operate as a leading professional medical organization, though it faced regulatory scrutiny from the FTC regarding the substantiation of claims in its pediatric gender dysphoria treatment guidelines.
dataType: Clinical records, medical guidance documents, financial records, membership information, communications with healthcare providers and patients
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts or practices)
FTC Act Section 20 (civil investigative demand authority)

companyDescription: The American Academy of Pediatrics is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit professional organization dedicated to improving child health through clinical guidance, education, and advocacy for pediatric medical professionals.
companyLongDescription: Founded in 1930, the AAP is the primary professional organization for pediatricians in the United States, with approximately 67,000 member physicians. The organization develops clinical practice guidelines, policy statements, and educational materials to inform pediatric medical practice. The AAP issued prominent guidance on gender-affirming care for transgender and gender-diverse youth in 2018 and reaffirmed it in 2023. While AAP describes itself as providing free educational materials rather than directly marketing or providing medical services, the FTC investigation examined whether its clinical guidance constituted deceptive or unfair marketing of pediatric gender dysphoria treatments.
caseDescription: The FTC issued a Civil Investigative Demand to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) investigating whether AAP or others made false or unsubstantiated representations about Pediatric Gender Dysphoria Treatment (PGDT) in violation of FTC Act Sections 5 and 12. AAP petitioned to quash the CID arguing it exceeded FTC authority, violated the First Amendment, lacked proper authorization, and was overbroad and unduly burdensome. The Commission denied the petition, finding the CID was properly issued within its investigatory authority and that AAP's constitutional arguments lacked merit.
violationSummary: The CID seeks to investigate potential false or unsubstantiated representations and unfair practices in the marketing and advertising of medical treatments. This falls under the Disclosure category as it concerns whether misleading information about health products and services was communicated to consumers and whether substantiation exists for claims made.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: The American Academy of Pediatrics issued clinical guidance on gender-affirming care for transgender youth.
whyTheyWereWrong: The FTC investigation suggests AAP's guidance may have misled medical professionals and families about the safety.

claimsVsReality.claim: AAP's guidance materials constitute non-commercial speech and are therefore outside FTC jurisdiction because they are offered free and AAP does not directly advertise or provide medical services.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC determined it has investigatory authority to examine whether AAP's statements about pediatric gender dysphoria treatment safety and efficacy constitute misleading commercial speech in a healthcare context, regardless of whether AAP directly profits from treatment provision.

claimsVsReality.claim: AAP is a nonprofit organization not organized to carry on business for profit, and therefore cannot violate the FTC Act as a 'corporation.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Under FTC Section 20, the agency can serve investigative demands on any 'legal entity' or 'person' regardless of nonprofit status or whether they fall within the enforcement definition of 'corporation,' to investigate potentially illegal conduct affecting consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5 – Prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
regulatoryFindings.description: Potential making of false or unsubstantiated representations regarding Pediatric Gender Dysphoria Treatment
violations: Potential making of false or unsubstantiated representations regarding Pediatric Gender Dysphoria Treatment
Potential engaging in unfair practices in connection with marketing and advertising of PGDT

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 12 – Prohibits false advertisements for foods, drugs, devices, or cosmetics
regulatoryFindings.description: Potential dissemination of false advertisements regarding safety and efficacy of medical interventions for minors with gender dysphoria
violations: Potential dissemination of false advertisements regarding safety and efficacy of medical interventions for minors with gender dysphoria

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 20 – Authorizes Commission to issue Civil Investigative Demands to any 'person' to investigate potential violations
regulatoryFindings.description: AAP challenged the scope and breadth of the CID but failed to demonstrate it exceeded the Commission's investigatory authority
violations: AAP challenged the scope and breadth of the CID but failed to demonstrate it exceeded the Commission's investigatory authority

outcome: The Commission denied AAP's petition to quash in its entirety. AAP is ordered to comply in full with the Civil Investigative Demand no later than 60 days after the Court's decision on AAP's Motion for Preliminary Injunction in AAP v. FTC, No. 1:26-cv-508 (D.D.C.), or at such other date as Commission staff determines. The CID requires AAP to produce documents and information concerning its membership, education programs, PGDT-related workshops, substantiation for specific representations (Covered Statements), development of policy statements, financial relationships with pharmaceutical companies and medical providers, investigations and lawsuits involving PGDT, financial statements, and records retention policies for the period January 1, 2021 forward (with certain specifications modified to January 1, 2015 forward).
companyNow: The AAP continues to operate as the leading professional organization for pediatricians in the United States, though it faces ongoing scrutiny regarding its positions on gender-affirming care for minors.
dataType: Medical records, health claims, internal communications, financial information, membership data
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts or practices)
FTC Act Section 20 (civil investigative demand authority)

companyDescription: Timegrip provides cloud-based time-tracking and HR management systems for retail and hospitality customers across multiple European countries. The company processes timesheets and employment data on behalf of employers.
companyLongDescription: Timegrip provides cloud-based time-tracking and HR management systems for retail and hospitality customers across multiple European countries. The company processes timesheets and employment data on behalf of employers.
caseDescription: Timegrip, a time-tracking system provider, unlawfully refused to provide employees with access to their own timesheets after their employer went bankrupt. The company claimed it could not grant access without instructions from the now-defunct employer, despite having sole control over the data and knowing the workers needed the records to claim unpaid wages. Datatilsynet found Timegrip was the de facto controller of the data and ordered it to pay 250,000 NOK.
violationSummary: The company refused to disclose personal data (timesheets) that individuals had a legal right to access under GDPR Article 15, despite being the only entity with control and knowledge of the data's importance to the data subjects.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Timegrip AS rejected 80 employees' requests to access their own timesheets following their employer's bankruptcy.
whyTheyWereWrong: Timegrip held sole control over workers' timesheet data and blocked access without legal justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Timegrip claimed it was only a data processor and could not release data without explicit instructions from the controller (Enklere Liv Retail AS).
claimsVsReality.reality: After the employer's bankruptcy, Timegrip was the sole entity with control over the data. It unilaterally determined retention periods, access, storage duration, and deletion—all hallmarks of a controller. No alternative controller emerged to give instructions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Timegrip stated the data handler agreement terminated upon bankruptcy, creating a legal vacuum where it had no obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Article 28(10) provides that processors who act outside their instructions become controllers. Timegrip's own actions—continuing storage, setting retention rules, denying access—made it a controller by operation of law.

claimsVsReality.claim: Timegrip claimed it could only provide raw data to the bankruptcy estate on a paid basis and only if the estate signed a new contract.
claimsVsReality.reality: Access rights under Article 15 are free and inalienable. The company cannot condition disclosure on payment, contract renegotiation, or third-party consent. Individual employees had a direct legal right regardless of any commercial dispute between Timegrip and the bankruptcy estate.

claimsVsReality.claim: Timegrip stated it acted in good faith based on legal advice about the ambiguous post-bankruptcy situation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Datatilsynet found no credible evidence of such advice, the company's legal position was self-contradictory (claiming both that the contract bound it and that the contract terminated), and a time-tracking company should understand basic GDPR controller/processor distinctions.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants every data subject the right to obtain confirmation of whether personal data is being processed and, if so, the right of access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Timegrip refused to provide copies of timesheets to employees requesting access, citing lack of instructions from the now-bankrupt employer.
violations: Timegrip refused to provide copies of timesheets to employees requesting access, citing lack of instructions from the now-bankrupt employer.

The company claimed it was only a data processor and could not disclose data without the controller's permission, ignoring the reality that it had sole actual control over the records and that no functioning controller existed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(10) provides that if a processor exceeds its authority by determining the purposes and means of processing without instructions, it becomes a controller for that processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Timegrip unilaterally decided to continue storing employee data indefinitely ('until 100% certain the company is liquidated'), determined how long records would be retained, and decided who could access them—all essential means and purposes—thereby becoming a controller.
violations: Timegrip unilaterally decided to continue storing employee data indefinitely ('until 100% certain the company is liquidated'), determined how long records would be retained, and decided who could access them—all essential means and purposes—thereby becoming a controller.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(3)(e) requires a processor to assist the controller in fulfilling the controller's obligations to respond to data subject requests for rights under Chapter III (including Article 15 access rights).
regulatoryFindings.description: After the employer ceased operations, Timegrip failed to identify an alternative controller or recognize its own controller status, and instead blocked all access requests, directly preventing employees from exercising their statutory rights.
violations: After the employer ceased operations, Timegrip failed to identify an alternative controller or recognize its own controller status, and instead blocked all access requests, directly preventing employees from exercising their statutory rights.

outcome: Datatilsynet found Timegrip was the de facto controller of the personal data after the employer's bankruptcy and had no legal grounds to refuse access. The company must pay 250,000 NOK. No structural remedies were imposed because the data has since been deleted (14 August 2020) and the complainant obtained wage compensation from NAV's wage guarantee fund. The case establishes that data processors cannot avoid controller obligations by pointing to contractual technicalities when they have sole actual control and no functioning controller exists.
companyNow: Timegrip was acquired by Timeplan International ApS (Denmark) in 2023. In 2024, Timeplan merged with TimeMap, operating under the Timegrip brand as part of a larger Scandinavian HR/time-tracking group.
dataType: Employment records, time logs, work hours, wage-related data

companyDescription: Allay Claims Limited is a claims management company acquired in 2015 that specialises in pursuing Personal Payment Insurance (PPI) tax refund claims on behalf of consumers. The company operates primarily through SMS marketing and online channels to identify and engage potential claimants.
companyLongDescription: Allay Claims Limited is a claims management company acquired in 2015 that specialises in pursuing Personal Payment Insurance (PPI) tax refund claims on behalf of consumers. The company operates primarily through SMS marketing and online channels to identify and engage potential claimants.
caseDescription: Allay Claims Limited sent 4.6 million unsolicited SMS marketing messages to consumers promoting PPI tax refund services between February 2023 and February 2024, without obtaining valid consent and failing to offer a simple means to opt out at the point of data collection. The company continued sending marketing messages even after the ICO's investigation commenced, resulting in a further 118,000+ complaints by January 2026.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic, large-scale collection and use of contact details for direct marketing without proper consent or opt-out mechanisms, fitting the surveillance category under Solove's framework. The deceptive representations about not using data for marketing exacerbate the surveillance aspect.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Allay Claims Limited sent 4,046,947 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to individuals between February 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: Recipients received promotional SMS messages about PPI tax refunds they never agreed to, despite the company's own online guarantee stating 'We do not cold call.

claimsVsReality.claim: Allay's online customer journey stated: 'PERSONAL INFORMATION GUARANTEE... We do not cold call, spam or pass on your data for marketing'
claimsVsReality.reality: Allay sent 4.6 million unsolicited SMS marketing messages to consumers, directly contradicting this guarantee.

claimsVsReality.claim: Allay claimed it relied on the 'soft opt-in' exemption and therefore consent was not required.
claimsVsReality.reality: Allay failed to comply with the conditions for soft opt-in under Regulation 22(3)(c), which requires a simple means of refusing marketing at initial data collection. Allay only offered opt-out via email hidden in the privacy policy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Allay later claimed the SMS messages were 'service messages' continuing a prior customer relationship, not direct marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The messages were explicitly promotional, encouraging recipients to join a class action ('Join them today!') and promoting a third-party law firm. The ICO found no reasonable interpretation by which these could be service messages.

claimsVsReality.claim: All recipients were 'previous customers' who had proactively engaged with Allay in 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: Contact details were obtained in 2019 for PPI claim services; many years later Allay sent unsolicited SMS promoting an unrelated group litigation order, with no evidence of fresh, explicit consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22(2) of PECR prohibits transmission of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Allay transmitted 4,046,947 direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: Allay transmitted 4,046,947 direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22(3)(c) of PECR requires that where soft opt-in applies, recipients must be given a simple means of refusing marketing use of contact details at the time details are initially collected and at each subsequent communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Allay failed to provide a simple opt-out mechanism at initial data collection; customers had to email a generic address to opt out. Online journey stated 'We do not cold call, spam or pass on your data for marketing' yet contained no upfront opt-out checkbox.
violations: Allay failed to provide a simple opt-out mechanism at initial data collection; customers had to email a generic address to opt out. Online journey stated 'We do not cold call, spam or pass on your data for marketing' yet contained no upfront opt-out checkbox.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A(1) of the DPA requires that before serving a monetary penalty for a serious contravention of PECR, the Commissioner must be satisfied that the contravention was either deliberate or negligent, with knowledge/reasonable awareness of the risk and failure to take reasonable steps to prevent it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Allay knew or ought to have known of PECR obligations; it was previously investigated in 2020 for similar breaches. Allay failed to suspend marketing activity despite ICO investigation and continued sending 118,088 complaints' worth of messages from February 2024 to January 2026. Company changed its legal position midway (from 'soft opt-in' to 'service messages'), indicating awareness of potential non-compliance.
violations: Allay knew or ought to have known of PECR obligations; it was previously investigated in 2020 for similar breaches. Allay failed to suspend marketing activity despite ICO investigation and continued sending 118,088 complaints' worth of messages from February 2024 to January 2026. Company changed its legal position midway (from 'soft opt-in' to 'service messages'), indicating awareness of potential non-compliance.

outcome: The Information Commissioner's Office issued a Monetary Penalty Notice on 15 January 2026 requiring Allay Claims Limited to pay £120,000 (reduced to £96,000 if paid by 16 February 2026 under the early payment discount). The penalty is enforceable by County Court (England, Wales, Northern Ireland) or Sheriff Court (Scotland). Allay has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber) within 28 days of the notice. The notice compels compliance with PECR Regulation 22 prospectively; Allay must ensure valid consent or full soft opt-in compliance for all future direct marketing.
companyNow: Allay Claims Limited remains active as of the notice date (15 January 2026), registered at Studio 20, The Kiln, Newcastle Upon Tyne. However, the company faces significant reputational damage, ongoing regulatory scrutiny, and continued SMS complaints (118,088 additional complaints from Feb 2024 to Jan 2026) indicating persistent non-compliance.
dataType: contact details (phone numbers, email addresses), personal identifiers related to PPI tax refund claims
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 22(2)
Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 22(3)(c)

companyDescription: The Greek Fire Service Headquarters (Αρχηγείο Πυροσβεστικού Σώματος) is the central executive and administrative authority of the Greek Fire Service, responsible for operations, human resources, and policy across all regional fire stations nationwide.
companyLongDescription: The Greek Fire Service Headquarters (Αρχηγείο Πυροσβεστικού Σώματος) is the central executive and administrative authority of the Greek Fire Service, responsible for operations, human resources, and policy across all regional fire stations nationwide.
caseDescription: The Fire Service Headquarters unlawfully recorded and distributed sensitive health data of an employee, including her medical condition, prescribed medications, and treatment details, in public daily orders and electronic systems accessible to hundreds of staff. The data was recorded 'in error' in common rather than confidential registers, distributed to multiple recipients beyond the Health Service, and made accessible without proper access restrictions in the Fire Service application system.
violationSummary: Health data were exposed to unauthorized individuals and kept accessible in unclassified systems without proper safeguards or data minimization, making them discoverable by all staff members.
violations: Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Fire Service Headquarters recorded an employee's health diagnosis, medications, and treatment details in common daily orders accessible to all staff.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's sensitive health data was exposed to hundreds of staff members across multiple fire service locations without her consent or any legitimate operational need.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Fire Service stated data were recorded 'by mistake' (εκ παραδρομής) in July-August 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even if recorded in error, the data remained visible in common registers, were reproduced in employee transfer documents, were sent to senior administration, and were accessible in unclassified electronic systems through at least February 2024 — long after discovery of the error in 2022.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Fire Service claimed it corrected the problem by designating the daily orders 'confidential' starting 01-06-2022 and later diagramming entries.
claimsVsReality.reality: By June 2022, an unknown number of staff had already seen the health information; the confidential redesignation came one year after the initial exposure; separate copies of the problematic entries persisted in other documents and electronic systems.

claimsVsReality.claim: Medical data must be recorded in daily orders per Presidential Decree 210/1992 articles 20, para. 4 (XIV-XV).
claimsVsReality.reality: The Decree required such data in CONFIDENTIAL orders for officers, not common ones. The Fire Service's own regulations mandated confidential classification; the Health Service circular (2022) explicitly prohibited sharing health data in non-confidential channels.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Fire Service Headquarters recorded the employee's health data (diagnosis, medication, treatment details) in common daily orders rather than confidential ones, violating the requirement that such sensitive information be processed lawfully and in accordance with applicable regulations.
violations: The Fire Service Headquarters recorded the employee's health data (diagnosis, medication, treatment details) in common daily orders rather than confidential ones, violating the requirement that such sensitive information be processed lawfully and in accordance with applicable regulations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: The Fire Service recorded and distributed extensive medical details including specific medications and treatment regimens beyond what was necessary for personnel management purposes, and kept this data accessible in unclassified electronic systems.
violations: The Fire Service recorded and distributed extensive medical details including specific medications and treatment regimens beyond what was necessary for personnel management purposes, and kept this data accessible in unclassified electronic systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 9 permits processing of special category data (including health data) only under specific conditions and with appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Health data were recorded in common registers and distributed to multiple recipients and systems without the specific protective measures required for special category data under Greek regulations and Fire Service internal rules.
violations: Health data were recorded in common registers and distributed to multiple recipients and systems without the specific protective measures required for special category data under Greek regulations and Fire Service internal rules.

outcome: The Authority found the Fire Service Headquarters liable as data controller for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(c). An administrative fine of €10,000 was imposed. The Fire Service was required to implement proper data protection policies and procedures, ensure confidential classification of health data, restrict access appropriately, and provide guidance to all subordinate services on compliance with data protection laws. The Authority emphasized the systemic (structural) nature of the violation affecting all employees of the Fire Service, not merely this individual case.
companyNow: The Greek Fire Service Headquarters continues operations as the central command authority for the Fire Service. The decision and fine are enforceable as of 08-01-2026.
dataType: Health data (medical conditions, medication, sick leave records)

companyDescription: Healthline Media is a digital health information and wellness platform providing medical content, articles, and health resources to consumers seeking health information and disease management guidance.
companyLongDescription: Healthline Media, LLC is one of the largest digital health information platforms in the United States, offering medical articles, health guides, symptom checkers, and wellness content covering hundreds of medical conditions. The company monetizes its platform through advertising and data partnerships. With millions of monthly visitors seeking sensitive health information, Healthline is a trusted resource for consumers researching diagnosed and undiagnosed medical conditions, treatments, and health management strategies.
caseDescription: Healthline Media violated California's Consumer Privacy Act by selling and sharing consumers' personal information through online tracking technologies without proper notice, particularly information indicating consumers had specific diagnosed medical conditions. violationSummary: Healthline disclosed consumers' personal information, including sensitive health data linked to diagnosed medical conditions, to third parties and service providers without proper consent or notice, and failed to respect opt-out signals. Upon full payment and compliance, all civil privacy and consumer protection claims relating to personal information collection, use, and disclosure are released.

companyDescription: Healthline is a medical information website that provides health and wellness articles to millions of monthly visitors and generates revenue through targeted advertising.
companyLongDescription: Healthline Media, LLC operates Healthline.com, a popular health and wellness information platform that attracts approximately 6.5 million California visitors monthly. The site publishes informational articles about medical and health topics and generates revenue by displaying targeted advertisements alongside its content. Healthline uses third-party online trackers, cookies, and pixels to collect data about readers and facilitate personalized advertising across multiple platforms. The company is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
caseDescription: Healthline allowed invisible online trackers and cookies to collect and share personal data about readers to advertising companies for targeted advertising, despite opt-out mechanisms that purportedly disabled such tracking. The company shared article titles strongly suggesting medical diagnoses (e.g., 'Newly Diagnosed with HIV') with third parties and failed to maintain compliant contracts with data recipients, violating CCPA purpose limitation and opt-out requirements.
violationSummary: Healthline disclosed personal information (article titles indicating health diagnoses and unique identifiers) to third-party advertisers and data brokers without proper consumer consent or contractual safeguards, despite opt-out requests and privacy policy promises.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Healthline allowed invisible online trackers and cookies to collect and share personal data about readers to advertising companies for targeted advertising.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of California readers had their sensitive health information—inferred from articles about diagnoses like HIV and Crohn's disease—shared with advertisers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Healthline's opt-out mechanisms would disable tracking and sharing of personal data for targeted advertising.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even after users opted out through all three mechanisms (direct opt-out form, Global Privacy Control, and cookie banner), Healthline continued transmitting 118 cookies and personal data including article titles to over a dozen advertising companies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Healthline had ensured its advertising contracts contain privacy protections for readers' data as required by CCPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: Healthline had not verified that third-party advertisers agreed to CCPA requirements; instead it assumed they had agreed to an industry contractual framework without verification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The cookie banner disabled targeted advertising cookies when users interacted with it.
claimsVsReality.reality: The cookie banner did not actually disable targeting cookies despite purporting to do so; tracking continued after users unchecked the targeting box.

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.120(a)/(d) and § 1798.135(a)/(c)(4) - Consumers have the right to opt out of sales and sharing of personal information for targeted advertising
regulatoryFindings.description: Healthline continued transmitting personal information to advertising companies even after consumers opted out via the 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' link
violations: Healthline continued transmitting personal information to advertising companies even after consumers opted out via the 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' link
Healthline's Global Privacy Control (GPC) opt-out mechanism was not properly implemented; trackers continued to function after opt-out
Healthline continued setting cookies and tracking users across websites despite triple opt-out attempts

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.100(c) - Purpose Limitation Principle requires data use consistent with consumer reasonable expectations and disclosed purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Healthline shared article titles strongly indicating medical diagnoses (e.g., 'Newly Diagnosed with HIV') to third parties without consumer reasonable expectation of such intimate health data sharing
violations: Healthline shared article titles strongly indicating medical diagnoses (e.g., 'Newly Diagnosed with HIV') to third parties without consumer reasonable expectation of such intimate health data sharing
Health-related information was shared for targeted advertising and data broker profiling purposes beyond what consumers would expect from visiting a health information website

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.100(d) - Businesses must have written contracts with data recipients specifying limited purposes and imposing required CCPA protections
regulatoryFindings.description: Several advertising company recipients lacked signed compliance with industry contractual framework
violations: Several advertising company recipients lacked signed compliance with industry contractual framework
Contracts with some data recipients used overly broad language ('any business purpose', 'any internal use', or undefined 'purposes contemplated') instead of limited, specified purposes
Contracts failed to address the U.S. Privacy String or require recipients to honor opt-out signals
Healthline did not verify that recipients agreed to CCPA-mandated protections; instead assumed compliance based on industry framework membership

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.135(f) and (g) - Recipients of opted-out data are prohibited from further sales; safe harbor requires no reason to believe recipient will violate this
regulatoryFindings.description: Healthline failed to secure contractual commitments ensuring recipients would honor the U.S. Privacy String and refrain from further sales of opted-out data
violations: Healthline failed to secure contractual commitments ensuring recipients would honor the U.S. Privacy String and refrain from further sales of opted-out data
Healthline had reason to believe recipients would violate opt-out requirements given expansive contractual language and lack of clear CCPA compliance terms

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 - Unfair Competition Law prohibits unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Cookie banner deceptively promised to disable advertising cookies but failed to do so
violations: Cookie banner deceptively promised to disable advertising cookies but failed to do so
Misrepresentation in consent mechanisms that purported to give consumers opt-out control that did not function as promised

outcome: Complaint filed by California Attorney General seeking injunctive relief, civil penalties of $2,663 per unintentional CCPA violation and $7,988 per intentional violation, civil penalties of $2,500 per unfair competition violation, disgorgement of revenue, and structural reforms to ensure Healthline's compliance systems function as intended. Healthline has already undertaken remedial measures including fixing misconfigured opt-out mechanisms, conducting manual reviews of online trackers, disabling trackers in response to opt-outs, and terminating data sales to non-compliant third parties.
companyNow: Healthline remains a major health information website, though it faces significant regulatory enforcement for its advertising and tracking practices under California's privacy laws.

companyDescription: Sling TV is an internet-based live TV and streaming service operated by Sling TV L.L.C., a subsidiary of Dish Network, offering on-demand and live content across multiple devices and platforms.
companyLongDescription: Sling TV is an app-based television streaming service that allows consumers to stream live and on-demand content over the internet via various devices including TVs, mobile devices, computers, gaming consoles, and the web. The service is operated by Sling TV L.L.C., a Delaware-incorporated limited liability company headquartered in Englewood, Colorado, which is a subsidiary of Dish Network Corporation. The company monetizes its service through advertising partnerships handled by its affiliate Dish Media Sales L.L.C., which manages customer data for targeted advertising purposes.
caseDescription: Sling TV and its affiliate Dish Media Sales failed to provide California consumers with clear, conspicuous notices and easy opt-out mechanisms for the sale and sharing of personal information, and failed to implement special protections for children and minors on its streaming platform. The company sold and shared personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising without proper consumer consent mechanisms.
violationSummary: The case involves systematic collection of personal information across platforms and contexts for behavioral targeting without adequate notice and opt-out mechanisms, coupled with failure to implement special protections for minors.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Sling TV sold and shared personal information of California consumers for cross-context behavioral advertising without providing clear opt-out mechanisms or proper notices about data sales.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Sling TV users had their viewing habits and personal data sold to advertisers across the internet without clear disclosure or easy ways to stop it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sling TV provided clear and conspicuous notices about data sales and sharing practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to provide California consumers with clear, conspicuous notices and easy opt-out mechanisms for the sale and sharing of personal information, as required by the CCPA.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers had easy mechanisms to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not provide a clear and conspicuous opt-out link on homepages or an easy-to-use opt-out system accessible across devices and browsers for logged-in users.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sling TV implemented special protections for children and minors on its streaming platform.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement special protections for children under 13 and minors ages 13-15 whose data was being sold and shared for behavioral advertising purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information was used only for purposes users understood and consented to.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sling TV conducted cross-context behavioral advertising using personal information obtained from third parties without meaningful consumer understanding or consent mechanisms.

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.100 and implementing regulations require clear and conspicuous notice that personal information is collected, sold, or shared
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide clear, conspicuous notice to consumers about collection of personal information from third parties
violations: Failed to provide clear, conspicuous notice to consumers about collection of personal information from third parties
Failed to adequately disclose that personal information was sold or shared for cross-context behavioral advertising
Did not provide meaningful understanding of data categories and sources

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.135 and regulations require easy, consumer-friendly opt-out mechanisms for sale and sharing of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Opt-out links were not clear and conspicuous on homepages and mobile apps
violations: Opt-out links were not clear and conspicuous on homepages and mobile apps
Opt-out system was overly complex, requiring multiple steps and form-filling
No simple toggle option for logged-in users; required users to fill out webforms with identification information
In-app opt-out methods were not implemented on mobile platforms

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA § 1798.120(c) and regulations (§§ 7070-7072) establish special protections for children under 13 and minors 13-15
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement 'kids' profiles that default off sale and sharing of personal information
violations: Failed to implement 'kids' profiles that default off sale and sharing of personal information
Failed to default off sale and sharing on children's programming channels
Made behavioral advertising available on children's channels without proper safeguards
Failed to delete personal information collected from known children and minors

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA requires businesses to honor valid consumer requests to opt-out across all accounts and devices
regulatoryFindings.description: Opt-out choices were not fully implemented account-wide across devices and browsers for logged-in users
violations: Opt-out choices were not fully implemented account-wide across devices and browsers for logged-in users
Non-logged-in users had limited opt-out scope, restricted to single browser or device

outcome: Sling TV and Dish Media Sales are permanently enjoined from violating the CCPA and UCL. The company must: (1) provide clear and conspicuous notices about personal information collection, sale, and sharing; (2) implement consumer-friendly opt-out mechanisms with minimal steps, including toggles for logged-in users and QR codes for in-app use where feasible; (3) create 'kids' profiles defaulting off sale/sharing and cross-context behavioral advertising; (4) default off sale/sharing on children's channels listed in Exhibit A; (5) delete personal information collected from known children and minors; (6) maintain a notice link titled 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' or 'Your Privacy Choices' on homepages and within apps; (7) avoid confusing language that could mislead consumers about opt-out choices; (8) implement compliance programs and provide annual reports for three years. The company must pay $530,000 ($265,000 within 30 days, $265,000 within one year).
companyNow: Sling TV continues to operate as a streaming service owned by Dish Network, now operating under the injunction and compliance obligations imposed by this California judgment.
