companyDescription: Sling TV is an internet-based live television and streaming service offering paid subscriptions and ad-supported options, owned by EchoStar Corporation through DISH subsidiaries.
companyLongDescription: Sling TV was the first internet-based live TV service, offering live and on-demand streaming of sports, movies, and shows across web, mobile, and connected living-room devices like Roku, Apple TV, and Fire TV Stick. The company generates revenue from both subscription fees and targeted advertising, purchasing third-party consumer data from brokers to enhance ad targeting capabilities. Sling TV is a subsidiary of DISH Network and operates under EchoStar Corporation's parent ownership.
caseDescription: Sling TV violated California's Consumer Privacy Act by failing to provide easy-to-use opt-out methods for the sale and sharing of personal information, instead deceptively directing consumers to cookie preferences that did not stop all data selling. The company also failed to implement sufficient privacy protections for children, continuing to collect, sell, and share personal information and engage in cross-context behavioral advertising when children were watching.
violationSummary: Sling TV engaged in deceptive disclosure practices by conflating cookie preferences with CCPA opt-out rights, making it difficult for consumers to exercise their right to stop the sale and sharing of personal information. This constitutes improper dissemination through deceptive interface design and dark patterns that obscured consumers' ability to control their data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Sling TV directed consumers to cookie preference controls instead of a straightforward opt-out method, required complicated URLs.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers lost meaningful control over their personal data being sold to advertisers, children's information was combined with third-party data for targeted advertising without parental consent,.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sling TV provided easy-to-use CCPA opt-out methods for consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sling TV directed users to cookie preferences instead of true opt-out, buried opt-out links in text, required 55-character URLs to type manually, had no in-app opt-out option despite most users accessing via apps, and required logged-in users to re-enter information already in the system.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sling TV's cookie preference controls were equivalent to CCPA opt-outs.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cookie preferences only blocked certain cookies on specific browsers and devices but did not stop Sling TV from selling or sharing personal information across offline channels, devices, and browsers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sling TV provided sufficient privacy protections for children watching the service.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite knowing children under 16 watched and offering parental controls, Sling TV did not allow parents to designate kid profiles, did not age-screen users, did not default off personalized advertising, and did not obtain parental opt-in consent before selling children's data combined with third-party information for cross-context behavioral advertising.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sling TV's terms of service address child privacy by stating the service is not intended for users under 18.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sling TV actively included children's programming channels, had demographic data identifying households with children under 16, and used that data to build targeted advertising groups for children without sufficient consent mechanisms.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.120(a) and § 1798.135(a) require businesses to provide methods for submitting opt-out requests that are easy for consumers to execute and require minimal steps
regulatoryFindings.description: Sling TV directed consumers to cookie preferences instead of a clear CCPA opt-out mechanism
violations: Sling TV directed consumers to cookie preferences instead of a clear CCPA opt-out mechanism
Required consumers to click through hard-to-find embedded links and fill out webforms
Required logged-in customers to provide information already available to Sling TV
Did not provide opt-out methods within the Sling TV app despite it being the primary access method

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.120(a) and § 1798.135(a) require easy-to-read and understandable disclosures without confusing or deceptive elements
regulatoryFindings.description: Labeled cookie choices as 'Do Not Sell/Share My Info' despite them not operating as CCPA opt-outs
violations: Labeled cookie choices as 'Do Not Sell/Share My Info' despite them not operating as CCPA opt-outs
Used dark patterns including unlabeled carets and confirmation pages asking 'Are you sure?' with warnings about losing customization
Combined CCPA opt-out with cookie preferences in a manner that confused consumers

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.120(a) and § 1798.135(c)(1) prohibit requiring logged-in consumers to provide additional information beyond what is necessary to direct the business to stop selling or sharing personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Required logged-in customers to re-enter name, address, phone number, and email address already in Sling TV's system
violations: Required logged-in customers to re-enter name, address, phone number, and email address already in Sling TV's system

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.120(a) requires opt-out methods that reflect the manner in which the business primarily interacts with customers
regulatoryFindings.description: Most customers access Sling TV via app on living-room devices but no in-app opt-out mechanism was provided
violations: Most customers access Sling TV via app on living-room devices but no in-app opt-out mechanism was provided
Consumers forced to use separate device and type 55-character URL to access website-based cookie preferences

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.120(c) requires affirmative authorization before selling or sharing personal information of consumers under 16 years of age
regulatoryFindings.description: Sling TV knew children under 16 watched its service but did not obtain required affirmative authorization
violations: Sling TV knew children under 16 watched its service but did not obtain required affirmative authorization
Did not implement kid's profile feature to disable data collection and sale for children
Did not age-screen users or obtain parental opt-in consent for consumers under 13
Continued cross-context behavioral advertising with knowledge or willful disregard of consumer age

outcome: This is a filed complaint seeking injunctive relief, civil penalties ($2,663 per violation or $7,988 for intentional violations and violations involving minors under CCPA; $2,500 per violation under UCL), disgorgement of profits, restoration of money or property, recovery of costs, and such other relief as the court deems just and proper. No settlement or final judgment has been reached yet.
companyNow: Sling TV remains an active streaming service operated by EchoStar/DISH as of 2025, continuing to offer both subscription and ad-supported streaming options.
dataType: Personal information including age, gender, income, location, interests, party affiliation, home and car ownership, demographic and psychographic attributes, children's data

companyDescription: Illuminate Education is an educational technology company that provides data management and assessment platforms to K-12 schools and school districts, including products like eSchoolData, eduCLIMBER, and SchoolCity.
companyLongDescription: Illuminate Education, Inc. is a provider of cloud-based educational software and data management solutions used by schools and districts to collect, analyze, and manage student data, assessment results, and educational information. The company offers multiple products designed to help educators track student performance and inform instructional decisions. Illuminate serves over 100 school districts across California and beyond, processing sensitive information including student records, test scores, and personal identifiers.
caseDescription: Illuminate Education failed to adequately secure student educational data, resulting in a data breach discovered in January 2022 affecting students across over 100 California schools and school districts. The company's inadequate security measures allowed unauthorized access to covered information stored on its network. The settlement requires Illuminate to implement comprehensive information security safeguards and pay $3.25 million.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the security, integrity, availability, and confidentiality of student educational data (covered information), resulting in unauthorized access during the data breach. This directly constitutes insecurity in information processing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Illuminate Education failed to implement adequate security measures to protect student educational data.
whyTheyWereWrong: Students' sensitive educational records were exposed to unauthorized access, putting minors' personal information at risk and violating the trust of schools.

claimsVsReality.claim: Illuminate maintained adequate security safeguards for student educational data stored on its network.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's inadequate security measures allowed unauthorized intruders to gain access to covered information affecting students across over 100 California schools and districts in January 2022.

claimsVsReality.claim: Student data would be protected in accordance with KOPIPA and CalOPPA requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Illuminate failed to adequately secure covered information, exposing sensitive student records and personal information to unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: KOPIPA (Business and Professions Code § 22584) requires companies collecting student data to implement reasonable safeguards to protect covered information
regulatoryFindings.description: Illuminate failed to implement adequate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect student educational records
violations: Illuminate failed to implement adequate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect student educational records
The company's security measures were insufficient to prevent unauthorized access during the January 2022 data breach
Inadequate access controls, monitoring, and database protection allowed intruders to gain unauthorized access to covered information

regulatoryFindings.description: Illuminate failed to maintain reasonable security procedures and practices for student personal information
violations: Illuminate failed to maintain reasonable security procedures and practices for student personal information

violations: Illuminate engaged in unfair competition by failing to properly safeguard covered information despite collecting it from schools and students

regulatoryFindings.act: FAL (Business and Professions Code § 17500) prohibits false or misleading representations about products and services
regulatoryFindings.description: Illuminate made representations regarding how it maintains and protects the privacy, security, or integrity of covered information that were not adequately supported by its actual security practices
violations: Illuminate made representations regarding how it maintains and protects the privacy, security, or integrity of covered information that were not adequately supported by its actual security practices

outcome: Illuminate Education is permanently enjoined to comply with all applicable California privacy and data protection laws. The company must implement a comprehensive information security program within 180 days, including specific safeguards such as zero trust architecture, multi-factor authentication, database activity monitoring, penetration testing, encryption, and employee training. The company must appoint a Chief Information Security Officer and conduct annual third-party security assessments for 5 years. All specific safeguards expire after 7 years. For any future security incidents affecting 500+ California residents, Illuminate must notify the Attorney General. The company must pay $3,250,000 in two installments to the California Attorney General's Office.
companyNow: As of 2025, Illuminate Education is operating under a permanent injunction requiring comprehensive information security safeguards and a $3.25 million settlement with California authorities following the 2022 data breach.
dataType: Student educational records, pupil data, covered information as defined under KOPIPA (K-12 Pupil Online Privacy Information Protection Act)

California Business and Professions Code §§ 22575-22577 (California Online Privacy Protection Act – CalOPPA)
California Business and Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law – UCL)

companyDescription: Illuminate Education is a K-12 education technology vendor that provides cloud-based software (IO Suite) for storing and analyzing student data, including academic, behavioral, and medical information for schools and school districts.
companyLongDescription: Illuminate Education, Inc. is a California-based education technology company and subsidiary of Renaissance Learning, Inc. The company provides IO Suite, a cloud-based platform designed to help educators monitor and assess student learning, manage behavioral and social-emotional needs, and store sensitive student data including academic records, demographics, special education information, and medical details. Illuminate contracts with school districts throughout California to handle data storage and analysis services for K-12 institutions.
caseDescription: Illuminate Education, a K-12 education technology vendor, failed to implement reasonable data security measures, resulting in a massive data breach affecting 49 California school districts and millions of students. A threat actor exploited unrevoked administrator credentials of a former employee to access and exfiltrate sensitive student data, including medical information, from both active and backup databases. Illuminate's security failures included inadequate access controls, lack of real-time monitoring and alerts, and unsecured backup systems.
violationSummary: Illuminate's failures to implement reasonable security procedures and practices—specifically inadequate account management, lack of monitoring for suspicious activity, and unsecured backup systems—resulted in unauthorized access and exfiltration of sensitive personal and medical information, directly falling under the Insecurity category of the Solove Privacy Taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Illuminate Education failed to terminate administrator credentials of a former employee who left in 2017, allowing a threat actor to access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of students had their personal, academic, behavioral, and medical records stolen, exposing them to identity theft, embarrassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Illuminate represented that its measures 'meet or exceed the requirements of applicable federal and state law' and signed the Student Privacy Pledge committing to 'maintain a comprehensive security program that is reasonably designed to protect the security, privacy, confidentiality and integrity of student personal information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Illuminate failed to implement basic security controls including unrevoked administrator credentials from a former employee (3 years after departure), no real-time alerts for suspicious activity, no log analysis, and backup databases stored in the same network segment as active databases, allowing a threat actor to compromise millions of student records.

regulatoryFindings.act: K-12 Pupil Online Personal Information Protection Act (Bus. & Prof. Code § 22584) requires operators of online services designed for K-12 purposes to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of covered information and protect such information from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure

violations: Illuminate failed to terminate administrator credentials of a former employee who left the company three years prior, allowing unauthorized access to student databases
Illuminate did not conduct credential audits to verify termination of former employee access
Illuminate did not monitor account creation and use or implement credential protection measures
Illuminate failed to detect suspicious activity despite having a threat detection tool that flagged over 40 anomalous events because alerts were not enabled
Illuminate stored backup databases in the same network segment as active databases, allowing compromise of both when the active system was breached

regulatoryFindings.act: Civil Code § 1798.81.5 (Reasonable Data Security Law) requires businesses maintaining personal information, including medical information, to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to implement reasonable account management and access controls
violations: Failure to implement reasonable account management and access controls
Failure to monitor and alert for suspicious logins and network activity
Failure to secure backup databases separately from active databases

violations: Permitted threat actor to access, acquire, modify, and delete medical data without students' authorization through inadequate security controls

violations: Failed to maintain, preserve, and store medical information in a manner that preserved confidentiality, through negligent security practices

violations: Violated KOPIPA, Reasonable Data Security Law, CMIA, and CalOPPA through inadequate security practices

outcome: This is a complaint for permanent injunction, civil penalties, and equitable relief filed by the California Attorney General. companyDescription: Home Improvement Marketing Ltd is a direct marketing organisation registered at Companies House (Number 14756152) that engaged in automated telephone marketing campaigns for home improvement products and services.
companyLongDescription: Home Improvement Marketing Ltd is a direct marketing organisation registered at Companies House (Number 14756152) that engaged in automated telephone marketing campaigns for home improvement products and services.
caseDescription: Home Improvement Marketing Ltd made 2.45 million automated marketing calls to subscribers without prior consent between May and August 2023, resulting in 274 complaints. The company violated PECR regulations 19 and 24 by using an automated calling system for recorded direct marketing calls without obtaining freely given, specific, informed consent from recipients, and failed to provide required identification information.
violationSummary: HIML engaged in mass unsolicited automated calling to subscribers without their knowledge or consent, constituting systematic surveillance-like collection of subscriber engagement through unwanted communications.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between May and August 2023, Home Improvement Marketing Ltd instigated 2,449,380 automated recorded marketing calls to subscribers without obtaining prior consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2.45 million people received unsolicited automated calls they never agreed to, resulting in 274 complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company implied through its marketing operations that subscribers had consented to receive automated marketing calls
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence of consent was obtained; HIML made no attempts to seek consent from any of the 2.45 million call recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 19(1) prohibits transmission or instigation of transmission of recorded direct marketing communications via automated calling systems except where the called subscriber has previously notified the caller of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: HIML instigated 2,449,380 automated marketing calls without evidence of prior subscriber consent
violations: HIML instigated 2,449,380 automated marketing calls without evidence of prior subscriber consent
HIML failed to obtain or maintain records of freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent from any subscribers

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(1) and (2) require that where electronic communications are used for direct marketing, the sender must provide the recipient with the sender's name and either their address or a free telephone number.
regulatoryFindings.description: HIML failed to provide recipients of automated calls with required identification information (name and contact details)
violations: HIML failed to provide recipients of automated calls with required identification information (name and contact details)

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) defines valid consent as freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes by clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: HIML obtained no affirmative consent from subscribers; consent was not freely given as subscribers had no genuine choice or control
violations: HIML obtained no affirmative consent from subscribers; consent was not freely given as subscribers had no genuine choice or control

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring HIML to: (1) cease transmission or instigation of automated recorded direct marketing calls except to subscribers who have previously notified HIML of consent; and (2) ensure recipients are provided with the name of the person/organisation and either address or free telephone number. These requirements must be met within 30 days. HIML has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: Unknown; enforcement notice issued 28 August 2025 with 30-day compliance deadline.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information

The company was controlled by Mathew Terry and used overseas call centres in the Philippines and Pakistan to generate leads for its loft insulation business.
companyLongDescription: Green Spark Energy Ltd was a UK-registered energy and home improvements company incorporated in February 2023, specialising in insulation products. The company was controlled by Mathew Terry and used overseas call centres in the Philippines and Pakistan to generate leads for its loft insulation business.
caseDescription: Green Spark Energy Ltd instigated 9.6 million automated recorded marketing calls promoting loft insulation products without valid subscriber consent between May 2023 and May 2024. The calls violated PECR regulations 19 and 24 by failing to obtain specific consent and failing to identify the caller with proper particulars. Evidence showed deliberate evasion of regulatory compliance and attempts to mislead the ICO.
violationSummary: GSE engaged in surveillance-like collection of individuals' telephone numbers and targeting them with automated calls without consent, using techniques designed to evade identification and regulatory oversight.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between May 2023 and May 2024, GSE instigated 9,587,050 automated recorded marketing calls via overseas call centres in the Philippines.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 9.5 million individuals received harassing unsolicited automated calls promoting insulation products, generating 497 complaints.

claimsVsReality.reality: GSE instigated 9,587,050 automated marketing calls through overseas call centres 1 in 3 BPO and 1 in 4 BPO, paid them £70,230+ for services, and directors sent daily instructions on which postcodes to dial

regulatoryFindings.description: Callers identified themselves as 'local energy advisor', 'energy hub', 'Helen', or 'Ian' rather than GSE
violations: Callers identified themselves as 'local energy advisor', 'energy hub', 'Helen', or 'Ian' rather than GSE

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty of £250,000 (reducible to £200,000 if paid by 29 September 2025, with payment deadline of 30 September 2025). GSE has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber) within 28 days.

companyDescription: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish financial microenterprise specializing in online loan provision. The company operates without published financial reporting.
companyLongDescription: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish financial microenterprise specializing in online loan provision. The company operates without published financial reporting.
caseDescription: KVIKU required customers to submit photographs holding their national ID card to process loan cancellations. This practice violated GDPR data minimization principles because less intrusive identification methods existed and complied with anti-money laundering requirements. The company processed personal data beyond what was strictly necessary.
violationSummary: The company collected excessive personal data (biometric + identity document combination) beyond what was strictly necessary for the stated purpose. This violated GDPR Article 5(1)(c) data minimization principle. The handling created security risks through unnecessary collection of sensitive biometric data when alternative, less intrusive methods existed.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: KVIKU required loan customers to submit photographs holding their national ID card in hand to process loan cancellations, collecting combined biometric.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' facial photographs combined with ID images exposed them to heightened identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: KVIKU claimed that photograph identification with DNI in hand was required to comply with anti-money laundering law (Law 10/2010 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism).
claimsVsReality.reality: Anti-money laundering law permits multiple identification methods (qualified electronic signatures, certified ID copies, first deposits from authorized accounts, or pre-approved secure procedures). Photograph identification is not mandated by law and was KVIKU's own choice, making it unjustifiable under data minimization principles.

claimsVsReality.claim: KVIKU's practice was justified by its obligation to identify customers for contract execution and legal compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer identification obligations could be fulfilled through less invasive, equally effective methods already available in the financial sector—certified document copies, electronic signatures, or existing customer account verification systems. KVIKU's method created unnecessary biometric and identity fraud risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: KVIKU argued the data retention was necessary because the customer had not satisfied the loan obligation.
claimsVsReality.reality: This argument was not relevant to the investigation, which concerned the data collection method itself, not retention post-satisfaction. The infraction occurred at the point of requesting the photograph for cancellation processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU required photographs with DNI in hand for loan cancellations despite alternative identification methods satisfying anti-money laundering requirements being available and less intrusive.
violations: KVIKU required photographs with DNI in hand for loan cancellations despite alternative identification methods satisfying anti-money laundering requirements being available and less intrusive.
The company failed to verify whether the stated purpose (identity verification for loan cancellation) could be achieved using fewer personal data, less detailed data, or data aggregation methods.

Facial biometric data combined with identity document images created unnecessary risk of identity fraud and suplantation when certified ID copies, electronic signatures, or existing customer account verification systems were available.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default, meaning controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU did not assess proportionality of its identification procedure or consider less invasive alternatives before implementing the photograph requirement.
violations: KVIKU did not assess proportionality of its identification procedure or consider less invasive alternatives before implementing the photograph requirement.
The company did not design its cancellation process to minimize data collection while achieving compliance with anti-money laundering obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 10/2010 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism permits identification through: qualified electronic signatures, certified copies of identity documents from public notaries, first deposits from equivalent accounts, or other secure procedures pre-approved by relevant authorities.
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU established a photograph identification requirement not expressly authorized by anti-money laundering law.
violations: KVIKU established a photograph identification requirement not expressly authorized by anti-money laundering law.
The company invoked anti-money laundering compliance to justify an excessive data collection practice not actually required by sectoral law.

outcome: AEPD issued a final resolution confirming the infraction and imposing a €8,000 fine (reduced 20% from €10,000 for voluntary payment on 9 December 2025). KVIKU was ordered within 1 month from the effective date to implement measures ensuring customer identity verification for loan cancellations complies with GDPR Article 5(1)(c) through less invasive means. The company must notify AEPD of compliance measures adopted. Failure to comply may trigger additional enforcement action. Resolution is final and enforceable; administrative remedies exhausted.
companyNow: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a microenterprise (fewer than 10 employees) founded in 2022 with €3,000 capital stock, operating as an online lending platform. Financial performance data is unavailable.
dataType: Biometric data (facial photography), identity documents (DNI), financial data, personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1)(b) – Lawful basis for contract performance
GDPR Article 25 – Data protection by design and by default

companyDescription: Greater Manchester Police is the territorial law enforcement agency responsible for policing Greater Manchester in Northwest England. As of March 2022, GMP employed 6,866 police officers, 3,524 police staff, and 560 police community support officers, covering 500 square miles and serving 2.8 million people.
companyLongDescription: Greater Manchester Police is the territorial law enforcement agency responsible for policing Greater Manchester in Northwest England. As of March 2022, GMP employed 6,866 police officers, 3,524 police staff, and 560 police community support officers, covering 500 square miles and serving 2.8 million people.
caseDescription: Greater Manchester Police systematically failed to respond to subject access requests (SARs) within legal timeframes under UK GDPR and DPA 2018. Between October 2022 and September 2024, GMP had compliance rates as low as 46%, with the oldest overdue request reaching 1,047 days. The backlog was caused by increased request volume (doubled from ~152 to ~300 per month in March 2020), COVID-19 response priorities, and insufficient staffing.
violationSummary: GMP systematically denied or delayed individuals' statutory right to access their personal data, preventing subjects from knowing what information police held or using that data, thereby excluding them from control over their own information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Greater Manchester Police failed to respond to hundreds of subject access requests within the legally required one-month deadline, with the oldest overdue request reaching 1,047 days.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens were systematically denied timely access to their personal data held by police for over two years.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP's prioritization of front-line policing during COVID-19 was a temporary, justified measure consistent with other organisations.
claimsVsReality.reality: This decision, combined with increased SAR volume (doubled from March 2020) and insufficient staffing, created a backlog that persisted until mid-2024 — over 4 years after the initial surge.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP acknowledged staffing difficulties and resource constraints prevented timely responses.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite resource challenges being known, GMP did not implement adequate staffing solutions until late 2023 (additional permanent staff) and early-mid 2024, leaving thousands of subjects without access for 18+ months beyond legal deadlines.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires the controller to provide information on action taken on data subject requests under Articles 15-22 without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, or within three months where complexity and number justify extension (with notice).
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to respond to hundreds of SARs within the one-month deadline
violations: GMP failed to respond to hundreds of SARs within the one-month deadline
GMP did not consistently inform data subjects of extensions within one month
In October 2023, GMP had 1277 overdue SARs; oldest request from 2021 (1047 days overdue)

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15 UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data concerning them is being processed and, where applicable, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP systematically denied or delayed individuals' right to access their personal data
violations: GMP systematically denied or delayed individuals' right to access their personal data
Delay periods ranging from months to years prevented data subjects from exercising this fundamental right

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 45, Part 3 DPA 2018 entitles data subjects to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and, where applicable, access to that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to provide timely confirmation or access to personal data held by the force
violations: GMP failed to provide timely confirmation or access to personal data held by the force

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 54, Part 3 DPA 2018 defines 'applicable time period' as one month from the relevant time, or up to three months where justified by complexity/volume, with a maximum of three months permitted.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP repeatedly exceeded the three-month maximum period; oldest request reached 1047 days overdue
violations: GMP repeatedly exceeded the three-month maximum period; oldest request reached 1047 days overdue

outcome: ICO issued a reprimand to GMP under Article 58(2)(b) UK GDPR and Schedule 13(2)(c) DPA 2018. No monetary fine imposed. GMP was already implementing significant remedial measures: SAR recovery action plan, staff increases, appointment of dedicated complaints officer, internalization of Data Protection Officer role, process improvements, and strategic oversight enhancements. By September 2024, GMP achieved 97% compliance rate on new SARs and reduced the backlog from 1277 to 39 overdue requests. ICO recommends ensuring sufficient resources to maintain compliance and completing outstanding action plan items. Failure to maintain improvements may trigger further enforcement action.
companyNow: Greater Manchester Police continues to operate as England's territorial police force for the Greater Manchester metropolitan county. As of September 2024, GMP had improved SAR compliance to 97% and substantially cleared its historical backlog, though remains subject to ICO monitoring.
dataType: Personal data routinely captured in law enforcement activities; body-worn video, CCTV footage, identification data

company: ZOUGLA TZI-AR ANONYMI ETAIREIA MESON ILEKTRONIKON MAZIKIS EPIKOINONIAS
companyDescription: ZOUGLA TZI-AR is a Greek media company operating the news website zougla.gr, which publishes news, reportage of public interest, and citizen complaints. The company positions itself as an investigative news outlet.
companyLongDescription: ZOUGLA TZI-AR is a Greek media company operating the news website zougla.gr, which publishes news, reportage of public interest, and citizen complaints. The company positions itself as an investigative news outlet.
caseDescription: A news website published an article containing the full personal details and address of a public official and his family members in relation to a private property dispute. The article included identifying information that was not necessary for the public interest story. The company failed to cooperate with the data protection authority for over 8 months and republished the content after claiming to have removed it.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data (name, address, professional details) of the complainant to the public without lawful basis and without necessity proportionate to the public interest being served. The disclosure was wider than needed to report the underlying news story.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Zougla.gr published an article identifying a public official by full name, home address, professional rank.
whyTheyWereWrong: The named official and his family suffered targeted exposure to public scrutiny and potential harassment over a private land dispute unrelated to his public duties.

claimsVsReality.claim: The article was based on a legitimate complaint from a citizen (Γ) seeking to expose alleged police misconduct and unlawful property disputes.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the underlying complaint may have had public interest merit, publishing the complainant's full name, address, and professional rank was not necessary to report that story. The news could have been published without identifying him.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company removed the article after receiving the authority's request (30-05-2023).
claimsVsReality.reality: The company republished the same article with identifying details three months later in August 2023, demonstrating that the initial removal was not final and the company did not genuinely remedy the violation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant was a 'public person' subject to press scrutiny by virtue of his public office.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the complainant held a public position, he was not a public figure in the sense of being a politician, celebrity, or someone who had voluntarily entered public life for scrutiny. His involvement in a private property dispute did not make him a legitimate target for full identification and public shaming.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires processing of personal data to be lawful, fair and transparent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company published full identifying details (name, address, professional rank) of the complainant without lawful basis under Art. 28 of Law 4624/2019, as the disclosure was not necessary and proportionate to the public interest in reporting the underlying property dispute story.
violations: Company published full identifying details (name, address, professional rank) of the complainant without lawful basis under Art. 28 of Law 4624/2019, as the disclosure was not necessary and proportionate to the public interest in reporting the underlying property dispute story.

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 4624/2019 Article 28 permits processing for freedom of expression only when the right to information outweighs data protection, the processing is limited to what is necessary, and it concerns matters of general public interest or public figures.
regulatoryFindings.description: The complainant was not a public figure requiring scrutiny; the property dispute was a private matter of lesser public concern; publishing his identifying details exceeded what was necessary—the news could have been reported without naming him; the company failed the necessity and proportionality test.
violations: The complainant was not a public figure requiring scrutiny; the property dispute was a private matter of lesser public concern; publishing his identifying details exceeded what was necessary—the news could have been reported without naming him; the company failed the necessity and proportionality test.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires processors and controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities upon request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company ignored the authority's requests on 12-08-2022 and 02-12-2022; only responded after a third letter on 30-05-2023 and a phone call; failed to provide views as requested; later republished the article after claiming removal, demonstrating non-cooperation and inconsistency.
violations: Company ignored the authority's requests on 12-08-2022 and 02-12-2022; only responded after a third letter on 30-05-2023 and a phone call; failed to provide views as requested; later republished the article after claiming removal, demonstrating non-cooperation and inconsistency.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority found the company violated GDPR Article 5(1)(a) and Law 4624/2019 Article 28 by publishing unnecessary identifying details without proportionate justification. It also violated GDPR Article 31 by failing to cooperate with the authority. The company was ordered to: (1) pay €2,000 for the unlawful publication; (2) contact websites www.theworldnews.net and www.opennews.gr to inform them the article was unlawful and has been removed, requesting they do the same; and (3) pay €1,000 for failure to cooperate. The article has since been removed from zougla.gr as of 15-05-2024.
companyNow: ZOUGLA is an active Greek news website (zougla.gr) that continues to operate. Following this decision, it is now subject to a compliance order to notify third-party republishers and to remove similar unlawfully published personal data.
dataType: Name, address, professional title, rank, family relationships, audio recordings
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 31 – Cooperation with supervisory authority
Law 4624/2019 Art. 28 – Processing for freedom of expression (proportionality requirement)

companyDescription: Plataforma Cabanillas is a mid-sized Spanish logistics company specializing in storage, transport, and distribution of goods, as well as customs and international trade services. With annual revenue of €31.04 million (2023), it operates cargo handling facilities with potential access to secure airport zones subject to air safety regulations.
companyLongDescription: Plataforma Cabanillas is a mid-sized Spanish logistics company specializing in storage, transport, and distribution of goods, as well as customs and international trade services. With annual revenue of €31.04 million (2023), it operates cargo handling facilities with potential access to secure airport zones subject to air safety regulations.
caseDescription: Plataforma Cabanillas requested criminal history certificates and personal family information (civil status, number of children) from job candidates during the recruitment process, before any employment contract existed. The company collected these sensitive data without a valid legal basis and in violation of data minimization principles under GDPR Article 5(1)(c).
violationSummary: The company systematically collected sensitive personal data (criminal records, family status) from job candidates during interviews without adequate legal justification, exceeding what was necessary for the hiring process and treating all participants as data sources before any employment relationship existed.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Plataforma Cabanillas requested criminal background certificates and family information (marital status.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of job applicants were forced to disclose sensitive criminal history and intimate family details during screening.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it was obligated by EU air safety regulations (Regulation 2015/1998) to verify criminal history 'during the selection process' to comply with aviation security requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual regulation refers to verification of 'selected persons'—those hired after selection is complete—not all interview candidates. The company was using an overbroad interpretation to justify pre-contractual collection of sensitive data from all participants.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it was collecting Form 145 family data 'in good faith' to improve recruitment efficiency and that this data would not be used for candidate evaluation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Form 145 family information is required only for employees after hiring. Requesting it during interviews from non-employees violated data minimization principles and collected far more data than necessary for hiring assessment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company argued that no negligence occurred because it was simply trying to comply with applicable regulations and improve process speed.
claimsVsReality.reality: A company conducting systematic personal data processing (recruitment) must apply heightened diligence to comply with data protection law. Collecting sensitive criminal data from all interview candidates without a valid legal basis prior to any employment contract constituted negligent violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(c).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: Company requested criminal history certificates from all interview candidates before any employment contract existed, exceeding necessity for hiring evaluation
violations: Company requested criminal history certificates from all interview candidates before any employment contract existed, exceeding necessity for hiring evaluation
Company requested family information (civil status, number of children) from candidates during interviews to populate Form 145, but this data is only required after employment begins

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 10 and LOPDGDD Article 10 restrict processing of criminal conviction data to circumstances authorized by EU or national law, with adequate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company relied on air safety regulations to justify requesting criminal certificates during selection phase, but those regulations refer to 'selected persons' (post-selection), not interview candidates
violations: Company relied on air safety regulations to justify requesting criminal certificates during selection phase, but those regulations refer to 'selected persons' (post-selection), not interview candidates
Company collected criminal data from all candidates, including those not selected, without proper legal authorization under GDPR Article 10

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed two administrative fines: €75,000 for requesting criminal history certificates during interviews before employment, and €25,000 for requesting Form 145 family data before employment contracts. The company was required to comply with updated selection procedures that defer collection of sensitive data until after final hiring decisions. No structural reforms or monitoring obligations were imposed, but the decision warns of further corrective measures if the company does not fully adopt the revised processes. The company has already updated its selection procedures to request criminal certificates and work-life documentation only after contracts are signed.
companyNow: Plataforma Cabanillas continues to operate as a logistics and customs services provider in Spain. Following the AEPD enforcement action, the company updated its recruitment procedures to request sensitive personal data only after employment contracts are finalized, effective January 2024.
dataType: Criminal history records, family status, number of children, identity documents
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 10 – Processing of criminal conviction data
LOPDGDD Art. 10 – Spanish implementation of criminal data processing restrictions

companyDescription: SERVACE, S.L. is a Spanish business services company founded in 1998, contracted to provide services to public agencies including work related to development/fomento (promotion/growth) initiatives.
companyLongDescription: SERVACE, S.L. is a Spanish business services company founded in 1998, contracted to provide services to public agencies including work related to development/fomento (promotion/growth) initiatives.
caseDescription: SERVACE, a contractor for a public agency, used an employee's personal email address for work communications without consent, and continued doing so even after being warned to stop. The company then displayed this personal email in visible copies to multiple colleagues and external parties. This violated GDPR requirements for lawful data processing and security.
violationSummary: The unauthorized use and visible disclosure of the personal email address to third parties (colleagues and government personnel) without the data subject's knowledge or consent constitutes a breach of confidentiality under GDPR Article 5(1)(f).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: SERVACE used an employee's personal email address for internal work communications without consent, ignored the employee's warning to stop.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's personal email address was processed and disclosed to numerous recipients without any legal authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: No implied evidence of claims; the company's conduct was simply non-compliant.
claimsVsReality.reality: SERVACE used personal email without any lawful basis and continued after being warned, then disclosed it to multiple parties without consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that personal data processing be lawful, based on at least one of six specified grounds (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: SERVACE processed the employee's personal email without obtaining consent and without any other lawful basis under Article 6(1).
violations: SERVACE processed the employee's personal email without obtaining consent and without any other lawful basis under Article 6(1).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed with integrity and confidentiality, with appropriate technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: SERVACE disclosed the personal email address in visible copies to multiple work colleagues and government personnel without authorization, violating the confidentiality principle.
violations: SERVACE disclosed the personal email address in visible copies to multiple work colleagues and government personnel without authorization, violating the confidentiality principle.

outcome: SERVACE recognized responsibility and paid the reduced sanction of €840 (after 40% cumulative reduction for early recognition and payment). The company was ordered to adopt corrective measures within 3 months: establish lawful bases for all personal data processing, implement stricter email list controls, and ensure personal email addresses are not used without explicit consent. The procedure terminated upon payment and commitment to remediation.
companyNow: SERVACE, S.L. is a small Spanish contractor (€90,730 annual revenue in 2023) that continues operations. The company has committed to implementing data protection compliance measures as ordered by AEPD.
dataType: Email addresses (personal and work), names

companyDescription: ECO4U is a sole trader business operated by Darian Bishop engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls. The company's business model involved high-volume outbound dialing for marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: ECO4U is a sole trader business operated by Darian Bishop engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls. The company's business model involved high-volume outbound dialing for marketing purposes.
caseDescription: Darian Bishop, trading as ECO4U, made 194,110 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and October 2023 to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), which prohibits such calls. The company failed to obtain valid consent from recipients before calling them and failed to provide required caller identification information during the calls.
violationSummary: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers. This represents systematic surveillance and targeting of individuals who explicitly opted out of marketing contact, without their knowledge or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 194,110 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between January and October 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: 194,110 individuals who had explicitly registered to block marketing calls received unwanted calls anyway, violating their opt-out choice.

claimsVsReality.claim: ECO4U implied or obtained consent from subscribers to receive marketing calls under Regulation 21(4).
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite Commissioner requests, Mr Bishop failed to demonstrate any valid notifications; individuals had explicitly opted out via TPS and received no clear opportunity to override that choice specifically for ECO4U.

claimsVsReality.claim: ECO4U provided required caller identification during direct marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company failed to provide the name or free-call contact details required by PECR Regulation 24 to any call recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the called number is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made 194,110 calls to TPS-registered numbers without 28+ day prior registration check or valid subscriber consent exception.
violations: Made 194,110 calls to TPS-registered numbers without 28+ day prior registration check or valid subscriber consent exception.
Failed to demonstrate valid consent under Regulation 21(4) despite Commissioner requests; did not show clear, positive individual notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(1) and 24(2) require provision of caller name and contact details with direct marketing calls upon request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide the name of the person/company or a free-call telephone number to recipients, breaching mandatory identification requirements.
violations: Failed to provide the name of the person/company or a free-call telephone number to recipients, breaching mandatory identification requirements.

outcome: Enforcement Notice issued 24 April 2025 under DPA Section 40. Mr Bishop is required within 30 days to: (1) cease making unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers or those who have notified ECO4U not to call; and (2) provide caller name and free-call contact details with all direct marketing calls. Right of appeal exists to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. No monetary penalty imposed; Commissioner found damage unlikely in this instance.
companyNow: Darian Bishop trading as ECO4U is subject to an active Enforcement Notice as of April 2025. The company is required to cease prohibited unsolicited calling practices and provide mandatory caller identification information.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information

companyDescription: D***Medien GmbH & Co KG is an Austrian digital media company operating a local news website. It was formed through transformation on 9 October 2024 from a predecessor entity and reported €8.35 million in annual revenues for 2023.
companyLongDescription: D***Medien GmbH & Co KG is an Austrian digital media company operating a local news website. It was formed through transformation on 9 October 2024 from a predecessor entity and reported €8.35 million in annual revenues for 2023.
caseDescription: An Austrian media company repeatedly violated GDPR Article 7 by maintaining a cookie consent banner that made withdrawing consent significantly harder than giving it. The company ignored a regulatory order to fix the banner for 5 months, constituting a failure to obey a supervisory authority directive under GDPR Article 58.
violationSummary: The company collected unique identifiers (UUIDs) via cookies using a deceptive consent mechanism that made refusal unreasonably burdensome, constituting unlawful surveillance of website visitors.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: D***Medien operated a website with a cookie banner that required significantly more user interactions to reject cookies than to accept them.
whyTheyWereWrong: Website visitors were manipulated into sharing tracking identifiers because declining cookies required multiple steps while accepting required only one click.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company implemented a standard cookie consent mechanism to gather user preferences.
claimsVsReality.reality: The banner was designed to make acceptance convenient (one click) while rejection required multiple additional steps, artificially steering users toward consent in violation of GDPR consent requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company complied with a regulatory order to redesign the banner.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not comply for 175 days after the regulatory order became enforceable, only updating the banner 5 months after the 10-week compliance deadline, triggering an administrative fine.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 7(1)–(3) requires that consent be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, and that withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's cookie banner required substantially more user interactions to decline or close without consent than to accept all cookies, making refusal materially harder.
violations: The company's cookie banner required substantially more user interactions to decline or close without consent than to accept all cookies, making refusal materially harder.
The company maintained this design for over 5 months after a regulatory order to fix it, continuing to burden visitors' ability to freely choose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(2)(d) grants supervisory authorities the power to order controllers to bring processing into compliance within a specified timeframe.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Austrian Data Protection Authority issued a binding 10-week order on 14 December 2023 to redesign the banner; the company complied only on 1 April 2025 (175 days late), constituting non-compliance with a supervisory directive.
violations: The Austrian Data Protection Authority issued a binding 10-week order on 14 December 2023 to redesign the banner; the company complied only on 1 April 2025 (175 days late), constituting non-compliance with a supervisory directive.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(6) permits fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover for violations of Articles 5–58.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company violated Article 58(2)(d) by failing to obey the regulatory order, an administrative violation subject to the fine in Article 83.
violations: The company violated Article 58(2)(d) by failing to obey the regulatory order, an administrative violation subject to the fine in Article 83.

outcome: The Austrian Data Protection Authority (Datenschutzbehörde) imposed an administrative fine of €6,200 plus €620 in procedural costs (€6,820 total). The company was ordered to immediately comply with the consent banner redesign required by the earlier December 2023 regulatory decision. The decision is enforceable if no appeal is filed within two weeks. The company had subsequently implemented the compliant banner design as of 1 April 2025, but only after the violation period had ended.
companyNow: The company appears to still operate its website (www.d***medien.at) as an Austrian local news publisher. It implemented a redesigned cookie banner in April 2025 following the enforcement action.
dataType: Unique identifiers (UUIDs), browsing data via cookies
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 58(2)(d) (compliance with supervisory authority directives)
GDPR Art. 83(1), (6) (administrative fines for violation of Art. 58)

companyDescription: ESTUDIO ALCAZAR DEL GENIL 2022, S.L. is a Spanish immobiliare (real estate) franchise operator. It acts as a real estate intermediary selling and renting properties. The company is a franchisee of a larger immobiliare network.
companyLongDescription: ESTUDIO ALCAZAR DEL GENIL 2022, S.L. is a Spanish immobiliare (real estate) franchise operator. It acts as a real estate intermediary selling and renting properties. The company is a franchisee of a larger immobiliare network.
caseDescription: An immobiliare agency collected personal data (names, addresses, apartment numbers) from mailbox photos in residential buildings without consent or legal basis, then stored the data in a customer management system. Employees were instructed to photograph community mailboxes to build prospecting databases. The company failed to inform affected individuals that their data was being processed.
violationSummary: The company conducted systematic collection of personal data from public property (mailbox photos) without subject awareness or consent, and created a database of non-clients for commercial targeting without any lawful basis. This is surveillance—covert, systematic data collection.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Instructed employees to photograph residential mailboxes, extract names and addresses without consent, and upload the data to a customer database for commercial prospecting purposes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of residents had their names, addresses, and door numbers extracted from mailboxes and stored in a commercial database without any knowledge, consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it only uses customer data that was obtained with proper consent and is properly legalised, and does not conduct the prospecting practices described by the complainant.
claimsVsReality.reality: Evidence showed the company systematically instructed employees to photograph residential mailboxes and extract names/addresses on 25 April 2023; the company's own database records show H.H.H.'s data was created that same day with source 'internal collaborator' (direct data entry by supervisor B.B.B.); supervisor acknowledged the mailbox practice in a recorded call and stated it was the company's standard 'zone management' methodology.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data concerning potential clients comes from public directory ***URL.2 and was obtained licitly from a public source.
claimsVsReality.reality: Public directory entries do not contain flat/apartment numbers, yet the company's database records show flat numbers alongside names and addresses, indicating the data was supplemented by mailbox observation or photography. No legitimate basis existed for collecting this additional identifying information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) establishes that processing is lawful only when at least one of six conditions is met: consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests (subject to balancing test).
regulatoryFindings.description: Company collected and stored names, addresses, and flat numbers from residential mailboxes without subject consent and with no lawful basis under Art. 6(1).
violations: Company collected and stored names, addresses, and flat numbers from residential mailboxes without subject consent and with no lawful basis under Art. 6(1).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 14 requires that when personal data is not obtained from the data subject, the controller must provide specified information (identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention period, rights) within one month or at first communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company extracted personal data from mailbox photographs without subject knowledge and never provided any privacy notice or information about the processing under Art. 14.
violations: Company extracted personal data from mailbox photographs without subject knowledge and never provided any privacy notice or information about the processing under Art. 14.

outcome: ESTUDIO ALCAZAR recognised responsibility on 21 February 2025 and paid €12,000 (applying 40% reduction for voluntary payment and early recognition). The company was ordered within 2 months from finalisation of the resolution to: (1) certify deletion of personal data collected from mailboxes; (2) certify communication to affected individuals of Art. 14 information; and (3) cease processing of mailbox-derived data. Procedure EXP202308051 terminated.
companyNow: ESTUDIO ALCAZAR is a small franchise immobiliare business established in 2022 with €3,000 capital. It operates under the ***EMPRESA.5 brand in a local district of Spain, subject to ongoing compliance monitoring.
dataType: Names, addresses, residential/property information, contact details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 14 – Information to be provided where personal data not obtained from subject

companyDescription: Bristol City Council is the local authority serving the city of Bristol in Southwest England, the eighth-largest city outside London with an estimated population of 483,000. It is responsible for local government services including education, social care, and community services.
companyLongDescription: Bristol City Council is the local authority serving the city of Bristol in Southwest England, the eighth-largest city outside London with an estimated population of 483,000. It is responsible for local government services including education, social care, and community services.
caseDescription: Bristol City Council failed to respond to subject access requests (SARs) within statutory timeframes. Over 230 SARs remained outstanding as of June 2025, with the oldest dating back to January 2022—over 3 years overdue. The council only responded to 42% of SARs within the required one-month deadline during 2023-24.
violationSummary: BCC's systemic failure to process and deliver SARs within legal timeframes, combined with inadequate resources, training, and procedures, denied data subjects timely access to their personal information and violated their statutory rights.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Bristol City Council failed to respond to 231 overdue subject access requests within the statutory one-month deadline, with the oldest request unanswered for over three years since January 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: Data subjects including children and vulnerable individuals were denied access to their personal records for years, preventing them from obtaining evidence for legal proceedings.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCC stated it would clear the SAR backlog in 50 months (over 3 years) as of February 2024.
claimsVsReality.reality: By August 2024, BCC revised the timeline to 36 months; by May 2025, it hoped to clear by end of 2026—demonstrating repeated deadline slippage and lack of concrete progress.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCC engaged an external organisation in July 2024 to assist with processing the oldest, most complex SARs.
claimsVsReality.reality: By March 2025 (8 months later), only 2 of the SARs sent to the external organisation had been completed. Quality issues required SARs to be returned for rework, causing further delays.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCC stated in its representations that it has 'made tangible progress with the 2022 cases' and that issuing an Enforcement Notice would be 'premature'.
claimsVsReality.reality: As of June 2025, only 1 SAR from 2022 remained outstanding (originally received 3 January 2022—over 3.5 years overdue). This represents minimal progress over 2+ years of engagement.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCC claimed to have training materials for the Disclosure Team per its Action Plan (high priority action: 'Review training and support offer').
claimsVsReality.reality: At a meeting on 8 May 2025, BCC stated there were no training materials for the Disclosure Team, contradicting documented representations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken on a subject access request without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCC failed to respond to SARs within the statutory one-month timeframe, with 231 SARs outstanding and 120 overdue from 2024 alone.
violations: BCC failed to respond to SARs within the statutory one-month timeframe, with 231 SARs outstanding and 120 overdue from 2024 alone.
No timely responses or progress updates provided to data subjects with outstanding requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide confirmation of whether personal data is being processed and, where applicable, provide access to personal data and specified information.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCC failed to provide confirmation or access to personal data for over 231 data subjects with outstanding SARs.
violations: BCC failed to provide confirmation or access to personal data for over 231 data subjects with outstanding SARs.
Some requesters waited over 3 years (since January 2022) without receiving required confirmation or data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing to data subjects.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCC did not provide copies of personal data to 231 data subjects with outstanding SARs.
violations: BCC did not provide copies of personal data to 231 data subjects with outstanding SARs.
Particularly acute in children's social care cases where individuals sought their own records.

outcome: Enforcement Notice issued requiring BCC to: (1) Contact all data subjects with overdue SARs to notify them of delays; (2) Respond to all outstanding SARs by tiered deadlines (30 days for 2022 cases, 90 days for 2023, 7 months for 2024, 8 months for 2025); (3) Provide weekly progress updates to the ICO; (4) Create a detailed action plan within 90 days addressing SAR prioritisation, assignment, and timelines; (5) Implement systemic changes within 12 months including adequate staffing and staff training. If BCC fails to comply, the ICO may serve a penalty notice up to £17,500,000 or 4% of annual worldwide turnover.
companyNow: Bristol City Council continues to operate as the local authority for Bristol. As of the enforcement notice date (27 August 2025), the council was under notice to resolve the backlog and had recruited additional disclosure staff, though structural compliance issues remained ongoing.
dataType: Personal data (including children's social care data, identity information)

companyDescription: IntelliVision Technologies Corp. is an artificial intelligence company specializing in deep learning-based facial recognition software for original equipment manufacturers, integrators, and developers. Its facial recognition technology has been integrated into consumer products including home security systems and smart home control panels.
companyLongDescription: IntelliVision Technologies Corp. is an artificial intelligence company specializing in deep learning-based facial recognition software for original equipment manufacturers, integrators, and developers. Its facial recognition technology has been integrated into consumer products including home security systems and smart home control panels.
caseDescription: IntelliVision made false and unsubstantiated claims about its facial recognition software, claiming it had one of the highest accuracy rates on the market, performed with zero racial and gender bias, was trained on millions of faces, and had anti-spoofing technology that could not be fooled by photos or videos. In reality, NIST testing showed the software had significant demographic disparities, was not among top performers, was trained on only ~100,000 unique individuals with duplicated variants, and lacked sufficient testing to support anti-spoofing claims.
violationSummary: The company's failure to adequately test for demographic bias and security vulnerabilities in facial recognition systems, combined with false marketing claims, constitutes insecure processing of sensitive biometric data. The lack of substantiation for anti-spoofing claims also represents inadequate safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: IntelliVision made false claims that its facial recognition software had one of the highest accuracy rates on the market, performed with zero gender and racial bias.
whyTheyWereWrong: IntelliVision's false claims about bias-free facial recognition exposed consumers and businesses to discriminatory outcomes.

claimsVsReality.claim: IntelliVision's facial recognition software has one of the highest accuracy rates on the market
claimsVsReality.reality: NIST testing showed IntelliVision's algorithms were not among the top 100 best-performing algorithms tested as of December 19, 2023, and had error rates that varied significantly across demographics.

claimsVsReality.claim: Zero gender or racial bias through model training with millions of faces from datasets around the world
claimsVsReality.reality: The software was trained on approximately 100,000 unique individuals, not millions, and NIST testing demonstrated significantly higher false positive rates for certain racial groups (West/East African, East Asian, American Indian) and for women compared to men.

claimsVsReality.claim: Can detect faces of all ethnicities without racial bias
claimsVsReality.reality: NIST testing found the algorithms produced significantly more false positive matches for certain demographics including West and East African, East Asian, and American Indian faces compared to Eastern European faces.

claimsVsReality.claim: Anti-spoofing technology ensures the system cannot be fooled by a photo or video image
claimsVsReality.reality: IntelliVision lacks sufficient testing to support this unqualified claim, and the company did not assess how the anti-spoofing technology performed across different demographic groups.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: IntelliVision represented that its facial recognition software had one of the highest accuracy rates on the market, but NIST testing showed error rates that differed significantly across demographics and the algorithms were not among the top 100 performers as of December 2023.
violations: IntelliVision represented that its facial recognition software had one of the highest accuracy rates on the market, but NIST testing showed error rates that differed significantly across demographics and the algorithms were not among the top 100 performers as of December 2023.

IntelliVision claimed zero gender or racial bias and that the software could detect faces of all ethnicities without racial bias, but NIST testing demonstrated significantly higher false positive rates for West/East African, East Asian, and American Indian faces compared to Eastern European faces, and higher false positives for women than men.

IntelliVision represented that the software was trained on millions of faces, but it was actually trained on approximately 100,000 unique individuals with synthetic variants created from the same images.

IntelliVision claimed its anti-spoofing technology ensures the system cannot be fooled by photos or videos, but the company lacked sufficient testing to support this unqualified claim and did not assess performance across demographic groups.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on January 8, 2025, against IntelliVision Technologies Corp. alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act through three counts: (I) Misrepresentations regarding facial recognition software accuracy and training, (II) False or unsubstantiated claims regarding facial recognition software bias and bias mitigation, and (III) False or unsubstantiated claims regarding anti-spoofing technology. The complaint triggers a formal administrative proceeding; no final order or remediation terms have been announced as of the document date. IntelliVision is required to cease making unsupported claims about its facial recognition technology's accuracy, bias performance, training dataset size, and anti-spoofing capabilities.
companyNow: IntelliVision Technologies Corp. remains active as a Delaware corporation with principal offices in San Jose, California. The company continues to market facial recognition software to OEMs, integrators, and end users, though facial recognition systems incorporating its technology have been sold through parent company Nice North America, LLC.
dataType: Biometric data (facial recognition images, facial features)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Staines Health Group is an NHS GP Surgery located in Staines, Middlesex, offering general healthcare services, antenatal and postnatal care, chronic disease management, family planning, vaccinations, and minor surgical procedures.
companyLongDescription: Staines Health Group is an NHS GP Surgery located in Staines, Middlesex, offering general healthcare services, antenatal and postnatal care, chronic disease management, family planning, vaccinations, and minor surgical procedures.
caseDescription: Staines Health Group, an NHS GP surgery, disclosed 23 years of a patient's medical records directly to their insurer (Vitality) when only 5 years were requested. The disclosure was not sent to the patient for review first as instructed, causing financial harm to the patient. The organisation also failed to report the breach to the ICO within the 72-hour deadline.
violationSummary: Unauthorised disclosure of excessive personal health data (23 years instead of 5) to a third party (insurer) without data subject review, and failure to notify regulator within statutory timeframe.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
