whatTheyDid: Staines Health Group sent 23 years of a patient's medical records directly to insurance company Vitality instead of the requested 5 years.
whyTheyWereWrong: A terminally ill patient suffered significant financial harm when their insurance claim payout was reduced because Vitality saw their complete 23-year medical history instead of just.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data Subject requested 5 years of medical records to be sent to them for review before forwarding to Vitality insurance for serious illness claim assessment.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staines Health Group sent 23 years of medical records directly to Vitality without sending to Data Subject first, resulting in claim payout reduction.

claimsVsReality.claim: Staff member had completed appropriate information governance training (March 2024) and a system was in place for insurance requests.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written procedures existed; staff relied on oral training from April 2022 (2 years prior); no peer review safeguards or contingencies for document access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Staines Health Group disclosed 23 years of medical records instead of the 5 years requested by Vitality for a serious illness insurance claim assessment.
violations: Staines Health Group disclosed 23 years of medical records instead of the 5 years requested by Vitality for a serious illness insurance claim assessment.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: No written procedures, no peer review safeguards, no contingency for password-protected documents; staff relied on 2-year-old oral training to process insurance requests.
violations: No written procedures, no peer review safeguards, no contingency for password-protected documents; staff relied on 2-year-old oral training to process insurance requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of documented policies for insurance request processing; no refresher training; password-protected files with no access contingency when staff member on leave; information governance policy not reviewed since 2020.
violations: Lack of documented policies for insurance request processing; no refresher training; password-protected files with no access contingency when staff member on leave; information governance policy not reviewed since 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Staines Health Group became aware of breach on 4 July 2024 but did not notify the ICO until 30 July 2024 (26 days late).
violations: Staines Health Group became aware of breach on 4 July 2024 but did not notify the ICO until 30 July 2024 (26 days late).

outcome: Reprimand issued by the ICO on 16 December 2025. Staines Health Group failed to provide representations. By 17 February 2025, the organisation had implemented remedial measures including: written procedures for insurance requests, new spreadsheet column flagging patient review requirements, staff training by Surrey Heartlands Information Governance Team (8 October 2024), sign-off checklist for insurance requests, disciplinary warning to employee, and 6-month supervision period. Infringements of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(1)(f), and 32 were remedied by 17 February 2025; Article 33 breach remains unresolved. No monetary fine imposed.
companyNow: Staines Health Group continues to operate as an NHS GP Surgery. The organisation has implemented documented procedures, staff training, and compliance controls following the enforcement action.
dataType: health data, medical records
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of breach to supervisory authority

companyDescription: ALVEA SOLUCIONES TECNOLÓGICAS, S.L. is a Spanish recruitment and staffing services company founded in 1918 that specializes in candidate selection and employment placement. The company processes large volumes of personal data from job applicants as part of its core business operations.
companyLongDescription: ALVEA SOLUCIONES TECNOLÓGICAS, S.L. is a Spanish recruitment and staffing services company founded in 1918 that specializes in candidate selection and employment placement. The company processes large volumes of personal data from job applicants as part of its core business operations.
caseDescription: ALVEA, a recruitment firm, sent job candidates a Google Form with two links—one public and one internal—that exposed a spreadsheet containing 10,837 candidates' names, surnames, and DNI numbers without authorization. The spreadsheet retained data dating back to 2020, violating the stated 18-month retention policy. The company failed to implement adequate security controls to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive personal data.
violationSummary: The company exposed a large volume of personal data (10,837 records) to unauthorized access due to failure to implement adequate technical and organizational measures. The data exposure was unintended but resulted from negligent controls and improper communication channels.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: ALVEA sent job candidates a recruitment email containing two hyperlinks: the intended consent form.
whyTheyWereWrong: 10,837 job applicants' sensitive personal information including names and ID numbers became accessible to anyone with the URL.

claimsVsReality.claim: ALVEA stated it implemented 'appropriate measures of diligence' and training for recruitment staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: A recently hired recruitment technician, despite receiving company training, sent recruitment candidates a link to an internal employee-only spreadsheet exposing 10,837 people's data, demonstrating training was insufficient or not enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: ALVEA's stated policy retained candidate data for a maximum of 18 months.
claimsVsReality.reality: The exposed spreadsheet contained candidate records dating back to 2020—over 4 years of retention—contradicting the stated policy and revealing no effective data lifecycle management.

claimsVsReality.claim: ALVEA claimed the incident was 'a single administrative error' by one employee.
claimsVsReality.reality: The error exposed 10,837 individuals and reflected systemic failures: no email controls, no link verification, no access restrictions, and no oversight mechanisms despite this being the company's primary business activity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed with appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction, or damage, through suitable technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: ALVEA failed to implement adequate technical controls to prevent unauthorized access to personal data. A recruiting staff member, despite receiving company training, sent both an internal and external link in a recruitment email, exposing 10,837 candidates' names, surnames, and DNI numbers to anyone with the URL.
violations: ALVEA failed to implement adequate technical controls to prevent unauthorized access to personal data. A recruiting staff member, despite receiving company training, sent both an internal and external link in a recruitment email, exposing 10,837 candidates' names, surnames, and DNI numbers to anyone with the URL.
The company did not enforce role-based access restrictions; data was accessible to anyone with the link rather than only to authorized personnel.
Data retention controls were ineffective: the spreadsheet contained records from 2020 despite a stated 18-month retention policy.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: ALVEA relied on a Google Form and Google Sheet with public sharing links, creating a single point of failure with no access restrictions, encryption, or logging of who accessed the data.
violations: ALVEA relied on a Google Form and Google Sheet with public sharing links, creating a single point of failure with no access restrictions, encryption, or logging of who accessed the data.
No preventive measures were in place to ensure that only properly vetted communications with correct links were sent to candidates.

outcome: ALVEA acknowledged responsibility and paid €21,000 (a 40% reduction from the initial €35,000 fine for early payment and admission of fault). The company is required within 6 months to: (1) implement measures preventing unauthorized data access through email communications, including restricting recipient access to only necessary data; (2) have its newly designated Data Protection Officer evaluate controls effectively implemented; and (3) notify the AEPD of compliance. The procedure has been terminated. The decision is final and executable unless challenged before Spain's National Court within 2 months.
companyNow: ALVEA SOLUCIONES TECNOLÓGICAS, S.L. remains active as a recruitment technology company. The company implemented immediate remedial measures following the discovery of the incident, including designating a Data Protection Officer, disabling the internal link, and restricting access controls. Annual revenue approximately €7.26 million (2023).
dataType: Names, surnames, national identity numbers (DNI), employment application data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality (Security Principle)
GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of Personal Data Breach (implied)

company: Η ΑΣΠΙΔΑ ΤΟΥ ΔΑΥΪΔ (Association for persons with autism spectrum disorders)
companyDescription: A Greek non-profit association providing therapeutic and educational programs for children and adults with autism spectrum disorders. The organization operates closed-circuit video surveillance systems on its premises and provides intervention and support services to beneficiaries.
companyLongDescription: A Greek non-profit association providing therapeutic and educational programs for children and adults with autism spectrum disorders. The organization operates closed-circuit video surveillance systems on its premises and provides intervention and support services to beneficiaries.
caseDescription: The association failed to provide parents access to video surveillance footage of their minor autistic child despite a lawful request, citing employee privacy concerns without evidence. The organization also shared the child's sensitive health and educational data with a third party without parental notification or consent, and publicly disseminated a court decision containing the child's personal data without proper authorization.
violationSummary: The association breached confidentiality by failing to honor the right of access; improperly disclosed sensitive health data of a minor to third parties without consent; and publicly shared personal data of a child in court documents without authorization.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The association failed to provide parents with video footage from its closed-circuit camera system showing their autistic child at the facility.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents sought video evidence to investigate visible injuries and marks on their child's body sustained while in the association's care.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed that withholding video footage was justified because employees appeared in the footage and would face privacy violations if it were disclosed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization provided no evidence that actual harm to employee rights would occur; the DPA found that proper redaction techniques could protect employee privacy while honoring the parents' lawful right of access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed that video recordings are automatically deleted from the system after 48 hours and therefore no footage was available to provide.
claimsVsReality.reality: During court proceedings for protective measures, the organization produced a USB drive containing video footage, photographs, and footage from mobile phone cameras for the same dates parents had requested, proving footage was available and retained.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization stated it did not know whether the child's health data had been transferred to the third-party company or on what legal basis.
claimsVsReality.reality: Records and parental investigation confirmed that sensitive health data, diagnostic assessments, and educational program information were transferred to the external company without parental notification or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization processed video surveillance data and shared sensitive health data without transparent disclosure to parents as data subjects exercising parental rights
violations: The organization processed video surveillance data and shared sensitive health data without transparent disclosure to parents as data subjects exercising parental rights

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to access personal data concerning them and information about the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization refused to provide video footage to parents without evidence that disclosure would harm employee rights, violating the right of access
violations: The organization refused to provide video footage to parents without evidence that disclosure would harm employee rights, violating the right of access

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires controllers to provide information about data processing, including recipients of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization transferred the child's health and educational data to a third party company without prior notification or consent from parents
violations: The organization transferred the child's health and educational data to a third party company without prior notification or consent from parents

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure and demonstrate compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization failed to implement measures ensuring lawful disclosure or to maintain proper records of data transfers and consent
violations: The organization failed to implement measures ensuring lawful disclosure or to maintain proper records of data transfers and consent

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities upon request.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization delayed and withheld complete responses to the DPA's inquiries about the basis and scope of data transfers
violations: The organization delayed and withheld complete responses to the DPA's inquiries about the basis and scope of data transfers

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (DPA) imposed four separate administrative fines totaling €10,000 for violations of GDPR Articles 5, 12, 13, 15, 24, and 31. The organization was required to: (1) immediately fulfill the right of access request by providing unredacted copies of video footage or properly redacted copies using technical measures such as blurring of employees' faces, after weighing and protecting employee rights; (2) cease unlawful transfers of personal data without proper legal basis, notice, or consent; (3) halt public dissemination of court decisions containing minor's personal data without authorization. The decision emphasizes that general concerns about employee privacy are insufficient to deny access rights; specific, case-by-case harm assessments are required.
companyNow: The organization continues to operate as a non-profit association serving individuals with autism spectrum disorder, supervised and funded by the Greek Ministry of Health.
dataType: Health data, sensitive personal data of minor child, educational records, intervention program information, diagnostic assessment
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12 – Transparency of exercising rights
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data collected from data subject
GDPR Art. 24 – Responsibility of the controller
GDPR Art. 31 – Cooperation with supervisory authority

companyDescription: BEEDIGITAL AI, S.A. (formerly Páginas Amarillas Soluciones Digitales) is an advertising and digital marketing company operating in Spain. It treats personal data of over 550,000 individuals as part of its business operations.
companyLongDescription: BEEDIGITAL AI, S.A. (formerly Páginas Amarillas Soluciones Digitales) is an advertising and digital marketing company operating in Spain. It treats personal data of over 550,000 individuals as part of its business operations.
caseDescription: BEEDIGITAL failed to encrypt or pseudonymise personal data including national ID numbers, resulting in unauthorised access by a third party affecting over 82,500 individuals. The company stored sensitive data without adequate technical and organisational security measures, violating the GDPR confidentiality principle. A data breach exposed customer and subscriber information, which the company notified the AEPD about.
violationSummary: BEEDIGITAL's failure to implement encryption, ciphetring, or pseudonymisation of personal data resulted in unauthorised third-party access, directly causing data exposure and loss of confidentiality — a core security/insecurity violation under Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: BEEDIGITAL stored personal data including DNI/NIF numbers, names, phone numbers, and emails without encryption, cifrado, or pseudonymisation.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 82,539 individuals had their complete identity data exposed to unauthorised access, enabling potential identity fraud, financial theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: BEEDIGITAL stated that it 'applies appropriate measures' for security and data protection, citing a data protection policy and security frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not encrypt, cipher, or pseudonymise personal data including national ID numbers. An actual breach exposed 82,539+ records, demonstrating that the 'appropriate measures' were materially inadequate.

claimsVsReality.claim: BEEDIGITAL claimed to have 'security measures in place' and a high level of compliance per audit reports.
claimsVsReality.reality: An independent security investigation found that encryption/cifrado and pseudonymisation measures were absent or insufficiently implemented, creating the vulnerability exploited in the breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: BEEDIGITAL asserted it took 'diligent reaction' and investigated rapidly, preventing greater harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach was only discovered through proactive monitoring; the absence of encryption meant that once unauthorised access occurred, all 82,539+ records were fully exposed, not mitigated by encryption-layer protections.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner that guarantees adequate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: BEEDIGITAL stored personal data including DNI/NIF numbers without encryption, cifrado, or pseudonymisation, failing to guarantee adequate security despite treating 550,000+ individuals' data and facing known risks of cyberattacks.
violations: BEEDIGITAL stored personal data including DNI/NIF numbers without encryption, cifrado, or pseudonymisation, failing to guarantee adequate security despite treating 550,000+ individuals' data and facing known risks of cyberattacks.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including encryption of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: BEEDIGITAL lacked encrypted/ciphered data storage and pseudonymisation measures despite an audit identifying security gaps. The company's preventive measures were insufficient to protect against the actual breach that exposed 82,539+ records.
violations: BEEDIGITAL lacked encrypted/ciphered data storage and pseudonymisation measures despite an audit identifying security gaps. The company's preventive measures were insufficient to protect against the actual breach that exposed 82,539+ records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24 establishes the principle of 'responsibility by design' — controllers must apply appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and be able to demonstrate compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: BEEDIGITAL's security measures were not proportionate to the risks; the company stored sensitive ID numbers unencrypted despite treating high volumes of personal data in an environment of exponentially increasing cyberattacks.
violations: BEEDIGITAL's security measures were not proportionate to the risks; the company stored sensitive ID numbers unencrypted despite treating high volumes of personal data in an environment of exponentially increasing cyberattacks.

outcome: BEEDIGITAL AI, S.A. was sanctioned with a €150,000 administrative fine, reduced to €120,000 following voluntary payment with 20% reduction. The company renounced any administrative appeal. BEEDIGITAL was ordered to demonstrate within 3 months of resolution becoming final and executive that it has implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures (encryption, ciphetring, or pseudonymisation) for all personal data it processes. Non-compliance with this order may trigger further enforcement action under GDPR Arts. 83.5–83.6.
companyNow: BEEDIGITAL AI, S.A. remains operational. The company was required to implement encryption and pseudonymisation of personal data within 3 months of the resolution becoming final. Compliance with the remedial order has not been publicly reported.
dataType: Name, surname, national ID number (DNI/NIF), telephone numbers, email address
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
GDPR Art. 24 – Responsibility of the Controller

companyDescription: Real Sociedad de Fútbol S.A.D. is a Spanish professional football club founded in 1992 competing in La Liga. The club processes personal data of subscribers, shareholders, players, employees, and fans for sports operations and fan engagement.
companyLongDescription: Real Sociedad de Fútbol S.A.D. is a Spanish professional football club founded in 1992 competing in La Liga. The club processes personal data of subscribers, shareholders, players, employees, and fans for sports operations and fan engagement.
caseDescription: Real Sociedad suffered a ransomware attack on 14 October 2023 that affected approximately 60,000 individuals' personal data stored across all virtualized servers. The club failed to implement adequate security measures such as encryption, network segmentation, and proper backup systems. Although no exfiltration was confirmed, the incident exposed the club's systemic lack of technical and organizational safeguards required by GDPR.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures (encryption, segmentation, backup isolation) required under Article 32 GDPR, resulting in a massive data breach affecting thousands of individuals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Real Sociedad failed to implement adequate security measures, allowing ransomware to encrypt all virtualized servers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 60,000 people's sensitive data including national ID numbers, bank accounts, health records, and biometric information became inaccessible, exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Real Sociedad claimed it promptly contained the ransomware incident and took immediate technical action to restore systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The club's recovery procedures eliminated forensic evidence; final backups were from 3 October 2023, leaving a 13-day gap; encryption was applied to all virtualized servers showing 100% network spread due to lack of segmentation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Real Sociedad asserted no exfiltration of data occurred based on forensic analysis.
claimsVsReality.reality: While no exfiltration was confirmed, the technical investigation was severely limited by evidence deletion and insufficient security logging; the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence.

claimsVsReality.claim: Real Sociedad claimed to have implemented security measures before the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: The club lacked critical security controls including encryption of sensitive data categories, network segmentation, isolated backups, and proper VPN security management; many documented policies lacked implementation dates.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner guaranteeing adequate security including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Real Sociedad failed to protect personal data against ransomware attack through unencrypted storage, lack of network segmentation, and improperly secured backups, compromising availability of 60,000 individuals' records.
violations: Real Sociedad failed to protect personal data against ransomware attack through unencrypted storage, lack of network segmentation, and improperly secured backups, compromising availability of 60,000 individuals' records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires data controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security adequate to the risk, including pseudonymization, encryption, ability to restore availability, and regular verification of measure effectiveness.
regulatoryFindings.description: Real Sociedad lacked critical security measures including encryption of sensitive data at rest, network segmentation to prevent lateral movement, isolated backup systems, and proper VPN vulnerability management despite handling health data, financial data, and biometric information.
violations: Real Sociedad lacked critical security measures including encryption of sensitive data at rest, network segmentation to prevent lateral movement, isolated backup systems, and proper VPN vulnerability management despite handling health data, financial data, and biometric information.

outcome: Real Sociedad recognized responsibility and paid €66,000 (40% reduction from initial €110,000 penalty for prompt payment and responsibility admission). The club was ordered within 3 months to implement effective security measures including encryption and other safeguards proportionate to the risks it processes. The procedure was closed without further enforcement, but the company must demonstrate compliance with corrective measures.
companyNow: Real Sociedad de Fútbol continues as one of Spain's major professional football clubs. The 2025 resolution marked closure of the AEPD investigation following the club's payment and commitment to enhanced data security practices.
dataType: Biometric data, identity documents (DNI/NIE/Passport), financial data (bank accounts), health data, location data, contact information, employment records, images/video

companyDescription: DHL Parcel Iberia is a subsidiary of Deutsche Post DHL Group, operating as a parcel delivery and logistics service provider in Spain. The company handles B2C and B2B shipments across Europe.
companyLongDescription: DHL Parcel Iberia is a subsidiary of Deutsche Post DHL Group, operating as a parcel delivery and logistics service provider in Spain. The company handles B2C and B2B shipments across Europe.
caseDescription: DHL included customers' phone numbers on shipping labels despite determining in 2019 that this was unnecessary. The company repeated this practice in 2023 at a new Polish warehouse, exposing personal data to unauthorized access. DHL failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures under GDPR Article 32.
violationSummary: DHL failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, as required by GDPR Art. 32. The company's own assessment in 2019 determined phone numbers were not essential for delivery, yet reintroduced them in 2023 without proper safeguards against unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: DHL printed customer phone numbers on shipping labels for B2C deliveries even though the field was optional, exposing private contact information to anyone handling or accessing the packages.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of customers had their personal phone numbers exposed to delivery workers, warehouse staff, and anyone intercepting packages, enabling unwanted calls, identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: DHL claimed in October 2019 that it approved removal of phone numbers from B2C shipping labels as unnecessary for delivery operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: In March 2023, DHL validated a new label template with phone numbers printed for the Polish warehouse, contradicting its 2019 determination and reintroducing the unnecessary data field.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated that phone numbers in its systems enable contact with recipients for failed delivery attempts and that immediate removal followed AEPD's request in March 2024.
claimsVsReality.reality: Phone numbers were printed on external labels visible to all handlers, creating unnecessary exposure risks even if internal systems retained them for legitimate delivery purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymization, encryption, confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: DHL included phone numbers on shipping labels without implementing safeguards to prevent unauthorized access or exposure, despite determining in 2019 that the field was not essential for logistics operations.
violations: DHL included phone numbers on shipping labels without implementing safeguards to prevent unauthorized access or exposure, despite determining in 2019 that the field was not essential for logistics operations.

DHL reintroduced the phone number field in 2023 at a new warehouse location despite prior agreement with suppliers to remove it, demonstrating gross negligence in failing to maintain consistent security standards.

outcome: DHL recognized responsibility and paid the administrative fine of €3,000 (reflecting a 40% reduction for voluntary payment and admission of liability). The company must implement adequate technical and organizational measures to remove unnecessary personal data from shipping labels and ensure data minimization in future operations. The procedure was terminated on September 2, 2025, following voluntary payment.
companyNow: DHL Parcel Iberia remains operational as a major logistics provider in Spain. Following this enforcement action, the company is required to implement enhanced data protection protocols and security measures across all facilities.
dataType: Name, address, telephone number, email address

companyDescription: The Institute of Mental Health is Singapore's specialist mental health hospital providing psychiatric inpatient, outpatient, and research services. It is a statutory authority under the Ministry of Health.
companyLongDescription: The Institute of Mental Health is Singapore's specialist mental health hospital providing psychiatric inpatient, outpatient, and research services. It is a statutory authority under the Ministry of Health.
caseDescription: The Institute of Mental Health used a patient's personal data (name, age, medical condition) to identify and recruit him for a research study without obtaining explicit consent beforehand. Although the organisation had displayed a notification in clinic areas stating it may use personal data for research recruitment, it failed to provide clear opt-out mechanisms, and the Commission found the notification approach insufficient for the sensitive nature of medical data.
violationSummary: The organisation collected patient data for medical treatment but used it for a secondary purpose (research recruitment) without clear express consent mechanisms or adequate opt-out procedures, violating principles of fair use and transparency.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A research officer approached a psychiatric patient in the clinic waiting area and identified him by name to recruit him for a medical study, using the patient's health information.
whyTheyWereWrong: The patient's sensitive mental health information was used to target and approach him for research participation without his express consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: IMH stated that only patient names and appointment times were provided to the research officer; no medical information was disclosed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commission found that IMH's actions necessarily involved assessment of patients' medical profiles and age group to identify suitable candidates, meaning medical data was effectively used in the recruitment process even if not explicitly 'disclosed' in summary form.

claimsVsReality.claim: IMH claimed patients could opt out by contacting the Data Protection Officer or speaking to counter staff or the Quality Service Manager.
claimsVsReality.reality: These mechanisms placed the burden on patients to navigate the organisation's administrative processes; IMH did not actively alert patients in the notification itself of how and when they could refuse research recruitment use of their data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.13(a) requires an organisation not to use personal data unless the individual has given or is deemed to have given consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: IMH used the complainant's health data, age, and name for research recruitment without first obtaining express written consent from the patient.
violations: IMH used the complainant's health data, age, and name for research recruitment without first obtaining express written consent from the patient.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.14(1) provides that consent is valid only if the individual has been notified of collection/use/disclosure purposes and has provided consent for those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: While IMH displayed a general notification in clinic areas, it did not obtain express consent before approaching the patient or clearly inform him of the specific manner and timeframe to opt out.
violations: While IMH displayed a general notification in clinic areas, it did not obtain express consent before approaching the patient or clearly inform him of the specific manner and timeframe to opt out.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.15A permits deemed consent by notification if the organisation: (a) conducts an adverse-effect assessment; (b) takes reasonable steps to inform the individual of the intended use; and (c) provides clear means and time for the individual to opt out.
regulatoryFindings.description: IMH satisfied requirements (a) and (b) but failed requirement (c): it did not take reasonable steps to alert the patient to how and when he could notify the organisation of his refusal to consent. The onus was placed on the individual to find DPO contact details on the website or speak to counter staff.
violations: IMH satisfied requirements (a) and (b) but failed requirement (c): it did not take reasonable steps to alert the patient to how and when he could notify the organisation of his refusal to consent. The onus was placed on the individual to find DPO contact details on the website or speak to counter staff.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found IMH in compliance with the Consent Obligation based on implied consent (the patient's 10+ years of visiting the clinic with knowledge of the notification and failure to object). However, the Commission held that IMH cannot rely on deemed consent by notification under s.15A because it failed to provide adequate opt-out mechanisms. The Commission commended IMH's voluntary reform: going forward, the clinical team will first inform potential participants about available research studies before direct contact by research staff, and patients will be asked for express consent before their medical information is used for research recruitment. IMH must also revise its notification to explicitly state how and within what timeframe patients may opt out of research recruitment use of their data.
companyNow: The Institute of Mental Health continues to operate as Singapore's specialist psychiatric institution. It has voluntarily revised its research recruitment procedures to require express consent and improved notice of opt-out mechanisms.
dataType: Health data, personal identifiers (name, age, medical condition history)
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.15A – Deemed Consent by Notification (failed third requirement)

companyDescription: People Central Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based cloud-based Human Resource (HR) solutions provider offering online HR management Software as a Service (SaaS) solutions to enterprise clients.
companyLongDescription: People Central Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based cloud-based Human Resource (HR) solutions provider offering online HR management Software as a Service (SaaS) solutions to enterprise clients.
caseDescription: People Central, a cloud-based HR SaaS provider, suffered a data breach affecting 95,000 employees and 24,765 emergency contacts/children due to SQL injection vulnerabilities, weak access controls (open RDP without 2FA), and insufficient security testing (vulnerability scans only every 2 years). The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements required under Singapore's PDPA, and personal data was deleted and exfiltrated, with data found for sale on the dark web.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (encryption, access controls, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing) to protect sensitive personal data in its possession, resulting in unauthorised access, deletion, and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect client employee data: no Web Application Firewall against SQL injections.
whyTheyWereWrong: 95,000 employees' highly sensitive personal data including names, NRIC numbers, salaries, bank account numbers, and dates of birth were exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had conducted vulnerability assessments and adhered to ISO procedures
claimsVsReality.reality: Vulnerability scans were conducted only every 2 years; no network vulnerability assessments were conducted; no regular penetration testing was performed (required annually per industry standards)

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation could not implement a WAF due to service disruption encountered previously
claimsVsReality.reality: WAF implementation is necessary and standard practice for organisations handling sensitive personal data; service disruption is not a valid mitigating circumstance

claimsVsReality.claim: Financial difficulties justified a waiver of the penalty (decline in sales, increased loans, reduced director salaries)
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation remained profitable; financial hardship does not justify non-compliance with data protection obligations

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews; vulnerability scans conducted only every 2 years instead of quarterly
violations: Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews; vulnerability scans conducted only every 2 years instead of quarterly
Did not implement Web Application Firewall (WAF) to defend against SQL injection attacks despite having SQL injection vulnerabilities
Maintained open RDP access to the internet without two-factor authentication (2FA)
Allowed network inbound traffic from all IP addresses in cloud environment without restrictions
Did not conduct network vulnerability assessments or regular penetration testing (should be at least annually per CIS Critical Security Controls)
Only encrypted passwords and salary information; did not encrypt all personal data fields

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation is required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $17,500 in 12 monthly instalments. Within 90 days, the organisation must: (1) review its web application for secure implementation per OWASP standards; (2) implement an adequately configured WAF; (3) complete regular annual external and internal penetration tests; (4) complete 2FA for RDP access; (5) implement encryption for all personal data fields; and (6) report completion to the Commission. Monitoring will continue to ensure compliance.
companyNow: People Central Pte. Ltd. remains operational. The company is implementing remedial security measures and is under compliance monitoring by the PDPC.
dataType: Name, gender, NRIC number, date of employment, place and date of birth, nationality, salary, marital status, religion, bank account number, mobile number, email address, physical address, emergency contact names and numbers, children's names and dates of birth

company: Asociación Nacional de Tasadores y Peritos Judiciales Informáticos (ANTPJI)
companyDescription: ANTPJI is a national Spanish association representing valuers (tasadores) and judicial computer experts (peritos judiciales informáticos). It maintains a website and processes personal data from website visitors and published judicial documents.
companyLongDescription: ANTPJI is a national Spanish association representing valuers (tasadores) and judicial computer experts (peritos judiciales informáticos). It maintains a website and processes personal data from website visitors and published judicial documents.
caseDescription: ANTPJI published a judicial resolution containing the personal data (name and surname) of an individual without consent on its website. The individual submitted deletion requests via registered mail, but ANTPJI failed to respond or remove the published document. The privacy policy also failed to provide adequate information about international data transfers to the US.
violationSummary: ANTPJI made personal data publicly accessible via website publication without consent or lawful basis, and failed to respond to subject access/deletion requests, directly exposing the individual's identity and information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: ANTPJI published a judicial ruling containing the complainant's full name and personal data on its website without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's personal data remained publicly accessible and searchable online for months after requesting removal.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy stated data is transferred to US but provided adequate safeguards and transparency.
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy failed to disclose existence or absence of adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards, or means to obtain copies, violating Article 13.1(f) transparency requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: ANTPJI's address listed in privacy policy (Calle Ponzano 52, 28005 Madrid) was valid contact information.
claimsVsReality.reality: First deletion request sent to this address on 30 Aug 2023 was returned as 'Unknown recipient.' Second request to same address on 12 Sept 2023 was received but never answered.

claimsVsReality.claim: Judicial resolution published on website was necessary and appropriately sourced.
claimsVsReality.reality: ANTPJI was not a party to the judicial proceedings; the resolution itself stated data should only be disclosed with prior dissociation of personal data and full respect for privacy; no authorization existed for publication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13(1)(f) requires controllers to provide information about international data transfers, including existence of adequacy decisions or appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: ANTPJI's privacy policy stated data would be transferred to US hosting servers but failed to disclose existence or absence of adequacy decisions or appropriate safeguards under GDPR Chapter 5.
violations: ANTPJI's privacy policy stated data would be transferred to US hosting servers but failed to disclose existence or absence of adequacy decisions or appropriate safeguards under GDPR Chapter 5.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 17(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain erasure of personal data without undue delay when grounds such as lack of necessity or withdrawal of consent apply.
regulatoryFindings.description: ANTPJI received two registered deletion requests (30 Aug 2023 and 12 Sept 2023) but never responded or removed the published judicial document containing claimant's personal data within the required one-month timeframe.
violations: ANTPJI received two registered deletion requests (30 Aug 2023 and 12 Sept 2023) but never responded or removed the published judicial document containing claimant's personal data within the required one-month timeframe.

outcome: ANTPJI was ordered to pay €1,000 for Article 13 violation and €1,000 for Article 17 violation. Within 3 months of the decision becoming final and enforceable, ANTPJI must: (1) update its privacy policy to include required information on international data transfers per Article 13.1(f) GDPR and include a valid postal address; and (2) respond to the claimant's deletion request. Failure to comply may result in additional enforcement action.
companyNow: Association status unknown; no evidence of remedial action to date. Document indicates organization maintains website presence and data processing operations.
dataType: Personal names, judicial case information

companyDescription: AUTOESCUELA A.A.A. is a Spanish driving school founded in 1999, with reported annual revenues of €920,920 as of 2015. It provides driver training and licensing services to the public.
companyLongDescription: AUTOESCUELA A.A.A. is a Spanish driving school founded in 1999, with reported annual revenues of €920,920 as of 2015. It provides driver training and licensing services to the public.
caseDescription: A driving school installed video surveillance cameras inside its premises without displaying the legally required informational signage notifying individuals of data processing. The AEPD determined this violated GDPR Article 13 (duty to inform data subjects) and ordered corrective measures and a penalty.
violationSummary: The company conducted continuous video surveillance without the required transparent notice to data subjects, failing to meet baseline transparency and lawfulness requirements for surveillance processing.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Operated a video surveillance system with at least one interior camera without displaying any visible informational notice identifying the data controller or explaining the recording.
whyTheyWereWrong: Students and clients whose images were captured had no way to know they were being recorded or how to access, delete, or exercise rights over their recorded biometric data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated in its response dated 18 March 2025 that it has maintained an informational notice ('distintivo informativo') and that surveillance has never involved illegal recording.
claimsVsReality.reality: No visible informational notice was present in the video surveillance areas according to photographs submitted by the complainant. The company failed to provide any documentary evidence of the claimed notice when asked to do so by the AEPD.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed to have engaged a specialized data protection service since 2013.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this claim, the company failed to implement the basic transparency requirement of a visible notice informing individuals of video surveillance, suggesting the engagement was ineffective or incomplete.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from a data subject, the controller must provide detailed information including the identity of the controller, the purposes of processing, and the rights of the individual, at the time of collection.
regulatoryFindings.description: AUTOESCUELA failed to place a visible informational notice in the video surveillance area identifying the existence of processing, the identity of the data controller, or the rights available to individuals under GDPR Articles 15-22.
violations: AUTOESCUELA failed to place a visible informational notice in the video surveillance area identifying the existence of processing, the identity of the data controller, or the rights available to individuals under GDPR Articles 15-22.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) (accountability principle) requires controllers to implement measures to demonstrate compliance with data protection requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: AUTOESCUELA provided no documentation or evidence of a visible warning notice when challenged by the AEPD, violating the duty to proactively demonstrate compliance.
violations: AUTOESCUELA provided no documentation or evidence of a visible warning notice when challenged by the AEPD, violating the duty to proactively demonstrate compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 22 specifies that the information duty for video surveillance can be fulfilled by placing a visible informational device in the monitored area identifying at minimum the existence of processing, the controller's identity, and the ability to exercise rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: AUTOESCUELA's video surveillance system lacked any visible informational device in the monitored zone, failing to meet the layered ('información por capas') transparency requirement.
violations: AUTOESCUELA's video surveillance system lacked any visible informational device in the monitored zone, failing to meet the layered ('información por capas') transparency requirement.

outcome: On 1 August 2025, the AEPD initiated a sanction procedure against AUTOESCUELA A.A.A. for violation of GDPR Article 13. The company subsequently recognized responsibility and paid the penalty voluntarily on 5 August 2025, obtaining a cumulative 40% reduction (20% for responsibility recognition + 20% for voluntary payment) under Article 85 of the LPACAP, reducing the initial €500 penalty to €300. The company was ordered to place a compliant informational notice in its video surveillance area within one month of the resolution becoming final and executable. The procedure was terminated on 18 July 2025 following voluntary payment and acceptance of the corrective measures. The resolution is final in administrative proceedings and fully executable.
companyNow: AUTOESCUELA A.A.A. remains operational. The company has been required to implement and maintain the mandatory informational signage in its video surveillance areas. Current compliance status unknown beyond the formal order.
dataType: Biometric data (facial images), personal identification data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 13 (information to be provided where personal data are obtained from the data subject)
LOPDGDD Article 22 (information duty for video surveillance)

companyDescription: EXCEL HOTELS & RESORTS, S.A. (founded 1987) is a Spanish hospitality company that manages hotel properties and serves as secretary-administrator for property owner communities. The company operates through property management services and guest accommodation.
companyLongDescription: EXCEL HOTELS & RESORTS, S.A. (founded 1987) is a Spanish hospitality company that manages hotel properties and serves as secretary-administrator for property owner communities. The company operates through property management services and guest accommodation.
caseDescription: EXCEL HOTELS failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to protect personal data of hotel guests and property community members. Security personnel routinely left printed lists containing names, passport numbers, DNI, and apartment details visible and unattended, allowing unauthorized third parties to photograph and access the information. The company did not report the security breach to the data protection authority despite internal discovery.
violationSummary: EXCEL HOTELS, as data controller, failed to implement Article 5(1)(f) of GDPR requiring adequate security measures (technical and organizational) to ensure confidentiality and integrity of personal data. The lists were left plainly visible despite being security-sensitive documents containing unique identifiers (DNI, passport numbers) that enable identity theft.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Left printed lists containing names, DNI numbers, passport numbers, and addresses of 37+ property owners and 40+ hotel guests visible.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 75 individuals had their identity documents and personal information exposed to unauthorized access and photography, creating serious risk of identity fraud, impersonation.

claimsVsReality.claim: EXCEL HOTELS claimed the security personnel habitually carried lists in a closed folder that was daily deposited in a locked guard station with exclusive access to security personnel.
claimsVsReality.reality: During the 21-22 March 2023 incident, security personnel left the lists openly visible on their work desk during their shift, where third parties photographed them from a window.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it evaluated the breach as low-risk and therefore did not communicate it to affected individuals or to the AEPD.
claimsVsReality.reality: Approximately 77 individuals had their DNI and passport numbers exposed and photographed, which are sensitive identifiers enabling identity fraud and requiring mandatory breach notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: EXCEL HOTELS asserted it had implemented appropriate security measures per GDPR Article 32.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented technical or organizational controls prevented security staff from leaving sensitive data lists unattended or visible, and no audit or training had verified compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed in such a way as to guarantee appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through application of appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: EXCEL HOTELS did not implement measures to prevent security personnel from leaving printed lists containing names, DNI, passport numbers, apartment numbers, and countries of residence visible and unattended on security desks.
violations: EXCEL HOTELS did not implement measures to prevent security personnel from leaving printed lists containing names, DNI, passport numbers, apartment numbers, and countries of residence visible and unattended on security desks.
Lists were accessible to third parties who photographed them on 21-22 March 2023.
No preventive controls were documented to ensure data handlers maintained confidentiality of sensitive personal data.
The company failed to account for the particular sensitivity of DNI and passport numbers, which uniquely identify individuals and enable identity fraud.

outcome: EXCEL HOTELS was found to have violated GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (Integrity and Confidentiality). The company paid €32,000 (originally €40,000 with 20% early payment reduction) and waived administrative appeal rights. The company must demonstrate, within three months, implementation of effective technical and organizational measures to prevent future incidents of this nature. The decision is fully enforceable. EXCEL HOTELS appointed an external Data Protection Officer, commissioned a compliance audit, and established periodic data protection audits and a security protocol for all personnel.
companyNow: EXCEL HOTELS continues operations as a hotel management and property administration company. Following the enforcement action, it engaged an external Data Protection Officer, conducted a compliance audit, and implemented a periodic audit framework for data protection across all departments.
dataType: Name, surname, apartment number, country of residence, passport number, national ID (DNI), accommodation regime

company: London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham Council
companyDescription: London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham is a local authority in West London responsible for providing public services and managing Freedom of Information requests. It is a UK public sector body with statutory data protection obligations.
companyLongDescription: London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham is a local authority in West London responsible for providing public services and managing Freedom of Information requests. It is a UK public sector body with statutory data protection obligations.
caseDescription: The Council prepared a Freedom of Information response containing 35 hidden Excel workbooks. Hidden personal data of 6,528 individuals—including 2,342 children and 96 unaccompanied asylum-seeking children—was inadvertently disclosed publicly for nearly three years. The Council lacked guidance, training, and technical controls to detect hidden data before release.
violationSummary: The personal data of thousands of individuals, particularly vulnerable children in Council care, was inadvertently exposed to the public through hidden spreadsheet data. This constitutes a breach of the confidentiality principle.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham published a Freedom of Information response containing 35 hidden Excel workbooks with personal data of 6,528 people without inspecting for or removing.
whyTheyWereWrong: 6,528 individuals including 2,342 children and 96 unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors had sensitive personal data exposed online for nearly three years because the Council failed to check.

claimsVsReality.claim: The FOI response was a routine disclosure prepared and published in accordance with FOI obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The response contained 35 hidden workbooks with sensitive personal data of 6,528 individuals (including 96 asylum-seeking children) that remained publicly accessible for nearly 3 years without detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Hidden data in Excel spreadsheets was not apparent and would not be readily discoverable.
claimsVsReality.reality: Anyone with basic Excel knowledge could use standard inspection tools to access the hidden workbooks and personal data within minutes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Council had adequate training and guidance in place for FOI disclosure practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Council provided only general training unrelated to Excel safety and had no written guidance, no specific training, and no technical checks for hidden data detection before disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council did not implement measures to detect or remove hidden data from Excel files before publishing FOI responses, exposing 6,528 individuals' sensitive data.
violations: Council did not implement measures to detect or remove hidden data from Excel files before publishing FOI responses, exposing 6,528 individuals' sensitive data.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(2) requires the controller to be responsible for and demonstrate compliance with the Regulation ('accountability').
regulatoryFindings.description: Council could not demonstrate compliance as it had no written guidance, training protocols, or technical checks in place for safe Excel disclosure.
violations: Council could not demonstrate compliance as it had no written guidance, training protocols, or technical checks in place for safe Excel disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(1) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing complies with the Regulation, and measures shall be reviewed and updated where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to implement or review measures for checking hidden data in spreadsheets before release, contrary to ICO best-practice guidance from June 2018.
violations: Council failed to implement or review measures for checking hidden data in spreadsheets before release, contrary to ICO best-practice guidance from June 2018.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(1) requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council did not implement security measures proportionate to the sensitivity of data disclosed (children's placements, asylum-seeker identities, special category data), relying on general training unrelated to Excel safety.
violations: Council did not implement security measures proportionate to the sensitivity of data disclosed (children's placements, asylum-seeker identities, special category data), relying on general training unrelated to Excel safety.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand (not a monetary fine) to the Council under Article 58(2)(b) of UK GDPR. The Council is required to comply with recommendations including: updating redaction and disclosure guidance for spreadsheets; mandating training on Excel safety and hidden data detection; implementing mandatory peer/manager review before disclosure; converting files to CSV format before release; and ensuring refresher training for all relevant staff. The Council must demonstrate rectification of these infringements; failure to do so may be treated as an aggravating factor in future enforcement action.
companyNow: London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham Council remains the local government authority serving West London. Following this enforcement action, the Council has implemented remedial measures including updated disclosure guidance, staff training, and process changes requiring CSV-only formats for information release.
dataType: Employment data, contact details, children's placement records, special category data, asylum-seeking children identifiers
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 24(1) – Responsibility of controller
UK GDPR Article 32(1) – Security of processing

companyDescription: A Spanish residential property management company managing a community of property owners. Operated an online portal to distribute community documents and facilitate resident communications.
companyLongDescription: A Spanish residential property management company managing a community of property owners. Operated an online portal to distribute community documents and facilitate resident communications.
caseDescription: A property management company operating a residential community website failed to implement basic security protections required by GDPR. The website used unencrypted HTTP protocol instead of HTTPS, lacked SSL certificates, and distributed login credentials (shared username/password) to all residents via physical documents. This exposed residents' personal and financial data to interception.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement mandatory technical and organizational security measures (Article 32 GDPR) to protect personal data transmitted via their web portal. The lack of encryption and SSL certificate created direct risk of unauthorized access and interception.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A property management company distributed shared login credentials to all residents in physical notices, operated its website without HTTPS encryption or SSL certificates.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents' names, addresses, impayment records, bank account details, and other sensitive personal information were transmitted over unencrypted HTTP protocol.

claimsVsReality.claim: The community management company claimed it had outsourced data protection consulting services and was handling data appropriately
claimsVsReality.reality: The website lacked basic encryption and security controls for months despite the complaint, indicating no meaningful implementation of security measures

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserted it stored no sensitive financial data beyond the community account itself
claimsVsReality.reality: Website contained residents' personal information, addresses, payment status, and references to bank account details accessible via unencrypted portal

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32 GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security adequate to the risk, including encryption of personal data and ability to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: Website used HTTP protocol without HTTPS or SSL encryption, exposing data transmission to interception attacks
violations: Website used HTTP protocol without HTTPS or SSL encryption, exposing data transmission to interception attacks
No SSL certificate installed despite processing personal and financial data
Shared username/password system prevented identification of individual access and breach detection
Failed to implement secure credential management and user authentication controls

outcome: Procedure terminated following voluntary payment and acknowledgment of responsibility. COMUNIDAD.1 paid €600.00 (representing 40% reduction for early payment and responsibility acknowledgment from base €1,000.00). Ordered to implement HTTPS protocol, install SSL certificates, and establish proper user/password management policies within 6 months of resolution becoming final. Failure to adopt corrective measures could trigger further administrative sanctions.
companyNow: Unknown. The entity remains a residential property management community subject to ongoing GDPR compliance obligations.
dataType: names, surnames, residential addresses, financial data (unpaid amounts), bank account details

companyDescription: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. is a Spanish company dedicated to the commercialization of electricity and energy services, operating as an energy advisor and service provider. The company engages in telemarketing and customer acquisition activities.
companyLongDescription: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. is a Spanish company dedicated to the commercialization of electricity and energy services, operating as an energy advisor and service provider. The company engages in telemarketing and customer acquisition activities.
caseDescription: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. unlawfully subcontracted personal data processing to third parties without explicit written authorization from the data controller (***EMPRESA.3). The company failed to maintain proper contractual safeguards and processor oversight, allowing unsolicited marketing calls and emails to be sent to complainants using data obtained without valid consent.
violationSummary: The company's failure to properly authorize and oversee subprocessors created systemic insecurity in personal data handling, allowing unauthorized processing and marketing activities without proper safeguards or consent mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. subcontracted personal data processing to third parties without obtaining prior written authorization from the data controller, violating Article 28 of the GDPR.
whyTheyWereWrong: A Spanish resident received unsolicited telemarketing calls and emails using his name, phone number, email address.

claimsVsReality.claim: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. claimed commitment to data protection compliance and stated it had implemented data processor agreements with safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written authorization existed for the subcontraction of ***EMPRESA.4; the subprocessor list (Annex IV) was blank; contractual safeguards were absent or unenforced; complainant received unsolicited calls and emails without valid consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that ***EMPRESA.5 guaranteed having obtained the complainant's free and express consent for marketing communications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainant explicitly denied providing consent, was not registered in Robinson (anti-marketing list), and had never been a customer. The certificate of consent was unverified and could not override the complainant's denial.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(2) requires that a processor shall not engage another processor without prior specific or general written authorization from the controller. In the case of general written authorization, the processor must inform the controller of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of other processors, giving the controller the opportunity to object.
regulatoryFindings.description: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. subcontracted data processing services to ***EMPRESA.4 without documented written authorization from ***EMPRESA.3 (the data controller). The contract between the controller and processor contained an empty Annex IV listing subprocessors, with no authorization for subcontracting reflected therein.
violations: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. subcontracted data processing services to ***EMPRESA.4 without documented written authorization from ***EMPRESA.3 (the data controller). The contract between the controller and processor contained an empty Annex IV listing subprocessors, with no authorization for subcontracting reflected therein.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(4) requires that where a processor engages another processor, the same data protection obligations must be imposed via contract, and the initial processor remains fully responsible to the controller for subprocessor compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: The contract between ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. and ***EMPRESA.4 lacked enforceable data protection obligations for consent and proper data sourcing. The subcontracted entities (***EMPRESA.5) provided data with only a unilateral certificate of consent dated 30 July 2023, which the complainant contests; no independent verification or safeguards existed to ensure validity.
violations: The contract between ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. and ***EMPRESA.4 lacked enforceable data protection obligations for consent and proper data sourcing. The subcontracted entities (***EMPRESA.5) provided data with only a unilateral certificate of consent dated 30 July 2023, which the complainant contests; no independent verification or safeguards existed to ensure validity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires lawful, fair, and transparent processing of personal data based on valid consent, legitimate interest, or other lawful basis.
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant's personal data was processed for telemarketing without demonstrable consent and without transparency. The data was obtained from ***EMPRESA.5's database allegedly with consent, but complainant asserts no such consent was given and was not on Robinson list (anti-marketing registry).
violations: Complainant's personal data was processed for telemarketing without demonstrable consent and without transparency. The data was obtained from ***EMPRESA.5's database allegedly with consent, but complainant asserts no such consent was given and was not on Robinson list (anti-marketing registry).

outcome: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. recognized responsibility and paid the penalty voluntarily in full on 16 May 2025, applying both the 20% reduction for early recognition of responsibility and the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, resulting in a final penalty of €12,000. The company submitted to the two accumulated reductions permitted under Article 85 of the Spanish Administrative Procedure Act (LPACAP). The procedure was terminated following payment. The company stated it had ceased working with ***EMPRESA.4 and ***EMPRESA.5 after determining they were not safe data processors, demonstrating post-violation remediation. The resolution is final in administrative proceedings and fully enforceable.
companyNow: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. is an energy commercialization company founded in 2021 with 2023 revenues of €6,257,181. Following this enforcement action, the company ceased engagement with the problematic subprocessors and stated commitment to GDPR compliance.
dataType: Name, surname, email, telephone, IBAN bank account code, postal address
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 28(2) — Processor cannot subcontract without prior written authorization
GDPR Art. 28(3) — Processor must ensure same data protection obligations in subprocessor contracts
GDPR Art. 28(4) — Processor remains fully liable for subprocessor compliance
GDPR Art. 6 — Lack of valid lawful basis for processing
GDPR Art. 14 — Failure to provide transparency information to data subjects

companyDescription: SILVANERGIA 2022, S.L. is a Spanish company that engaged in telemarketing services for energy contract recruitment. Founded in 2022, the company attempted to act as a customer acquisition agent for Bassols Energía but never formalized a legal processing agreement.
companyLongDescription: SILVANERGIA 2022, S.L. is a Spanish company that engaged in telemarketing services for energy contract recruitment. Founded in 2022, the company attempted to act as a customer acquisition agent for Bassols Energía but never formalized a legal processing agreement.
caseDescription: SILVANERGIA conducted telemarketing campaigns to recruit customers for an energy company without a signed processing agreement or legal basis. The company obtained personal data from a third-party provider and made unsolicited calls using sensitive identifiers like DNI and partial bank account information, without lawful consent or contractual authority.
violationSummary: The company failed to establish lawful legitimacy (Article 6.1) for processing personal data. Personal data was acquired from a third party without evidence of lawful consent from data subjects, and processed without a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) despite acting as a processor.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SILVANERGIA made unsolicited telemarketing calls to consumers using personal data including names, national ID numbers, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' sensitive personal information including national IDs and financial details were processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: SILVANERGIA claimed it was acting as an authorized agent of Bassols Energía and that the call was to 'update tariffs' per new government regulations.
claimsVsReality.reality: SILVANERGIA had no signed Data Processing Agreement with Bassols Energía; preliminary discussions began in July 2023 but were never formalized. Bassols later terminated contact in August 2023 due to non-receipt of the signed contract and SILVANERGIA's poor financial condition. The company was not authorized to process customer data on Bassols' behalf.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it obtained data from a legitimate source ('companies like...') and that the data provider guaranteed Robinson List filtering.
claimsVsReality.reality: SILVANERGIA provided only an invoice from a data provider dated 10 June 2023 (pre-call), with no documentation of lawful consent from data subjects or proof that the provider obtained the data legitimately. No evidence was submitted that the data transaction was compliant with GDPR or that the complainant had ever consented to sale/transfer of her data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if it complies with at least one of six legal bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests (with a balance test for the last).
regulatoryFindings.description: SILVANERGIA processed the complainant's personal data (name, DNI, address, bank details) without establishing any lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained from the data subject; no contractual relationship existed; no legal obligation applied; and no legitimate interest justified processing without consent.
violations: SILVANERGIA processed the complainant's personal data (name, DNI, address, bank details) without establishing any lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained from the data subject; no contractual relationship existed; no legal obligation applied; and no legitimate interest justified processing without consent.

The company acquired data from a third-party provider without evidence that the provider had obtained it lawfully or with consent from data subjects, and failed to provide documentation of legitimacy of the data transaction.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28 requires that where processing is carried out on behalf of a controller, there must be a contract or other legally binding document binding the processor to the controller, establishing the subject, duration, nature, and purpose of the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: SILVANERGIA entered into preliminary discussions with Bassols Energía Comercial in July 2023 but never formalized a Data Processing Agreement (DPA). Despite this, the company began customer acquisition activities in July–August 2023 without a signed contract, meaning all processing lacked proper contractual legitimacy.
