whyTheyWereWrong: By refusing to cooperate with the investigation, 4USPORT obstructed the authority's ability to determine whether personal data of gym members had been mishandled.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) requires that each supervisory authority shall have the power to order a controller and processor and, where applicable, the controller's or processor's representative, to provide any information the authority requires for the performance of its functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: 4USPORT did not provide requested information to AEPD despite three separate information requests sent between November 2024 and February 2025
violations: 4USPORT did not provide requested information to AEPD despite three separate information requests sent between November 2024 and February 2025

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(e) provides that failure to facilitate access in breach of Article 58(1) constitutes an infringement subject to administrative fines.
regulatoryFindings.description: 4USPORT's non-compliance with information requests was classified as a breach of GDPR Article 58(1), triggering sanction authority under Article 83(5)(e)
violations: 4USPORT's non-compliance with information requests was classified as a breach of GDPR Article 58(1), triggering sanction authority under Article 83(5)(e)

outcome: AEPD imposed a €600 administrative fine and ordered 4USPORT to provide the requested information within 10 business days from when the decision becomes final and enforceable. The company was warned that continued non-compliance may trigger further enforcement action and additional sanctions up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover. The decision is final after expiration of the one-month appeal period.
companyNow: 4USPORT INSTALACIONES DEPORTIVAS, S.L. is a sports facilities company incorporated in 2021. Per AXESOR data, the company has not filed financial statements publicly.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified categories)

companyDescription: LVMH IBERIA, S.L. is the Spanish subsidiary of LVMH, operating luxury retail stores. The entity was founded in 1997 and had reported annual turnover of €541,845,000 in 2023, making it a major retail employer in Spain.
companyLongDescription: LVMH IBERIA, S.L. is the Spanish subsidiary of LVMH, operating luxury retail stores. The entity was founded in 1997 and had reported annual turnover of €541,845,000 in 2023, making it a major retail employer in Spain.
caseDescription: LVMH IBERIA added an employee's personal mobile phone number to a WhatsApp work group without consent, despite the employee explicitly stating she would not use her personal device for work communications. The company lacked any legal basis to process this personal data and continued the practice even after being informed of the employee's withdrawal.
violationSummary: The company failed to establish and maintain adequate legal grounds (lawful basis) for processing employees' personal mobile phone data. Processing without consent or another valid Article 6 basis constitutes a fundamental breach of GDPR's licidity principle.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: LVMH IBERIA added an employee's personal mobile phone number to a work WhatsApp group without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's personal phone number was processed without any legal basis, exposing her to unwanted work communications on her private device despite her clear rejection of this practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it adopted a 'guarantor posture' and acted respectfully toward employee privacy, pointing to its decision to allow temporary withdrawal from WhatsApp groups during vacation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company added an employee to a WhatsApp group on 5 June 2023, only days after she explicitly notified management on 11 May 2023 that she would no longer use her personal phone for work communications. This contradicts any claimed respect for privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company argued the employee had not requested permanent removal from WhatsApp groups, only temporary absence during vacation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee's email explicitly stated 'ya no seguiré utilizando mi móvil personal para cuestiones laborales' (I will no longer use my personal phone for work matters) and announced she would 'saldré de los grupos a final de mi jornada el día viernes' (exit groups by end of Friday), indicating a permanent change in her work communication preferences.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed the personal data processed was minimal and necessary — only name, surname, mobile number, and work tasks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the volume of data, processing personal mobile phone numbers without a valid legal basis violates GDPR Article 6. Necessity does not cure lack of lawfulness.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data be lawful and based on at least one of six specified conditions: consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: LVMH IBERIA processed the employee's personal mobile phone number without obtaining her consent, and without establishing any other lawful basis. The employee had expressly stated she would not use her personal phone for work, yet the company added her number to a WhatsApp group days later.
violations: LVMH IBERIA processed the employee's personal mobile phone number without obtaining her consent, and without establishing any other lawful basis. The employee had expressly stated she would not use her personal phone for work, yet the company added her number to a WhatsApp group days later.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data processing be lawful, fair, and transparent.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's processing was neither lawful (lacking a valid Article 6 basis) nor transparent (no prior notice or consent was sought). The processing was opaque and contrary to the employee's explicit wishes.
violations: The company's processing was neither lawful (lacking a valid Article 6 basis) nor transparent (no prior notice or consent was sought). The processing was opaque and contrary to the employee's explicit wishes.

outcome: LVMH IBERIA recognized responsibility and paid €42,000 (following application of 40% cumulative reduction for early admission and voluntary payment). The AEPD issued a compliance order requiring LVMH IBERIA to adopt measures ensuring compliance with GDPR Article 6(1) within one month. The company must notify the AEPD of adoption of necessary measures. The resolution is final and not subject to administrative appeal.
companyNow: LVMH IBERIA is a large luxury retail subsidiary of LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, one of the world's largest luxury goods conglomerates. The parent company remains a major global business with significant operations in retail and fashion.
dataType: Personal mobile phone number
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 83.5 – Administrative fines for violations of Articles 5–7

companyDescription: School Fitness Holiday & Franchising, S.L. is a Spanish fitness company founded in 2001 that operates Holiday Gym franchise locations. The company provides gym memberships and fitness services including personal training and group classes.
companyLongDescription: School Fitness Holiday & Franchising, S.L. is a Spanish fitness company founded in 2001 that operates Holiday Gym franchise locations. The company provides gym memberships and fitness services including personal training and group classes.
caseDescription: School Fitness grabbed and published client images and videos without valid consent, failed to establish proper data processor contracts, and indefinitely retained promotional footage. Clients explicitly objected but the company ignored their refusals and continued recording.
violationSummary: Images of clients were published on social media platforms (Instagram, Facebook) without valid consent, exposing their likenesses to public access. The company's vague contractual consent and bundled acceptance mechanism rendered their consent invalid under GDPR Article 7.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: School Fitness recorded and published gym clients' images and videos in fitness classes on social media for promotional purposes without obtaining their specific, informed consent beforehand.
whyTheyWereWrong: Gym members had their likenesses captured and distributed online without clear knowledge or agreement; some clients explicitly objected but were ignored.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clients consent to image recording and publication by signing the membership contract.
claimsVsReality.reality: Contracts contained vague, bundled language about 'image use' that did not clearly notify clients of filming during classes or social media publication; many clients explicitly objected and were ignored.

claimsVsReality.claim: Verbal consent is obtained at the start of sessions to be recorded.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented evidence of systematic verbal consent collection; inspectors found no audio recordings or sign-in sheets proving verbal consent was requested or granted.

claimsVsReality.claim: No images of non-consenting clients are stored or published.
claimsVsReality.reality: Inspectors discovered images sent to marketing department on 25 May 2023 with no documented consent; clients who objected in writing were still captured in background of group fitness videos.

claimsVsReality.claim: School Fitness and Holiday Fit are joint controllers (co-responsible) for image handling.
claimsVsReality.reality: In practice, School Fitness (the parent company) determined when, how, and why images were captured and published via its centralized marketing department; Holiday Fit was subordinate, acting as a processor, but no processor agreement existed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 7 requires that consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous.
regulatoryFindings.description: School Fitness embedded image recording consent into bundled contract terms, making it non-specific and coercive; clients could not opt out without rejecting the entire gym membership.
violations: School Fitness embedded image recording consent into bundled contract terms, making it non-specific and coercive; clients could not opt out without rejecting the entire gym membership.
Consent form provided during online registration did not clearly separate image/video recording consent from general service terms.
No separate, granular consent was obtained in writing before recording sessions; reliance on verbal consent at class start was unreliable and undocumented.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) requires personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: School Fitness stated in its Records of Processing that images would be retained 'indefinitely' rather than for the specific promotional period necessary.
violations: School Fitness stated in its Records of Processing that images would be retained 'indefinitely' rather than for the specific promotional period necessary.
Indefinite retention breached the storage limitation principle and exceeded the original purpose of promotional marketing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28 requires a written contract between processor and controller, specifying obligations including data security, sub-processing restrictions, and deletion protocols.
regulatoryFindings.description: Holiday Fit Tres Cantos (the gym operator) and School Fitness (the corporate entity) had no formal processor agreement in place specifying terms for image handling, retention, and deletion.
violations: Holiday Fit Tres Cantos (the gym operator) and School Fitness (the corporate entity) had no formal processor agreement in place specifying terms for image handling, retention, and deletion.
The roles of controller vs. processor were misaligned in documentation, creating ambiguity over who was responsible for data protection compliance.

outcome: School Fitness voluntarily recognized responsibility and paid €21,600 (40% reduction applied for early payment and responsibility admission). AEPD ordered the company to: (1) ensure image recording/publication is conducted with valid consent and suppress non-consensual content within 6 months; (2) adopt measures to comply with Article 5(1)(e) storage limits; (3) execute a formal processor contract with Holiday Fit Tres Cantos. Procedure terminated upon payment.
companyNow: School Fitness Holiday & Franchising operates a network of gyms under the Holiday Gym brand across Spain. The company has acknowledged the data protection violations and implemented corrective measures as mandated.
dataType: Biometric data (fingerprints), images, video recordings, personal contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 28 — processor obligations and contract requirements

companyDescription: South Wales Police is a statutory police force maintained under the Police Act 1996, covering the South Wales police area in Wales. It serves a population of 1.3 million (approximately 42% of Wales), employing almost 3,000 police officers and over 2,200 police staff. It covers Cardiff and Swansea, Wales' two largest cities.
companyLongDescription: South Wales Police is a statutory police force maintained under the Police Act 1996, covering the South Wales police area in Wales. It serves a population of 1.3 million (approximately 42% of Wales), employing almost 3,000 police officers and over 2,200 police staff. It covers Cardiff and Swansea, Wales' two largest cities.
caseDescription: South Wales Police failed to respond to subject access requests within statutory timeframes, leaving 352 requests outstanding as of August 2025, with the oldest request nearly two years overdue. The force violated data subjects' right of access under UK GDPR Articles 12, 15 and Data Protection Act 2018 sections 45, by systematically delaying responses due to resource constraints and operational challenges. Data subjects reported distress and detriment from the delays.
violationSummary: SWP systematically excluded data subjects from accessing and learning about their own personal data by failing to respond to access requests within legally required timeframes, effectively denying the right of access itself.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: South Wales Police failed to respond to 352 subject access requests within the one-month statutory deadline, with the oldest request outstanding for approximately 24 months as of August 2025.
whyTheyWereWrong: Data subjects experienced prolonged delays of up to two years waiting for copies of their personal data, causing documented emotional distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: SWP attributed delays to the complexity and volume of SARs involving body-worn video footage and sensitive law enforcement data, and to resource constraints.
claimsVsReality.reality: While complexity is a factor, SWP admitted 'continuously infringing' obligations 'for a while' and had received a clear recommendation in August 2019 (over six years prior) to ensure adequate resourcing. Delays persisted despite this prior notice, with 352 requests still outstanding as of August 2025, including one nearly two years old.

claimsVsReality.claim: SWP stated it was implementing recovery and action plans focused on resource recruitment, technology improvements, and demand prioritisation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commissioner noted these plans as 'reassuring' but expressed concern that SWP continued 'large-scale non-compliance' despite similar recommendations issued six years earlier, indicating a pattern of failure to remediate.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on action taken on a data subject access request without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months only where necessary considering complexity and number of requests.
regulatoryFindings.description: SWP failed to respond to 352 outstanding SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe; oldest request was nearly two years overdue as of March 2025
violations: SWP failed to respond to 352 outstanding SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe; oldest request was nearly two years overdue as of March 2025
SWP did not inform data subjects of any extension within one month, nor provided reasons for delays
SWP's compliance rate was 29% (201 of 689 requests) for the period April 2023–March 2024

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(1) entitles data subjects to confirmation whether personal data is being processed and to access the data and specified information (purposes, categories, recipients, retention period, rights, complaint mechanism, data source, automated decision-making logic).
regulatoryFindings.description: SWP failed to provide data subjects with confirmation or access to their personal data within the statutory timeframe
violations: SWP failed to provide data subjects with confirmation or access to their personal data within the statutory timeframe
SWP failed to provide the mandatory information set out in Article 15(1)(a)–(h) to waiting data subjects

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(3) requires controllers to provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing in a commonly used electronic form when requested electronically.
regulatoryFindings.description: SWP failed to provide copies of personal data to 352 data subjects within the statutory deadline
violations: SWP failed to provide copies of personal data to 352 data subjects within the statutory deadline

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018 Section 45 places equivalent obligations on competent authorities (police forces) processing personal data for law enforcement purposes to facilitate data subjects' right of access within one month (s.54).
regulatoryFindings.description: SWP failed to provide confirmation or access to personal data for law enforcement processing within one month
violations: SWP failed to provide confirmation or access to personal data for law enforcement processing within one month
SWP failed to provide mandatory information set out in s.45(2)(a)–(g) to data subjects making requests

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice on 9 October 2025 requiring SWP to: (1) By 1 June 2026, provide 352 data subjects with confirmation and copies of their personal data plus mandatory information under Article 15(1)(a)–(h) [UK GDPR] or s.45(2) [DPA 2018]; (2) By 1 June 2026, fully implement outstanding recommendations from SWP's Action Plan (dated 5 March 2025) addressing resource, technology, and demand prioritisation; (3) By 24 April 2026, implement changes to internal systems, procedures, and policies to ensure future SARs are identified and complied with within statutory timeframes. SWP was granted a six-month extension (beyond the PEN proposal) to Terms 1 and 2 in recognition of internal resource challenges and detailed remediation plans. SWP may appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 calendar days. The notice is not suspended pending appeal determination.
companyNow: South Wales Police continues to operate as the largest police force in Wales, serving 1.3 million people. As of August 2025, the force's SAR backlog had reduced to 352 outstanding requests (from 376 in June 2024), indicating ongoing remediation efforts, though systematic delays persist.
dataType: Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes; sensitive information including body-worn video footage

company: FUNDACIÓ PRIVADA DE SERVEIS PER ALS USUARIS DEL HABITATGE SOCIAL DE CATALUNYA
companyDescription: FUNDACIÓ PRIVADA DE SERVEIS PER ALS USUARIS DEL HABITATGE SOCIAL DE CATALUNYA is a private foundation established in 2001 providing social housing services and property administration in Catalonia, Spain. With annual turnover of approximately €1.96 million as of 2022, it manages residential communities.
companyLongDescription: FUNDACIÓ PRIVADA DE SERVEIS PER ALS USUARIS DEL HABITATGE SOCIAL DE CATALUNYA is a private foundation established in 2001 providing social housing services and property administration in Catalonia, Spain. With annual turnover of approximately €1.96 million as of 2022, it manages residential communities.
caseDescription: A property management foundation unlawfully added a resident's personal banking details to a water utility domiciliation order without authorization. The resident's account was then charged for community water bills, constituting unauthorized personal data processing and financial harm. The foundation paid €4,800 in settlement after recognizing responsibility.
violationSummary: Personal data (banking details, contact information) were collected for property administration purposes but repurposed without consent to charge the individual for community expenses, exemplifying unlawful secondary use and unauthorized processing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The property manager changed the water utility's payment domiciliation from the community account to the resident's personal bank account without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: The resident suffered financial harm and loss of control over their personal bank account when unauthorized water bill charges were debited without consent or legal basis.

claimsVsReality.claim: The foundation acted as a legitimate property administrator with proper authorization to manage the water utility billing domiciliation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The foundation had ceased its contractual relationship with the community by January 2024 but continued to use resident personal data to redirect billing without consent, suggesting intentional misuse of information accessed during its administration role.

claimsVsReality.claim: The water company required the change to the domiciliation account.
claimsVsReality.reality: The water company proceeded with the account change without requesting proof of account ownership or verification that the account holder authorized the change, and the foundation provided no such authorization from the resident.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1) requires that processing of personal data shall be lawful only if it complies with at least one lawful basis: consent, contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests with appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: The foundation processed the resident's personal banking data and contact details without any lawful basis under Art. 6(1), incorporating them into a domiciliation order without express authorization.
violations: The foundation processed the resident's personal banking data and contact details without any lawful basis under Art. 6(1), incorporating them into a domiciliation order without express authorization.
No lawful basis existed: the resident did not consent; processing was not necessary for any contract; no legal obligation required it; vital interests or public task did not apply.
The foundation intentionally exploited prior access to personal data from its administrative role to redirect charges after ceasing its contractual relationship with the community.

outcome: On 10 March 2025, the AEPD initiated a sanctioning procedure against the foundation for violation of GDPR Art. 6(1). On 28 March 2025, the foundation recognized responsibility and paid €4,800 (original sanction €8,000 with 40% cumulative reduction for early admission of guilt and voluntary payment). The procedure was terminated under Art. 85 LPACAP. The foundation is ordered to implement measures within 2 months to ensure compliance with Art. 6(1) requirements, including establishment of lawful bases for any data processing. The resolution is final and executable upon notification.
companyNow: The foundation continues operating as a social housing service provider in Catalonia. The case is now closed following voluntary payment and recognition of responsibility.
dataType: Name, surname, DNI, postal address, telephone number, email, bank account details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle

companyDescription: Jam City is a mobile gaming developer that creates free-to-play games based on licensed intellectual properties from Disney and Warner Bros., generating revenue through in-app advertising and in-game purchases.
companyLongDescription: Jam City is a mobile gaming developer that creates free-to-play games based on licensed intellectual properties from Disney and Warner Bros., generating revenue through in-app advertising and in-game purchases.
caseDescription: Jam City created free-to-play mobile games that collected personal information and sold it to third parties for targeted advertising without providing CCPA-compliant opt-out mechanisms. The company failed to implement in-app opt-out links and improperly handled minors' data, selling information of children ages 13-16 without affirmative consent required by law.
violationSummary: Jam City disclosed consumer personal information to third-party advertisers without compliant opt-out mechanisms and without affirmative consent from minors, enabling cross-context behavioral targeting.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Jam City collected device identifiers, IP addresses, and gameplay behavior from users, then sold this data to third-party advertisers for targeted ads without providing CCPA-compliant opt-out.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of California consumers had their personal data sold to advertisers without any way to opt out within the apps where Jam City collected it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jam City's privacy policy stated consumers could opt out by emailing cepaoptout@jamcity.com under a 'Cookies and Interest Based Advertising' section.
claimsVsReality.reality: This email-based method did not meet CCPA requirements, which mandate a link within apps and websites reflecting how the business interacts with the consumer.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jam City provided child versions of age-gated games for users who submitted an age below 16, preventing data sharing for minors.
claimsVsReality.reality: Six games failed to enforce age gates properly, allowing consumers between 13-16 to access full versions with data-sharing functionality without affirmative parental or minor consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.120(a)-(b) requires businesses to provide a clear, conspicuous, and easy-to-use opt-out mechanism reflecting how the business interacts with the consumer; for mobile app developers, this means in-app opt-out links.
regulatoryFindings.description: Jam City did not provide CCPA-compliant opt-out links in 20 of 21 apps despite primarily operating through mobile applications.
violations: Jam City did not provide CCPA-compliant opt-out links in 20 of 21 apps despite primarily operating through mobile applications.
Only one app provided a 'Data Privacy' control that did not reference CCPA and was unclear about whether enabling it would stop data sales.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.135(a)(c)(2) prohibits businesses from selling or sharing personal information of consumers known to be less than 16 years of age without first obtaining opt-in consent from the consumer or parent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Jam City failed to maintain proper age gates for six games, allowing consumers between ages 13-16 to use full versions that shared data with third parties without affirmative consent.
violations: Jam City failed to maintain proper age gates for six games, allowing consumers between ages 13-16 to use full versions that shared data with third parties without affirmative consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent acts or practices in commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Jam City's failure to provide compliant opt-out mechanisms and improper handling of minors' data constitutes unfair competition and deceptive practices affecting California consumers.
violations: Jam City's failure to provide compliant opt-out mechanisms and improper handling of minors' data constitutes unfair competition and deceptive practices affecting California consumers.

outcome: The Attorney General filed a Complaint for Injunction, Civil Penalties, and Other Equitable Relief on November 21, 2025, seeking injunctive orders to prevent further CCPA violations; civil penalties of $2,663 per violation or $7,988 per intentional violation involving minors' data; restoration of improperly acquired money; disgorged revenue; and attorney fees. Jam City is required to implement CCPA-compliant opt-out mechanisms within all apps and establish proper age verification procedures.
companyNow: Jam City remains a Delaware corporation headquartered in Culver City, California, operating mobile gaming apps as of the complaint filing date in November 2025. The company faces ongoing injunctive oversight and remediation obligations.
dataType: Device identifiers, IP addresses, in-app purchase history, gameplay behavior, age data
legalBasisViolated: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 et seq.

company: NN Ελληνική Μονοπρόσωπη Ανώνυμη Ασφαλιστική Εταιρία Ζωής (NN Hellas)
companyDescription: NN Hellas (successor to METLIFE AEAZ) is a Greek life insurance company that offers health and dental care coverage through provider networks. It operates dental care programs via partner call centers and provider networks.
companyLongDescription: NN Hellas (successor to METLIFE AEAZ) is a Greek life insurance company that offers health and dental care coverage through provider networks. It operates dental care programs via partner call centers and provider networks.
caseDescription: NN Hellas failed to provide a policyholder access to recorded telephone calls he made to a dental care call center as required under GDPR Article 15. The company misrepresented its role as data controller and did not respond to multiple requests over 6+ months. Additionally, MEDIADENT refused to cooperate with the data protection authority's investigation.
violationSummary: The company failed to fulfill data subject's right of access (Art. 15 GDPR) and did not provide information about the action taken in response to the request within the prescribed deadline (Art. 12(3) GDPR). This constitutes a failure to maintain transparency and protect the data subject's ability to exercise their rights.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: NN Hellas failed to provide recorded telephone calls to an insured customer despite repeated requests from December 2023 through January 2024.
whyTheyWereWrong: The insured customer needed these recordings as critical evidence to support a legal dispute but was denied access for over a month.

claimsVsReality.claim: NN Hellas stated that MEDIADENT alone (as a processor) controlled the recorded telephone calls and that NN Hellas had no access to them.
claimsVsReality.reality: The 30/10/2015 contract between METLIFE and MEDIADENT explicitly shows that METLIFE (NN Hellas' predecessor) specified the purpose of recording ('for customer service and quality assurance'), required technical specifications (Art. 10 xii), required monthly reporting of calls, and retained ownership of all call archives. This made NN Hellas the controller, not merely a third party.

claimsVsReality.claim: The call center number 2315555535 was identified as belonging to 'MEDIADENT' and the complainant knew the service came from a third-party provider.
claimsVsReality.reality: NN Hellas itself advertised this number as the 'Dental Care of NN Hellas' coordinating center on its website and to policyholders. The recorded greeting stated 'Dental Care of NN Hellas,' deliberately obscuring MEDIADENT's role from policyholders.

claimsVsReality.claim: NN Hellas claimed it had already repeatedly answered the complainant's allegations and requests.
claimsVsReality.reality: NN Hellas only sent two emails (11/01/2024 and 23/01/2024) telling the complainant to contact MEDIADENT directly, without providing the requested data or substantively addressing the access right.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data concerning them is being processed, and if so, the right of access to such data.
regulatoryFindings.description: NN Hellas did not respond to the complainant's multiple access requests (December 2023, repeated through January 2024) for recorded telephone calls made to the dental care call center.
violations: NN Hellas did not respond to the complainant's multiple access requests (December 2023, repeated through January 2024) for recorded telephone calls made to the dental care call center.
The company failed to provide the requested data within one month as required by Art. 12(3) GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(7) defines a controller as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing. Where purposes and means are determined by EU or national law, the controller or specific criteria for its designation may be established by such law.
regulatoryFindings.description: NN Hellas (as successor to METLIFE under merger) contractually specified that the call center would record calls for quality assurance and customer service purposes, and set performance requirements (Art. 10 xii of the MEDIADENT contract).
violations: NN Hellas (as successor to METLIFE under merger) contractually specified that the call center would record calls for quality assurance and customer service purposes, and set performance requirements (Art. 10 xii of the MEDIADENT contract).
NN Hellas presented the service as 'Dental Care of NN Hellas' to policyholders, creating the appearance that NN Hellas, not MEDIADENT, was the service provider.
The company claimed MEDIADENT alone was the controller to avoid fulfilling the data subject's access request, contradicting its own contractual control over purposes and means.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires controllers and processors, and representatives where applicable, to cooperate with supervisory authorities on request.
regulatoryFindings.description: MEDIADENT failed to respond to two Authority requests for clarifications (Γ/ΕΞΕ/1307/02-05-2024 and Γ/ΕΞΕ/2577/23-09-2024) and did not appear at the mandatory hearing on 21-5-2025.
violations: MEDIADENT failed to respond to two Authority requests for clarifications (Γ/ΕΞΕ/1307/02-05-2024 and Γ/ΕΞΕ/2577/23-09-2024) and did not appear at the mandatory hearing on 21-5-2025.
This non-cooperation obstructed the Authority's investigation into the access right violation.

outcome: NN Hellas was ordered to provide the complainant with the recorded telephone calls within 10 days and was fined €20,000 for violation of GDPR Art. 15. MEDIADENT was fined €2,000 for violation of GDPR Art. 31 (failure to cooperate with the Authority). NN Hellas must report compliance to the Authority.
companyNow: NN Hellas remains a major insurance provider in Greece and part of NN Group. The company must now provide recorded calls to the data subject and faces ongoing Authority scrutiny for data protection compliance.
dataType: Audio recordings of telephone conversations, personal identification data (name, telephone number), health data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12(3) – Timely response to data subject requests
GDPR Art. 31 – Cooperation with supervisory authority
GDPR Art. 4(7) – Definition of controller (determination of purposes and means)

company: Φ (newspaper/publishing company, operating as individual enterprise)
companyDescription: A Greek newspaper publisher operating as a sole proprietorship (individual enterprise) that maintained a digital platform for article publication and reader access. The company employed the complainant under an indefinite-term employment contract.
companyLongDescription: A Greek newspaper publisher operating as a sole proprietorship (individual enterprise) that maintained a digital platform for article publication and reader access. The company employed the complainant under an indefinite-term employment contract.
caseDescription: A newspaper publisher denied an employee's lawful request to access personal data concerning their login records and work activities during employment. The publisher falsely claimed the data belonged to the company rather than the employee, and rejected the access request without valid legal basis under GDPR Article 15.
violationSummary: The respondent denied the data subject's fundamental right to access personal data concerning them (GDPR Art. 15), excluding the individual from knowledge of their own personal information and processing activities.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Denied a former employee's request for access to personal data including login records and activity logs from the newspaper platform where the employee worked.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee was deprived of evidence documenting their work hours and activities on the platform, preventing them from defending themselves against employment disputes.

claimsVsReality.claim: All information concerning the newspaper platform is company property/intellectual property and not personal data of the employee.
claimsVsReality.reality: Login records, access timestamps, and activity logs relating to the individual's work are personal data concerning that individual under GDPR Art. 4(1), not corporate intellectual property.

claimsVsReality.claim: The requested data relates to third parties (readers/customers) and cannot be disclosed due to their privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee requested only their own login and activity records, not content uploaded or reader information. No third-party data limitation applied.

claimsVsReality.claim: The system lacks technical capability to record connection logs.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system manages user credentials, access controls, and password resets—functions requiring logging capability. No credible evidence of technical impossibility was provided.

claimsVsReality.claim: Responding to the access request would impose disproportionate burden and compromise system security.
claimsVsReality.reality: No supporting documentation was provided before the hearing; the claim was advanced only at the final submission stage and contradicted by the publisher's ability to manage user accounts and security measures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee's access request is abusive/malicious because he intends to use the data for litigation about working hours.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Art. 15 imposes no precondition that the data subject justify the purpose of their request. Controllers may not interrogate or refuse access based on the intended use of the information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation and access to personal data concerning them being processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: The publisher refused to provide the employee access to login records and activity timestamps despite them being clearly personal data concerning the individual's work activities.
violations: The publisher refused to provide the employee access to login records and activity timestamps despite them being clearly personal data concerning the individual's work activities.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(3)-(4) requires controllers to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing, free of charge.
regulatoryFindings.description: The publisher denied provision of connection logs and activity records, falsely characterizing them as company property rather than personal data subject to disclosure.
violations: The publisher denied provision of connection logs and activity records, falsely characterizing them as company property rather than personal data subject to disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(5) establishes that controllers bear the burden of proving access requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive; they cannot refuse based on speculative harm or claimed inconvenience.
regulatoryFindings.description: The publisher invoked technical difficulty and security concerns without providing evidence, and belatedly claimed disproportionate burden. The burden to prove such grounds rested with the controller.
violations: The publisher invoked technical difficulty and security concerns without providing evidence, and belatedly claimed disproportionate burden. The burden to prove such grounds rested with the controller.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) (accountability) requires controllers to demonstrate compliance and cannot rely on unsubstantiated technical limitations to deny statutory rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: The publisher claimed the system lacked logging capability without supporting documentation, contradicting its own ability to manage user credentials and access—a failure to design systems compliant with data subject rights.
violations: The publisher claimed the system lacked logging capability without supporting documentation, contradicting its own ability to manage user credentials and access—a failure to design systems compliant with data subject rights.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority ordered the publisher to satisfy the employee's access request within one month, granting the individual their right to obtain personal data concerning their work activities on the platform. A fine of €1,000 was imposed for violation of GDPR Articles 15(1)-(3) and 12(5). The Authority rejected all of the publisher's defenses (company ownership fiction, third-party data conflation, technical inability, security risks, and abusive-exercise claims) as lacking merit or proper substantiation.
dataType: Login/access logs, activity records, employment data, system access timestamps
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 15(3) — Duty to provide copy of personal data
GDPR Art. 12(5) — Obligation to respond to access requests

companyDescription: ADMINISTRACIONES BENIPON, S.L. is a small property management company (€55,289 revenue in 2021) that administers residential communities in Spain, providing services including accounting, data management, and administrative support to property owners' associations.
companyLongDescription: ADMINISTRACIONES BENIPON, S.L. is a small property management company (€55,289 revenue in 2021) that administers residential communities in Spain, providing services including accounting, data management, and administrative support to property owners' associations.
caseDescription: A property management company subcontracted cloud server hosting to a third party without prior authorization from the data controller (property owners' community). The third-party vendor suffered a cyberattack in May 2023 compromising personal data. The company failed to notify both the controller and authorities within required timeframes and lacked a proper data processing contract with the subcontractor.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures by subcontracting data processing without proper authorization, contractual safeguards, or notification protocols, resulting in exposure of personal data to a cyberattack.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ADMINISTRACIONES BENIPON subcontracted personal data processing to a cloud service provider (EMPRESA.1) without obtaining written authorization from the property owners' community.
whyTheyWereWrong: Property owners' personal data including names, addresses, banking details, and contact information were compromised when the unauthorized subcontractor suffered a cyberattack in May 2023,.

claimsVsReality.claim: BENIPON stated the cyberattack was caused by the third-party vendor and was outside its control.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the cyberattack occurred at the vendor, BENIPON was contractually liable for proper subprocessor oversight and bore responsibility for breach notification regardless of fault attribution.

claimsVsReality.claim: BENIPON claimed it informed property owners by placing notices on building walls on 5 May 2023.
claimsVsReality.reality: No formal notification meeting GDPR Art. 33(2) requirements occurred; property owners were only informed via an incidental note in meeting minutes dated 16 June 2023, over 40 days after the breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: BENIPON stated the vendor assured them data would not be disseminated due to economic interest only.
claimsVsReality.reality: This unverified claim provided no basis for omitting mandatory breach notification to the controller; formal notification procedures were legally required regardless of attacker motivation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 28(2) requires that a processor shall not engage another processor without prior specific or general written authorization from the controller, and must inform the controller of any intended changes.
regulatoryFindings.description: BENIPON engaged cloud hosting vendor ***EMPRESA.1 without written authorization from the property owners' community and without a formal subprocessor agreement containing equivalent data protection obligations.
violations: BENIPON engaged cloud hosting vendor ***EMPRESA.1 without written authorization from the property owners' community and without a formal subprocessor agreement containing equivalent data protection obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 28(4) requires that when a processor engages a sub-processor, the same data protection obligations must be imposed via contract, and the processor remains fully liable to the controller for sub-processor performance.
regulatoryFindings.description: No contract was established between BENIPON and the cloud vendor that included mandatory data protection obligations required by Art. 28(3), leaving the subprocessor relationship non-compliant.
violations: No contract was established between BENIPON and the cloud vendor that included mandatory data protection obligations required by Art. 28(3), leaving the subprocessor relationship non-compliant.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33(2) requires processors to notify the controller without undue delay of any personal data breach of which they become aware.
regulatoryFindings.description: BENIPON learned of the cyberattack on 4 May 2023 but did not formally notify the property owners' community (the controller) through official channels; notification occurred only incidentally on 16 June 2023 via meeting minutes, over 40 days late.
violations: BENIPON learned of the cyberattack on 4 May 2023 but did not formally notify the property owners' community (the controller) through official channels; notification occurred only incidentally on 16 June 2023 via meeting minutes, over 40 days late.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed total fines of €1,100 across three articles. BENIPON was ordered to: (1) provide written authorization and execute a compliant data processing agreement with any subprocessor within 6 months; and (2) provide evidence of notification to the property owners' community regarding the breach in compliance with GDPR Art. 33(2). Failure to comply may trigger additional enforcement. The resolution is final upon exhaustion of administrative remedies.
companyNow: BENIPON remains in operation as a property management firm. The enforcement decision is final pending potential judicial review.
dataType: Names, addresses, contact information, email addresses, financial/banking data of property owners

company: RED ESPAÑOLA DE IDENTIFICACIÓN DE ANIMALES DE COMPAÑÍA (REIAC)
companyDescription: RED ESPAÑOLA DE IDENTIFICACIÓN DE ANIMALES DE COMPAÑÍA (REIAC) is a Spanish national registry for pet identification and tracking (NIF: G60616521). It maintains personal data of pet owners linked to animal identification records.
companyLongDescription: RED ESPAÑOLA DE IDENTIFICACIÓN DE ANIMALES DE COMPAÑÍA (REIAC) is a Spanish national registry for pet identification and tracking (NIF: G60616521). It maintains personal data of pet owners linked to animal identification records.
caseDescription: REIAC failed to respond to four separate information requests from Spain's Data Protection Authority (AEPD) during a regulatory investigation, obstructing the authority's investigative powers under GDPR Article 58.1. The company ignored lawful requests for documentation despite multiple notification attempts via postal and electronic means. REIAC subsequently recognized responsibility and paid a reduced penalty of €360.
violationSummary: The violation is fundamentally about obstruction of regulatory oversight and failure to facilitate investigation — a procedural breach that prevents proper safeguarding of personal data. This fits 'Insecurity' as it demonstrates lack of organizational accountability and transparency mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: REIAC failed to provide required information and documentation in response to four separate information requests from Spain's data protection authority during an investigation into potential.
whyTheyWereWrong: REIAC's non-cooperation prevented the regulator from investigating whether pet owner personal data was being improperly handled.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.1(a) grants each supervisory authority the power to order data controllers and processors to provide any information required to perform its functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: REIAC failed to comply with four separate information requests issued by AEPD under Article 58.1(a), obstructing the regulator's investigative powers and preventing the authority from properly investigating alleged data protection violations.
violations: REIAC failed to comply with four separate information requests issued by AEPD under Article 58.1(a), obstructing the regulator's investigative powers and preventing the authority from properly investigating alleged data protection violations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(e) classifies as a very serious infraction the failure to facilitate access in breach of Article 58, and permits fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: REIAC's refusal to provide required information constitutes a violation of Article 58.1(a), classified as a very serious infraction under Article 83.5(e), warranting administrative penalties.
violations: REIAC's refusal to provide required information constitutes a violation of Article 58.1(a), classified as a very serious infraction under Article 83.5(e), warranting administrative penalties.

outcome: REIAC acknowledged responsibility and voluntarily paid €360 (40% reduction from base fine of €600: 20% for recognition of responsibility + 20% for voluntary payment under LPACAP Article 85). The procedure was terminated on 2025-05-14. REIAC remains obligated to provide the required information within ten business days from the resolution becoming final and enforceable. The company waived all administrative remedies as a condition of the penalty reduction.
companyNow: Unknown. REIAC is a Spanish registry organization for pet identification (microchip/ID services). Current operational status not documented in this enforcement resolution.
dataType: Personal data of pet owners (names, addresses, contact information); animal identification data

company: UNIÓN DE CRÉDITO PARA LA FINANCIACIÓN MOBILIARIA E INMOBILIARIA EFC (CREDIFIMO)
companyDescription: CREDIFIMO is a Spanish credit union (Unión de Crédito para la Financiación Mobiliaria e Inmobiliaria) providing mortgage and personal loan financing services. The company was founded in 1971 and maintains ongoing financial operations.
companyLongDescription: CREDIFIMO is a Spanish credit union (Unión de Crédito para la Financiación Mobiliaria e Inmobiliaria) providing mortgage and personal loan financing services. The company was founded in 1971 and maintains ongoing financial operations.
caseDescription: CREDIFIMO included a guarantor's personal data in the ASNEF credit reporting registry without proper legal basis or prior notice. A court had already ruled that the underlying debt was invalid and ordered dismissal of the lender's counterclaim. The data subject was included despite no legitimate requirement to pay and never having been formally notified of the possibility of registry inclusion.
violationSummary: CREDIFIMO processed personal data (credit information) without any valid legal basis under GDPR Article 6(1). The company failed to meet the specific procedural requirements under Spanish LOPDGDD Article 20 for lawful inclusion in credit reporting systems, including mandatory prior notice and proof of legitimate debt.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CREDIFIMO included a guarantor's personal data in the ASNEF credit registry without proving it had sent required payment notices or informed them of the inclusion risk beforehand.
whyTheyWereWrong: The guarantor's creditworthiness was harmed when their data remained in the delinquent registry for years despite a court ruling that the underlying loan payments were current.

claimsVsReality.claim: CREDIFIMO claimed it had informed the guarantor of possible inclusion in ASNEF at the time of the payment demand (allegedly sent in 2009)
claimsVsReality.reality: CREDIFIMO could not produce the payment demand letters despite repeated requests from the AEPD. The company acknowledged it had outsourced communications and could not retrieve documents from a system abandoned in 2017, contradicting its assertion of prior notice.

claimsVsReality.claim: CREDIFIMO asserted the debt was unpaid since September 2009 and was in default when reported to ASNEF
claimsVsReality.reality: A court judgment from May 2023 ruled the underlying mortgage debt was current and valid, ordering dismissal of CREDIFIMO's counterclaim for unpaid amounts. The guarantor had provided proof of payments made by the loan principals.

claimsVsReality.claim: CREDIFIMO claimed the data subject did not appear in ASNEF registries from 2024 onwards
claimsVsReality.reality: The data remained registered until removal was ordered as a remedial measure in this enforcement action. The company's statement was irrelevant because the unlawful processing had already occurred and caused harm.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the specified conditions applies (consent, contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests not overridden by data subject rights).
regulatoryFindings.description: CREDIFIMO processed the complainant's personal data by reporting them to ASNEF without demonstrating any lawful basis under Article 6(1). The company relied solely on claiming the debt was unpaid but could not prove compliance with the mandatory procedural requirements, leaving no valid legal ground for the processing.
violations: CREDIFIMO processed the complainant's personal data by reporting them to ASNEF without demonstrating any lawful basis under Article 6(1). The company relied solely on claiming the debt was unpaid but could not prove compliance with the mandatory procedural requirements, leaving no valid legal ground for the processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 20(1) establishes that processing of personal data relating to non-payment in credit systems shall be presumed lawful only when the creditor has: (a) provided the data; (b) the debt is certain, due and enforceable and not subject to administrative/judicial challenge; and (c) informed the affected party at contract or payment demand time about the possibility of inclusion, with notice of which systems participate.
regulatoryFindings.description: CREDIFIMO failed to prove it had informed the complainant about the possibility of registry inclusion. The company could not produce the pre-inclusion payment demand letters despite being required to do so. A court judgment showed the underlying debt was disputed and ultimately ruled invalid, further undermining the lawfulness of the initial inclusion.
violations: CREDIFIMO failed to prove it had informed the complainant about the possibility of registry inclusion. The company could not produce the pre-inclusion payment demand letters despite being required to do so. A court judgment showed the underlying debt was disputed and ultimately ruled invalid, further undermining the lawfulness of the initial inclusion.

outcome: CREDIFIMO recognized responsibility and paid €120,000 voluntarily (€200,000 initial fine reduced by 40% for early recognition and payment). The company was ordered to remove the complainant's data from the ASNEF credit registry within one month of the resolution becoming final and executable. The procedure was terminated under Article 85 of the Administrative Procedure Act. The company must submit evidence of compliance with the data removal order to the AEPD.
companyNow: CREDIFIMO is a Spanish financial entity (Unión de Crédito) established in 1971, with annual turnover of approximately €22.2 million (2023). The company continues financial services operations after recognition of this data protection violation.
dataType: Personal identification data (name, surname, postal address), financial/credit data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
LOPDGDD Art. 20 – Credit information systems requirements

companyDescription: SPRINTER MEGACENTROS DEL DEPORTE, S.L. is a Spanish retail company specialising in sports equipment and clothing, operating both physical stores and e-commerce across multiple European countries. It is a subsidiary of the JD Sports group.
companyLongDescription: SPRINTER MEGACENTROS DEL DEPORTE, S.L. is a Spanish retail company specialising in sports equipment and clothing, operating both physical stores and e-commerce across multiple European countries. It is a subsidiary of the JD Sports group.
caseDescription: SPRINTER suffered a ransomware breach in October 2023 affecting 6.38 million customers and employees across multiple EU countries. The company failed to maintain adequate technical and organisational security measures, and delayed notification to affected individuals by one month. SPRINTER admitted responsibility and paid €1.56 million in fines.
companyWorth: €662.2 million (2024 annual revenue; part of larger JD Sports group)
violationSummary: The breach exposed millions of personal records (names, IDs, contact details, health data, financial information) to unauthorised third parties, with delayed notification preventing individuals from taking timely protective action.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: SPRINTER failed to implement adequate security measures, allowing attackers to access its systems, exfiltrate personal data of 6.38 million customers and employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of customers and employees across five European countries had their names, ID numbers, addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, photos, health information.

claimsVsReality.claim: SPRINTER had 'a continuous improvement process for information security management' since 2018 and maintained security protocols.
claimsVsReality.reality: Critical security gaps existed: no multi-factor authentication for key systems, inadequate monitoring of alert systems, poor credential management, and insufficient network segmentation—all identified post-breach as necessary improvements.

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident 'could not have been avoided' despite being external in origin.
claimsVsReality.reality: SPRINTER's own breach notification forms (Oct 31, 2023) admitted the breach 'could have been prevented with additional security measures' and was caused by 'security control failures.' The company later contradicted this claim in Nov 30 notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data availability was unaffected due to backup redundancy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Initial Oct/Nov 2023 notifications stated availability was 'still not recovered,' contradicting later claims of unaffected availability via backup systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires data controllers to ensure integrity and confidentiality of personal data through appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: SPRINTER maintained inadequate security controls prior to the breach, failing to implement multi-factor authentication, proper network segmentation, and monitoring despite identifying such deficiencies in its own risk assessments.
violations: SPRINTER maintained inadequate security controls prior to the breach, failing to implement multi-factor authentication, proper network segmentation, and monitoring despite identifying such deficiencies in its own risk assessments.
Security measures in place were insufficient to prevent initial credential compromise, lateral movement within systems, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment affecting millions of records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 34 requires controllers to communicate personal data breaches to affected individuals without undue delay in clear, simple language, describing the nature of the breach and providing information on measures adopted to remedy the breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: SPRINTER delayed breach notification by one month (Oct 24 detection to Nov 27–28 notification), violating the 'without undue delay' requirement.
violations: SPRINTER delayed breach notification by one month (Oct 24 detection to Nov 27–28 notification), violating the 'without undue delay' requirement.
Initial notification on Nov 28 was incomplete, omitting specific details of security measures implemented to address the breach, contrary to Art. 34(2) requirements.

outcome: SPRINTER recognised responsibility and paid €1.56 million (after 40% reduction for early payment and admission). Agreed to implement mandatory security measures within 6 months, including enhanced technical and organisational controls. Procedure closed via settlement on Nov 5, 2025. Fine subject to publication in Spanish Official Gazette (BOE). No appeal filed; resolution final and immediately executable.
companyNow: SPRINTER (part of JD Sports group) continues operations as a sportswear retailer with physical and online presence across Europe. Company has since implemented post-incident security improvements and established enhanced breach management procedures.
dataType: Customer and employee personal data: name, surname, date of birth, national ID (DNI/NIF), address, telephone, email, photos/videos, health data (disability status for employees), financial data (payroll, bank account numbers)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality (inadequate security measures)
GDPR Art. 32 – Security of Processing (failure to implement appropriate technical/organisational measures)
GDPR Art. 34 – Communication of a Personal Data Breach to Data Subjects (untimely and incomplete notification)

companyDescription: Rising Sun Car Rental S.L. (NIF B09973165) is a Spanish car rental company operating from offices in Spain. The company had contracted with a security company (***EMPRESA.1) to maintain video surveillance systems, including two cameras—one exterior and one interior.
companyLongDescription: Rising Sun Car Rental S.L. (NIF B09973165) is a Spanish car rental company operating from offices in Spain. The company had contracted with a security company (***EMPRESA.1) to maintain video surveillance systems, including two cameras—one exterior and one interior.
caseDescription: Rising Sun Car Rental installed surveillance cameras with audio recording capabilities in its offices and employee break areas without proper legal justification, proportionality assessment, or worker consent. The company recorded conversations between employees and clients, and captured audio in rest areas designated for employee breaks, violating GDPR principles on data minimization and transparency requirements. The company also failed to provide compliant privacy notices on external signage identifying the data controller and explaining data subject rights.
violationSummary: The cameras captured audio of private conversations and rest areas, exceeding the scope of legitimate security surveillance. This constitutes unlawful surveillance affecting both employees and customers without adequate prior notice or justification.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Rising Sun Car Rental installed video surveillance cameras with audio recording capability in office and employee break areas, capturing conversations between workers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees and customers had their private conversations recorded without consent, exposing them to unauthorized surveillance that violated their fundamental right to privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated the cameras were necessary to preserve security of installations, goods, workers, and clients, and to enable labor control.
claimsVsReality.reality: The audio recording capability was disproportionate to these stated goals; exterior camera captured only parking area; interior camera could record private employee-client conversations; no necessity was demonstrated for audio capture when existing security measures sufficed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed external signage identified the presence of surveillance cameras.
claimsVsReality.reality: The external sign was provided by the security company and failed to identify Rising Sun Car Rental as the data controller or explain how affected persons could exercise their GDPR rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted cameras did not capture rest, break, or employee changing areas.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company acknowledged in its own RAT (Record of Activities of Treatment) that cameras captured audio in exterior rest and break areas designated for worker leisure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing (data minimization principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Rising Sun Car Rental captured audio recordings in office areas where employees and clients conducted private conversations without necessity or proportionality, exceeding the scope of legitimate security purposes.
violations: Rising Sun Car Rental captured audio recordings in office areas where employees and clients conducted private conversations without necessity or proportionality, exceeding the scope of legitimate security purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from a data subject, the controller must provide comprehensive information about identity, contact details, processing purposes, legal basis, data retention, and data subject rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Rising Sun Car Rental's external privacy notice was displayed on a sign provided by the security company, failing to identify the actual data controller (Rising Sun Car Rental), explain how to exercise rights, or provide required transparency information.
violations: Rising Sun Car Rental's external privacy notice was displayed on a sign provided by the security company, failing to identify the actual data controller (Rising Sun Car Rental), explain how to exercise rights, or provide required transparency information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Spanish Organic Law 3/2018 Article 89(2) absolutely prohibits installation of audio recording systems or video surveillance in places designated for worker rest, leisure, changing rooms, bathrooms, and similar spaces.
regulatoryFindings.description: Rising Sun Car Rental installed cameras capable of recording audio in employee break and rest areas, directly violating the categorical prohibition.
violations: Rising Sun Car Rental installed cameras capable of recording audio in employee break and rest areas, directly violating the categorical prohibition.

regulatoryFindings.act: Spanish Organic Law 3/2018 Article 89(3) permits audio recording in work areas only when substantial safety risks justify it, and only if proportionality, minimum intervention, and statutory protections are observed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Rising Sun Car Rental failed to demonstrate proportionality or necessity for capturing audio of employee-customer conversations; existing security systems made audio recording unnecessary and excessive.
violations: Rising Sun Car Rental failed to demonstrate proportionality or necessity for capturing audio of employee-customer conversations; existing security systems made audio recording unnecessary and excessive.

outcome: Rising Sun Car Rental voluntarily recognized responsibility and paid €3,600 on 9 September 2025, triggering termination of the enforcement procedure under Spanish administrative law (LPACAP Article 85). The payment reflected two cumulative 20% reductions: one for early recognition of responsibility and one for prompt voluntary payment. The company informed the AEPD that it had adopted necessary measures to prevent recurrence of the violations, though this declaration carried no AEPD pronouncement on the adequacy of remedial measures. Final resolution is firm and executively enforceable; the company waived any administrative appeal rights as a condition of the penalty reduction.
companyNow: No current status information provided in the document. The company has acknowledged the violations and implemented unspecified corrective measures.
dataType: Images, audio recordings, employee conversations, customer interactions
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) – Principle of data minimization
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided when data obtained from data subject
GDPR Art. 22.4 LOPDGDD – Duty to provide visible notice of processing
Spanish Organic Law 3/2018 Art. 89(2) – Prohibition of audio recording in rest areas
Spanish Organic Law 3/2018 Art. 89(3) – Proportionality requirement for audio recording

companyDescription: ENDESA ENERGIA, S.A.U. is a Spanish electricity and gas commercializer and subsidiary of the ENDESA Group, founded in 1998. It is one of the leading energy suppliers in Spain, serving millions of residential and commercial customers.
companyLongDescription: ENDESA ENERGIA, S.A.U. is a Spanish electricity and gas commercializer and subsidiary of the ENDESA Group, founded in 1998. It is one of the leading energy suppliers in Spain, serving millions of residential and commercial customers.
caseDescription: ENDESA ENERGIA erroneously associated the utility supply codes (CUPS) of the complainant with a third party during a supplier change process, causing the complainant's electricity and gas to be disconnected without authorization. The company failed to verify the relationship between the contractor and the supply point, violating the data accuracy principle. The regulatory authority found negligent handling of personal data in a high-risk operation involving third-party rights.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate verification procedures (checking CUPS against actual titleholder, requiring prior utility bills or proof of residency) before processing a supply point transfer. This administrative negligence created a data integrity failure affecting a third party's essential services.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ENDESA ENERGIA associated the electricity and gas supply codes (CUPS) belonging to complainant A.A.A.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant lost essential electricity and gas service for two days due to ENDESA's failure to verify the contractor's legitimate ownership of the supply point.

claimsVsReality.claim: The error originated solely from the contractor's DNI, which listed an incomplete address without the portal identifier, and ENDESA acted diligently by verifying the document.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contractor's DNI correctly showed her residential address (floor 4, letter C). ENDESA associated the complainant's CUPS (at a different building with the same street number but different portal letter) to this contract without cross-checking with the distribution company or requiring prior utility bills, creating a false match.

claimsVsReality.claim: The error was 'invincible' due to confusing street numbering in the neighborhood (two buildings with similar numbers differing only by a letter).
claimsVsReality.reality: Such situations are routine in urban areas and do not eliminate the controller's duty of care. The CUPS system is specifically designed to avoid address-only confusion. ENDESA had technical means (distribution company verification, prior bill requests) but chose not to deploy them.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant was alerted by SMS of the supply change and failed to act promptly, contributing to the error not being corrected.
claimsVsReality.reality: A consumer's delayed reaction does not excuse the controller's failure to verify data accuracy. GDPR places the compliance burden on the data controller, not on data subjects to detect and correct the company's errors.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires that personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; all reasonable measures must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate personal data without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: ENDESA ENERGIA associated the complainant's CUPS codes with a third party's contract in error, treating inaccurate data (wrong address without portal identifier) as valid without verification.
violations: ENDESA ENERGIA associated the complainant's CUPS codes with a third party's contract in error, treating inaccurate data (wrong address without portal identifier) as valid without verification.
Company failed to implement diligence checks to confirm the contractor's legitimate relationship to the supply point before processing a title transfer and commercializer change.
No verification of CUPS ownership, no demand for prior utility bills, no confirmation with the distribution company that the applicant was the actual titleholder.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 imposes on the controller the responsibility to comply with the principles in Article 5 and be capable of demonstrating such compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: ENDESA ENERGIA as the commercial entity (entering commercializer) was the sole point of contact during the supply change and bore responsibility for verifying the validity of the title transfer documentation.
violations: ENDESA ENERGIA as the commercial entity (entering commercializer) was the sole point of contact during the supply change and bore responsibility for verifying the validity of the title transfer documentation.
The company's delegate agent (Salesland S.L.) failed to apply the mandatory 'Change of Titleholder' procedure correctly, omitting the portal identifier without confirming it with the applicant.
Company did not require proof of rightful entitlement ('justo título') to proceed with the transfer, despite sector regulations and the CNE guidance requiring such verification.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72 classifies as 'very serious' infractions the treatment of personal data that violates the principles and guarantees in GDPR Article 5.
regulatoryFindings.description: Error resulted in real harm: temporary loss of essential utility services to the complainant for two days.
violations: Error resulted in real harm: temporary loss of essential utility services to the complainant for two days.
Complainant was forced to escalate to the Xunta de Galicia, which confirmed the unlawful suspension was attributable to ENDESA's errors.
The company's negligence affected both the contractor (who received incorrect CUPS) and the complainant (whose essential rights were interrupted).

outcome: ENDESA ENERGIA S.A.U. was ordered to pay €200,000 and comply within six months by implementing measures to ensure that any future supply point transfers with simultaneous title changes comply with GDPR Article 5(1)(d). The company must demonstrate that new contracting procedures for electricity and gas supply include adequate verification of the contractor's relationship to the supply point. Failure to comply may result in further enforcement action under GDPR Articles 83.5–83.6.
companyNow: ENDESA ENERGIA is a subsidiary of the ENDESA Group, Spain's largest energy company. As of 2022, the group reported revenues of €20.003 billion, operating across Spain and Portugal in electricity and gas supply.
dataType: Name, address, CUPS (utility supply point identifier), contact information

companyDescription: BANCO INVERSIS, S.A. is a Spanish credit institution founded in 2001 that offers technological and service outsourcing solutions to financial entities, insurance companies, and investment product distributors. The company acts as a custodian bank for investment portfolios and provides online banking services to individual and institutional clients.
companyLongDescription: BANCO INVERSIS, S.A. is a Spanish credit institution founded in 2001 that offers technological and service outsourcing solutions to financial entities, insurance companies, and investment product distributors. The company acts as a custodian bank for investment portfolios and provides online banking services to individual and institutional clients.
caseDescription: BANCO INVERSIS suffered a data breach affecting approximately 2 million individuals' personal data when an attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to customer data via the bank's web service. The breach resulted from inadequate security measures, including a weak authentication exemption that failed to require multi-factor authentication for 90 days after initial login, allowing attackers to exploit a vulnerable parameter in the web service to access data beyond the user's authorized scope.
violationSummary: The breach resulted from inadequate technical and organizational security measures violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f), which requires integrity and confidentiality protections. The weak password policies, overly permissive authentication exemption, and vulnerable web service parameter represent systemic security failures that enabled unauthorized access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: BANCO INVERSIS failed to implement adequate security measures, allowing attackers to use compromised credentials with weak authentication requirements to access customer data through.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 2 million customers had their names, birth dates, national ID numbers, and addresses exposed to unauthorized third-party access.
