claimsVsReality.claim: GRUPO BONATEL committed contractually to implement 'appropriate technical and organizational measures' to guarantee confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of systems and services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Basic security controls were absent: active unupdated generic VPN account, no login attempt limits, obsolete unpatched systems, no multi-factor authentication, no encryption of sensitive files—controls that are standard industry practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security measures were in place to protect employee data from unauthorized access and data exfiltration.
claimsVsReality.reality: A single brute-force attack on a generic VPN account compromised the entire system, exposing 976 employees' DNI numbers, financial data, and contact information across five companies, with evidence of public publication of exfiltrated data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRUPO BONATEL failed to implement adequate technical measures including: (1) active generic VPN user ('Guest') with outdated credentials vulnerable to brute force attack; (2) no maximum login attempt limits before access denial; (3) obsolete domain controller with known exploitable vulnerabilities; (4) absence of multi-factor authentication for remote access; (5) insufficient encryption and access controls on employee records containing DNI, banking data, and payroll information.
violations: GRUPO BONATEL failed to implement adequate technical measures including: (1) active generic VPN user ('Guest') with outdated credentials vulnerable to brute force attack; (2) no maximum login attempt limits before access denial; (3) obsolete domain controller with known exploitable vulnerabilities; (4) absence of multi-factor authentication for remote access; (5) insufficient encryption and access controls on employee records containing DNI, banking data, and payroll information.

The security failures resulted in unauthorized access via VPN compromise, enabling attackers to encrypt databases and exfiltrate 976 employees' personally identifiable information (name, surname, DNI/NIE, contact details, banking information) across five related companies.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including inter alia: (a) the pseudonymization and encryption of personal data; (b) the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: As processor for four of the five companies (BONATEL BUSINESS, SI DREAMS, SINEDIE, AGRUPACIÓN), GRUPO BONATEL committed to implementing security measures 'appropriate to the risk' but failed to provide basic protections—no encryption of sensitive employee files, no resilience mechanisms, no incident response capability despite handling sensitive personal data including national identity numbers.
violations: As processor for four of the five companies (BONATEL BUSINESS, SI DREAMS, SINEDIE, AGRUPACIÓN), GRUPO BONATEL committed to implementing security measures 'appropriate to the risk' but failed to provide basic protections—no encryption of sensitive employee files, no resilience mechanisms, no incident response capability despite handling sensitive personal data including national identity numbers.

outcome: GRUPO BONATEL recognized responsibility and made voluntary payment of €18,000 (40% reduction from original €30,000 fine: 20% for responsibility recognition + 20% for voluntary payment). Final resolution issued July 2025. Company ordered to adopt corrective measures within 6 months: acredit effective implementation of appropriate technical and organizational security measures aligned with GDPR Article 32, specifically addressing confidentiality, integrity, and risk-appropriate security controls. Resolution is final and enforceable in administrative law.
companyNow: GRUPO BONATEL SL continues operations with reported 2023 turnover of €5.88 million. Company has been ordered to implement enhanced security measures within 6 months of resolution finality and must demonstrate compliance to AEPD.
dataType: Employee personal data (name, surname, DNI/NIE, passport, contact details, banking information, payroll data)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of a Personal Data Breach

companyDescription: IBERCAJA BANCO, S.A. (NIF A99319030) is a Spanish banking entity providing digital banking, payment services, and transfer operations to personal and business customers. The company is incorporated as a public limited company with substantial business volume.
companyLongDescription: IBERCAJA BANCO, S.A. (NIF A99319030) is a Spanish banking entity providing digital banking, payment services, and transfer operations to personal and business customers. The company is incorporated as a public limited company with substantial business volume.
caseDescription: IBERCAJA BANCO disclosed a customer's full postal address to a transfer recipient through a bank transfer receipt when no such disclosure was required or authorized. The customer's address appeared in a field labeled 'Ampliación remitente de la transferencia' on the beneficiary's receipt, violating data confidentiality obligations under GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The company acknowledged responsibility and paid a reduced fine of €42,000.
violationSummary: Customer's address was improperly exposed to a third party (transfer beneficiary) through the bank's receipt generation process, making it accessible when it should have remained confidential.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Ibercaja Bank transmitted a customer's complete postal address including street, number, postal code.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer's home address was disclosed to an unrelated third party without consent, exposing the customer to potential stalking, theft, or identity fraud from someone who received the transfer.

claimsVsReality.claim: The address information was transmitted between payment processors under SEPA Scheme Rulebook requirements for transfer execution.
claimsVsReality.reality: While SEPA standards do permit address transmission between PSPs for execution and anti-money-laundering compliance, the standards explicitly state that such information must NOT be included in the customer receipt provided to the beneficiary.

claimsVsReality.claim: The document was not generated or sent by IBERCAJA BANCO.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation confirmed IBERCAJA BANCO generated and transmitted the receipt containing the address, through its standard banking operations and receipt generation process.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner guaranteeing appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: IBERCAJA BANCO failed to ensure confidentiality by transmitting the customer's postal address to the transfer recipient in the receipt, when SEPA standards explicitly prohibit including sender address information in beneficiary-facing transfer documents.
violations: IBERCAJA BANCO failed to ensure confidentiality by transmitting the customer's postal address to the transfer recipient in the receipt, when SEPA standards explicitly prohibit including sender address information in beneficiary-facing transfer documents.

outcome: IBERCAJA BANCO recognized its responsibility and paid €42,000 (reduced from initial €70,000 by 40% for early recognition and voluntary payment). The company is required within 3 months to notify AEPD of measures adopted to guarantee personal data confidentiality in transfer operations, ensuring compliance with GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The procedure is terminated and the resolution is final and executable as of notification.
companyNow: IBERCAJA BANCO, S.A. is a major Spanish financial institution established in 2011 with significant banking operations. The company continues operations under compliance obligations imposed by this enforcement action.
dataType: Address, account information, name, IBAN

companyDescription: TRUEBA SPORT S.L. is a Spanish sports management company established in 1994 that organizes the Vuelta Hispania, a Sub-23 cycling competition. The company generates revenue through sponsorships, municipal contributions, and product sales via the Correos Market platform.
companyLongDescription: TRUEBA SPORT S.L. is a Spanish sports management company established in 1994 that organizes the Vuelta Hispania, a Sub-23 cycling competition. The company generates revenue through sponsorships, municipal contributions, and product sales via the Correos Market platform.
caseDescription: TRUEBA SPORT sent a bulk email to over 300 product inquirers about a new cycling competition jersey without using the BCC (blind copy) field, exposing all recipients' email addresses to each other. The company failed to provide required transparency information in its privacy notices and on its website where personal data was collected.
violationSummary: Unintended disclosure of email addresses to unrelated third parties through failure to use confidentiality protection (BCC field), exposing personal contact information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: TRUEBA SPORT sent a bulk email to over 300 recipients about a product launch, disclosing all recipients' email addresses in visible To/CC fields instead of using BCC.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 300 people's email addresses were exposed to strangers without their knowledge or consent, enabling unsolicited contact and creating privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: TRUEBA SPORT stated it had established email management protocols and data protection policies incorporating BCC best practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed these policies (dated June 2024) were created after the October 2023 incident, proving no such protocols existed at the time of the violation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed to include data protection information in email signatures and privacy terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The email in the complaint contained no controller identification or processing information; the website entirely lacked privacy notices or legal disclaimers.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in such a manner as to guarantee adequate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: TRUEBA SPORT sent a bulk email on 30 October 2023 to over 300 recipients without using the BCC function, causing all recipients' email addresses to be visible to each other, violating the confidentiality principle by failing to prevent unauthorized disclosure of personal data to third parties.
violations: TRUEBA SPORT sent a bulk email on 30 October 2023 to over 300 recipients without using the BCC function, causing all recipients' email addresses to be visible to each other, violating the confidentiality principle by failing to prevent unauthorized disclosure of personal data to third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from a data subject, the controller must provide specified information including the controller's identity, processing purposes, legal basis, data retention details, and rights of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: TRUEBA SPORT's website at vueltahispania.com collected personal data through registration and equipment reservation forms but did not provide a Privacy Policy or Legal Notice identifying the data controller or explaining the treatment and individual rights, failing to comply with transparency obligations.
violations: TRUEBA SPORT's website at vueltahispania.com collected personal data through registration and equipment reservation forms but did not provide a Privacy Policy or Legal Notice identifying the data controller or explaining the treatment and individual rights, failing to comply with transparency obligations.

outcome: TRUEBA SPORT recognized responsibility and paid €1,200 (original proposed fine €2,000 with 40% reduction for early recognition and payment). The company was ordered to provide Art. 13 transparency information on its website within one month of the resolution becoming enforceable. The procedure was terminated on 2 June 2025 following payment. The company must maintain compliance with data protection principles and demonstrate active accountability.
companyNow: TRUEBA SPORT S.L. remains active as a small sports event management company. The enforcement decision is final and unappealable at administrative level; judicial review is available at the National Court.
dataType: Email addresses
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are obtained from the data subject

company: GACM SEGUROS GENERALES, COMPAÑIA DE SEGUROS Y REASEGUROS S.A.U.
companyDescription: GACM SEGUROS is a Spanish insurance and reinsurance company established in 1991 with estimated annual revenue of approximately €1.48 million (2022 figures).
companyLongDescription: GACM SEGUROS is a Spanish insurance and reinsurance company established in 1991 with estimated annual revenue of approximately €1.48 million (2022 figures).
caseDescription: GACM SEGUROS, a Spanish insurance company, violated the data accuracy principle by sharing a customer's personal information with an unrelated third party and sending communications containing another customer's data. The company failed to implement adequate procedures to ensure data accuracy, resulting in customer data being mixed between different policy holders.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to ensure data accuracy and prevent unauthorized mixing of personal data across different customer records, constituting a breach of data security fundamentals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: GACM Seguros sent personal data including names, addresses, and claim details of one customer to a different customer, mixing client information in letters, emails.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two customers received each other's private personal information including addresses and claim details, exposing them to privacy breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: GACM SEGUROS maintained appropriate data handling practices consistent with data protection law
claimsVsReality.reality: The company sent insurance claim communications containing one customer's personal data to another customer, and shared claim information between unrelated policyholders

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(d) requires personal data to be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. All reasonable measures must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate data without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: GACM SEGUROS mixed customer data across different insurance policies, sending one customer's personal information (name, address, claim details) to another customer
violations: GACM SEGUROS mixed customer data across different insurance policies, sending one customer's personal information (name, address, claim details) to another customer
The company failed to implement procedures to verify data accuracy before communicating with customers
Despite being alerted by the complainant, no immediate corrective measures were demonstrated

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Art. 4 specifies that data handlers are not liable for inaccurate data when they have adopted all reasonable measures to suppress or correct it, unless exceptions apply.
regulatoryFindings.description: GACM SEGUROS failed to demonstrate adequate organizational measures to prevent data association errors
violations: GACM SEGUROS failed to demonstrate adequate organizational measures to prevent data association errors
The insurance company, handling sensitive customer data daily, did not maintain sufficient diligence in preventing cross-customer data leakage

outcome: GACM SEGUROS recognized responsibility and paid €4,800.00 (original fine €8,000.00 reduced by 20% for acknowledgment of responsibility and 20% for voluntary payment). The company must adopt measures within 3 months to guarantee compliance with GDPR Art. 5(1)(d) by establishing procedures to verify data accuracy and prevent cross-customer data association. The procedure is terminated; resolution is final and executable upon notification.
companyNow: GACM SEGUROS continues operating as an insurance company. The company acknowledged the violation and implemented corrective measures as required by the AEPD enforcement order.
dataType: name, surname, address, claim reference number

companyDescription: STRATESYS TECHNOLOGY SOLUTIONS, S.L. is a Spanish company providing payroll management, HR outsourcing, and employee administration services to multiple client organizations. As of 2023, the company reported annual revenue of approximately €100.9 million.
companyLongDescription: STRATESYS TECHNOLOGY SOLUTIONS, S.L. is a Spanish company providing payroll management, HR outsourcing, and employee administration services to multiple client organizations. As of 2023, the company reported annual revenue of approximately €100.9 million.
caseDescription: STRATESYS suffered a ransomware cyberattack on August 24-28, 2023 that compromised the confidentiality and availability of personal data it processed both as a controller and processor. The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures, including encryption and perimeter security, allowing attackers to access and exfiltrate sensitive employee and client information. STRATESYS recognized responsibility and paid a reduced fine of €60,000.
violationSummary: The company failed to maintain adequate technical and organizational measures to ensure data security, leading to unauthorized access and potential exfiltration of personal data by cyberattackers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: STRATESYS operated payroll and HR management systems with inadequate security controls, allowing a ransomware attack between August 24-28.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's negligent failure to implement basic security measures like data encryption and access controls exposed employees and clients to identity theft, financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: STRATESYS claimed it had implemented proactive monitoring and detection mechanisms
claimsVsReality.reality: Detection only occurred 4 days after the attack began; earlier detection would have been possible with adequate perimeter monitoring

claimsVsReality.claim: STRATESYS stated the attackers' download link was never activated, limiting exposure
claimsVsReality.reality: The forensic investigation confirmed attackers gained access to and exfiltrated unencrypted personal data; actual public disclosure was prevented only by INTERPOL takedown action

claimsVsReality.claim: STRATESYS claimed to have implemented security policies (ITPOL document dated June 28, 2023)
claimsVsReality.reality: Critical measures such as encryption and network segmentation were absent or inadequately configured at the time of the breach one month later

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: STRATESYS failed to implement encryption of data at rest and in transit on affected servers
violations: STRATESYS failed to implement encryption of data at rest and in transit on affected servers
STRATESYS lacked adequate network segmentation and perimeter security controls
STRATESYS did not implement adequate monitoring and detection mechanisms prior to the breach
The combination of missing security controls allowed attackers to access systems and exfiltrate unencrypted personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 imposes on processors and controllers the obligation to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, and risks presented by processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: STRATESYS, as both processor and controller, failed to maintain current security policies and implement recommended controls
violations: STRATESYS, as both processor and controller, failed to maintain current security policies and implement recommended controls
Security measures were not proportionate to the risks of processing large volumes of sensitive employee and client data
Controls identified as missing in the forensic report were only implemented after the breach occurred

outcome: STRATESYS recognized responsibility and made voluntary payment of €60,000 on July 24, 2025, applying two cumulative 20% reductions to the initial €100,000 proposed fine. The company is required within 3 months of the executive resolution to implement and certify adoption of effective technical and organizational measures to ensure data integrity, confidentiality, and treatment security appropriate to identified risks. The procedure (EXP202318355) was terminated following payment and recognition of responsibility. STRATESYS must implement the 61 security controls identified in the forensic report and notify AEPD of compliance.
companyNow: STRATESYS continues operating as a payroll and HR management service provider in Spain. The company has undertaken remedial security measures post-breach and is subject to 3-month compliance verification by AEPD.
dataType: Employee personal data, client data (names, identification numbers, financial information, employment records)

companyDescription: SOBLADA RESTAURACIÓN, S.L. is a Spanish restaurant company founded in 2022 with limited annual revenue (reported as redacted in the document). It operates a single restaurant location.
companyLongDescription: SOBLADA RESTAURACIÓN, S.L. is a Spanish restaurant company founded in 2022 with limited annual revenue (reported as redacted in the document). It operates a single restaurant location.
caseDescription: A restaurant installed video surveillance cameras in excessive and poorly signaled locations, capturing customers' faces and movements without proper transparency or consent. The company failed to comply with GDPR requirements for data minimization and failed to provide required information notices about the surveillance system.
violationSummary: The company conducted video surveillance without proper legal basis, transparency mechanisms, or necessity justification. Cameras captured individuals in intimate leisure settings (dining) without their knowledge, constituting systematic surveillance that exceeded security needs.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed at least four surveillance cameras on the restaurant terrace oriented toward customer dining tables, and additional cameras inside pointing at the bar.
whyTheyWereWrong: Restaurant diners and employees were captured on video in moments of leisure and work without their knowledge or consent, exposing their faces, movements.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cameras were installed for security purposes
claimsVsReality.reality: Cameras were positioned to capture customer dining tables and faces, areas with no legitimate security need; at least four outdoor cameras directly recorded customers at leisure, inconsistent with any documented security objective

claimsVsReality.claim: System was properly communicated to users
claimsVsReality.reality: No informational signs were present; customers and staff were not informed of the surveillance, its purposes, the controller's identity, or their rights

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: SOBLADA RESTAURACIÓN installed at least four cameras on the outdoor terrace directed at customer dining tables, capturing facial images and movements in intimate leisure moments where such surveillance had no legitimate security justification and exceeded what was necessary or proportionate.
violations: SOBLADA RESTAURACIÓN installed at least four cameras on the outdoor terrace directed at customer dining tables, capturing facial images and movements in intimate leisure moments where such surveillance had no legitimate security justification and exceeded what was necessary or proportionate.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 requires controllers to provide data subjects with prescribed information including the identity of the controller, the purposes of processing, and rights available to them.
regulatoryFindings.description: No informational signage was displayed in the surveillance areas, and customers were not informed about the existence of the treatment, the controller's identity, or their rights. The restaurant failed to meet the transparency obligation required by LOPDGDD Art. 22.4.
violations: No informational signage was displayed in the surveillance areas, and customers were not informed about the existence of the treatment, the controller's identity, or their rights. The restaurant failed to meet the transparency obligation required by LOPDGDD Art. 22.4.

outcome: SOBLADA RESTAURACIÓN was found to have violated GDPR Arts. 5(1)(c) and 13. The company paid €800 (original sanction €1,000 reduced by 20% for voluntary payment under Art. 85 LPACAP). The company must, within one month: (1) remove or reorient cameras that do not comply with proportionality requirements; (2) place informational signage in all surveilled areas identifying the treatment, controller identity, and rights. The resolution is final and immediately executable; any appeal must be filed within two months before the National Court.
companyNow: SOBLADA RESTAURACIÓN, S.L. (CIF B72719073) is a micro-enterprise operating a restaurant in Spain. As of June 2025, the company complied with the administrative penalty and was ordered to correct its surveillance systems within one month.
dataType: Biometric data (facial images/video recordings), location data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 – Right to information from data controller

company: The Management Corporation - Strata Title Plan No. 4599
companyDescription: A management corporation responsible for control, management and administration of a residential condominium complex in Singapore, engaged in property management and common facility oversight.
companyLongDescription: A management corporation responsible for control, management and administration of a residential condominium complex in Singapore, engaged in property management and common facility oversight.
caseDescription: A condominium management corporation rejected a resident's request for CCTV footage from a traffic accident and failed to preserve the footage pending resolution. The organisation had no data protection policies, failed to designate a data protection officer, and gave no instructions to its managing agents or security company on handling access requests.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate accountability measures (policies, DPO designation, operational procedures) required under PDPA sections 11(3) and 12, creating systemic insecurity in personal data handling and access request management.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The management corporation rejected a resident's request for CCTV footage of a traffic accident, failed to develop its own data protection policies.
whyTheyWereWrong: The blanket refusal to provide CCTV footage from a public road caused the resident to lose evidence of the accident without being offered alternatives like masking other individuals' images,.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed it was not obliged to provide CCTV footage because the complainant did not fall within categories under section 47(1)(b)(viii) of the BMSMA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The BMSMA section applies only to persons entitled under that provision; since the complainant did not fall within those categories, the PDPA section 21 access right applied independently, and the organisation should have handled the request under PDPA provisions

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed it could not provide CCTV footage because it would reveal personal data of other individuals in breach of section 21(3)(c).
claimsVsReality.reality: Publicly-captured data may be disclosed without consent; CCTV of a public road captures publicly-available data, and the organisation could have masked other individuals' images rather than denying access outright

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation relied on its managing agent's data protection policy as sufficient for compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The managing agent's policy was designed for the agent's own operations and did not address the organisation's specific operational needs (e.g., access request procedures for CCTV), and organisations cannot outsource PDPA compliance to managing agents

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 21 of the PDPA requires an organisation to provide personal data about an individual upon request, as soon as reasonably possible, provided the data is in the organisation's possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organisation wrongfully denied the access request relying on section 21(3)(c) without considering that CCTV footage of a public road captures publicly-available data and could have been provided with masking of other individuals
violations: The organisation wrongfully denied the access request relying on section 21(3)(c) without considering that CCTV footage of a public road captures publicly-available data and could have been provided with masking of other individuals
The organisation incorrectly relied on section 47(1)(b)(viii) of the BMSMA to deny access when the complainant did not fall under those categories; the PDPA applies where BMSMA does not

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 11(3) of the PDPA requires every organisation to designate one or more individuals as a data protection officer to ensure compliance with the Act.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organisation admitted it had not appointed a DPO at the time of the incident, constituting a breach of section 11(3)
violations: The organisation admitted it had not appointed a DPO at the time of the incident, constituting a breach of section 11(3)

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the PDPA requires an organisation to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet its obligations under the Act.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organisation failed to develop its own contextualised data protection policy; it provided only its managing agent's policy which did not address the organisation's specific needs
violations: The organisation failed to develop its own contextualised data protection policy; it provided only its managing agent's policy which did not address the organisation's specific needs

The organisation gave no written instructions or standard operating procedures to managing agents or security company on handling access requests for personal data including CCTV footage, leading to inability to preserve and provide footage

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 22A of the PDPA requires preservation of personal data for at least 30 days from refusal date where an organisation refuses an access request.
regulatoryFindings.description: The CCTV footage was overwritten on 30 April 2024 before the organisation communicated its refusal on 2 May 2024, so section 22A did not apply; however, the systemic failure to implement access request procedures contributed to this outcome
violations: The CCTV footage was overwritten on 30 April 2024 before the organisation communicated its refusal on 2 May 2024, so section 22A did not apply; however, the systemic failure to implement access request procedures contributed to this outcome

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation negligently breached the Accountability Obligation under PDPA sections 11(3) and 12 by failing to designate a DPO and failing to develop contextualised data protection policies and procedures. The Commission made observations (non-binding findings) regarding the improper handling of the access request but could not determine whether access should have been granted since the CCTV footage no longer existed. The organisation is directed within 60 days to: (a) develop and implement policies under section 12 of the PDPA; (b) establish procedures for managing CCTV footage on receipt of section 21 access requests; (c) communicate policies and procedures to data intermediaries and contractors; and (d) furnish written updates to the Commission within 7 days of completion. The organisation has since appointed a DPO.
companyNow: The Management Corporation - Strata Title Plan No. 4599 operates The Scotts Tower Condominium in Singapore and has since appointed a Data Protection Officer and is implementing required data protection policies and procedures.
dataType: CCTV footage, video personal data
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s. 11(3) – Failure to designate data protection officer
PDPA s. 12 – Failure to develop and implement policies and practices
PDPA s. 21 – Access obligation (observations on improper denial)
PDPA s. 22A – Preservation of personal data (did not apply as data overwritten before refusal)

companyDescription: GESTIÓN DE VENTAS IBERIA S.L. (NIF B72598329) is a Spanish sales/marketing company engaged in energy supplier switching campaigns via telemarketing. Ceased collaboration with energy marketing firm on 20 November 2023.
companyLongDescription: GESTIÓN DE VENTAS IBERIA S.L. (NIF B72598329) is a Spanish sales/marketing company engaged in energy supplier switching campaigns via telemarketing. Ceased collaboration with energy marketing firm on 20 November 2023.
caseDescription: GESTIÓN DE VENTAS IBERIA S.L. made an unsolicited commercial call to a complainant on 3 January 2024 regarding electricity supplier switching, possessing full personal data without consent. The company failed to provide mandatory transparency information required under GDPR Article 14 and violated Spanish telecommunications law by making unwanted commercial calls without prior consent or valid legal basis.
violationSummary: The company conducted unsolicited contact and data-driven telemarketing targeting with personal information obtained without transparency. This falls under surveillance as the company monitored and targeted the individual without notice or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: GESTIÓN DE VENTAS IBERIA S.L. made an unsolicited commercial telephone call on January 3, 2024 to a consumer without prior consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The consumer received an invasive cold call from an unknown company with access to their full banking details including IBAN, creating serious risk of financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company could have lawfully obtained and used complainant's personal data for commercial contact
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation found no documentation of prior consent, valid contract, or other lawful basis; company did not respond to requests for evidence

claimsVsReality.claim: Complainant was informed about the company's identity and data processing purposes during the call
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence that company provided mandatory transparency information required by GDPR Article 14 before or at first contact

regulatoryFindings.act: LGTEL Article 66.1(b): Right to protection against unwanted commercial calls without prior consent or valid lawful basis under GDPR Article 6.1
regulatoryFindings.description: Company made commercial call soliciting electricity supplier switch without complainant's prior consent
violations: Company made commercial call soliciting electricity supplier switch without complainant's prior consent
No lawful basis documented for processing contact data for commercial call

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 14: When personal data not obtained directly from data subject, controller must provide identity of controller, purposes of processing, categories of data, data source, and rights available
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant received no information about data source, processing purpose, or rights before or during call
violations: Complainant received no information about data source, processing purpose, or rights before or during call
Company did not provide mandated transparency information within one month or at first contact

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1: Processing must have a lawful basis such as explicit consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests
regulatoryFindings.description: No evidence of prior consent obtained by company
violations: No evidence of prior consent obtained by company
No contractual relationship existed between complainant and company
No other lawful basis identified in investigation

outcome: AEPD imposed total administrative fine of €4,000 (€2,000 for LGTEL Article 66.1(b) violation; €2,000 for GDPR Article 14 violation). Company ordered to bring conduct into compliance with data protection rules within 3 months of resolution becoming final and executable. Company did not respond to agency inquiries throughout investigation. Resolution is enforceable once voluntary appeal period (one month) expires. Payment due via CAIXABANK transfer to AEPD restricted account.
companyNow: Unknown. Company address is registered in Granada, Spain. Did not respond to AEPD investigative requests; postal notifications returned 'Unknown' or 'Incorrect address'.
dataType: Name, address, telephone number, email, bank account IBAN
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 14 (Information to be provided when personal data not obtained from the data subject)
LGTEL Art. 66.1(b) (Right to protection from unwanted commercial calls without prior consent)
GDPR Art. 6 (Lawful basis requirement for processing)

companyDescription: Smart Home Ensured Limited is a UK-registered company (Companies House Registration No. 13624736) based in London, operating in the smart home technology sector. The company engaged in unsolicited direct marketing activities in 2023.
companyLongDescription: Smart Home Ensured Limited is a UK-registered company (Companies House Registration No. 13624736) based in London, operating in the smart home technology sector. The company engaged in unsolicited direct marketing activities in 2023.
caseDescription: Smart Home Ensured Limited made 14,508 unsolicited direct marketing calls between July and August 2023 to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), violating PECR regulation 21. The company failed to respect consumers' explicit opt-out preferences despite having access to the TPS register. The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring immediate cessation of such practices.
violationSummary: Systematic unsolicited direct contact to individuals who had explicitly opted out through TPS registration constitutes surveillance and intrusion into individual privacy choices.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Smart Home Ensured Limited made 14,508 unsolicited direct marketing calls between July and August 2023 to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 14,508 consumers who took affirmative steps to opt out of marketing calls by registering with TPS received unwanted calls anyway.

claimsVsReality.claim: Implied: SHE had valid consent to call TPS-registered subscribers
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence of clear, positive opt-in notifications from consumers; TPS registration indicates explicit opt-out preference

claimsVsReality.claim: Implied: SHE was conducting lawful direct marketing
claimsVsReality.reality: 14,508 calls made to consumers who had registered with TPS to avoid such contact, violating PECR regulation 21(1)(b)

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits persons from using or instigating the use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the called line number is listed on the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: SHE used public telecommunications service to make 14,508 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
violations: SHE used public telecommunications service to make 14,508 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
Calls were made without valid opt-in consent as required under regulation 21(4)
No evidence of clear, positive notification from subscribers overriding TPS registration

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR regulation 26 requires the Commissioner to maintain a register of numbers where subscribers have notified they do not wish to receive unsolicited direct marketing calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: SHE failed to comply with TPS register requirements despite having access to it
violations: SHE failed to comply with TPS register requirements despite having access to it
Numbers had been on the register for at least 28 days before the calls were made

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 section 40 empowers the Commissioner to serve enforcement notices where a person has contravened PECR requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: SHE's systematic violation of PECR regulation 21 triggered enforcement action
violations: SHE's systematic violation of PECR regulation 21 triggered enforcement action

outcome: The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring SHE to cease unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers and to individuals who have notified SHE directly not to call. Within 30 days, SHE must comply by: (1) neither using nor instigating use of public electronic communications for unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers or those who opted out; and (2) providing recipients with caller identification information upon request. SHE has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal within 28 days.
dataType: telephone numbers, direct marketing contact information

companyDescription: Servicios Financieros Carrefour, E.F.C., S.A. is a financial credit establishment and hybrid payment entity regulated by Spain's Banco de España. It offers payment cards (Carrefour Pass), consumer loans, and other financial products to Carrefour supermarket customers and the general public.
companyLongDescription: Servicios Financieros Carrefour, E.F.C., S.A. is a financial credit establishment and hybrid payment entity regulated by Spain's Banco de España. It offers payment cards (Carrefour Pass), consumer loans, and other financial products to Carrefour supermarket customers and the general public.
caseDescription: Carrefour Financial Services suffered a data breach on December 19, 2023, exposing personal and financial data of customers through phishing and compromised credentials. The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures despite maintaining customer financial data on a critical backend system. Following investigation, the company paid a €1.5M penalty after acknowledging responsibility for inadequate data protection controls.
companyWorth: €2B (estimated, as subsidiary of Carrefour Group with ~€100B+ market cap)
violationSummary: The company failed to maintain adequate technical and organizational security measures to protect personal data from unauthorized access and breach, directly violating the integrity and confidentiality principle of GDPR Article 5(1)(f).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Carrefour Financial Services failed to implement adequate security measures on a critical backend service.
whyTheyWereWrong: The breach exposed DNI numbers, financial records, payment details, and contact information of customers to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: SFC maintained appropriate security measures for customer data protection
claimsVsReality.reality: The backend service handling customer financial data had a vulnerable configuration since 2017, lacked proactive security reviews, and had no adequate controls to prevent unauthorized access via compromised credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach affected a limited number of customers with restricted data exposure
claimsVsReality.reality: Attackers using 19 compromised credentials successfully accessed customer records from multiple IP addresses, exposing basic data, contact information, DNI numbers, financial data, and payment card information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner guaranteeing appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and protection against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: SFC maintained a critical backend service handling sensitive customer financial data without adequate security controls, including: vulnerable configuration in place since 2017, lack of proactive service review for years, absence of adequate access controls, and insufficient monitoring of anomalous activity patterns.
violations: SFC maintained a critical backend service handling sensitive customer financial data without adequate security controls, including: vulnerable configuration in place since 2017, lack of proactive service review for years, absence of adequate access controls, and insufficient monitoring of anomalous activity patterns.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5 establishes that infringements of Article 5 principles shall be subject to administrative fines of up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover, whichever is higher.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's failure to implement security measures constituted a substantial violation of fundamental data protection principles, warranting a significant administrative fine.
violations: The company's failure to implement security measures constituted a substantial violation of fundamental data protection principles, warranting a significant administrative fine.

outcome: On August 27, 2025, Servicios Financieros Carrefour paid a penalty of €1,500,000 after recognizing responsibility and exercising voluntary payment under Spanish administrative procedure law. This represented a 40% reduction from the initial €2,500,000 proposed sanction. The company must implement enhanced security controls, conduct regular vulnerability assessments, apply timely patches to all critical systems, and undergo monitoring to ensure compliance with GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requirements.
companyNow: Servicios Financieros Carrefour, a subsidiary of the Carrefour Group, continues to operate as a financial services entity regulated by Banco de España. The company is classified as a hybrid payment entity and is considered small and non-complex.
dataType: Financial data, payment card information, identification documents (DNI), contact data, customer IDs

companyDescription: Piraeus Bank A.E. is one of Greece's largest banking institutions, headquartered in Athens. It provides retail and corporate banking services, including loan origination, asset management, and payment processing.
companyLongDescription: Piraeus Bank A.E. is one of Greece's largest banking institutions, headquartered in Athens. It provides retail and corporate banking services, including loan origination, asset management, and payment processing.
caseDescription: Piraeus Bank erroneously registered a customer as a loan guarantor due to employee data entry error, causing personal data to be processed without legal basis. The bank sent multiple notification letters to the complainant despite his explicit objection, and failed to correct the error promptly. The processing violated the lawfulness and accuracy principles of GDPR Articles 5 and 6.
violationSummary: The violation stems from a data quality/integrity failure (erroneous categorization of a data subject) combined with unlawful processing without a valid legal basis. The employee error that caused misidentification falls under insecurity in data handling practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Piraeus Bank incorrectly recorded a customer as a loan guarantor due to employee error, then sent him three notification letters about debt collection without legal basis.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer had no actual relationship to the loan and received threatening debt collection letters about his brother's obligation, causing him emotional distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data entry error was a one-off, isolated incident caused by a single employee's mistake, not indicative of systemic dysfunction.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the Authority accepted this argument and classified it as isolated human error, the bank continued sending notifications after the complainant objected, indicating inadequate compliance procedures.

claimsVsReality.claim: No data was actually transferred to the debt manager or SPV because the complaining party was never incorporated into their perimeter.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although no actual transfer occurred, the notification letters themselves processed the complainant's data without lawful basis, and the third parties were aware of his existence from the notification sent to them.

claimsVsReality.claim: The erroneous registration could be attributed to the complainant's co-ownership of the property securing the loan.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant held only a 50% ownership stake in a property used as collateral for his brother's loan. This property interest did not establish a guarantor relationship, which requires a separate contractual commitment.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Piraeus Bank processed the complainant's data without a valid legal basis under Article 6, as no guarantor relationship existed. The bank relied on an erroneous system record to justify processing.
violations: Piraeus Bank processed the complainant's data without a valid legal basis under Article 6, as no guarantor relationship existed. The bank relied on an erroneous system record to justify processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires personal data to be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. Reasonable measures must be taken for the prompt deletion or correction of inaccurate data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The complainant was incorrectly recorded as a loan guarantor due to employee data entry error. The bank failed to correct this inaccuracy promptly despite the complainant's objections.
violations: The complainant was incorrectly recorded as a loan guarantor due to employee data entry error. The bank failed to correct this inaccuracy promptly despite the complainant's objections.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires processing to be based on at least one lawful basis such as consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: The bank processed the complainant's data without any valid legal basis under Article 6, as the assumed guarantor relationship did not exist.
violations: The bank processed the complainant's data without any valid legal basis under Article 6, as the assumed guarantor relationship did not exist.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) imposes accountability: the data controller must be able to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: The bank failed to maintain adequate data quality controls and continued sending notifications after the complainant explicitly objected, demonstrating lack of accountability.
violations: The bank failed to maintain adequate data quality controls and continued sending notifications after the complainant explicitly objected, demonstrating lack of accountability.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority found Piraeus Bank in violation of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(d), 5(2), and 6(1). The Authority imposed a fine of €50,000. The bank must cease the unlawful processing, correct the complainant's erroneous designation in its systems, and implement measures to prevent recurrence. A district court judgment also upheld the complainant's claim for moral damages, awarding €1,500. The bank has acknowledged the systemic error and initiated corrective measures in its data systems.
companyNow: Piraeus Bank remains a major Greek financial institution. The bank has implemented corrective measures and acknowledged the erroneous processing. The decision was issued in June 2025, following formal proceedings.
dataType: Personal data related to banking customers and guarantors; property/real estate information

companyDescription: Blue Team Flight School, S.L. is a flight training school established in Spain in 2020. According to AXESOR data cited in the decision, it is classified as a microenterprise with reported annual revenue of less than €100,000 in 2022.
companyLongDescription: Blue Team Flight School, S.L. is a flight training school established in Spain in 2020. According to AXESOR data cited in the decision, it is classified as a microenterprise with reported annual revenue of less than €100,000 in 2022.
caseDescription: Blue Team Flight School failed to respond to three information requests from Spain's data protection authority during a formal investigation into a privacy complaint. The company refused to provide documents and evidence needed by the AEPD to conduct its investigation, obstructing the authority's enforcement powers under GDPR Article 58(1).
violationSummary: The violation stems from obstruction of the regulatory authority's investigative powers, preventing oversight of how personal data is handled and protected. This failure to cooperate impedes the authority's ability to identify and remedy data protection breaches.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Blue Team Flight School failed to respond to three formal information requests from Spain's data protection authority (AEPD) during a GDPR investigation.
whyTheyWereWrong: By refusing to provide required information, the company prevented the AEPD from investigating potential data protection violations affecting individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) grants each supervisory authority powers to order the controller or processor to provide any information required for the authority to perform its functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: Blue Team Flight School failed to comply with three separate formal information requests issued by AEPD in the course of investigating a privacy complaint, despite proper notification on 6 October 2024, 25 October 2024, and 28 October 2024.
violations: Blue Team Flight School failed to comply with three separate formal information requests issued by AEPD in the course of investigating a privacy complaint, despite proper notification on 6 October 2024, 25 October 2024, and 28 October 2024.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(e) classifies failure to provide access to required information in contravention of Article 58(1) as a serious infraction subject to administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: By obstinately refusing all three information requests without explanation or response, the company directly violated Article 58(1), obstructing the AEPD's investigative and supervisory function.
violations: By obstinately refusing all three information requests without explanation or response, the company directly violated Article 58(1), obstructing the AEPD's investigative and supervisory function.

outcome: The AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €6,000 on Blue Team Flight School, S.L. for violation of GDPR Article 58(1). The company was also ordered to provide the requested information within 10 business days from the date this resolution becomes final and enforceable. The resolution is enforceable once the voluntary appeal period (one month from notification) expires without the company filing a challenge. Non-compliance with the information order may trigger a separate enforcement action under GDPR Article 83(6).
companyNow: Blue Team Flight School, S.L. is a microenterprise registered in Spain (NIF B01862572) founded in 2020. Current compliance status and operational status unknown.
dataType: Unknown

companyDescription: Marina Bay Sands Pte. Ltd. is an integrated resort in Singapore operating a hotel, casino, shopping mall, and ArtScience Museum. The company operates membership programmes (Sands Rewards Lifestyle and ArtScience Friends) managing data for approximately 1.9 million individuals.
companyLongDescription: Marina Bay Sands Pte. Ltd. is an integrated resort in Singapore operating a hotel, casino, shopping mall, and ArtScience Museum. The company operates membership programmes (Sands Rewards Lifestyle and ArtScience Friends) managing data for approximately 1.9 million individuals.
caseDescription: Marina Bay Sands failed to implement adequate security measures during a middleware migration, causing a misconfiguration that exposed customer data for 6+ months. A threat actor exploited this vulnerability to access and exfiltrate personal data of 665,495 members. The company's reliance on manual API replication without verification checks or automation led to the omission of critical security configurations.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (automated processes, independent verification) to prevent unauthorised access to personal data, allowing a misconfiguration to create a vulnerability exploitable by threat actors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Marina Bay Sands manually replicated API configurations during a middleware migration without independent verification or automated checks.
whyTheyWereWrong: 665,495 customers' personal data including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and countries of residence were exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had implemented adequate security arrangements including testing, vulnerability assessments, and security monitoring tools
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, the organisation failed to implement the most fundamental security practice for high-risk migrations: independent verification or automation of critical configuration changes

claimsVsReality.claim: The Employee's expertise and training made reliance on single-person manual process appropriate
claimsVsReality.reality: Expertise does not render employees infallible; organisations must implement systemic processes and controls to protect against human error, not depend on individual competence

claimsVsReality.claim: Token Verification Policy and segregated access controls adequately protected customer data
claimsVsReality.reality: These controls were rendered ineffective by the misconfiguration that excluded the ASF webpage from token verification, allowing unrestricted access to 665,495 customer records

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Marina Bay Sands failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by relying solely on manual API replication by a single employee without independent verification checks or automation
violations: Marina Bay Sands failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by relying solely on manual API replication by a single employee without independent verification checks or automation
The organisation did not put in place downstream controls to detect the API misconfiguration during or after the migration
For high-volume personal data, the organisation should have implemented more robust processes to mitigate human error risks, such as automated deployment or secondary verification

outcome: Marina Bay Sands was found to have negligently breached the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. The Commission imposed a financial penalty of SGD 315,000 (reduced from the preliminary decision of SGD 450,000 based on the organisation's representations regarding prompt remedial actions, voluntary notification to affected individuals, and cooperation with the investigation). The organisation must pay within 30 days. No further directions were issued as the organisation had already implemented remedial measures including enabling token verification, penetration testing, conducting security audits, implementing automated deployment checks, and establishing digital accounts with stronger authentication.
companyNow: Marina Bay Sands continues to operate as a major integrated resort in Singapore. Following the incident, the company has implemented comprehensive security enhancements and remediation measures to strengthen its data protection infrastructure.
dataType: Names, email addresses, phone numbers, countries of residence, membership numbers and tiers

companyDescription: YUNEXPRESS SPAIN, S.L. is a logistics and parcel delivery company operating in Spain, providing warehouse storage, merchandise receipt, and distribution services. The company had reported €1,318,342 in annual revenue in 2022.
companyLongDescription: YUNEXPRESS SPAIN, S.L. is a logistics and parcel delivery company operating in Spain, providing warehouse storage, merchandise receipt, and distribution services. The company had reported €1,318,342 in annual revenue in 2022.
caseDescription: YUNEXPRESS failed to establish a properly documented data processing agreement with its subcontractor URVAAM that complied with GDPR Article 28.3 requirements. The deficient contract permitted uncontrolled subcontracting chains without adequate safeguards, leading to a delivery error where a recipient's personal data was mixed with another person's DNI and signature on a delivery receipt, compromising data accuracy and control.
violationSummary: YUNEXPRESS's failure to enforce binding processor obligations through a compliant Article 28 contract resulted in insecure handling of personal data throughout the subcontracting chain, leading to data inaccuracy and unauthorized exposure of identity information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: YUNEXPRESS failed to establish a properly detailed processor contract with URVAAM that specified required security measures, subcontracting authorization procedures.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer's delivery receipt contained another person's DNI and signature, exposing two individuals' personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: URVAAM claimed it was not the responsible party for data protection because YUNEXPRESS was the client and contractually responsible.
claimsVsReality.reality: YUNEXPRESS, as the data controller, bore responsibility for ensuring all processors and subprocessors complied with GDPR, regardless of subcontracting arrangements. Responsibility cannot be delegated away through contractual disclaimers.

claimsVsReality.claim: YUNEXPRESS stated it had authorized subcontracting and visibility into platform details showing subcontractors, implying adequate oversight.
claimsVsReality.reality: Visibility into a logistics platform does not constitute compliance with Article 28 processor contract requirements. The actual written processor agreement lacked required security specifications, proper subcontracting controls, and assistance procedures.

claimsVsReality.claim: LAN COURIER and B.B.B. claimed short-term collaboration and informal arrangements did not require formal contracts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Article 28.3 and 28.4 of GDPR mandate written contracts or formal legal instruments for all processor and subprocessor relationships, regardless of duration or informality of the business arrangement.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28.3 requires that processing by a processor must be governed by a contract that establishes the object, duration, nature and purpose of processing, specifies security measures, processor obligations, and conditions for subcontracting.
regulatoryFindings.description: YUNEXPRESS failed to include specific security measures in the contract; only general language was included without defining what measures the processor must actually implement.
violations: YUNEXPRESS failed to include specific security measures in the contract; only general language was included without defining what measures the processor must actually implement.
The subcontracting clause authorized subcontracting without requiring the processor to inform the controller of planned changes or give the controller opportunity to object.
No mechanism required the processor to inform the controller of changes to subcontractors or timeline for approval/opposition.
The contract did not specify how the processor would assist the controller in meeting GDPR security and accountability obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires personal data to be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date, with all reasonable measures taken to rectify or erase inaccurate data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Delivery receipts contained the complainant's name and address linked to a third party's DNI and signature, creating inaccurate and confused records.
violations: Delivery receipts contained the complainant's name and address linked to a third party's DNI and signature, creating inaccurate and confused records.
Contradictory system records (delivery marked both 'Delivered' and 'Lost' at same timestamp) compromised data accuracy.
The processor chain lacked controls to verify identity and prevent mixing of different individuals' data on delivery documents.

outcome: YUNEXPRESS recognized responsibility and paid the reduced fine of €5,400 (reflecting 40% cumulative reduction for early recognition and voluntary payment). The company was ordered to update its processor agreement with URVAAM within 3 months to comply with Article 28.3, including detailed security measures, explicit subcontracting limitations, and processor assistance procedures. Procedural termination confirms no further administrative appeal available.
companyNow: YUNEXPRESS SPAIN, S.L. (B02704062) is an active Spanish logistics company operating in warehouse and parcel distribution. The company must demonstrate contract compliance within 3 months of the final resolution becoming enforceable.
dataType: Name, address, telephone number, national ID number (DNI), signature

companyDescription: Post Office Limited is a UK public sector company providing mail, financial, and government services through a nationwide network of over 11,500 branches, the majority operated by independent postmasters and franchise partners.
companyLongDescription: Post Office Limited is a UK public sector company providing mail, financial, and government services through a nationwide network of over 11,500 branches, the majority operated by independent postmasters and franchise partners.
caseDescription: Post Office Limited failed to implement appropriate security measures for personal data of 502 postmasters involved in the Horizon IT scandal settlement. An unredacted settlement deed containing sensitive personal data was accidentally uploaded to the Post Office's public website on 25 April 2024, remaining publicly accessible for 55 days until removed. The Post Office had no documented policies, quality assurance processes, or centralized data controls in place to prevent such disclosures.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of confidential personal data to the public internet breaches the confidentiality principle. The Post Office failed to maintain adequate technical and organizational safeguards required by law, resulting in sensitive personal information becoming publicly accessible.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Post Office Limited uploaded an unredacted Settlement Deed containing 502 postmasters' full names, home addresses, and financial details to its public website on 25 April 2024.
whyTheyWereWrong: 502 postmasters already traumatized by wrongful prosecutions based on faulty Horizon IT evidence had their identities, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Post Office staff completed required annual data protection and information security refresher training.
claimsVsReality.reality: While staff training was completed, no specific training covered uploading information to the corporate website, and there were no documented procedures or controls to prevent uploading unredacted documents.

claimsVsReality.claim: Post Office had information classification policies in place requiring confidential information not be published to the internet.
claimsVsReality.reality: Classification policy existed but was not enforced; no quality assurance process, document checks, or sign-off procedures existed to prevent publishing classified information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Impact of the 25 April Incident on data subjects was overstated.
claimsVsReality.reality: Incident caused considerable stress and anxiety documented by legal representatives of 365 affected postmasters and media reports; individuals faced vulnerability to fraud, burglary, and targeted scams due to public exposure of names, addresses, and settlement amounts.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised processing, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Post Office failed to implement any documented policies, procedures, or guidance for uploading documents to the corporate website
violations: Post Office failed to implement any documented policies, procedures, or guidance for uploading documents to the corporate website
No quality assurance or sign-off process existed for documents uploaded to the public website
No centralized document storage, labeling, or segregation protocols were in place
Risk register was neither complete nor accurate and did not identify risks of inadvertently publishing confidential information
No checks were conducted on documentation prior to upload, allowing an unredacted settlement deed to be published

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account state of the art, costs, nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Post Office failed to assess information risks or classify how valuable, sensitive, or confidential information held was
violations: Post Office failed to assess information risks or classify how valuable, sensitive, or confidential information held was
Risk profile focused on reputational risks only, not on risks of inadvertently publishing or sharing confidential information
Despite knowing personal data involved highly sensitive settlement information related to wrongfully prosecuted postmasters, appropriate security measures were not implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(2) requires assessment of risks presented by processing, in particular from unauthorised disclosure of personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Post Office did not conduct adequate risk assessment of the sensitive nature of unredacted settlement deed data
violations: Post Office did not conduct adequate risk assessment of the sensitive nature of unredacted settlement deed data
Failed to identify specific risks of accidentally publishing confidential information to the public internet
Internal assurance review concluded the control environment was not fit for purpose with fundamental weaknesses in governance and risk management

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal Reprimand to Post Office Limited on 2 December 2025 for violations of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1), and 32(2) UK GDPR. No monetary penalty was imposed due to the Commissioner's public sector enforcement approach, which prioritizes reprimands and compliance orders over fines. However, the Commissioner calculated that had the public sector approach not been in place, a monetary penalty of up to £1.094 million would have been appropriate. Post Office has implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: (1) Data control framework with document classification protocols (Public, Internal, Confidential, Strictly Confidential); (2) Three-step quality assurance and approval process for publishing confidential data; (3) Updated risk and controls register identifying data security risks; (4) Centralized document storage on SharePoint with restricted access; (5) Outreach to affected data subjects with apologies and compensation to 440 of 502 individuals; (6) 24 months of identity fraud protection services (Experian); (7) Removal of documents from web caches (Wayback Machine, Google, National Archives); (8) Dark web monitoring. All remedial actions were completed by 15 November 2024. Infringements have been remedied as of that date.
companyNow: Post Office Limited continues to operate as the primary postal and government services provider in the UK with 11,500+ branches run by franchise partners. The company remains subject to ongoing monitoring and must maintain the implemented data security controls.
dataType: Full names, home addresses, postmaster status, settlement payment amounts
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (integrity and confidentiality principle)
UK GDPR Article 32(2) (risk assessment for security)

companyDescription: MAD COOL FESTIVAL, S.L. is a Spanish company (founded 2015) that organizes music festivals and events. The company had annual revenue of approximately €357,000 as of 2021.
companyLongDescription: MAD COOL FESTIVAL, S.L. is a Spanish company (founded 2015) that organizes music festivals and events. The company had annual revenue of approximately €357,000 as of 2021.
caseDescription: MAD COOL Festival launched a form to confirm attendee shipping details on 11 April 2023. During a server migration that morning, a 2-second micro-cache was left enabled, allowing users to see other users' personal data when logging in within that window. The incident exposed data of approximately 406 users with certainty during a 30-minute window (14:45–15:15), though potentially up to 827 users had access to the form.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal data. The micro-cache vulnerability resulted from inadequate testing and monitoring protocols, leaving sensitive personal information accessible.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MAD COOL migrated its user data platform to a new server on the same day it launched a confirmation form, failing to disable the server's default micro-cache.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least 406 festival attendees had their names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses exposed to strangers without consent due to the company's failure to verify basic server security.

claimsVsReality.claim: MAD COOL stated the breach posed 'no risk or high risk to the fundamental rights and freedoms' and therefore did not require notification to the AEPD or affected individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The AEPD investigation confirmed that at least 406 individuals' personal data (name, surname, address, phone, email) were definitively exposed without authorization. The data types involved were sensitive enough that notification obligations existed regardless of MAD COOL's unilateral risk assessment.

claimsVsReality.claim: MAD COOL claimed the incident was caused by 'a one-off human error, completely involuntary' during server configuration.
claimsVsReality.reality: The incident stemmed from systemic failures: (1) the decision to perform a critical server migration on the same day as a major form launch without adequate testing; (2) absence of pre-deployment verification protocols to check server parameters like micro-cache settings; and (3) lack of VPN and other standard security controls in the development environment. These reflect organizational negligence, not isolated human error.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate technical and organizational measures in place per audit dated March 2022.
claimsVsReality.reality: Post-breach investigation revealed the absence of VPN protection, inadequate verification procedures for server configurations before production deployment, and insufficient security testing protocols. VPN was only implemented reactively after the breach occurred, demonstrating that pre-breach security posture was inadequate for the risks.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner that ensures adequate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: MAD COOL failed to guarantee confidentiality of personal data during the server migration. A micro-cache configuration error allowed unauthorized users to view other users' personal data for up to 2 seconds per login attempt, exposing 406 users' names, addresses, phone numbers, and emails without their knowledge or consent.
violations: MAD COOL failed to guarantee confidentiality of personal data during the server migration. A micro-cache configuration error allowed unauthorized users to view other users' personal data for up to 2 seconds per login attempt, exposing 406 users' names, addresses, phone numbers, and emails without their knowledge or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires that the controller and processor implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including through pseudonymization, encryption, ability to ensure ongoing confidentiality and integrity, regular testing of security measures, and capacity to restore availability in case of incidents.
