regulatoryFindings.description: MAD COOL did not implement VPN protection for remote access to its development environment prior to the breach. Security measures in place (HTTPS, CSRF protection) were insufficient for internal configuration risks. The company performed a critical server migration without adequate pre-deployment verification protocols to check server parameters such as cache settings, demonstrating negligent risk assessment and management.
violations: MAD COOL did not implement VPN protection for remote access to its development environment prior to the breach. Security measures in place (HTTPS, CSRF protection) were insufficient for internal configuration risks. The company performed a critical server migration without adequate pre-deployment verification protocols to check server parameters such as cache settings, demonstrating negligent risk assessment and management.

outcome: MAD COOL was found to have committed infringements of GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32. Total fines of €3,500 were imposed (€2,000 for Article 5(1)(f) and €1,500 for Article 32), reduced by 20% to €2,800 following early payment on 20 January 2025. The company waived its right to administrative appeal. The resolution is fully enforceable as of notification, though the company may pursue judicial review in administrative courts if desired.
companyNow: MAD COOL Festival continues to operate as an events organizer. Post-breach, the company implemented remedial security measures including VPN protection, enhanced deployment protocols, and additional monitoring systems to prevent similar incidents.
dataType: Name, surname, postal address, telephone number, email address

companyDescription: Private gynecologist operating a medical practice in Greece providing pregnancy monitoring and obstetric care.
companyLongDescription: Private gynecologist operating a medical practice in Greece providing pregnancy monitoring and obstetric care.
caseDescription: A private gynecologist illegally accessed a patient's electronic health record after terminating their professional relationship, obtaining repeated unauthorized access to the patient's health data via the national eHealth system without consent. The physician also failed to provide a complete medical file upon the patient's access request following pregnancy loss and fetal death.
violationSummary: Physician obtained confidential health information after termination of the doctor-patient relationship without authorization, consent, or legitimate basis, violating the duty of medical confidentiality and data protection principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A private gynecologist accessed a former patient's electronic health records 13+ times between October 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: The patient's sensitive health data—including pregnancy status, ultrasounds, blood tests, and genetic information—was repeatedly accessed by a physician who no longer provided care.

claimsVsReality.claim: Physician claimed no medical records were maintained in electronic form due to sensitive data concerns.
claimsVsReality.reality: Physician did maintain complete medical records; only claimed non-retention to avoid providing copies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Physician stated ultrasound images and cardiotocography recordings were already provided to patient during visits.
claimsVsReality.reality: Patient submits that fundamental test results including ultrasound measurements, hormone and blood tests, and the cardiotocography from two days before fetal death were never received.

claimsVsReality.claim: Physician claimed continued access to patient file during October 2021-May 2022 was to 'collect information' for potential handover to next physician.
claimsVsReality.reality: Patient had explicitly terminated the relationship on 13 October 2021; physician had no legitimate basis for 13+ subsequent accesses to monitor for new pregnancy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Physician accessed records only after learning (from third party) that patient was pregnant again.
claimsVsReality.reality: Access logs show 4 accesses between 13-21 October 2021 (immediately after termination), 9 accesses between 22 October 2021-25 January 2022, and 1 access on 31 May 2022—pattern inconsistent with chance discovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Physician accessed patient health data without lawful basis after terminating professional relationship and without patient knowledge or consent
violations: Physician accessed patient health data without lawful basis after terminating professional relationship and without patient knowledge or consent

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 9(1) prohibits processing of special categories of personal data including health data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Physician accessed sensitive health data (pregnancy status, ultrasounds, test results, genetic screening) without proper legal basis or safeguards
violations: Physician accessed sensitive health data (pregnancy status, ultrasounds, test results, genetic screening) without proper legal basis or safeguards

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 9(3) permits processing of health data only by healthcare professionals under professional confidentiality obligations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Physician accessed data after care relationship ended, lacking any continuing professional duty or legitimate healthcare purpose
violations: Physician accessed data after care relationship ended, lacking any continuing professional duty or legitimate healthcare purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Medical Code of Ethics Art. 14 requires physicians to maintain complete medical records and provide copies upon patient request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Physician initially claimed no records existed, then provided incomplete medical file omitting ultrasounds and examination images
violations: Physician initially claimed no records existed, then provided incomplete medical file omitting ultrasounds and examination images

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 grants data subjects the right to access complete personal data processed about them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Physician provided incomplete medical file lacking ultrasound results, hormone tests, blood work, and cardiotocography records that existed at time of request
violations: Physician provided incomplete medical file lacking ultrasound results, hormone tests, blood work, and cardiotocography records that existed at time of request

outcome: The Data Protection Authority found the physician violated GDPR Article 5(1)(a) by accessing the patient's electronic health records without lawful basis after terminating the professional relationship. The Authority determined the physician's claims of collecting information for file handover and subsequent re-engagement were pretextual. The physician was ordered to cease the unlawful processing and comply with GDPR requirements. A monetary penalty of €5,000 was imposed as an effective, proportionate, and deterrent sanction. The decision is final; no evidence was found of data transmission to third parties, and the access right violation was rejected as the documents provided covered the material available at time of request.
dataType: Health data, pregnancy records, ultrasound images, medical test results, genetic mutation screening, blood test results, hormone test results, cardiotocography records
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
GDPR Art. 9(1) – Prohibition on processing special categories of data (health data)
GDPR Art. 9(3) – Lack of proper safeguards for health data processing
Greek Medical Code of Ethics (N. 3418/2005) Art. 14 – Obligation to maintain complete medical records
GDPR Art. 15 – Right of access to personal data

company: REPSOL COMERCIALIZADORA DE ELECTRICIDAD Y GAS S.L.U.
companyDescription: REPSOL S.A. is a multinational energy corporation headquartered in Spain, operating primarily in petroleum, natural gas, and electricity commercialisation. REPSOL COMERCIALIZADORA operates as its regulated tariff and free-market electricity and gas retail subsidiary.
companyLongDescription: REPSOL S.A. is a multinational energy corporation headquartered in Spain, operating primarily in petroleum, natural gas, and electricity commercialisation. REPSOL COMERCIALIZADORA operates as its regulated tariff and free-market electricity and gas retail subsidiary.
caseDescription: REPSOL erred in assigning gas and electricity utility contracts to an existing customer due to a similar name match, then failed to implement adequate security procedures to prevent such errors. The customer received invoices and personal data exposure for services she never requested, and the company's procedures lacked verification controls despite handling thousands of customer records.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures (Article 32 GDPR) to ensure adequate security for the data processing involved in customer identity verification and contract management, resulting in an identifiable individual's data being processed incorrectly.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: REPSOL assigned gas and electricity contracts to an existing customer based solely on name similarity.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer received multiple invoices and had her name, DNI, and consumption data wrongly associated with unknown utility accounts she never contracted.

claimsVsReality.claim: REPSOL stated the error was 'a simple human mistake' and a 'one-off incident' due to similarity of names, and that appropriate security measures were already in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The error resulted from a structural procedural deficiency – the system relied solely on name matching without verifying DNI or other identifiers despite handling thousands of customer records. Post-incident 'fixes' (such as DNI-only searches) do not address the underlying risk that DNI entry errors could also occur, confirming the procedures were inadequate to the risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: REPSOL claimed to have 'appropriate measures' and said the factual cause was merely an error by one agent in identifying the customer.
claimsVsReality.reality: Invoices continued to be issued to the affected customer even after REPSOL became aware of the error, and the company maintained no adequate preventive or detective controls to catch such mix-ups despite the scale of their operations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires that personal data shall be 'accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; all reasonable measures shall be taken to erase or rectify without delay personal data that is inaccurate with respect to the purposes for which it is processed.'
regulatoryFindings.description: REPSOL associated the complainant's personal data (name, surname, DNI) to utility contracts she never requested due to procedural failure to verify all identifying information prior to contract modification.
violations: REPSOL associated the complainant's personal data (name, surname, DNI) to utility contracts she never requested due to procedural failure to verify all identifying information prior to contract modification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires the controller and processor to apply technical and organisational measures appropriate to ensure a level of security adequate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: REPSOL's procedure for contract ownership changes relied on name matching alone without verifying DNI, account details or other identifiers; no sequential verification controls existed despite handling thousands of customer records and foreseeable risk of human error in name-based identification.
violations: REPSOL's procedure for contract ownership changes relied on name matching alone without verifying DNI, account details or other identifiers; no sequential verification controls existed despite handling thousands of customer records and foreseeable risk of human error in name-based identification.

outcome: REPSOL was ordered to pay €1,380,000 total (€130,000 for Article 5(1)(d) violation; €1,250,000 for Article 32 violation). The company must implement improved security procedures including mandatory DNI-based client identification searches, enhanced pre-verification of all customer data prior to contract modifications, and centralised handling of complex cases to prevent human error. REPSOL has committed to design improvements in data blocking and deletion automation. The resolution is enforceable once the optional repositioning appeal period (one month) expires without challenge.
companyNow: REPSOL S.A. is a large multinational energy company, one of Spain's largest corporations. It continues operations as a major electricity and gas commercialiser while under obligation to implement the compliance measures ordered.
dataType: Name, surname, DNI (national ID), telephone, bank account, address, consumption data

companyDescription: CREMA GAMES, S.L. is a Spanish video game developer offering online games. The company processes personal data including IP addresses, MAC addresses, and game user identifiers for players across multiple EU member states.
companyLongDescription: CREMA GAMES, S.L. is a Spanish video game developer offering online games. The company processes personal data including IP addresses, MAC addresses, and game user identifiers for players across multiple EU member states.
caseDescription: CREMA GAMES obstructed a user's right of access under GDPR Article 15 by requesting identification documents containing data it did not possess and could not verify. The company failed to implement proper authentication mechanisms and imposed unnecessary barriers to accessing personal data, denying the subject's access request for months.
violationSummary: The company's identification requirements effectively prevented the data subject from exercising their fundamental GDPR right of access by imposing conditions that were technically impossible for the company to verify and that created unnecessary security risks.
violations: Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: CREMA GAMES repeatedly requested a complete identification document from a user exercising data access rights.
whyTheyWereWrong: The user could not access their own personal data for months because the company demanded a full ID document containing data fields it couldn't verify against its own records.

claimsVsReality.claim: CREMA GAMES stated the game user IDs (IDENTIFICADOR.1 and IDENTIFICADOR.2) are 'anonymous' and not linked to any identifying personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The IDs are pseudonymous, not anonymous, as they are associated with IP addresses, MAC addresses, connection timestamps, and potentially location data that allow identification when combined. The company's own Privacy Policy acknowledged collecting name, address, email, phone, and other personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it could not identify the user without a complete identification document because the user initiated contact only via email.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had sufficient data to verify identity through the game account itself, and GDPR Guidelines permit blocking unnecessary document information before submission. The company's own authentication system (managed by the platform distributor) could have verified ownership of the game accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: CREMA GAMES stated it had 'no intention to obstruct' the access right and was merely requiring 'inequivocal identification' as permitted by RGPD.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's requests for full identification documents it could not verify constituted obstruction; Guidelines 01/2022 explicitly warns that identity document authentication creates security risks and should not be the primary method in online contexts.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and to receive a copy of such data.
regulatoryFindings.description: CREMA GAMES demanded full identification documents containing data elements (national ID number, issue/expiry dates, photograph) it did not possess and could not verify, creating an unnecessary barrier to exercising the access right.
violations: CREMA GAMES demanded full identification documents containing data elements (national ID number, issue/expiry dates, photograph) it did not possess and could not verify, creating an unnecessary barrier to exercising the access right.
The company failed to implement proper digital authentication despite Guidelines 01/2022 (paragraph 66) stating controllers must implement authentication procedures to verify identity online.

The company denied the access request on 27 February 2023, citing insufficient identity verification, despite the subject providing a partially redacted identification document with name, date of birth, country, and signature.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12 requires controllers to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights without undue delay and in an easily accessible manner.
regulatoryFindings.description: CREMA GAMES imposed identification requirements that went beyond what was necessary, as per EDPB Guidelines paragraph 75, which permits blocking unnecessary information before submission to the controller.
violations: CREMA GAMES imposed identification requirements that went beyond what was necessary, as per EDPB Guidelines paragraph 75, which permits blocking unnecessary information before submission to the controller.
The company's insistence on full document identification created a prolonged dispute spanning 67 days (21 January to 27 February 2023) without resolution.

outcome: On 8 May 2024, AEPD initiated a sanctions procedure against CREMA GAMES for violating GDPR Article 15. A penalty of €5,000 was proposed with a 20% reduction for voluntary payment. CREMA GAMES paid €4,000 on 19 March 2025 and agreed to notify AEPD within one month of providing proper access to the claimant's personal data using appropriate authentication mechanisms. The procedure was terminated on payment; compliance with the remedial order is pending.
companyNow: CREMA GAMES' current operational status is unknown. The company is subject to ongoing compliance monitoring under the GDPR Article 58.2(d) order to implement proper authentication procedures.
dataType: IP address, MAC address, game user identifiers, pseudonymous user data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12 (Facilitating the exercise of data subject rights)

companyDescription: EDA TV Consulting, S.L. is a Spanish news media portal (edatv.news) founded in 2020. It operates an online news service and handles user data for account/rights management.
companyLongDescription: EDA TV Consulting, S.L. is a Spanish news media portal (edatv.news) founded in 2020. It operates an online news service and handles user data for account/rights management.
caseDescription: EDA TV required users to submit full photocopies of their national ID documents (DNI) to exercise data subject rights, violating the GDPR data minimization principle. The company collected excessive biometric and identity data far beyond what was necessary for identity verification. This practice exposed users' sensitive identity information unnecessarily.
violationSummary: The company's practice of collecting full ID document scans exceeded necessary data scope for identity verification, storing sensitive biometric and identity information (photos, parent names) that posed unnecessary risk if mishandled or breached. This violates data minimization principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: EDA TV required users to submit full photocopies of their national ID cards (both sides) to exercise GDPR data rights.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users were forced to disclose excessive personal data from ID documents to access their basic GDPR rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: EDA TV claimed requiring full DNI photocopies was a 'reasonable measure' to verify identity per GDPR Recital 64 and was 'compliant with GDPR.'
claimsVsReality.reality: AEPD found alternative methods (partial documents, other identity verification) existed and were equally reliable. Full DNI scans contained unnecessary sensitive data (biometric images, parental names, document numbers) beyond what identification requires, violating Article 5(1)(c) data minimization.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: EDA TV collected full DNI photocopies containing images, document numbers, and parental names from users exercising rights. These elements exceeded what was necessary for identity verification, violating data minimization by collecting disproportionate identity information.
violations: EDA TV collected full DNI photocopies containing images, document numbers, and parental names from users exercising rights. These elements exceeded what was necessary for identity verification, violating data minimization by collecting disproportionate identity information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Recital 64 permits controllers to use 'all reasonable measures' to verify requestor identity in online services, but must apply proportionality.
regulatoryFindings.description: EDA TV justified full DNI collection under Recital 64, but AEPD found alternative verification methods (partial documents, cryptographic verification, other identity proofs) existed and were equally valid, making DNI photocopies unnecessary and disproportionate.
violations: EDA TV justified full DNI collection under Recital 64, but AEPD found alternative verification methods (partial documents, cryptographic verification, other identity proofs) existed and were equally valid, making DNI photocopies unnecessary and disproportionate.

outcome: EDA TV admitted responsibility and paid €3,000 (40% reduction from €5,000 base for early payment + responsibility recognition). AEPD imposed a one-month compliance order requiring EDA TV to implement proportionate identity verification methods compliant with Article 5(1)(c) and to reflect the updated method in its privacy policy. Procedure terminated via settlement under LPACAP Article 85.
companyNow: Unknown. EDA TV is a small media/news portal founded in 2020 with modest revenue. The settlement was finalized in February 2025.
dataType: National ID documents (DNI – scans/copies containing identity images, numbers, parental names)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 4(1) – Definition of Personal Data
GDPR Recital 64 – Reasonable measures for identity verification

companyDescription: NOVATES ALIMENTACIÓN MADRID, S.L. is a Spanish supermarket/food retail operator established in 2017, operating grocery store locations in Madrid with security camera systems.
companyLongDescription: NOVATES ALIMENTACIÓN MADRID, S.L. is a Spanish supermarket/food retail operator established in 2017, operating grocery store locations in Madrid with security camera systems.
caseDescription: A supermarket operator unlawfully shared video surveillance footage of a customer with another employee via WhatsApp without proper security controls. The footage contained identifiable images of multiple customers, and employees accessed and transmitted the recordings without adequate technical and organizational safeguards required under GDPR Article 32.
violationSummary: NOVATES failed to maintain confidentiality of recorded personal data by allowing unauthorized employees to access, copy via mobile devices, and transmit video surveillance footage through unsecured messaging platforms, breaching the duty to protect against unauthorized access and disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: NOVATES employees shared surveillance video footage containing customers' facial images via personal WhatsApp messages without implementing proper security controls or authorization protocols.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least three customers' identifiable faces were transmitted through unsecured personal messaging channels to unauthorized recipients.

claimsVsReality.claim: NOVATES stated it had implemented data protection policies and contracted external data protection consulting services (***EMPRESA.1)
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claimed compliance measures, the company had no effective technical or organizational controls preventing employees from accessing, copying, and sharing surveillance footage via personal mobile devices without authorization

claimsVsReality.claim: NOVATES claimed the customer 'voluntarily provided her phone number and authorized transmission of the video via WhatsApp'
claimsVsReality.reality: Even assuming consent to receive the footage, this does not exempt NOVATES from implementing mandatory security controls preventing unauthorized employee access and initial unauthorized copying/capture of surveillance data by staff

claimsVsReality.claim: NOVATES asserted proper signage was in place informing customers of video surveillance and data security measures
claimsVsReality.reality: Signage alone does not satisfy GDPR Article 32 requirements for technical and organizational security measures; the actual security infrastructure was inadequate

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires data controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security of personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: NOVATES failed to implement access controls preventing staff from viewing, copying and transmitting surveillance video footage without authorization
violations: NOVATES failed to implement access controls preventing staff from viewing, copying and transmitting surveillance video footage without authorization
No security measures restricted which employees could access surveillance recordings or prevented their distribution via personal mobile devices
Video footage was transmitted via unsecured WhatsApp messaging application without encryption or protective controls

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(4) requires that the controller and processor take measures to ensure that any natural person acting under the authority of the controller or processor and having access to personal data only processes such data on instructions from the controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: NOVATES employees accessed and transmitted surveillance footage containing identifiable customer images without documented authorization or instruction protocols
violations: NOVATES employees accessed and transmitted surveillance footage containing identifiable customer images without documented authorization or instruction protocols
No evidence of training, policies, or controls limiting employee access to surveillance system data
Staff member unilaterally decided to share video footage via WhatsApp without oversight mechanisms

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 22 governs video surveillance treatments and requires compliance with data protection security requirements for such processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Video surveillance system lacked adequate technical safeguards to prevent unauthorized access and transmission of recordings
violations: Video surveillance system lacked adequate technical safeguards to prevent unauthorized access and transmission of recordings
No organizational procedures governed which personnel could view, copy, or share surveillance footage
System failed to maintain audit trails or controls over unauthorized sharing via personal devices

outcome: NOVATES recognized responsibility and paid €12,000 (40% reduction applied for early recognition and voluntary payment from initial €20,000 proposal). The company must implement within 1 month appropriate technical and organizational security measures for surveillance data, including access controls, employee authorization protocols, and restrictions on copying/sharing footage. Procedure terminated upon payment and conditional on company's renunciation of administrative remedies.
companyNow: NOVATES ALIMENTACIÓN MADRID, S.L. remains operational as a food/supermarket retailer in Madrid, Spain with 2023 annual revenue of €6,118,562.
dataType: Biometric data - video surveillance footage showing customer images and identifiable faces
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32(1) - Security of Processing (technical and organizational measures)
GDPR Art. 32(4) - Ensuring only authorized persons under data controller instruction can access personal data
LOPDGDD Art. 22 - Video surveillance treatment requirements
LOPDGDD Art. 73(f) - Failure to adopt appropriate security measures

companyDescription: NAROBESA INV, S.L. is a small Spanish enterprise classified as a microenterprise under AXESOR data, founded in 2021, with 2023 revenues of approximately €241,000.
companyLongDescription: NAROBESA INV, S.L. is a small Spanish enterprise classified as a microenterprise under AXESOR data, founded in 2021, with 2023 revenues of approximately €241,000.
caseDescription: NAROBESA INV, S.L. failed to provide requested information to the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) during an investigation into a data protection complaint. The company received two information requests but did not respond to the second request within the prescribed timeframe, obstructing the authority's investigative powers under GDPR Article 58(1).
violationSummary: The violation concerns obstruction of regulatory authority's investigative powers under GDPR Article 58(1), which falls under failure to facilitate access to information needed for enforcement.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: NAROBESA INV, S.L. failed to provide information required by the Spanish Data Protection Authority in response to two separate investigative requests made under Article 58.1 of the GDPR.
whyTheyWereWrong: By refusing to provide the requested information, NAROBESA obstructed the data protection authority's investigation into potential violations of individuals' data rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: NAROBESA claimed in its 7 March 2025 response that it had presented all required documentation on 29 November 2024 with registration number REGAGE24e00089934868.
claimsVsReality.reality: That submission responded only to the first information requirement (notified 15 November 2024), not the second requirement with different content (notified 21 January 2025), to which NAROBESA provided no response.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) grants supervisory authorities investigative powers, including the ability to order controllers and processors to provide any information required for the performance of the authority's functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: NAROBESA failed to respond to a second information requirement issued on 21 January 2025 within the ten working day deadline, obstructing the AEPD's investigation into a data protection complaint.
violations: NAROBESA failed to respond to a second information requirement issued on 21 January 2025 within the ten working day deadline, obstructing the AEPD's investigation into a data protection complaint.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(e) provides that failure to facilitate access in breach of Article 58(1) is a serious infraction punishable by administrative fines.
regulatoryFindings.description: NAROBESA's non-compliance with the information request constituted a failure to facilitate access to information required by the investigative authority.
violations: NAROBESA's non-compliance with the information request constituted a failure to facilitate access to information required by the investigative authority.

outcome: On 29 November 2025, NAROBESA INV, S.L. made voluntary payment of €1,600.00 (the original proposed sanction of €2,000.00 reduced by 20% for early payment). The procedure was terminated upon payment, conditional on the company's waiver of any administrative remedies. The AEPD also ordered NAROBESA to provide the information required under the original investigation (EXP202410265) within ten working days from the date the resolution became final and enforceable.
companyNow: NAROBESA INV, S.L. is a microenterprise incorporated in 2021 with reported business volume of €241,168 in 2023. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Unknown

companyDescription: SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC is a Spanish trade union organization (sindicato). The entity is identified by NIF G61762241.
companyLongDescription: SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC is a Spanish trade union organization (sindicato). The entity is identified by NIF G61762241.
caseDescription: The Spanish Data Protection Authority initiated sanctions proceedings against SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC for failing to comply with information requests issued during a data protection investigation. The union failed to respond to two formal requests for information required under GDPR Article 58.1, obstructing the authority's investigative powers. The company recognized responsibility and paid a reduced fine of €360 following a 40% reduction for voluntary payment and acknowledgment of fault.
violationSummary: The organization's failure to facilitate regulatory access to information and documents constitutes obstruction of data protection enforcement, which falls under insecurity as it prevented proper investigation of underlying data handling practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC failed to respond to two formal information requests from the Spanish Data Protection Authority during an investigation into potential data protection violations.
whyTheyWereWrong: The union's refusal to provide requested information obstructed the regulator's ability to investigate whether personal data was being mishandled.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.1(a) grants data protection authorities the power to order the data controller and processor, and their representatives, to provide any information required for the authority to perform its functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC failed to provide information requested in two formal requerimientos issued by AEPD in the context of investigative proceedings
violations: SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC failed to provide information requested in two formal requerimientos issued by AEPD in the context of investigative proceedings
The organization did not respond despite valid electronic notification and attempted postal delivery to its registered fiscal address
This non-compliance obstructed the authority's investigative powers under GDPR Article 58.1

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(e) provides that failure to facilitate access in violation of Article 58.1 constitutes an infraction subject to administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: The non-response to information requests was classified as a violation of Article 58.1 under Article 83.5(e)
violations: The non-response to information requests was classified as a violation of Article 58.1 under Article 83.5(e)
Initial fine of €600 was proposed; reduced to €360 following voluntary payment and recognition of responsibility

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72.1 classifies failure to facilitate access to data, information, and equipment to data protection authorities as a 'very grave' infraction with a 3-year prescription period.
regulatoryFindings.description: The conduct was classified as a very grave infraction under LOPDGDD Article 72.1(ñ)
violations: The conduct was classified as a very grave infraction under LOPDGDD Article 72.1(ñ)

outcome: The Agencia Española de Protección de Datos issued a final resolution confirming the infraction and imposing a €360 monetary penalty (40% reduction applied for voluntary payment and recognition of responsibility). The organization was ordered to provide the requested information within 10 business days from the date the resolution became final and executable. The resolution is final in the administrative sphere and fully executable as the organization waived any administrative remedies.
companyNow: The organization's current status is not described in the document. SINDICAT CATAC-CTSC is a Spanish trade union that continues to operate.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Mobilewalla is a Delaware data broker that collects, aggregates, and sells vast quantities of consumer location and behavioral information to advertisers, data brokers, analytics firms, and government entities. The company operated primarily from 2018–2022 by collecting location data from real-time bidding exchanges and data suppliers.
companyLongDescription: Mobilewalla is a Delaware data broker that collects, aggregates, and sells vast quantities of consumer location and behavioral information to advertisers, data brokers, analytics firms, and government entities. The company operated primarily from 2018–2022 by collecting location data from real-time bidding exchanges and data suppliers.
caseDescription: Mobilewalla, a data broker, collected and sold precise location data tied to mobile devices that could identify individual consumers and their visits to sensitive locations including medical facilities, places of worship, and LGBTQ+ services. The company collected data from real-time bidding exchanges in violation of their terms, created audience segments targeting consumers based on sensitive characteristics like pregnancy and sexual orientation, and retained this data indefinitely without adequate consumer consent verification.
violationSummary: Mobilewalla collected consumer data from RTB exchanges for non-advertising purposes (government use, union tracking, employee poaching), violating the express prohibition on secondary use in RTB exchange terms. Also qualifies as 'Information Dissemination – Disclosure' (selling sensitive location data) and 'Invasion – Intrusion' (indefinite tracking).
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Mobilewalla collected over 2 billion mobile advertising identifiers paired with precise geolocation data from real-time bidding exchanges without winning bids.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' movements to sensitive locations like abortion clinics, places of worship, and protest sites were tracked.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mobilewalla's data collection from RTB exchanges complied with RTB exchange terms and purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Mobilewalla collected and retained bid request data even without winning bids, violating RTB exchange prohibitions on such collection and use for non-advertising purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mobilewalla's suppliers obtained informed consumer consent to share data with Mobilewalla and for Mobilewalla's uses.
claimsVsReality.reality: Mobilewalla failed to contractually require suppliers to obtain consent, did not verify accuracy of certification claims, and only spot-checked 3–5 apps from suppliers handling thousands, never re-verifying as disclosures changed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mobilewalla's location data was sufficiently anonymized and could not identify individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: Raw location data included MAIDs, precise latitude/longitude, and timestamps; MAIDs are used by data brokers to match offline information (names, addresses); Mobilewalla's CEO stated ability to identify home addresses more accurately due to long-term data retention.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mobilewalla's audience segmentation and tracking practices served only legitimate advertising purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Mobilewalla used location data to create geofences for union organizer tracking, employee poaching, government surveillance, and litigation support unrelated to advertising or consumer consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Collected and sold precise location data identifying visits to sensitive locations (medical facilities, places of worship, LGBTQ+ services, domestic abuse shelters) tied to individual consumers via MAIDs, causing loss of privacy and risk of discrimination, physical violence, and emotional distress.
violations: Collected and sold precise location data identifying visits to sensitive locations (medical facilities, places of worship, LGBTQ+ services, domestic abuse shelters) tied to individual consumers via MAIDs, causing loss of privacy and risk of discrimination, physical violence, and emotional distress.

Created and sold audience segments targeting consumers based on sensitive characteristics (pregnancy, sexual orientation, religious beliefs, political activity) derived from location data, without consumer knowledge or consent.

Collected approximately 77-273 million advertising identifiers paired with location data annually from RTB exchanges even when bids were unsuccessful, violating RTB terms prohibiting such collection and non-advertising use.
Transferred consumer location data to government entities and used location-based tracking to identify union organizers and facilitate employee poaching, for purposes beyond original consent.
Retained sensitive location data indefinitely (5+ years) for all 2+ billion devices, enabling retrospective tracking via geofences and increasing risk of stalking, scams, and reputational harm.

Failed to take reasonable steps to verify consumer consent through data suppliers—only spot-checking 3-5 apps from suppliers collecting from thousands of apps, never re-verifying as disclosures changed.

outcome: Complaint issued by FTC on 13 January 2025. No settlement terms or monetary penalty specified in the complaint document itself. The complaint alleges five counts of unfair practices under FTC Act Section 5(a) and seeks compliance measures. The proceeding remains pending; no final resolution has been issued yet.
companyNow: Mobilewalla's business practices were exposed by news outlets in early 2022, which halted new data collection. The complaint, filed in January 2025, represents formal enforcement action by the FTC against the company's historical practices.
dataType: Location data, Mobile Advertising Identifiers (MAIDs), device information, app names, timestamps, phone numbers, email addresses, IP addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(n) – Unfairness standard (substantial injury not reasonably avoidable)

companyDescription: Apitor Technology Co., Ltd. is a Chinese corporation based in Shenzhen that designs and sells programmable robot toys marketed as STEM/coding education products for children ages 6-14. The company sold products primarily through Amazon and other online retailers, with accompanying mobile apps for iOS and Android.
companyLongDescription: Apitor Technology Co., Ltd. is a Chinese corporation based in Shenzhen that designs and sells programmable robot toys marketed as STEM/coding education products for children ages 6-14. The company sold products primarily through Amazon and other online retailers, with accompanying mobile apps for iOS and Android.
caseDescription: Apitor Technology Co., Ltd. developed and sold programmable robot toys directed to children ages 6-14 with a companion mobile app that secretly collected precise geolocation data from thousands of children under 13 through an integrated third-party SDK (JPush). The company failed to provide required parental notice or obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting this sensitive location information, violating COPPA and the FTC Act.
violationSummary: Covert collection of precise geolocation data through required app permissions constitutes surveillance. Children were unable to use purchased toy without enabling location tracking they could not see or control.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Apitor Technology integrated JPush SDK into its Android app for robot toys marketed to children ages 6-14, which secretly collected precise geolocation data from child users.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of children's precise location coordinates were transmitted to an undisclosed third party without parental knowledge or consent, exposing minors to unauthorized tracking.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apitor's Privacy Policy stated: 'We care about children's privacy. We are committed to complying with the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).'
claimsVsReality.reality: The app secretly collected and transmitted precise geolocation data to third-party JPush servers without parental notice or consent, directly violating COPPA requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy Policy disclosed only app usage data collection ('app profile name, user-created programs, time spent in app') with no uploading to Apitor servers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Geolocation data was actively collected by integrated JPush SDK and transmitted to external servers, undisclosed in privacy documentation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Location permission request message suggested it was necessary for Bluetooth connectivity: 'Enable location information permission for users to connect to the robot using Bluetooth.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Location data had no functional purpose for Bluetooth robot control; it was collected solely for JPush SDK analytics and third-party use.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule § 312.4(b)-(c): Operators of services directed to children must provide clear, understandable, and complete notice of information practices directly to parents.
regulatoryFindings.description: Apitor failed to disclose to parents that geolocation data would be collected by third-party JPush SDK
violations: Apitor failed to disclose to parents that geolocation data would be collected by third-party JPush SDK
Privacy policy did not mention geolocation collection, only listed app usage data
Parents received no direct notice before geolocation collection began

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule § 312.5(a): Operators must obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Apitor never requested or obtained parental consent for geolocation collection
violations: Apitor never requested or obtained parental consent for geolocation collection
App allowed guest use and account creation without any parental consent mechanism
Geolocation data collection occurred automatically upon location permission grant, with no consent step

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule § 312.4(d): Operators must provide sufficient notice on their website or online service of all information they collect online from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Privacy policy claimed COPPA compliance but did not disclose geolocation collection
violations: Privacy policy claimed COPPA compliance but did not disclose geolocation collection
Material omission: third-party JPush SDK geolocation access not mentioned anywhere in privacy disclosures

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act § 45(a): Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce are prohibited.
regulatoryFindings.description: Deceptive: Privacy policy claimed COPPA compliance while secretly enabling third-party location tracking
violations: Deceptive: Privacy policy claimed COPPA compliance while secretly enabling third-party location tracking
Unfair: Geolocation collection required for app functionality but undisclosed, forcing consent through coercion rather than informed choice

outcome: Complaint filed seeking permanent injunction to prevent future COPPA violations, civil penalties for each violation of the COPPA Rule, and other relief. Case is in the United States District Court, Northern District of California. No settlement or final judgment has been entered as of the complaint filing date (September 2, 2025).
companyNow: Chinese toy/robotics company; status post-complaint unknown. Case pending in U.S. District Court as of September 2025.
dataType: Geolocation data (precise location)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act § 45(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: GoDaddy Inc. is a global domain registrar and web hosting company serving approximately 5 million customers worldwide. It provides website hosting, domain name registration, website builders, and related services primarily to small businesses and individuals.
companyLongDescription: GoDaddy Inc. is a global domain registrar and web hosting company serving approximately 5 million customers worldwide. It provides website hosting, domain name registration, website builders, and related services primarily to small businesses and individuals.
caseDescription: GoDaddy, a major web hosting company with ~5 million customers, made security commitments it failed to keep. Since 2018, the company deployed inadequate security tools and practices, leading to multiple breaches (2019-2022) where attackers accessed customer websites, credentials, and sensitive data. GoDaddy's security program was unreasonable for a company its size, leaving it blind to vulnerabilities and threats.
violationSummary: GoDaddy's unreasonable data security program (absence of standard tools, poor monitoring, lack of segmentation) directly caused the processing insecurity that led to multiple compromises of customer personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: GoDaddy failed to implement standard security tools and practices to protect its hosting environment, including asset inventory, security patch management, multi-factor authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 2019 and 2022, attackers repeatedly compromised GoDaddy's servers, stealing approximately 28,000 customer credentials, 1,000 payment card numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: GoDaddy's security team is on the job 24/7 to meticulously monitor, thwart suspicious activity and deflect DDoS attacks.
claimsVsReality.reality: GoDaddy relied on manual ad hoc reviews prior to 2020 and did not deploy SIEM with detection capability until Spring 2020; the first threat actor remained undetected for 6 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data protection, security and privacy are at the core of everything we do.
claimsVsReality.reality: GoDaddy failed to inventory ~435,000 devices, did not centrally track patches, had 30,000 end-of-life vulnerable servers, and lacked file integrity monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: Our monitoring and detection mechanisms are built to prevent threats before they ever impact you or your customers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple attackers compromised the environment and remained undetected; breaches were discovered via customer complaints or external incident response, not internal detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Get peace of mind, knowing network security and DDoS protection is monitored around the clock.
claimsVsReality.reality: GoDaddy had no centralized monitoring, inconsistent logging, and lacked controls like multi-factor authentication and network segmentation until after breaches occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: We've got your back. Our award-winning security team monitors your site around the clock to thwart attackers.
claimsVsReality.reality: GoDaddy was blind to vulnerabilities and threats; the first breach went undetected for 6 months despite attackers replacing application files with malicious versions.

claimsVsReality.claim: GoDaddy has certified compliance with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: GoDaddy did not implement the reasonable and appropriate security measures required by the Privacy Shield Security Principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: GoDaddy failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures, causing substantial injury to consumers (Count I – Unfair Data Security Practices)
violations: GoDaddy failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures, causing substantial injury to consumers (Count I – Unfair Data Security Practices)
GoDaddy represented it used reasonable security measures when it did not (Count II – Data Security Misrepresentations)
GoDaddy certified compliance with Privacy Shield Security Principle but failed to implement required protections (Count III)

outcome: FTC issued a complaint alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act across three counts: unfair data security practices, data security misrepresentations, and false Privacy Shield compliance claims. The complaint was issued in 2025 and marks the initiation of formal enforcement proceedings. Remedies typically include mandatory compliance orders requiring implementation of reasonable security measures, regular third-party audits, and ongoing monitoring.
companyNow: GoDaddy remains one of the world's largest web hosting companies. The FTC complaint is the latest in a series of security incidents that have damaged the company's reputation for security and data protection.
dataType: Customer website data, SSH credentials, email addresses, database credentials, FTP credentials, private encryption keys, payment card numbers, personally identifiable information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework – Security Principle (Principle 4)
Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework – Security Principle (Principle 4)

companyDescription: LastPass UK Limited is a subsidiary of LastPass Ireland Limited, which is part of the LMI Parent, L.P. corporate group that was separated from the GoTo Business in December 2021. LastPass is a market-leading password management and single sign-on solution provider offering encrypted password vaults and identity management services to individuals, small and medium-sized businesses, and enterprises.
companyLongDescription: LastPass UK Limited is a subsidiary of LastPass Ireland Limited, which is part of the LMI Parent, L.P. corporate group that was separated from the GoTo Business in December 2021. LastPass is a market-leading password management and single sign-on solution provider offering encrypted password vaults and identity management services to individuals, small and medium-sized businesses, and enterprises.
caseDescription: LastPass failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures to protect customer personal data, allowing senior employees to access business accounts containing critical encryption keys from unmanaged personal devices. A sophisticated threat actor exploited this weakness, compromised a senior engineer's personal computer via a third-party vulnerability, captured their master password via keylogger malware, and gained access to backup databases containing encrypted customer vault data and unencrypted metadata of over 1.6 million UK users.
companyWorth: Unknown (private company; parent LMI Parent, L.P. reported ~$1.1 billion global turnover in 2024, of which approximately $100-150 million was generated by LastPass Business)
violationSummary: LastPass failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of customer personal data, in direct violation of UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (integrity and confidentiality principle) and Article 32(1)(b) (ongoing confidentiality and integrity of processing systems).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: LastPass allowed senior employees with access to highly confidential corporate credentials to access Employee Business accounts from unmanaged personal devices.
whyTheyWereWrong: A sophisticated threat actor exploited these security failures to access personal devices via a Plex vulnerability, captured master passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: LastPass advertises 'best-in-class encryption' and 'zero knowledge' architecture that protects customers' private data.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the zero knowledge encryption successfully protected the contents of customer vaults, the company's failure to secure the keys and credentials needed to access those vaults, combined with poor employee security practices, allowed a threat actor to access 1.6+ million customers' email addresses, IP addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, and other metadata.

claimsVsReality.claim: LastPass holds multiple third-party security certifications including ISO 27701:2019, ISO 27001:2022, SOC2 Type II, and BSI C5, demonstrating compliance with industry security standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite holding these certifications, LastPass's actual practices (allowing access to business accounts from personal devices, permitting linked account structures, storing encryption keys in employee vaults) violated fundamental principles of these standards and GDPR security requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: The threat actor could not access the sensitive personal data stored in customer vaults because it remained encrypted.
claimsVsReality.reality: While vault data remained encrypted, 1.6+ million customers' plaintext personal identifiers, contact information, and website URLs were exfiltrated, enabling phishing, brute-force attacks, and credential stuffing targeting the exposed individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: LastPass allowed senior employees with access to highly confidential corporate credentials (including encryption keys required to decrypt customer backup databases) to access Employee Business accounts from personal devices on which unverified, potentially insecure third-party applications could be installed.
violations: LastPass allowed senior employees with access to highly confidential corporate credentials (including encryption keys required to decrypt customer backup databases) to access Employee Business accounts from personal devices on which unverified, potentially insecure third-party applications could be installed.
LastPass permitted employees to link Personal and Employee Business accounts so they could be accessed by a single master password, significantly increasing the impact of password compromise.

The decryption key needed to decrypt the AWS SSE-C Key (which protects the Backup Database) was stored in the Employee Business account vault of only four senior developers, accessible from personal devices, creating a single point of failure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(b) UK GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: LastPass failed to implement measures to restrict access to Employee Business accounts containing critical infrastructure credentials to company-managed devices only.
violations: LastPass failed to implement measures to restrict access to Employee Business accounts containing critical infrastructure credentials to company-managed devices only.
LastPass failed to enforce separation of Personal and Employee Business accounts for senior employees with access to highly confidential corporate data.
LastPass did not implement adequate controls to prevent the linking of Personal and Business accounts where the same master password would grant access to both, creating cascading compromise risk.
The infrastructure protecting customer data (backup encryption keys) was accessible from personal devices vulnerable to third-party software exploits.

outcome: LastPass UK Limited was issued a monetary penalty of £1,228,283 by the Information Commissioner (reduced from the initially proposed £2,696,745 due to mitigating factors including LastPass' 'zero knowledge' encryption system which kept customer vault data encrypted even when exfiltrated, and subsequent remediation measures). The penalty requires LastPass to implement comprehensive security reforms including: prohibition of linking Employee Business and Personal accounts; provision of company-issued devices to all employees; implementation of hardware authentication keys (FIDO2) for multi-factor authentication; deployment of endpoint protection, privileged access management, and web filtering solutions; secrets scanning of code repositories; subscriptions to threat intelligence platforms; engagement of phishing takedown services; and additional employee security training. Compliance monitoring is ongoing. LastPass must pay the penalty by 19 December 2025 or face enforcement action in County or High Court.
companyNow: LastPass has implemented significant remediation measures including company-issued laptops and mobile phones for all employees, prohibition of linked Personal/Business accounts, FIDO2 authentication keys for enhanced MFA, deployment of multiple third-party security tools (endpoint protection, privileged access management, vulnerability scanning, secrets scanning, threat intelligence platforms), and phishing takedown services. The company continues to operate and process customer personal data.
dataType: Email addresses, IP addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, website usernames, passwords, secure notes, billing information

companyDescription: INDEPENDENTS DE VALLROMANES (IVALL, NIF G63674006) is a local political party based in Vallromanes, Catalonia, Spain. Limited public information available regarding its budget or operational scale.
companyLongDescription: INDEPENDENTS DE VALLROMANES (IVALL, NIF G63674006) is a local political party based in Vallromanes, Catalonia, Spain. Limited public information available regarding its budget or operational scale.
caseDescription: IVALL published a judicial sentence containing the full name and identifying information of a private citizen on its social media account on 12 May 2021. The published data included complete facts, court details, and other identifying information of persons involved in the case. The party continued to keep the publication accessible even after being ordered by AEPD to remove it, violating the data minimisation principle.
violationSummary: IVALL exposed personal identifying data (names, case facts, court details) on a public social media platform without necessity or justification. This constitutes exposure of sensitive personal information to an unlimited audience.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: INDEPENDENTS DE VALLROMANES published a complete judicial sentence on social media containing the complainant's full name, detailed case facts, court information.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's personal data was publicly exposed on social media without necessity, allowing unlimited online access to sensitive information about their private legal case that could enable.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) establishes that personal data shall be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimisation'). The data controller is responsible for compliance and demonstrating accountability.
regulatoryFindings.description: IVALL published complete judicial sentence containing plaintiff's full name and identifying details without necessity or proportionality
violations: IVALL published complete judicial sentence containing plaintiff's full name and identifying details without necessity or proportionality
The data disclosed (full names, case facts, court details, other parties' identities) exceeded what was required or relevant for information purposes
IVALL failed to apply data minimisation principles in design and execution of the publication

outcome: AEPD imposed a fine of €2,000 on IVALL for violation of GDPR Art. 5(1)(c). The enforcement decision confirmed a provisional measure ordering removal of the judicial sentence from IVALL's social media account. IVALL was given 10 business days from notification to remove the publication and provide proof of compliance. IVALL failed to respond to multiple compliance notices and did not remove the post before the deadline (last verification showed it remained accessible as of 20 September 2024). The resolution is final once the one-month deadline for lodging an optional appeal (recurso de reposición) expires without action. If not appealed, IVALL must pay the €2,000 fine within the statutory payment period.
companyNow: INDEPENDENTS DE VALLROMANES is a political party in Vallromanes, Catalonia. The enforcement indicates it may not have responsive administrative capacity, as it did not acknowledge official notifications from AEPD.
dataType: Personal data from judicial proceedings (names, identities, case details)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 83.5 — Classification as very grave infraction

companyDescription: Blackbaud is a publicly traded cloud-based software-as-a-service company providing solutions for nonprofits, foundations, educational institutions, healthcare organizations, and other entities to manage operations and resources.
companyLongDescription: Blackbaud, founded in 1981, is a major SaaS provider serving over 45,000 customers across more than 100 countries with solutions for resource management, operations delivery, program management, and impact measurement. The company maintains sensitive personal information for its customers' constituents, including names, Social Security numbers, bank account information, and medical data. Despite claims of following industry-standard security practices, the company suffered a significant 2020 data breach affecting over 13,000 customers. Blackbaud is headquartered in Charleston, South Carolina and is a Delaware corporation.
caseDescription: Blackbaud, a cloud-based software company, suffered a 2020 data breach affecting over 13,000 customers including California residents. The company failed to implement reasonable security measures such as multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, and encryption, allowing a threat actor to access and exfiltrate sensitive personal data. Blackbaud further violated consumer protection laws by making false and misleading statements about its security practices both before and after the breach, initially denying that Social Security numbers and bank account information were compromised when it knew or should have known they were.
violationSummary: Blackbaud failed to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect personal information from unauthorized access, including inadequate password controls, lack of multi-factor authentication, poor network segmentation, unencrypted data storage, excessive data retention, and insufficient threat detection mechanisms. This insecurity enabled the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Blackbaud failed to implement reasonable security measures including multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, encryption.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive personal information including Social Security numbers, bank account details, and medical records were stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud's security, privacy, and risk-management teams work every day to ensure the safety of customers' data by adhering to industry standard practices, conducting ongoing risk assessments, aggressively testing security, and continually assessing infrastructure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Blackbaud failed to implement multi-factor authentication, proper password controls, network segmentation, encryption for sensitive fields, adequate data retention policies, and threat detection systems, allowing a threat actor to access systems undetected for four months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud protects its databases with various physical, technical and procedural measures and restricts access to information by unauthorized persons.
claimsVsReality.reality: A threat actor gained entry using a compromised customer login without multi-factor authentication, escalated to administrator access due to lack of network segmentation, and moved across multiple environments to access unencrypted personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The threat actor did not access bank account information or Social Security numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: By early August 2020, Blackbaud knew that bank account information and Social Security numbers had been exfiltrated, but continued making this false statement until late September 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud follows industry-standard best practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Blackbaud lacked reasonable security procedures and practices to protect personal information from unauthorized access or disclosure, as evidenced by the successful breach and multiple critical security gaps.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) requires businesses to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information and to protect it from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement password controls such as mandatory rotation and prohibition of default/weak passwords
violations: Failed to implement password controls such as mandatory rotation and prohibition of default/weak passwords
Failed to mandate multi-factor authentication as a security layer
Failed to implement appropriate network segmentation

Tilting Point Media integrates third-party software development kits (SDKs) into its games to monetize user data. caseDescription: Tilting Point Media violated COPPA and CCPA by collecting personal information from children under 13 and teens aged 13-15 without proper parental consent, failing to provide adequate notice, and selling/sharing children's data through software development kits (SDKs) in games featuring SpongeBob SquarePants and other apps directed to children.

outcome: Tilting Point Media agreed to a permanent injunction and settlement requiring: (1) payment of $500,000 ($250,000 to California Attorney General, $250,000 to Los Angeles City Attorney) plus $10,079.66 cost recovery paid over 3 years; (2) comprehensive compliance program including determination of apps directed to children, implementation of verifiable parental consent for children under 13 and opt-in mechanisms for teens 13-15; (3) data minimization requirements restricting collection to only necessary information; (4) SDK governance framework with annual assessments; (5) implementation of neutral age screens with appropriate data handling; (6) enhanced advertising compliance using commercially reasonable measures; (7) annual compliance assessments and reporting to California authorities for 3 years; (8) training of employees on data minimization and SDK configuration; (9) all apps featuring SpongeBob SquarePants designated as directed to children; (10) CEO certification of third-party compliance reports if used.

companyLongDescription: RivX Automation Corp., based in Doral, Florida, was the primary vehicle for a coordinated fraud scheme operated by Antonio Rivodo (Founder/CEO) and Noah Wooten (Vice President). The enterprise used multiple interrelated LLC and corporate entities to market and sell fake trucking automation business opportunities to consumers nationwide. Defendants falsely promised that consumers investing $75,000-$85,000+ would receive trucks, logistics management, load booking services, and $5,000-$7,000 monthly passive income, with full investment recovery within 12-24 months. In reality, consumers received neither trucks nor promised earnings, losing their entire investments while operators extracted millions in profits and used non-disparagement clauses to silence complaints.
caseDescription: RivX engaged in a multi-year scheme to defraud consumers by falsely promising $5,000-$7,000 monthly passive income through trucking business opportunities in exchange for $75,000-$85,000+ investments. Defendants made millions in profits while failing to disclose required information and using non-disparagement clauses to silence complaints.

caseDescription: L.A.D.H Limited, a financial services company, sent 31,329 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages between March and April 2022 promoting debt advice services without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients. The company relied on verbal assurances from a third-party data supplier rather than written confirmation that recipients had opted in, and most messages lacked opt-out mechanisms. The company failed to cooperate with the ICO's investigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A DPA 1998 authorises monetary penalties for serious contraventions of PECR where the contravention was deliberate or where the organisation knew or ought to have known of the risk but failed to take reasonable steps.

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £50,000 (reducible to £40,000 with early payment by 12 February 2024). LADH was required to pay by 13 February 2024. The penalty was issued under Section 55A of the Data Protection Act 1998 for serious contraventions of PECR Regulations 22 and 23. LADH has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The company is subject to monitoring and compliance expectations under PECR.

caseDescription: BBVA bank branch employee forged customer signatures on data protection documents without consent, falsely marking consent boxes for marketing and profiling. The bank acknowledged the isolated procedural breach and agreed to preventive measures. BBVA paid a reduced penalty of €120,000 after recognizing responsibility.
violationSummary: The failure to obtain genuine, informed consent through proper signature procedures represents a breakdown in data controller security and procedural integrity, exposing personal data to unauthorized processing.

whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal data was unlawfully processed for marketing and profiling without their genuine consent, exposing them to unwanted commercial communications.

violations: BBVA processed personal data of the complainant and spouse without valid consent basis because signatures on consent documents were forged by branch staff, rendering purported consent invalid.

violations: Processing was neither transparent nor fair; customers did not authorize their signatures and were unaware their personal data was being processed for commercial and profiling purposes.

outcome: BBVA acknowledged responsibility and paid €120,000 (40% reduction from initial €200,000 for prompt payment and admission). The bank implemented corrective measures including staff retraining videos distributed to 12,617 commercial banking employees and 2,602 central service staff, annual quality audits of tablet signatures (750 reviews/month), office visits to ~1,000 branches annually, and internal audit procedures. Procedure investigated by Internal Audit; findings elevated to Discipline Committee. Mandatory awareness notices issued in March 2024 and planned for May 2024. The enforcement action terminated on 17 December 2024.
