whatTheyDid: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL failed to implement adequate security measures for its electronic banking platform, allowing attackers to access thousands of customers' personal, contact.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of the bank's customers lost control over their personal and financial data, exposing them to identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed that adequate security measures were in place and cited security certifications held by its processor (RSI).
claimsVsReality.reality: The Ruralvía Clásica application lacked multi-factor authentication and other controls adequate to protect against credential-based attacks. Security certifications in information security are distinct from GDPR compliance certifications and do not guarantee protection of fundamental rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company and processor asserted that attackers required legitimate credentials to access data, suggesting the breach was inevitable.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was responsible for implementing security measures appropriate to the risk level. Inadequate controls allowing credential-based attacks to succeed represent a failure of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, regardless of attack method.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed to have conducted audits and held security certifications, demonstrating compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite audits and certifications in information security standards, the company failed to implement adequate measures to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of personal data, particularly multi-factor authentication for a financial application accessible via the internet.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that guarantees appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures for the Ruralvía Clásica application, allowing attackers to access customer data through credential-based attacks between November and December 2022.
violations: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures for the Ruralvía Clásica application, allowing attackers to access customer data through credential-based attacks between November and December 2022.
The company did not implement multi-factor authentication or other controls adequate to the risk level despite handling thousands of customers' financial data accessible via the internet.
Security audits performed before the breach identified vulnerabilities that were not remediated before the attack occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including capacity to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's legacy banking system lacked adequate access controls and multi-factor authentication despite handling sensitive financial data at scale.
violations: The company's legacy banking system lacked adequate access controls and multi-factor authentication despite handling sensitive financial data at scale.
Although the company contracted with a processor (RSI) to implement security measures, it failed in its supervisory obligation to ensure those measures were appropriate and effective.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33 requires controllers to notify supervisory authorities of data breaches without undue delay and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: This charge was archived during proceedings; the company demonstrated it had instructed its processor to notify the AEPD and that notification occurred within required timeframes.
violations: This charge was archived during proceedings; the company demonstrated it had instructed its processor to notify the AEPD and that notification occurred within required timeframes.

outcome: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL S.C.C. was ordered to pay €90,000 in fines for violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The company availed itself of a 20% voluntary payment reduction, resulting in a final penalty of €72,000, paid on 20 December 2024. The fine was imposed as the company failed to maintain adequate security measures protecting customer data. Charges under Articles 32 and 33 were archived. The case was terminated following the company's voluntary payment and waiver of administrative appeals.
companyNow: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL S.C.C. is a Spanish cooperative credit entity and part of the Caja Rural banking group. Following the enforcement action, the company is required to implement enhanced security measures and ongoing compliance monitoring.
dataType: Personal data, contact information, financial data including bank account details and transaction history
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of Data Breach

companyDescription: Kent Police is the local law enforcement agency responsible for policing Kent, England. It operates under the supervision of the Kent Police and Crime Commissioner and is subject to UK data protection and law enforcement regulations.
companyLongDescription: Kent Police is the local law enforcement agency responsible for policing Kent, England. It operates under the supervision of the Kent Police and Crime Commissioner and is subject to UK data protection and law enforcement regulations.
caseDescription: A Kent Police officer photographed an individual's identity document on a personal mobile phone and uploaded it to Telegram, a messaging app used by multiple police forces and international law enforcement for vehicle crime investigation. The officer did not inform the data subject of further processing, purpose, or how their data would be used. Kent Police failed to adequately inform staff of data protection responsibilities and lacked sufficient policies governing personal device use for official duties.
violationSummary: Personal data was disclosed to unauthorised recipients (international law enforcement on social media) without data subject knowledge or consent, and stored insecurely on third-party servers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A Kent Police officer photographed an individual's identity document using a personal mobile phone and uploaded it to Telegram, a social media application shared by 25 Kent officers.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unknown number of individuals' identity documents were exposed on an unencrypted social media platform with international access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telegram use was not officially sanctioned by Kent Police and the app was blocked on official devices
claimsVsReality.reality: 25 officers had downloaded the app onto personal devices and were active members of the distribution group; two officers held admin rights; the group had been in sustained use for years without management detection

claimsVsReality.claim: Only five officers had previously used Telegram to share personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: At least 25 officers were group members with capability to share; full extent of data sharing prior to investigation discovery could not be determined

claimsVsReality.claim: Officers needed to make operational decisions and personal devices were permitted for limited scenarios (recording incidents, photography, sensitive calls)
claimsVsReality.reality: Officers used personal devices to upload identity documents to international social media without operational justification or authorisation

claimsVsReality.claim: Data protection policies and training were in place
claimsVsReality.reality: Policies existed but failed to adequately communicate that personal device use for official data processing was prohibited; sustained group use undetected indicates training was ineffective

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40: Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed with appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kent Police failed to ensure personal data (identity documents) was processed with appropriate security measures
violations: Kent Police failed to ensure personal data (identity documents) was processed with appropriate security measures
Data was uploaded to Telegram, a social media application, without adequate encryption or access controls
Data was stored on Telegram servers hosted internationally, creating uncontrolled access risks
Personal devices were used to process law enforcement data without adequate technical or organisational safeguards
No policy existed to prevent or restrict use of personal devices for official data processing
Supervisory oversight failed to detect sustained misuse of unsanctioned apps by 25 officers over significant period

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to the Chief Constable of Kent Police under DPA 2018 Schedule 13(2)(c) and UK GDPR Article 58(2)(b) for infringement of Section 40. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps taken: incident reported to ICO and originating organisation; officers instructed to cease use; disciplinary action imposed on identified officers. The ICO issued four recommendations: (1) regularly review ICT Acceptable Use Policy with clear guidance on personal device use; (2) enhance procedure for policy distribution with documented compliance monitoring; (3) expand data protection training to include acceptable personal device use and real incident examples; (4) provide force-wide guidance on social media app compliance. Kent Police invited to update ICO on implementation progress. No monetary penalty imposed but failure to rectify infringements may be treated as aggravating factor in future enforcement action.
companyNow: Kent Police remains the primary law enforcement agency for Kent, England. Following this incident, the force has implemented corrective measures and is subject to ICO monitoring regarding data protection compliance.
dataType: Identity documents, personal identification data
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 (sixth data protection principle – security)
UK GDPR Article 58(2)(b) (authority to issue reprimand)

companyDescription: Avanza Bank AB is a Swedish digital bank and online investment broker offering trading, savings, and banking services. The company operates primarily through digital channels and web/mobile applications.
companyLongDescription: Avanza Bank AB is a Swedish digital bank and online investment broker offering trading, savings, and banking services. The company operates primarily through digital channels and web/mobile applications.
caseDescription: Avanza Bank AB unintentionally activated two advanced tracking functions (AAM and AH) within Meta's pixel tracking tool between November 2019 and June 2021, causing approximately 500,000–1,000,000 customer personal records to be transmitted to Meta without authorization. The data included highly sensitive information such as personal identity numbers, account details, loan amounts, and securities holdings. The bank failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to prevent this unauthorized disclosure, and was unaware of the ongoing data transfers for over 18 months until notified externally.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to implement adequate technical and organizational safeguards resulted in unauthorized disclosure of confidential banking information to Meta, a third party. Statutory banking secrecy obligations were breached, and personal data were exposed through inadequate security.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Avanza Bank deployed Meta-pixel tracking on its website and app without adequate security controls, allowing two automated data-transfer functions to activate without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 500,000 and 1 million customers had their personal identity numbers, account numbers, loan amounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank claimed it had formalized routines and documented procedures to ensure proper data protection before implementing new features.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these documented procedures, the bank failed to follow them when implementing Meta-pixel functions, resulting in unauthorized activation of two tracking functions without the knowledge of the data controller.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank stated the two functions (AAM and AH) were activated accidentally and that it was not possible to verify how or by whom they were activated.
claimsVsReality.reality: The failure to verify activation occurred because the bank did not document the implementation of these features in accordance with its own stated protocols, leaving no audit trail.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank asserted that the data transmitted posed no risk because Meta did not use the information for its own purposes and eventually deleted the data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data remained exposed and accessible to Meta for over 18 months; the unauthorized transmission itself constituted a breach of banking secrecy and GDPR security obligations regardless of Meta's eventual deletion.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Avanza Bank transmitted approximately 500,000–1,000,000 customer records containing identity numbers, account details, loan amounts, and other highly sensitive financial information to Meta without authorization over 18 months.
violations: Avanza Bank transmitted approximately 500,000–1,000,000 customer records containing identity numbers, account details, loan amounts, and other highly sensitive financial information to Meta without authorization over 18 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires data controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to follow its own formalized data protection protocols when Meta-pixel functions were activated, lacked systematic monitoring to detect unauthorized data transfers, and had no controls to identify unintended configuration changes to third-party scripts.
violations: Bank failed to follow its own formalized data protection protocols when Meta-pixel functions were activated, lacked systematic monitoring to detect unauthorized data transfers, and had no controls to identify unintended configuration changes to third-party scripts.

regulatoryFindings.act: Swedish Banking Act § 1 kap. 10 prohibits unauthorized disclosure of information concerning a customer's dealings with a credit institution.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank disclosed detailed customer financial information (account numbers, loan amounts, credit limits, securities holdings) to Meta through inadequate security controls on tracking tools.
violations: Bank disclosed detailed customer financial information (account numbers, loan amounts, credit limits, securities holdings) to Meta through inadequate security controls on tracking tools.

outcome: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (Swedish Data Protection Authority) determined that Avanza Bank AB violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) by failing to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures. The bank was ordered to pay an administrative fine of 15,000,000 SEK. The decision found the breach serious enough to constitute violation of both the integrity principle and the security requirement. Meta confirmed deletion of transferred data. Avanza implemented additional governance documents, enhanced third-party script management processes, and established monitoring for data exfiltration. The decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Avanza Bank AB continues to operate as a Swedish digital bank and online broker. Following the regulatory decision, the company has strengthened its data protection and information security governance frameworks.
dataType: Financial data, account numbers, loan amounts, credit limits, securities holdings, personal identity numbers, contact information, employment details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
Swedish Complementary GDPR Act § 3 kap. 10 (Personal identity numbers)

companyDescription: Quick Tax Claims Limited is a tax claims service provider registered in Manchester, UK (Companies House Reg. No. 14377745). The company operated a direct marketing campaign via SMS using purchased lead lists without obtaining valid consumer consent.
companyLongDescription: Quick Tax Claims Limited is a tax claims service provider registered in Manchester, UK (Companies House Reg. No. 14377745). The company operated a direct marketing campaign via SMS using purchased lead lists without obtaining valid consumer consent.
caseDescription: Quick Tax Claims Limited transmitted 4.98 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages between February and May 2023 without valid recipient consent, violating PECR Regulations 22 and 23. The company failed to obtain freely-given, specific, and informed consent, and did not provide valid opt-out mechanisms. The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring immediate compliance with PECR within 30 days.
violationSummary: QTC conducted direct marketing surveillance via SMS without consent, collecting and using phone numbers for unsolicited commercial contact, which is a form of privacy-intrusive information collection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Quick Tax Claims Limited transmitted 4,983,499 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers between February.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 5 million subscribers received intrusive marketing texts they never clearly consented to.

claimsVsReality.claim: Leads arranged as 'single use' means subscribers will not receive multiple messages from QTC
claimsVsReality.reality: 7726 spam complaints data documented 50 instances where subscribers received multiple messages from QTC with no opt-out option

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent obtained from data suppliers was valid and informed
claimsVsReality.reality: Consent was conditioned on service access (not freely-given), obtained from vague lists of dozens of companies (not specific), and users could not have seen QTC named in privacy policies at time of consent (not informed)

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: QTC transmitted 4,983,499 unsolicited SMS messages without valid prior consent from recipients
violations: QTC transmitted 4,983,499 unsolicited SMS messages without valid prior consent from recipients
Consent obtained was not freely-given (made conditional on service access), specific (vague lists of dozens of companies), or informed (privacy policy language unclear)

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23(b) requires a valid address where recipients may request cessation of direct marketing communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: 93% of SMS messages lacked a valid opt-out mechanism
violations: 93% of SMS messages lacked a valid opt-out mechanism
50 instances documented where subscribers received multiple messages from QTC with no opt-out option provided, despite company claim that leads were 'single use'

outcome: The ICO issued a binding Enforcement Notice dated 26 September 2024 requiring Quick Tax Claims Limited to cease all unsolicited direct marketing via electronic mail within 30 days, except where valid freely-given and specific consent exists. The notice mandates compliance with PECR Regulations 22 and 23, including providing valid opt-out mechanisms. QTC has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. No monetary penalty was issued; compliance is mandatory.
dataType: Phone numbers (SMS recipients)
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 22(2) – unsolicited direct marketing communications
PECR Regulation 23(b) – failure to provide valid opt-out mechanism

companyDescription: Penny Appeal is a UK-registered charity supporting vulnerable populations in crisis situations. The organisation collects donations and maintains donor databases for fundraising and direct marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: Penny Appeal is a UK-registered charity supporting vulnerable populations in crisis situations. The organisation collects donations and maintains donor databases for fundraising and direct marketing purposes.
caseDescription: Penny Appeal transmitted 461,650 unsolicited direct marketing emails to individual subscribers without obtaining valid prior consent, contrary to PECR Regulation 22. The organisation could not evidence that recipients had freely, specifically, and informedly consented to receive marketing messages. Messages were sent to donors who had explicitly opted out of marketing communications.
violationSummary: Unsolicited electronic direct marketing communications without prior explicit consent constitute surveillance-based marketing targeting of individuals without their knowledge or agreement.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between April 22 and May 1, 2022, Penny Appeal transmitted and instigated transmission of approximately 461,650 unsolicited direct marketing emails to 52,179 customers without valid consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of subscribers received marketing emails they had never consented to, including donors who had explicitly opted out, causing unwanted invasions of their email accounts and privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Penny Appeal could rely on existing customer relationships to send marketing emails without separate consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 22(2) requires explicit prior notification of consent for unsolicited direct marketing; soft opt-in exemption (Reg 22(3)) does not apply to non-commercial charity fundraising, and Penny Appeal held no valid consent evidence.

claimsVsReality.claim: Marketing emails sent to opted-in customers were legitimately targeted.
claimsVsReality.reality: Messages were sent to 52,179 customers including donors who had explicitly opted out of marketing from Penny Appeal; no valid consent was obtained or evidenced.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission or instigation of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail to individual subscribers unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent for such communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: Penny Appeal transmitted 461,650 unsolicited marketing emails without prior explicit consent from recipients.
violations: Penny Appeal transmitted 461,650 unsolicited marketing emails without prior explicit consent from recipients.
No evidence of freely given, specific, informed consent as required by UK GDPR Article 4(11).
Messages sent to donors who had explicitly opted out of marketing from Penny Appeal.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(3) permits direct marketing only where contact details were obtained in course of sale/negotiation, marketing concerns similar products/services only, and recipient given simple means to refuse at collection and with each subsequent communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Penny Appeal could not demonstrate compliance with soft opt-in exemption conditions.
violations: Penny Appeal could not demonstrate compliance with soft opt-in exemption conditions.
No evidence that opt-out mechanism was provided to recipients at initial collection or with each communication.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40(1)(a) empowers the Commissioner to serve enforcement notices if satisfied a person has contravened requirements of the Regulations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Commissioner satisfied Penny Appeal contravened PECR through systematic transmission of 461,650 non-consensual marketing emails.
violations: Commissioner satisfied Penny Appeal contravened PECR through systematic transmission of 461,650 non-consensual marketing emails.

outcome: ICO issued an Enforcement Notice (dated 18 April 2024, varied pursuant to DPA 1998 Section 41(1)) requiring Penny Appeal to cease transmission and instigation of unsolicited direct marketing emails within 30 days, except where: (1) circumstances under PECR Regulation 22(3) or other legal exemption apply, or (2) recipient has previously notified Penny Appeal of ongoing consent. No monetary penalty imposed. Commissioner determined damage unlikely despite contravention severity. Right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) available.
companyNow: Penny Appeal continues to operate as a UK-registered charity (Companies House No. 06578382). The Enforcement Notice requires immediate cessation of non-consensual direct marketing or compliance with PECR exemptions.
dataType: Email addresses, phone numbers

companyDescription: West Midlands Police is a statutory police force serving the West Midlands region of England. It processes personal data for law enforcement purposes including criminal investigations, victim protection, and safeguarding.
companyLongDescription: West Midlands Police is a statutory police force serving the West Midlands region of England. It processes personal data for law enforcement purposes including criminal investigations, victim protection, and safeguarding.
caseDescription: West Midlands Police incorrectly linked and merged the personal data records of two individuals with the same name and date of birth on multiple occasions from January 2020 onwards. This resulted in inaccurate data being processed, leading to officers attending the wrong addresses and disclosing sensitive information. The force failed to maintain adequate records of incidents, implement proper technical safeguards, and provide sufficient employee training.
violationSummary: The core failure involves inadequate technical and organisational measures to prevent inaccurate data merging, resulting in security breaches (disclosure to wrong recipient) and inability to maintain data accuracy, falling squarely under information processing insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: West Midlands Police incorrectly merged and linked personal data records of two individuals with identical names.
whyTheyWereWrong: One individual received a letter disclosing another person's victim assault information, and officers conducted home visits.

claimsVsReality.claim: WMP had systems and processes in place to accurately manage and distinguish between records of individuals with similar identifiers
claimsVsReality.reality: Records of two identically-named individuals were repeatedly and incorrectly merged without clear technical or organisational safeguards to prevent or quickly identify such errors

claimsVsReality.claim: Adding system notes and manually unlinking records would prevent future incidents
claimsVsReality.reality: These remedial actions proved ineffective; records continued to be incorrectly linked and merged despite multiple instances of manual intervention

claimsVsReality.claim: WMP could track and manage security incidents and inaccurate data processing
claimsVsReality.reality: Inadequate record-keeping meant WMP could not determine the true number of times records were incorrectly linked, when incidents occurred, which employees were involved, or the full extent of inappropriate disclosures

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 34(3): The controller in relation to personal data is responsible for, and must be able to demonstrate, compliance with the data protection principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: WMP failed to demonstrate adequate records and systems to ensure accuracy and security of personal data relating to the two individuals
violations: WMP failed to demonstrate adequate records and systems to ensure accuracy and security of personal data relating to the two individuals
Inadequate record-keeping and incident management prevented WMP from monitoring and rectifying non-compliance

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 38(1): Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be accurate, kept up to date, and inaccurate data must be erased or rectified without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Information relating to one individual was incorrectly linked to the other's record on numerous occasions throughout 2020-2022
violations: Information relating to one individual was incorrectly linked to the other's record on numerous occasions throughout 2020-2022
WMP unable to demonstrate inaccurate data was rectified without delay; some records remain incorrectly merged
True number and duration of inaccuracies unknown due to inadequate record-keeping

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 38(3): A clear distinction must be made between personal data relating to different categories of data subject (suspects, convicted persons, victims, witnesses).
regulatoryFindings.description: One individual known as a crime victim while the other was both a suspect and victim; incorrect linking prevented clear distinction between these categories
violations: One individual known as a crime victim while the other was both a suspect and victim; incorrect linking prevented clear distinction between these categories

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 40: Personal data processed for law enforcement must be processed with appropriate security using technical and organisational measures to prevent unauthorised processing, loss, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Letter disclosing victim assault information sent to wrong individual on 12 July 2022
violations: Letter disclosing victim assault information sent to wrong individual on 12 July 2022
Multiple incidents involving actual or potential inappropriate disclosure; WMP unable to determine full extent due to inadequate records
Failed to demonstrate personal data kept secure across incidents affecting both individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 57(1): Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data protection principles effectively.
regulatoryFindings.description: Testing and risk assessment of new systems failed to prevent inaccurate merging of records
violations: Testing and risk assessment of new systems failed to prevent inaccurate merging of records
Manual editing tool needed to separate merged records not developed in timely manner, delaying rectification
Employees not provided clear policies and procedures for system use; mandatory training completion only 30-35% of workforce
Inadequate records prevented identifying affected employees for refresher training following incidents

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to West Midlands Police for violations of DPA 2018 sections 34(3), 38(1), 38(3), 40, and 57(1). No monetary penalty was imposed. WMP was required to implement remedial steps including: maintaining adequate processing records and governance measures; distinguishing and preventing future merging of the two individuals' records by completing technical changes to unmerge records on relevant systems; sharing security incident learnings organisation-wide; ensuring all employees complete mandatory data protection training and system-specific training; and implementing an action plan to improve refresher training completion rates. WMP submitted representations on 16 January 2024 confirming progress on these recommendations. A further progress update was requested within six months of the reprimand date.
companyNow: West Midlands Police remains a large regional police force serving the West Midlands region. The force is implementing governance and technical improvements to address data protection compliance gaps identified in the reprimand.
dataType: Criminal records, victim data, suspect data, witness information, personal identifiers, address information

companyDescription: Cortina Watch Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based retailer specializing in the import, export, and retail of timepieces, branded pens, and luxury accessories.
companyLongDescription: Cortina Watch Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based retailer specializing in the import, export, and retail of timepieces, branded pens, and luxury accessories.
caseDescription: Cortina Watch experienced a ransomware attack via a compromised VPN testing account between April–June 2023, leading to the exfiltration and public posting of 3,953 individuals' personal data. The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements, including multi-factor authentication, strong password policies, and proper access controls on privileged accounts. Despite prompt remedial action post-breach, the company was found in breach of section 24 of Singapore's PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession/control, specifically inadequate access controls, weak authentication, and lack of encryption, leading to unauthorised access and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Cortina Watch failed to implement multi-factor authentication for VPN accounts, enforce strong password complexity requirements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data of 3,953 customers including names, contact numbers, addresses, identification numbers, and bank account details were stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had reasonable security arrangements in place to protect personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: Security arrangements were inadequate: VPN testing accounts were not properly managed, MFA was not implemented on privileged accounts despite being an established baseline requirement, password policies were weak, and data was not encrypted

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for VPN accounts with remote access to personal data, despite this being established as a baseline requirement in Lovebonito Singapore Pte. Ltd. [2022] SGPDPC 3 published before the Incident
violations: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for VPN accounts with remote access to personal data, despite this being established as a baseline requirement in Lovebonito Singapore Pte. Ltd. [2022] SGPDPC 3 published before the Incident

Failed to enforce a strong password policy, requiring only 8 characters minimum without alphanumeric complexity, contrary to Commission guidance recommending 12 alphanumeric characters with mixed case, numeric, and special characters
Failed to implement proper 'housekeeping' and access controls on test VPN user accounts, allowing a brute force attack to compromise the 'test' VPN account and gain lateral access across servers
Failed to secure personal data with encryption, leaving stored data vulnerable to exfiltration once network access was compromised

outcome: The Commission declined to impose a monetary penalty in lieu of remedial actions already undertaken and the organisation's cooperation. Instead, the Commission directed Cortina Watch to: (1) engage a third-party cyber security vendor to conduct a targeted security audit to enhance access control to personal data within its network, and (2) complete this Direction within 60 days and submit a comprehensive report to PDPC within 7 days of completion. The organisation implemented multiple remedial measures post-breach including endpoint detection tools, centralised logging, certificate-based VPN authentication with 2FA, firewall VPN access with 2FA, decommissioning legacy Windows Server 2008 R2, hardened network environments with mandatory password complexity, folder/file encryption, and managed backup services.
dataType: Full names, contact numbers, addresses, email addresses, dates of birth, NRIC/passport numbers, bank account numbers
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24(a) – Protection of personal data

companyDescription: InMarket Media is a digital marketing platform and data aggregator that collects consumer location data through a proprietary SDK embedded in mobile apps, purchases additional consumer data from third parties, and uses this combined data to create targeted advertising audiences for brands and advertising agencies.
companyLongDescription: InMarket Media is a digital marketing platform and data aggregator that collects consumer location data through a proprietary SDK embedded in mobile apps, purchases additional consumer data from third parties, and uses this combined data to create targeted advertising audiences for brands and advertising agencies.
caseDescription: InMarket Media collected precise location data from approximately 100 million unique devices annually through its SDK and apps without adequately disclosing it would be used for targeted advertising and audience profiling. The company failed to obtain informed consent in its own apps (CheckPoints and ListEase) and failed to verify that third-party apps incorporating its SDK obtained proper consumer consent. Additionally, InMarket retained sensitive location data for up to five years—far longer than necessary for its stated purposes.
violationSummary: InMarket conducted systematic, ongoing surveillance of consumer location at high frequency (from idle to every few seconds), tracking sensitive movements over time and across multiple apps without transparent disclosure or meaningful consent. This constitutes mass surveillance under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Collected precise location data from approximately 100 million devices annually through software embedded in over 300 third-party apps and two proprietary apps (CheckPoints.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers using CheckPoints and ListEase were told their location data would only be used for earning rewards or shopping reminders.

claimsVsReality.claim: CheckPoints app: 'Allow CheckPoints to access your location? This allows us to award you extra points for walking into stores.' (iOS) and 'CheckPoints finds nearby earning opportunities by using your device's location' (Android).
claimsVsReality.reality: InMarket used location data not just for earning points, but to build detailed consumer profiles tracking where users live, work, worship, receive medical care, and attend protests. This data was combined with purchased demographic information and used for targeted advertising across third-party platforms. Data was retained for up to 5 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: ListEase app: 'Allow ListEase to use your location? Uses location so you don't forget items on your list when you are at the store.' (iOS) and 'Allow Location Permissions to unlock reminders. Get a reminder when you're in the store so you never forget to grab the items you need!' (Android).
claimsVsReality.reality: Location data was collected multiple times per hour (regardless of store proximity) and shared with InMarket for creation of advertising audiences based on consumer movement patterns, income level, family structure, religion, and predicted behavior. Data was retained for 5 years and made available on real-time bidding platforms.

claimsVsReality.claim: Third-party app example: 'Your location is used to provide you with rewards and discounts when you visit retail partners.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Location data was collected continuously multiple times per day and shared with InMarket, which combined it with other data sources, created detailed consumer profiles, and used it to target advertising without user knowledge that a third party (InMarket) was amassing and monetizing their movement data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.'
regulatoryFindings.description: InMarket represented that CheckPoints and ListEase would use location only for awarding points and list reminders, but actually used it for targeted advertising and consumer profiling without disclosure.
violations: InMarket represented that CheckPoints and ListEase would use location only for awarding points and list reminders, but actually used it for targeted advertising and consumer profiling without disclosure.
InMarket failed to disclose to CheckPoints and ListEase users that location data would be used for advertising, supplemented with purchased data, shared with third parties, and retained for 5 years.
InMarket failed to verify that third-party apps incorporating its SDK obtained informed consumer consent for its use of location data for advertising.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines unfairness as acts causing substantial injury to consumers that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that are not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: InMarket's collection of location data without disclosure caused substantial loss of privacy about day-to-day movements of millions of consumers and increased risk of disclosure of sensitive information (home, workplace, places of worship, medical facilities, protests).
violations: InMarket's collection of location data without disclosure caused substantial loss of privacy about day-to-day movements of millions of consumers and increased risk of disclosure of sensitive information (home, workplace, places of worship, medical facilities, protests).
InMarket's retention of location data for 5 years exposed consumers to unnecessary risk of data breach, misuse, and re-identification without consumer awareness or ability to avoid.
Consumers could not reasonably avoid the injury because they were not aware of the scope of InMarket's data collection, use, and retention practices due to misleading consent screens.

outcome: FTC issued a Complaint (April 29, 2024) alleging four counts: (1) Unfair Collection and Use of Consumer Location Data from InMarket's own apps; (2) Unfair Collection and Use of Consumer Location Data from third-party apps; (3) Unfair Retention of Consumer Location Data; (4) Deceptive Failure to Disclose use of location data. The complaint is pending adjudication. No settlement or final order has been issued as of the complaint date. InMarket must respond to the allegations and the case will proceed through FTC administrative proceedings.
companyNow: InMarket Media, LLC remains in operation as a digital marketing platform and data aggregator. The company is facing FTC enforcement proceedings alleging violations of consumer privacy protection standards. Current operations and any changes to practices are unknown pending resolution of the case.
dataType: Location data, device identifiers, purchasing history, demographic and socioeconomic information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair and deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(n) – unfairness standard (substantial injury not reasonably avoidable)

company: ROCA & ASOCIADOS ABOGADOS Y ECONOMISTAS, S.L.P.
companyDescription: ROCA & ASOCIADOS ABOGADOS Y ECONOMISTAS, S.L.P. is a Spanish law firm (despacho de abogados) classified as a microenterprise, founded in 2017. The firm provides legal and economic consulting services.
companyLongDescription: ROCA & ASOCIADOS ABOGADOS Y ECONOMISTAS, S.L.P. is a Spanish law firm (despacho de abogados) classified as a microenterprise, founded in 2017. The firm provides legal and economic consulting services.
caseDescription: A law firm published employee photographs, names, and professional information on its website without obtaining valid, informed, and explicit consent from the employees. The company claimed consent was given through informal email communications, but failed to provide proper data protection information and evidence of affirmative consent as required by GDPR Article 6(1).
violationSummary: The company exposed employees' personal data (photographs, names, professional details) publicly on the internet without proper consent, making the data accessible to the general public and increasing privacy risks.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Published employee photographs with names and professional details on the company website without obtaining valid prior consent from the employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees had their images, names, and professional information exposed publicly without their informed agreement, creating privacy harm and loss of control over their personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated that the employee gave consent by posing for the photograph and providing curriculum data, and was informed through emails about photo availability.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR requires free, specific, informed, and unequivocal consent obtained through affirmative action before processing begins. Informal email stating 'new employees who want them' is not affirmative consent; company provided no Article 13 mandatory information; consent must be documented and demonstrable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company argued that the employee had published the same data on LinkedIn, implying prior consent or public disclosure justifying republication.
claimsVsReality.reality: Publication by the data subject on a personal social media account does not constitute consent to corporate publication. Each processing activity requires separate, valid consent under GDPR. The employee's LinkedIn publication does not waive their right to control corporate use of their image.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data shall only be lawful if at least one of the specified conditions is met, including explicit consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: ROCA & ASOCIADOS published employee photographs and personal data without valid consent meeting GDPR requirements.
violations: ROCA & ASOCIADOS published employee photographs and personal data without valid consent meeting GDPR requirements.
Consent was not free, specific, informed, and unequivocal; company relied on informal email and presumed consent rather than affirmative action.
Company failed to provide information required by Article 13 GDPR before obtaining consent.
No evidence of proper consent documentation or mechanism to demonstrate valid consent had been obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(11) defines valid consent as a free, specific, informed, and unequivocal manifestation of will by which the data subject accepts processing through a clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: Email communication mentioning 'new employees who want them' was not an affirmative declaration of consent.
violations: Email communication mentioning 'new employees who want them' was not an affirmative declaration of consent.
Silence, pre-marked checkboxes, and inaction do not constitute valid consent; company did not obtain clear affirmative action.
Fact that complainant had previously posted photos on LinkedIn did not constitute consent to employer's publication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from the data subject, the controller shall provide specific information including identity of controller, purposes of processing, right to withdraw consent, and other mandatory details.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company provided no formal information sheet or privacy notice to employees before taking and publishing their photographs.
violations: Company provided no formal information sheet or privacy notice to employees before taking and publishing their photographs.
Employees were not informed of the purposes of processing, the legal basis, their rights, or other Article 13 requirements.
Informal emails did not constitute adequate provision of mandatory transparency information.

outcome: AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Authority) imposed a €5,000 administrative fine on ROCA & ASOCIADOS for violation of GDPR Article 6(1). Additionally, the company was ordered to adopt compliance measures within 3 months to ensure that personal data are not published on its website without complying with Article 6(1) GDPR requirements. The company must demonstrate implementation of these measures to the AEPD. The resolution is final after one month from notification if no appeal is filed. The company has the right to request a suspension of the resolution if it intends to file an administrative appeal before the National Court.
companyNow: Unknown. ROCA & ASOCIADOS is a Spanish legal services firm established in 2017 with approximately €[undisclosed] in annual business volume as of 2022. Current operational status not documented.
dataType: Photographs, names, first surnames, professional information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 4(11) – Definition of valid consent
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided to data subjects

company: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
companyDescription: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust is one of the largest acute hospital trusts in England, providing acute and specialist healthcare services across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties through four hospital sites (Lincoln, Boston, Grantham, and Louth). It employs approximately 9,136 staff with an annual income of £740 million.
companyLongDescription: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust is one of the largest acute hospital trusts in England, providing acute and specialist healthcare services across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties through four hospital sites (Lincoln, Boston, Grantham, and Louth). It employs approximately 9,136 staff with an annual income of £740 million.
caseDescription: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust failed to respond to 32% of Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month timeframe during March 2021 to March 2022. The Trust's deficient case management systems, lack of adequate resources, and poor oversight meant data subjects could not timely access their personal health information. The ICO issued a reprimand under UK GDPR Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3).
violationSummary: The Trust systematically excluded data subjects from accessing their personal health information by failing to meet statutory response deadlines, preventing individuals from exercising their data access rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Between March 2021 and March 2022, the Trust failed to respond to 32% of Subject Access Requests within the required one-month statutory timeframe.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients requesting their own medical records experienced significant delays accessing their health data, with some waiting months beyond the legal deadline.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Trust claimed it had responded to approximately 68% of SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe during the relevant period.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Trust had actually failed to respond to 32% of SARs within statutory deadlines. The Trust later acknowledged serious data quality issues and could not guarantee the accuracy of its quantitative reporting due to system failures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Trust stated it had processes and procedures in place for managing SARs effectively.
claimsVsReality.reality: The case management system lacked basic compliance-tracking functionality, the Trust was still operating primarily with paper records, and there was no adequate oversight or resource allocation for SAR processing for several years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Trust indicated its data provided to the ICO was reliable.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Trust acknowledged data quality issues, later advised that quantitative data was inaccurate because it included deceased individuals' records (outside GDPR scope), and admitted it could not guarantee data accuracy throughout the investigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken in response to data subject rights requests without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two months where necessary, with notice to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to respond to 32% of SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe
violations: Trust failed to respond to 32% of SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe
Trust could not confirm how many SARs received the extended three-month timeframe or how many were answered within it
Trust's case management system lacked functionality to record or track compliance data

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide data subjects with confirmation of whether personal data concerning them is being processed and, where applicable, access to the personal data and specified information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal health data to data subjects
violations: Trust failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal health data to data subjects
32% of data subjects were unable to exercise their right of access within the required timeframe

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing to data subjects.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to provide copies of personal health data within statutory deadlines due to system deficiencies and resource constraints
violations: Trust failed to provide copies of personal health data within statutory deadlines due to system deficiencies and resource constraints
Inadequate paper-based record systems and lack of oversight prevented timely fulfilment of data access requests

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand on 13 December 2024. The Trust acknowledged the infringements and did not submit representations. As remedial steps, the Trust has implemented an Information Asset Management Strategy (IAMS), procured a bespoke SAR management system and Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) solution (concluded March 2024), updated its Access to Records Policy, provided staff training, and recruited additional temporary staff. The Trust is planning to digitise patient records by March 2025 in line with NHS England's digital health plan. The Commissioner notes the backlog is improving but continues monitoring. Future failure to rectify these infringements could result in escalated enforcement action including substantial fines.
companyNow: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust continues to operate as a major acute hospital trust in England, serving approximately 769,474 people annually across four hospital sites. It is implementing significant systemic improvements to SAR handling and digitising health records.
dataType: Health data, Personal medical records

companyDescription: WerepairUK Ltd is a repair services company registered in the UK. The company conducted direct marketing operations via unsolicited telephone calls.
companyLongDescription: WerepairUK Ltd is a repair services company registered in the UK. The company conducted direct marketing operations via unsolicited telephone calls.
caseDescription: WerepairUK Ltd made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between September 2022 and May 2023, violating PECR Regulation 21. The company failed to obtain valid consent from TPS-registered subscribers before calling them for marketing purposes. Despite being notified of the Commissioner's concerns, the company continued its unlawful calling activity.
violationSummary: The company systematically contacted individuals who had explicitly registered to avoid such contact, constituting surveillance-type collection through unsolicited direct marketing calls.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service between September 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: 42,688 individuals who had explicitly registered to block marketing calls experienced unwanted sales calls, violating their stated privacy preferences.

claimsVsReality.claim: Implied by compliance: WerepairUK obtained valid consent from subscribers to receive marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: WerepairUK failed to demonstrate any valid notifications from the 42,688 called individuals overriding their TPS registration.

claimsVsReality.claim: Implied: The company respected TPS opt-out preferences.
claimsVsReality.reality: WerepairUK made 42,688 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid exceptions under Regulation 21(4).

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(1)(b) of PECR prohibits using public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the called number is listed in the TPS register kept under Regulation 26.
regulatoryFindings.description: WerepairUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS for at least 28 days prior without valid subscriber notification under Regulation 21(4).
violations: WerepairUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS for at least 28 days prior without valid subscriber notification under Regulation 21(4).
The company failed to obtain clear and positive action from individuals to override their TPS registration.
Notification (if any) did not clearly indicate willingness to receive marketing calls specifically from WerepairUK.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered numbers only where the subscriber has notified the caller they do not object to such calls, requiring clear and positive action.
regulatoryFindings.description: WerepairUK demonstrated no valid notifications from subscribers overriding their TPS registration.
violations: WerepairUK demonstrated no valid notifications from subscribers overriding their TPS registration.
The company could not demonstrate that signing up to use products/services constituted clear consent to receive marketing calls.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring WerepairUK Ltd to cease making unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers and subscribers who have previously notified the company not to call within 30 days. The company must also ensure direct marketing communications recipients receive the caller's name and contact details on request. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: WerepairUK Ltd remains a registered company (Companies House Registration 12080599) based in Tonbridge, UK. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Telephone numbers
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 21(1)(b)

company: Comunidad de Propietarios Conjunto Hotel Apartamentos Don B.B.B.
companyDescription: A residential property owners' collective managing a hotel apartment complex in Spain. The association is responsible for common areas and facilities including security systems for the building.
companyLongDescription: A residential property owners' collective managing a hotel apartment complex in Spain. The association is responsible for common areas and facilities including security systems for the building.
caseDescription: A property owners' association installed video surveillance cameras that were improperly oriented toward public space without adequate signage or access controls. The system exceeded permissible limits by capturing images of public areas, which is exclusively the competence of state security forces under Spanish law, and failed to provide proper transparency to individuals whose data was being collected.
violationSummary: The primary violation involved unauthorized video surveillance oriented toward public space beyond the property's legitimate interest, combined with lack of transparency to data subjects and inadequate access controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed video surveillance cameras oriented toward public streets without prior authorization, inadequate warning signs, and allowed unauthorized personnel access to the system.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents and passersby captured on video had no meaningful notice of surveillance and no way to exercise their data rights, exposing them to undisclosed monitoring in public areas.

claimsVsReality.claim: The property association claimed the cameras do not record or permit viewing of the community swimming pool.
claimsVsReality.reality: While pool monitoring may have been excluded, the cameras still recorded public space and areas beyond the property's legitimate scope, violating data minimization principles.

claimsVsReality.claim: The association provided documents showing approval by general assembly of owners and establishment of a protocol for system operation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite procedural approval by owners, the physical installation exceeded legal limits by capturing public space, which no private entity may do regardless of internal authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, pertinent and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: The property association installed cameras capturing public space beyond the building's curtilage, exceeding permissible scope for a private entity.
violations: The property association installed cameras capturing public space beyond the building's curtilage, exceeding permissible scope for a private entity.
The system was not limited to necessity for security of the property and its residents.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are collected from an individual, the controller must provide specified information including the identity of the controller, purposes of processing, legal basis, and rights of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Surveillance signage was inadequate and not properly identifying the responsible party or providing required information.
violations: Surveillance signage was inadequate and not properly identifying the responsible party or providing required information.
Data subjects passing through or near the property had no clear notice of the surveillance system.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 22(4) establishes that the information duty is satisfied through placement of an informative device in a sufficiently visible location identifying the existence of processing, controller identity, and rights available.
regulatoryFindings.description: The property association failed to install adequate signage complying with visibility and completeness standards.
violations: The property association failed to install adequate signage complying with visibility and completeness standards.

outcome: The property owners' association paid €600 (original proposed fine of €1,000 reduced by 40% through voluntary payment and responsibility recognition). The association was ordered to reorient and/or remove cameras improperly pointed toward public space and to install compliant warning signage within 30 days. The procedure was terminated upon payment with acknowledgment of responsibility. The association must notify AEPD within one month of implementing corrective measures once the resolution becomes final and enforceable.
companyNow: The property owners' association (Comunidad de Propietarios) was ordered to bring its video surveillance system into compliance with GDPR and Spanish data protection law by reorienting cameras away from public space and installing proper transparency signage.
dataType: Images/footage from video surveillance cameras
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
LOPDGDD Art. 22(4) – Information requirements for video surveillance

companyDescription: CH Offshore Ltd. is an owner-operator and ship manager of offshore support vessels serving the offshore marine oil and gas sector.
companyLongDescription: CH Offshore Ltd. is an owner-operator and ship manager of offshore support vessels serving the offshore marine oil and gas sector.
caseDescription: CH Offshore Ltd. suffered a ransomware attack on 28 March 2023 that encrypted files containing personal data of 5,906 individuals. Investigation revealed the company failed to implement reasonable security measures, including unpatched firewall firmware (not updated since December 2021), lack of multi-factor authentication on VPN access, weak network segmentation, and inadequate vendor oversight. The breach resulted in data exfiltration and unauthorized access to sensitive information.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal of personal data, directly resulting in a ransomware attack that compromised and exfiltrated sensitive data of thousands of individuals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CH Offshore failed to patch its firewall firmware for over 15 months, did not implement multi-factor authentication for remote VPN access, granted employees local administrator rights.
whyTheyWereWrong: Ransomware attackers encrypted and exfiltrated sensitive data of 5,906 individuals including health records, bank account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation expected its IT vendor to conduct periodic security reviews and maintenance as part of contracted IT services.
claimsVsReality.reality: The IT vendor contract contained only a general stipulation for monthly maintenance. The organisation failed to exercise adequate oversight—the last audit was in December 2021, and no audit cycle was due before the March 2023 incident. Without clear specification and regular monitoring, the vendor did not conduct the necessary security reviews.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data exfiltration could not be conclusively determined.
claimsVsReality.reality: Event logs showed 2.38TB of data transferred over suspicious VPN connections, and sample files from the threat actor contained 33 employee performance appraisal forms with full names and work appraisals, proving data exfiltration had occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had review processes and oversight of the IT vendor.
claimsVsReality.reality: The audit cycle occurred only every 2-3 years. With the last audit in December 2021 and the incident in March 2023 (15 months later), the next audit had not yet commenced, indicating insufficient frequency and timeliness of oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to patch firewall firmware since December 2021, exposing the network to multiple known remote code execution vulnerabilities for 15 months
violations: Failed to patch firewall firmware since December 2021, exposing the network to multiple known remote code execution vulnerabilities for 15 months
Did not implement multi-factor authentication for remote access VPN logins, allowing attackers to compromise user accounts and gain network access
Gave employees local administrator rights on laptops, enabling the threat actor to disable endpoint security software before deploying ransomware
Maintained a high-risk IT infrastructure without proper network segmentation or access controls, allowing lateral movement across all systems
Failed to conduct periodic security reviews or establish robust patch management processes despite outsourcing to an IT vendor
Exercised insufficient oversight of IT vendor performance, with audits conducted only every 2-3 years and last audit in December 2021

outcome: CH Offshore Ltd. is required to pay a financial penalty of SGD 18,000 within 30 days. The organisation must furnish a schedule within 30 days for completion of remedial actions including: reviewing and enhancing asset and patch management processes; enhancing servers and infrastructure to CIS benchmarks; implementing network segmentation and tightening access controls; improving logging capabilities with centralised log server; hardening perimeter firewall with 2FA for VPN; conducting periodic vulnerability assessments and penetration testing; implementing MFA for privileged accounts; installing Endpoint Detection and Response; implementing Managed Detection and Response/Managed Security Services; ensuring all systems are patched; implementing measures against lateral movement; conducting employee cybersecurity awareness training; and obtaining Cyber Essentials certification. The organisation must report to the Commission upon completion of all remedial actions.
companyNow: Unknown current operational status. The company was required to implement comprehensive cybersecurity remediation measures and report compliance to the Personal Data Protection Commission.
dataType: Name, address, date of birth, email, NRIC number, foreign ID, passport number, telephone, photograph, thumbprints, health information (medical records, lab tests, vaccinations), financial information (bank account numbers, pay slips), educational certificates, seaman's book details

companyDescription: Glasgow City Council is the local government authority for Glasgow City Area in Scotland, responsible for providing services to approximately 622,820 residents and managing 27,064 employees across multiple departments including social work, housing, and administration.
companyLongDescription: Glasgow City Council is the local government authority for Glasgow City Area in Scotland, responsible for providing services to approximately 622,820 residents and managing 27,064 employees across multiple departments including social work, housing, and administration.
caseDescription: Glasgow City Council failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory timeframes, with only 45% of SARs answered within one month during April 2023–March 2024. As of July 2024, the council had a backlog of 427 cases and failed to provide data subjects with progress updates or inform them of extension requests as required by UK GDPR Article 12(3). These failures prevented thousands of data subjects from exercising their right to access their personal data within statutory deadlines.
violationSummary: GCC systematically denied data subjects timely access to their personal data by failing to respond to Subject Access Requests within statutory timeframes and refusing to provide meaningful communication about delays, effectively excluding them from exercising their legal rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Glasgow City Council failed to respond to 55% of Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory deadline, maintaining a backlog of 427 cases as of July 2024.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 622,820 residents and employees were systematically denied timely access to their personal data, with many never informed of request extensions or case progress.

claimsVsReality.claim: GCC acknowledged the backlog was due to increased demand from the Scottish Government's Redress Scheme with staffing challenges and no additional funding.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite cited constraints, GCC failed to meet statutory obligations for 55% of SARs and did not proactively communicate with data subjects, as required by law regardless of workload.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on action taken on requests under Articles 15–22 to data subjects without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, with possibility of two-month extension if necessary with notice to data subject of reasons.
regulatoryFindings.description: GCC responded to only 45% of SARs within the one-month statutory deadline during April 2023–March 2024
violations: GCC responded to only 45% of SARs within the one-month statutory deadline during April 2023–March 2024
GCC failed to inform data subjects of extension requests or reasons for delays
GCC provided only an initial acknowledgment email and did not regularly update data subjects on case progression

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(1) establishes the right to obtain from a controller confirmation as to whether personal data concerning the data subject are being processed, and where that is the case, access to the personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GCC failed to respond to over 50% of SARs within the statutory timeframe of one month (or three months for complex SARs)
violations: GCC failed to respond to over 50% of SARs within the statutory timeframe of one month (or three months for complex SARs)
GCC failed to demonstrate provision of timely confirmation of processing or access to personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(3) requires the controller to provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: GCC failed to provide copies of personal data due to significant delays in SAR responses persisting over 12 months
violations: GCC failed to provide copies of personal data due to significant delays in SAR responses persisting over 12 months
427 cases remained in backlog as of July 12, 2024

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Glasgow City Council for infringements of UK GDPR Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3). Additionally, an Assessment Notice was issued to provide ongoing assurance of compliance. GCC committed to implementing a new system to support timely SAR completion and engaged transparently with the ICO. The reprimand serves as a warning that future non-compliance may be treated as an aggravating factor in escalated enforcement action under Article 83(2)(i) of the UK GDPR.
companyNow: Glasgow City Council remains the local government authority serving 622,820 residents and 27,064 employees in Glasgow, Scotland. The council is actively implementing remedial measures and pursuing procurement of new SAR management systems to improve compliance.
dataType: Social care records, employment records, personal identifiers

companyDescription: Payroll2U Pte. Ltd. is a payroll service provider offering payroll outsourcing services and online payroll Software as a Service (SaaS) solutions to corporate clients in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Payroll2U Pte. Ltd. is a payroll service provider offering payroll outsourcing services and online payroll Software as a Service (SaaS) solutions to corporate clients in Singapore.
caseDescription: Payroll2U, a payroll service provider, suffered a ransomware attack in December 2022 where attackers exfiltrated 81.95 GB of employee data from 5,640 individuals via a compromised user account. The company failed to implement reasonable access controls such as multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, and restricted administrator rights, allowing the threat actor to access sensitive financial and personal data stored on unsecured shared drives.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable organisational and technical measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access, resulting in a large-scale data breach and exfiltration of sensitive financial and identity information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Payroll2U failed to implement reasonable access controls and stored 81.95 GB of sensitive employee data including bank account numbers, salary information.
whyTheyWereWrong: A ransomware attack exposed the personal and financial data of 5,640 employees to criminals who posted it on the dark web, causing identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had 'proactive cybersecurity controls' in place
claimsVsReality.reality: These controls were inadequate; critical access controls were missing (no MFA, unrestricted admin rights), allowing a single compromised account to access and exfiltrate 81.95 GB of sensitive employee data

claimsVsReality.claim: The company was storing data securely in line with best practices
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive financial data including bank account numbers and salary information was stored on unsecured internal shared drives accessible to any compromised account with basic credentials

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to implement reasonable organisational and technical measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access, processing, use, or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Payroll2U failed to implement MFA for administrator accounts and non-administrative accounts with access to personal data
violations: Payroll2U failed to implement MFA for administrator accounts and non-administrative accounts with access to personal data
Payroll2U stored sensitive personal data (bank account numbers, salary information) on unsecured internal shared drives without restrictive access controls
Payroll2U granted local administrator rights to all employees, enabling unauthorized software installation and removal of endpoint protection
Payroll2U failed to implement network segmentation to restrict access to sensitive data on a need-to-know basis
Payroll2U lacked effective incident response and monitoring controls, allowing unauthorised activity to remain undetected for 18 days (29 December 2022 to 16 January 2023)

outcome: Payroll2U admitted to breach of the Protection Obligation under the Commission's Expedited Breach Decision Procedure and agreed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $4,000 within 30 days. The company implemented comprehensive remedial actions including: deactivation of compromised accounts; implementation of MFA for all internal and remote access; quarterly reviews of network drive and folder access with monthly log reviews; endpoint protection verification for all workstations; host-checking for VPN users; firewall configuration review and web-filtering enhancement; and regular service account validation. The company must maintain these security controls going forward.
