regulatoryFindings.description: NDA relied on generic loan decline data without verifying that consent covered NDA specifically or was obtained freely and informed
violations: NDA relied on generic loan decline data without verifying that consent covered NDA specifically or was obtained freely and informed
No evidence of separate consent for NDA direct marketing; recipients had only consented to calls, texts, and emails generically through the original loan application process

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A authorizes monetary penalties for serious contraventions of PECR where the contravention was deliberate or negligent.
regulatoryFindings.description: NDA knew or ought to have known of risks in relying on third-party data and failed to conduct substantive due diligence
violations: NDA knew or ought to have known of risks in relying on third-party data and failed to conduct substantive due diligence
NDA had been registered with the ICO for 7 years and should have been aware of PECR requirements and enforcement action against similar breaches

outcome: NDA was issued a monetary penalty of £30,000 (reducible to £24,000 if paid by 21 October 2024). The penalty must be paid by BACS transfer or cheque by 22 October 2024. NDA has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner found NDA failed to take reasonable steps to prevent the contraventions despite having 8 years of business experience and 7 years of registration with the ICO. No mitigating factors were identified.
companyNow: National Debt Advice Limited remains registered with the Financial Conduct Authority for debt counselling (FCA registration number 789258) and with the ICO as a data controller. The company's current operational status and compliance measures are not detailed in the decision.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, personal contact details

company: Caja Rural Ntra Madre del Sol S.C.A.C.
companyDescription: Caja Rural Ntra Madre del Sol S.C.A.C. is a regional rural savings bank operating in Spain as part of the broader Caja Rural cooperative group. It offers traditional banking services including electronic banking platforms to retail and small business customers.
companyLongDescription: Caja Rural Ntra Madre del Sol S.C.A.C. is a regional rural savings bank operating in Spain as part of the broader Caja Rural cooperative group. It offers traditional banking services including electronic banking platforms to retail and small business customers.
caseDescription: A rural savings bank's electronic banking platform (Ruralvía Clásica) suffered a data breach in November 2022 that exposed customers' personal and financial data due to inadequate security measures. The bank failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational safeguards required to protect the confidentiality and integrity of personal data, despite being a financial institution with a duty of care to protect large volumes of customer data.
violationSummary: The company failed to apply appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure adequate security of personal data treatment, directly enabling unauthorized access to confidential customer information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Caja Rural Ntra Madre del Sol failed to implement adequate security measures for its Ruralvía Clásica online banking platform.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of bank customers lost control of their personal data, account credentials, and financial information when attackers exploited security vulnerabilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank stated its data processor (Rural Servicios Informáticos) had implemented security measures detailed in the service agreement annexes and held security certifications.
claimsVsReality.reality: The security certifications cited were only for information security (ISO standards), not data protection compliance. The actual security measures proved inadequate, with the processor and bank both acknowledging additional safeguards could have prevented the breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach was caused solely by an external cyber-attack that the bank could not have foreseen or prevented.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed the attackers exploited known vulnerabilities that had been identified in prior audits but were not remediated. The bank had received audit reports identifying specific security weaknesses before the breach occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank had conducted regular audits and maintained high security standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: While audits were performed, they revealed vulnerabilities (including those used in the attack) that remained unresolved at the time of the breach, indicating audit findings were not acted upon promptly.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in such a manner as to ensure appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural failed to guarantee adequate confidentiality and integrity of customer personal and financial data, resulting in unauthorized access to banking credentials, account information, and sensitive financial records between 10 November and 23 November 2022.
violations: Caja Rural failed to guarantee adequate confidentiality and integrity of customer personal and financial data, resulting in unauthorized access to banking credentials, account information, and sensitive financial records between 10 November and 23 November 2022.
The bank did not deploy sufficient protective measures despite handling sensitive banking data at scale, with thousands of customers affected by potential identity theft and financial fraud risks.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires that the controller and processor shall apply technical and organizational measures appropriate to the risk to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, considering state of the art, implementation costs, and the nature and scope of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Security evaluation reports and audits revealed known vulnerabilities in the system that were not remediated prior to the breach. The bank acknowledged that additional security measures could have prevented the incident.
violations: Security evaluation reports and audits revealed known vulnerabilities in the system that were not remediated prior to the breach. The bank acknowledged that additional security measures could have prevented the incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) establishes the accountability principle, making the controller responsible for demonstrating compliance with data protection requirements through proactive measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: The bank failed in its duty of prior vigilance and ongoing supervision of data processing operations, including failure to ensure its data processor implemented adequate safeguards or to conduct sufficient oversight of security measures.
violations: The bank failed in its duty of prior vigilance and ongoing supervision of data processing operations, including failure to ensure its data processor implemented adequate safeguards or to conduct sufficient oversight of security measures.

outcome: The Administrative Authority for Data Protection imposed an administrative fine of €10,000. The entity exercised the right to voluntary payment under Article 85 of the Common Administrative Procedure Act (LPACAP), paying €8,000 (20% reduction) on 18 December 2024. This payment terminated the procedure; no further remediation or monitoring was imposed beyond the administrative fine. The bank renounced all rights to appeal or pursue administrative remedies.
companyNow: Caja Rural Ntra Madre del Sol S.C.A.C. remains operational as a member of the Caja Rural group, a Spanish cooperative banking network. The 2022 incident and resulting fine have not been reported to affect its current operational status.
dataType: Financial data, personal contact information, account credentials, banking transaction data

companyDescription: Money Bubble Ltd is a direct marketing company registered in England (Companies House Registration No. 11785059) based in Oldham, which conducted telemarketing campaigns for financial or consumer products/services.
companyLongDescription: Money Bubble Ltd is a direct marketing company registered in England (Companies House Registration No. 11785059) based in Oldham, which conducted telemarketing campaigns for financial or consumer products/services.
caseDescription: Money Bubble Ltd made 168,852 unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers between October and November 2022 without valid subscriber consent. The company failed to obtain clear notifications from registered subscribers that they did not object to receiving such calls, and failed to provide required identification information (name and contact details) with the calls.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic unsolicited telephone contact (surveillance-like behaviour) to individuals who had explicitly registered to opt-out, and failed to disclose caller identity, preventing individuals from knowing who was contacting them.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Money Bubble Ltd made 168,852 unsolicited direct marketing calls between October and November 2022 to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 168,852 individuals who had registered their numbers to opt out of marketing calls received unwanted calls anyway, violating their explicit privacy preference.

claimsVsReality.claim: Money Bubble Ltd presumably claimed or acted as though it had authority to make marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no valid consent from 168,852 subscribers who had explicitly registered with TPS to opt-out of such calls, and provided no evidence of notifications overriding their TPS registration.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use or instigation of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the called line number is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: Money Bubble Ltd permitted its lines to be used or instigated the use of a telecommunications service to make 168,852 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with TPS at least 28 days prior, with no valid opt-out notifications obtained.
violations: Money Bubble Ltd permitted its lines to be used or instigated the use of a telecommunications service to make 168,852 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with TPS at least 28 days prior, with no valid opt-out notifications obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(1)–(2) requires that where public electronic communications services are used for direct marketing, the person using or instigating the service must provide the recipient with the name of the person making the call, and if requested, an address or free telephone number.
regulatoryFindings.description: Money Bubble Ltd failed to provide recipients of the 168,852 calls with the required particulars (name and contact details), preventing subscribers from knowing who was calling them or how to reach the caller.
violations: Money Bubble Ltd failed to provide recipients of the 168,852 calls with the required particulars (name and contact details), preventing subscribers from knowing who was calling them or how to reach the caller.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring Money Bubble Ltd to, within 30 days: (1) cease making or instigating unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers or those who have notified the company not to call; and (2) ensure all future direct marketing calls include the caller's name and, if requested, address or free-access telephone number. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
dataType: telephone numbers, subscriber contact information
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) – prohibition on unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
PECR Regulation 21(2) – subscriber duty not to permit lines for prohibited use
PECR Regulation 24(1)–(2) – requirement to provide caller name and contact details

companyDescription: Dr Telemarketing Ltd is a telemarketing company registered in London that conducted direct marketing campaigns by telephone.
companyLongDescription: Dr Telemarketing Ltd is a telemarketing company registered in London that conducted direct marketing campaigns by telephone.
caseDescription: Dr Telemarketing Ltd made 80,240 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) without obtaining valid prior notification from recipients that they consented to receive such calls. The company violated Regulation 21 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 (PECR) by systematically calling TPS-registered subscribers between February 2021 and March 2022.
violationSummary: DRT systematically contacted individuals who had registered with TPS to avoid unwanted marketing calls, violating their privacy expectations and right to be left alone from direct marketing solicitation.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 80,240 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between February 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 80,240 people who had explicitly registered to stop receiving marketing calls were harassed with unwanted calls anyway, invading their privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recipients had validly consented to receive marketing calls from DRT
claimsVsReality.reality: DRT provided no evidence of valid prior notification from any recipient that they did not object to calls; individuals had registered with TPS specifically to avoid such calls

claimsVsReality.claim: Generic opt-in to receive marketing communications constitutes valid consent under PECR Regulation 21(4)
claimsVsReality.reality: Valid notification requires explicit, specific indication of willingness to receive calls from that particular company, not generic marketing consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits a person from using or instigating the use of a public electronic communications service for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the called line number is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: DRT instigated 80,240 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
violations: DRT instigated 80,240 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
Called individuals had registered with TPS at least 28 days prior to calls
DRT failed to provide evidence that recipients had given valid notification they did not object to calls from DRT specifically
DRT did not demonstrate clear and positive action by individuals to override TPS registration for DRT calls

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered numbers only where the subscriber has previously notified the caller that they do not object to such calls being made by that caller.
regulatoryFindings.description: DRT provided no evidence of valid notification from any of the 80,240 called individuals
violations: DRT provided no evidence of valid notification from any of the 80,240 called individuals
Generic consent to receive marketing communications does not satisfy the requirement for specific notification regarding telephone calls from that company
Conditional signup terms do not constitute clear and positive notification separate from product/service terms

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice under DPA Section 40 requiring Dr Telemarketing Ltd to cease making unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers and to those who have previously requested no calls, within 30 days of 15 February 2024. DRT has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner found that while the contravention was serious, damage to individuals was unlikely (no monetary penalty was imposed).
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information

companyDescription: The Labour Party is a major British political party that processes personal data relating to employees, members, and supporters. The organisation faced operational challenges managing data protection requests after experiencing a cyber-attack in October 2021.
companyLongDescription: The Labour Party is a major British political party that processes personal data relating to employees, members, and supporters. The organisation faced operational challenges managing data protection requests after experiencing a cyber-attack in October 2021.
caseDescription: The Labour Party failed to respond to thousands of subject access requests and erasure requests within statutory timeframes following a cyber-attack in October 2021. An unmonitored privacy inbox discovered during investigation contained approximately 646 unresponded subject access requests and 597 unresponded erasure requests. The backlog persisted for over a year, with 82% of requests in November 2022 exceeding the one-month response deadline.
violationSummary: The Labour Party systematically excluded data subjects from exercising their rights by failing to acknowledge, respond to, or process legitimate access and erasure requests within required timeframes, denying individuals information about how their data was being handled.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Labour Party failed to respond to 646 subject access requests and 597 erasure requests found in an unmonitored privacy inbox from November 2021 to October 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1,200 individuals were systematically denied access to their personal data or had erasure requests ignored for up to two years, with some requests dating back to 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy inbox was used to handle cyber-incident correspondence and was moved to standard data protection inbox
claimsVsReality.reality: Privacy inbox was abandoned without proper monitoring from November 2021 to October 2023, leaving 1,243 requests completely unaddressed

claimsVsReality.claim: Subject access request backlog resulted from a spike due to cyber-attack
claimsVsReality.reality: While cyber-attack triggered initial spike, failure to adequately staff, monitor, and process requests left 82% of requests overdue one year later

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on action taken on data subject requests under Articles 15-22 without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt (extendable by two further months where necessary for complexity/number).
regulatoryFindings.description: Labour Party had 352 actionable subject access requests in November 2022; 82% (289) were older than one month; 78% (274) were older than three months
violations: Labour Party had 352 actionable subject access requests in November 2022; 82% (289) were older than one month; 78% (274) were older than three months
In unmonitored privacy inbox, approximately 646 subject access requests had no evidence of response

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain from the controller confirmation whether personal data concerning them is being processed and to access that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: 56% (198) of subject access requests in November 2022 backlog were 12+ months old
violations: 56% (198) of subject access requests in November 2022 backlog were 12+ months old
Approximately 646 subject access requests in unmonitored inbox, many dating to 2021, received no response

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 17(1) grants data subjects the right to erasure without undue delay and requires controllers to erase personal data without undue delay, with obligation to respond to erasure requests even if erasure is not ultimately required.
regulatoryFindings.description: Approximately 597 erasure requests found in unmonitored privacy inbox with no evidence of Labour Party response
violations: Approximately 597 erasure requests found in unmonitored privacy inbox with no evidence of Labour Party response
Privacy inbox left unmonitored from November 2021 to October 2023 (nearly 24 months), resulting in undue delay in handling erasure requests

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand (not a monetary fine) against the Labour Party under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner noted significant mitigating factors and remedial steps taken by the Labour Party, including: hiring temporary staff and a senior data protection consultant; recruiting a new Data Protection Officer (July 2023); allocating extra funds; contacting all 646 affected data subjects; actioning all 597 erasure requests; deleting the unmonitored inbox; and updating data subject request processes and privacy notices. By October 2023, the Labour Party had reduced the backlog to four outstanding requests; by April 2024, zero outstanding requests remained. The Commissioner issued non-binding recommendations to ensure future compliance, noting that failure to rectify the infringements could constitute an aggravating factor in any future enforcement action.
companyNow: The Labour Party has significantly improved its data protection compliance posture. As of April 2024, all outstanding subject access requests have been resolved, no open complaints remain at the national party level, and a permanent Data Protection Officer is in place.
dataType: Personal data of party employees, members, and supporters; subject access request data

companyDescription: Academy of Medicine Singapore is a professional institution providing postgraduate medical education and specialist training in Singapore, serving current and former members, event participants, and examination candidates.
companyLongDescription: Academy of Medicine Singapore is a professional institution providing postgraduate medical education and specialist training in Singapore, serving current and former members, event participants, and examination candidates.
caseDescription: Academy of Medicine Singapore suffered a ransomware attack in July 2023 that exposed personal data of 6,574 individuals, including full credit card information of over 1,000 people. The breach resulted from multiple critical security failures: unpatched firewall vulnerable to known exploits, outdated end-of-life operating systems, disabled endpoint detection, lack of vulnerability scanning, and absence of robust patch management processes. The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements required under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data, resulting in a ransomware breach that exfiltrated sensitive financial and identity information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Academy of Medicine Singapore failed to patch its firewall for over two years, deployed servers with obsolete operating systems.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data of 6,574 individuals was stolen and posted on the dark web, including complete credit card information with CVV numbers for 1,083 people.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had recently onboarded a new IT vendor in April 2023 and was conducting IT infrastructure reviews.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite ongoing reviews completed June 26, 2023, the firewall remained unpatched for over 2 years, end-of-life systems were still deployed, and no documented patch management processes existed at time of breach on July 13, 2023.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Firewall FortiOS not patched since July 2021; vulnerable to CVE-2023-27997 critical heap buffer overflow allowing pre-authentication remote code execution without credentials.
violations: Firewall FortiOS not patched since July 2021; vulnerable to CVE-2023-27997 critical heap buffer overflow allowing pre-authentication remote code execution without credentials.
Two affected servers deployed end-of-life operating systems (no support since July 2015 and January 2020 respectively).
Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) manager compromised early and disabled by threat actors.
Credit host and staff computers not regularly scanned for vulnerabilities.
Credit card data with CVV stored in plain text without password protection or encryption.
No documented robust processes for regular patching and updates of critical software and firmware.
No data protection requirements or clear job specifications stipulated in IT vendor contract.

outcome: The Commission found Academy of Medicine Singapore breached the Protection Obligation under PDPA s.24. The organization was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 9,000 within 30 days. Additionally, the organization must complete seven remedial actions within 60 days: assess perimeter firewall needs, conduct security architecture review with network segregation, implement endpoint hardening, identify and encrypt sensitive data per PCI-DSS standards, delete stored CVV numbers and implement anti-storage policy, conduct annual security reviews, and submit written completion report to the Commissioner.
companyNow: Academy of Medicine Singapore continues operations. The organization has completed remedial actions including firewall upgrades, two-factor authentication implementation, automated patch management, and engagement of third-party credit monitoring services for affected individuals.
dataType: Names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, NRIC numbers, passport numbers, ID photographs, dates of birth, bank account details, credit card numbers with CVV and expiry dates

companyDescription: Service Box Group Limited is a UK-registered company (Companies House 10664393) engaged in direct marketing and telemarketing operations, based in Hove, East Sussex.
companyLongDescription: Service Box Group Limited is a UK-registered company (Companies House 10664393) engaged in direct marketing and telemarketing operations, based in Hove, East Sussex.
caseDescription: Service Box Group Limited made 5,361 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), contrary to PECR regulation 21. The company failed to obtain valid consent from individuals before making these calls and did not adequately consider compliance requirements in its customer journey.
violationSummary: The company systematically contacted individuals despite explicit privacy preferences recorded on the TPS register, constituting targeted surveillance of a particular demographic group without consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between August 2022 and January 2023, Service Box Group Limited instigated 5,361 unsolicited telemarketing calls to numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service without obtaining valid.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of people who had explicitly registered to opt out of marketing calls were repeatedly contacted anyway, violating their privacy choice.

claimsVsReality.claim: SBG provided evidence to the Commissioner indicating valid notifications had been obtained from recipients
claimsVsReality.reality: The evidence showed no valid notifications meeting PECR requirements had actually been obtained; the company had not adequately considered compliance in its customer journey

claimsVsReality.claim: Generic opt-in language for 'marketing communications' constitutes valid notification under regulation 21(4)
claimsVsReality.reality: Regulation 21(4) requires specific, clear notification about marketing calls from that particular company; generic opt-ins do not meet this standard

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits any person from using or instigating the use of a public electronic communications service to make unsolicited calls for direct marketing where the number is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: SBG instigated 5,361 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers between August 2022 and January 2023
violations: SBG instigated 5,361 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers between August 2022 and January 2023
Called subscribers had registered with TPS at least 28 days prior and had not notified SBG that they accepted marketing calls
SBG failed to obtain valid consent as required under regulation 21(4), which mandates clear and positive notification specific to that company

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) requires that for calls to TPS-registered numbers, the individual must have notified the caller that they do not object to such calls, through clear and positive action.
regulatoryFindings.description: SBG did not demonstrate valid notifications had been obtained from any of the 5,361 called individuals
violations: SBG did not demonstrate valid notifications had been obtained from any of the 5,361 called individuals
The company did not adequately consider the customer journey in relation to PECR compliance
SBG relied on generic opt-in language regarding 'marketing communications' rather than specific notification about telephone marketing calls

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40(1)(a) empowers the Commissioner to serve an enforcement notice if satisfied that a person has contravened the PECR requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: SBG's systematic contravention of PECR regulation 21 constituted a serious breach warranting enforcement action
violations: SBG's systematic contravention of PECR regulation 21 constituted a serious breach warranting enforcement action
The violations caused or risked causing damage and distress to subscribers who received unwanted calls targeting their demographic group

outcome: The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring SBG to cease instigating unsolicited calls to subscribers who have previously notified the company not to call them or who are registered with TPS (unless they have provided clear, specific notification that they consent to marketing calls from SBG). SBG must comply within 30 days. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days of the notice date (13 August 2024).
dataType: telephone numbers, personal contact information

companyDescription: 20 AÑOS DE MÚSICA A.I.E. is a Spanish music event and concert organizer that manages public entertainment events. The company required parental authorization and ID verification for minors attending concerts.
companyLongDescription: 20 AÑOS DE MÚSICA A.I.E. is a Spanish music event and concert organizer that manages public entertainment events. The company required parental authorization and ID verification for minors attending concerts.
caseDescription: A music event organizer collected excessive personal data from parents/guardians attending concerts with minors, including full photocopies of national ID documents containing unnecessary information. The authorization forms lacked proper data protection disclosures and were based on outdated privacy legislation, failing to inform data subjects of their rights or data retention periods.
violationSummary: The company collected and retained excessive personal data (full ID photocopies) that contained sensitive information unnecessary for the stated purpose (age verification). This represents inadequate data minimization and security practices under GDPR Article 5(1)(c) and Article 32.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Collected complete photocopies of ID documents from parents authorizing minors' concert attendance and retained them without updating privacy notices or specifying data retention periods.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents and minors received no clear information about data collection, retention duration, or their rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed ID photocopies were necessary to comply with Cantabrian regional law (Ley 3/2017) requiring age verification before allowing minors into venues.
claimsVsReality.reality: While age verification is legally required, the company collected unnecessary data beyond verification—full ID photocopies with all embedded information—and retained them. Simple in-situ age verification without copying or storing documents would have satisfied the legal requirement while minimizing data exposure.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed a Privacy Policy was available and met GDPR Article 13 requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The authorization forms used to collect data lacked proper privacy disclosures, referenced repealed 1999 legislation, and failed to explain data handling, retention periods, or data subject rights. The document itself was the collection mechanism but contained outdated and insufficient information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated deficiencies were caused by human error and were under review.
claimsVsReality.reality: The AEPD noted that technical and organizational measures must account for human error throughout the entire data lifecycle, not just be revised after violations occur. The company's error-reactive approach did not meet proactive accountability requirements under GDPR Article 5(2).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: 20 AÑOS DE MÚSICA collected full photocopies of national ID documents containing all information (including unnecessary sensitive data) when only age verification was required. A simple in-situ age verification would have sufficed without collecting or storing excess data.
violations: 20 AÑOS DE MÚSICA collected full photocopies of national ID documents containing all information (including unnecessary sensitive data) when only age verification was required. A simple in-situ age verification would have sufficed without collecting or storing excess data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from a data subject, the controller must provide comprehensive information including: identity and contact details of controller, data protection officer contact, purposes and legal basis of processing, data retention periods, and rights of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The 'documento de acceso a menores' used outdated privacy language referencing the repealed 1999 Spanish Data Protection Act. It failed to inform parents/guardians of data handling practices, retention periods, or their GDPR rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability). No clear information was provided about what would be done with the ID data once collected.
violations: The 'documento de acceso a menores' used outdated privacy language referencing the repealed 1999 Spanish Data Protection Act. It failed to inform parents/guardians of data handling practices, retention periods, or their GDPR rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability). No clear information was provided about what would be done with the ID data once collected.

outcome: The company paid €3,000 in fines on 4 June 2024 using both available reductions (20% for recognition of responsibility and 20% for voluntary payment), acknowledging liability. The company was ordered to: (1) update the minor access authorization document with current GDPR-compliant privacy information, removing references to the 1999 repealed law; (2) revise privacy clauses to comply with data protection requirements; and (3) eliminate the requirement for ID photocopies in the authorization documents. The company reported adopting measures to prevent recurrence. Procedure terminated following voluntary payment with recognition of responsibility.
companyNow: 20 AÑOS DE MÚSICA A.I.E. is a microenterprise registered in Spain (NIF V09865601) established in 2022, active in music events and concert organization. The company has adopted corrective measures following the enforcement action.
dataType: Identity documents (DNI), personal information of minors and parents/guardians, name, contact details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

companyDescription: A Spanish residential homeowners' association managing a multi-unit apartment building. The organization maintains records of residents' personal data including names, addresses, and financial obligations and holds general assemblies where minutes are recorded.
companyLongDescription: A Spanish residential homeowners' association managing a multi-unit apartment building. The organization maintains records of residents' personal data including names, addresses, and financial obligations and holds general assemblies where minutes are recorded.
caseDescription: A homeowners' association publicly displayed meeting minutes containing residents' names, initials, and debt information in a locked display case in the building lobby for nearly 8 months. The exposed personal data violated GDPR confidentiality principles, as the disclosure exceeded the legally permitted 3-day notification period and lacked justification.
violationSummary: The company exposed sensitive personal data (names, addresses, financial debts) to an indeterminate number of third parties in a public building common area, without proper safeguards or justification, directly violating the principle of integrity and confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Published assembly meeting minutes in a locked lobby display case from August 2023 through April 2024, exposing resident names, initials, postal addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 12 residents had their names, addresses, and debt information publicly displayed in a common building area.

claimsVsReality.claim: The assembly minutes were displayed in a locked display case as a lawful notification mechanism under Spanish property law.
claimsVsReality.reality: While Spanish law permits public notice of assembly minutes when direct notification is impossible, it limits such public notice to 3 days and requires documented justification; the association displayed the minutes for 8 months without proper legal grounds or time limitation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The locked display case provided adequate protection for sensitive resident data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The case was located in the building's public vestibule and was visible to all persons entering the building, including third-party visitors, delivery personnel, and guests, providing no meaningful protection against unauthorized access or disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner guaranteeing adequate security and confidentiality, including protection against unauthorized access, use, and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Homeowners association displayed assembly minutes containing resident names, initials, postal addresses, and debts in a public lobby display case for approximately 8 months (August 3, 2023 – April 2, 2024), exposing sensitive personal data to all building occupants and visitors without adequate safeguards.
violations: Homeowners association displayed assembly minutes containing resident names, initials, postal addresses, and debts in a public lobby display case for approximately 8 months (August 3, 2023 – April 2, 2024), exposing sensitive personal data to all building occupants and visitors without adequate safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: Spanish Horizontal Property Law (Ley 49/1960) Article 9.h) permits public notice of assembly proceedings only when direct notification is impossible, and requires such notice to produce legal effect for only 3 days, with a signed record by the community secretary.
regulatoryFindings.description: The association displayed the meeting minutes well beyond the 3-day legal notification period without documenting justification for the public display or the reasons for exceeding the legally permitted timeframe.
violations: The association displayed the meeting minutes well beyond the 3-day legal notification period without documenting justification for the public display or the reasons for exceeding the legally permitted timeframe.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a €1,000 administrative fine for breach of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The homeowners association was ordered to: (1) certify adoption of measures to ensure compliance with GDPR confidentiality requirements; (2) confirm that assembly minutes will no longer be displayed in public areas except where mandated by the Horizontal Property Law; (3) remove the offending minutes from the display case within one month of the resolution becoming final. The association may appeal this resolution to Spain's National Court (Audiencia Nacional) within two months of notification. Resolution became enforceable after the one-month optional repositioning appeal period expired without challenge.
companyNow: The homeowners association remains active and subject to ongoing compliance obligations. Failure to comply with the corrective measures may result in additional enforcement proceedings.
dataType: Names, surnames, postal addresses, financial debts

companyDescription: NHS FIFE is a medium-sized territorial Health Board in Scotland responsible for delivering acute, community, and health and social care partnership services across the Fife region. The organisation processes special category health data as part of routine patient care.
companyLongDescription: NHS FIFE is a medium-sized territorial Health Board in Scotland responsible for delivering acute, community, and health and social care partnership services across the Fife region. The organisation processes special category health data as part of routine patient care.
caseDescription: NHS FIFE failed to secure personal health data when an unauthorised individual gained ward access due to inadequate identification checks and unclear processes, obtaining a document (SBAR) containing personal data of 14 patients and special category health information. The SBAR was removed from the site and never recovered, compounded by disabled CCTV and lack of document tracking procedures. The organisation had insufficient staff training (42% overall), outdated policies, and no robust data protection measures.
violationSummary: Unauthorised access to and removal of personal health records from physical premises due to inadequate security measures, lack of access controls, and disabled monitoring systems, resulting in exposure of special category data to unknown third party.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: An unauthorised individual gained access to a hospital ward due to lack of identification checks, received a document (SBAR) containing personal data and health records of 14 patients.
whyTheyWereWrong: Fourteen patients' personal identifiers and sensitive health data were exposed to an unknown person whose intentions remain unknown, with the data never recovered.

claimsVsReality.claim: NHS FIFE had CCTV installed within the hospital and a CCTV policy in place to monitor security.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CCTV wall socket was accidentally turned off by staff as part of an energy-saving exercise prior to the incident, rendering the installed CCTV non-functional and unable to identify the unauthorised individual or aid recovery of stolen data.

claimsVsReality.claim: NHS FIFE operates with staff identification and verification procedures for ward access.
claimsVsReality.reality: No formal ID verification process existed at the time of the breach; the unauthorised individual gained access due to lack of identification checks and unclear processes, and was handed confidential patient documents without verification.

claimsVsReality.claim: SBAR documents containing patient data are appropriately secured and tracked.
claimsVsReality.reality: No procedure existed to document whether SBARs were destroyed correctly or collected at the end of shifts; the SBAR containing 14 patients' health data was removed from site by the unauthorised individual and has not been recovered.

claimsVsReality.claim: Staff training on data protection is up-to-date and comprehensive.
claimsVsReality.reality: Overall staff training rate was only 42% (though ward staff reached 82%); refresher training occurred only every three years, which the ICO deemed insufficient for managing data protection risks.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: NHS FIFE failed to implement identification verification procedures, allowing an unauthorised individual to access a ward
violations: NHS FIFE failed to implement identification verification procedures, allowing an unauthorised individual to access a ward
No document tracking system existed for SBAR documents containing patient health data
CCTV security was disabled prior to the incident due to energy-saving measures, removing physical surveillance protection
No clear process in place to verify and restrict access to sensitive health records

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32 requires that appropriate levels of security shall account for risks presented by processing, particularly from accident or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: NHS FIFE lacked adequate technical and organisational measures to prevent unauthorised access to health data
violations: NHS FIFE lacked adequate technical and organisational measures to prevent unauthorised access to health data
No procedure to document whether SBAR documents were correctly destroyed or collected at end of shift
Low staff training rates (42% organisation-wide, though 82% for ward staff) and three-yearly refresher cycles insufficient for risk management
Outdated and incorrectly labelled policies indicated poor data protection governance

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to NHS FIFE under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. NHS FIFE has implemented remedial measures including a ward system for signing documents in and out each shift, revisited ID verification procedures requiring identification verification before commencing shifts, and is developing a standard operating procedure for bank staff. The ICO invited a progress update within six months (by 6 June 2024) covering: effectiveness of the standard operating procedure for bank staff; implementation and effectiveness of the ID process; data protection training rates improvements; and policy updates in line with UK GDPR. Recommendations include: more frequent refresher training (beyond three-yearly); development of written guidance/policy for bank staff ID verification; review of all intranet policies with clear archival marking; and revisiting data breach reporting processes to ensure 72-hour notification compliance under Article 33(1).
companyNow: NHS FIFE is an ongoing medium-sized territorial Health Board in Scotland. The organisation continues to operate its Acute Services, Community Services (Health and Social Care Partnership), and Corporate Services divisions while implementing the remedial measures required by this reprimand.
dataType: Health data, personal identifiers, special category data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 32 – Security of Processing

company: Υπουργείο Αγροτικής Ανάπτυξης και Τροφίμων (Ministry of Agricultural Development and Food)
companyDescription: Greek Ministry of Agricultural Development and Food is a government department responsible for agricultural policy, rural development, and food safety in Greece. As a public body, it is subject to mandatory GDPR compliance requirements including Data Protection Officer designation.
companyLongDescription: Greek Ministry of Agricultural Development and Food is a government department responsible for agricultural policy, rural development, and food safety in Greece. As a public body, it is subject to mandatory GDPR compliance requirements including Data Protection Officer designation.
caseDescription: Greek data protection authority found that the Ministry of Agricultural Development and Food failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for over 10 months (August 2022–June 2023), in breach of GDPR Article 37. The ministry also failed to cooperate adequately with the authority's investigation and did not timely submit a required questionnaire about DPO definition and role.
violationSummary: Lack of DPO appointment meant no independent oversight mechanism for data processing activities, creating structural governance failure that undermines data protection safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Ministry failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer for nearly 10 months after the previous officer's term ended on August 4, 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens' personal data processed by the ministry lacked dedicated oversight and protection mechanisms during this period, creating exposure to potential unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ministry claimed that during the DPO vacancy period (August 2022–June 2023), a data protection and security plan existed and data subjects suffered no harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: The absence of a formally designated DPO for over 10 months violated statutory requirements regardless of claim of mitigating safeguards; no independent oversight mechanism was in place during this period.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ministry attributed delayed questionnaire response to technical difficulties encountered by staff at the Directorate of Administrative Organization and Legal Supervision after receiving the 26 May 2023 letter.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ministry provided no advance notice to the authority of technical problems and failed to submit completed questionnaire until after receiving formal notice of hearing before the authority's plenary on 19 December 2023—nearly 7 months after the original May deadline.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ministry contended that answers to the questionnaire could be inferred from its 15 December 2023 memorandum describing the DPO's role, duties, and qualifications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority determined that the ministry's obligation to complete and timely submit the structured questionnaire was not satisfied by indirect inference; direct, timely cooperation was required by Article 31 GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 37(1) requires data controllers and processors to designate a Data Protection Officer in cases where processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except courts acting in judicial capacity.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ministry failed to appoint a DPO from 4 August 2022 until 20 June 2023 (10.5 months), despite statutory obligation as a public body.
violations: Ministry failed to appoint a DPO from 4 August 2022 until 20 June 2023 (10.5 months), despite statutory obligation as a public body.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires data controllers and processors to cooperate with the supervisory authority upon request in exercising the authority's duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ministry did not respond to initial questionnaire (3 May 2023 deadline, no response). Did not respond to second request (26 May 2023 deadline, no response). Only submitted completed questionnaire after receiving formal notice of hearing (20 December 2023), citing technical difficulties as excuse but providing no advance notice to authority.
violations: Ministry did not respond to initial questionnaire (3 May 2023 deadline, no response). Did not respond to second request (26 May 2023 deadline, no response). Only submitted completed questionnaire after receiving formal notice of hearing (20 December 2023), citing technical difficulties as excuse but providing no advance notice to authority.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1)(a) gives supervisory authorities power to order controllers and processors to provide information necessary to fulfil the authority's duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ministry delayed and failed to provide timely responses to authority's structured information requests, obstructing the coordinated EDPB-wide investigation into DPO definitions and positions in public sector.
violations: Ministry delayed and failed to provide timely responses to authority's structured information requests, obstructing the coordinated EDPB-wide investigation into DPO definitions and positions in public sector.

outcome: Greek Data Protection Authority (ΑΡΧΗ ΠΡΟΣΤΑΣΙΑΣ ΔΕΔΟΜΕΝΩΝ ΠΡΟΣΩΠΙΚΟΥ ΧΑΡΑΚΤΗΡΑ) imposed administrative fines totalling €25,000: €5,000 for Article 31 breach (failure to cooperate) and €20,000 for Article 37 breach (failure to appoint DPO for extended period). Authority found that mitigating factors included: (i) no material harm to data subjects, (ii) no previous similar violations, (iii) ministry had since signed a 2-year DPO service contract (June 2023), and (iv) late submission of questionnaire. Authority determined penalties were effective, proportionate, and deterrent measures to restore compliance and punish unlawful conduct.
companyNow: The Ministry of Agricultural Development and Food has since appointed a Data Protection Officer under a two-year service contract commencing 20 June 2023, restoring compliance with mandatory DPO designation requirements.
dataType: Personal data processed by public ministry (unspecified types)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 37 (designation of Data Protection Officer)
GDPR Article 38 (position of Data Protection Officer)

companyDescription: Join the Triboo Limited is a UK-registered company that operated online platforms including job recruitment websites. The company collected email addresses and contact details from job applicants and used them to send direct marketing emails on behalf of third-party 'business partners' and 'clients'.
companyLongDescription: Join the Triboo Limited is a UK-registered company that operated online platforms including job recruitment websites. The company collected email addresses and contact details from job applicants and used them to send direct marketing emails on behalf of third-party 'business partners' and 'clients'.
caseDescription: Join the Triboo Limited transmitted 107 million unsolicited direct marketing emails without valid consent between August 2019 and August 2020. The consent obtained was vague and non-specific, failing to clearly identify the sender or describe the types of marketing. The ICO found the company violated PECR Regulation 22 by sending unsolicited marketing emails without freely given, specific, and informed consent.
violationSummary: The company engaged in mass unsolicited direct marketing communication without valid prior consent from recipients, exploiting ambiguous consent mechanisms to target millions of individuals.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between August 2019 and August 2020, Join the Triboo Limited transmitted 107 million direct marketing emails to individual subscribers without obtaining valid consent compliant with PECR.
whyTheyWereWrong: 107 million subscribers received unsolicited marketing emails based on vague consent statements like 'I agree with marketing activity' that did not clearly identify which organizations would.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent statements stated 'I agree with marketing activity' or referenced receipt of emails from 'selected companies'
claimsVsReality.reality: These statements were too vague to constitute valid consent; recipients could not identify which organisations would contact them or what types of marketing they would receive

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy referenced 'similar organisations', 'business partners', and 'clients' across 'any business sector'
claimsVsReality.reality: This was too generic and broad to inform individuals about specific senders, rendering consent non-specific and non-informed

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent was obtained from job website applicants
claimsVsReality.reality: Data was not collected during a sale or negotiation with JTT, so the 'soft opt-in' exemption under PECR Regulation 22(3) did not apply

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited communications for direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent to such communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: JTT transmitted 107 million direct marketing emails without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: JTT transmitted 107 million direct marketing emails without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
Consent statements were vague and generic, failing to specify the sender or types of marketing, violating the 'specific' and 'informed' requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(11) defines consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of agreement via affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent statements such as 'I agree with marketing activity' lack specificity regarding sender identity and marketing types.
violations: Consent statements such as 'I agree with marketing activity' lack specificity regarding sender identity and marketing types.
Consent was pre-packaged across multiple channels without separate granular consent options, violating the 'freely given' principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Recital 32 requires that when processing has multiple purposes, consent should be given for all of them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Single vague consent statements were used to authorize marketing on behalf of multiple 'business partners', 'clients', and organisations across 'any business sector' without separate consent for each purpose.
violations: Single vague consent statements were used to authorize marketing on behalf of multiple 'business partners', 'clients', and organisations across 'any business sector' without separate consent for each purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Recital 42 requires that for consent to be informed, the data subject should be aware of the identity of the controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent statements referred to marketing by 'similar organisations', 'selected companies', and generic categories without identifying which specific entities would send marketing.
violations: Consent statements referred to marketing by 'similar organisations', 'selected companies', and generic categories without identifying which specific entities would send marketing.

outcome: The ICO issued an Enforcement Notice under section 40 of the Data Protection Act 1998 requiring JTT to cease unsolicited direct marketing via electronic mail unless recipients have previously notified JTT of clear and specific consent. JTT must comply within 30 days. The company has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days of the notice date (12 April 2023).
companyNow: Unknown. Join the Triboo Limited remains registered at Companies House (Registration No. 07152223) but current operational status is not disclosed in the document.
dataType: Email addresses, contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Recital 32 – multiple purposes require separate consent
GDPR Recital 42 – consent must be informed
GDPR Recital 43 – consent presumed not freely given without separate consent options

company: Mobile Chat (Koh Wei Ming @ Muhammad Amin Koh, trading as Mobile Chat)
companyDescription: Mobile Chat is a small retail business operating since 2015 from Geylang, Singapore, engaged in the sale and servicing of mobile phones, prepaid SIM cards, and mobile phone accessories. It acted as an M1 telecommunications retailer.
companyLongDescription: Mobile Chat is a small retail business operating since 2015 from Geylang, Singapore, engaged in the sale and servicing of mobile phones, prepaid SIM cards, and mobile phone accessories. It acted as an M1 telecommunications retailer.
caseDescription: KWM, a mobile phone retailer, exploited the SIM card registration process to illegally register prepaid SIM cards using customers' personal data without consent. He used two methods: duplicate scanning and incomplete transactions to register unwanted SIM cards that were then sold to anonymous purchasers, generating approximately $35,000 profit over 4 years. These illicit SIM cards were subsequently used to send unsolicited marketing messages to DNC-registered numbers, affecting at least 1,391 complainants.
violationSummary: KWM collected and used personal data ostensibly for legitimate SIM card registration but then misused that data for an entirely different, undisclosed purpose: registering SIM cards for unauthorized resale. This is a classic secondary use violation where data collected for one purpose was repurposed without consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Koh Wei Ming registered prepaid SIM cards using customers' personal data without consent by scanning their identity documents twice or activating incomplete transactions.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 1,000 individuals' names, addresses, and ID numbers were misused to register SIM cards that sent 1,391 unsolicited marketing messages to phone numbers registered with the Do Not.

claimsVsReality.claim: KWM claimed financial hardship as a sole breadwinner and sought to avoid a financial penalty due to anticipated imprisonment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commission found these representations unsubstantiated and insufficiently documented. Criminal sentencing arising from the same conduct does not exempt an organisation from regulatory enforcement under the PDPA.

claimsVsReality.claim: KWM claimed he was seeking mental health treatment at the Institute of Mental Health as a mitigating factor.
claimsVsReality.reality: Without substantiation of the specific conditions or nexus to the breaches, mental health treatment cannot serve as a mitigating factor in PDPA enforcement.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 13 of the PDPA: Organisations are prohibited from collecting, using or disclosing an individual's personal data unless the individual gives, or is deemed to have given, his consent, unless otherwise authorised under the PDPA or any other written law.
regulatoryFindings.description: KWM used customers' personal data without consent to register duplicate SIM cards in Method 1 (Duplicate Scanning), where customers consented only to registration of the number of SIM cards they requested.
violations: KWM used customers' personal data without consent to register duplicate SIM cards in Method 1 (Duplicate Scanning), where customers consented only to registration of the number of SIM cards they requested.
In Method 2 (Incomplete Transactions), customers withdrew consent by declining to complete the purchase, but KWM proceeded to use their personal data to activate and register SIM cards anyway.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 18 of the PDPA: An organisation may collect, use or disclose personal data about an individual only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances, and where that individual has been informed of the said purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: KWM used personal data for the purpose of registering SIM cards to sell to third parties for profit, a purpose that no reasonable person would consider appropriate and that customers did not consent to or could have anticipated.
violations: KWM used personal data for the purpose of registering SIM cards to sell to third parties for profit, a purpose that no reasonable person would consider appropriate and that customers did not consent to or could have anticipated.

outcome: The Commissioner found KWM liable for breaches of both the Consent Obligation (section 13) and Purpose Limitation Obligation (section 18) of the PDPA. KWM was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD 48,000 (approximately USD 35,748) within 30 days, with interest accruing at the rate specified in the Rules of Court for judgment debts if unpaid. The Commission noted that the Organisation has ceased the unauthorised sale of preregistered SIM cards and no further directions were required. KWM was separately sentenced to 16 months' imprisonment on 14 September 2023 under the Computer Misuse Act.
companyNow: Mobile Chat, a sole proprietorship operated by Koh Wei Ming, has ceased the unauthorised sale of preregistered SIM cards. The proprietor was sentenced to 16 months' imprisonment in September 2023 for related criminal offences under the Computer Misuse Act.
dataType: Names, addresses, NRIC/FIN/passport numbers

companyDescription: Nomad was a cryptocurrency cross-chain bridging platform founded circa 2021 that allowed users to transfer digital assets between different blockchain networks. The company raised $22 million in seed funding and positioned itself as a 'security-first' solution for interoperability.
companyLongDescription: Nomad was a cryptocurrency cross-chain bridging platform founded circa 2021 that allowed users to transfer digital assets between different blockchain networks. The company raised $22 million in seed funding and positioned itself as a 'security-first' solution for interoperability.
caseDescription: Nomad operated a cross-chain cryptocurrency bridge while making prominent security claims, but implemented inadequate software security practices including insufficient code testing, no circuit breakers, and no incident response plan. In August 2022, hackers exploited a vulnerability in their smart contracts and drained approximately $186 million in user assets; over $100 million in user losses resulted.
violationSummary: Nomad failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures for a financial services platform handling user assets worth hundreds of millions. The company's inadequate security practices directly led to a massive breach of user funds despite explicit security representations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Nomad marketed its cryptocurrency token bridge as 'security-first' and 'high security' while failing to implement basic secure coding practices, adequate testing, circuit breakers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users lost over $100 million in cryptocurrency assets when hackers exploited a preventable vulnerability that Nomad's leadership knew about but ignored despite internal warnings.

claimsVsReality.claim: Nomad is a 'security-first cross-chain messaging protocol' with 'high security'
claimsVsReality.reality: Nomad implemented inadequate testing (only 'happy-path' scenarios), no circuit breakers, no incident response plan, and insufficient security staff—failures that enabled a catastrophic $186M breach

claimsVsReality.claim: Users get 'high security, low cost, and fast bridging' and Nomad 'keeps the entire system (and your funds/messages) safe'
claimsVsReality.reality: Over $100 million in user funds were stolen within hours on August 1, 2022 due to a preventable vulnerability that exploited inadequate code testing

claimsVsReality.claim: Nomad developers 'securely build cross-chain applications' and Nomad 'strives to take advantage of every tool that protects users'
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal communications showed Nomad leadership knew of critical missing protections (circuit breakers, automated detection) but failed to implement them before launch

claimsVsReality.claim: The company prioritizes 'safety, simplicity, and our users' and is 'security-first'
claimsVsReality.reality: Executives overrode employee suggestions to reimburse an earlier loss, asserting there were 'no guarantees of safety' despite public security promises

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Nomad represented that it implemented secure software development practices and was 'security-first' while failing to implement well-known secure coding practices such as adequate unit testing prior to production deployment.
violations: Nomad represented that it implemented secure software development practices and was 'security-first' while failing to implement well-known secure coding practices such as adequate unit testing prior to production deployment.

Nomad failed to employ reasonable and appropriate software development security practices, including no circuit breakers, inadequate incident response systems, insufficient security staff, and no automated anomaly detection systems.

Users relied on Nomad's explicit security claims ('High security', 'security-first protocol', 'keep the entire system safe') when entrusting it with substantial financial assets, yet the company internally acknowledged inadequate testing and protective measures.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act on two counts: (1) Unfair Security Practices—failure to employ reasonable and appropriate software development security practices; (2) Security Misrepresentations—false or misleading representations regarding implementation of secure development practices. As of the complaint date, Nomad had recovered approximately $37.5 million in nominal asset value with the assistance of white-hat hackers and law enforcement, and partnered with third parties to return recovered funds to users. The document does not indicate a final settlement or judgment, only the issuance of the complaint.
companyNow: Nomad Bridge suffered a catastrophic security breach in August 2022 and was effectively shut down. The company faced an FTC enforcement action. Current operational status is unclear; the bridge became inoperable following the exploit.
dataType: Financial assets, transaction data, cryptographic keys, user wallet information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: LEADDESK, S.L. was a Spanish microenterprise founded in 2019, operating in the technology or software sector. Limited financial information is available.
companyLongDescription: LEADDESK, S.L. was a Spanish microenterprise founded in 2019, operating in the technology or software sector. Limited financial information is available.
caseDescription: LEADDESK, S.L. failed to respond to four information requests issued by Spain's data protection authority during an investigation into alleged GDPR violations. The company's non-cooperation obstructed the regulator's investigative powers. The company paid a €400 fine voluntarily, terminating the proceeding.
violationSummary: The violation relates to obstruction of regulatory authority's investigative powers and failure to cooperate with supervisory authority requests, which falls under processing security and regulatory compliance failures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: LEADDESK, S.L. received four information requests from Spain's data protection authority but failed to provide any response to the agency within the required ten business day deadline.
whyTheyWereWrong: By refusing to respond to regulatory inquiries, LEADDESK obstructed the investigation into whether personal data had been unlawfully processed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.1 grants supervisory authorities the power to order controllers and processors to provide any information required for the exercise of their functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: LEADDESK, S.L. did not provide any response to four separate information requests issued by AEPD between October 2022 and January 2023, obstructing the authority's investigation into alleged GDPR violations.
violations: LEADDESK, S.L. did not provide any response to four separate information requests issued by AEPD between October 2022 and January 2023, obstructing the authority's investigation into alleged GDPR violations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(e) establishes that failure to provide access in breach of Article 58.1 constitutes an infraction punishable by administrative fine up to €20,000,000 or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: LEADDESK, S.L.'s non-cooperation with regulatory information requests constituted a violation of Article 58.1, typified as a 'very grave' infraction under LOPDGDD Article 72.1.
violations: LEADDESK, S.L.'s non-cooperation with regulatory information requests constituted a violation of Article 58.1, typified as a 'very grave' infraction under LOPDGDD Article 72.1.

outcome: LEADDESK, S.L. paid €400 voluntarily on 29 March 2023, applying a 20% reduction to the proposed €500 fine. The payment terminated the administrative sanction procedure. The company waived any administrative appeals or further remedies regarding the matter. No admission of responsibility was recorded.
companyNow: Unknown. LEADDESK, S.L. was a microenterprise (PYME) with €296,619 in revenue in 2020 and was classified as inactive or dissolved in later years.
dataType: Unknown

companyDescription: Telefónica de España is a Spanish multinational telecommunications company founded in 1924, providing mobile, fixed-line, internet, and television services across Spain, Latin America, and Europe. It operates with approximately 40 million customers and is one of the largest telecommunications operators in the Spanish-speaking world.
companyLongDescription: Telefónica de España is a Spanish multinational telecommunications company founded in 1924, providing mobile, fixed-line, internet, and television services across Spain, Latin America, and Europe. It operates with approximately 40 million customers and is one of the largest telecommunications operators in the Spanish-speaking world.
caseDescription: Telefónica failed to provide complete and truthful responses to multiple information requests from Spain's data protection authority during an investigation into unauthorized domiciliation of a customer's bank account. The company initially refused to provide information, later gave incomplete answers, and did not justify its inability to locate the relevant contract until the penalty phase. This obstruction prevented the authority from properly investigating a potential data protection violation.
violationSummary: The core violation is obstruction of regulatory investigation powers (GDPR Art. 58.1). The company's failure to provide required information prevented effective enforcement of data protection rules, constituting an operational security and compliance failure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Telefónica failed to provide complete responses to multiple information requests from Spain's data protection authority.
whyTheyWereWrong: Telefónica's incomplete and delayed responses obstructed the authority's investigation into how a customer's bank account number was used without authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica claimed it could not provide the requested information because Serviguit Servicios 1970 S.L. was a legal entity outside the scope of GDPR and data protection law.
claimsVsReality.reality: The investigation concerned the complainant's personal bank account data, which is personal data under GDPR. The authority's power to request information under Article 58.1 does not depend on whether the intermediary is a legal entity or natural person; it applies to any information necessary to perform regulatory functions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica stated it had facilitated all available information and complied with the reiterative requests.
claimsVsReality.reality: Telefónica's responses were incomplete and evasive across five separate requests. It confirmed the bank account was associated with Serviguit Servicios 1970 S.L. from October 2021 to February 2022 only after multiple reiterations, and did not disclose until the penalty phase that it lacked the initial contract—information that should have been communicated immediately to allow the authority to pursue alternative investigative paths.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.1(a) requires control authorities to have the power to order the controller and processor to provide any information required for the authority to carry out its functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica refused to provide information on grounds that data about a legal entity fell outside GDPR scope, despite explicit authority requests.
violations: Telefónica refused to provide information on grounds that data about a legal entity fell outside GDPR scope, despite explicit authority requests.
Telefónica failed to provide complete information in response to three successive reiterative requests about whether Serviguit Servicios 1970 S.L. supplied the complainant's bank account number.
Until the penalty phase, Telefónica did not disclose that it could not locate the initial contract, preventing the authority from pursuing alternative investigative paths earlier.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(e) classifies as a serious infraction the failure to facilitate access in violation of Article 58(1), punishable by administrative fine up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica's incomplete and delayed responses constituted a failure to facilitate the authority's access to necessary information for investigation.
violations: Telefónica's incomplete and delayed responses constituted a failure to facilitate the authority's access to necessary information for investigation.
The obstruction directly caused expiration of the statutory limitations period on the underlying investigation (EXP202205067) without resolution.

outcome: Telefónica was ordered to pay an administrative fine of €90,000 for failure to facilitate information access under GDPR Article 58.1, as classified in Article 83.5(e). The authority rejected Telefónica's arguments that the request concerned a legal entity outside GDPR scope, that lack of culpability excused non-response, and that procedural fairness required reduction of the proposed €100,000 fine based on cooperation and conduct codes.
