The authority removed one aggravating factor (nexus to data processing activities) that had inflated the initial proposal but maintained the €90,000 penalty as proportionate to the seriousness of obstructing regulatory investigation.
companyNow: Telefónica remains one of Spain's largest telecommunications providers and a major operator in Europe, with continued regulatory oversight of data protection compliance.
dataType: Bank account numbers, personal identifiers, telephone line information

companyDescription: The Crown Prosecution Service is a public authority responsible for prosecuting criminal cases investigated by police and other investigative organisations in England and Wales. It is a controller of personal data under UK data protection law.
companyLongDescription: The Crown Prosecution Service is a public authority responsible for prosecuting criminal cases investigated by police and other investigative organisations in England and Wales. It is a controller of personal data under UK data protection law.
caseDescription: The CPS copied highly sensitive case files concerning historic child abuse from its secure computer system to an unencrypted personal USB device without proper security controls. The device was retained by the employee for months and later given to a family member, who viewed the contents. The breach would have remained undetected but for the family member's responsible action in reporting it.
companyWorth: Unknown (public sector body; no commercial valuation)
violationSummary: CPS failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of personal data, violating the sixth data protection principle. Unencrypted storage on self-procured devices without asset management, access controls, or encryption represents a fundamental insecurity in data handling.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: CPS allowed an employee to copy sensitive child abuse case files containing medical records, police reports.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 10 people including child abuse victims and witnesses experienced exposure of their most sensitive personal data to unauthorised access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CPS Electronic Media Policy prohibited use of self-procured USB devices and the employee contravened it.
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence showed the employee was aware of or trained on the policy; the policy existed but was not rigorously enforced or communicated. CPS conceded that self-procurement of USBs was a known practice that it had not controlled through technical measures.

claimsVsReality.claim: It would be a 'considerable exercise' to determine how many Active Directory group members were wrongly included and the management of portable media is inherently 'complex'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commissioner found this admission to be evidence of failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational controls. Basic asset management and encryption are standard data protection measures, not complex undertakings.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee acted on his own volition, not in discharge of employment duties, because the colleague had similar access rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee accessed and downloaded the data as part of his role and job responsibilities. His initial intent was to share information with a colleague for a legitimate business purpose (case preparation), making it a controller responsibility issue.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40 DPA 2018 requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: CPS failed to implement appropriate measures for Active Directory group management; the employee was wrongly included in an AD group of ~1,500 persons with broad access to sensitive data.
violations: CPS failed to implement appropriate measures for Active Directory group management; the employee was wrongly included in an AD group of ~1,500 persons with broad access to sensitive data.
CPS did not prevent self-procurement of USB devices by staff or implement countermeasures; ~1,500 staff had write access to data but only 800 had encryption software access.
CPS did not encrypt highly sensitive data stored on the USB device.
CPS maintained no asset register, supervision, or recording of self-procured USB device use despite awareness of the practice.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 66(1) DPA 2018 requires each controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to processing risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: CPS was aware of self-procurement of USB devices but did not implement technical measures (e.g., blocking USB access, mandatory encryption, device restrictions) to manage the risk.
violations: CPS was aware of self-procurement of USB devices but did not implement technical measures (e.g., blocking USB access, mandatory encryption, device restrictions) to manage the risk.
CPS rejected prior audit recommendations to procure USBs centrally and maintain distribution records, leaving gaps in control and visibility.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring CPS to comply with five specific remediation steps within 3 months: (1) prohibit and prevent use of self-procured USB devices; (2) provision CPS-procured USB devices with appropriate controls; (3) implement asset management for CPS USB devices including registration and tracking; (4) ensure encryption and compliance with CPS data protection policies; (5) limit USB use by considering available alternatives such as secure file transfer solutions (Egress). Failure to comply may result in a penalty notice up to £17.5 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. The Notice is effective immediately; CPS has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 calendar days.
companyNow: The Crown Prosecution Service remains the primary prosecuting authority in England and Wales. The Notice and remediation requirements are binding; ongoing monitoring by the ICO is expected to verify compliance with the data security measures.
dataType: Medical records, social care records, police investigation reports, witness names and addresses, defendant interview records, highly sensitive personal data
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018 Section 40 (sixth data protection principle – security)
Data Protection Act 2018 Section 66(1) (technical and organisational measures)
Data Protection Act 2018 Section 34(3) (controller responsibility for compliance)

company: TransUnion Rental Screening Solutions, Inc. (TURSS) and Trans Union LLC
companyDescription: TransUnion is a major credit reporting and background screening company providing consumer reports for employment, rental, credit, and identity verification purposes. TURSS, its wholly-owned subsidiary headquartered in Greenwood Village, Colorado, specializes in tenant and employment background screening.
companyLongDescription: TransUnion is a major credit reporting and background screening company providing consumer reports for employment, rental, credit, and identity verification purposes. TURSS, its wholly-owned subsidiary headquartered in Greenwood Village, Colorado, specializes in tenant and employment background screening.
caseDescription: TransUnion's tenant screening reports contained numerous inaccuracies in eviction records, including duplicate entries for single cases, missing or incorrect case dispositions, and mislabeled monetary amounts. The company also failed to disclose its third-party data vendors as information sources in consumer file disclosures, preventing consumers from disputing errors at the source.
violationSummary: TURSS failed to implement reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of consumer report data, and failed to identify data sources, violating FCRA requirements for consumer reporting agencies.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: TransUnion furnished hundreds of thousands of tenant screening reports annually with multiple duplicate entries for single eviction cases, missing or incorrect case dispositions.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers faced prolonged housing searches, rental application denials, higher rental payments, and spent time.

claimsVsReality.claim: TURSS contract with LexisNexis stated LexisNexis 'will use reasonable efforts' to provide accurate data and TURSS accepted all information 'AS IS'
claimsVsReality.reality: TURSS furnaced hundreds of thousands of inaccurate reports with duplicate entries, outdated dispositions, and sealed records to clients, despite receiving tens of thousands of consumer disputes

claimsVsReality.claim: File Disclosures identified the jurisdiction (e.g., local court) as the sole source of criminal record and eviction proceeding information
claimsVsReality.reality: Much of this information was actually sourced from third-party vendors like LexisNexis, and consumers requesting disclosures were not given the true sources needed to dispute errors

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(b) of the FCRA requires that whenever a Consumer Reporting Agency prepares a Consumer Report it shall follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.
regulatoryFindings.description: TURSS displayed multiple separate entries for single eviction cases, making eviction histories appear more voluminous than actual cases
violations: TURSS displayed multiple separate entries for single eviction cases, making eviction histories appear more voluminous than actual cases
TURSS reported eviction cases without accurate final dispositions, leaving cases appearing as merely initiated even when final decisions were available in public records months or years prior
TURSS labeled a field 'Judgment Amount' when it actually contained amounts alleged by landlords, not court judgments, misleading consumers about liability
TURSS reported sealed eviction records that were no longer accessible to the public, continuing to include them without procedures to identify and delete sealed records

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 609(a) of the FCRA requires Consumer Reporting Agencies to clearly and accurately disclose to consumers all information in the consumer's file and the sources of the information upon request.
regulatoryFindings.description: TURSS identified only the jurisdiction as the source of criminal records and eviction proceeding records in File Disclosures, even when TURSS obtained the information from third-party vendors such as LexisNexis, preventing consumers from disputing errors at the true source
violations: TURSS identified only the jurisdiction as the source of criminal records and eviction proceeding records in File Disclosures, even when TURSS obtained the information from third-party vendors such as LexisNexis, preventing consumers from disputing errors at the true source

outcome: Complaint filed October 12, 2023 seeking permanent injunctive relief, civil money penalties, restitution, disgorgement, compensatory damages, and FTC/Bureau cost recovery. Case status: Complaint initiated; no settlement or final judgment reported in document.
companyNow: TransUnion remains a major consumer reporting agency and credit data provider. TURSS operates as a subsidiary under Trans Union LLC (parent company based in Chicago). The company has implemented some compliance improvements (e.g., grouping eviction entries as of April 2021, disclosing vendor sources as of June 2021), though these changes only occurred after FTC investigative demands.
dataType: Criminal records, eviction proceedings, credit information, personal identification
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(b) – 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(b)
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 609(a) – 15 U.S.C. § 1681g(a)
Consumer Financial Protection Act Sections 1054(a) and 1055 – 12 U.S.C. §§ 5564(a) and 5565

companyDescription: Cover Appliance Limited is a UK-registered company (incorporated 16 September 2020) that provides home appliance cover and warranty products. The company conducted direct marketing via telephone calls but systematically violated regulations protecting consumers from unsolicited marketing.
companyLongDescription: Cover Appliance Limited is a UK-registered company (incorporated 16 September 2020) that provides home appliance cover and warranty products. The company conducted direct marketing via telephone calls but systematically violated regulations protecting consumers from unsolicited marketing.
caseDescription: Cover Appliance Limited made 511,499 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between January and December 2021, violating PECR regulations. The calls targeted vulnerable elderly individuals with misleading and threatening language, repeatedly attempted unauthorised bank debits, and used spoof caller identities to avoid detection. The company failed to obtain proper consent, provide identifying information, or respond adequately to ICO investigations.
violationSummary: PECR Regulation 21 prohibits unsolicited marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers without explicit prior consent. CAL systematically circumvented this protective measure by targeting vulnerable populations, using deceptive identification, and ignoring regulatory warnings.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Cover Appliance Limited made 511,499 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service, used multiple deceptive company names.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 511,000 vulnerable individuals—many elderly and explicitly registered to refuse such calls—were repeatedly harassed with misleading threats about insurance policies.

claimsVsReality.claim: CAL claimed it screened data prior to receipt and obtained valid consent from subscribers
claimsVsReality.reality: CAL made 511,499 calls to TPS-registered numbers with no valid prior consent; subscribers had not positively notified CAL they wished to receive calls; CAL was in fact making calls to solicit consent, which itself violates regulation 21(4)

claimsVsReality.claim: CAL claimed it introduced the company on calls and asked if recipients were happy to continue; consent was obtained on the call
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence was provided; the pattern of repeated calls to the same vulnerable individuals despite objections, use of deceptive company names, and complaints about misleading statements demonstrate consent was not genuinely obtained

claimsVsReality.claim: CAL stated details of individuals who do not wish to be contacted are entered into their CRM system to prevent future calls
claimsVsReality.reality: Complaints show CAL continued calling the same vulnerable individuals multiple times per day despite explicit requests to stop, including after individuals stated they were on the TPS register

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing to numbers listed on the Telephone Preference Service register kept under regulation 26, unless the subscriber has specifically notified the caller they do not object to such calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAL made 511,499 calls to TPS-registered numbers without obtaining valid prior consent from subscribers
violations: CAL made 511,499 calls to TPS-registered numbers without obtaining valid prior consent from subscribers
CAL obtained data claiming prior consent but had no evidence subscribers had positively and clearly notified CAL they were willing to receive marketing calls from CAL specifically
CAL made calls to illicit consent, which breaches regulation 21(4) requirements for valid notification

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(1)–(2) requires persons using public electronic communications services for direct marketing to provide the caller's name and either an address or free-call telephone number with each communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAL failed to provide identifying information to call recipients
violations: CAL failed to provide identifying information to call recipients
CAL used multiple deceptive company names ('Cover Appliance', 'UK Home Cover', 'Home Care Solutions', 'Platinum Cover') to avoid detection
CAL did not provide a valid callback number identifying CAL itself, preventing individuals from contacting the company to complain or withdraw consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A(1) permits the ICO to serve a monetary penalty where there has been a serious contravention of PECR by the person, and the contravention was either deliberate or negligent (the person knew or ought to have known of the risk but failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it).
regulatoryFindings.description: CAL deliberately contravened PECR by failing to provide adequate responses to ICO investigations despite multiple requests and warnings
violations: CAL deliberately contravened PECR by failing to provide adequate responses to ICO investigations despite multiple requests and warnings

CAL was negligent: it knew or ought to have known of the legal risks (published ICO guidance, TPS complaint notification in July 2021, industry knowledge) but failed to screen against TPS register, implement proper consent procedures, or respond to regulatory warnings
CAL's volume of calls (511,499 to TPS numbers in 7 months) and deliberate use of spoof identities demonstrate systematic and reckless disregard for consumer protection laws

outcome: The ICO issued a Monetary Penalty Notice of £200,000 (reduced to £160,000 if paid by 31 August 2023) against Cover Appliance Limited on 2 August 2023. The penalty is payable by BACS or cheque by 1 September 2023. CAL has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner found deliberate and/or negligent contraventions of PECR Regulations 21 and 24 and imposed the penalty to promote compliance with PECR and deter similar non-compliance. Enforcement will not proceed unless all appeals are exhausted and the payment deadline passes.
companyNow: Cover Appliance Limited (Companies House No. 12883535) remains registered but was subject to enforcement action in 2023. Current operational status is unclear; the company failed to respond to regulatory enquiries during the investigation.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal contact information

companyDescription: 1Health.io Inc., doing business as Vitagene, provides DNA health test kits and personalized health reports combining genetic analysis with consumer health questionnaires. The company sells products directly to consumers and through retailers like Amazon, with pricing from $29 to $259.
companyLongDescription: 1Health.io Inc., doing business as Vitagene, provides DNA health test kits and personalized health reports combining genetic analysis with consumer health questionnaires. The company sells products directly to consumers and through retailers like Amazon, with pricing from $29 to $259.
caseDescription: Vitagene made prominent promises about privacy and security of genetic and health data, but failed to deliver. The company publicly exposed over 2,600 consumers' sensitive health and genetic information in unencrypted cloud storage and ignored three security warnings before a breach was disclosed. Additionally, Vitagene retroactively changed privacy policies to permit much broader sharing of data without consumer consent.
violationSummary: The core violation is the public exposure of sensitive health and genetic information due to inadequate security practices combined with deceptive claims about security standards. This also involves Information Processing – Insecurity (failure to implement promised safeguards) and Information Dissemination – Breach of Confidentiality (retroactive policy changes enabling third-party sharing without consent).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Vitagene made prominent false claims about exceeding industry-standard security practices, storing DNA results without identifying information.
whyTheyWereWrong: More than 2,600 consumers' sensitive health and genetic information was publicly exposed online for years because Vitagene failed to encrypt data, restrict access.

claimsVsReality.claim: We exceed industry-standard security practices to protect your privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vitagene stored 2,600+ consumers' unencrypted health and genetic data in publicly accessible cloud storage buckets from 2016-2019 without access controls, encryption, logging, or monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your results and DNA sample are stored without your name or any other common identifying information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Health Reports listed consumer names, dates of birth, referring doctors; raw genetic data was stored with first names and identifying information alongside genetic information.

claimsVsReality.claim: You can delete your data at any time. This will remove your information from all of our servers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vitagene lacked a data inventory system and could not search or identify consumers' data in exposed buckets, making complete deletion impossible for consumers who requested it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vitagene destroys your physical DNA saliva sample after it has been analyzed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Beginning December 2016, Vitagene had no contractual requirement with its genotyping lab partner to destroy physical samples, leaving samples retained indefinitely.

claimsVsReality.claim: We will not sell your data to any third party individually or in aggregate form.
claimsVsReality.reality: In 2020, Vitagene retroactively changed privacy policies to permit sharing of sensitive health and genetic data with pharmacies, supermarkets, supplement makers, and other third parties for marketing—applied to all customers including those predating the policy without consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Claimed to exceed industry-standard security practices but maintained publicly accessible unencrypted cloud storage with consumer health and genetic data for years
violations: Claimed to exceed industry-standard security practices but maintained publicly accessible unencrypted cloud storage with consumer health and genetic data for years
Represented DNA results were stored without identifying information, but actually stored names and identifying data with genetic information
Promised consumers could delete all their data, but lacked inventory systems preventing complete deletion from exposed buckets
Claimed to destroy physical DNA saliva samples after analysis, but had no contractual requirement with lab partner for destruction
Retroactively applied expanded data-sharing policies to consumers who purchased services under prior privacy terms without notice or consent

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Vitagene on September 6, 2023 (Docket No. C-4798). The complaint alleges five counts of unfair and deceptive practices. As of the document date, this is an initial complaint; the case appears to be in the early litigation phase. Expected outcome likely includes a consent order requiring comprehensive privacy and security remediation, data inventory implementation, deletion of exposed data, monitoring and audit provisions, and corrective advertising. No final settlement or monetary penalty amount is specified in the complaint document itself.
companyNow: 1Health.io (formerly Vitagene) operates a DNA testing and health reporting service. The company faces significant regulatory exposure and consumer trust damage following the public exposure of genetic data.
dataType: Genetic data, health information, DNA test results, medical history, family health history, lifestyle data, enrollment information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Count I: Security Misrepresentation – Exceeding Industry Standards
Count II: Security Misrepresentation – Storing DNA Results without Identifying Information
Count III: Privacy Misrepresentation – Data Deletion
Count IV: Privacy Misrepresentation – Saliva Sample Destruction
Count V: Unfair Adoption of Material Retroactive Privacy Policy Changes

companyDescription: Trygg-Hansa is an insurance company operating as a filial (branch) of Danish insurer Tryg Forsikring A/S, which is a subsidiary of Tryg A/S. It provides insurance products in Sweden and merged with Moderna Försäkringar in April 2022 under the Trygg-Hansa name.
companyLongDescription: Trygg-Hansa is an insurance company operating as a filial (branch) of Danish insurer Tryg Forsikring A/S, which is a subsidiary of Tryg A/S. It provides insurance products in Sweden and merged with Moderna Försäkringar in April 2022 under the Trygg-Hansa name.
caseDescription: Trygg-Hansa failed to implement adequate technical security measures for sensitive insurance customer data, making approximately 650,000 customers' records accessible via manipulated URLs for over 2 years. Unauthorised individuals could access documents containing health records, personal numbers, and financial information by simply changing digits in web addresses. The company received a tip about the vulnerability in November 2020 but did not report or remediate it until contacted by the regulator in February 2021.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures (authentication, encryption, access controls) to protect sensitive personal data from unauthorised access, directly violating security and integrity principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: From October 2018 to February 2021, Trygg-Hansa made approximately 650,000 insurance customers' sensitive personal data accessible via unencrypted internet links that could be modified.
whyTheyWereWrong: The security breach exposed 650,000 customers' health information, social security numbers, financial data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Trygg-Hansa claimed that accessing documents required special knowledge of URL structure and manipulation of specific digits in document IDs.
claimsVsReality.reality: In practice, a single digit change in many cases was sufficient (first six of eight digits were identical across different URLs), making access trivial. IMY was able to access documents directly via shared URLs without any modification whatsoever.

claimsVsReality.claim: Trygg-Hansa claimed it had implemented comprehensive security measures before the incident, including IT security policy, regular penetration testing, logging, and annual data protection training.
claimsVsReality.reality: These claimed measures did not prevent the deployment of a system with fundamental security flaws (no authentication, no encryption, predictable URLs), and the flaws went undetected for 28 months despite being relatively obvious.

claimsVsReality.claim: Trygg-Hansa received a phone tip in November 2020 and claimed the recipient did not understand it was a potential incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to investigate or escalate the tip, and the vulnerability remained unfixed for three more months until the regulator contacted them in February 2021.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing, loss, destruction or damage by accident.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trygg-Hansa made 650,000 customers' sensitive personal data directly accessible in plaintext on the internet for 28 months without authentication or encryption, in breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle.
violations: Trygg-Hansa made 650,000 customers' sensitive personal data directly accessible in plaintext on the internet for 28 months without authentication or encryption, in breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32.1 requires data controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, considering latest developments, implementation costs, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trygg-Hansa failed to implement basic technical controls: no user authentication, no encryption of sensitive data, no access controls. Document URLs were modifiable, allowing unauthorised parties to access any customer record by changing URL digits. The company deployed this system with these fundamental flaws and did not detect or remediate them for 28 months.
violations: Trygg-Hansa failed to implement basic technical controls: no user authentication, no encryption of sensitive data, no access controls. Document URLs were modifiable, allowing unauthorised parties to access any customer record by changing URL digits. The company deployed this system with these fundamental flaws and did not detect or remediate them for 28 months.

outcome: Trygg-Hansa ordered to pay administrative fine of 35,000,000 SEK (approximately €3.24 million or $3.24 million). Decision dated 28 August 2023. Company must implement enhanced security measures including encryption, access controls, authentication, independent penetration testing, architectural security review, improved testing procedures, and additional staff training. Registered individuals were notified by letter and website notice. Decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Trygg-Hansa Försäkring filial continues as a branch of Tryg Forsikring A/S (Danish parent company Tryg A/S). Following the enforcement action, it has implemented enhanced security measures including independent penetration testing, architectural security controls, code review processes, and expanded employee training programmes.
dataType: Health data, personal identification numbers, contact information, financial data, ownership information, accident details, union membership

companyDescription: Century Evergreen Private Limited is a manpower contracting services company that provides recruitment and staffing services, requiring jobseekers to submit identification documents for identity verification and suitability assessment.
companyLongDescription: Century Evergreen Private Limited is a manpower contracting services company that provides recruitment and staffing services, requiring jobseekers to submit identification documents for identity verification and suitability assessment.
caseDescription: Century Evergreen Private Limited exposed 96,889 images of identification documents belonging to 23,940 jobseekers on its website due to an unpatched Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) vulnerability that existed since 2015. The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements or include data protection requirements in its vendor contract, allowing unauthorised access and download of sensitive identification data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection and disclosure of personal data. An IDOR vulnerability allowed attackers to manipulate URLs and download sensitive identification documents without restriction for seven years.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to implement reasonable security arrangements and left an Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) vulnerability unpatched from 2015 to 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: 23,940 jobseekers had their national identity card images and personal identification documents exposed publicly for seven years, enabling potential identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had engaged an IT vendor to develop and maintain the website, suggesting vendor responsibility for security
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation remained solely responsible for protecting personal data under the PDPA regardless of vendor engagement; organisation failed to include data protection requirements in vendor contract

claimsVsReality.claim: Functionality testing was conducted when website launched
claimsVsReality.reality: No security testing was conducted prior to launch or thereafter; only functionality testing was performed

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Century Evergreen failed to implement any security measures to prevent the IDOR vulnerability that existed from website launch in 2015 until December 2022
violations: Century Evergreen failed to implement any security measures to prevent the IDOR vulnerability that existed from website launch in 2015 until December 2022
Failed to conduct security testing prior to website launch or at any point thereafter
Failed to include security requirements in its contract with the IT vendor who developed and maintained the website
Did not implement access controls or authorization checks to prevent URL manipulation attacks

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of section 24(a) of the PDPA. Directed to pay a financial penalty of S$9,000 within 30 days. The organisation has already implemented remedial actions including fixing the IDOR vulnerability, making server configuration changes, implementing vulnerability scans, migrating backup to encrypted remote server, deploying additional security software, and securing a new vendor contract for website security management.
companyNow: Status unknown; organisation had admitted culpability and cooperated with investigation, taking prompt remedial actions upon discovery of the breach in December 2022.
dataType: Identification documents (National Registration Identity Cards), identification document images

companyDescription: Plymouth City Council is a local authority serving the city of Plymouth in Devon, England. As a public body, it processes personal data for statutory functions including housing, education, social services, and local governance.
companyLongDescription: Plymouth City Council is a local authority serving the city of Plymouth in Devon, England. As a public body, it processes personal data for statutory functions including housing, education, social services, and local governance.
caseDescription: Plymouth City Council failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory one-month deadlines over a three-year period, with compliance rates as low as 45% for on-time responses. Some SARs took up to two years to complete, and 20 SARs remained outstanding for over a year. The ICO issued a reprimand for violations of Articles 12(3) and 15 of the UK GDPR.
violationSummary: The council's systemic failure to provide timely access to personal data constitutes exclusion—the denial of individuals' right to access information about themselves, a core data protection principle.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Plymouth City Council failed to respond to Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory deadline over three years.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents were systematically denied timely access to their own personal data for extended periods.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) of the UK GDPR requires the controller to provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15 to 22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request, extendable by two further months where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Plymouth City Council failed to provide information to data subjects within one month of receipt; compliance rate was only 45% within statutory deadline over three years
violations: Plymouth City Council failed to provide information to data subjects within one month of receipt; compliance rate was only 45% within statutory deadline over three years

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) of the UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation from the controller as to whether personal data concerning them are being processed and, where applicable, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Plymouth City Council failed to provide timely access to personal data, with 18 SARs taking up to two years and 8 remaining incomplete after two years
violations: Plymouth City Council failed to provide timely access to personal data, with 18 SARs taking up to two years and 8 remaining incomplete after two years

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) of the UK GDPR requires the controller to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Plymouth City Council's significant delays in SAR responses (up to two years) prevented provision of copies of personal data within reasonable timeframes
violations: Plymouth City Council's significant delays in SAR responses (up to two years) prevented provision of copies of personal data within reasonable timeframes

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Plymouth City Council. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps including £110,000 investment to increase team capacity from 2.6 FTE to 5.6 FTE (April 2021–August 2022), employment of new staff, monthly KPI tracking, and weekly SAR assessment. The Commissioner recommended six further actions: (1) ensure SARs are responded to within statutory deadlines; (2) continue monitoring SAR compliance data; (3) complete outstanding SARs; (4) consider additional process improvements; (5) ensure adequate staff resources; (6) provide staff training council-wide on SAR recognition and monitor completion. Plymouth City Council remains subject to ICO oversight for compliance with these recommendations.
companyNow: Plymouth City Council continues as a local authority in the UK providing public services and governance to the city of Plymouth. The council has implemented remedial measures and increased resources for data subject access request handling.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Swinburne Snowball and Jackson is a legal practice specialising in probate and estate matters. The firm handles sensitive financial transactions and beneficiary information for clients.
companyLongDescription: Swinburne Snowball and Jackson is a legal practice specialising in probate and estate matters. The firm handles sensitive financial transactions and beneficiary information for clients.
caseDescription: A law firm's employee email account was compromised via spear phishing, allowing a threat actor to divert fraudulent payments totalling an undisclosed sum from probate beneficiaries. The firm lacked multi-factor authentication, had no formal IT security contracts defining responsibilities, and did not achieve cybersecurity accreditation. The ICO found violations of UK GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(b) and issued a reprimand.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures required by GDPR Article 32, resulting in unauthorised access to personal data via email account compromise.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Swinburne Snowball and Jackson failed to implement multi-factor authentication on employee email accounts and lacked formal IT security contracts defining security responsibilities and standards.
whyTheyWereWrong: An employee's email account was compromised via spear phishing, allowing a threat actor to make four fraudulent payments totaling a large sum from probate beneficiaries' funds.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firm had taken reasonable security precautions and its IT contractors had advised on appropriate measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The firm lacked MFA, had no formal IT security contracts defining responsibilities, and IT contractors had not suggested MFA despite it being widely recommended by the NCSC, SRA, and Law Society.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firm was a small practice and had promptly reported to the SRA and insurers within 24 hours.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite prompt reporting to regulators and insurers, the firm failed to notify the ICO within the mandatory 72-hour window, breaching Article 33 of the UK GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data is processed securely, with integrity and confidentiality ensured through appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: SSJ processed financial and probate beneficiary data without multi-factor authentication, formal IT security contracts, or security accreditation, allowing a spear phishing attack to compromise an employee email account.
violations: SSJ processed financial and probate beneficiary data without multi-factor authentication, formal IT security contracts, or security accreditation, allowing a spear phishing attack to compromise an employee email account.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(b) of the UK GDPR requires appropriate measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk and ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: SSJ failed to implement MFA, lacked documented security responsibilities with its IT provider, and could not demonstrate preventative, detective or auditing measures for email account security.
violations: SSJ failed to implement MFA, lacked documented security responsibilities with its IT provider, and could not demonstrate preventative, detective or auditing measures for email account security.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 33 of the UK GDPR requires notification of a personal data breach to the ICO without undue delay and no later than 72 hours of becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: SSJ notified the ICO on 26 January 2021, 12 days after the breach was discovered on 14 January 2021, citing unawareness of the 72-hour deadline.
violations: SSJ notified the ICO on 26 January 2021, 12 days after the breach was discovered on 14 January 2021, citing unawareness of the 72-hour deadline.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand in accordance with Article 58 of the GDPR. SSJ must implement multi-factor authentication, establish formal IT security contracts, undergo cybersecurity accreditation (e.g. NCSC Cyber Essentials), conduct regular security assessments, deliver mandatory data protection and cybersecurity training to staff, and ensure senior management accountability for data security. All affected clients were repaid in full on 3 February 2021. The matter is now closed, though further regulatory action may be considered if additional incidents are reported.
companyNow: Swinburne Snowball and Jackson is a solicitor's practice based in Consett, County Durham. Post-incident, the firm has implemented multi-factor authentication and engaged with third-party cyber security consultants.
dataType: Financial data, beneficiary information, probate matter details

companyDescription: Gain Capital UK Limited is a financial services provider operating in the online trading and financial technology sector, offering trading platforms and services to UK-based customers.
companyLongDescription: Gain Capital UK Limited is a financial services provider operating in the online trading and financial technology sector, offering trading platforms and services to UK-based customers.
caseDescription: Gain Capital UK Limited suffered a data breach on 14 April 2020 when an unauthorised third party exploited an unpatched SiteCore vulnerability to exfiltrate 17.92 GB of data containing personal information of 72,361 UK individuals. The company lacked a patch management programme and failed to apply security patches to their systems as specified in their vendor support contract, violating GDPR Article 32 requirements for appropriate technical and organisational security measures.
violationSummary: The core failure was inadequate technical and organisational security measures (GDPR Art. 32). The company failed to implement appropriate safeguards (patch management) that would have prevented the vulnerability exploitation, resulting in a large-scale data breach affecting financial data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Gain Capital UK Limited failed to implement a patch management programme and did not apply security patches to its systems despite their support contract explicitly requiring them to do so.
whyTheyWereWrong: 72,361 UK customers had their bank account numbers, sort codes, names, and email addresses stolen when attackers exploited unpatched SiteCore vulnerabilities that Gain Capital should have fixed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company was not notified by the third-party vendor about the SiteCore vulnerabilities that were exploited.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor support contract explicitly stipulated that Gain Capital UK Limited was responsible for installing security patches and upgrades; the company failed to apply them despite this contractual obligation and the availability of the patches.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Gain Capital UK Limited failed to implement a patch management programme and did not apply security patches to their systems despite their vendor support contract stipulating this was their responsibility, leaving systems vulnerable to known SiteCore vulnerabilities.
violations: Gain Capital UK Limited failed to implement a patch management programme and did not apply security patches to their systems despite their vendor support contract stipulating this was their responsibility, leaving systems vulnerable to known SiteCore vulnerabilities.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's systems lacked essential security measures to ensure resilience and integrity. Unpatched vulnerabilities directly led to unauthorized access and exfiltration of 17.92 GB of sensitive personal data including bank account numbers and sort codes.
violations: The company's systems lacked essential security measures to ensure resilience and integrity. Unpatched vulnerabilities directly led to unauthorized access and exfiltration of 17.92 GB of sensitive personal data including bank account numbers and sort codes.

outcome: The ICO issued Gain Capital UK Limited a formal reprimand under GDPR Article 58(2)(b). The company was directed to take steps to ensure compliance with GDPR requirements. The ICO recommended implementing a structured patch management programme, consulting the ICO's security checklist, and following NCSC guidance including Cyber Essentials. The ICO noted that if further incidents or complaints are reported, the matter will be revisited and further formal regulatory action may be considered. The investigation is now closed.
companyNow: Gain Capital UK Limited continues to operate as a financial services company. The reprimand serves as formal notice of non-compliance; the company is expected to implement recommended security measures to prevent future incidents.
dataType: Financial data (bank account numbers, sort codes), names, email addresses

companyDescription: House Hold Appliances 247 Limited (HHA247L) was a UK-based appliance service and repair company offering service plans and maintenance products for domestic white goods. The company engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls.
companyLongDescription: House Hold Appliances 247 Limited (HHA247L) was a UK-based appliance service and repair company offering service plans and maintenance products for domestic white goods. The company engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls.
caseDescription: HHA247L made 19,069 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between June and November 2021, violating regulation 21 of PECR. The company purchased data from a third party without proper screening against the TPS register and failed to implement adequate due diligence. Two complaints were filed, including one from an elderly vulnerable individual who received consecutive unwanted calls about insurance products.
violationSummary: The company conducted systematic unsolicited direct marketing telephone calls to individuals who had explicitly registered their preference not to receive such communications, constituting surveillance-type collection in violation of privacy preferences.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 19,069 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between June.
whyTheyWereWrong: Elderly and vulnerable individuals registered to reject marketing calls received unwanted calls anyway.

claimsVsReality.claim: HHA247L stated it 'presumed' purchased data had been screened against the TPS
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not screen the data itself and had no documented evidence of TPS screening; only 100 of 20,000 purchased records were screened by the supplier

claimsVsReality.claim: HHA247L claimed the second complaint was a 'called in error' incident
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed 19,069 systematic calls to TPS-registered numbers over 6 months, with 80% of connected calls reaching TPS subscribers; calls were part of deliberate marketing campaign

claimsVsReality.claim: Company advised it purchased data from legitimate third-party suppliers
claimsVsReality.reality: Data sourced from persons formerly associated with a company the ICO had previously fined £40,000 for PECR breaches and which was in compulsory liquidation; total failure of due diligence

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(1)(b) of PECR prohibits use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers are registered on the TPS register, unless the subscriber has notified the caller they do not object to such calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: HHA247L made 19,069 calls to TPS-registered numbers without subscriber consent or opt-out notifications
violations: HHA247L made 19,069 calls to TPS-registered numbers without subscriber consent or opt-out notifications
No evidence presented that any TPS-registered subscriber had notified HHA247L they did not object to receiving calls
Company purchased third-party data without verifying TPS screening or obtaining required regulation 21(4) notifications

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(A1) requires that when making direct marketing calls, the CLI (calling line identifier) must not be withheld.
regulatoryFindings.description: HHA247L made all outbound calls from a 'withheld number', constituting an additional breach of regulation 21(A1)
violations: HHA247L made all outbound calls from a 'withheld number', constituting an additional breach of regulation 21(A1)

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A DPA (as applied to PECR cases) permits monetary penalties where serious contravention is deliberate or negligent (organisation knew or ought to have known of risk but failed to take reasonable steps).
regulatoryFindings.description: HHA247L knew or ought to have known PECR requirements as a business engaged in direct marketing
violations: HHA247L knew or ought to have known PECR requirements as a business engaged in direct marketing
ICO published detailed PECR guidance and operates a helpline explaining TPS screening obligations
Company received TPS contact notifications on each complaint but failed to implement prevention measures
Failed to undertake due diligence on third-party data supplier (previously fined by ICO, in liquidation)
Did not screen data against TPS register despite purchasing it; merely 'presumed' supplier had screened

outcome: Monetary penalty of £55,000 imposed (reducible to £44,000 with early payment discount by 3 September 2023). Payment due by 4 September 2023 by BACS transfer or cheque. Penalty recoverable by County Court, High Court, or Scottish sheriff court if unpaid. Right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. Company must comply with PECR requirements, implement TPS screening, cease calls to TPS-registered numbers without consent, and ensure training and documentation are in place.
companyNow: House Hold Appliances 247 Limited was still operating as of May 2022 (website active). Current operational status unknown; company registered with ICO as of January 2022.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber information

company: SERVICIOS E INTERVENCIONES EN EDIFICACION DEL MEDITERRÁNEO, S.L.
companyDescription: SERVICIOS E INTERVENCIONES EN EDIFICACION DEL MEDITERRÁNEO, S.L. is a Spanish construction and building services company (NIF B54803101). Details about its size, revenue, or founding date are not disclosed in the decision.
companyLongDescription: SERVICIOS E INTERVENCIONES EN EDIFICACION DEL MEDITERRÁNEO, S.L. is a Spanish construction and building services company (NIF B54803101). Details about its size, revenue, or founding date are not disclosed in the decision.
caseDescription: A construction services company published a photograph of an individual on its website without consent. The image was identifiable and made public to illustrate company work. The company violated GDPR Article 6.1 by processing personal data (the image) without any lawful basis.
violationSummary: The company disclosed an identifiable photograph of the complainant on its public website without authorization, making personal data (the image) accessible to the public without lawful basis.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Published an identifiable photograph of an individual on their website to showcase construction work without obtaining the person's prior written consent or establishing any lawful basis.
whyTheyWereWrong: The person's identifiable image was publicly displayed online without consent, exposing their likeness to potential misuse, reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's publication of the image served a legitimate business purpose (illustrating work performed).
claimsVsReality.reality: No lawful basis under Article 6.1 GDPR was established; the company processed personal data without consent and without legal justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The image was not fully identifiable because the face was not completely visible.
claimsVsReality.reality: The image was identifiable because, combined with the company name and context, it permitted identification of the individual. The court cited Spanish jurisprudence showing that partial facial obscuring does not prevent identification when other contextual information makes attribution possible.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1 requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if it complies with at least one of the specified conditions: consent, contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company processed the complainant's image (personal data) without consent and without any other lawful basis under Article 6.1.
violations: Company processed the complainant's image (personal data) without consent and without any other lawful basis under Article 6.1.
No evidence that processing fell under contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, or public task exception.
No legitimate interest assessment demonstrating that company's interests overrode the data subject's fundamental rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5.1(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company's processing of the image was unlawful (no legal basis) and lacked transparency (no notice to the data subject).
violations: Company's processing of the image was unlawful (no legal basis) and lacked transparency (no notice to the data subject).
Data subject had no knowledge that their image would be used for marketing/illustrative purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 71 defines infringements of GDPR Articles 5, 6, 7, and 9 as serious violations subject to administrative sanctions.
regulatoryFindings.description: Violation of GDPR Article 6.1 constituted a serious infraction under Spanish law.
violations: Violation of GDPR Article 6.1 constituted a serious infraction under Spanish law.

outcome: On 29 May 2023, the AEPD Director initiated a sanctioning procedure against the company. The company recognized responsibility and paid the reduced penalty of €1,200 on 10 June 2023, using two available reductions (20% for early responsibility recognition + 20% for voluntary payment, applied cumulatively to the original €2,000 penalty). The procedure was terminated on 10 June 2023 pursuant to Article 85 of the Spanish Administrative Procedure Act (LPACAP). The company had already removed the image from its website prior to resolution.
companyNow: Unknown. The company appears to be a small-to-medium construction services firm based in Spain; current operational status unknown.
dataType: Biometric data (photograph/image), identifying information

companyDescription: Fortis Insolvency Limited operates within the financial sector, providing advice and services to businesses and individuals facing financial and operational problems, including IVAs (Individual Voluntary Arrangements) and debt management solutions.
companyLongDescription: Fortis Insolvency Limited operates within the financial sector, providing advice and services to businesses and individuals facing financial and operational problems, including IVAs (Individual Voluntary Arrangements) and debt management solutions.
caseDescription: Fortis Insolvency Limited sent 558,354 unsolicited SMS direct marketing messages to individuals without valid consent between July 2020 and July 2021. The company obtained data from third-party lead generators but failed to ensure individuals had provided informed, specific consent to receive SMS marketing. The contravention affected financially vulnerable individuals seeking debt advice.
violationSummary: Unsolicited SMS messages were transmitted to subscribers' personal devices without consent, exposing them to unwanted direct marketing and creating nuisance (810 complaints to spam service). This constitutes exposure of contact information and personal circumstances to unauthorized marketing communications.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Between July 2020 and July 2021, Fortis Insolvency Limited sent 558,354 unsolicited SMS direct marketing messages (527,481 delivered) to individuals obtained from third-party websites.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 527,000 financially vulnerable individuals in debt received unwanted SMS marketing messages for debt relief services they never agreed to receive.

claimsVsReality.claim: FIL claimed it 'contracts with third parties who collect specific consent to allow their customers details to be passed on' and implements Data Sharing Agreements and due diligence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Third-party websites failed to provide meaningful consent for SMS marketing from FIL; FIL was not identified as a trusted third party; individuals had no opportunity to opt in/out of FIL marketing during data collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: FIL maintained that messages sent were 'solicited by the individual' and therefore fell outside PECR.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals entering details into third-party websites were not sufficiently informed they were requesting solicited marketing from FIL; messaging appeared to indicate interaction would be with the website owner, not FIL.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 requires that unsolicited direct marketing by electronic mail must not be transmitted unless the recipient has previously notified consent or falls within specific exemptions (e.g., soft opt-in).
regulatoryFindings.description: FIL transmitted 527,481 SMS direct marketing messages without obtaining valid, informed, and specific consent from recipients
violations: FIL transmitted 527,481 SMS direct marketing messages without obtaining valid, informed, and specific consent from recipients
Consent obtained from third-party websites was generic and failed to identify FIL or SMS as a communication channel
FIL was not listed as a trusted third party on privacy policies where data was collected, making it improbable recipients anticipated FIL contact
No opportunity to opt in/out of FIL marketing was provided at point of data collection on third-party platforms

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A of the Data Protection Act 1998 permits a monetary penalty where there is a serious contravention of PECR and the person either acted deliberately or knew/ought to have known of risk but failed to take reasonable steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: Contravention was serious: 558,354 messages sent, 527,481 delivered, directed at financially vulnerable individuals in debt
violations: Contravention was serious: 558,354 messages sent, 527,481 delivered, directed at financially vulnerable individuals in debt
FIL was aware of PECR obligations and had published compliance policies, establishing knowledge of legal requirements
FIL failed to implement reasonable measures to verify consent despite availability of ICO guidance, helpline, and published enforcement examples
810 complaints to the 7726 spam reporting service indicated FIL should have known of systemic compliance failures

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty of £30,000 (reducible to £24,000 upon early payment by 26 July 2023) to be paid by 27 July 2023. The penalty was imposed under Section 55A of the Data Protection Act 1998. FIL has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner emphasized the seriousness of marketing to financially vulnerable individuals without consent and noted that the penalty serves as general deterrent to industry compliance.
companyNow: Fortis Insolvency Limited continues to operate in the financial services sector. The company's current compliance status and whether remediation measures were implemented is not specified in the notice.
dataType: Phone numbers, personal contact details
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 22

companyDescription: Tokyo Century Leasing (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is a leasing and hire-purchase financing company that operates a website for customer applications.
companyLongDescription: Tokyo Century Leasing (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is a leasing and hire-purchase financing company that operates a website for customer applications.
caseDescription: Tokyo Century Leasing suffered a ransomware attack encrypting personal data of 141,412 individuals due to an unpatched vulnerability in its firewall that had been available for 2 years 9 months. The company failed to implement basic cybersecurity measures including patch monitoring, patch management processes, and multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 PDPA. Specifically: failure to monitor for patches, lack of patch management processes, and absence of MFA for privileged accounts created foreseeable vulnerabilities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Tokyo Century Leasing left a known firewall vulnerability unpatched for 2 years 9 months, failed to monitor for security updates.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers exploited the unpatched vulnerability to encrypt personal data of 141,412 individuals including names, NRIC numbers, bank account information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's IT vendor had responsibility for upgrading the firewall, so patching was handled externally
claimsVsReality.reality: While the vendor had technical capability, the contract contained no requirement for proactive monitoring; patching only occurred on ad-hoc request. The company failed to request or monitor for the patch for 2 years 9 months despite it being publicly available.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ransomware attack was an external threat beyond the company's control
claimsVsReality.reality: The attack exploited a known vulnerability that the company could have patched within weeks or months of its May 2019 release. The company's own failure to implement basic security practices (patch monitoring, MFA, patch management processes) created the preventable vulnerability window.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal, having regard to the volume and sensitivity of the data and possible impact of breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct regular monitoring for software patches despite FortiOS firewall running outdated version 6.0.4 with known CVE-2018-13379 vulnerability for 2 years 9 months
violations: Failed to conduct regular monitoring for software patches despite FortiOS firewall running outdated version 6.0.4 with known CVE-2018-13379 vulnerability for 2 years 9 months
Did not implement processes to manage software patches and upgrades; patching was ad-hoc and only triggered by organisation request, with no requirement in IT vendor contract for proactive monitoring

Failed to implement MFA for administrator accounts accessing large volumes of sensitive personal data (NRIC, financial info, bank accounts) despite Commission guidance since May 2022 that MFA is a baseline requirement

outcome: Tokyo Century Leasing was found in breach of section 24 PDPA and ordered to pay SGD 82,000 penalty within 30 days. Post-incident, the company patched the vulnerability, implemented MFA for VPN access, changed admin passwords, conducted anti-virus scans, and engaged forensic monitoring (no exfiltration detected). The Commission found no further directions necessary based on remedial actions already taken.
companyNow: Tokyo Century Leasing (Singapore) continues to operate as a leasing and hire-purchase finance company. Following the incident and enforcement action, it has implemented the required security controls.
dataType: NRIC numbers, names, dates of birth, addresses, contact numbers, income statements, email addresses, employer information, bank account details, passport numbers, employment pass numbers, medical check-up information

companyDescription: Ascentis Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based software company specialising in developing, providing, and integrating Customer Relationship Management (CRM) and eCommerce solutions. The company was engaged by Starbucks Coffee Singapore to develop and host both a CRM system for the loyalty program and a separate eCommerce platform.
companyLongDescription: Ascentis Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based software company specialising in developing, providing, and integrating Customer Relationship Management (CRM) and eCommerce solutions. The company was engaged by Starbucks Coffee Singapore to develop and host both a CRM system for the loyalty program and a separate eCommerce platform.
caseDescription: Ascentis developed and hosted an eCommerce platform for Starbucks that suffered a data breach affecting 332,774 individuals. The breach occurred because Ascentis failed to disable an administrator account belonging to a former contractor employee, allowing a malicious actor to gain access and exfiltrate personal data. The Commission found Ascentis breached its obligation to implement reasonable security arrangements.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements required under PDPA s.24, specifically failing to disable dormant admin accounts and failing to implement multi-factor authentication, which directly enabled the unauthorised access and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to disable an administrative account after a contractor employee departed, permitting continued use of weak credentials shared via Google Sheet to access a platform holding 332,774.
whyTheyWereWrong: 332,774 people's names, email addresses, phone numbers, birthdays, and physical addresses were stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ascentis maintained control and management of the Project and retained responsibility for the development and management of the Platform, including creation and management of administrator accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this responsibility, Ascentis failed to disable an admin account after a contractor employee departed and did not create individual accounts for contractors taking over duties, instead allowing credential sharing via Google Sheet.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Platform's password complexity requirements were met by the password 'Kyanon@123456' (minimum 8 characters, 1 upper/lower case, 1 special character, not repeating previous 5 passwords).
claimsVsReality.reality: The password incorporated the company name 'Kyanon' and sequential digits '123456', making it easily guessable and insecure despite technical compliance with stated requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ascentis had plans to implement MFA for admin accounts as part of unified access controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Implementation was delayed due to COVID-19 related manpower shortages and had not occurred prior to the breach, despite the large volume of personal data accessible from the Platform.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA (Protection Obligation) requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ascentis failed to disable Peter's Admin Account after the contractor employee left Kyanon in May 2022, allowing continued use by remaining team members
violations: Ascentis failed to disable Peter's Admin Account after the contractor employee left Kyanon in May 2022, allowing continued use by remaining team members
Ascentis permitted the admin credentials to be shared via an insecure Google Sheet
Ascentis failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) on admin accounts with access to large volumes of personal data
Ascentis failed to create new individual accounts for contractors who took over duties, instead reusing a shared admin account
Ascentis did not establish sufficiently clear data protection requirements with Kyanon regarding account management and access controls
The weak password 'Kyanon@123456' (incorporating company name and sequential digits) was easily guessable despite meeting technical complexity requirements

outcome: The Commission found Ascentis in breach of PDPA s.24 and imposed a financial penalty of SGD $10,000, payable within 30 days. No further directions were issued as Ascentis had already implemented remedial measures including disabling all accounts, resetting administrator credentials, implementing MFA, blocking the malicious actor's IP address, and requiring vendors to perform anti-virus scans. Starbucks SG (the data controller) accepted a separate voluntary undertaking to implement enhanced security arrangements.
companyNow: Ascentis Pte. Ltd. continues to operate as a software development and eCommerce solutions provider. The company demonstrated cooperation with regulatory authorities and swift remediation of security controls following the breach.
dataType: Names, email addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, physical addresses, membership details

companyDescription: PPLingo Pte Ltd operates LingoAce, an online Chinese and English language learning platform offering virtual classes to students aged 4-15 globally. The platform includes an operations support system managing student, teacher, and staff data.
companyLongDescription: PPLingo Pte Ltd operates LingoAce, an online Chinese and English language learning platform offering virtual classes to students aged 4-15 globally. The platform includes an operations support system managing student, teacher, and staff data.
caseDescription: PPLingo's online education platform suffered a data breach affecting 557,144 users when attackers exploited a weak administrator password ('lingoace123') via brute force attacks. The company lacked basic password security controls and had failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer since incorporation. Personal data of approximately 303,238 minors and sensitive financial information were accessed.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (adequate password policies, 2FA, DPO oversight) to prevent unauthorised access to personal data, resulting in large-scale breach of confidential and sensitive information including minors' data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PPLingo failed to implement adequate password security for administrator accounts, using only an 8-character minimum requirement with no expiry, complexity requirements.
whyTheyWereWrong: A threat actor used brute force attacks to compromise the admin account with password 'lingoace123', exposing personal data of 557,144 individuals including 303,238 minors' names.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation had in place a written data protection policy and certain security measures including network access control and firewall protection
claimsVsReality.reality: Security measures were inadequate; admin password lacked expiry, complexity requirements, or 2FA; password remained unchanged for 2+ years and was easily guessable

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation organised two rounds of security awareness training for IT development team in April 2022
claimsVsReality.reality: Training had no practical effect; brute force attack succeeded within days exploiting basic password vulnerabilities that should have been prevented

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to implement password expiry or mandatory password change for administrator account over 2 years
violations: Organisation failed to implement password expiry or mandatory password change for administrator account over 2 years
Organisation failed to require minimum password complexity for privileged accounts
Password 'lingoace123' incorporated guessable components (company name and common sequence '123'), vulnerable to brute force attacks
No 2FA/MFA implemented for admin accounts despite handling large volume of sensitive personal data including minors' data and financial information

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.11(3) requires all organisations to designate an individual to be responsible for compliance with the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer from incorporation in 2016 until 18 May 2022 (over 5 years)
violations: Organisation failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer from incorporation in 2016 until 18 May 2022 (over 5 years)
No designated person responsible for ensuring PDPA compliance, implementing data protection policies, managing complaints, or alerting management to data protection risks

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 74,000 payable within 30 days. The organisation is required to pay interest at Rules of Court rates on any outstanding amount. No further directions issued as the organisation had already implemented remedial measures including: engaging forensic experts, resetting admin passwords, implementing 2FA for all OPS System accounts, implementing enhanced password requirements, appointing a DPO, notifying affected users, implementing 2FA for email accounts, conducting security audits, enhancing firewall protection, and increasing security training frequency.
companyNow: PPLingo continues to operate its LingoAce online language learning platform for students aged 4-15. The company has implemented significant security improvements including 2FA, enhanced password policies, bug testing services, and appointed a Data Protection Officer.
dataType: Name, date of birth, gender, photos, email, phone number, address, financial data (bank account), identity card number, salary, educational background, learning data
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation – reasonable security arrangements)
PDPA s.11(3) (Accountability Obligation – designate Data Protection Officer)

company: Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC)
companyDescription: MOPAC is a functional body of the Greater London Authority responsible for oversight of the Metropolitan Police. It determines the purpose and means of data processing on its website, while GLA serves as its data processor hosting MOPAC's pages and webforms on London.gov.uk.
companyLongDescription: MOPAC is a functional body of the Greater London Authority responsible for oversight of the Metropolitan Police. It determines the purpose and means of data processing on its website, while GLA serves as its data processor hosting MOPAC's pages and webforms on London.gov.uk.
caseDescription: MOPAC's data processor GLA accidentally made two webforms public on the London.gov.uk website between November 2022 and February 2023, allowing unauthorized access to 394 individuals' personal data submitted via the London Victims' Commissioner contact form. The organization lacked specific training and policies on permission management, violating data security requirements under UK GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32.
violationSummary: Personal data was unintentionally exposed to the public due to lack of technical safeguards, security procedures, and staff training, resulting in unauthorized disclosure to a broad audience.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
