whyTheyWereWrong: A threat actor exploited a single compromised credential to infiltrate the network and steal personal data for 2,022 employees including National Insurance numbers, bank details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company had adequate security measures in place for data protection
claimsVsReality.reality: No multi-factor authentication on internet-facing Remote Desktop Service; no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing conducted; no formal Incident Response Plan existed

claimsVsReality.claim: Data Breach Policy referenced an appointed Data Protection Officer for breach handling
claimsVsReality.reality: GRS (Roadstone) Limited did not actually have an appointed Data Protection Officer at the time of the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of the UK GDPR requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRS (Roadstone) Limited failed to ensure the ongoing confidentiality of systems as required by Article 32(1)(b). Specifically, the company deployed a Remote Desktop Service without multi-factor authentication despite ICO guidance explicitly stating that single-factor authentication should not be used on internet-facing services that can lead to access to personal data. This vulnerability was left unpatched for over 4 years after the acquisition of the subsidiary that operated the service.
violations: GRS (Roadstone) Limited failed to ensure the ongoing confidentiality of systems as required by Article 32(1)(b). Specifically, the company deployed a Remote Desktop Service without multi-factor authentication despite ICO guidance explicitly stating that single-factor authentication should not be used on internet-facing services that can lead to access to personal data. This vulnerability was left unpatched for over 4 years after the acquisition of the subsidiary that operated the service.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(d) requires organisations to implement a process for regular testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRS (Roadstone) Limited conducted no formalised testing on their IT infrastructure prior to the incident, including no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing. The organisation operates across 41 sites in the UK, and given the size and scale, regular assessment was clearly necessary. A threat actor was able to exploit a documented Common Vulnerabilities and Exposure (CVE) published over 2 years before the incident. Had periodic vulnerability assessments been conducted, this threat would have been identified and mitigated.
violations: GRS (Roadstone) Limited conducted no formalised testing on their IT infrastructure prior to the incident, including no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing. The organisation operates across 41 sites in the UK, and given the size and scale, regular assessment was clearly necessary. A threat actor was able to exploit a documented Common Vulnerabilities and Exposure (CVE) published over 2 years before the incident. Had periodic vulnerability assessments been conducted, this threat would have been identified and mitigated.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to GRS (Roadstone) Limited under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. While no monetary fine was imposed, the company was found in infringement of Articles 32(1), 32(1)(b), and 32(1)(d). GRS (Roadstone) Limited has since taken remedial actions including: deployment of vulnerability management tools, centralised logging, increased employee security awareness training, and significant expansion of multi-factor authentication across applications. The ICO recommended further actions: implementation, testing and periodic review of a formal Incident Response Plan; and clarification of breach handling procedures with clear documentation regarding who is responsible for managing data breaches (correcting references to a non-existent Data Protection Officer). The company also provided credit monitoring services and paid for replacement driving licences and passports for affected individuals.
companyNow: GRS (Roadstone) Limited continues to operate as an independent supplier of materials to the construction industry with at least 800 employees across 41 UK sites. Following the incident and ICO enforcement action, the company has implemented enhanced security infrastructure and practices.
dataType: Names, addresses, National Insurance numbers, passports, driving licences, birth/marriage certificates, bank details, dates of birth, HR records, medical information

companyDescription: RedMart Limited is a Singapore-based online grocery and fresh produce retailer that operates warehouses for storage and distribution of goods sold through its platform. The organisation implemented security measures at its Jalan Buroh warehouses to manage visitor access and deter food safety incidents.
companyLongDescription: RedMart Limited is a Singapore-based online grocery and fresh produce retailer that operates warehouses for storage and distribution of goods sold through its platform. The organisation implemented security measures at its Jalan Buroh warehouses to manage visitor access and deter food safety incidents.
caseDescription: RedMart collected photographic images of physical NRICs and identification documents from suppliers accessing its warehouses without proper legal basis or notification. The organisation failed to obtain valid consent and did not initially provide transparency about the collection purpose. While the company later implemented a Legitimate Interests Exception framework with enhanced security controls, the prior collection violated PDPA provisions on consent, notification, and lawful processing.
violationSummary: The organisation conducted systematic photographic collection of identification documents containing sensitive personal identifiers (NRIC numbers) without legal authority, notice, or consent. This constitutes surveillance under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: RedMart collected photographs of suppliers' physical NRICs and identification documents at warehouse security checkpoints without notifying visitors of the purpose or obtaining valid legal basis.
whyTheyWereWrong: Suppliers were exposed to collection of sensitive personal data including full NRIC numbers with no meaningful choice to refuse.

claimsVsReality.claim: RedMart claimed collection of ID photographs was necessary to establish visitor identities and deter food security incidents.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the legitimate interest was recognised as valid, the organisation had no legal basis for the collection prior to July 2022—neither valid consent nor a documented legitimate interest assessment was conducted beforehand. The collection occurred without notice or proper safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: RedMart argued the collection fell under the National Interest Exception (national defence/security) and Investigations Exception (ongoing investigations).
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commission rejected both claims. Food security at a private warehouse is not 'national interest' in the sense of national defence or security. The Investigations Exception requires an ongoing investigation, not hypothetical future investigations. Neither exception applied.

claimsVsReality.claim: RedMart claimed visitors voluntarily provided their IDs and that collection was obvious and reasonable.
claimsVsReality.reality: Visitors had no choice—ID photograph collection was a mandatory condition for warehouse entry as part of their employment or delivery obligation. It would not have been obvious to suppliers that photographic images of IDs would be taken and retained.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 13 of the PDPA requires organisations to obtain consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal data unless an exception applies.
regulatoryFindings.description: RedMart did not obtain valid consent from suppliers. The collection of ID photographs was a mandatory condition for warehouse entry—not a voluntary product or service the suppliers chose to access. Consent cannot be inferred from participation in employment or business delivery obligations.
violations: RedMart did not obtain valid consent from suppliers. The collection of ID photographs was a mandatory condition for warehouse entry—not a voluntary product or service the suppliers chose to access. Consent cannot be inferred from participation in employment or business delivery obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Sections 14(1)(a) and 18(b) of the PDPA, read with section 20, require organisations to notify individuals of the purpose for which personal data is collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: RedMart failed to inform suppliers of the purpose for collecting ID photographs prior to the incident. No notices were posted at security checkpoints explaining why photographs were being taken. This breached the transparency requirement even if consent had otherwise been valid.
violations: RedMart failed to inform suppliers of the purpose for collecting ID photographs prior to the incident. No notices were posted at security checkpoints explaining why photographs were being taken. This breached the transparency requirement even if consent had otherwise been valid.

regulatoryFindings.act: Paragraph 1, Part 3 of the First Schedule of the PDPA permits collection without consent where a legitimate interest of the organisation outweighs adverse effects to individuals, provided assessments are conducted and reasonable mitigation measures are implemented.
regulatoryFindings.description: Prior to July 2022, RedMart relied on no legitimate legal basis—neither valid consent nor documented legitimate interest assessment. The organisation did not conduct the required assessment or implement safeguards until after the Commission's investigation. Retroactive reliance on this exception was not available for prior collection.
violations: Prior to July 2022, RedMart relied on no legitimate legal basis—neither valid consent nor documented legitimate interest assessment. The organisation did not conduct the required assessment or implement safeguards until after the Commission's investigation. Retroactive reliance on this exception was not available for prior collection.

outcome: The Commission found that RedMart's collection of ID photographs prior to 8 July 2022 breached the PDPA because it lacked valid consent, proper notification, and a documented legitimate interest assessment. After investigation, RedMart submitted a Legitimate Interests Exception Assessment dated 22 July 2022 demonstrating: (1) identification of a legitimate interest in deterring and investigating food security incidents; (2) implementation of six specific access controls to mitigate risks (limiting collection to high-risk areas, restricting tablet access, encrypting transmission, immediate server upload, limiting access to DevOps team, one-year retention cap); and (3) commitment to notify visitors via posted notices. The Commission accepted the organisation had met the Legitimate Interests Exception requirements going forward. No monetary penalty was issued. The preliminary direction requiring a 60-day assessment was deemed satisfied by the LIE Assessment already provided. The organisation must continue implementing the identified safeguards and maintain notification to visitors.
companyNow: RedMart Limited continues operations as an online grocery and retail platform in Singapore. The company implemented the required data protection measures and now relies on legitimate interest basis for ID photograph collection from warehouse visitors.
dataType: National ID numbers (NRIC), identity documents, photographs

companyDescription: Bank of Ireland Group plc is a major financial services organisation providing retail and commercial banking services across Ireland and internationally via online platforms including Banking365, a digital banking service offering account access, fund transfers, payments, and bill payment functionality to hundreds of thousands of customers.
companyLongDescription: Bank of Ireland Group plc is a major financial services organisation providing retail and commercial banking services across Ireland and internationally via online platforms including Banking365, a digital banking service offering account access, fund transfers, payments, and bill payment functionality to hundreds of thousands of customers.
caseDescription: Bank of Ireland failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures on its Banking365 platform, resulting in ten personal data breaches between January and May 2020. Six breaches were caused by staff failing to follow procedures correctly; four resulted from a flaw in the Customer Information System's account merging algorithm. Unauthorised persons gained access to customer accounts and viewed sensitive financial data.
violationSummary: Bank failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures required by Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data processed via Banking365.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Bank of Ireland failed to implement adequate security measures on its Banking365 platform, allowing staff to manually grant account access without proper validation controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Ten customers had their sensitive financial transaction data and account details unauthorisedly accessed and disclosed to third parties, exposing them to risks of fraud and identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank stated 'there has never been an instance of fraud or identity theft arising from these types of events' and 'risk of fraud and/or identity theft is a potential harm'.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ten customers' accounts were compromised and unauthorised third parties gained access to sensitive financial transaction details, creating genuine fraud and identity theft risk regardless of whether realised harm occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank claimed it had adequate data protection policies and procedures in place and quality assurance frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Procedures existed but were not followed; quality assurance testing (10% sampling of account merges) was insufficient; training did not adequately address risks; and internal audit identified the CIS flaw in 2019 but remediation took 21 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to implement robust validation procedures and quality assurance controls to prevent staff errors when manually populating user access fields on Banking365 platform.
violations: Bank failed to implement robust validation procedures and quality assurance controls to prevent staff errors when manually populating user access fields on Banking365 platform.
Bank did not implement adequate testing measures for account merging operations in Customer Information System, allowing a known 2019 coding flaw to persist unremediable for 21 months.
Training materials did not adequately emphasise importance of data protection procedures or detail risks of account merging and potential for unauthorised disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymisation, encryption, ability to ensure confidentiality and integrity, ability to restore availability in timely manner, and processes for regularly testing and evaluating effectiveness of measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Monthly call monitoring sampled only one call per agent per month, insufficient oversight for high-risk manual data entry on widely-used platform.
violations: Monthly call monitoring sampled only one call per agent per month, insufficient oversight for high-risk manual data entry on widely-used platform.
Quality assurance procedures did not include additional controls to minimise human error in account access provisioning despite documented risks.
Security measures including proprietary fraud detection and SIEM system failed to identify over-merged accounts until late remediation in 2021, revealing inadequate ongoing effectiveness evaluation.

outcome: Bank of Ireland ordered to: (1) upgrade validation controls and implement quality assurance controls for data input within 90 days; (2) implement staff training on data protection and account merging risks within 90 days; (3) implement appropriate testing measures for coding errors within 90 days; (4) implement process ensuring coding errors affecting customer account access are remediated without delay within 90 days. Additionally, Bank received formal reprimand recognising serious nature of infringements. Bank required to submit compliance report within one month of notification. Administrative fine of €750,000 imposed.
companyNow: Bank of Ireland Group plc remains operational as one of Ireland's major financial institutions. The bank has since implemented enhanced data protection governance and account management systems in response to this enforcement decision.
dataType: financial data, account balances, transaction details, credit card information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) — Integrity and Confidentiality Principle

companyDescription: Argentum Data Solutions Limited is a UK-based telecommunications and SMS messaging services provider that offers bulk SMS transmission infrastructure to businesses for marketing campaigns.
companyLongDescription: Argentum Data Solutions Limited is a UK-based telecommunications and SMS messaging services provider that offers bulk SMS transmission infrastructure to businesses for marketing campaigns.
caseDescription: Argentum Data Solutions sent 2.33 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers between January 2021 and January 2022, the vast majority (2.3 million) through third parties using the company's lines. The company failed to obtain valid prior consent from recipients and did not identify the sender in any messages, violating PECR Regulations 22 and 23.
violationSummary: ADS collected and used subscriber contact information for direct marketing surveillance without obtaining freely given, specific, and informed consent as required by PECR Regulation 22. The company enabled mass unsolicited contact to individuals who had not explicitly agreed to receive such communications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between January 2021 and January 2022, Argentum Data Solutions sent 24,309 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 2.3 million individuals received unwanted marketing messages they had never consented to, were unable to identify the sender.

claimsVsReality.claim: ADS claimed that 'legitimate interest' was the lawful basis for sending direct marketing SMS messages.
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 22 explicitly requires prior consent from recipients for unsolicited direct marketing communications; legitimate interest is not a permissible alternative basis under PECR.

claimsVsReality.claim: ADS operates a compliant SMS platform for direct marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: Of 2.33 million messages transmitted, 99% lacked valid recipient consent and violated PECR; sender identity was concealed in all messages, violating Regulation 23.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited direct marketing electronic communications unless the recipient has previously notified the sender that they consent to such communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: ADS sent 24,309 direct marketing SMS messages directly without valid prior consent from recipients
violations: ADS sent 24,309 direct marketing SMS messages directly without valid prior consent from recipients
ADS allowed third parties to send 2,306,114 direct marketing SMS messages via company lines without valid recipient consent
No evidence of valid consent was provided; ADS claimed 'legitimate interest' which is not a lawful basis under PECR Regulation 22

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23(b) requires that direct marketing communications identify the person on whose behalf the communication is sent and provide a valid address where recipients can request cessation of communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: None of the SMS messages sent or transmitted by ADS identified the sender of the communication
violations: None of the SMS messages sent or transmitted by ADS identified the sender of the communication
Recipients were unable to determine who initiated the marketing message and therefore could not exercise their right to refuse

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) defines consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes by statement or clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: ADS failed to demonstrate freely given consent (no evidence consent was not conditional on service receipt)
violations: ADS failed to demonstrate freely given consent (no evidence consent was not conditional on service receipt)
No evidence of specific consent to direct marketing from ADS or third parties
Consent could not have been informed as recipients did not know the identity of senders

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring ADS to cease sending unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages without valid prior consent within 30 days. ADS is required to: (1) obtain clear and specific consent from recipients before sending or allowing others to send direct marketing communications; (2) identify the sender in all direct marketing emails; (3) provide valid addresses for unsubscribe requests; and (4) ensure communications comply with Electronic Commerce Regulations 2002. The case involves ongoing monitoring compliance. Right of appeal exists to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights).
companyNow: Argentum Data Solutions Limited remains registered at Companies House (Registration Number 08935427) as of the enforcement notice date. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Phone numbers (SMS recipients), subscriber contact information

company: Piraeus Leasing (Πειραιώς Leasing) / Piraeus Financial Leasing MAE (formerly CPB Leasing)
companyDescription: Piraeus Leasing/Piraeus Financial Leasing MAE is a financial leasing company and subsidiary of Piraeus Bank Group. It engaged in financing and leasing of vehicles and real property, including property marketing and management services through affiliated entities.
companyLongDescription: Piraeus Leasing/Piraeus Financial Leasing MAE is a financial leasing company and subsidiary of Piraeus Bank Group. It engaged in financing and leasing of vehicles and real property, including property marketing and management services through affiliated entities.
caseDescription: A leasing company collected and stored a photograph containing a vehicle's clearly visible license plate number (personal data) without consent. The photo was shared internally within the Piraeus Group and sent externally to third parties, allowing a narrow social circle to identify the complainant's family financial hardship. When the complainant requested access to his personal data, the company falsely claimed the license plate was not visible and denied possessing the incriminating photograph.
violationSummary: The company failed to apply data minimization (Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR) by retaining and transmitting a high-resolution photograph with clearly visible personal identifiers (license plate) when a redacted version would have sufficed for legitimate business purposes. The violation also encompasses failure to provide honest and transparent access to personal data as required by Art. 15 GDPR.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Collected and stored a photograph showing a vehicle with a clearly visible license plate number, then distributed it to a third party without the vehicle owner's knowledge or consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's license plate became linked to his family's property loss, enabling his social circle to learn of their financial devastation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company initially stated to the complainant that the license plate number in the published photograph was not visible, claiming the image posed no data protection concern.
claimsVsReality.reality: A second high-resolution version of the same photograph was retained in the company's files showing the license plate number in crystal-clear detail, which had been transmitted to Piraeus Real Estate and distributed to third parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: During the investigation, the company represented that the photograph had already been deleted from its archives and could not be produced.
claimsVsReality.reality: The photograph remained in company files and was produced only at the oral hearing. The company provided no documentary evidence (deletion logs, timestamps) to support its deletion claims, violating the accountability principle.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted the license plate number alone cannot identify an individual because license plates are held by vehicle owners and are not directly linked to personal identity without access to official registry records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The license plate, combined with the property location shown in the photograph and the complainant's known narrow social circle, allowed his identification. The Data Protection Authority confirmed that indirect identification through combined data elements within a small social group constitutes personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which they are processed' (data minimization principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Piraeus Leasing collected and retained a high-resolution photograph containing the complainant's vehicle license plate number when a redacted or lower-resolution image without the visible plate would have sufficed for property marketing purposes.
violations: Piraeus Leasing collected and retained a high-resolution photograph containing the complainant's vehicle license plate number when a redacted or lower-resolution image without the visible plate would have sufficed for property marketing purposes.

The company transmitted the incriminating photograph in full clarity to Piraeus Real Estate and subsequently to third parties, failing to implement technical measures (e.g., license plate blurring) before distribution.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of whether personal data concerning them is being processed, and to receive a copy of that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: When the complainant exercised his access rights, Piraeus Leasing falsely stated it did not hold a photograph with a clearly visible license plate, despite maintaining such an image in its files.
violations: When the complainant exercised his access rights, Piraeus Leasing falsely stated it did not hold a photograph with a clearly visible license plate, despite maintaining such an image in its files.

The company asserted it had already deleted the image as justification for non-compliance, yet provided no documentary evidence (audit logs, deletion records) to support this claim, violating the accountability principle (Art. 5(2) GDPR).

outcome: The Hellenic Data Protection Authority found that Piraeus Leasing MAE (as successor entity absorbing the two originally-named respondents through universal succession) violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(c) and 15(1). The Authority imposed two administrative fines of €10,000 each (total €20,000): one for failure to apply data minimization principles, and one for non-compliance with the access right request. The decision found that the complainant's identity could be derived from the license plate in combination with the property location within his narrow social circle, making the photograph personal data. The company was ordered to comply with all GDPR obligations going forward, including implementing technical safeguards to minimize personal data in images before internal distribution and external sharing.
companyNow: Piraeus Financial Leasing is a subsidiary of Piraeus Bank Group, Greece's second-largest banking group. The entity continues to operate as a wholly-owned leasing subsidiary of Piraeus Bank following the absorption of predecessor companies.
dataType: Vehicle license plate number, vehicle ownership details, property location information

company: Fullerton Healthcare Group Pte Limited & Agape CP Holdings Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: Fullerton Healthcare Group is an enterprise healthcare service provider serving individuals and corporate employees. Agape CP Holdings is a business process outsourcing provider and social enterprise that engages prison inmates in work programmes.
companyLongDescription: Fullerton Healthcare Group is an enterprise healthcare service provider serving individuals and corporate employees. Agape CP Holdings is a business process outsourcing provider and social enterprise that engages prison inmates in work programmes.
caseDescription: FHG and Agape failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect customer data processed by Agape as a data intermediary. Agape created an internet-facing file server with disabled password protection for 20 months, enabling unauthorised access and exfiltration of 156,900 customers' sensitive health and financial records. Both organisations failed to conduct adequate security reviews and maintain proper vendor oversight.
violationSummary: Both organisations failed to implement and maintain reasonable security safeguards as required by PDPA s.24. Agape's inadequate password management, failure to conduct comprehensive security reviews, and use of internet-facing storage without proper access controls directly enabled unauthorized access and exfiltration of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Agape downloaded FHG customer data onto a computer, re-uploaded it to an internet-facing file server without password protection for 20 months.
whyTheyWereWrong: 156,900 patients and employees had their health records, bank account numbers, identity documents, and surgical procedure codes stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: FHG's understanding with Agape was that customer data would only be held on a local computer for emergency/exceptional situations during SharePoint downtime, with no additional copies made.
claimsVsReality.reality: Agape routinely downloaded and re-uploaded customer data to an internet-facing file server (Online Drive) as the primary working system for agents, contrary to FHG's stated understanding. FHG failed to discover or monitor this practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agape had appropriate security measures in place when the Online Drive was created in December 2017 with a password meeting complexity standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: By the time of the incident in October 2021, the password had been disabled for approximately 20 months (since December 2019) due to an unknown cause, leaving the server as an unprotected public directory on the internet without any access controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agape conducted periodic security reviews to ensure protection of customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Security reviews were improperly scoped and failed to cover the internet-facing Online Drive, which was treated as a legacy system unique to FHG and not reviewed, allowing critical vulnerabilities to go undetected for years.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.24 requires organisations to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agape failed to conduct periodic security reviews covering all IT systems including the internet-facing Online Drive
violations: Agape failed to conduct periodic security reviews covering all IT systems including the internet-facing Online Drive
Agape implemented inadequate password management with shared credentials and no expiry dates
Agape's Online Drive password was disabled for approximately 20 months, creating an unprotected public directory
FHG failed to exercise reasonable oversight of vendor data handling processes despite awareness that third-party access was required
FHG inadvertently disclosed unnecessary sensitive financial and health data to Agape, increasing breach impact

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.4(2) makes data intermediaries subject to the same Protection Obligation as data controllers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agape, as a data intermediary, breached security obligations through inadequate system reviews and password management
violations: Agape, as a data intermediary, breached security obligations through inadequate system reviews and password management

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.4(3) makes data controllers liable for intermediaries' compliance and requires exercise of reasonable oversight.
regulatoryFindings.description: FHG failed to conduct regular monitoring of Agape's data handling processes despite contractual security requirements
violations: FHG failed to conduct regular monitoring of Agape's data handling processes despite contractual security requirements
FHG did not make reasonable enquiries about how customer data would be stored, transmitted, and accessed when outsourcing to third party

outcome: FHG ordered to pay SGD 58,000; Agape ordered to pay SGD 10,000. Both entities required to complete within 60 days: comprehensive reviews of vendor data handling processes and contractual obligations; ensure security reviews cover all systems; establish written data protection requirements with oversight mechanisms; implement direct individual user accounts with multi-factor authentication for system access; reconfigure SharePoint with view-only access and file segregation; establish audit rights; implement vulnerability assessments and penetration testing requirements. Compliance notifications due within 14 days of completion. Both organisations have voluntarily implemented enhanced security policies, staff training, and external cybersecurity assessments.
companyNow: Both organisations remain operational. FHG continues as an enterprise healthcare provider. Agape continues as a business process outsourcing and social enterprise provider, with enhanced data protection practices.
dataType: Health information, financial data, identity numbers, personal contact details, medical diagnosis codes, surgical procedure information, bank account details
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation — reasonable security arrangements)
PDPA s.4(3) (data controller obligations regarding intermediary oversight)

companyDescription: Outsource Strategies Ltd is a UK-registered company (based in Cardiff, Wales) that provided outsourced telemarketing and direct marketing services, including unsolicited direct marketing calls.
companyLongDescription: Outsource Strategies Ltd is a UK-registered company (based in Cardiff, Wales) that provided outsourced telemarketing and direct marketing services, including unsolicited direct marketing calls.
caseDescription: Outsource Strategies Ltd made 1,346,503 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between February 2021 and March 2022, violating PECR regulation 21. The calls targeted subscribers who had not provided valid opt-in consent and whose numbers had been on the TPS register for at least 28 days. The company failed to respect do-not-call preferences despite having access to TPS data.
violationSummary: OSL systematically contacted individuals via unsolicited calls without consent, targeting those who had explicitly registered to avoid such contact. This constitutes surveillance-based collection of consumer engagement through non-consensual direct marketing.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between February 2021 and March 2022, Outsource Strategies Ltd made 1,346,503 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS).
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals who registered with TPS explicitly opted out of receiving unsolicited marketing calls, but OSL ignored this choice.

claimsVsReality.claim: OSL implied or relied on product sign-up terms indicating willingness to receive marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Valid opt-in under PECR requires clear, positive, separate notification reflecting the individual's choice, not conditional terms buried in service agreements.

claimsVsReality.claim: Calling TPS-registered numbers was acceptable if the company believed it had consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: 1,346,503 TPS-registered subscribers (on the register for 28+ days) had no valid opt-in on record; calls were unlawful regardless of company belief.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes to numbers listed in the national do-not-call register (TPS).
regulatoryFindings.description: OSL made 1,346,503 unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers in breach of this regulation.
violations: OSL made 1,346,503 unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers in breach of this regulation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered numbers only if the subscriber has provided valid opt-in notification that they do not object to calls from that specific company.
regulatoryFindings.description: OSL failed to obtain valid, clear, positive opt-in consent from subscribers. The Commissioner found that signing up for a service cannot automatically constitute valid opt-in for marketing calls; consent must be explicit and separate.
violations: OSL failed to obtain valid, clear, positive opt-in consent from subscribers. The Commissioner found that signing up for a service cannot automatically constitute valid opt-in for marketing calls; consent must be explicit and separate.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(a) prohibits unsolicited marketing calls where the subscriber has previously notified the caller not to call.
regulatoryFindings.description: TPS registration itself constitutes notification; OSL disregarded this standing notification by calling 1.3+ million registered subscribers.
violations: TPS registration itself constitutes notification; OSL disregarded this standing notification by calling 1.3+ million registered subscribers.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring OSL to cease making unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers within 30 days. OSL must ensure recipients of direct marketing communications receive the caller's name and, upon request, contact details. The company must respect TPS registration and obtain valid, explicit opt-in consent (separate from product/service sign-up) before calling. OSL has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: Unknown. Outsource Strategies Ltd (Companies House Registration 12553312) is subject to the Enforcement Notice and compliance obligations as of October 2023.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal contact information

companyDescription: Fortytwo Pte. Ltd. is an online furniture store operating in Singapore. The company operates a website for direct consumer sales of furniture products.
companyLongDescription: Fortytwo Pte. Ltd. is an online furniture store operating in Singapore. The company operates a website for direct consumer sales of furniture products.
caseDescription: Fortytwo Pte. Ltd., an online furniture store, suffered a malicious code injection attack on its website that exposed the personal data of 6,241 individuals, including email addresses and passwords, plus financial details of 98 customers. The breach occurred because the organization failed to apply four critical security patches to its outdated Magento 1.9.x platform, despite Adobe ending support for the version in June 2020 and announcing the timeline in November 2015.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and data collection. Unpatched software vulnerabilities directly led to the malicious code injection and capture of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to apply four critical security patches to Magento 1.9.x software despite receiving patches from Adobe in November 2017, June 2019, October 2019, and April 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: 6,241 customers had their email addresses and passwords stolen by attackers exploiting the unpatched vulnerabilities through malicious code injection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The impact of the Incident might be more limited as some of the users' names may be incomplete, fictitious or pseudonymous, potentially reducing the dataset at risk.
claimsVsReality.reality: Section 2(1) of the PDPA defines personal data as 'data, whether true or not' about an identifiable individual. The organization's PDPA obligations apply to the entire customer database regardless of data accuracy. Even incomplete or fictitious names remain personal data requiring protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had planned to upgrade to Magento version 2 in early 2020 but the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted those plans, limiting the period of non-compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Adobe announced end-of-support for Magento 1.x in November 2015 (providing 36 months notice) and formally ended support on 30 June 2020. The organization took no action from November 2015 to early 2020 despite ample advance notice and only made a decision to upgrade 6 months before end-of-support.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Fortytwo failed to apply four critical security patches released by Adobe in November 2017, June 2019, October 2019, and April 2020 to address high-severity vulnerabilities including malicious code injection risks.
violations: Fortytwo failed to apply four critical security patches released by Adobe in November 2017, June 2019, October 2019, and April 2020 to address high-severity vulnerabilities including malicious code injection risks.
Fortytwo did not upgrade from Magento 1.9.x to a supported version (2.0) despite Adobe announcing end-of-support in November 2015 (36-month timeline) and formally ending support on 30 June 2020.

This failure to patch created exploitable vulnerabilities that allowed threat actors to inject malicious code and capture 6,241 users' email addresses and passwords, plus 98 users' credit card details.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found Fortytwo in breach of section 24(a) of the PDPA. The organization was directed to pay a financial penalty of S$8,000 within 30 days. Additionally, Fortytwo was required to: (1) complete the upgrading of its website to a supported software version, including vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, within 6 months; and (2) inform the Commission within 14 days of completion. The organization received a reduced penalty due to its cooperation throughout the investigation, voluntary admission of breach, and prompt post-incident remediation (notifying affected individuals and implementing technical security measures).
companyNow: Fortytwo Pte. Ltd. is taking steps to upgrade to Magento version 2 and has implemented additional security measures following the breach. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Email addresses, passwords, names, credit card numbers, expiry dates, CVV/CVN, billing addresses, shipping addresses, date of birth
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24(a) – Protection Obligation (reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure)

companyDescription: MCP Online Ltd is a lead generation and direct marketing business registered in April 2020. The company conducted unsolicited telemarketing campaigns targeting consumers in finance, pensions, and claims sectors, operating through subsidiary accounts and multiple trading names including 'The Review Team TRT', 'My HDR Claim', and 'My Lead Locker'.
companyLongDescription: MCP Online Ltd is a lead generation and direct marketing business registered in April 2020. The company conducted unsolicited telemarketing campaigns targeting consumers in finance, pensions, and claims sectors, operating through subsidiary accounts and multiple trading names including 'The Review Team TRT', 'My HDR Claim', and 'My Lead Locker'.
caseDescription: MCP Online Ltd made 20,939 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between January and September 2022, violating PECR regulations. The company failed to provide required caller identification information and showed deliberate disregard for TPS registration, displaying wilful non-compliance despite regulatory investigation.
violationSummary: The company systematically contacted individuals on TPS registry without consent, treating their explicit preference not to receive unsolicited calls as irrelevant; this constitutes surveillance-like targeting of vulnerable individuals.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 20,939 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service; sent 92,265 unsolicited text messages generating 386 spam complaints; failed.
whyTheyWereWrong: 20,939 individuals who had explicitly registered with the TPS to stop unwanted calls received unwanted marketing calls anyway, violating their stated preferences.

claimsVsReality.claim: Craig Power (director/owner) claimed to have relocated to Thailand in July 2018 with no UK ties and that companies were nothing to do with him
claimsVsReality.reality: Companies House and telecom records showed Power remained the active director and subscriber for MCP and related accounts through 2022; contact details matched his registered address; correspondence came from accounts associated with him

claimsVsReality.claim: Power claimed someone obtained his passport and impersonated him, setting up the companies
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed Power was directly involved: he signed correspondence as 'Craig Power of MCP', CSP records confirmed subscriber name, multiple accounts diverted to his personal mobile number, he was director until termination filed September 2023 (backdated)

claimsVsReality.claim: MCP operated legitimately with proper consent from subscribers
claimsVsReality.reality: 20,939 calls made to TPS-registered numbers with no valid opt-in consent; internal correspondence showed MCP deliberately requesting lists of people who had opted out to call them again; callers unable to explain data source

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing to numbers listed on the TPS register without prior consent from the subscriber.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCP made 20,939 connected calls to TPS-registered numbers between 8 January 2022 and 28 September 2022
violations: MCP made 20,939 connected calls to TPS-registered numbers between 8 January 2022 and 28 September 2022
No evidence of valid opt-in notifications from subscribers overriding TPS registration
Calls were for direct marketing purposes (pension schemes, HDR claims, lifestyle surveys)

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(2) requires that direct marketing calls must include the caller's name and either address or freephone number.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCP failed to provide required caller identification information with calls
violations: MCP failed to provide required caller identification information with calls
Recordings showed generic names ('TRT', 'Best Card Payments') without adequate contact details

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A DPA 1998 permits monetary penalties for serious contraventions where conduct is deliberate or negligent with failure to take reasonable steps to prevent the breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: Contravention was deliberate: MCP masked operations, used multiple subsidiary accounts, deliberately obscured directorship relationships
violations: Contravention was deliberate: MCP masked operations, used multiple subsidiary accounts, deliberately obscured directorship relationships
Negligent: Failed to screen data against TPS/CTPS, no training materials or compliance procedures provided, complete lack of engagement with investigation

outcome: MCP Online Ltd issued monetary penalty of £55,000 (reducible to £44,000 with early payment by 31 October 2023). Penalty issued under section 55A DPA 1998. MCP required to cease unsolicited marketing to TPS-registered numbers and implement TPS screening. Notice of Intent issued 6 July 2023; no representations received. Right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: MCP Online Ltd remains registered at 20-22 Wenlock Road, London N1 7GU, with James Miller listed as director (appointed September 2022, backdated to January 2021). Company appears to have continued operations and later established 'MCP Online Group Limited' potentially to evade regulatory action.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal contact information

companyDescription: It's OK Limited is a UK-based company registered at Suite 12, 4th Floor, New England Road, Brighton, East Sussex (Companies House Registration: 10196140) engaged in direct marketing operations via telephone.
companyLongDescription: It's OK Limited is a UK-based company registered at Suite 12, 4th Floor, New England Road, Brighton, East Sussex (Companies House Registration: 10196140) engaged in direct marketing operations via telephone.
caseDescription: It's OK Limited made 1.75 million unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), violating PECR Regulation 21. The company sourced telephone data from a third party without conducting adequate due diligence and failed to obtain valid consent from TPS-registered subscribers. This resulted in 71 complaints to the TPS and the Information Commissioner's Office.
violationSummary: The company systematically made unsolicited calls to individuals who had explicitly opted out via TPS registration, constituting unauthorized surveillance and collection of personal contact information for direct marketing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: It's OK Limited made 1,752,149 unsolicited direct marketing calls between July 2019 and June 2020 to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1.75 million people had explicitly registered their numbers to avoid marketing calls; It's OK ignored these preferences and called them anyway, generating 71 complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: It's OK sourced its telephone data from third-party providers in the normal course of business.
claimsVsReality.reality: The third-party data included millions of TPS-registered numbers; It's OK failed to conduct due diligence to verify status or obtain valid consent from any of the 1.75 million subscribers called.

claimsVsReality.claim: It's OK could rely on product signup consent as valid notification under PECR Regulation 21(4).
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commissioner found that consent to use a product/service conditional on receiving marketing calls does not constitute clear and positive notification of willingness to receive marketing calls specifically, and does not override TPS registration.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(1)(b) of PECR prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes to numbers listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: It's OK made 1,752,149 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers between July 2019 and June 2020.
violations: It's OK made 1,752,149 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers between July 2019 and June 2020.
The company failed to obtain valid notification from TPS subscribers that they did not object to receiving calls.
It's OK sourced telephone data from third parties without conducting sufficient due diligence to verify consent or TPS status.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(4) of PECR allows calls to TPS-registered numbers only where the subscriber has notified the caller they do not object, and notification must reflect a clear and positive action.
regulatoryFindings.description: It's OK could not demonstrate valid notification meeting the standard of clear and positive action to override TPS registration.
violations: It's OK could not demonstrate valid notification meeting the standard of clear and positive action to override TPS registration.
The company failed to verify that individuals had taken affirmative steps to opt in to marketing calls from It's OK specifically.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 1998 Section 40(1)(a) empowers the Information Commissioner to serve an enforcement notice if satisfied a person has contravened PECR requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Commissioner found a serious contravention of PECR Regulation 21 and issued an enforcement notice under this power.
violations: The Commissioner found a serious contravention of PECR Regulation 21 and issued an enforcement notice under this power.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice on 13 February 2023 requiring It's OK Limited to cease making unsolicited marketing calls to subscribers within 30 days where: (a) the subscriber has previously notified them not to call, or (b) the subscriber has registered with TPS for at least 28 days and has not notified It's OK they consent to calls. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information

company: Autobahn Rent A Car Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: Autobahn Rent A Car Pte. Ltd. operates Shariot, a car-sharing mobile application service in Singapore. The organisation provides vehicle-sharing solutions to customers in the Singapore market.
companyLongDescription: Autobahn Rent A Car Pte. Ltd. operates Shariot, a car-sharing mobile application service in Singapore. The organisation provides vehicle-sharing solutions to customers in the Singapore market.
caseDescription: Autobahn Rent A Car's car-sharing service Shariot suffered a data breach when a threat actor accessed an unrevoked administrator account belonging to a terminated ex-employee. The attacker exploited the dormant credentials to exfiltrate personal data of 53,000 users. The organisation failed to implement reasonable security measures including timely credential revocation and multi-factor authentication.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure, specifically through inadequate access control (failure to revoke credentials) and absence of enhanced authentication mechanisms (MFA) for accounts with access to sensitive data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to revoke administrator account credentials of an ex-employee after employment ended in May 2022, leaving dormant login credentials active in their backend system.
whyTheyWereWrong: 53,000 car-sharing users had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, NRIC numbers, and location data stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation maintained reasonable security arrangements to protect user personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Administrator credentials remained active for a terminated employee for approximately four months, and the system lacked multi-factor authentication, allowing unauthorised access and exfiltration of 53,000 user records.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, disclosure, and similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Autobahn failed to revoke login credentials of an administrator account belonging to a terminated employee, leaving the dormant account active and exploitable.
violations: Autobahn failed to revoke login credentials of an administrator account belonging to a terminated employee, leaving the dormant account active and exploitable.
The organisation did not implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrator accounts with access to its user database containing 53,000 personal data records.
The absence of these access controls enabled a threat actor to breach the system and exfiltrate sensitive personal data (NRIC numbers, contact details, location data) of 53,000 users.

outcome: The organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $3,000 within 30 days. In addition, Autobahn was directed to: (a) implement credential revocation processes within reasonable timeframes upon employee cessation; (b) strengthen access control measures to administrator accounts; (c) conduct a security review of technical and administrative arrangements within 60 days; (d) rectify identified security gaps; and (e) report completion to the Commission within 1 week. The organisation has implemented remedial actions including internal account audits, NRIC masking in software, and cyber hygiene training.
companyNow: Autobahn Rent A Car Pte. Ltd. continues to operate the Shariot car-sharing service in Singapore following implementation of mandatory security improvements and compliance measures.
dataType: Names, email addresses, mobile phone numbers, NRIC numbers, general location data

companyDescription: Simply Connecting Ltd operated as a marketing agency specializing in lead generation for housing disrepair claims, debt solutions, and personal injury claims. The company marketed services through websites including home-disrepair.com, debt-reduced.com, debt-deduct.com, and quick-claims.co.
companyLongDescription: Simply Connecting Ltd operated as a marketing agency specializing in lead generation for housing disrepair claims, debt solutions, and personal injury claims. The company marketed services through websites including home-disrepair.com, debt-reduced.com, debt-deduct.com, and quick-claims.co.
caseDescription: Simply Connecting Ltd sent 441,830 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients, violating PECR. The company purchased data from third-party providers but failed to conduct proper due diligence to verify consent was genuinely obtained. The company's director had a history of similar violations and ignored prior assurances to the ICO.
violationSummary: SCL transmitted unsolicited marketing communications without recipient consent, constituting surveillance-based collection. The company obtained and used contact details without valid prior notification or affirmative consent from subscribers.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Sent 441,830 unsolicited SMS direct marketing messages to individuals without valid consent between December 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: 3,959 people reported receiving spam texts they never agreed to, with some complainants expressing concern their numbers had been obtained without authorization, causing distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data provider had 'full optin status' and customers were 'fully aware they opted in for contact'
claimsVsReality.reality: SCL could not produce evidence of valid consent; the data provider (dissolved company) had never provided opt-in documentation; 3,959 complaints from individuals denying they consented

claimsVsReality.claim: SCL purchased data from a credible and compliant data provider
claimsVsReality.reality: The data provider company had been dissolved over 2 years before the data purchase; former director was selling data from a dissolved entity; no valid consent records were available

claimsVsReality.claim: Director would no longer rely on generic third-party consent (assurance given in 2015)
claimsVsReality.reality: Director again relied entirely on generic third-party data with no independent verification of consent in 2020-2022

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) states: 'a person shall neither transmit, nor instigate the transmission of, unsolicited communications for the purposes of direct marketing by means of electronic mail unless the recipient of the electronic mail has previously notified the sender that he consents for the time being to such communications.'
regulatoryFindings.description: SCL transmitted 441,830 direct marketing SMS messages without evidence of prior recipient consent
violations: SCL transmitted 441,830 direct marketing SMS messages without evidence of prior recipient consent
SCL failed to verify that purchasedphone numbers had consented to receive marketing from SCL specifically
SCL relied on unverified third-party assurances of consent without conducting proper due diligence

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A allows monetary penalties for serious contraventions if the person knew or ought to have known of the risk and failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it.
regulatoryFindings.description: SCL's director had managed similar companies investigated by ICO in 2015 for identical PECR violations
violations: SCL's director had managed similar companies investigated by ICO in 2015 for identical PECR violations
Director had previously given assurances he would no longer rely on generic third-party consent
SCL failed to seek independent legal advice despite operating a direct marketing business
SCL did not request evidence of valid consent from data provider or conduct due diligence on data source

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £40,000 (reduced to £32,000 if paid early). The company must comply with PECR requirements: only send unsolicited direct marketing to those who have provided specific, informed, freely-given consent. SCL must implement proper due diligence procedures for third-party data, obtain written agreements with suppliers confirming valid consent, and seek legal advice on PECR compliance. The penalty is enforceable by County Court or High Court order.
companyNow: Simply Connecting Ltd remained registered with Companies House as of the notice date (August 2023). The ICO noted the company may no longer be operating from its registered London address; the sole director, Kieran Flannery, is a British national resident in Thailand.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, names, personal contact details

companyDescription: Wee Jing Kai Leon is an individual real estate salesperson registered with Propnex Realty Pte Ltd since 2006 operating as an independent contractor. He owns DGK Global Pte Ltd, which he used to register SMS sender IDs under Singapore's SMS Sender ID Regime.
companyLongDescription: Wee Jing Kai Leon is an individual real estate salesperson registered with Propnex Realty Pte Ltd since 2006 operating as an independent contractor. He owns DGK Global Pte Ltd, which he used to register SMS sender IDs under Singapore's SMS Sender ID Regime.
caseDescription: A real estate salesperson sent approximately 6,120 unsolicited SMS marketing messages to telephone numbers registered on Singapore's Do Not Call Registry between November 2022 and March 2023. He failed to obtain valid confirmation that the numbers were not registered or clear and unambiguous consent from subscribers before sending the messages. The Commission found he negligently breached section 43(1) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012.
violationSummary: The individual disclosed (sent) specified marketing messages to telephone numbers registered on the DNC Registry without valid confirmation or documented consent, violating recipients' explicit opt-out preferences.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Between November 2022 and March 2023, Wee Jing Kai Leon sent approximately 6,120 unsolicited SMS marketing messages promoting his real estate services to telephone numbers on his marketing list,.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1,224 individuals had explicitly registered their phone numbers to opt out of unsolicited marketing messages, but received repeated monthly SMS messages anyway.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Individual stated he was under the impression that since he had obtained the telephone numbers prior to the enactment of the PDPA, he could use them for marketing purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PDPA and its DNC Provisions came into effect on 2 January 2014. Merely obtaining numbers before the law was enacted does not provide authorization to use them for marketing to numbers that subscribers have since registered on the DNC Registry. Consent must be documented in writing or other retrievable form.

claimsVsReality.claim: By using the sender ID 'Propnex LW' registered under the SSIR, the Individual demonstrated regulatory compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Registration of a sender ID, while showing willingness to comply with the SSIR, does not constitute compliance with DNC requirements, which mandate checking the DNC Registry and obtaining valid confirmation before sending marketing messages.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 43(1) of the PDPA requires that before sending a specified message (marketing message) to a Singapore telephone number, the sender must have valid confirmation that the number is not listed in the Do Not Call Registry.
regulatoryFindings.description: Wee Jing Kai Leon sent SMS messages advertising real estate services to 1,224 telephone numbers registered on the DNC Registry without obtaining valid confirmation from the Commission or a checker that these numbers were not listed.
violations: Wee Jing Kai Leon sent SMS messages advertising real estate services to 1,224 telephone numbers registered on the DNC Registry without obtaining valid confirmation from the Commission or a checker that these numbers were not listed.

He did not obtain documented clear and unambiguous consent from any of the telephone subscribers before sending the marketing messages, either before or after 2 January 2014 (the effective date of the DNC Provisions).

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 43(4) of the PDPA provides a defence to section 43(1) if the subscriber gave clear and unambiguous consent evidenced in writing or other accessible form.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Individual failed to satisfy this defence, as no evidence of such consent was found for any subscriber on the Marketing List.
violations: The Individual failed to satisfy this defence, as no evidence of such consent was found for any subscriber on the Marketing List.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 48(2) of the PDPA provides a defence for employees acting in good faith in the course of employment; however, this defence is only available to employees in an employer-employee relationship.
regulatoryFindings.description: Wee Jing Kai Leon was self-employed as a registered real estate salesperson with Propnex, not an employee, and therefore this defence was not available.
violations: Wee Jing Kai Leon was self-employed as a registered real estate salesperson with Propnex, not an employee, and therefore this defence was not available.

outcome: Wee Jing Kai Leon was administered a written warning in respect of his negligent breach of section 43(1) of the PDPA. No financial penalty or other directions were imposed, taking into account his cooperation with the Commission's investigation, his otherwise compliant practices (providing unsubscribe options, registering sender IDs under the SMS Sender ID Regime, including identification information), and his voluntary cessation of marketing messages to the list. The Commission noted it will monitor future cases involving property agents and calibrate enforcement decisions to ensure compliance with DNC Provisions, particularly given concurrent media reports of property scams.
dataType: Telephone numbers

companyDescription: Poxell Ltd was a construction and home improvements company specialising in energy-saving products (double glazing, doors, solar panels, resin driveways). Sole director Marcel Kellman was appointed in February 2022. The company operated www.poxellhomeimprovements.co.uk.
companyLongDescription: Poxell Ltd was a construction and home improvements company specialising in energy-saving products (double glazing, doors, solar panels, resin driveways). Sole director Marcel Kellman was appointed in February 2022. The company operated www.poxellhomeimprovements.co.uk.
caseDescription: Poxell Ltd made 2.65 million unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), violating PECR regulations 21 and 24. The company used multiple phone lines to avoid detection ('snowshoeing'), failed to provide caller identification, and ignored the Information Commissioner's investigation attempts. This generated 413 consumer complaints, including from vulnerable elderly individuals.
violationSummary: Poxell conducted systematic, non-consensual collection of consumer attention and personal information through unsolicited calls to opted-out individuals, combined with intentional obfuscation of caller identity.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Poxell Ltd made 2,647,805 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between March.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 413 consumers who had explicitly registered to opt out of unsolicited marketing calls received repeated unwanted calls, including vulnerable individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: Poxell's online presence promoted home improvement and energy efficiency services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Poxell conducted systematic unsolicited marketing calls to 2.65 million consumers, many on TPS opt-out lists, causing distress especially to vulnerable elderly individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The calls came from legitimate business operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Poxell deliberately obtained multiple phone numbers in sequence to distribute complaints across different CLIs ('snowshoeing'), a known evasion tactic used by non-compliant call centres.

claimsVsReality.claim: Poxell was a legitimate company open to regulatory oversight.
claimsVsReality.reality: Poxell failed to respond to multiple investigation letters, a voicemail from the Commissioner, formal warnings, Information Notices, and chaser letters. The director provided no evidence or cooperation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits the use of a public electronic communications service to make unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes to any line listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: Poxell made 2,647,805 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with the TPS for more than 28 days, without valid consent under Regulation 21(4).
violations: Poxell made 2,647,805 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with the TPS for more than 28 days, without valid consent under Regulation 21(4).

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(2) requires that direct marketing communications provide the name of the person making the call and either their address or a freephone callback number.
regulatoryFindings.description: Poxell failed to identify themselves, provide their contact address, or offer a freephone number for the recipient to call back.
violations: Poxell failed to identify themselves, provide their contact address, or offer a freephone number for the recipient to call back.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A(1) permits a monetary penalty where there is a serious contravention and either the contravention was deliberate or the person knew/ought to have known of the risk and failed to take reasonable steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: Poxell deliberately obtained multiple phone lines ('snowshoeing') to spread complaints across several numbers and evade detection. After receiving the investigation letter, Poxell continued making calls until its service was terminated. The director did not respond to multiple contact attempts, an Information Notice, or formal letters.
violations: Poxell deliberately obtained multiple phone lines ('snowshoeing') to spread complaints across several numbers and evade detection. After receiving the investigation letter, Poxell continued making calls until its service was terminated. The director did not respond to multiple contact attempts, an Information Notice, or formal letters.

Poxell relied on direct marketing but failed to screen data against the TPS register every 28 days, maintain records of notifications, or establish a robust suppression list. No evidence of due diligence on data sources was provided.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty of £150,000 (reduced to £120,000 if paid by 4 September 2023). Poxell is subject to compliance with PECR regulations going forward. The company's account was already terminated by its telecommunications provider in August 2022 for non-payment. Appeal rights are available to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: Poxell Ltd's telecommunications service was terminated by its provider in August 2022 for non-payment. Current operational status is unknown; the company was not responsive to regulatory communications.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal contact data
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) – Unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers
PECR Regulation 24(2) – Failure to provide caller identification and contact details
Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A – Serious contravention of PECR

companyDescription: The Chartered Institute for Securities & Investment (CISI) is a UK-based professional body and regulatory authority for financial services professionals, offering qualifications, professional standards and training in the securities and investment sector.
companyLongDescription: The Chartered Institute for Securities & Investment (CISI) is a UK-based professional body and regulatory authority for financial services professionals, offering qualifications, professional standards and training in the securities and investment sector.
caseDescription: CISI suffered a data breach on 17 February 2020 when an unauthorised third party exploited a known vulnerability in unsupported Sitefinity software to upload malicious code to the website checkout page, capturing payment details and personal data of approximately 3,883 individuals. The breach resulted from CISI's failure to implement timely security upgrades, conduct penetration testing, or establish effective vulnerability management processes required under GDPR Article 32.
violationSummary: CISI failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures (Article 32) resulting in a preventable breach. The vulnerability had a patch available for years but was not applied, demonstrating systemic security negligence.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: CISI ran unsupported Sitefinity software with a critical vulnerability for which a security patch had been available since 2017.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unauthorized attacker exploited the unpatched vulnerability to inject malicious code into CISI's checkout page, capturing payment details of 3,883 customers.

claimsVsReality.claim: CISI maintained a secure website for customer transactions
claimsVsReality.reality: The website ran unsupported, vulnerable software for which security patches had been available for over 3 years

claimsVsReality.claim: CISI had security testing and vulnerability management processes
claimsVsReality.reality: No penetration testing or web application scanning had been conducted prior to the breach

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, taking into account state of the art, implementation costs, and nature and scope of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: CISI ran unsupported software with known critical vulnerabilities and did not implement timely security upgrades despite patches being available since 2017
violations: CISI ran unsupported software with known critical vulnerabilities and did not implement timely security upgrades despite patches being available since 2017

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires controllers to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: CISI's systems lacked resilience and were vulnerable to brute-force attacks due to unpatched software
violations: CISI's systems lacked resilience and were vulnerable to brute-force attacks due to unpatched software

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(d) requires controllers to have a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: CISI had not conducted any penetration testing or web application scanning prior to the incident
violations: CISI had not conducted any penetration testing or web application scanning prior to the incident

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand under GDPR Article 58(2)(b) to CISI for breaches of Article 32. The Commissioner recommended CISI implement: (1) a formal testing procedure specifying timing and nature of security tests; (2) a patching policy to identify and manage vulnerabilities; (3) designated responsibility for patch management. CISI had already taken remedial steps including installing a web application firewall, updating software, notifying affected individuals, offering credit monitoring, and providing financial compensation for verified losses. The case remains under ICO oversight for compliance verification.
