companyNow: CISI continues to operate as a professional body for financial services professionals in the UK. Following the enforcement action, the organisation has implemented enhanced security measures and vulnerability management processes.
dataType: Payment card details, names, email addresses
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32(1)(b) — Confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience
GDPR Art. 32(1)(d) — Regular testing, assessing and evaluating security measures

companyDescription: Rite Aid Corporation is one of the largest pharmacy chains in the United States, operating thousands of retail pharmacy locations nationwide selling prescription and non-prescription medicines, medical supplies, groceries, cosmetics, and personal care items.
companyLongDescription: Rite Aid Corporation is one of the largest pharmacy chains in the United States, operating thousands of retail pharmacy locations nationwide selling prescription and non-prescription medicines, medical supplies, groceries, cosmetics, and personal care items.
caseDescription: Rite Aid deployed facial recognition technology in hundreds of pharmacy stores from 2012–2020 without implementing reasonable safeguards, resulting in thousands of false-positive matches that led store employees to wrongfully accuse, surveil, ban, and call police on innocent customers—particularly Black, Asian, Latino, and women consumers. The company failed to test accuracy, enforce image quality standards, train employees, monitor results, or remediate problematic enrollments. Additionally, Rite Aid violated a prior 2010 FTC order by failing to implement a comprehensive information security program for vendor management and document retention.
violationSummary: Rite Aid's failure to implement reasonable measures to prevent harm from its facial recognition technology—including lack of accuracy testing, enforcement of quality standards, employee training, and monitoring—constitutes insecurity in information processing that enabled widespread misidentification and harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Rite Aid deployed facial recognition technology in hundreds of stores to identify and eject suspected shoplifters, but failed to test accuracy, used low-quality enrollment images.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of innocent customers—disproportionately Black, Asian, Latino, and women—were wrongly identified as criminals, publicly accused in front of coworkers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Rite Aid's internal presentation identified only '[m]edia attention and customer acceptance' as a risk associated with facial recognition deployment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The technology generated thousands of false-positive matches causing severe harm to consumers including wrongful accusation, public humiliation, banning from stores, searches, and police involvement—risks that were reasonably foreseeable to Rite Aid.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facial recognition technology would help 'drive and keep persons of interest out of [Rite Aid's] stores.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The technology frequently misidentified innocent customers, leading employees to take action (surveillance, bans, accusations, police calls) against people who had committed no wrongdoing, particularly harming Black, Asian, Latino, and women consumers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Rite Aid had policies and procedures to select vendors capable of safeguarding personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Rite Aid routinely conducted vendor assessments via phone calls without obtaining written responses, failed to maintain documentation, did not consistently reassess vendors, and entered contracts with minimal or no cybersecurity requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Rite Aid deployed facial recognition technology without taking reasonable steps to address foreseeable risks of false-positive matches that caused substantial injury to consumers.
violations: Rite Aid deployed facial recognition technology without taking reasonable steps to address foreseeable risks of false-positive matches that caused substantial injury to consumers.
Failed to assess, test, or monitor accuracy before and after deployment despite knowing the technology would generate false positives.
Failed to enforce image quality standards, resulting in use of low-quality enrollment images that increased false-positive risk.
Failed to train employees on facial recognition limitations or how to evaluate matches, leading to wrongful actions against innocent customers.
Generated thousands of false-positive matches that led store employees to surveil, accuse, ban, and call police on innocent customers.

regulatoryFindings.act: 2010 FTC Order Section II requires Rite Aid to establish, implement, and maintain a comprehensive information security program with reasonable steps to select and retain service providers capable of appropriately safeguarding personal information and requiring them by contract to implement appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct comprehensive security assessments of service providers; instead conducted assessments via phone calls and meetings without written documentation.
violations: Failed to conduct comprehensive security assessments of service providers; instead conducted assessments via phone calls and meetings without written documentation.
Failed to maintain risk assessment documentation for vendors between November 2019 and November 2021.
Failed to consistently reassess vendors' information security programs on a periodic basis.
Failed to consistently use contract renewal processes to include cybersecurity provisions in vendor contracts.
Numerous vendor contracts lacked or had minimal information security requirements, breach notification language, or confidential data return provisions.

regulatoryFindings.act: 2010 FTC Order Section IV requires Rite Aid to maintain and make available documents relating to compliance, including documents that contradict, qualify, or call into question compliance with the order.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to produce hundreds of contracts with service providers and security assessments to the FTC as required.
violations: Failed to produce hundreds of contracts with service providers and security assessments to the FTC as required.
For numerous service providers, did not maintain or produce records demonstrating steps taken to ensure they were capable of safeguarding personal information.
Failed to maintain adequate documentation of its information security program implementation.

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint for permanent injunction and other relief seeking to prevent future violations. The complaint alleges two counts: (1) unfair facial recognition technology practices, and (2) unfair failure to implement or maintain a comprehensive information security program in violation of the 2010 Order. As of the filing date (December 19, 2023), Rite Aid was in bankruptcy proceedings. The FTC sought a permanent injunction to prevent future violations and awarded any additional relief the court determines just and proper.
companyNow: Rite Aid Corporation filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 15, 2023. As of the FTC complaint filing in December 2023, the company was operating under bankruptcy protection with jointly administered cases. The company continues to operate retail pharmacy locations.
dataType: Facial images, biometric data, enrollment database records, personal information (names, dates of birth, criminal history allegations)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
2010 FTC Order Section II – Requirement to establish and maintain comprehensive information security program
2010 FTC Order Section IV – Document retention requirements

companyDescription: Nottinghamshire County Council is a local government authority in the East Midlands, England. Its Council Assessment Service is responsible for preparing Child and Family Assessments to evaluate the needs of vulnerable children and support from social services.
companyLongDescription: Nottinghamshire County Council is a local government authority in the East Midlands, England. Its Council Assessment Service is responsible for preparing Child and Family Assessments to evaluate the needs of vulnerable children and support from social services.
caseDescription: Nottinghamshire County Council failed to implement adequate organisational measures to protect highly sensitive personal data in child and family assessments. A social worker sent unredacted assessment reports containing domestic violence information to ex-partners, creating a volatile and dangerous situation. The council lacked robust redaction procedures, staff training, and had experienced 16 similar incidents in the prior two years.
violationSummary: Sensitive personal data relating to domestic violence and child welfare was disclosed to third parties without proper redaction due to inadequate organisational and technical security measures.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Nottinghamshire County Council's social worker sent unredacted Child and Family Assessment reports containing sensitive domestic violence information to ex-partners without adequate safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: A mother and two children faced actual physical harm when an ex-partner who had previously committed domestic violence against them received confidential assessment details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Council had procedures in place requiring team manager sign-off of all Child and Family Assessments before dissemination
claimsVsReality.reality: Procedure was not sufficiently robust; team manager approved a report with significant unredacted sensitive information containing domestic violence disclosures

claimsVsReality.claim: Failure to redact was described as an isolated human error or oversight by the social worker
claimsVsReality.reality: Pattern of 16 similar incidents in prior two years indicated systemic organisational failure, not isolated error; root cause was lack of training and clear policies

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of the UK GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, including robust procedures, regular testing, and effective security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to implement appropriate organisational measures including lack of robust redaction procedures prior to document dissemination
violations: Council failed to implement appropriate organisational measures including lack of robust redaction procedures prior to document dissemination
Insufficient training and guidance on disclosure and redaction was not provided to staff until April 2022, after the incident
Procedure requiring team manager sign-off was not sufficiently robust to prevent disclosure of inadequately redacted sensitive documents
Pattern of 16 similar incidents in the two years prior demonstrated systemic failure in security measures

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a Reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The council was required to remedy the infringement. In mitigation, the Commissioner acknowledged that Nottinghamshire County Council implemented comprehensive remedial steps in April 2022, including detailed Disclosure and Redaction Guidance for staff. The council introduced enhanced training and policies designed to prevent future incidents.
companyNow: Nottinghamshire County Council remains a local government authority providing social services in the East Midlands region. It has implemented enhanced data protection procedures and training following this enforcement action.
dataType: Sensitive personal data including information about domestic violence, child welfare assessments, family circumstances

companyDescription: Ring LLC designs and sells internet-connected video security cameras, doorbells, and related accessories and services. The company markets its products primarily for home security and monitoring, with customers using devices to monitor private spaces including bedrooms, bathrooms, and children's rooms.
companyLongDescription: Ring LLC designs and sells internet-connected video security cameras, doorbells, and related accessories and services. The company markets its products primarily for home security and monitoring, with customers using devices to monitor private spaces including bedrooms, bathrooms, and children's rooms.
caseDescription: Ring marketed security cameras as privacy-enhancing devices while systematically failing to secure them from hacking and giving hundreds of employees and contractors unrestricted access to intimate video footage without customer knowledge or consent. Over 55,000 customers suffered account compromises from credential stuffing attacks between January 2019 and March 2020, with hackers harassing and threatening children and families via two-way camera audio.
violationSummary: Ring failed to implement reasonable safeguards against well-known attacks (credential stuffing, brute force) and granted excessive access to sensitive video data. This resulted in unauthorized access to and misuse of intimate personal information on a massive scale.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Ring gave all employees and hundreds of Ukraine-based contractors unrestricted access to customers' intimate home videos without technical safeguards, monitoring, or security training.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 55,000 customers suffered account compromises exposing bedroom and bathroom videos; hackers sexually harassed children, elderly women.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ring's mission is to 'Make Neighborhoods Safer' and its tagline for cameras is 'Smart security here, there, everywhere.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Between 2016 and January 2020, Ring gave all employees and contractors unrestricted access to customer video data without training or monitoring; 55,000+ customers were hacked between January 2019 and March 2020 via well-known attacks Ring failed to prevent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ring Stick Up Cam lets users '[a]dd security anywhere you need it,' '[p]rotect your home,' and '[w]atch over home.' Indoor Cam is 'Small in size. Big on peace of mind.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Devices were highly insecure: hackers accessed intimate bedroom and bathroom footage of tens of thousands of customers; employees viewed thousands of women's videos for sexual gratification; Ring made two-factor authentication optional and only <2% of customers adopted it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ring's Terms of Service and Privacy Policy informed customers of employee access and data use practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Before December 2017, terms did not disclose that hundreds of employees and Ukraine contractors had unrestricted access to all video recordings. Between December 2017 and January 2018, disclosure was buried in dense legalese with only a checkbox for 'consent.'

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ring represented its cameras as secure means to monitor private home areas but failed to implement reasonable security measures; 55,000+ customers compromised via credential stuffing attacks Ring knew about but did not prevent.
violations: Ring represented its cameras as secure means to monitor private home areas but failed to implement reasonable security measures; 55,000+ customers compromised via credential stuffing attacks Ring knew about but did not prevent.
Ring allowed thousands of employees and contractors to access intimate video recordings without customer knowledge or explicit consent, causing substantial injury to consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines unfair acts as those causing substantial injury to consumers that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ring's overbroad employee access to sensitive video data, combined with inadequate monitoring and zero security training, resulted in multiple instances of employee misconduct and customer harm—incidents Ring only discovered through chance employee reporting, not technical safeguards.
violations: Ring's overbroad employee access to sensitive video data, combined with inadequate monitoring and zero security training, resulted in multiple instances of employee misconduct and customer harm—incidents Ring only discovered through chance employee reporting, not technical safeguards.

outcome: The FTC filed a civil complaint in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seeking permanent injunctive relief and other remedies. The complaint alleges three counts: deceptive security representations (Count I), unfair employee access practices without consent (Count II), and unfair failure to provide reasonable security against credential stuffing/brute force attacks (Count III). As of the complaint filing (May 31, 2023), the case is pending. Relief sought includes a permanent injunction and monetary damages.
companyNow: Ring LLC remains a subsidiary of Amazon (acquired 2018) and continues to operate as a home security and smart home device manufacturer. The FTC enforcement action and reputational damage from widespread hacking incidents have prompted Ring to implement enhanced security measures and privacy controls.
dataType: Video recordings, personal video data from private spaces (bedrooms, bathrooms, children's rooms)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 13(b) – Authority to seek injunctive relief

companyDescription: Gap Personnel Holdings Limited is a UK-based recruitment company providing temporary and permanent employment services across multiple sectors including construction, IT, science, healthcare, human resources, sales, and finance.
companyLongDescription: Gap Personnel Holdings Limited is a UK-based recruitment company providing temporary and permanent employment services across multiple sectors including construction, IT, science, healthcare, human resources, sales, and finance.
caseDescription: Gap Personnel Holdings Limited suffered two unauthorized data breaches in 2022 (March and August) affecting over 18,000 UK data subjects. The breaches resulted from multiple unpatched security vulnerabilities including outdated MySQL and PHP versions, poorly written code, and insufficient logging. The ICO found the company failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures and did not conduct regular security testing.
violationSummary: Gap failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures to protect personal data, resulting in unauthorized access and data exfiltration through exploitable vulnerabilities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Gap Personnel Holdings Limited operated recruitment systems using unsupported MySQL 5.6 and PHP 7.1 versions with poorly written code lacking input validation.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unauthorized attacker exploited these preventable security failures to breach the systems twice within five months, exposing personal data including names, addresses, email addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Gap stated they were planning to replace the affected system, with delays due to Covid-19
claimsVsReality.reality: The system remained in production for 12+ months with multiple unpatched vulnerabilities, allowing the same attacker to breach it twice

claimsVsReality.claim: Gap believed updating MySQL could stop the system from working, so decided to replace it instead
claimsVsReality.reality: The outdated MySQL version received no security support after February 2021, leaving the system exposed to known vulnerabilities

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) UK GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, and nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Gap did not have appropriate technical and organisational measures in place to ensure security appropriate to risk
violations: Gap did not have appropriate technical and organisational measures in place to ensure security appropriate to risk
Gap maintained unsupported MySQL version 5.6 (out of support since February 2021) despite knowing the vulnerability
Gap maintained unsupported PHP version 7.1 (last update October 2019) due to legacy coding incompatibility
Gap did not have an active patching policy in place at the time of the incidents

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(b) UK GDPR requires organisations to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Poorly written PHP code failed to validate user input, enabling SQL injection attacks
violations: Poorly written PHP code failed to validate user input, enabling SQL injection attacks
Insufficient logging prevented effective detection and analysis of security incidents
Software vulnerabilities and lack of logging/monitoring limited ability to detect and quickly mitigate incidents

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(d) UK GDPR requires organisations to have a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Gap did not conduct regular vulnerability scans; NCSC recommends at least monthly scans
violations: Gap did not conduct regular vulnerability scans; NCSC recommends at least monthly scans
No regular security testing was performed on web applications

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Gap Personnel Holdings Limited for violations of UK GDPR Articles 32(1), 32(1)(b), and 32(1)(d). No monetary fine was imposed. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps taken by Gap including: prompt notification to data subjects in April 2022 with links to NCSC guidance; implementation of a new system in October 2022 with enhanced security measures and regular penetration testing; and introduction of policies for data retention, patching, and vulnerability management. Gap is required to maintain appropriate technical and organisational measures going forward to detect and respond to incidents promptly.
companyNow: Gap Personnel Holdings Limited has since implemented a new system with enhanced security measures, regular penetration testing, and formalized policies for patching and vulnerability management as of October 2022.
dataType: names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, right to work status, bank account numbers

companyDescription: The Patient and Client Council (PCC) is an independent health and social care advocacy organisation in Northern Ireland, established to represent the interests of patients and clients in the health and social care system.
companyLongDescription: The Patient and Client Council (PCC) is an independent health and social care advocacy organisation in Northern Ireland, established to represent the interests of patients and clients in the health and social care system.
caseDescription: PCC staff sent an email to 15 members of a Gender Identity Liaison Panel using CC instead of BCC, inadvertently disclosing all recipients' email addresses to each other. The email addresses revealed the identity of individuals with lived experience of gender dysphoria, constituting special category data. PCC lacked adequate policies and procedures to guide staff on secure email practices, particularly for sensitive data.
violationSummary: The unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data (email addresses containing identifying information and inferred special category data regarding gender dysphoria) to unintended recipients constitutes a breach of confidentiality and failure to maintain data security.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: On 20 January 2021, PCC staff sent an email to 15 Gender Identity Liaison Panel members using carbon copy (CC) instead of blind carbon copy (BCC).
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals with gender dysphoria had their email addresses and inferred sensitive medical condition disclosed to strangers on the panel, causing potential distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: PCC had policies in place (PCC Use of Electronic Email Policy) requiring encryption of sensitive/patient data sent to external addresses.
claimsVsReality.reality: The email involved in the incident containing special category data was not encrypted, indicating staff either were unaware of the requirement or failed to implement it in practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: PCC stated additional training framed the functionality of BCC and CC for staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented evidence was provided that such training was in place prior to the incident; only one limited slide within elearning training module addressed the topic at time of breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of UK GDPR requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: PCC failed to use suitably secure methods for communicating special category data (gender identity information). Email with BCC function was used instead of more secure alternatives such as individual emails or encrypted secure sending software.
violations: PCC failed to use suitably secure methods for communicating special category data (gender identity information). Email with BCC function was used instead of more secure alternatives such as individual emails or encrypted secure sending software.

PCC's own 'PCC Use of Electronic Email Policy' required sensitive/patient data to be encrypted when emailed to addresses outside a specified list, but the email in question was not encrypted, indicating lack of staff awareness or failure to implement the requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of UK GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, considering state of the art, implementation costs, nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: PCC failed to provide sufficient documented policies, procedures or guidance detailing staff requirements when using BCC function for email communications.
violations: PCC failed to provide sufficient documented policies, procedures or guidance detailing staff requirements when using BCC function for email communications.

At time of incident, PCC's policies contained no guidance on BCC use, and references to outdated Data Protection Act 1998. Only one limited slide in elearning module addressed BCC/CC functionality, with no evidence of documented guidance accessible to staff prior to the incident.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to PCC for infringements of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32(1) of UK GDPR. PCC took remedial steps including: swift notification to all recipients requesting deletion of email and non-use of disclosed addresses; staff refresher training on information governance, data protection policies and appropriate email use; individual and team meetings on data protection responsibilities; staff agency day training on BCC/CC functionality (7 March 2023); and initiation of company-wide policy review. The Commissioner recommended PCC: (1) review and update policies/procedures/guidance on BCC use when sending emails to multiple recipients; (2) communicate updated policies to staff; (3) undertake Data Protection Impact Assessment to evaluate whether email/BCC is suitable for special category data. PCC required to provide progress update within three months (by 11 October 2023).
companyNow: The Patient and Client Council (PCC) is a health and social care advocacy organisation operating in Northern Ireland. Current status and compliance with Commissioner recommendations unknown.
dataType: Email addresses, special category data (gender identity/dysphoria information)

companyDescription: E-Commerce Enablers Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce platform offering cashback rewards, coupons, voucher codes, and price comparison features for users making purchases through affiliated merchant programs.
companyLongDescription: E-Commerce Enablers Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce platform offering cashback rewards, coupons, voucher codes, and price comparison features for users making purchases through affiliated merchant programs.
caseDescription: E-Commerce Enablers Pte. Ltd. suffered a data breach affecting 1.46 million users when an AWS administrative access key was inadvertently committed to GitHub, remained compromised for 15 months after failed key rotation, and was exploited by a malicious actor in September 2020. The company lacked sufficiently robust key management processes and failed to conduct periodic security reviews that would have detected the exposed key.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data. Specifically, it lacked robust processes for AWS key management (no independent verification of key rotation/deletion) and failed to conduct periodic security reviews to detect the exposed key during the 15-month window before exploitation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: E-Commerce Enablers failed to fully disable an AWS administrative access key during key rotation on 21 June 2019.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1.4 million customers had their email addresses, names, bank account numbers, NRIC numbers, and partial credit card information exfiltrated.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed the compromise of the AWS Key arose solely from human error by a senior SRE team member and was not indicative of systemic security issues.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach revealed systemic failures: no independent verification of key rotation completion, no periodic audits to detect the unexpired key over 15 months, and a 15-day delay in responding to the GitHub exposure. These gaps affected 1.46 million users' financial and identification data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The SRE team member's record showed competence; he was senior and had properly rotated other keys in the same rotation cycle.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite completing rotation of other keys, he failed to fully disable the critical AWS Key with full administrative privileges, and the organisation had no process to verify completion, allowing the key to remain usable for 15 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or similar risks to personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to ensure AWS key management processes were sufficiently robust; relied solely on employee seniority without independent verification that a critical administrative key was properly deleted during out-of-cycle rotation on 21 June 2019
violations: Failed to ensure AWS key management processes were sufficiently robust; relied solely on employee seniority without independent verification that a critical administrative key was properly deleted during out-of-cycle rotation on 21 June 2019
Failed to conduct regular security reviews on AWS keys, which could have detected that the key remained active and accessible for 15 months between June 2019 and September 2020

Failed to implement timely incident management processes; took 15 days after inadvertent GitHub commit (4–6 June) to initiate key rotation (21 June) despite handling a full administrative privilege access key

outcome: The Commissioner determined E-Commerce Enablers breached the Protection Obligation under PDPA s.24 in two respects: lack of sufficiently robust AWS key management processes and failure to conduct periodic security reviews. The organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $74,400 within 30 days. No further directions were imposed given the remedial measures already implemented post-incident, including key separation, VPN/IP whitelisting, database encryption, enhanced monitoring, and development/production account segregation.
companyNow: E-Commerce Enablers Pte. Ltd. continues to operate its cashback and coupon platform. Following the incident, it has implemented comprehensive security improvements including temporary time-limited keys, secure key sharing policies, enhanced monitoring, and structural separation of development and production environments.
dataType: email addresses, names, mobile numbers, addresses, gender, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, bank account numbers, partial credit card information

companyDescription: Digivo Media Limited is a debt management lead generation company operating the Rid My Debt website, which collects personal information and outstanding debt details from individuals and passes them to debt solution providers on a panel basis.
companyLongDescription: Digivo Media Limited is a debt management lead generation company operating the Rid My Debt website, which collects personal information and outstanding debt details from individuals and passes them to debt solution providers on a panel basis.
caseDescription: Digivo Media Limited sent 415,041 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to individuals between March and September 2021 without valid consent. The company obtained contact details through its Rid My Debt website but made consent to receive marketing a mandatory condition of service rather than a genuine opt-in. The ICO found this breached PECR Regulation 22 and imposed a £50,000 penalty.
violationSummary: Unsolicited transmission of personal contact information for direct marketing purposes to individuals who did not freely consent, constituting unauthorized disclosure via electronic communications.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Digivo sent 415,041 unsolicited marketing text messages between March and September 2021, making consent to SMS marketing a mandatory tick-box condition of using their debt advice website.
whyTheyWereWrong: Financially vulnerable individuals seeking debt help received repeated unwanted marketing texts they could not refuse without abandoning access to the service.

claimsVsReality.claim: We have a checkbox where the customer agrees to give their consent to receive email, SMS and telephone communication.
claimsVsReality.reality: The checkbox was mandatory to submit an application and could not be skipped, making consent non-freely given and therefore invalid under UK GDPR.

claimsVsReality.claim: We only send out marketing communication in alignment with legitimate interests.
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 22 does not permit legitimate interests as a basis for unsolicited direct marketing; only valid consent or the soft opt-in exemption apply. Legitimate interests cannot be used for SMS marketing under PECR.

claimsVsReality.claim: At the point of application we will not make any contact to the applicant only our partners will contact them directly.
claimsVsReality.reality: Digivo sent 415,041 marketing SMS directly to individuals, not just data-sharing to partners, and all 479,017 messages sent were marketing messages without valid consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2): A person shall neither transmit nor instigate transmission of unsolicited direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digivo transmitted and instigated 415,041 unsolicited marketing SMS without valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: Digivo transmitted and instigated 415,041 unsolicited marketing SMS without valid prior consent from recipients.
Consent obtained via mandatory tick-box was not freely given, as it was a condition of service.
Consent was not specific, as individuals could not select between SMS, email, and telephone channels.
Consent was not informed, as the statement did not reference marketing and only mentioned debt solution providers, not Digivo itself.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 1998 Section 55A: Commissioner may serve monetary penalty if satisfied there has been serious contravention of PECR and contravention was deliberate or negligent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Contravention was serious: 415,041 messages delivered over 6 months; 1,396 complaints received; potential for 1.15M messages annually based on database size.
violations: Contravention was serious: 415,041 messages delivered over 6 months; 1,396 complaints received; potential for 1.15M messages annually based on database size.
Contravention was deliberate: apparent connection to affiliated companies in sub-prime market; high volume of complaints during and after investigation.
Contravention was negligent: organisation should have been aware of PECR obligations via published ICO guidance; failed to take reasonable steps despite complaints and investigation notice.

outcome: The ICO issued a Monetary Penalty Notice on 3 October 2023 requiring payment of £50,000 by 2 November 2023 (reducible to £40,000 if paid by 1 November 2023). Digivo has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The penalty is payable to the Consolidated Fund. Digivo must cease unsolicited marketing practices and implement compliant consent mechanisms.
companyNow: Digivo Media Limited (trading as Rid My Debt) remains active but under regulatory scrutiny. The company is required to comply with PECR and implement validated consent procedures for all future direct marketing communications.
dataType: Phone numbers, personal contact details

companyDescription: Lee Chee Meng is an individual real estate salesperson registered under the Estate Agents Act 2010 and appointed by ERA Realty Network Pte Ltd to engage in estate agency work. He operated as an independent agent earning commissions on real estate transactions.
companyLongDescription: Lee Chee Meng is an individual real estate salesperson registered under the Estate Agents Act 2010 and appointed by ERA Realty Network Pte Ltd to engage in estate agency work. He operated as an independent agent earning commissions on real estate transactions.
caseDescription: Lee Chee Meng, a real estate salesperson, purchased approximately 420,000 records of personal data from an unknown online seller without verifying consent or legitimate sources, and used this data to send unsolicited telemarketing emails and SMS messages. He failed to perform due diligence on the data provenance and did not obtain or verify that individuals had consented to the collection, use, and disclosure of their data. The purchased data may have originated from a data breach.
violationSummary: The respondent purchased personal data from a third party and used it for a secondary purpose (telemarketing) without obtaining or verifying that the original data subjects had consented to this use and disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Lee Chee Meng purchased approximately 420,000 personal data records from an unknown online seller for S$1,200 and used names, emails, contact numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 420,000 individuals had their personal data used for marketing communications without their consent or knowledge, exposing them to unwanted contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondent claimed he was unaware that using email addresses for telemarketing purposes was a violation of the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ignorance of the law is not a legitimate excuse for breaching data protection obligations, and the respondent was acting for profit in furtherance of his business as a real estate salesperson.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondent stated he had no malicious intentions and was only seeking to provide for his family.
claimsVsReality.reality: The respondent's actions were ultimately done for profit in furtherance of his business; personal motivations do not excuse data protection breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondent claimed to have provided opt-out options in emails and checked DNC registry.
claimsVsReality.reality: While these measures showed some awareness of compliance, they did not cure the fundamental breach of failing to obtain or verify consent before collection and use of the data in the first place.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 13 of the PDPA requires organisations to obtain consent of individuals before collecting, using or disclosing personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent failed to ascertain that consent of the individuals had been obtained before purchasing their personal data from the seller and subsequently sending unsolicited telemarketing communications to them.
violations: Respondent failed to ascertain that consent of the individuals had been obtained before purchasing their personal data from the seller and subsequently sending unsolicited telemarketing communications to them.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 20 of the PDPA requires organisations to inform individuals of the purposes for which personal data is being collected, used or disclosed before collection, use or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent did not perform due diligence to ensure individuals had been informed of the purposes for which their personal data was subsequently collected, used and/or disclosed by the respondent and the seller.
violations: Respondent did not perform due diligence to ensure individuals had been informed of the purposes for which their personal data was subsequently collected, used and/or disclosed by the respondent and the seller.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data controllers buying marketing lists from third parties must make rigorous checks to satisfy themselves that the third party obtained the personal data fairly and lawfully, that individuals understood their details would be passed on for marketing purposes, and that they have the necessary consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent purchased data from unknown seller without any verification checks, without asking how the data was obtained, without confirming consent was obtained, and without contacting individuals directly to obtain consent.
violations: Respondent purchased data from unknown seller without any verification checks, without asking how the data was obtained, without confirming consent was obtained, and without contacting individuals directly to obtain consent.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the respondent in breach of sections 13 and 20 of the PDPA. The respondent was ordered to: (1) pay a financial penalty of S$16,800 (reduced from the initially proposed S$28,000 due to exceptional financial hardship); (2) cease use of all purchased data immediately; (3) cease retention of all purchased data within 7 days; and (4) inform the Commission within 7 days of completion of these steps. The penalty was reduced based on the respondent's evidence of severe financial difficulties and medical expenses for a family member, though the Commission made clear this reduction was exceptional and not precedent-setting.
companyNow: Lee Chee Meng remains a registered salesperson under the Estate Agents Act 2010 appointed by ERA Realty Network Pte Ltd, though subject to the directions and financial penalty imposed by this decision.
dataType: Name, email address, contact number, residential address, partial credit card number (last 4 digits)

companyDescription: Google, LLC is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Mountain View, California, and a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. Google's primary business is advertising, generating over $220 billion in annual advertising revenue (2022), with location-based geotargeting as a critical feature.
companyLongDescription: Google, LLC is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Mountain View, California, and a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. Google's primary business is advertising, generating over $220 billion in annual advertising revenue (2022), with location-based geotargeting as a critical feature.
caseDescription: Google deceived millions of California users into enabling location tracking through misleading prompts and false claims about privacy controls. The company misrepresented that disabling Location History would stop location collection, when it continued tracking users through Web & App Activity. Google also falsely claimed users could opt out of location-based advertising by disabling Ads Personalization, but continued geotargeting regardless.
violationSummary: Google engaged in systematic surveillance of user location through deceptive account-level settings and misleading interface disclosures, allowing continuous geolocation tracking without informed consent.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Google used deceptive prompts from 2014–2018 to trick users into enabling Location History, misrepresented that disabling it stopped all location tracking.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of California users had their precise daily movements continuously tracked and recorded without meaningful consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Location History is off by default and can be disabled to stop location tracking
claimsVsReality.reality: Google showed deceptive prompts (2014–2018) tricking users into enabling Location History; even when disabled, Google continued collecting precise location via Web & App Activity

claimsVsReality.claim: Turning off Location History means 'the places you go are no longer stored'
claimsVsReality.reality: Google continued recording and storing precise location coordinates through Web & App Activity and continued using historical location data to serve geotargeted ads

claimsVsReality.claim: Disabling Ads Personalization stops Google from serving personalized/geotargeted ads
claimsVsReality.reality: Google continued using real-time location information to geotarget ads even after users disabled Ads Personalization

claimsVsReality.claim: Web & App Activity merely 'saves your activity on Google sites and apps'
claimsVsReality.reality: Web & App Activity collected and stored precise latitude/longitude coordinates (2015–2019) without explicit user disclosure, enabling location tracking independent of Location History setting

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17500 prohibits making or disseminating false or misleading statements with intent to induce use of services or products when the defendant knew or should have known the statements were false.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google made false/misleading statements about Location History, claiming users could turn it off to stop location tracking, when Google continued collecting location data via Web & App Activity
violations: Google made false/misleading statements about Location History, claiming users could turn it off to stop location tracking, when Google continued collecting location data via Web & App Activity
Google misrepresented that disabling Ads Personalization would stop geotargeted advertising, when it continued using real-time location data for ad targeting
Google failed to disclose that Web & App Activity collected and stored precise latitude/longitude coordinates (2015–2019)

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent acts or practices in commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by using misleading prompts (e.g., 'Enhance your Google Maps experience') that obscured the true scope of location data collection
violations: Google engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by using misleading prompts (e.g., 'Enhance your Google Maps experience') that obscured the true scope of location data collection
Google created false appearance of user control by offering settings that did not function as described
Google's default-enabled settings combined with obscured disclosures constituted fraudulent practice designed to maximize location data harvesting for advertising profit

outcome: Complaint for permanent injunction, civil penalties, and equitable relief filed September 14, 2023 in Superior Court of California, County of Santa Clara. The People seek: (1) permanent injunction to prevent future violations; (2) civil penalties of $2,500 per UCL violation; (3) civil penalties of $2,500 per FAL violation; (4) costs; and (5) additional relief as determined by court. Case remains pending; no settlement or judgment has been entered as of document date.
companyNow: Google, LLC (subsidiary of Alphabet Inc.) remains one of the world's largest technology and advertising companies, though facing increased regulatory scrutiny over data practices globally.
dataType: Geolocation data, precise location coordinates, behavioral/activity data
legalBasisViolated: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law)
California Business and Professions Code § 17500 et seq. (False Advertising Law)

companyDescription: OrangeTee & Tie Pte Ltd is a real estate enterprise based in Singapore that has operated since 2000, offering property brokerage and related services.
companyLongDescription: OrangeTee & Tie Pte Ltd is a real estate enterprise based in Singapore that has operated since 2000, offering property brokerage and related services.
caseDescription: OrangeTee & Tie suffered a ransomware attack in August 2021 that exfiltrated personal data of 256,583 individuals (employees, customers, and agents). The company breached PDPA Section 24 by using unencrypted production data in development servers without security safeguards and failing to conduct periodic security reviews, leaving outdated SQL Server vulnerable to injection attacks.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, exposing it to unauthorised access through both inadequate development environment safeguards and unpatched vulnerabilities in internet-facing servers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: OrangeTee & Tie stored unencrypted personal data of 256,583 people in poorly-secured development servers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Threat actors exploited outdated, unpatched database software to steal full names, national ID numbers, bank account details, and financial information from employees.

claimsVsReality.claim: The threat actor ALTDOS claimed to have stolen 'hundreds of databases'
claimsVsReality.reality: Forensic investigation confirmed exfiltration from only 11 databases across the four servers

claimsVsReality.claim: Microsoft's auto-scan function would reliably alert to all required patches including Service Pack 4
claimsVsReality.reality: The tool failed to detect that Service Pack 4 (available since October 2017) needed installation, despite being configured to run monthly

claimsVsReality.claim: Live production data was necessary in development servers for accurate testing
claimsVsReality.reality: PDPC guidance and best practices recommend using anonymised, synthetic, or pseudonymised data for development/testing purposes to reduce breach impact

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Stored unencrypted personal data from 256,583 individuals in development servers accessible to threat actors via SQL injection vulnerabilities
violations: Stored unencrypted personal data from 256,583 individuals in development servers accessible to threat actors via SQL injection vulnerabilities
Failed to conduct periodic security reviews that would have identified vulnerabilities in outdated Microsoft SQL Server 2012 (unsupported since October 2018)
Used live production personal data in development environment without sufficiently robust security assessment, contrary to PDPC guidance recommending anonymisation or pseudonymisation
Relied solely on automated Microsoft patch alerts for 4 years without consciously reviewing or applying critical Service Pack 4 update

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 37,000 payable within 30 days. The organisation had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures including server isolation, security patching, vulnerability testing, enterprise anti-malware deployment, security hardening to CIS benchmarks, firewall configuration review, web application firewall implementation, and liaison with forensic experts. No further directions were deemed necessary given the remedial actions already completed.
companyNow: OrangeTee & Tie Pte Ltd remains a Singapore-based real estate enterprise. The company has implemented significant security infrastructure improvements following the incident and continues operations.
dataType: Names, national identification numbers (NRIC/FIN/passport), bank account numbers, commission amounts, property transaction amounts

companyDescription: Sussex Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing the Sussex region in southeastern England. The force serves a population of approximately 1.7 million people across East Sussex, West Sussex, and Brighton and Hove.
companyLongDescription: Sussex Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing the Sussex region in southeastern England. The force serves a population of approximately 1.7 million people across East Sussex, West Sussex, and Brighton and Hove.
caseDescription: Sussex Police deployed a call-recording app to 1,015 staff members without adequate data protection safeguards. Over 202,000 telephone conversations were automatically recorded and retained on officers' devices, capturing sensitive data across many non-law-enforcement topics. Data subjects were never informed of the recording, denying them access and other rights under data protection law.
violationSummary: The app conducted mass surveillance of telephone conversations without knowledge or consent of the individuals involved. This represents systematic surveillance across a broad range of topics, not limited to law enforcement purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Sussex Police deployed a call-recording app to all 1,015 staff members without restricting access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Victims, witnesses, and suspected criminals had their telephone conversations recorded without knowledge or consent, denying them the right to object, request erasure.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app was initially requested by a specific cadre of officers for critical operational policing support.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app was made available to all 1,015 staff members without limiting deployment, capturing 202,000+ recordings across a broad range of non-law-enforcement topics.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app was technically necessary and beneficial for law enforcement operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app was deployed without risk assessment, approval documentation, staff guidance, or compliance review, capturing indiscriminate recordings without data subject knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app complied with Electronic Devices policies.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app breached the Forces-issued Electronic Devices policy by using it to 'record notes or other investigative details' in a manner that captured sensitive personal data across many non-law-enforcement conversations.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 35(1) requires that the processing of personal data for any of the law enforcement purposes must be lawful and fair.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sussex Police made the app available to all 1,015 staff members despite it being technically possible to limit it to specific officers, capturing data across broad topics including non-law-enforcement conversations
violations: Sussex Police made the app available to all 1,015 staff members despite it being technically possible to limit it to specific officers, capturing data across broad topics including non-law-enforcement conversations
No adequate risk assessment was undertaken before making the app available
Devices captured calls indiscriminately and without knowledge of affected data subjects
No documentation evidenced how the app was approved for release

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 45(1) entitles data subjects to confirmation of processing and access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Data subjects were not informed that their telephone calls were being recorded
violations: Data subjects were not informed that their telephone calls were being recorded
Data subjects were denied the opportunity to exercise rights of access, objection, rectification, and erasure
The lack of transparency and fair processing denied data subjects the ability to exercise their rights under DPA 2018

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 37 requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be adequate, relevant, and not excessive in relation to the purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Retention of call recordings on officers' mobile devices was not subject to any review or oversight
violations: Retention of call recordings on officers' mobile devices was not subject to any review or oversight
Every call made from or received by devices was recorded regardless of relevance to law enforcement

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 39(1) and 39(2) require that personal data be kept no longer than necessary and that appropriate time limits for periodic review be established.
regulatoryFindings.description: Recordings were retained until individual devices were remotely wiped with no retention schedule or review process
violations: Recordings were retained until individual devices were remotely wiped with no retention schedule or review process

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 40 requires appropriate security of personal data using technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Copies of call recordings were manually transferred onto removable media, compromising security
violations: Copies of call recordings were manually transferred onto removable media, compromising security
A subsequently identified additional app processing personal information had unmitigated security risks identified in a Data Protection Impact Assessment

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to the Chief Constable of Sussex Police. Although the ICO considered imposing a £1.0 million administrative penalty, it adopted a revised approach to public sector enforcement in June 2022 and decided not to impose a financial penalty. The Commissioner requires Sussex Police to: (1) establish a specific team to assess new apps with adequate consideration of data protection and data subject rights; (2) document and authorise app deployment processes; (3) issue adequate staff instruction with confirmation of understanding; (4) review existing policies to ensure data subject rights are considered; and (5) review data protection training to emphasise data subject rights. Sussex Police must report on compliance actions by 4 July 2023. The app has been withdrawn and recordings other than evidential material have been destroyed.
companyNow: Sussex Police remains the primary law enforcement agency for the Sussex region of England. The organisation has implemented remedial steps including forming a Gold Group oversight body, withdrawing the app, and destroying non-evidential recordings.
dataType: Telephone conversation recordings, personal data, special category data (sensitive personal data)
legalBasisViolated: DPA 2018 Section 35(1) – lawful and fair processing for law enforcement purposes
DPA 2018 Section 37 – adequacy, relevance, and non-excessive processing
DPA 2018 Section 39(1) – retention only as long as necessary
DPA 2018 Section 39(2) – periodic review of retention necessity
DPA 2018 Section 40 – appropriate security of personal data
DPA 2018 Section 45(1) – data subject right to confirmation and access

companyDescription: RHAP Limited is a UK-registered company that conducted direct marketing via telephone calls. The company appears to have worked with or made calls on behalf of 'APUK' or 'Appliance Plan UK' based on call recordings referenced in the enforcement notice.
companyLongDescription: RHAP Limited is a UK-registered company that conducted direct marketing via telephone calls. The company appears to have worked with or made calls on behalf of 'APUK' or 'Appliance Plan UK' based on call recordings referenced in the enforcement notice.
caseDescription: RHAP Limited made 15,288 unsolicited marketing calls to individuals registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between January and August 2021, violating UK telemarketing regulations. The company failed to obtain proper consent from TPS-registered subscribers and failed to provide required caller identification information on the calls. Recipients reported distress from the violations.
violationSummary: RHAP systematically circumvented individuals' explicit privacy preferences (TPS registration) by making unsolicited marketing calls without consent, representing surveillance-based collection contrary to stated preferences.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: RHAP made 15,288 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and August 2021 to phone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 15,288 individuals who had explicitly registered their numbers to block unwanted marketing calls received those calls anyway, resulting in documented complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: RHAP claimed to have obtained consent from call recipients to receive marketing calls
claimsVsReality.reality: RHAP provided minimal evidence of valid consent and no documentation showing subscribers notified RHAP they did not object to calls; references to third party 'APUK' gaining consent were unsupported

claimsVsReality.claim: RHAP's marketing calls provided required identification information
claimsVsReality.reality: RHAP failed to provide required caller identification particulars (name and contact details on request) to call recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits using public electronic communications services to make unsolicited calls for direct marketing to numbers listed on the Telephone Preference Service register.
regulatoryFindings.description: RHAP made 15,288 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers without evidence of valid consent from subscribers
violations: RHAP made 15,288 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers without evidence of valid consent from subscribers
Company provided no documentation showing subscribers had notified RHAP they did not object to calls
Subscribers had registered with TPS at least 28 days before receiving calls, meeting the statutory threshold

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(2) requires that direct marketing communications include the name of the person making the call and, if requested, contact details.
regulatoryFindings.description: RHAP failed to provide required caller identification particulars to call recipients
violations: RHAP failed to provide required caller identification particulars to call recipients
Company did not ensure recipients could obtain address or free telephone number for contact

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered subscribers only where they have given clear, positive notification of willingness to receive calls from that specific company.
regulatoryFindings.description: RHAP provided limited evidence of any valid notifications from call recipients
violations: RHAP provided limited evidence of any valid notifications from call recipients
On call recordings, agents referenced third party 'APUK' gaining consent without demonstrating how
No evidence showed RHAP obtained consent specifically from RHAP, rather than generic consent

outcome: Enforcement Notice issued requiring RHAP to cease unsolicited marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers without valid consent within 30 days, and to provide required caller identification information on all direct marketing calls. The notice specifies that valid consent must be based on clear, positive action by the individual and must specifically reference RHAP (not generic third parties). RHAP has right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: RHAP Limited (Companies House Registration 11856484) is a limited company registered in Bury, UK. Current operational status and activities unknown from the document.
dataType: telephone numbers, personal contact information

companyDescription: Devon and Cornwall Police is the statutory police force responsible for policing Devon and Cornwall in South West England. In April 2017, it formed an operational alliance with Dorset Police covering over 30 administrative and operational business areas, including data protection.
companyLongDescription: Devon and Cornwall Police is the statutory police force responsible for policing Devon and Cornwall in South West England. In April 2017, it formed an operational alliance with Dorset Police covering over 30 administrative and operational business areas, including data protection.
caseDescription: Devon and Cornwall Police failed to respond to subject access requests within statutory timeframes for over four years, with a backlog of hundreds of overdue requests. In August 2022, the force had 373 overdue requests, with 33% older than seven months and 19% older than a year. As of November 2023, 83% of 347 pending requests exceeded the one-month statutory deadline.
violationSummary: The organisation systematically failed to provide data subjects with timely access to their personal data, effectively denying them the ability to exercise their statutory right of access under GDPR Article 15 and equivalent DPA 2018 provisions.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Devon and Cornwall Police failed to respond to hundreds of subject access requests within the one-month statutory deadline required by UK GDPR Article 12(3).
whyTheyWereWrong: Data subjects were systematically denied timely access to their personal information, with 33% of overdue requests languishing over seven months.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Alliance claimed to have comprehensive action plans to bring subject access request compliance back in line with statutory requirements (submitted 24 February 2023).
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite action plans, the force maintained over 300 overdue requests months later, with 287 of 347 pending requests still exceeding the one-month deadline as of November 2023.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) of the UK GDPR and Part 3, Chapter 3, Section 54 of the DPA 2018 require controllers to provide information on action taken on requests under Articles 15-22 to data subjects without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request (extendable by two further months where necessary).
regulatoryFindings.description: Devon and Cornwall Police continuously infringed this provision for over four years, maintaining a persistent backlog of subject access requests since 2018
violations: Devon and Cornwall Police continuously infringed this provision for over four years, maintaining a persistent backlog of subject access requests since 2018
In August 2022, 373 requests were overdue, with 128 (33%) older than seven months and 71 (19%) older than one year
As of November 2023, 287 out of 347 pending requests (83%) exceeded the one-month deadline, with 78 (22%) older than four months

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Devon and Cornwall Police under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR and Schedule 13(2)(c) of the DPA 2018. The Commissioner recommended that the force continue to ensure adequate staffing resources and follow its action plan to meet statutory deadlines. The force had already begun remedial steps by July 2023, increasing staff by 8 full-time data protection advisors (37 hours/week) and 2 advisors (30 hours/week), and securing month-by-month overtime funding. Statistics showed improving compliance by November 2023.
companyNow: Devon and Cornwall Police remains operational and continues to implement compliance improvements. As of November 2023, increased staffing and overtime measures were showing measurable progress in reducing the age of pending subject access requests.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (various types under GDPR/DPA 2018)
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018 Part 3, Chapter 3, Section 54

companyDescription: Complete Marketing Services Ltd is a UK-based telemarketing and direct marketing services provider registered at Companies House (Company Number 11745446) and located at Stanmore Business Innovative Centre, Middlesex.
companyLongDescription: Complete Marketing Services Ltd is a UK-based telemarketing and direct marketing services provider registered at Companies House (Company Number 11745446) and located at Stanmore Business Innovative Centre, Middlesex.
caseDescription: Complete Marketing Services Ltd made 242,497 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) register between June 2021 and February 2022, violating Regulations 21 and 24 of PECR. The company failed to obtain clear consent from subscribers and did not provide required identification information during calls. This resulted in 106 valid complaints to the TPS and Information Commissioner.
violationSummary: CMS systematically made unsolicited marketing calls to individuals who had registered with TPS to prevent such contact, constituting targeted surveillance of subscribers' preference data without permission or valid override consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between June 2021 and February 2022, Complete Marketing Services made 242,497 unsolicited direct marketing calls to phone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 106 people who had explicitly registered to stop receiving marketing calls were contacted anyway, causing repeated unwanted intrusions into their privacy.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits using or instigating the use of public electronic communications services to make unsolicited calls for direct marketing where the called number is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: CMS made 242,497 unsolicited calls to numbers listed on the TPS register, contrary to Regulation 21(1)(b).
violations: CMS made 242,497 unsolicited calls to numbers listed on the TPS register, contrary to Regulation 21(1)(b).

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(2) requires that for direct marketing calls, the caller must provide their name and either their address or a telephone number on which they can be reached free of charge.
regulatoryFindings.description: CMS failed to provide the required identification information (name, address, or contact telephone number) to call recipients as mandated by Regulation 24(2).
violations: CMS failed to provide the required identification information (name, address, or contact telephone number) to call recipients as mandated by Regulation 24(2).

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered numbers only if the subscriber has given clear and positive notification that they do not object to receiving such calls from that company.
regulatoryFindings.description: CMS provided no evidence that subscribers had given valid, clear and positive notification consenting to receive marketing calls from CMS specifically.
violations: CMS provided no evidence that subscribers had given valid, clear and positive notification consenting to receive marketing calls from CMS specifically.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice dated 9 November 2023 requiring Complete Marketing Services Ltd to cease making unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers within 30 days and to ensure provision of caller identification information (name and address or reachable telephone number) on all future direct marketing calls. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003

companyDescription: The Ministry of Justice is the UK government department responsible for administering courts, prisons, probation services, and criminal justice policy. HMP is a prison facility within its remit where the security incident occurred.
companyLongDescription: The Ministry of Justice is the UK government department responsible for administering courts, prisons, probation services, and criminal justice policy. HMP is a prison facility within its remit where the security incident occurred.
caseDescription: The Ministry of Justice failed to implement adequate security measures for confidential waste at a prison facility, resulting in 14 bags of sensitive personal data—including medical records and security vetting information—being left unsecured for 18 days where up to 44 individuals, including prisoners, could access them. The prison lacked robust policies for handling confidential waste, designated secure storage areas, and failed to ensure staff completed mandatory data protection training, creating systemic vulnerabilities.
violationSummary: Confidential personal data was left exposed in an unsecured, accessible location where unauthorised individuals (prisoners and staff) could view and remove it, directly resulting in disclosure and increased accessibility of sensitive information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Ministry of Justice left 14 bags of confidential waste containing medical records, security vetting details.
whyTheyWereWrong: Up to 44 prisoners and staff accessed sensitive personal data including medical records and security information, exposing individuals to identification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Policies in operation clearly emphasised the need to securely shred records.
claimsVsReality.reality: No specific instructions were provided to prison staff regarding designated storage areas for confidential waste, and there were no pre-agreed secure areas for staff to leave confidential waste at the facility.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data protection training was in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The prison did not hold accurate data on staff completion rates, there were no robust measures to ensure mandatory training completion, and staff lacked awareness of processes for handling sensitive waste and understanding of breach reporting requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: A shredder would usually collect the confidential waste.
claimsVsReality.reality: On the incident date, the shredder lorry failed to collect the bags within the allotted time, leaving them unsecured for 18 days, and staff did not report this failure despite evidence of prisoners accessing the material.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction, or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ministry of Justice failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, leaving confidential waste unsecured in an accessible prison area for 18 days.
violations: Ministry of Justice failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, leaving confidential waste unsecured in an accessible prison area for 18 days.
No designated secure storage areas were established for confidential waste prior to disposal.
Bags were not properly sealed or shredded, exposing medical data and security vetting details to prisoners and staff.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR requires controllers to implement a process for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ministry of Justice did not conduct adequate testing or evaluation of waste handling procedures.
violations: Ministry of Justice did not conduct adequate testing or evaluation of waste handling procedures.
No evidence of systematic assessment of risks posed by confidential waste storage and disposal.
Lack of robust quality assurance for the shredding and waste collection process.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(2) of the UK GDPR requires an appropriate level of security commensurate with the risks of processing, including risks of accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Security measures were grossly inadequate given the high-risk prison environment where both prisoners and staff had access to confidential waste.
violations: Security measures were grossly inadequate given the high-risk prison environment where both prisoners and staff had access to confidential waste.
No risk assessment demonstrated appropriate mitigation for sensitive information (medical, security vetting) in a correctional facility.
Failure to shred waste before collection created foreseeable risk of unauthorised access.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to the Ministry of Justice for violations of UK GDPR Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(d), and 32(2). The ICO welcomed remedial steps taken post-incident, including implementation of a new confidential waste collection process, designation of secure storage areas, installation of on-site shredders, and issuance of staff guidance. The Commissioner recommended further actions: a thorough review of all data protection policies (noting outdated references to DPA 1998 and GDPR), creation of a separate data breach reporting policy, testing of residual risks to affected individuals, execution of a data processing agreement with the NHS Trust, and timely completion of staff training initiatives. The Ministry of Justice was required to provide a progress update to the ICO by 27 October 2023.
companyNow: The Ministry of Justice remains the government department responsible for criminal justice in England and Wales. Post-incident remediation measures at HMP have been implemented to prevent recurrence.
