dataType: Health data, security vetting details, prison staff and prisoner personal information
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Security and integrity
UK GDPR Art. 32(1)(d) – Testing and evaluation of security measures
UK GDPR Art. 32(2) – Appropriate level of security

companyDescription: Piraeus Bank is a major Greek bank founded in 1891, operating in retail and corporate banking, asset management, and capital markets across Greece and southeastern Europe. It is one of the four largest banks in Greece.
companyLongDescription: Piraeus Bank is a major Greek bank founded in 1891, operating in retail and corporate banking, asset management, and capital markets across Greece and southeastern Europe. It is one of the four largest banks in Greece.
caseDescription: Piraeus Bank unlawfully processed personal data of 23,259 customers by sending them notifications about debt collection transfers due to a systematic software error in recipient list generation. The bank failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to prevent sending notifications to customers with zero-balance accounts who were not subject to collection. The bank also failed to properly respond to the complainant's data access request.
violationSummary: The bank failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures (Article 25 GDPR) to ensure lawful processing, resulting in systematic unauthorized processing of personal data of thousands of individuals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Piraeus Bank sent 23,259 personalized letters to customers due to systemic technical errors.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers with fully paid loans received debt collection notices about data transfers they didn't authorize, causing confusion.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank claimed the inclusion of 23,259 zero-balance accounts in the notification list was purely a 'systematic technical error' with no actual data transfer to the debt collector.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of whether actual transfer occurred, the bank unlawfully processed the personal data of 23,259 individuals by generating and sending the notification letters, as the recipients had no outstanding debt requiring collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank stated it had provided 'proper notice and transparent information' to customers about the debt collection transfer.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bank failed to implement adequate safeguards to prevent sending notices to customers with fully-paid zero-balance loans who should never have received notification, and failed to respond properly to the complainant's specific data access questions.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank processed data of 23,259 customers without lawful basis because recipients had zero-balance fully-paid loans not subject to debt collection
violations: Bank processed data of 23,259 customers without lawful basis because recipients had zero-balance fully-paid loans not subject to debt collection

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires at least one lawful basis to exist for any processing of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: No lawful basis existed for processing data of customers with zero-balance accounts as they were not owed funds requiring collection
violations: No lawful basis existed for processing data of customers with zero-balance accounts as they were not owed funds requiring collection

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25(1) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure processing complies with GDPR and protects rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to implement safeguards in recipient list generation system, allowing systematic inclusion of zero-balance accounts; discovered error only after customer complaints, not through own controls
violations: Bank failed to implement safeguards in recipient list generation system, allowing systematic inclusion of zero-balance accounts; discovered error only after customer complaints, not through own controls

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) provides the right to access personal data and information about processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank sent generic apology letter instead of clearly confirming whether complainant's data was actually transferred to debt collector; failed to answer four specific questions about data collection and scope
violations: Bank sent generic apology letter instead of clearly confirming whether complainant's data was actually transferred to debt collector; failed to answer four specific questions about data collection and scope

outcome: Authority found Piraeus Bank violated Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 15(1), and 25(1) GDPR. Bank ordered to pay €210,000 in administrative fines: €100,000 for unlawful processing (Art. 5/6), €100,000 for failure to implement adequate safeguards (Art. 25), €10,000 for inadequate access response (Art. 15). Bank directed to properly satisfy the complainant's data access right with specific answers to all four original questions. No transfer of data to debt collector (Intrum) was confirmed to have occurred as listed recipients did not meet collection criteria.
companyNow: Piraeus Bank remains one of Greece's largest banking institutions, though it underwent significant restructuring and recapitalization following the 2008 financial crisis and Greek debt crisis. The bank continues operating as a major lender in Greece.
dataType: Financial data, loan contract details, personal identification information, debt status, contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of lawful basis for processing
GDPR Art. 15(1) – Right of access / failure to provide adequate response
GDPR Art. 25(1) – Data protection by design and by default / lack of adequate technical and organizational measures

companyDescription: Amazon.com, Inc. is a multinational technology and e-commerce company founded in 1994, operating globally with over 1.4 million employees and annual revenues exceeding $380 billion. Through its Alexa voice assistant, Echo smart speakers, and FreeTime children's services, Amazon serves millions of consumers worldwide.
companyLongDescription: Amazon.com, Inc. is a multinational technology and e-commerce company founded in 1994, operating globally with over 1.4 million employees and annual revenues exceeding $380 billion. Through its Alexa voice assistant, Echo smart speakers, and FreeTime children's services, Amazon serves millions of consumers worldwide.
caseDescription: Amazon collected and indefinitely retained voice recordings and transcripts from millions of Alexa users, including over 800,000 children under 13, despite representing that it would delete this data upon request. The company failed to honor deletion requests, retained transcripts after voice files were deleted, and allowed excessive employee access to sensitive recordings. Amazon misled parents about their ability to control and delete children's voice data in violation of COPPA.
violationSummary: Amazon collected voice data ostensibly to fulfill user requests but retained it indefinitely for product improvement, using children's unique speech patterns to train algorithms without proportionate necessity or parental consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Amazon retained children's voice recordings and transcripts indefinitely by default, deleted audio files but secretly kept transcripts after deletion requests.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 800,000 children had their voice recordings, speech patterns, and location data retained without parental knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Amazon's Alexa Privacy Hub states 'Alexa and Echo devices are designed to protect your privacy' and 'provide transparency and control.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Amazon retained voice recordings indefinitely by default, made deletion non-functional (kept transcripts), and gave 30,000 employees unnecessary access to sensitive data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Alexa Privacy Settings webpage: 'You have control over your Alexa experience' and 'View, hear, and delete your voice recordings at any time.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Until mid-2019, deletion requests deleted voice files but retained transcripts for product improvement, rendering user control illusory. Geolocation deletion requests failed repeatedly across multiple calendar years (2018–2022).

claimsVsReality.claim: Amazon will delete users' voice and geolocation data upon request and carefully limits employee access to voice data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between August 2018 and September 2019, 30,000 employees could access voice recordings; approximately 15,000 lacked any business justification, violating Amazon's own 'least permission' policies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Parents can exercise control over children's voice recordings through simple deletion mechanisms.
claimsVsReality.reality: Parents could not delete transcripts, which Amazon retained indefinitely and used for algorithm training. Parents received no notification that deletion was incomplete.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Amazon falsely represented that Alexa App users could delete geolocation information at any time, but retained data in secondary storage locations insulated from deletion requests across multiple discovery cycles (Feb 2018 – early 2022).
violations: Amazon falsely represented that Alexa App users could delete geolocation information at any time, but retained data in secondary storage locations insulated from deletion requests across multiple discovery cycles (Feb 2018 – early 2022).

Amazon falsely represented that users could delete voice recordings and transcripts, but deleted only audio files while retaining transcripts in residual data stores for product improvement without user notification.

Amazon engaged in unfair privacy practices by failing to ensure children's voice recordings were retained only as long as reasonably necessary, retaining data indefinitely by default even for inactive accounts.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.10 requires operators to retain personal information from children online only as long as reasonably necessary to fulfill the purpose for which collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: Amazon retained children's voice recordings indefinitely by default setting from product launch until September 2019, two months after receiving FTC Civil Investigative Demand, despite only needing seconds to process requests.
violations: Amazon retained children's voice recordings indefinitely by default setting from product launch until September 2019, two months after receiving FTC Civil Investigative Demand, despite only needing seconds to process requests.

Amazon retained transcripts of deleted voice recordings in perpetuity, claiming three justifications (responding to commands, parental review, algorithm improvement), none of which reasonably required indefinite retention.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. §§ 312.4(a) and 312.4(d)(3) require complete, truthful, clear notice to parents regarding their ability to request deletion of children's personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Amazon's privacy disclosures asserted control and deletion capability but omitted that transcripts were retained indefinitely after voice file deletion, making notice incomplete and misleading.
violations: Amazon's privacy disclosures asserted control and deletion capability but omitted that transcripts were retained indefinitely after voice file deletion, making notice incomplete and misleading.
Amazon directed parents to deletion options that appeared to delete both audio and text, but UI design (disappearing 'play' button) created false impression of complete deletion.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.6(a)(2) requires operators to provide parents with a meaningful opportunity to delete children's personal information at any time.
regulatoryFindings.description: When parents requested deletion of children's voice recordings via Alexa Privacy Hub or Alexa App, Amazon deleted voice files but retained transcripts in residual data stores, continuing product improvement use without parental knowledge.
violations: When parents requested deletion of children's voice recordings via Alexa Privacy Hub or Alexa App, Amazon deleted voice files but retained transcripts in residual data stores, continuing product improvement use without parental knowledge.
Amazon failed to honor complete deletion requests for over one year (until mid-2019), denying parents' effective opportunity to control children's data.

outcome: Complaint filed May 31, 2023, seeking permanent injunction to prevent future violations of FTC Act and COPPA Rule, monetary civil penalties for each violation of COPPA Rule, and additional equitable relief. The complaint alleges unfair and deceptive practices through indefinite data retention, misleading deletion claims, and excessive employee access to sensitive children's voice data. No settlement agreement or final judgment yet disclosed as of document date.
companyNow: Amazon remains one of the world's largest technology and e-commerce companies. As of 2023, the company continues to operate Alexa services and has undertaken remediation steps including auto-delete features introduced in September 2019, though litigation was ongoing.
dataType: Voice recordings, transcripts, geolocation data, children's personal information (name, birth date, gender)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
COPPA Section 1303(c) – Retention of children's personal information longer than reasonably necessary
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312.10 – Data retention limits
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.6(a)(2) – Parental deletion rights

companyDescription: Region Skåne is a regional government body (Regionstyrelsen) in Sweden responsible for healthcare delivery in Skåne region. As a public authority, it manages patient data from quality registries and conducts medical research.
companyLongDescription: Region Skåne is a regional government body (Regionstyrelsen) in Sweden responsible for healthcare delivery in Skåne region. As a public authority, it manages patient data from quality registries and conducts medical research.
caseDescription: Region Skåne stored unencrypted patient health data and ID numbers on a USB drive, which was lost on 1 November 2020. The drive contained sensitive health information for 1,934 patients from a cardiac care registry. Sweden's data protection authority found the region failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures required under GDPR Article 32.
violationSummary: The region failed to implement appropriate technical safeguards (encryption) for sensitive health data processed on portable storage, creating material risk of unauthorised access, disclosure, and loss through ordinary negligence.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Region Skåne stored unencrypted health records and patient ID numbers on a portable USB drive and lost control of the device when it was misplaced in a laundry bag in November 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,934 patients' sensitive health information and personal ID numbers were exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data controller claimed the breach resulted solely from a single employee's carelessness in leaving the USB drive in laundry, not a failure of organisational security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the employee's negligence, the organisation was responsible under GDPR for implementing encryption and other safeguards. Encrypted USB devices were available internally but not mandated for use, revealing systemic security gaps.

claimsVsReality.claim: Some data values were encoded as binary (1s and 0s) representing yes/no responses, suggesting reduced sensitivity because data was not in plain text.
claimsVsReality.reality: Binary-encoded health data remains sensitive personal information; encoding does not constitute adequate encryption. Direct linkage to patient ID numbers meant individuals remained readily identifiable.

claimsVsReality.claim: There was no evidence the data had actually been accessed or distributed by unauthorised parties because the USB was lost within the organisation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The unrecovered state of the device created ongoing material risk of breach, and lack of evidence of unauthorised access does not excuse the failure to implement preventive security measures beforehand.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32.1 requires the data controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security proportionate to the risks posed by processing, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Skåne stored unencrypted health data and ID numbers on a portable USB drive without encryption despite organisational policies recommending encrypted USB devices for sensitive information.
violations: Region Skåne stored unencrypted health data and ID numbers on a portable USB drive without encryption despite organisational policies recommending encrypted USB devices for sensitive information.
The region failed to ensure adequate security appropriate to the high-risk nature of health data and personally identifiable numbers, resulting in loss of the device and unrecovered data.
No technical safeguards (such as encryption) were implemented to prevent unauthorised access if the USB drive were lost or stolen, contrary to GDPR Article 32 requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, or damage by appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Health data concerning 1,934 patients was processed on unencrypted portable storage, exposing it to material risk of loss and unauthorised access.
violations: Health data concerning 1,934 patients was processed on unencrypted portable storage, exposing it to material risk of loss and unauthorised access.
The region's failure to encrypt the data breached the security principle and created a high-risk scenario inconsistent with the sensitive nature of health information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24.1 makes the data controller responsible for implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and be able to demonstrate that processing is compliant with the Regulation.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Skåne as the data controller failed to ensure compliance with security requirements by permitting storage of sensitive health data on unencrypted portable media.
violations: Region Skåne as the data controller failed to ensure compliance with security requirements by permitting storage of sensitive health data on unencrypted portable media.
The controller could not demonstrate implementation of adequate safeguards proportionate to the risks, particularly for health data processed for research purposes.

outcome: The Swedish Data Protection Authority (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten – IMY) issued a binding administrative fine of 200,000 SEK (approximately €19,000 USD). The decision is enforceable immediately and can be appealed to the Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks. Region Skåne subsequently compensated affected data subjects under GDPR Article 82, implemented encryption tools (7-zip), created a secure external storage facility for sensitive personal data, strengthened internal controls over removable media use, and intensified data protection support to research units. The case demonstrates that employee negligence does not excuse the data controller's fundamental responsibility to implement adequate security measures.
companyNow: Region Skåne is a regional healthcare authority in southern Sweden providing public health services. It continues to operate but has implemented remedial security measures including encryption infrastructure and enhanced data protection oversight.
dataType: Health data, personal identification numbers (personnummer)

companyDescription: Tipros is a sole proprietorship engaged in wholesale and repair of electrical appliances, operating under the business name '24hr fridge refrigerator #1 Quick repair service Trusted in Singapore' on Google reviews (later renamed 'Tipros.sg').
companyLongDescription: Tipros is a sole proprietorship engaged in wholesale and repair of electrical appliances, operating under the business name '24hr fridge refrigerator #1 Quick repair service Trusted in Singapore' on Google reviews (later renamed 'Tipros.sg').
caseDescription: Tipros disclosed a customer's residential address and mobile number in a public Google reviews response to a 1-star service complaint. The Commission found this disclosure unreasonable and disproportionate, as neither contact detail was necessary to respond to the customer's grievances about service quality. The organisation failed to cooperate with the investigation and disclosed similar personal data for 13 other customers.
violationSummary: The organisation unreasonably disclosed personal data (residential address and mobile number) in a public forum without proportionate justification, violating the customer's reasonable expectation of privacy when providing a review.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Tipros posted a customer's residential address and mobile number in a public Google reviews response to a 1-star service complaint.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' home addresses and phone numbers were publicly exposed without consent, enabling unwanted contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tipros advertised itself as providing '24hr' (round-the-clock) repair service
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation's technician was not available over the weekend when the complainant needed service, contradicting the advertised availability

claimsVsReality.claim: Tipros sought to provide explanations for service complaints by disclosing customer contact details
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosure of residential address and mobile number was unnecessary to address the customer's grievances about service quality, fees, and technician availability

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.18(a) requires organisations to collect, use or disclose personal data only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances.
regulatoryFindings.description: Tipros disclosed complainant's residential address and mobile number in a public Google review response. The disclosure was unreasonable and disproportionate because the location and phone number were unnecessary to respond to service complaints about repairs, fees, and technician availability.
violations: Tipros disclosed complainant's residential address and mobile number in a public Google review response. The disclosure was unreasonable and disproportionate because the location and phone number were unnecessary to respond to service complaints about repairs, fees, and technician availability.
Tipros disclosed personal data of 13 other customers in similar fashion without proportionate justification.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.18(b) read with s.20(1)(b) requires individuals to be informed of the purpose prior to collection, use or disclosure of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customers did not authorise or consent to disclosure of their contact details in public responses. While the Commission recognised that individuals initiating public complaints may be deemed informed of reasonable response purposes, the disclosure here exceeded what was proportionate or necessary.
violations: Customers did not authorise or consent to disclosure of their contact details in public responses. While the Commission recognised that individuals initiating public complaints may be deemed informed of reasonable response purposes, the disclosure here exceeded what was proportionate or necessary.

outcome: The Commission found Tipros in breach of s.18(a) PDPA. Aggravating factors included the organisation's failure to respond to the Notice to Produce Documents and its refusal to attend interviews. No mitigating factors existed as the organisation took no action to remove or amend the disclosures. The Commission directed Tipros to: (1) Remove disclosure of the complainant's residential address and mobile number from its Google reviews response; and (2) Review the 13 other customer responses and remove any personal data disclosures that are not reasonable or proportionate. The organisation was given 30 days to comply.
companyNow: Tipros appears to be a small sole proprietorship in electrical appliance repair. The organisation's registered business address was vacant at the time of investigation, and the sole proprietor was contacted at a residential address, suggesting ongoing operations may be limited.
dataType: Residential address, mobile phone number
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.18(a) – Purpose Limitation Obligation (unreasonable disclosure)
PDPA s.18(b) – Lack of prior notice

companyDescription: Sembcorp Marine Ltd is a Singapore-based company specialising in marine and offshore engineering, including shipbuilding, ship repair, and conversion services. The company employs thousands and is a significant player in the global marine industry.
companyLongDescription: Sembcorp Marine Ltd is a Singapore-based company specialising in marine and offshore engineering, including shipbuilding, ship repair, and conversion services. The company employs thousands and is a significant player in the global marine industry.
caseDescription: Sembcorp Marine suffered a data breach via Log4J zero-day vulnerability exploitation on 4 January 2022, resulting in exfiltration of personal data of 25,925 individuals between 10-23 June 2022. The organisation was found to have made reasonable security arrangements and complied with its protection obligations under PDPA Section 24, resulting in no enforcement action.
violationSummary: The breach resulted from inadequate security measures (unpatched vulnerabilities) that failed to prevent unauthorized access and exfiltration of personal data. However, the Commission found the organisation had taken reasonable precautions given the early timing of the breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Sembcorp Marine failed to promptly patch Log4J vulnerabilities in its application, allowing threat actors to exploit the zero-day vulnerability.
whyTheyWereWrong: 25,925 individuals had their highly sensitive personal data exfiltrated, including bank account details, medical screening results, NRIC numbers, passports.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had made reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in relation to the Incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the organisation had good cybersecurity practices in place, its systems contained unpatched Log4J vulnerabilities that allowed threat actors to gain unauthorised access as early as 4 January 2022 and exfiltrate data of 25,925 individuals. However, the Commission accepted that the organisation had acted promptly upon discovering the vulnerability and that being an early target made prevention difficult.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks, and loss of storage media.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sembcorp Marine's systems contained unpatched Log4J vulnerabilities that were exploited by threat actors, allowing unauthorised access to servers and exfiltration of personal data of 25,925 individuals. However, the Commission found the organisation had adopted good cybersecurity practices including vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and security monitoring, and had acted promptly upon discovering the vulnerability, applying patches immediately when available.
violations: Sembcorp Marine's systems contained unpatched Log4J vulnerabilities that were exploited by threat actors, allowing unauthorised access to servers and exfiltration of personal data of 25,925 individuals. However, the Commission found the organisation had adopted good cybersecurity practices including vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and security monitoring, and had acted promptly upon discovering the vulnerability, applying patches immediately when available.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that Sembcorp Marine had met its Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the PDPA. The Commission was satisfied that the organisation had made reasonable security arrangements, including cybersecurity testing programmes, regular vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and security monitoring. Given that the Log4J vulnerability was disclosed in December 2021 and the breach occurred as early as 4 January 2022 (making Sembcorp one of the early targets), and considering the organisation's prompt remedial actions, no enforcement action was taken.
companyNow: Sembcorp Marine Ltd remains a major Singapore-based marine and offshore engineering company. As of 2023, the company continues operations in shipbuilding, ship repair, and offshore engineering.
dataType: Name, address, email, NRIC number, telephone, passport number, photograph, date of birth, bank account details, salary, medical screening results

companyDescription: CHINA CENTER LLEIDA is a commercial establishment (likely retail or cultural center) located in Lleida, Spain, operating a premises with video surveillance systems for security purposes.
companyLongDescription: CHINA CENTER LLEIDA is a commercial establishment (likely retail or cultural center) located in Lleida, Spain, operating a premises with video surveillance systems for security purposes.
caseDescription: CHINA CENTER LLEIDA operated a video surveillance system in its establishment without displaying mandatory privacy notices informing customers of the surveillance and their rights under GDPR. The company failed to provide required first-layer information signage in a sufficiently visible location and did not maintain accessible data protection information documents for individuals. This violated GDPR Article 13 requirements for transparent data processing.
violationSummary: Customers' images were collected without proper transparency safeguards. Lack of mandatory privacy signage and informational materials meant individuals could not identify the controller, understand the processing, or exercise rights like access or deletion—exposing them to unregulated use of their biometric data.
violations: Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: China Center Lleida installed video surveillance cameras in its establishment without displaying mandatory signage informing visitors of surveillance or providing data protection information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers and visitors entered the premises unaware they were being videotaped, with no way to know their facial images were being captured or understand their rights to access or delete their.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that where personal data are obtained from data subjects, the controller must provide specified information at the time the personal data are obtained.
regulatoryFindings.description: CHINA CENTER LLEIDA failed to provide mandatory first-layer privacy information (existence of processing, controller identity, GDPR rights) via visible signage in surveillance zones.
violations: CHINA CENTER LLEIDA failed to provide mandatory first-layer privacy information (existence of processing, controller identity, GDPR rights) via visible signage in surveillance zones.
No second-layer informational documents were made available to customers, preventing access to full transparency obligations under Article 13.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12 requires information to be provided to data subjects in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.
regulatoryFindings.description: The establishment provided no informational devices in sufficiently visible locations to communicate surveillance activities and data subject rights to individuals.
violations: The establishment provided no informational devices in sufficiently visible locations to communicate surveillance activities and data subject rights to individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 22 establishes that video surveillance for security purposes must include a layered information system: first layer minimum (treatment existence, controller identity, rights), and second layer (full Article 13 elements) available in easily accessible locations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Neither layer of required information was provided. No warning signs identified the surveillance or controller; no accessible information documents were made available.
violations: Neither layer of required information was provided. No warning signs identified the surveillance or controller; no accessible information documents were made available.

outcome: Procedure terminated by voluntary payment. On 25 July 2023, CHINA CENTER LLEIDA paid €420 (original proposed fine €700, reduced by two 20% reductions: one for voluntary payment, one for admission of responsibility). Payment occurred within the allegation period and constituted acceptance of responsibility and waiver of administrative remedies. The company was ordered to notify the AEPD within one month of implementing the required compliance measures: placement of mandatory informational signage in all surveillance zones identifying the treatment, controller, and GDPR rights; and provision of accessible second-layer information documents (Articles 13–14 RGPD) in a visible public location. Procedure closed with no further enforcement action.
dataType: Biometric data (video footage/images)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 13 (information to be provided where personal data are collected)
LOPDGDD Article 22 (video surveillance requirements and layered information obligations)
GDPR Article 58.2(d) (corrective powers of supervisory authorities)

companyDescription: H&M Hennes & Mauritz is a multinational fashion retail company founded in 1947, headquartered in Stockholm, Sweden. It operates thousands of stores worldwide and manages millions of customer email subscriptions for direct marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: H&M Hennes & Mauritz is a multinational fashion retail company founded in 1947, headquartered in Stockholm, Sweden. It operates thousands of stores worldwide and manages millions of customer email subscriptions for direct marketing purposes.
caseDescription: H&M failed to process customer opt-out requests from direct marketing over extended periods (up to 18 months), sending unwanted newsletters after customers explicitly objected. The company lacked adequate internal systems and processes to handle unsubscribe requests reliably across multiple newsletter categories.
violationSummary: H&M continued using personal data for direct marketing purposes after the data subject exercised the unconditional right to object (Article 21.2 GDPR), which is a form of prohibited secondary use without proper legal basis.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: H&M continued sending unwanted marketing emails to six customers for 4 to 18 months after each customer explicitly requested to stop receiving them.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers were forced to receive repeated marketing messages against their explicit wishes, exposing them to unwanted commercial surveillance and manipulation despite their clear objections.

claimsVsReality.claim: H&M stated it offers three ways for customers to unsubscribe: account settings, unsubscribe links in emails, and customer service contact.
claimsVsReality.reality: These mechanisms operated unreliably; customers used the same methods multiple times (up to 10+ times in some cases) without success. The unsubscribe link often failed silently or unsubscribed customers from only one newsletter category while leaving them subscribed to others.

claimsVsReality.claim: H&M claimed that 'only in a very small part' of unregistration requests did problems occur and that the company handles a very large number of subscribers annually.
claimsVsReality.reality: At least 6 customers from 3 different countries reported systematic failures over an 18-month period, indicating systemic process defects, not isolated incidents.

claimsVsReality.claim: H&M stated it had adequate internal procedures and systems for handling objections to direct marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system and processes had critical gaps: partial unsubscription was possible, technical bugs prevented synchronization across multiple systems, and customer service staff did not follow proper procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21.3 requires that if a data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 1 for nearly 4 months after objection (5 April – 2 August 2019)
violations: H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 1 for nearly 4 months after objection (5 April – 2 August 2019)
H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 2 for nearly 3 months after objection (4 July – 3 October 2019)
H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 3 for 5 months after objection (3 September 2019 – 5 February 2020)
H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 4 for 18 months after objection (31 July 2018 – 16 February 2020)
H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 5 for 9 months after objection (July 2018 – 20 May 2019)
H&M continued sending marketing emails to Complaint 6 for 1 month after objection (8 August – 15 September 2019)

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1 requires that processing of personal data must be based on at least one lawful basis.
regulatoryFindings.description: After customers objected to direct marketing under Article 21.2, H&M had no lawful basis to continue processing their personal data for marketing purposes yet continued sending newsletters
violations: After customers objected to direct marketing under Article 21.2, H&M had no lawful basis to continue processing their personal data for marketing purposes yet continued sending newsletters

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12.2 requires that the controller shall facilitate the exercise of data subject rights in a simple and transparent manner.
regulatoryFindings.description: H&M's systems allowed partial unsubscription (from general newsletter but not club newsletter), preventing customers from fully exercising their right to object
violations: H&M's systems allowed partial unsubscription (from general newsletter but not club newsletter), preventing customers from fully exercising their right to object
Multiple unsubscribe mechanisms (link, web form, customer service) operated inconsistently, causing customer requests to fail silently
Customer service personnel did not properly handle objection requests despite receiving them repeatedly

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12.3 requires the controller to provide information on the measures taken in response to an objection request without undue delay, and in any case within one month.
regulatoryFindings.description: H&M did not act on objections without undue delay; instead took months to fully process them
violations: H&M did not act on objections without undue delay; instead took months to fully process them
H&M did not reliably inform customers that their objections had been processed

outcome: The Swedish Data Protection Authority (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten – IMY) determined H&M violated Articles 6.1, 12.2, 12.3, and 21.3 of the GDPR. IMY ordered H&M to pay an administrative fine of 350,000 SEK (approximately €33,600 USD). The authority noted that H&M had established a dedicated task force in October 2019 to address the deficiencies, implemented bug fixes, system improvements, and staff retraining, and in May 2020 deployed a manual verification process to ensure all systems were updated when a customer unsubscribed. These remedial measures were recognized as mitigating factors in determining the relatively modest fine. The decision can be appealed to the Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: H&M remains one of the world's largest fashion retailers. Following this enforcement action, the company has continued investing in data protection compliance and customer preference management systems.
dataType: Email addresses, customer subscription preferences, marketing profile data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6.1 (lack of legal basis for processing)
GDPR Art. 12.2 (failure to facilitate exercise of rights)
GDPR Art. 12.3 (failure to act without undue delay on objection)
GDPR Art. 21.3 (failure to cease processing after objection to direct marketing)

companyDescription: Whiz Communications Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore telecommunications service provider offering broadband internet access, local and long-distance digital IP telephony, and prepaid/postpaid calling plans.
companyLongDescription: Whiz Communications Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore telecommunications service provider offering broadband internet access, local and long-distance digital IP telephony, and prepaid/postpaid calling plans.
caseDescription: Whiz Communications' customer management system had a design flaw allowing Python scripts to extract personal data. Attackers exploited this vulnerability over 5 days in March–April 2023, successfully exfiltrating identification documents and supporting papers for 24,323 individuals. The organisation failed to implement basic security requirements when commissioning the system, weak password policies, and inadequate access controls.
violationSummary: The core violation involves failure to implement reasonable security arrangements as required by PDPA s.24. The system's insecure design (accepting any Python script), weak authentication, and poor access controls exposed sensitive personal data to unauthorised access and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Whiz Communications deployed a customer management system without security requirements to prevent Python script exploitation, allowing attackers to extract personal data for 7 days.
whyTheyWereWrong: 24,323 customers had their identity documents and work permit letters stolen because the company failed to specify security requirements to vendors.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CMS was professionally designed and developed by an external vendor in 2016
claimsVsReality.reality: The system had a fundamental design flaw from inception: it accepted any Python script request without validation, creating an inherent security vulnerability

claimsVsReality.claim: Standard password requirements were in place for admin access
claimsVsReality.reality: The CMS required only 9 alphanumeric characters with one uppercase letter, falling far below PDPC's recommended 12+ characters with mixed character types

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide security requirements to the CMS vendor, particularly regarding Python script requests and web application security
violations: Failed to provide security requirements to the CMS vendor, particularly regarding Python script requests and web application security
Failed to enforce a sufficiently complex password policy (only 9 alphanumeric characters with one uppercase; PDPC recommends minimum 12 with mixed character types)
Failed to implement reasonable access control beyond password protection (no multi-factor authentication, no IP restrictions, no web application firewall)

outcome: The organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD 9,000 (approximately USD 6,550) within 30 days. Post-incident remedial actions included rejecting all Python requests, restricting overseas IP access, implementing two-factor authentication with enhanced password complexity, and conducting penetration testing. The organisation cooperated fully during investigation and voluntarily admitted the breach under the Expedited Decision Procedure.
companyNow: Whiz Communications continues operations as a Singapore-based telecommunications service provider. Following the incident, the organisation implemented enhanced security measures including multi-factor authentication, stronger password policies, and access restrictions.
dataType: Identity documents (NRIC, passport, student pass, dependent pass), tenancy agreements, work permit approval letters

companyDescription: DPG Professional Services Ltd is a company registered in Manchester, England (Companies House Registration Number 13435544) that engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls.
companyLongDescription: DPG Professional Services Ltd is a company registered in Manchester, England (Companies House Registration Number 13435544) that engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls.
caseDescription: DPG Professional Services Ltd made 74,119 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between August 2021 and August 2022, violating PECR Regulation 21. The company called subscribers who had registered with the TPS to opt out and had not provided valid consent to receive such calls. The Information Commissioner found this to be a serious contravention and issued an enforcement notice requiring compliance within 30 days.
violationSummary: DPG conducted systematic unsolicited calls targeting individuals who had explicitly opted out via TPS registration, surveilling and contacting them without consent for direct marketing purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: DPG Professional Services Ltd made 74,119 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between August 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: These calls harassed 74,119 people who had explicitly registered to block unsolicited marketing calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: DPG could make unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 21 prohibits such calls unless the subscriber has provided valid prior notification of willingness to receive them; DPG provided no evidence of such notifications

claimsVsReality.claim: General opt-in to marketing communications constitutes valid notification for telephone calls under Regulation 21(4)
claimsVsReality.reality: Valid notification must be clear, positive, specific to telephone calls, and specific to that company; general marketing consent is insufficient

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes where the number allocated to the subscriber is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: DPG made 74,119 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
violations: DPG made 74,119 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
Called subscribers who had been registered with TPS at least 28 days prior to the calls
Did not obtain valid notifications from subscribers under Regulation 21(4) consenting to receive calls

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) provides that valid notification must be a clear, positive action by the individual to override TPS registration, must be specific to telephone calls, and must be specific to that company.
regulatoryFindings.description: DPG provided no evidence of receiving valid notifications from any of the 74,119 called subscribers
violations: DPG provided no evidence of receiving valid notifications from any of the 74,119 called subscribers
DPG did not demonstrate clear, positive consent from individuals to receive marketing calls specifically from DPG

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring DPG to cease making unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers within 30 days. DPG must neither use nor instigate use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls to: (a) subscribers who have previously notified DPG not to call, or (b) subscribers registered with TPS for at least 28 days who have not notified DPG of willingness to receive calls. Right of appeal exists to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information

company: Διαδημοτική Επιχείρηση Ύδρευσης – Αποχέτευσης Χ (ΔΕΥΑ Χ)
companyDescription: ΔΕΥΑ Χ is a municipal/intermunicipal public utility enterprise responsible for water supply and sewerage services. The organization operates as a legal entity under private law with public welfare objectives, governed by the principles of commercial economy.
companyLongDescription: ΔΕΥΑ Χ is a municipal/intermunicipal public utility enterprise responsible for water supply and sewerage services. The organization operates as a legal entity under private law with public welfare objectives, governed by the principles of commercial economy.
caseDescription: A municipal water utility in Greece unlawfully shared an employee's sensitive health data (COVID-19 test results and medical certificates) with multiple internal recipients and an external regional civil protection authority without proper legal basis or data minimization. The company sent detailed medical information in emails to board members and government officials to address questions about whether the employee could attend a meeting, despite the information being unnecessary for that purpose.
violationSummary: The company disclosed special category data (health information) to third parties both internally and externally without a lawful basis, adequate necessity assessment, or the data subject's knowledge or consent, constituting unauthorized disclosure.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ΔΕΥΑ Χ shared an employee's COVID-19 test results, medical certificates, and detailed health records with board members.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's sensitive health information was exposed to multiple internal and external recipients who had no legitimate business need for it, violating her privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The General Director claimed the disclosure was necessary to inform board members about an employee's health status so they could adjust work priorities and ensure smooth operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Board members were already aware the employee was ill from her in-person attendance at the meeting. Sharing detailed medical records weeks after the meeting served no operational purpose and could not have influenced any contemporaneous decision-making.

claimsVsReality.claim: The utility argued it needed to share health data with the regional civil protection authority to determine what COVID-19 containment measures to implement.
claimsVsReality.reality: The regional authority confirmed it had no authority to advise individual employers on containment measures and that designated national health agencies handled such policy. The medical records were unnecessary for the authority to answer generic protocol questions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed that disclosing health data was required to protect the health of board members (some immunocompromised) and ensure effective administration.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee had already attended and left the meeting. Retroactive disclosure of her detailed medical history could not protect anyone and was not required for administrative function. Simpler notification of her illness status would have sufficed if health protection were the genuine concern.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: ΔΕΥΑ Χ shared comprehensive medical documentation (test results, certificates, medical opinions) with multiple internal recipients and an external authority when only confirmation of test status was needed
violations: ΔΕΥΑ Χ shared comprehensive medical documentation (test results, certificates, medical opinions) with multiple internal recipients and an external authority when only confirmation of test status was needed
The company disclosed sensitive health data to board members and administrative staff who had no functional need to receive full medical details
Medical records were appended to correspondence sent to the regional civil protection authority when the authority required only policy guidance, not individual patient health histories

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(2) (Accountability) requires the controller to demonstrate compliance with principles through appropriate measures, policies, and documentation.
regulatoryFindings.description: ΔΕΥΑ Χ had no internal written policies governing recipient categories for employee health data or tiered access controls
violations: ΔΕΥΑ Χ had no internal written policies governing recipient categories for employee health data or tiered access controls
The company failed to establish data recipient guidelines despite handling sensitive employee health information
No Data Protection Impact Assessment or minimization procedures were documented for this class of processing

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 9 restricts processing of special categories (health data) and requires explicit lawful basis.
regulatoryFindings.description: Health data was processed and shared without explicit consent or clear necessity
violations: Health data was processed and shared without explicit consent or clear necessity
The sharing served administrative convenience rather than legitimate occupational health or legal compliance purposes

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority found the water utility guilty of violating GDPR Article 5(1)(c) on data minimization in three separate processing operations. The Authority imposed a €1,000 administrative fine. The company was ordered to establish internal data protection policies within three months governing: (1) designated recipient categories for employee personal data; (2) tiered access controls for health-related information within the organization; and (3) documentation of necessity assessments before sharing employee health data. The company must ensure that sensitive information is restricted to the minimum recipients necessary for legitimate purposes.
companyNow: ΔΕΥΑ Χ (Intermunicipal Water and Sewerage Enterprise) continues to operate as a public utility providing essential water and sewerage services in Greece. The company is subject to ongoing compliance monitoring under the Data Protection Authority's corrective measures.
dataType: Health data (COVID-19 test results, medical certificates), personal identifiers (social security number, tax number, contact information)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
GDPR Art. 9 – Processing of special categories of data (health data)

companyDescription: Expressen Lifestyle AB is a Swedish media and publishing company operating digital magazine subscriptions and related lifestyle content. The company was formed through the 2022 merger of Bonnier Magazine and Brands AB into Expressen Lifestyle AB.
companyLongDescription: Expressen Lifestyle AB is a Swedish media and publishing company operating digital magazine subscriptions and related lifestyle content. The company was formed through the 2022 merger of Bonnier Magazine and Brands AB into Expressen Lifestyle AB.
caseDescription: Expressen Lifestyle AB (formerly Bonnier Magazine and Brands AB) failed to accurately disclose the legal basis for processing customer personal data on its website registration form. Between May 2018 and June 2019, the company displayed a checkbox stating consent was required when it actually relied on contract and legitimate interest as its primary legal bases. This misrepresentation violated GDPR Article 13.1(c) requirements for transparent legal basis disclosure.
violationSummary: The company deliberately or negligently presented false information about its legal basis for processing, distorting the facts about why and how customer data would be used, deceiving individuals about the true nature of their data processing.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Expressen Lifestyle AB displayed a misleading checkbox stating 'I consent to personal data processing within Bonnier group' on its Magasinshoppen webshop registration form from May 2018 to June.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 1,372 customers were deceived about why their personal data was being collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: We base customer data processing on consent
claimsVsReality.reality: The company actually based processing on contract (subscription terms) and legitimate interest (marketing, analytics), not consent

claimsVsReality.claim: The registration form accurately disclosed our legal basis for data processing
claimsVsReality.reality: The registration form on Magasinshoppen falsely indicated consent as the basis while omitting the actual bases (contract and legitimate interest)

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13.1(c) requires that when a data controller collects personal data directly from a data subject, the controller must provide information about the legal basis for the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Expressen Lifestyle AB displayed checkbox text indicating consent as the legal basis, when the company actually relied on contract (Art. 6.1(b)) or legitimate interest (Art. 6.1(f))
violations: Expressen Lifestyle AB displayed checkbox text indicating consent as the legal basis, when the company actually relied on contract (Art. 6.1(b)) or legitimate interest (Art. 6.1(f))

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12.1 requires data controllers to provide required information in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.
regulatoryFindings.description: The registration form's text 'I consent to personal data processing within Bonnier group' was ambiguous and suggested consent as the basis, contradicting the company's actual reliance on contract and legitimate interest
violations: The registration form's text 'I consent to personal data processing within Bonnier group' was ambiguous and suggested consent as the basis, contradicting the company's actual reliance on contract and legitimate interest

outcome: The Swedish Data Protection Authority (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten) issued a reprimand to Expressen Lifestyle AB under GDPR Article 58.2(b) for the violation of Article 13.1(c). The authority found this a minor violation given that: (1) the company immediately corrected the webshop registration form upon inspection initiation; (2) the webshop affected only 1,372 customers of a much larger customer base; (3) the error resulted from failure to update the webshop during the 2018 GDPR compliance review, not intentional deception; and (4) no serious consequences resulted for affected individuals. No monetary fine was imposed. The company must ensure all registration forms accurately communicate that processing is based on contract terms and legitimate interest, with appropriate privacy policy disclosures.
companyNow: Expressen Lifestyle AB (formerly Bonnier Magazine and Brands AB) continues to operate as a media and publishing company in Sweden. The company has updated its data processing disclosures and registration forms to comply with GDPR requirements.
dataType: Email address, phone number, digital contact information

companyDescription: Bank Of Ireland (UK) PLC is a UK-incorporated banking subsidiary of BOI Group plc, established in 2009. It provides financial services and is required to report customer account information to credit reference agencies.
companyLongDescription: Bank Of Ireland (UK) PLC is a UK-incorporated banking subsidiary of BOI Group plc, established in 2009. It provides financial services and is required to report customer account information to credit reference agencies.
caseDescription: Bank Of Ireland failed to ensure accurate personal data was sent to credit reference agencies, affecting 3,284 customers' credit profiles between 2018 and 2020. A manual process error caused defaulted loan accounts sold to debt collectors to be incorrectly reported as still owned by BOI with outstanding balances, resulting in double defaults on customers' credit records. BOI lacked adequate oversight and assurance controls to detect and prevent the error.
violationSummary: The failure to maintain accurate data through inadequate process controls and lack of assurance reviews constitutes a data processing security/quality deficiency under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Bank Of Ireland (UK) PLC failed to accurately flag 3,284 loan accounts sold to debt collectors in its credit reporting system.
whyTheyWereWrong: 3,284 customers suffered damaged credit profiles with false or duplicate default entries, unfairly preventing them from obtaining credit, refinancing existing loans.

claimsVsReality.claim: BOI had risk management measures in place for debt sales
claimsVsReality.reality: Risk management was inadequate and did not identify the sold debt flag as a granular risk despite it being a critical manual process step

claimsVsReality.claim: Accounts affected in 2019 were rectified by a local fix
claimsVsReality.reality: BOI provided no documentary evidence of the fix, failed to escalate the incident internally, did not perform historic checks, and did not implement preventive measures—115 errors continued for up to 33 months

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires that personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that inaccurate personal data are erased or rectified without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: BOI failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accurate personal data was recorded with CRAs, affecting 3,284 data subjects over 2–33 months
violations: BOI failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accurate personal data was recorded with CRAs, affecting 3,284 data subjects over 2–33 months
BOI did not detect or correct inaccuracies in the debt sale flag during 2019 despite correcting some accounts, allowing errors to persist

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(2) requires the controller to be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, the data processing principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: BOI lacked adequate risk management granularity—the sold debt flag was not identified as a granular risk despite being a critical manual step
violations: BOI lacked adequate risk management granularity—the sold debt flag was not identified as a granular risk despite being a critical manual step
BOI conducted no specific assurance reviews or audits of the debt sale flag and provided no documentary evidence of escalation or remediation in 2019
BOI could not demonstrate why historic checks were not performed or why new preventive processes were not implemented after discovering the error

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand under UK GDPR Article 58(2)(b). BOI was required to continue supporting affected data subjects, has corrected all inaccurate accounts, suspended debt sales pending process review, and committed to a wider assurance review of CRA reporting processes during 2024. The ICO recognizes BOI has already completed two of three recommended compliance steps and is sharing lessons across the organization.
companyNow: Bank Of Ireland (UK) PLC remains a UK-based subsidiary of the Dublin-headquartered BOI Group plc, operating as a financial services provider. The company is implementing enhanced governance and assurance controls over credit reporting processes following this enforcement action.
dataType: Financial data, credit account information, default status, outstanding balances

companyDescription: SGS Home Protect Limited is an insurance and home protection services company registered in Poole, England. The company rebranded from Finesta Limited in October 2021 and was engaged in direct marketing of blocked drain insurance and other home protection products.
companyLongDescription: SGS Home Protect Limited is an insurance and home protection services company registered in Poole, England. The company rebranded from Finesta Limited in October 2021 and was engaged in direct marketing of blocked drain insurance and other home protection products.
caseDescription: SGS Home Protect Limited made 24,241 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), violating PECR Regulation 21. The company deliberately failed to screen calls against the TPS register and did not respond to the ICO's investigation. The violation resulted in a £70,000 monetary penalty.
violationSummary: The company systematically made unsolicited calls to individuals who had explicitly registered their preference not to receive direct marketing calls, constituting a surveillance-like intrusion into consumer privacy through persistent unwanted contact.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: SGS Home Protect Limited made 24,241 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and June 2021 to phone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: Vulnerable consumers, including an elderly 90-year-old man who had been scammed 35 times previously.

claimsVsReality.claim: SGS's marketing calls were legitimate unsolicited direct marketing communications
claimsVsReality.reality: 81% of calls were made to consumers who had explicitly registered with TPS to block such calls, indicating systematic non-compliance with legal requirements

claimsVsReality.claim: SGS had systems and procedures in place for PECR compliance
claimsVsReality.reality: SGS made 24,241 calls to TPS-registered numbers with no evidence of TPS screening procedures or compliance controls

claimsVsReality.claim: The calls targeted willing consumers
claimsVsReality.reality: One documented call targeted an elderly, vulnerable 90-year-old with serious memory loss who had been scammed 35 times previously; he was nearly defrauded again by the call

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use or instigation of unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes where the called line number is listed on the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: SGS made 24,241 calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with TPS for 28+ days without obtaining their prior written consent that they do not object to receiving such calls
violations: SGS made 24,241 calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with TPS for 28+ days without obtaining their prior written consent that they do not object to receiving such calls
SGS failed to screen telephone numbers against the TPS register before making calls
SGS did not respond to ICO investigation requests, providing no evidence of subscriber consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A(1) permits monetary penalties where there is a serious contravention of PECR requirements and either the contravention was deliberate or the person knew or ought to have known of the risk but failed to take reasonable steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: SGS deliberately contravened PECR by making systematic calls to TPS-registered numbers without screening
violations: SGS deliberately contravened PECR by making systematic calls to TPS-registered numbers without screening
As a direct marketing business, SGS ought to have known of TPS requirements and published ICO guidance
SGS failed to take reasonable steps (TPS screening) to prevent the contravention despite knowledge of legal obligations

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £70,000 (reduced to £56,000 if paid by 31 August 2023). SGS was ordered to cease unlawful calling practices and implement TPS screening procedures. SGS has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal within 28 days. The penalty is recoverable by court order if not paid by 1 September 2023.
companyNow: SGS Home Protect Limited (formerly Finesta Limited) remains registered as a company but the enforcement action indicates serious compliance failures. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Telephone numbers, contact information

companyDescription: Daniel George Bentley operated as a sole trader direct marketer under the name Daniel George, registered with the ICO from December 2021 to November 2022. He engaged in SMS marketing campaigns targeting subscribers for the purposes of promoting financial products and services.
companyLongDescription: Daniel George Bentley operated as a sole trader direct marketer under the name Daniel George, registered with the ICO from December 2021 to November 2022. He engaged in SMS marketing campaigns targeting subscribers for the purposes of promoting financial products and services.
caseDescription: Daniel George Bentley sent over 2.26 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers without valid consent between May and October 2022. He admitted obtaining data indiscriminately through third parties and attempted to conceal his identity using hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards. The enforcement notice requires him to cease such activity and obtain clear, specific consent before any future marketing communications.
violationSummary: Bentley engaged in mass surveillance-scale collection and transmission of direct marketing communications to individual subscribers without consent, exploiting electronic communications channels to target large populations indiscriminately.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between May and October 2022, sent 2,261,352 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers using data obtained indiscriminately from third parties.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 2 million individuals received unwanted marketing messages without their knowledge or consent, including financially vulnerable people targeted with loans.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bentley implied he was operating a legitimate direct marketing business with proper data acquisition.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bentley admitted he could not obtain sufficient legally-compliant data and resorted to sending SMS messages 'indiscriminately' using data obtained indirectly through third parties without valid consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The messages came from an identifiable sender with proper contact information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bentley used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards and non-identifying websites to conceal his identity and prevent recipients from identifying the actual sender or requesting cessation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited communications for direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of their consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bentley transmitted 2,261,352 SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: Bentley transmitted 2,261,352 SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
He admitted obtaining data indiscriminately through third parties, which does not constitute the clear and specific consent required for electronic marketing.
Indirect consent obtained through third-party data sources is insufficient under PECR for SMS/electronic marketing.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23 prohibits direct marketing communications where the sender's identity is disguised or concealed, or where a valid address to refuse further communications is not provided.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bentley used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal his identity as the sender.
violations: Bentley used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal his identity as the sender.
He used websites that did not correctly identify the sender or instigator of the messages.
Recipients had no valid means of identifying who was sending the messages or where to request cessation.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) defines valid consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes signifying agreement to processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent obtained indirectly through third parties was not freely given by the actual recipients.
violations: Consent obtained indirectly through third parties was not freely given by the actual recipients.
Consent was not specific—recipients had not agreed to receive marketing from Bentley specifically.
Consent was not informed—recipients did not understand they were consenting to SMS marketing from an unidentified sender.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice under Data Protection Act 1998 s.40, requiring Daniel George Bentley to cease all unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail within 30 days unless he obtains clear and specific prior consent from recipients. The notice further requires him to cease all direct marketing communications where his identity is disguised, no valid opt-out address is provided, or communications would violate the Electronic Commerce Regulations 2002. The recipient has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days of the notice date (5 December 2023).
dataType: Phone numbers (SMS contact details)

companyDescription: Tai Shin Fatt is an insurance director managing a team of 25 insurance agents at a large, well-known insurance company in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Tai Shin Fatt is an insurance director managing a team of 25 insurance agents at a large, well-known insurance company in Singapore.
caseDescription: An insurance director used dictionary attack methods to generate 18,809 random telephone numbers for automated marketing calls without proper validation. The system made 433 calls to the SCDF emergency line (995), which was not registered in the Do Not Call Registry, disrupting critical emergency services.
violationSummary: The use of dictionary attack to generate and target telephone numbers without consent constitutes indiscriminate surveillance-type collection under the framework of generating applicable telephone numbers through automated means.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Generated 18,809 telephone numbers using automated means by combining common prefixes with randomly generated last 4 digits, then authorized 22,268 automated marketing calls to these numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: The method exposed critical infrastructure to disruption — 433 calls reached the SCDF emergency line, preventing genuine emergency responses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Engaged Call Automation Vendor and Checker services to conduct marketing calls more efficiently with DNCR compliance built-in
claimsVsReality.reality: System failed to filter calls to the SCDF emergency line (995), resulting in 433 unwanted calls to emergency services despite stated intent to comply with DNCR

claimsVsReality.claim: Used commonly seen telephone prefixes to generate realistic test numbers for system validation
claimsVsReality.reality: Method generated completely random and invalid telephone numbers through dictionary attack, indiscriminately targeting any possible combination without validation

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 48B(1) of the PDPA provides that a person must not send, cause to be sent or authorise the sending of an applicable message.
regulatoryFindings.description: Individual authorized sending of 22,268 automated marketing calls (messages in sound form) to telephone numbers
violations: Individual authorized sending of 22,268 automated marketing calls (messages in sound form) to telephone numbers
Telephone numbers were generated using dictionary attack method (combining common prefixes with randomly generated 4-digit permutations via Microsoft Excel)
Messages had Singapore link (originated in Singapore)
System was not designed to exclude emergency service numbers, resulting in 433 calls to SCDF emergency line

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 48A(1) of the PDPA defines 'applicable telephone number' as a number generated or obtained through dictionary attack or address-harvesting software.
regulatoryFindings.description: Dictionary attack was performed using automated means via Microsoft Excel to generate permutations of telephone numbers
violations: Dictionary attack was performed using automated means via Microsoft Excel to generate permutations of telephone numbers
18,809 unique telephone numbers were created through this method without validation against critical infrastructure numbers

outcome: The Commission determined the Individual contravened Section 48B of the PDPA. Administrative warning issued without monetary penalty. No further directions necessary due to remedial actions already taken by the Individual (immediate cessation of calls upon discovery, deletion of number lists, cooperation with investigation). Individual had made efforts to comply with DNCR obligations and demonstrated no prior PDPA violations.
companyNow: No public information available regarding current status of Tai Shin Fatt as of document date (February 2023).
dataType: Telephone numbers (personal contact information)

companyDescription: Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is the police service responsible for law enforcement across Greater Manchester, England. It operates multiple police stations including Pendleton Police Station and maintains custody suites, forensic services, and professional standards departments.
companyLongDescription: Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is the police service responsible for law enforcement across Greater Manchester, England. It operates multiple police stations including Pendleton Police Station and maintains custody suites, forensic services, and professional standards departments.
caseDescription: GMP failed to provide a detained individual's CCTV footage within the one-month subject access request deadline and lost two hours of footage due to inadequate quality checks and security measures when retaining data beyond the standard 90-day period.
