The force lacked documented procedures, clear responsibility assignments, and a required Data Protection Impact Assessment for CCTV processing.
violationSummary: GMP failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures to protect against accidental loss of CCTV data, resulting in the loss of two hours of footage. Additionally, the failure to provide complete data in response to a SAR within the statutory timeframe constitutes a separate breach of the right of access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Greater Manchester Police retained CCTV footage of a detainee held for 48 hours without implementing quality checks to verify data integrity.
whyTheyWereWrong: A detainee was unable to obtain their own personal data (CCTV recording from custody) within the legally required timeframe.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP staff at Professional Standards Department believed data retention procedures were being followed and quality checks were conducted before the data subject's SAR.
claimsVsReality.reality: No quality checks were actually performed. Two hours of CCTV footage was lost because neither PPS nor PSD checked data integrity, each assuming the other had done so. The loss went undetected until May 2022, over a year after retention was authorized in April 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP had a data protection regime in place providing staff training during induction.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite the training regime, GMP's Custody Inspector did not receive data protection training because GMP failed to deploy appropriate administrative monitoring to ensure all staff actually received it.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 s.45(3)(a) and (b) requires that where a data subject requests access to their personal data, it must be provided in writing without undue delay and in any event before the end of the applicable time period (one month).
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to provide the data subject with their complete CCTV footage within one month of the SAR request. After exemptions expired, GMP could not release all applicable data as two hours of footage had been lost due to inadequate retention procedures.
violations: GMP failed to provide the data subject with their complete CCTV footage within one month of the SAR request. After exemptions expired, GMP could not release all applicable data as two hours of footage had been lost due to inadequate retention procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Sixth Data Protection Principle requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, protecting against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to protect CCTV data from accidental loss. The CCTV system could only download footage in half-hour/one-hour segments without chronological ordering or backup error alerts. No quality checks were performed when data was retained beyond 90 days. The 2017 SOP was never updated or reviewed. No DPIA was conducted. Staff confusion about responsibility meant two hours of footage was lost undetected until May 2022.
violations: GMP failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to protect CCTV data from accidental loss. The CCTV system could only download footage in half-hour/one-hour segments without chronological ordering or backup error alerts. No quality checks were performed when data was retained beyond 90 days. The 2017 SOP was never updated or reviewed. No DPIA was conducted. Staff confusion about responsibility meant two hours of footage was lost undetected until May 2022.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to GMP under Schedule 13(2)(c) of DPA 2018. No monetary fine was imposed, taking into account mitigating factors (form 708G authorisation requirement in place, sealed evidence bag storage) and remedial steps undertaken by GMP. GMP has undertaken significant remediation including: system upgrade in 2023 with restricted access controls; centralized SAR administration within Information Access team; improved auditing with comprehensive officer access logs and timestamps; complete rewrite of SOP with annual review requirement; improved data protection training monitoring. The Commissioner issued non-binding recommendations for further compliance improvements including mandatory DPIA completion, enhanced staff training, and breach reporting procedures.
companyNow: Greater Manchester Police continues to operate as a major police force serving Greater Manchester, England. Following the reprimand, GMP has invested significantly in system upgrades and procedural improvements to ensure data protection compliance.
dataType: CCTV footage, biometric data (video recording of individual in custody)
legalBasisViolated: DPA 2018 s.45(3)(a) – provide information without undue delay
DPA 2018 s.45(3)(b) – provide information within one month
DPA 2018 Sixth Data Protection Principle – appropriate security of personal data

companyDescription: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A.U. is a major Spanish mobile telecommunications operator providing wireless services to millions of customers. As a large-scale processor of personal data, it manages customer identities, contact information, billing records, and service requests.
companyLongDescription: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A.U. is a major Spanish mobile telecommunications operator providing wireless services to millions of customers. As a large-scale processor of personal data, it manages customer identities, contact information, billing records, and service requests.
caseDescription: Telefónica issued a duplicate SIM card to an identity thief without verifying the requester's identity, enabling unauthorized access to the customer's phone, banking data, and personal accounts. The company failed to apply adequate identity verification procedures during SIM card replacement, breaching GDPR Article 6 (lawfulness of processing) by processing personal data without a valid legal basis.
violationSummary: Telefónica's failure to verify identity before issuing the SIM duplicate exposed the customer's personal data and enabled a third party to gain unauthorized access to sensitive information including banking credentials.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Issued a duplicate SIM card to an unauthorized third party without verifying the person's identity or obtaining the legitimate account holder's consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The fraudster used the duplicate SIM to intercept the victim's banking access, steal passwords and financial data, and execute unauthorized transfers that drained the victim's bank account.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica stated it has consolidated and adequate customer identity verification procedures that provide sufficient guarantees to identify SIM duplicate requesters.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to apply those procedures in this case, issuing a duplicate SIM to an identity thief without verifying the requester's identity, demonstrating that the procedures either did not exist or were not properly implemented.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica claimed the fraud was perpetrated by an external attacker ('hacker') and that the company lacked responsibility.
claimsVsReality.reality: Telefónica bears responsibility for failing to implement adequate identity verification controls; the third party's ability to obtain the SIM depended entirely on Telefónica's negligent issuance process.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) provides that processing is lawful only if at least one lawful basis applies: consent, contract execution, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica processed the customer's personal data (phone number, SIM identifiers) for SIM card issuance without consent and without verifying the requester's identity, lacking any valid lawful basis.
violations: Telefónica processed the customer's personal data (phone number, SIM identifiers) for SIM card issuance without consent and without verifying the requester's identity, lacking any valid lawful basis.
The company failed to verify the identity of the person requesting the duplicate SIM, enabling an unauthorized third party to process the customer's personal data without any legal justification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica failed to implement adequate security measures during SIM card issuance, specifically the identity verification procedures required to prevent unauthorized access.
violations: Telefónica failed to implement adequate security measures during SIM card issuance, specifically the identity verification procedures required to prevent unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires data controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company did not demonstrate that proper identity verification procedures were followed before issuing the duplicate SIM, indicating inadequate organizational measures.
violations: The company did not demonstrate that proper identity verification procedures were followed before issuing the duplicate SIM, indicating inadequate organizational measures.

outcome: Telefónica was fined €70,000 for violating GDPR Article 6(1) by processing personal data without lawful basis. The company failed to verify the identity of the person requesting a duplicate SIM card, enabling identity fraud. The agency found that Telefónica, as a professional data handler with extensive customer data processing obligations, was negligent in applying inadequate due diligence. The company previously blocked the fraudulent line and refunded the customer's SIM card fee. Telefónica indicated it would implement enhanced identity verification procedures, OTP authentication, and digital onboarding with biometric verification for sensitive operations. The resolution is final and enforceable.
companyNow: Telefónica Móviles España remains one of Spain's largest mobile operators. The company stated it is implementing enhanced security measures including OTP-based authentication and digital identity verification for sensitive operations.
dataType: Personal identifiers (phone number, SIM card identifiers), banking data, email addresses, passwords

companyDescription: London Borough of Lewisham is a local government authority in London responsible for delivering public services including housing, adult social care, highways, and other municipal functions. As a public authority, it is subject to FOIA obligations to provide information transparency to citizens.
companyLongDescription: London Borough of Lewisham is a local government authority in London responsible for delivering public services including housing, adult social care, highways, and other municipal functions. As a public authority, it is subject to FOIA obligations to provide information transparency to citizens.
caseDescription: London Borough of Lewisham systematically failed to respond to Freedom of Information requests within statutory 20 working day timeframes, leaving 338 requests overdue as of enforcement date, with 221 outstanding for over 12 months. The oldest request dated back to December 2020. The Council prioritised new requests over clearing its substantial backlog, breaching FOIA sections 1(1) and 10(1).
violationSummary: The failure to respond to FOI requests constitutes a breach of the public's right to access government-held information and accountability, though not 'confidentiality' in the traditional sense. Better categorized as an administrative/procedural failure under FOIA, but within Solove framework this maps closest to breach of duty to disclose.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Failed to respond to 338 overdue Freedom of Information requests within the required 20 working days, with 221 requests outstanding over 12 months old and the oldest dating to December 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens seeking critical information about Adult Social Care and Housing were left without responses for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Council reported 73% compliance rate for responding to FOI requests within 20 working days (April-September 2022)
claimsVsReality.reality: Even at 73%, this meant 27% of requests were already overdue; corrected data (April-December 2022) revealed 338 total overdue requests, not the originally stated 100, with 221 over 12 months old

claimsVsReality.claim: Council's strategy was to focus resources on new requests to prevent backlog growth
claimsVsReality.reality: This strategy abandoned existing requestors for years; oldest request from December 2020 remained unanswered, effectively adding to backlog rather than clearing it

claimsVsReality.claim: Council put new management structure in place and agreed to recruit additional staff
claimsVsReality.reality: These measures came only after Commissioner's escalated inquiry (October-January 2022-2023) and were insufficient to address existing backlog within statutory timescales

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 1(1) FOIA requires public authorities to inform requestors in writing whether they hold information requested and, if so, communicate it to them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to provide written confirmation or communication for 338 overdue requests
violations: Council failed to provide written confirmation or communication for 338 overdue requests
Council did not comply with duty to respond to information requestors

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 10(1) FOIA requires public authorities to comply with section 1(1) promptly and in any event not later than the twentieth working day following receipt of a request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council responded to only 73% of requests within 20 working days (April-December 2022)
violations: Council responded to only 73% of requests within 20 working days (April-December 2022)
221 requests were outstanding for over 12 months
Oldest unanswered request submitted 3 December 2020, unresponded for over 2 years

outcome: Information Commissioner issued Enforcement Notice under FOIA Section 52 requiring Council to: (1) within 6 months, respond to all overdue requests (either provide information per section 1(1)(b) or issue valid refusal notice per section 17 FOIA), and (2) within 35 calendar days, devise and publish an action plan formalising measures to comply with statutory duties and clear backlog. Failure to comply may result in Commissioner certification to High Court for contempt of court proceedings. Council has right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 calendar days.
companyNow: London Borough of Lewisham is an operational London local authority. As of the enforcement date (March 2023), the Council acknowledged the problem and had implemented a new FOI management structure (December 2022) and agreed to recruit additional FOI team staff, indicating ongoing remediation efforts.
dataType: Government service requests; information potentially includes Adult Social Care, Housing, Highways data
legalBasisViolated: FOIA 2000 Section 1(1)(a) – duty to confirm holding of information
FOIA 2000 Section 1(1)(b) – duty to communicate information
FOIA 2000 Section 10(1) – duty to respond within 20 working days

companyDescription: Ice Telecommunications Ltd is a business-to-business telecommunications solutions provider incorporated in 2014 (originally as Talkfair Converged Solutions Ltd). The company operates a direct marketing calling operation targeting businesses to promote telecom services. It has three active directors: James Taylor (Managing Director), Stuart William Bonell, and Jamie Steven Ward.
companyLongDescription: Ice Telecommunications Ltd is a business-to-business telecommunications solutions provider incorporated in 2014 (originally as Talkfair Converged Solutions Ltd). The company operates a direct marketing calling operation targeting businesses to promote telecom services. It has three active directors: James Taylor (Managing Director), Stuart William Bonell, and Jamie Steven Ward.
caseDescription: Ice Telecommunications Ltd made 72,682 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) and Corporate Telephone Preference Service (CTPS) between September 2021 and January 2022, violating PECR regulation 21. Despite receiving 23 complaints to TPS and 7 to the ICO, plus 19 warning letters from TPS, the company continued making contravening calls for months after the investigation began. The company failed to implement adequate due diligence on data providers and did not properly screen contact lists against TPS/CTPS registers.
violationSummary: The company systematically conducted unsolicited direct marketing calls (surveillance activity) to individuals who had explicitly registered their preference not to receive such calls, violating their explicit opt-out and privacy preference.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Ice Telecommunications made 72,682 unsolicited marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between September 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 72,682 individuals who had explicitly registered to block marketing calls were repeatedly contacted anyway, including some who asked multiple times to be removed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ice Comms claimed they obtained marketing lists from [data broker] which were screened against TPS and CTPS
claimsVsReality.reality: While lists may have been screened by the broker, Ice Comms could not produce a contract or evidence of due diligence; some staff members independently sourced unscreened data from public websites like Yell.com, Thomson Local, and Google

claimsVsReality.claim: Ice Comms stated staff were 'fully trained with the knowledge that calling individuals and businesses registered with the TPS and CTPS was prohibited'
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claimed training, a minority of staff breached policy by obtaining and using unscreened prospect data; the company had no written PECR policy and received 19 TPS warning letters and 30+ complaints that were not adequately acted upon

claimsVsReality.claim: Ice Comms claimed they 'take their responsibilities under PECR and data protection legislation seriously' and had implemented an 'internal suppression list'
claimsVsReality.reality: The company continued making 72,682 contravening calls over a 4.5-month period despite complaints, failed to respond to TPS warnings, and did not implement TPS screening service until January 2022—only after ICO investigation began

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1) requires that a person shall not use or instigate the use of a public electronic communications service for unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes where the called line is that of a subscriber registered with TPS/CTPS.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ice Comms made 72,682 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS/CTPS for more than 28 days prior to the calls
violations: Ice Comms made 72,682 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS/CTPS for more than 28 days prior to the calls
The company did not obtain explicit prior notification from subscribers that they did not object to receiving such calls as required by Regulation 21(4)
Company obtained marketing lists from data brokers without rigorous due diligence; some staff sourced unscreened data from public websites in violation of policy

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A DPA 1998 permits the ICO to issue monetary penalties where there is a serious contravention of PECR that was either deliberate or involved negligence (knowing or ought to know risk but failing to take reasonable steps).
regulatoryFindings.description: The contravention was serious—involving multiple breaches, 30 complaints during the violation period, and calls made to 72,682 subscribers
violations: The contravention was serious—involving multiple breaches, 30 complaints during the violation period, and calls made to 72,682 subscribers
Ice Comms knew or ought to have known of the risk: registered with ICO since 2015, received 19 letters from TPS, received direct complaints, and operates in direct marketing sector

Ice Comms failed to take reasonable steps: no written PECR policy, no verification of data broker screening, no proper investigation of TPS complaints, inadequate staff training and controls, delayed implementation of TPS screening service until January 2022

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £80,000 (reducible to £64,000 with early payment by 8 June 2023). Ice Comms must comply with PECR going forward and has implemented screening procedures with a TPS service provider (effective 7 January 2022). The company must pay by 9 June 2023. Ice Comms has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days, though exercising this right forfeits the early payment discount. Enforcement action will not be taken unless payment is not made after appeal periods expire.
companyNow: Ice Telecommunications Ltd remains operational. Following the investigation, the company implemented TPS screening procedures (effective 7 January 2022) and stated measures had been taken to prevent recurrence, though further complaints were received post-investigation period, suggesting continued compliance challenges.
dataType: Telephone numbers, business contact information

companyDescription: Kingsforce Management Services Pte Ltd is a recruitment and job search services provider that operates a jobseeker database platform. The company was based in Singapore and engaged in matching jobseekers with employment opportunities.
companyLongDescription: Kingsforce Management Services Pte Ltd is a recruitment and job search services provider that operates a jobseeker database platform. The company was based in Singapore and engaged in matching jobseekers with employment opportunities.
caseDescription: Kingsforce Management Services failed to protect a jobseeker database containing approximately 54,900 records, which was compromised and sold on RaidForums in December 2021. The breach was caused by outdated website coding with critical vulnerabilities. The organisation had not conducted periodic security reviews or vulnerability scans since launch, and failed to provide adequate data protection specifications to IT vendors.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and collection of personal data, as required by PDPA section 24(a). Specific failures included lack of periodic vulnerability scanning and inadequate vendor management.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Kingsforce failed to conduct periodic security reviews or vulnerability scans on its jobseeker website since launch and provided insufficient data protection specifications to IT vendors.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 54,900 jobseekers had their personal data including names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, qualifications and salary information exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation subsequently engaged IT maintenance vendors in an effort to ensure the security of the website
claimsVsReality.reality: Maintenance was ad-hoc and limited to troubleshooting functionality issues from bugs, glitches and page failures, rather than proactive security measures

claimsVsReality.claim: Work was not completed on the website at launch owing to contractual disputes with the developer, but security would be addressed through IT maintenance vendors
claimsVsReality.reality: The website was launched with outdated coding technology containing critical vulnerabilities that were never identified or remedied through periodic security reviews

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews, including vulnerability scans, since website launch
violations: Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews, including vulnerability scans, since website launch
Failed to provide sufficient clarity and specifications to IT vendors on how to protect the database and personal data
Failed to exercise reasonable oversight over vendors to ensure adherence to data protection requirements
Engaged in ad-hoc maintenance limited to troubleshooting functionality rather than proactive security hardening

outcome: The Commission accepted the organisation's request for expedited breach decision procedure. The organisation was found in breach of section 24(a) of the PDPA. The Commission imposed a compliance order directing the organisation to: (a) submit within 21 days a plan to ensure regular patching, updates and upgrades for all software and firmware supporting its websites; (b) state whether implementation will use qualified external services or internal resources, and if external, provide detailed job specifications; (c) outline implementation steps with deadlines ensuring completion within 60 days. The Commission noted mitigating factors including the organisation's cooperation, voluntary admission, and prompt remediation including immediate website suspension and engagement of a new developer.
dataType: Name, address, email address, telephone number, date of birth, job qualifications, salary information, educational qualifications, job search related data
legalBasisViolated: PDPA section 24(a) – Protection of personal data

companyDescription: Alpha Bank is a major Greek financial services provider offering retail and corporate banking, investment services, and financial products. It is one of the four largest banks in Greece.
companyLongDescription: Alpha Bank is a major Greek financial services provider offering retail and corporate banking, investment services, and financial products. It is one of the four largest banks in Greece.
caseDescription: Alpha Bank failed to timely respond to a data subject's access request for CCTV footage and subsequently destroyed the requested data before fulfilling the request. The bank delayed its response by 13 days beyond the legal one-month deadline and then cited data retention policy expiration to refuse access, despite the data still being within the retention period when the request was made.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to preserve personal data after receiving an access request, and subsequent destruction of that data before fulfilling the request, constitutes a breach of data processing integrity and security obligations under GDPR Article 5(1)(f) and denial of access rights under Article 15.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Alpha Bank received a data subject access request for CCTV footage within its 45-day retention window, failed to respond within the required 30 days.
whyTheyWereWrong: The bank's delay and destruction of the requested footage prevented the requester from obtaining evidence of a fraudulent transaction affecting his business.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank claimed it responded to the request and satisfied its substantive scope by providing a written confirmation of the visit date and time, along with web banking access logs.
claimsVsReality.reality: A written confirmation is not a statutory equivalent to providing a copy of the requested personal data (CCTV footage). The data subject has a specific right to obtain the data itself, not just a summary or confirmation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank stated that high workload caused the delay and justified the late response by citing operational pressure.
claimsVsReality.reality: As a large financial institution processing vast amounts of personal data, the bank has an obligation to maintain adequate procedures and mechanisms to handle data subject requests within the legal timeframe regardless of workload.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's retention policy permitting 45-day retention excused the later destruction of the data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Once an access request is submitted, the retention policy's automatic deletion schedule must be suspended to preserve the data until the request is fulfilled, even if the standard retention period expires in the interim.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) establishes that personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank destroyed CCTV footage after receiving an access request but before providing the data to the requester, rendering fulfillment impossible and violating the principle of lawfulness.
violations: Alpha Bank destroyed CCTV footage after receiving an access request but before providing the data to the requester, rendering fulfillment impossible and violating the principle of lawfulness.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) and (3) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and receive a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank refused to provide the requested CCTV footage copy despite the data being within its 45-day retention policy when the request was submitted, denying the fundamental right of access.
violations: Alpha Bank refused to provide the requested CCTV footage copy despite the data being within its 45-day retention policy when the request was submitted, denying the fundamental right of access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on actions taken in response to rights requests without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt, with possible two-month extension if justified.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank responded 13 days late (43 days instead of 30) and failed to notify the requester of the extension or reasons for delay, as required by the regulation.
violations: Alpha Bank responded 13 days late (43 days instead of 30) and failed to notify the requester of the extension or reasons for delay, as required by the regulation.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (Αρχή Προστασίας Δεδομένων Προσωπικού Χαρακτήρα) imposed a €10,000 administrative fine on Alpha Bank for violating Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 12(3), and 15(1)–(3) of the GDPR. The Authority found that the bank unlawfully destroyed CCTV data after receiving an access request and failed to timely respond or preserve the requested information. The decision emphasizes that once an access request is received while data is within the retention period, the controller must immediately take steps to prevent scheduled deletion and preserve the data until the request is fulfilled. This decision sets binding precedent that data destruction following a rights request constitutes a fundamental breach of processing lawfulness.
companyNow: Alpha Bank remains one of Greece's largest financial institutions and continues to operate under enhanced regulatory scrutiny following this and prior GDPR enforcement decisions (2014, 2018).
dataType: CCTV video footage, web banking access logs, financial transaction records
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Legal basis for processing
GDPR Art. 12(3) – Timely response to requests
GDPR Art. 15(3) – Provision of copy of data

companyDescription: Norfolk County Council is a local government authority in England responsible for providing public services including education, social care, highways, and other functions across Norfolk. As a public sector body, it is subject to UK GDPR compliance obligations for personal data processing.
companyLongDescription: Norfolk County Council is a local government authority in England responsible for providing public services including education, social care, highways, and other functions across Norfolk. As a public sector body, it is subject to UK GDPR compliance obligations for personal data processing.
caseDescription: Norfolk County Council failed to respond to 251 out of 511 Subject Access Requests (SARs) within the statutory one-month deadline (or three-month extension) during April 2021 to April 2022. The Council violated Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3) of the UK GDPR by failing to provide timely confirmation of data processing and access to personal data. While COVID-19 pandemic restrictions and subsequent remedial staffing measures were considered mitigating factors, the Commissioner issued a reprimand and required compliance improvements.
violationSummary: The Council systematically excluded data subjects from timely access to information about their data processing by failing to meet statutory deadlines, denying individuals prompt exercise of their rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Norfolk County Council failed to respond to 251 out of 511 Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month deadline between April 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 251 individuals experienced significant delays in exercising their fundamental right to access their personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Council had appropriate capacity to process Subject Access Requests in a timely manner
claimsVsReality.reality: The Council responded to only 260 out of 511 SARs (51%) within statutory deadlines, indicating capacity issues

claimsVsReality.claim: COVID-19 pandemic access restrictions were the primary cause of delay
claimsVsReality.reality: While COVID-19 contributed to backlog, the Council's failure to meet deadlines for nearly half of requests suggests systemic resource management issues beyond pandemic-related factors

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken on data subject rights requests (Articles 15–22) without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months only where necessary, with notification of extension within one month.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council responded to only 260 of 511 SARs within the statutory one-month (or extended three-month) deadline
violations: Council responded to only 260 of 511 SARs within the statutory one-month (or extended three-month) deadline

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation from the controller whether personal data concerning them are being processed and, where applicable, access to the personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to provide timely confirmation of data processing and access to personal data for 251 data subjects
violations: Council failed to provide timely confirmation of data processing and access to personal data for 251 data subjects

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires the controller to provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council's failure to respond to requests within statutory deadlines prevented data subjects from obtaining copies of their data
violations: Council's failure to respond to requests within statutory deadlines prevented data subjects from obtaining copies of their data

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Norfolk County Council for infringements of Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner acknowledged mitigating factors including COVID-19 pandemic impacts on building access and manual record retrieval, and welcomed the Council's remedial measures including increased staffing dedicated to SAR processing and backlog closure. The Commissioner required the Council to provide details of actions taken to address three recommendations by 6 November 2023: (1) ensure SARs are responded to within statutory deadlines, (2) maintain adequate staff resources for SAR processing and continue monitoring, and (3) continue implementing effective measures to address the backlog.
companyNow: Norfolk County Council continues to operate as a local government authority in Norfolk, England. The Council has implemented remedial measures including increased staffing and a dedicated SAR response team to address identified compliance gaps.
dataType: Personal data (general); may include sensitive categories based on council functions

companyDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. (formerly Vodafone Group España) is a leading telecommunications provider in Spain offering mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. (formerly Vodafone Group España) is a leading telecommunications provider in Spain offering mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers.
caseDescription: Vodafone España failed to verify the identity of a person who obtained a duplicate SIM card for a customer's line without authorization. This enabled SIM swapping fraud, allowing unauthorized access to the customer's mobile line and attempted account takeover. The company's inadequate identity verification procedures violated GDPR Article 6 requirements for lawful processing.
violationSummary: Vodafone failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures (Art. 32) to prevent unauthorized access to customer data via SIM duplication. The insecure process allowed a third party to obtain control of personal data (mobile line) without consent, violating the lawfulness principle.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Vodafone staff issued a duplicate SIM card to an unauthorized third party without verifying the person's identity or obtaining the customer's consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: An attacker gained control of the customer's phone line, attempted to port it to another carrier.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone stated that 'all SIM changes realized by Vodafone surpass the security policy established for these effects' and that the company had implemented policies requiring ID verification for in-store SIM changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite security policies on paper, Vodafone staff facilitated a SIM duplication to an unauthorized person without verifying their identity against the account holder's ID, demonstrating the policies were not effectively enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone claimed the physical distributor would be penalized for failure to obtain and retain identity documentation, shifting responsibility downstream.
claimsVsReality.reality: The responsibility for ensuring lawful processing rests with Vodafone as the controller; inadequate training, monitoring, or enforcement of partner compliance does not eliminate Vodafone's legal liability for the unlawful processing that occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data be lawful only if it meets at least one of the specified conditions: consent, contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone processed the customer's personal data (mobile line credentials, identity details) through SIM duplication without the customer's consent and without any lawful basis, enabling unauthorized third-party access.
violations: Vodafone processed the customer's personal data (mobile line credentials, identity details) through SIM duplication without the customer's consent and without any lawful basis, enabling unauthorized third-party access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone failed to implement adequate identity verification controls for SIM duplication requests, allowing an unauthorized person to obtain a duplicate SIM without authentication, enabling fraud.
violations: Vodafone failed to implement adequate identity verification controls for SIM duplication requests, allowing an unauthorized person to obtain a duplicate SIM without authentication, enabling fraud.

outcome: Vodafone made voluntary payment of €56,000 on 21 October 2022, equivalent to one 20% reduction from the proposed €70,000 penalty. The company waived administrative appeals. The procedure was terminated under Article 85 of Law 39/2015. Vodafone committed to additional security measures including mandatory ID photocopying for in-store SIM changes (since May 2019) and €300 penalties for non-compliant distributors.
companyNow: Vodafone España remains a major Spanish telecom operator, part of Vodafone Group plc. The company has since implemented enhanced SIM security protocols and fraud detection measures.
dataType: Mobile phone number, SIM card access, personal identity data

companyDescription: Direct Clothing Co. (UK) Limited is a retail clothing company operating an e-commerce website from which it collects customer payment card information.
companyLongDescription: Direct Clothing Co. (UK) Limited is a retail clothing company operating an e-commerce website from which it collects customer payment card information.
caseDescription: Direct Clothing Co. failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer payment card data on its website. A malicious actor exploited a WordPress vulnerability to inject code that harvested payment card details from customers. The company had not applied security patches since February 2019, conducted no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing, and lacked a contractual security arrangement with its third-party IT provider.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures required by GDPR Article 32, directly enabling unauthorized access to payment card data through known exploitable vulnerabilities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Direct Clothing Co. failed to apply security patches or updates since at least February 2019, conducted no vulnerability scanning or penetration tests.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customer payment card details were stolen when attackers exploited unpatched WordPress vulnerabilities on the company's website, exposing customers to fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: A third-party IT provider was responsible for the security and maintenance of the affected website.
claimsVsReality.reality: No contractual security agreement was actually in place with any third-party provider at the time of the incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Direct Clothing Co. failed to apply security patches or updates since at least February 2019, contrary to NCSC guidance recommending regular vulnerability scanning.
violations: Direct Clothing Co. failed to apply security patches or updates since at least February 2019, contrary to NCSC guidance recommending regular vulnerability scanning.
The company conducted no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing despite NCSC guidance recommending regular scanning.
The company lacked a contractual security agreement with its third-party IT provider, resulting in no regular patching, testing, or monitoring.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires implementing measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Direct Clothing Co. failed to maintain system integrity and availability by allowing WordPress vulnerabilities to remain unpatched, enabling malicious code injection that compromised customer payment data.
violations: Direct Clothing Co. failed to maintain system integrity and availability by allowing WordPress vulnerabilities to remain unpatched, enabling malicious code injection that compromised customer payment data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(d) requires a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Direct Clothing Co. did not conduct any vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, or regular security assessments of its website systems.
violations: Direct Clothing Co. did not conduct any vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, or regular security assessments of its website systems.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to Direct Clothing Co. (UK) Limited under Article 58(2)(b) of the GDPR. The company was advised to implement the security guidance provided and warned that if further incidents or complaints are reported, further formal regulatory action may be considered. The matter is now closed, but the ICO reserves the right to revisit if new information emerges.
dataType: Payment card details, financial data

companyDescription: Thomson Medical Pte. Ltd. is a healthcare provider in Singapore that operates medical clinics and facilities, including maternity and general medical services.
companyLongDescription: Thomson Medical Pte. Ltd. is a healthcare provider in Singapore that operates medical clinics and facilities, including maternity and general medical services.
caseDescription: Thomson Medical's Health Declaration Portal stored visitor data in a publicly accessible CSV file on their web server from April to September 2020, exposing personal data of 44,679 visitors. An in-house developer failed to remove legacy code and change default server configuration despite instructions to migrate data to a secured database. The Commission found the organisation breached the Protection Obligation by failing to implement adequate security controls and pre-launch testing.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement and enforce reasonable security arrangements (access controls, encryption, authentication) to protect personal data in its possession, resulting in unauthorised access vulnerability.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Thomson Medical stored visitor health declaration data for 44,679 people in an unsecured, publicly accessible CSV file on its web server instead of a protected database from April to September.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 44,000 visitors' sensitive personal information including names, ID numbers, contact details, clinic visits.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation's existing policies required visitor data to be stored in a secured database with proper access controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data was simultaneously stored in an unprotected public CSV file for 5 months, with no security testing performed before portal launch to verify the policies were enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: In-house developer was instructed to switch data storage from CSV file to secured database exclusively.
claimsVsReality.reality: Developer omitted removing legacy code that continued writing to the CSV file and failed to change default web server configuration allowing public access.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, disclosure, and similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to ensure processes were in place to enforce its own policies requiring data storage in secured database, relying solely on one employee with no oversight.
violations: Organisation failed to ensure processes were in place to enforce its own policies requiring data storage in secured database, relying solely on one employee with no oversight.
Organisation conducted only acceptance and technical testing but no security testing before portal launch to verify access controls existed.
Organisation omitted to remove legacy code and change default web server configuration, leaving CSV file with 44,679 records publicly accessible.

outcome: Commission imposed directions instead of financial penalty due to limited impact (no evidence of actual exposure to unauthorised third parties, only 4 file accesses from 3 local IPs likely from complainant and Commission). Organisation must within 60 days: (1) implement reasonable pre-launch security testing for all future applications processing personal data; (2) develop and implement a data retention policy; (3) conduct Clear/Surface Web and renewed Dark Web scans to confirm no online publication of affected data; (4) submit written update to Commission within 14 days of completion. Organisation had already removed the CSV file, changed database passwords, reviewed deployment processes, and rectified vulnerability scan gaps.
companyNow: Unknown – Thomson Medical is a private healthcare provider in Singapore. The decision does not provide current operational status.
dataType: health declaration information, visitor names, contact numbers, NRIC/FIN/passport numbers, clinic/room visited, temperature readings, COVID-19 exposure declarations

companyDescription: QCP Capital Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based cryptocurrency and digital asset trading company that provides trading services and account management for customers.
companyLongDescription: QCP Capital Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based cryptocurrency and digital asset trading company that provides trading services and account management for customers.
caseDescription: QCP Capital Pte Ltd suffered a data breach on 30 August 2021 through unauthorised access to employee accounts, resulting in the exfiltration of personal data for 675 individuals including names, NRIC numbers, passport scans, and trading records. The organisation was found to have implemented reasonable security measures and responded promptly with remedial action, resulting in no enforcement action.
violationSummary: The breach involved unauthorised access and exfiltration of sensitive personal data held in confidence by the organisation, resulting in disclosure of confidential customer information to threat actors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: QCP Capital failed to prevent threat actors from accessing two employee accounts, resulting in the exfiltration of personal data belonging to 675 customers including names.
whyTheyWereWrong: 675 customers' highly sensitive identity documents, financial account balances, and transaction histories were exposed to criminals who gained access through insufficiently protected employee.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: QCP Capital implemented reasonable security arrangements including internal monitoring systems that detected and escalated anomalous transactions, allowing suspension of affected trading accounts, thereby maintaining compliance with the Protection Obligation despite the breach occurring through compromised employee credentials.
violations: QCP Capital implemented reasonable security arrangements including internal monitoring systems that detected and escalated anomalous transactions, allowing suspension of affected trading accounts, thereby maintaining compliance with the Protection Obligation despite the breach occurring through compromised employee credentials.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found that QCP Capital Pte Ltd was in compliance with its Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation had provided reasonable security arrangements, maintained an internal monitoring system that detected the breach, and took prompt and extensive remedial action including notifying affected individuals, layering access controls, and introducing mandatory hardware key authentication. No enforcement action was taken.
dataType: Financial data, identity documents, contact information, trading records, biometric data (photographs)

companyDescription: South Wales Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing South Wales, serving a large civilian population across multiple local authority areas. The force is a public sector law enforcement organisation accountable to the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner.
companyLongDescription: South Wales Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing South Wales, serving a large civilian population across multiple local authority areas. The force is a public sector law enforcement organisation accountable to the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner.
caseDescription: South Wales Police disclosed the identities of two vulnerable women who had applied for information under domestic violence and child sexual offender disclosure schemes. Officers carelessly revealed their identities during conversations with offenders and while performing safeguarding duties, causing significant distress. The ICO found the force failed to provide adequate data protection training and had no proper guidance on handling such sensitive disclosures.
violationSummary: The core violation was breach of confidentiality under data protection law. Sensitive personal data (identities of domestic violence and child protection applicants) was disclosed without authorization to third parties (offenders), breaching the duty of confidentiality and appropriate security measures required under law enforcement data processing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Police officers disclosed the identities of two women to individuals they had sought protection information about through domestic violence and child sex offender disclosure schemes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two vulnerable women seeking safety assessments had their identities exposed to the very people they feared, causing documented emotional distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: Officers were appropriately trained and aware of their obligations under DVDS and CSODS schemes when dealing with offenders and applicants
claimsVsReality.reality: First officer had received no DVDS training and minimal Sexual Offences Liaison training, with no data protection training since July 2018. Second officer had no CSODS training since 2015 and no data protection training since December 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: South Wales Police had implemented improvements in data protection practices following ICO audit recommendations in September 2019
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite ICO audit identifying lack of formal training programme and warning of increased breach risk, South Wales Police failed to implement adequate training before both incidents occurred in February and April 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clear procedures existed to ensure confidentiality of applicant identities under domestic violence and child protection disclosure schemes
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented processes or guidance existed for officers regarding what could and could not be communicated, particularly where MAPPA and DVDS overlapped, resulting in confused officers making disclosures.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40, Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires that data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: South Wales Police failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data by disclosing applicant identities to offenders without authorization
violations: South Wales Police failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data by disclosing applicant identities to offenders without authorization
Officers and staff failed to act in a manner expected to preserve identity of data subjects
Police failed to provide full and appropriate training to officers and staff on handling sensitive disclosures under DVDS and CSODS schemes
No documented processes or guidance existed for officers regarding confidentiality obligations when MAPPA and DVDS overlapped
Officers had not received relevant data protection training (2018 and 2015 respectively) or scheme-specific training (DVDS, CSODS)
Prior ICO audit in September 2019 identified lack of formal training programme but South Wales Police failed to remediate before these incidents occurred

outcome: ICO issued a formal reprimand to South Wales Police under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018 for infringement of Section 40, Part 3. The force is required to: (1) fully implement all recommendations from the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) report; (2) establish clear lines of communication and guidance on disclosure responsibilities across all officers and staff; (3) conduct a comprehensive review of data protection reporting procedures to ensure incidents are reported within 72 hours; (4) implement comprehensive data protection and scheme-specific training for all relevant officers. The ICO noted it will revisit the matter and consider further formal regulatory action if additional incidents or complaints are reported. The matter is closed but subject to ongoing monitoring.
companyNow: South Wales Police continues operations as the regional police force for South Wales. The force has begun implementing recommendations from the IOPC and ICO investigations but remains under ICO monitoring.
dataType: Identity information, personal information of domestic violence and child protection applicants

companyDescription: Sjukhusstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is a Swedish regional public authority that oversees hospital administration for Akademiska sjukhuset (Academic Hospital), providing specialized healthcare services including international patient care.
companyLongDescription: Sjukhusstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is a Swedish regional public authority that oversees hospital administration for Akademiska sjukhuset (Academic Hospital), providing specialized healthcare services including international patient care.
caseDescription: Sjukhusstyrelsen sent sensitive patient health data via unencrypted email over the internet to patients and referrers in third countries, and stored this data in Outlook. The organization failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to protect health data, despite knowing of the risks through its own guidelines.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect sensitive personal data (health information) from unauthorized access or disclosure, exposing it to interception during transmission and unauthorized access in storage.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Sent approximately 500–1,000 unencrypted email messages monthly containing patient health records to recipients in third countries.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 300 patients annually had sensitive health data exposed via unencrypted internet transmission where unauthorized parties could intercept it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sjukhusstyrelsen used Microsoft's standard TLS encryption settings for email transmission to protect data in transit.
claimsVsReality.reality: The encryption used (opportunistic TLS 1.2) fell back to unencrypted transmission when recipient servers lacked TLS support, and the organization did not verify or control how many sensitive patient emails were actually sent unencrypted over the internet.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Uppsala's guidelines permitted sensitive patient data transmission via email.
claimsVsReality.reality: Region Uppsala's own email handling guidelines explicitly stated that sensitive personal data must not be communicated via email, yet Sjukhusstyrelsen continued the practice systematically for over one year.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sjukhusstyrelsen transmitted unencrypted patient health data over open internet, exposing it to unauthorized access and interception by third parties.
violations: Sjukhusstyrelsen transmitted unencrypted patient health data over open internet, exposing it to unauthorized access and interception by third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the risks to individuals' rights and freedoms.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization used opportunistic TLS encryption that fell back to unencrypted transmission when recipient email servers did not support TLS; stored sensitive patient health data in Outlook, an internet-exposed email system inherently unsuitable for long-term storage of sensitive data; did not verify how many emails were sent unencrypted despite knowing about the vulnerability.
violations: The organization used opportunistic TLS encryption that fell back to unencrypted transmission when recipient email servers did not support TLS; stored sensitive patient health data in Outlook, an internet-exposed email system inherently unsuitable for long-term storage of sensitive data; did not verify how many emails were sent unencrypted despite knowing about the vulnerability.

outcome: Sjukhusstyrelsen must pay 1,600,000 SEK administrative penalty for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32. The decision found that the organization systematically transmitted and stored sensitive health data without adequate protection for over 12 months despite awareness of security risks through its own regional guidelines. The organization implemented a file encryption solution in September 2019 after the incident was reported. The decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Sjukhusstyrelsen i Region Uppsala continues operations as a regional hospital administration board in Sweden. The organization has implemented file encryption measures following the May 2019 incident and is undergoing systematic improvement efforts.
dataType: Health data, patient names, contact information, identification numbers

companyDescription: North Yorkshire Police is a law enforcement agency responsible for policing North Yorkshire in England. The force handles criminal prosecutions, including driving offences, through the Single Justice Procedure.
companyLongDescription: North Yorkshire Police is a law enforcement agency responsible for policing North Yorkshire in England. The force handles criminal prosecutions, including driving offences, through the Single Justice Procedure.
caseDescription: North Yorkshire Police generated a duplicate Single Justice Procedure (SJP) for a driving offence on 3 July 2018, resulting in a data subject being convicted twice of the same offence. The individual received a second fine and driving disqualification. Although the disqualification was later removed, the police failed to notify their compliance team of the breach until 31 August 2021 (nearly 3 years later), delaying ICO notification until 8 September 2021—well beyond the 72-hour reporting requirement.
violationSummary: Lack of adequate safeguards and processes to ensure accuracy of sensitive criminal justice data, combined with failure to detect and prevent duplicate processing of law enforcement data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: North Yorkshire Police generated a duplicate Single Justice Procedure record for a driving offense on 3 July 2018 without documented processes to check for existing records before creating new.
whyTheyWereWrong: A person was wrongly convicted twice for the same offense, paid duplicate fines and prosecution costs, suffered a driving disqualification due to 'totting up' on false records.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disqualification had minimal impact on the data subject as they had already decided not to renew their driving licence.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data subject suffered significant financial loss from paying two fines and prosecution costs, and the stress from the breach exacerbated an existing eye condition with negative effects on eyesight.

claimsVsReality.claim: NYP had suitable data protection processes in place for generating SJPs.
claimsVsReality.reality: There was no documented process in place requiring staff to check for duplicates before generating a new SJP, and no specific DPA 2018 training had been provided to staff prior to the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Part 3, Chapter 2, Section 38(1) requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be accurate and kept up to date, and every reasonable step must be taken to ensure inaccurate data is erased or rectified without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: NYP generated a duplicate SJP without documented process to check for existing records, resulting in inaccurate duplicate conviction data
violations: NYP generated a duplicate SJP without documented process to check for existing records, resulting in inaccurate duplicate conviction data
No specific data protection training was provided to staff on the importance of accurate recording of personal data prior to the breach

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Part 3, Chapter 4, Section 67(1) requires controllers to notify the Commissioner of a personal data breach without undue delay and where feasible not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: NYP became aware of the breach on 4 October 2018 but multiple staff failed to notify the Compliance Team
violations: NYP became aware of the breach on 4 October 2018 but multiple staff failed to notify the Compliance Team
Compliance Team only learned of the breach on 31 August 2021 (nearly 3 years later) upon notification of a civil claim
ICO was not notified until 8 September 2021, approximately 3 years after the breach occurred

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to North Yorkshire Police under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018. NYP has implemented remedial measures including: a documented SJP process with additional steps to avoid duplicate processing, a mandatory Managing Information e-learning package for all staff, and governance improvements. The Commissioner recommended NYP review data breach reporting policies, implement contingency planning for data protection issues, and ensure regular data protection training for all employees. The matter is now closed, but further incidents may trigger additional formal regulatory action.
companyNow: North Yorkshire Police continues to operate as the police force for the North Yorkshire area in England. Following this investigation, the organisation has implemented documented processes and enhanced training to prevent similar incidents.
dataType: Criminal offence data, driving offence records, conviction data, personal identifiers

companyDescription: Grindr LLC operates a location-based social networking and dating application primarily used by LGBTQ+ individuals worldwide, with a significant user base in the United Kingdom.
companyLongDescription: Grindr LLC operates a location-based social networking and dating application primarily used by LGBTQ+ individuals worldwide, with a significant user base in the United Kingdom.
caseDescription: Grindr failed to provide transparent and clear privacy information to UK users regarding how their personal and special category data was being processed and shared with advertising partners. The company's privacy policy contained contradictions and omissions about data sharing practices, legal bases for processing, and the distinction between different categories of personal data. The ICO found systematic failures in transparency compliance under UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a).
violationSummary: Grindr disclosed personal and special category data to third-party advertisers without providing clear, transparent information to users about the scope, legal basis, and recipients of such disclosures, violating the transparency principle.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Grindr's Privacy Policy contradicted its actual data-sharing practices by claiming it only shared user data with advertisers based on consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of UK users, including vulnerable LGBTQ+ individuals, were unable to understand how their intimate personal and special category data was being collected, processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that user personal data is only shared with advertising partners on the basis of consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grindr's Privacy and Cookie Policy table explicitly referenced 'legitimate interest' as a legal basis for sharing data with third-party ad partners in rows 5 and 9.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that it does not share users' profile information for advertising purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Profile information was listed in multiple rows (5, 9, 21, 22) of the 'EEA and U.K Legal Basis For Processing' table as being shared for advertising.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that IP address and advertising ID do not constitute personal data and therefore should not be reflected in privacy information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The ICO determined that IP address and advertising ID may constitute personal data in certain circumstances (e.g., when combined with other data) and must be disclosed transparently.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that it does not 'process' special category data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grindr processes special category data through voluntary user input and storage on its platform, regardless of whether it shares such data with third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(a) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Grindr failed to provide effective and transparent privacy information to UK data subjects regarding the processing of their personal data, including contradictions between stated and actual data sharing practices, unclear disclosure of profile information processing, and insufficient clarity on special category data handling and third-party recipients.
violations: Grindr failed to provide effective and transparent privacy information to UK data subjects regarding the processing of their personal data, including contradictions between stated and actual data sharing practices, unclear disclosure of profile information processing, and insufficient clarity on special category data handling and third-party recipients.

outcome: The ICO issued Grindr with a formal reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR. The company was required to amend its Privacy and Cookie Policy and 'EEA and U.K Legal Basis For Processing' table to eliminate contradictions and clarify actual data sharing practices. Grindr must provide users with clearer information about: the distinction between personal and special category data; data flow restrictions with advertising partners; the full list of third-party recipients; information collected via third-party sign-up processes; and SDK integration security measures. The company was instructed to ensure special category data remains subject to appropriate safeguards and to submit a progress update to the ICO by 26 January 2023. The ICO indicated that further breaches could result in formal regulatory action.
companyNow: Grindr LLC remains operational as a dating application for LGBTQ+ users globally. Following the ICO investigation, the company has faced continued scrutiny over data privacy practices and has made updates to its privacy policies.
dataType: Sexual orientation, profile information, location data, IP address, advertising ID, personal data, special category data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, transparency

company: Secretary of State for the Home Department (Home Office)
companyDescription: The Home Office is the UK government department responsible for immigration, crime, policing, counterterrorism, and related policy. It processes sensitive personal data from millions of individuals seeking asylum, visas, and other immigration services.
companyLongDescription: The Home Office is the UK government department responsible for immigration, crime, policing, counterterrorism, and related policy. It processes sensitive personal data from millions of individuals seeking asylum, visas, and other immigration services.
caseDescription: The Home Office failed to respond to Subject Access Requests within statutory timescales under UK GDPR. Only 45.73% of SARs received between April 2020 and December 2021 were answered within the required one-month deadline, leaving 20,862 requests unanswered. The ICO issued a reprimand and required compliance improvements and progress reporting.
violationSummary: The Home Office excluded data subjects from their statutory right to access personal data by failing to respond within required timescales, preventing individuals from exercising their rights under Article 15 of UK GDPR.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Home Office failed to respond to 54.27% of Subject Access Requests within the required one-month statutory deadline, leaving 20,862 requests unanswered between April 2020 and December 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 20,862 individuals were denied timely access to their personal data held by the Home Office, preventing them from understanding what information the government held about them.

claimsVsReality.claim: Home Office had implemented a Subject Access Request Unit (SARU) Improvement Plan to address SAR compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Home Office failed to improve its SAR compliance during the investigation period; SARU continued to have a backlog of cases and did not meet statutory timescales for the vast majority of requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires a controller to provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15–22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt (or within two months for complex requests), with notice of any extension.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office did not provide responses within the statutory one-month deadline for 54.27% of requests (20,862 cases) during the review period.
violations: Home Office did not provide responses within the statutory one-month deadline for 54.27% of requests (20,862 cases) during the review period.
Failed to inform data subjects of extensions or reasons for delay as required.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and, if so, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office denied thousands of individuals their right to access their own personal data by failing to respond within statutory timescales.
violations: Home Office denied thousands of individuals their right to access their own personal data by failing to respond within statutory timescales.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires a controller to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office failed to provide copies of personal data to requesters within required timeframes, breaching the right to receive data in accessible form.
violations: Home Office failed to provide copies of personal data to requesters within required timeframes, breaching the right to receive data in accessible form.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand under Article 58 UK GDPR. The Home Office was required to: (1) take steps to ensure Subject Access Requests are responded to within statutory deadlines in line with Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3); (2) ensure adequate staff resources are in place to process and respond to SARs. The Home Office was required to provide progress updates to the ICO three months from 21 September 2022 (by 21 December 2022) and again at six months (by 21 March 2023). The ICO indicated it may pursue further formal regulatory action if additional information comes to light or further incidents occur. The matter is now considered closed.
companyNow: The Home Office remains the UK government department responsible for immigration, justice, and policing policy. As a government ministry, it continues to process Subject Access Requests but faces ongoing compliance scrutiny.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (SAR) — nature not specified in findings

companyDescription: Editorial Ribadeo S.L. is a Spanish publishing company incorporated in 2020 (NIF B01864982). No financial statements have been deposited, indicating either minimal operations or non-compliance with corporate reporting obligations.
companyLongDescription: Editorial Ribadeo S.L. is a Spanish publishing company incorporated in 2020 (NIF B01864982). No financial statements have been deposited, indicating either minimal operations or non-compliance with corporate reporting obligations.
caseDescription: Editorial Ribadeo failed to comply with a prior AEPD enforcement decision requiring implementation of GDPR information transparency measures within 15 days. Despite two follow-up notices, the company provided no evidence of compliance or corrective action, resulting in enforcement for non-compliance with authority orders.
violationSummary: Company excluded data subjects from required information by failing to implement mandatory transparency disclosures ordered by regulator. This directly violates GDPR transparency principles and regulatory authority to enforce compliance.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Editorial Ribadeo S.L. failed to comply with a corrective order requiring it to adopt measures ensuring compliance with GDPR articles 12.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals who provided personal data to Editorial Ribadeo received no required transparency about how their data would be processed, stored, or protected.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.2(d) permits supervisory authorities to order controllers to adjust processing to comply with GDPR provisions in a specified manner within a specified timeframe.
