regulatoryFindings.description: Editorial Ribadeo ignored binding order to adopt transparency measures within 15 days and failed to respond to two subsequent compliance notices over three months.
violations: Editorial Ribadeo ignored binding order to adopt transparency measures within 15 days and failed to respond to two subsequent compliance notices over three months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.6 imposes administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% global annual turnover for non-compliance with supervisory authority corrective orders under Article 58.2.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to comply with enforceable AEPD decision requiring GDPR Articles 12-13 transparency implementation, triggering Article 83.6 penalty authority.
violations: Company failed to comply with enforceable AEPD decision requiring GDPR Articles 12-13 transparency implementation, triggering Article 83.6 penalty authority.

outcome: AEPD imposed €1,000 administrative fine for non-compliance with prior enforcement decision. Company required to demonstrate adoption of all transparency measures within 15 days of notification. Failure to comply may trigger additional enforcement. Resolution is final; administrative remedies exhausted.
companyNow: Editorial Ribadeo S.L. is a micro-enterprise incorporated in 2020 with no publicly available financial disclosures, suggesting minimal operational activity or financial viability.
dataType: Personal data subject to GDPR Articles 12-13 information requirements

company: Warrington and Halton Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
companyDescription: Warrington and Halton Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is an NHS healthcare organization providing hospital and medical services in the North West of England.
companyLongDescription: Warrington and Halton Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is an NHS healthcare organization providing hospital and medical services in the North West of England.
caseDescription: An appointments administrator uploaded a patient's urgent referral form to another patient's electronic record. When the second patient requested their records via subject access request, the mistakenly filed document was included, disclosing seven pages of sensitive health information to an unauthorized individual. The breach was discovered only after the recipient contacted the affected patient directly.
violationSummary: The filing error resulted in special category personal data being disclosed to an unauthorized third party. The disclosure occurred because the organization lacked basic verification procedures and safeguards before releasing requested records.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: An appointments administrator uploaded a patient's urgent referral form to the wrong patient's electronic record.
whyTheyWereWrong: A seven-page form containing one patient's full demographic details, referral reason, family medical history, medications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Administrative staff were following the process in place
claimsVsReality.reality: The process in place was not robust and lacked basic verification procedures, allowing sensitive health data to be uploaded to wrong patient records without detection

claimsVsReality.claim: Computer-generated PDFs can contain 1-6000 pages and capacity constraints prevent checking
claimsVsReality.reality: Volume of records alone does not justify absence of verification procedures; organizations must implement safeguards appropriate to their systems regardless of document size

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of UK GDPR requires data controllers to process personal data securely by means of appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: WHH had no checking process in place for subject access request responses either for paper or electronic notes, and no process to identify misfiled records, constituting inadequate security measures
violations: WHH had no checking process in place for subject access request responses either for paper or electronic notes, and no process to identify misfiled records, constituting inadequate security measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(d) of UK GDPR requires data controllers to ensure that personal data remains accurate and up to date in line with the purposes for which it is being processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: One patient had an incorrect letter on their electronic record and the other was missing the letter, resulting in both records being inaccurate or incomplete. WHH had no policy, written procedure or guidance for safe document uploads or verification of correct record selection
violations: One patient had an incorrect letter on their electronic record and the other was missing the letter, resulting in both records being inaccurate or incomplete. WHH had no policy, written procedure or guidance for safe document uploads or verification of correct record selection

outcome: ICO issued a Reprimand under Article 58 of UK GDPR. WHH implemented remedial steps including: correction of records, updated standard operating procedure with two-tier checking process, monthly audit process, policy review, staff briefing, and incident reporting for all detected misfiled records. WHH required to provide progress update within 6 months (by 27 November 2022) on four recommended actions: building sufficient checks into procedures, ensuring staff awareness of updated procedures, completing a Data Protection Impact Assessment for subject access request processes, and reviewing data protection training content and frequency.
companyNow: Warrington and Halton Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust continues to operate as an NHS healthcare provider in England. Following this investigation, the organization implemented enhanced data protection procedures and continues to undergo ICO monitoring.
dataType: Health data, patient demographics, medical history, family medical history, clinical information, medication records

companyDescription: Budgetcars Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based logistics company providing parcel delivery services to customers on behalf of retailers.
companyLongDescription: Budgetcars Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based logistics company providing parcel delivery services to customers on behalf of retailers.
caseDescription: Budgetcars operated a delivery tracking function that exposed personal data of 44,357 individuals due to insecure direct object reference vulnerability. Users could modify Tracking IDs to access other customers' personal information including names, addresses, contact numbers, and signature photographs. The company failed to implement reasonable access controls or archive completed delivery data, violating Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security arrangements (access controls and data archival) resulted in predictable and exploitable vulnerability that exposed sensitive personal information to unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Budgetcars adopted Tracking IDs from retailers without implementing access controls, allowing anyone to modify ID numbers to retrieve other customers' personal data including names.
whyTheyWereWrong: 44,357 customers' personal data was exposed to unauthorized access through a simple attack, enabling strangers to view delivery addresses, contact information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Budgetcars failed to implement reasonable access controls when adopting Tracking IDs, allowing modification of IDs to access other individuals' personal data
violations: Budgetcars failed to implement reasonable access controls when adopting Tracking IDs, allowing modification of IDs to access other individuals' personal data
Budgetcars did not archive personal data relating to completed delivery orders after a reasonable period, leaving 44,357 individuals' data at risk for longer than necessary

outcome: The Commission found Budgetcars in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. No monetary penalty was imposed due to the company's voluntary admission of liability and prompt remedial action. Instead, the Commission directed Budgetcars to: (1) implement appropriate contractual provisions defining data controller and intermediary obligations; (2) engage a qualified security provider to conduct a thorough security audit of its website and technical arrangements within 60 days; (3) rectify identified security gaps and update personal data protection policies within 60 days of audit completion; and (4) inform the Commission within 1 week of completion. Post-incident, Budgetcars removed all personal data from the tracking page, engaged IT solutions providers for re-examination, implemented 14-day post-delivery Tracking ID expiry, and prevented sequential IDs from upload.
dataType: Name, address, contact number, signature photographs

company: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust
companyDescription: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust is a major National Health Service teaching trust in London providing acute hospital care, clinical research, and medical education. Founded in 1828, it operates multiple hospitals including the Royal Free Hospital.
companyLongDescription: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust is a major National Health Service teaching trust in London providing acute hospital care, clinical research, and medical education. Founded in 1828, it operates multiple hospitals including the Royal Free Hospital.
caseDescription: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust stored hysteroscopy scans on three USB sticks over nine years without proper backup, encryption management, or risk assessment. Two encrypted USB sticks became inaccessible on 5 April 2018, affecting 4,000–10,000 data subjects. The Trust failed to recognise the inaccessibility as a data breach and delayed reporting to the ICO.
violationSummary: The Trust failed to implement and maintain appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data held on USB sticks, resulting in loss of data accessibility and confidentiality, breach of integrity principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Stored hysteroscopy scans for 4,000–10,000 patients on three USB sticks for nine years without backing up data to Trust servers, failed to conduct risk assessments.
whyTheyWereWrong: Encrypted USB sticks containing sensitive medical imaging data became permanently inaccessible in April 2018, leaving thousands of patients unable to access their own health records.

claimsVsReality.claim: USB sticks were encrypted
claimsVsReality.reality: Encryption keys were lost or forgotten, rendering the encrypted data inaccessible for years; no secondary backup existed

claimsVsReality.claim: Data protection policies were in place requiring USB data to be backed up to Trust servers
claimsVsReality.reality: Policies existed but were not enforced, monitored, or communicated; staff lacked awareness and there was no accountability mechanism

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident was managed appropriately
claimsVsReality.reality: The Trust did not initially recognise the inaccessibility as a data protection breach and delayed reporting to the ICO

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data on USB sticks over nine years
violations: Trust failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data on USB sticks over nine years
No backup of data to Trust servers despite policy requiring it
Inaccessibility of data relating to 4,000–10,000 data subjects due to loss of USB encryption keys or device failure

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(1) requires controllers to implement and maintain appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the Regulation, and to review and update these measures where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: No risk assessments completed over nine-year period beyond basic initial considerations
violations: No risk assessments completed over nine-year period beyond basic initial considerations
Lack of training and awareness of correct handling procedures for USB devices
No Information Asset Owners or System managers appointed to manage USB usage
Failure to oversee policy compliance or raise awareness of data protection obligations

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR on 10 November 2022. The Trust is required to provide an update on progress against seven recommended measures by 10 February 2023, including: reviewing data protection training; incorporating anonymised incident examples; ensuring regular risk assessments; naming Information Asset Owners for all assets; obtaining Asset Owner policy confirmations; reviewing data breach reporting procedures; and ensuring staff understand breach reporting obligations. The Trust has already begun an overhaul of policies, information asset mapping, USB review, and ceased storing images on USB. The matter is closed, but the ICO warned that further incidents may trigger additional formal regulatory action.
companyNow: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust continues to operate as one of the UK's leading NHS teaching trusts. The organisation has implemented remedial governance measures and information asset management processes following the investigation.
dataType: Medical imaging data (hysteroscopy scans)
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Security of personal data
UK GDPR Article 24(1) – Controller's responsibility to implement and review security measures

company: Epsom & St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust
companyDescription: Epsom & St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust is a public healthcare provider in England operating two hospital sites (St Helier Hospital in Carshalton, Surrey and Epsom Hospital) providing acute hospital services to local populations.
companyLongDescription: Epsom & St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust is a public healthcare provider in England operating two hospital sites (St Helier Hospital in Carshalton, Surrey and Epsom Hospital) providing acute hospital services to local populations.
caseDescription: A staff member removed error-correcting coding from a test result report following a consultant's request, causing test results to be falsely reported as positive. This led individuals to receive incorrect NHS Test and Trace isolation instructions and triggered closure of three schools and a nursery. The Trust lacked adequate policies, change management procedures, and information-sharing protocols to prevent the error.
violationSummary: The Trust failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure ongoing integrity and resilience of processing systems, allowing a single staff member's uncontrolled change to propagate false data to external recipients affecting hundreds of people.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: A staff member modified coding in a live laboratory reporting system without adequate testing, removing a duplicate comment entry that had been requested by a consultant.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of individuals were erroneously notified they had tested positive for COVID-19 and were told to isolate, leading to staff unable to work, postponed surgical procedures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The SGSS reporting mechanism did not allow Trust staff to see results that would be automatically produced, so they could not check them themselves.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Trust was responsible for ensuring appropriate security controls regardless of system limitations; the lack of visibility was itself a sign that testing and validation procedures were inadequate

claimsVsReality.claim: The staff member was aware of the code's purpose and uncertain the action would succeed; he requested checks by PHE which responded affirmatively.
claimsVsReality.reality: The staff member proceeded with a change in a live environment without conducting proper testing first, and no formal validation process existed despite the critical nature of the data being transmitted

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to implement adequate controls to ensure ongoing integrity and confidentiality of test result data processed in the SGSS reporting system
violations: Trust failed to implement adequate controls to ensure ongoing integrity and confidentiality of test result data processed in the SGSS reporting system
Trust permitted live system changes without prior testing in a safe environment or adequate consultation with PHE

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) and (d) require controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems, including regular testing and evaluation of security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust lacked formal policies and procedures for change management in the microbiology department
violations: Trust lacked formal policies and procedures for change management in the microbiology department
Trust failed to establish a test environment for validating coding changes before live implementation
Trust had no documented procedure for recording and cascading externally received information about system impacts
Trust did not conduct Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for the SGSS processing arrangement
Trust had no formal contract or data sharing agreement with PHE regarding SGSS use

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand under Article 58 of the GDPR. The Trust is required to: implement procedures for recording and cascading external information; build risk analysis into change management for coding changes; undertake a DPIA; establish a test environment for validating amendments; strengthen staff training on data protection policies; and negotiate a formal data sharing agreement with PHE. The case is closed pending any further information or incidents.
companyNow: The Epsom & St Helier University Hospitals NHS Trust continues to operate as an NHS provider in England. The Trust has implemented the recommended remedial measures, including updated Microbiology Computing Policy and Protocol.
dataType: COVID-19 test results, health data

companyDescription: PINC Interactive Pte. Ltd. operates pincstyle.com, a fashion and lifestyle e-commerce website. The company was incorporated in 2018 and has been experiencing significant operational losses.
companyLongDescription: PINC Interactive Pte. Ltd. operates pincstyle.com, a fashion and lifestyle e-commerce website. The company was incorporated in 2018 and has been experiencing significant operational losses.
caseDescription: PINC Interactive exposed the personal data of 3,916 real users when a staging database was accessed and exfiltrated from its servers in October 2019. The breach occurred because developers stored database copies on personal devices without security controls and the staging API lacked authentication despite containing real user data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, creating significant risk of unauthorised access, collection, and disclosure through insecure storage and lack of access controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PINC Interactive allowed developers to store copies of a staging database containing 3,916 real users' personal data on unencrypted personal computers with minimal security controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Real users' names, email addresses, contact numbers, and password hashes were exposed and exfiltrated when developers' computers were compromised.

claimsVsReality.claim: Developers had antivirus software installed on personal devices to protect the staging database
claimsVsReality.reality: PINC could not verify the product names, versions, or update frequencies of the antivirus software when questioned

claimsVsReality.claim: The staging database was used only for development and testing with mostly synthetic/dummy data
claimsVsReality.reality: The database contained personal data of 3,916 real users (1.6% of total records) including names, usernames, emails, contact numbers, and password hashes, making it a valuable target

claimsVsReality.claim: Strong password instructions were sufficient security control for employee-held staging databases
claimsVsReality.reality: Developers' computers were compromised despite password instructions, resulting in exfiltration of real user data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: PINC allowed employees to store the staging database on personal devices without implementing any additional security requirements beyond basic password instructions
violations: PINC allowed employees to store the staging database on personal devices without implementing any additional security requirements beyond basic password instructions
PINC left security management to individual employee discretion and was unable to verify what antivirus products, versions, or update frequencies were actually in place
PINC failed to require authentication for the staging API (accessible over the internet) for five months despite it pointing to a database containing real user personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12(a) of the PDPA requires an organisation to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet its obligations under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: PINC admitted it had no data protection policies or practices in place for non-technical employees with access to user data
violations: PINC admitted it had no data protection policies or practices in place for non-technical employees with access to user data
PINC's onboarding briefings and code standards for technical staff did not constitute data protection policies and could not guide employees on PDPA compliance

outcome: PINC Interactive was directed to: (1) pay a financial penalty of SGD $12,500 within 30 days; (2) develop and implement internal data protection policies and practices compliant with the PDPA within 60 days; (3) ensure no local database copies are stored on employee personal computers within 60 days; (4) notify the Commission within one week of completion. The penalty was reduced from a higher amount due to the organisation's financial circumstances (significant operational losses since 2018 inception) and mitigation factors including cooperation during investigation and remedial actions taken post-incident.
companyNow: PINC Interactive Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based fashion/lifestyle e-commerce company operating www.pincstyle.com. The company has been implementing data protection reforms following the 2022 enforcement action.
dataType: Name, username, email address, contact number, password hash

companyDescription: The respondent is a private individual who installed outdoor surveillance cameras on a residential property. The case does not involve a commercial entity.
companyLongDescription: The respondent is a private individual who installed outdoor surveillance cameras on a residential property. The case does not involve a commercial entity.
caseDescription: A private individual installed two outdoor surveillance cameras on their residential property that captured excessive public street space without proper authorization or privacy safeguards. The cameras violated GDPR Article 5(1)(c) by capturing third parties' images without proportionality, affecting pedestrians and neighbors. The authority ordered camera removal or reorientation and imposed a fine.
violationSummary: The cameras conducted ongoing surveillance of public space and third parties beyond the respondent's private property, capturing biometric data (images) of pedestrians without lawful basis or prior notice.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed two residential surveillance cameras on property exterior that captured excessive public street space beyond the homeowner's boundaries, recording pedestrians.
whyTheyWereWrong: The cameras recorded facial images and identities of pedestrians and the complainant's family transiting public streets.

claimsVsReality.claim: The cameras capture approximately one meter of public space and are properly labeled with information notices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Photographs examined by AEPD showed the cameras captured excessive public street space beyond one meter, with field of view not proportional to residential security needs.

claimsVsReality.claim: The third camera on the access stairway captures only the respondent's property and entrance due to family disputes requiring evidence.
claimsVsReality.reality: The stairway camera's field of view was unclear; AEPD could not confirm it did not capture neighboring windows or shared spaces without explicit clarification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be processed with necessity and proportionality — data collection must be limited to what is necessary for the stated purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: The respondent's two outdoor cameras captured excessive public street space beyond minimal necessity for residential security, recording images of pedestrians and neighbors without consent or legal basis.
violations: The respondent's two outdoor cameras captured excessive public street space beyond minimal necessity for residential security, recording images of pedestrians and neighbors without consent or legal basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Art. 22(2) limits videovigilance to capture public space 'only insofar as it is essential' for the stated security purpose; capture beyond this scope is prohibited.
regulatoryFindings.description: The respondent's cameras captured more public space than necessary for property security, failing the proportionality test and creating unjustified surveillance of third parties.
violations: The respondent's cameras captured more public space than necessary for property security, failing the proportionality test and creating unjustified surveillance of third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6 requires a lawful basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests) for any processing of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The respondent processed the images of third parties without establishing any lawful basis; no consent was obtained, and residential security interest does not override third parties' rights to avoid excessive capture.
violations: The respondent processed the images of third parties without establishing any lawful basis; no consent was obtained, and residential security interest does not override third parties' rights to avoid excessive capture.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 & 14 and LOPDGDD Art. 22(4) require transparent notice to data subjects regarding surveillance via infographics or signs identifying the controller and processing purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: While the respondent claimed to display information notices, the cameras' scope was excessive and no proportionality was demonstrated; notice alone does not remedy unlawful scope.
violations: While the respondent claimed to display information notices, the cameras' scope was excessive and no proportionality was demonstrated; notice alone does not remedy unlawful scope.

outcome: The Director of AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Authority) imposed a €300 administrative fine on the respondent for violation of GDPR Art. 5(1)(c). The authority also issued a compliance order (Art. 58.2.d) requiring the respondent, within 10 days, to either: (1) remove the cameras from their current locations, or (2) reorient them to capture only their private property. The respondent was further ordered to provide images captured by the cameras with a site plan indicating which portions correspond to their own property. Non-compliance with the order could trigger a second administrative enforcement action. The decision is final but subject to administrative appeal.
companyNow: Unknown; the case involved a private residential individual, not a registered company. No information about current status is available.
dataType: Biometric data (facial images), location data (public street)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) - Principle of necessity and proportionality
GDPR Art. 6 - Lack of lawful basis for processing third-party data
GDPR Art. 13/14 - Failure to provide transparency information
LOPDGDD Art. 22(2) - Excessive capture of public space

companyDescription: Piraeus Bank (founded 1891) is a major Greek commercial and investment bank providing retail, corporate, and investment banking services. It operates through multiple subsidiaries across Greece and the Eastern Mediterranean.
companyLongDescription: Piraeus Bank (founded 1891) is a major Greek commercial and investment bank providing retail, corporate, and investment banking services. It operates through multiple subsidiaries across Greece and the Eastern Mediterranean.
caseDescription: Piraeus Bank repeatedly sent banking transaction notifications (Winbank Alerts) to a third party's email address due to a typo in a co-account holder's declared email. Despite the complainant reporting the breach multiple times and requesting correction, the bank failed to stop the unauthorized disclosures, did not notify the authority or data subject, and took no remedial measures to mitigate the ongoing confidentiality breach.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to prevent and stop unauthorized disclosure of financial transaction data to a third party (due to an erroneous email address) directly breached the confidentiality principle and the data subject's right to data security.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Piraeus Bank continued sending banking transaction alerts to a wrong email address belonging to an unrelated person with the same name, even after the customer reported the breach.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's confidential transaction data was repeatedly disclosed to a third party without authorization, exposing her banking activity and financial information to someone else for months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank claimed no unauthorised forwarding of data occurred because it sent notifications to the address declared by the co-account holder and the Gmail system treated the two addresses (differing only by a period) as identical due to Google's error.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the technical cause, the bank became aware that financial transaction data was being received by an unauthorised third party and did nothing to stop the disclosures; the bank had a duty to mitigate the breach immediately.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank asserted that because the email address was declared by the co-account holder (not the complainant), the complaint did not concern the complainant's own personal data and the right of correction did not apply.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was the account holder and data subject whose banking transaction details were being disclosed; she had standing to report the breach and request cessation of unauthorised processing, regardless of who declared the erroneous address.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank stated it was powerless to intervene because any unilateral correction of the co-account holder's declared address without his explicit request would constitute unlawful processing of his data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank had legal and technical ability to suspend the alert service or redirect notifications while investigating and waiting for the co-account holder to correct the error, especially after being notified of the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed with integrity and confidentiality; appropriate technical and organisational measures must protect data from unauthorised or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank sent banking notifications containing transaction data to unauthorised third party for extended period despite receiving explicit notice from data subject
violations: Bank sent banking notifications containing transaction data to unauthorised third party for extended period despite receiving explicit notice from data subject

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24 requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to demonstrate compliance and ensure lawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank lacked adequate verification procedures to confirm correctness of declared email addresses at account opening and failed to implement safeguards against foreseeable user error
violations: Bank lacked adequate verification procedures to confirm correctness of declared email addresses at account opening and failed to implement safeguards against foreseeable user error

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires the controller to apply appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including regular testing and evaluation of measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to implement confirmation mechanisms or validation steps for email address declarations despite known risk of typographical errors with significant privacy consequences
violations: Bank failed to implement confirmation mechanisms or validation steps for email address declarations despite known risk of typographical errors with significant privacy consequences

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where possible, within 72 hours of becoming aware.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank did not report the breach to the authority after learning from the data subject that her transaction information was being disclosed to a third party
violations: Bank did not report the breach to the authority after learning from the data subject that her transaction information was being disclosed to a third party

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 34 requires controllers to notify data subjects without undue delay when a breach is likely to result in high risk to their rights and freedoms, with clear description of the breach and information on measures taken.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank did not notify the affected data subject of the breach or provide information about the ongoing disclosure of her financial transaction data
violations: Bank did not notify the affected data subject of the breach or provide information about the ongoing disclosure of her financial transaction data

outcome: The Hellenic Data Protection Authority imposed a €10,000 fine on Piraeus Bank for violating the confidentiality principle (GDPR Art. 5(1)(f)) and failing to comply with breach notification obligations (GDPR Arts. 33–34). The authority also issued a compliance order requiring the bank to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to verify the correctness of email addresses declared by customers for receipt of transaction notifications (Winbank Alerts), adding confirmation steps where necessary to ensure declared addresses belong to the person who declared them.
companyNow: Piraeus Bank remains one of the largest banking groups in Greece and operates across the Eastern Mediterranean region as of 2024. The bank has undergone restructuring and capital increases since the financial crisis.
dataType: Financial transaction data, banking activity notifications, email addresses
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 – Breach Notification to Authority
GDPR Art. 34 – Breach Notification to Data Subject

company: WIND Ελλάς Τηλεπικοινωνίες ΑΕΒΕ (WIND Hellas Telecommunications)
companyDescription: WIND Hellas Telecommunications (now Vodafone Greece after rebranding) is a major Greek telecommunications company providing fixed-line, mobile, and internet services through retail stores and direct channels.
companyLongDescription: WIND Hellas Telecommunications (now Vodafone Greece after rebranding) is a major Greek telecommunications company providing fixed-line, mobile, and internet services through retail stores and direct channels.
caseDescription: A Wind Hellas store manager failed to respond to a customer's data access request regarding CCTV footage for over four months, only rejecting it after the authority intervened. The manager claimed the video data had been destroyed due to a hard disk failure, but provided no contemporaneous evidence. The store's identification procedure during contract renewal also deviated from the company's stated policy by relying solely on verbal confirmation of tax ID rather than document verification.
violationSummary: The failure to respond to a lawful data subject access request within the prescribed timeframe and the lack of adequate technical and organizational measures to preserve recorded data (CCTV footage) constitutes both a procedural violation and a security/availability failure. The exposure category applies because the customer's right to access information about themselves was effectively denied.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: WIND store manager ignored a customer's July 2020 request for CCTV footage for four months, then rejected it by claiming the video had been destroyed without providing timely notice or proof.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was left without access to evidence of a contract renewal transaction for 120 days, exposing them to potential disputes over what actually occurred during that store visit with no.

claimsVsReality.claim: The store manager claimed the customer was known and recognizable to store staff, requiring no identification document.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer stated he had never seen the employee who served him before and only provided his phone number; no actual recognition occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: The store manager stated CCTV footage could not be provided due to a hard disk failure affecting archived files.
claimsVsReality.reality: No contemporaneous evidence or timely notice of the technical failure was provided; the claim was made only four months after the access request, following regulatory intervention.

claimsVsReality.claim: Wind Hellas stated identification procedures required document verification for all contract renewals.
claimsVsReality.reality: In this case, identification relied solely on verbal confirmation of the tax ID number without document presentation or verification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants the data subject the right to obtain confirmation of whether personal data is being processed and to receive a copy of the data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The store manager, as data controller for the CCTV system under the franchisee arrangement, did not respond to the customer's July 29, 2020 data access request within any reasonable timeframe, only rejecting it on November 28, 2020 (4 months later) after the authority's intervention.
violations: The store manager, as data controller for the CCTV system under the franchisee arrangement, did not respond to the customer's July 29, 2020 data access request within any reasonable timeframe, only rejecting it on November 28, 2020 (4 months later) after the authority's intervention.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken within one month of receipt of the request, without undue delay, or to inform the data subject of any extension.
regulatoryFindings.description: No response was given within one month or any extension notification. The store manager did not acknowledge or respond to the access request submitted on July 29, 2020 until November 28, 2020.
violations: No response was given within one month or any extension notification. The store manager did not acknowledge or respond to the access request submitted on July 29, 2020 until November 28, 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(2) and (4) require the controller to implement technical and organizational measures to ensure security and availability of personal data processed, including against accidental loss.
regulatoryFindings.description: The store failed to maintain backup or recovery procedures for CCTV data; a single hard disk failure resulted in claimed permanent loss of all recorded footage. No evidence was provided that adequate safeguards, redundancy, or backup systems were in place.
violations: The store failed to maintain backup or recovery procedures for CCTV data; a single hard disk failure resulted in claimed permanent loss of all recorded footage. No evidence was provided that adequate safeguards, redundancy, or backup systems were in place.

outcome: The Hellenic Data Protection Authority (DPA) found the store manager (identified as 'B') liable as data controller for the CCTV surveillance system and imposed a fine of €2,000 for failure to respond to the data subject's access request within the statutory deadline. The authority determined that under the franchise agreement, the store manager retained autonomous decision-making authority over the store's security measures, including CCTV. The fine reflects the nature and gravity of the violation, the fact that only one individual was affected (who suffered no direct economic harm), the absence of intent, prior violations, or special category data, and the low risk profile of fixed-line service renewal. The company is now required to comply with all applicable GDPR requirements in processing personal data.
companyNow: WIND Hellas Telecommunications remains operational in Greece as a major telecom provider. The company operates numerous retail locations and continues to provide fixed-line, mobile, and internet services.
dataType: Personal identification data (name, tax ID number), CCTV video footage

companyDescription: EDYTE A.E. is an electronic voting platform provider that operated the ZEUS e-voting system used for the EDOEA (journalist union) elections. It acted as a data processor handling sensitive voter registration and ballot data.
companyLongDescription: EDYTE A.E. is an electronic voting platform provider that operated the ZEUS e-voting system used for the EDOEA (journalist union) elections. It acted as a data processor handling sensitive voter registration and ballot data.
caseDescription: EDYTE A.E., a processor handling electronic voting data for EDOEA, disclosed approximately 4,500 voters' personal data to three political candidates despite explicit objections from the data controller. The disclosure included sensitive voting information and voter identification details without proper authorization or data subject notification. This violated GDPR requirements for processor conduct and data subject transparency.
violationSummary: EDYTE improperly disclosed confidential voter data to third parties without lawful basis or data subject knowledge, violating the confidentiality obligations of a data processor under GDPR.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: EDYTE A.E. transmitted personal data of approximately 4,500 voters including names, email addresses, IP addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: The disclosure exposed thousands of voters' sensitive information revealing their voting patterns, submission times, and unique identifiers, enabling the recipients to identify.

claimsVsReality.claim: EDYTE claimed it was obligated by law to comply with the prosecutor's order and therefore had to disclose the voter data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The prosecutor's order was issued to a public sector body (EDOEA is an NPID not covered by the statutory disclosure obligation under Law 1756/1988), was later recalled as non-binding, and did not override EDYTE's GDPR obligations as a processor to follow only the controller's instructions.

claimsVsReality.claim: EDYTE asserted the documents were public administrative records subject to right-of-access legislation.
claimsVsReality.reality: EDOEA is a private non-profit organization; its records are private, not public documents. The data also included sensitive personal information protected under GDPR, which cannot be treated as mere administrative records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 29 requires a processor to process personal data only on instructions of the controller unless required to do so by EU or Member State law.
regulatoryFindings.description: EDYTE disclosed voter data to third parties despite the controller's explicit written objection and without evidence of a legal obligation requiring disclosure.
violations: EDYTE disclosed voter data to third parties despite the controller's explicit written objection and without evidence of a legal obligation requiring disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(10) provides that if a processor determines purposes and means of processing in violation of GDPR, the processor becomes an independent controller and bears all obligations of a controller, including notification duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: EDYTE acted as an independent controller by unilaterally disclosing data and failed to notify data subjects of the disclosure as required.
violations: EDYTE acted as an independent controller by unilaterally disclosing data and failed to notify data subjects of the disclosure as required.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (APDPPC) imposed an administrative fine of €5,000 on EDYTE A.E. for violating Article 28(10) of the GDPR by acting as an independent data controller and failing to notify data subjects of the disclosure. The Authority found EDYTE had breached Article 29 GDPR by processing data outside its processor role and without proper controller authorization. No evidence of compliance remediation or monitoring beyond the fine was specified in the decision.
dataType: voter personal data including names, email addresses, IP addresses, voting behavior, tax identification numbers (AFM), and unique voter IDs

companyDescription: BAYARD REVISTAS, S.A. is a Spanish magazine and digital media publisher that operates a web portal offering cultural and literary content. The company processes personal data from users who register through the portal to access its publications and services.
companyLongDescription: BAYARD REVISTAS, S.A. is a Spanish magazine and digital media publisher that operates a web portal offering cultural and literary content. The company processes personal data from users who register through the portal to access its publications and services.
caseDescription: BAYARD REVISTAS, a magazine and online portal company, failed to implement adequate security measures, leading to unauthorized access to approximately 464,762 users' personal data. The company also delayed notification to the regulator and affected individuals beyond GDPR requirements. The AEPD initiated enforcement action for violations of data security, risk assessment, and breach notification obligations.
violationSummary: The company failed to apply appropriate technical and organizational measures to guarantee adequate security of personal data, as required by GDPR Article 32. This resulted in unauthorized access to a large volume of user data, exemplifying insecurity in processing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: BAYARD REVISTAS operated a website with inadequate security measures that allowed unauthorized access to user databases containing approximately 464,762 people's contact.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 465,000 users had their personal information, including children's identities and home locations.

claimsVsReality.claim: BAYARD claimed it contracted cybersecurity expert ACUNETIX to identify and remediate vulnerabilities after the breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had not deployed adequate security measures before the breach, and vulnerabilities were only discovered when reported by a third party on 22 October 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: BAYARD claimed to have conducted a risk analysis using the AEPD's GESTIONA tool prior to the breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: The risk assessment provided was merely the output of GESTIONA EIDP and failed to identify web-based attack threats or any technology-related risks, making it insufficient for actual risk mitigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: BAYARD stated it could not be certain the breach was real at the time of discovery and therefore did not notify the AEPD immediately.
claimsVsReality.reality: On 28 October 2021, the company was aware enough to consult its data protection advisor, establishing that the breach was real. No notification to the AEPD occurred until 11 November, a 14-day delay.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized processing and accidental loss, destruction, or damage through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: BAYARD failed to ensure adequate security of contact, location, and children's identification data. Data in the database was exposed to unauthorized third-party access due to web vulnerabilities that had not been identified or remediated.
violations: BAYARD failed to ensure adequate security of contact, location, and children's identification data. Data in the database was exposed to unauthorized third-party access due to web vulnerabilities that had not been identified or remediated.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) requires the controller and processor to implement technical and organizational measures appropriate to the risk, considering the state of the art, costs, nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, including pseudonymization, encryption, and regular verification of measure effectiveness.
regulatoryFindings.description: BAYARD's risk analysis using the AEPD's GESTIONA tool was insufficient and failed to identify web attack threats. Pre-breach security measures were ineffective, and no clear link existed between the risk assessment and deployed safeguards. Contingency and recovery procedures were inadequate.
violations: BAYARD's risk analysis using the AEPD's GESTIONA tool was insufficient and failed to identify web attack threats. Pre-breach security measures were ineffective, and no clear link existed between the risk assessment and deployed safeguards. Contingency and recovery procedures were inadequate.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33(1) requires notification to the competent authority without undue delay and, where possible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: BAYARD became aware of the breach on 22 October 2021 but did not notify the AEPD until 11 November 2021, a 14-day delay. The company also delayed notifying affected individuals until approximately 20 November 2021, exceeding the 72-hour requirement.
violations: BAYARD became aware of the breach on 22 October 2021 but did not notify the AEPD until 11 November 2021, a 14-day delay. The company also delayed notifying affected individuals until approximately 20 November 2021, exceeding the 72-hour requirement.

outcome: On 27 July 2022, BAYARD REVISTAS paid €31,200 in penalties, utilizing both a 20% reduction for recognizing responsibility and a 20% reduction for voluntary payment (cumulative). This payment terminated the administrative procedure. The company acknowledged responsibility and waived any administrative appeals. No ongoing monitoring or mandatory remediation orders are specified in the resolution, though the company was required to implement security improvements, which it claimed to have done (hiring cybersecurity firm ACUNETIX, contracting a DPO, implementing encryption).
companyNow: Unknown. BAYARD REVISTAS claims to have resolved all vulnerabilities and implemented additional security measures, including encryption and periodic security audits. Current operational status is not specified in the document.
dataType: Identification data, contact information, location data, children's personal data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of a Personal Data Breach to the Authority

company: MARIA PEDIOTI KAI SIA O.E. (operating as 'Slim Way Rejuvenation Center')
companyDescription: MARIA PEDIOTI KAI SIA O.E. is a small Greek partnership operating a rejuvenation and wellness center offering customer programs and services. The company serves clients through in-person sessions and maintains customer contracts and financial records.
companyLongDescription: MARIA PEDIOTI KAI SIA O.E. is a small Greek partnership operating a rejuvenation and wellness center offering customer programs and services. The company serves clients through in-person sessions and maintains customer contracts and financial records.
caseDescription: A rejuvenation center failed to provide a customer with copies of signed contracts and information about attended sessions and deposited funds despite repeated requests. The company ignored 11 months of successive requests from the Greek DPA and failed to cooperate with the regulator's investigation.
violationSummary: Company excluded the data subject from knowledge and control of her own personal data by refusing to acknowledge access requests or cooperate with regulatory oversight despite explicit legal obligations.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The company ignored a customer's written request for copies of her signed contracts, session attendance records.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was unable to obtain or verify her own personal data and financial records held by the company, leaving her without documentation of services paid for or amounts owed to her.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed contracts were active and customer relationship was ongoing (implying they maintained records and services).
claimsVsReality.reality: Company could not or would not produce copies of signed contracts, attendance records, or information about customer deposits despite years of relationship.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company provided an unsigned, undated document with vague program information after DPA intervention (appearing to attempt compliance).
claimsVsReality.reality: Document was unsigned, undated, had no legal significance, and still failed to provide the specific requested information about contracts, sessions, or balances.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) and (3) grant data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of whether their personal data is being processed and to receive a copy of such data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to provide the complainant with copies of signed contracts and requested information about attended sessions and deposited funds despite written request.
violations: Company failed to provide the complainant with copies of signed contracts and requested information about attended sessions and deposited funds despite written request.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken on a data subject's request without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company never acknowledged the customer's access request and provided no response within one month or any other timeframe.
violations: Company never acknowledged the customer's access request and provided no response within one month or any other timeframe.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(4) requires the controller to inform the data subject of reasons for not acting on a request and of their right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company provided no explanation, reasons, or information about remedies despite the complainant's repeated inquiries.
violations: Company provided no explanation, reasons, or information about remedies despite the complainant's repeated inquiries.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities when requested to assist in their investigative duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company ignored five separate letters from the DPA sent between December 2020 and November 2021, confirmed receipt in one instance, and never provided substantive response despite explicit warnings of administrative penalties.
violations: Company ignored five separate letters from the DPA sent between December 2020 and November 2021, confirmed receipt in one instance, and never provided substantive response despite explicit warnings of administrative penalties.

outcome: The DPA found the company violated Articles 12(3), 12(4), 15(1), and 15(3) GDPR by failing to timely satisfy the customer's access request. It also violated Article 31 GDPR by refusing to cooperate with the regulator. The company was ordered to: (1) pay €2,000 for the access denial violations; (2) pay €5,000 for failure to cooperate with the DPA; and (3) properly satisfy the complainant's outstanding access request for any data not yet provided.
companyNow: Unknown current status. Company operated under the business name 'Slim Way Rejuvenation Center' offering wellness and rejuvenation services in Greece.
dataType: personal customer data, contract details, program attendance records, financial transaction records

company: Toll Logistics (Asia) Limited; Toll Global Forwarding (Singapore) Pte. Limited; Toll Offshore Petroleum Services Pte. Ltd.; Toll (TZ) Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: Toll Holdings Limited is an integrated logistics services provider headquartered in Australia with a multinational group structure including Singapore-registered entities providing logistics, forwarding, offshore petroleum services, and related corporate services.
companyLongDescription: Toll Holdings Limited is an integrated logistics services provider headquartered in Australia with a multinational group structure including Singapore-registered entities providing logistics, forwarding, offshore petroleum services, and related corporate services.
caseDescription: Toll's Singapore entities transferred 1,748 employees' personal data to an Australian server without adequate legal safeguards, violating Singapore's data transfer rules. A ransomware attack later compromised the Australian server. While no employee data was actually exfiltrated, the unauthorized transfer itself breached the Personal Data Protection Act.
violationSummary: Unprotected cross-border transfer of personal data resulted in loss of control over data protection standards and exposed it to offshore storage without adequate safeguards, constituting breach of confidentiality obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Transferred 1,748 Singapore employees' personal data including names, addresses, ages, and salaries to an Australian server without legally binding contracts ensuring comparable data protection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees' personal information was exposed to inadequate legal safeguards during transfer, leaving 1,748 workers vulnerable to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Toll Holdings represented that personal data transferred to Australian server was for purposes of performing services under the CSAs with appropriate protections.
claimsVsReality.reality: Organisations had no contractual safeguards ensuring Toll Holdings was bound by comparable data protection standards when receiving the transferred personal data; CSAs contained no data protection provisions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Threat monitoring software detected malicious activity and alerted the MSSP during the Incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: No alerts were brought to Toll Holdings' attention despite detection, enabling the attack to proceed and compromise the Australian server containing unprotected employee data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 26 of the PDPA prohibits transfer of personal data outside Singapore except in accordance with prescribed requirements. Regulation 9(1)(b) of PDPR 2014 and Regulation 10(1) of PDPR 2021 require transferring organisations to take appropriate steps to ensure recipients are bound by legally enforceable obligations providing comparable data protection standards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisations transferred 1,748 employees' personal data to Australian server without ensuring Toll Holdings was bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide comparable protection
violations: Organisations transferred 1,748 employees' personal data to Australian server without ensuring Toll Holdings was bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide comparable protection
While the contract between Toll Holdings and HR Vendor included data protection terms, the Organisations were not parties to that agreement
CSAs between Organisations and Toll Holdings contained no data protection provisions or obligations regarding transferred personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisations did not breach the Protection Obligation as industry-standard security solutions were implemented (end-point protection, logging, monitoring, firewall, intrusion prevention, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing) prior to and at time of Incident
violations: Organisations did not breach the Protection Obligation as industry-standard security solutions were implemented (end-point protection, logging, monitoring, firewall, intrusion prevention, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing) prior to and at time of Incident
Security lapse enabling malicious actor occurred abroad from theft of third-party vendor credentials and was beyond Organisations' control

outcome: Deputy Commissioner administered a warning to all four Organisations in respect of breach of Transfer Limitation Obligation under PDPA s.26. No monetary penalties issued. Organisations had already implemented mitigating measures: (1) executed 'Singapore Data Export Agreement' with Toll Holdings to govern future intra-group transfers with comparable protection standards; (2) implemented comprehensive remedial security measures post-Incident including system upgrades, multi-factor authentication, enhanced monitoring, new MSSP engagement, and cyber awareness training. No other directions necessary.
companyNow: Toll Holdings Limited is an active integrated logistics services provider headquartered in Australia, with Singapore-registered subsidiaries continuing operations. Group has implemented enhanced data protection and cybersecurity governance.
dataType: Name, address, age, salary, driver's licence number, emergency contact details, national ID, fingerprint, medical details, passport details

companyDescription: Farrer Park Hospital Pte Ltd is a private tertiary healthcare institute providing a range of healthcare services in Singapore. The organization handles sensitive personal data of past, present, and prospective patients as part of routine medical operations.
companyLongDescription: Farrer Park Hospital Pte Ltd is a private tertiary healthcare institute providing a range of healthcare services in Singapore. The organization handles sensitive personal data of past, present, and prospective patients as part of routine medical operations.
caseDescription: Farrer Park Hospital failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive patient data processed by its marketing department. For 18 months (March 2018–October 2019), two employees' email accounts were compromised and automatically forwarded 9,271 emails containing the personal data of 3,539 individuals, including 1,923 with medical information, to an unknown third party. The hospital did not detect the breach for over a year, and had not implemented multi-factor authentication or other enhanced controls appropriate for highly sensitive healthcare data.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data (medical information) via compromised email accounts due to inadequate security arrangements, resulting in breach of confidentiality of healthcare records.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Farrer Park Hospital failed to implement multi-factor authentication or enhanced security controls for marketing department email accounts that routinely processed patients' sensitive medical.
whyTheyWereWrong: 9,271 emails containing personal data of 3,539 individuals, including 1,923 patients' medical diagnoses, histories, test results.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had implemented various IT and data protection policies and current market technical security solutions (firewalls, endpoint protection, user behavior analytics, etc.).
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, the organization failed to implement multi-factor authentication for internet-accessible email accounts and did not detect or prevent 19 months of automatic email forwarding of sensitive medical data to an external party.

claimsVsReality.claim: No guidelines, standards, or industry benchmarks existed at the material time for disabling email auto-forwarding in Office 365.
claimsVsReality.reality: Email auto-forwarding had been documented as a known security risk internationally (e.g. Maersk breach in 2018); the absence of formal guidelines does not excuse failure to assess risks from default software settings.

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident was less serious than comparable cases because there was no evidence of further exploitation or misuse of the data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of detected misuse does not mitigate the breach itself; 3,539 individuals' sensitive medical data was exposed, 50 times more than in the SMA case cited, and the hospital took no appropriate preventive action despite handling medical information daily.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication for marketing department's web-mail accounts handling sensitive medical data despite known internet-facing risks
violations: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication for marketing department's web-mail accounts handling sensitive medical data despite known internet-facing risks
Did not conduct risk assessment of Microsoft Office 365's default email auto-forwarding feature or disable it despite documented security risks
Failed to implement enhanced access controls (e.g. IP whitelisting, secure portals, data purging policies) proportionate to the volume and sensitivity of medical information processed
Lack of detective controls meant auto-forwarding continued undetected for 19 months (March 2018 to October 2019)

outcome: Farrer Park Hospital was ordered to pay SGD 58,000 in financial penalty within 30 days. The organization had already implemented remedial measures including disabling auto-forwarding for end-users, increasing cybersecurity training frequency, and upgrading network and endpoint security by 2022. The Commission accepted the hospital's voluntary acceptance of liability but rejected arguments that lack of misuse, prompt remediation, or comparison to less serious prior cases warranted further reduction. No additional compliance directions were imposed given the remedial actions already undertaken.
companyNow: Farrer Park Hospital is a private tertiary healthcare provider operating in Singapore. Current operational status and any subsequent security incidents not disclosed in this decision.
dataType: Medical information (diagnoses, health conditions, medical history, test results/reports), name, gender, nationality, date of birth, NRIC number, passport details, contact number, photograph
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation — reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Small hospitality establishment (bar/café) operating in Madrid, Spain. Regented by individual proprietor with limited data protection knowledge.
companyLongDescription: Small hospitality establishment (bar/café) operating in Madrid, Spain. Regented by individual proprietor with limited data protection knowledge.
caseDescription: Bar owner installed security cameras that captured public street, sidewalks, and parked vehicles without justification. One camera focused entirely on the public sidewalk and opposite street, recording third parties and vehicle data. No external warning sign was posted about video surveillance in the public-facing area.
violationSummary: Unauthorized video surveillance of public space and third parties exceeding the scope necessary for private security. Excessive orientation toward public space violates data minimization (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c)) and intrudes on individuals' privacy in public areas.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: BAR NEW TEMPO installed a security camera oriented toward public street that captured the entire sidewalk, parked vehicles on both sides of the street.
whyTheyWereWrong: The camera recorded personal data of strangers including their faces, vehicle license plates, and movements in public space without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Owner claimed an informational sign was installed inside the bar with name, DNI, and postal address, plus information on rights exercise procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sign was only placed inside the bar; no external warning sign existed in the public-facing area where cameras recorded public space—third parties outside could not see any notice.

claimsVsReality.claim: Owner stated Camera 5 was part of the business security system.
claimsVsReality.reality: Camera 5's orientation captured an entire public sidewalk, opposite sidewalk, and parked vehicles across the street—data collection far exceeded what is necessary for securing the private establishment.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Bar owner oriented Camera 5 to capture entire public sidewalk, parked vehicles, opposite sidewalk and vehicles—data collection exceeded necessary scope for legitimate business security
violations: Bar owner oriented Camera 5 to capture entire public sidewalk, parked vehicles, opposite sidewalk and vehicles—data collection exceeded necessary scope for legitimate business security
Captured vehicle registration plates and images of unknown third parties without legal basis or justification
No external warning sign posted in public area informing people of video surveillance

outcome: Administrative penalty of €400 imposed. Owner ordered within 10 business days to: (1) Remove the cameras capturing public space with documentary proof (date/time stamped), OR (2) Regularise the system in compliance with applicable law. AEPD warned that failure to comply may trigger further administrative sanction proceedings. Resolution is final in administrative proceedings; owner may appeal to National Court within 2 months.
companyNow: Unknown status. Bar appears to be small, privately-operated establishment in Madrid. Compliance required or cameras must be removed.
dataType: Facial images, vehicle registration plates, location data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lawful basis for processing (none established for public surveillance)

companyDescription: CPR Vision Management Pte Ltd is a CRM system vendor that processes personal data on behalf of e-commerce retailers, including luxury brands L'Oreal and L'Occitane. The company acts as a data intermediary/processor for customer relationship management services.
companyLongDescription: CPR Vision Management Pte Ltd is a CRM system vendor that processes personal data on behalf of e-commerce retailers, including luxury brands L'Oreal and L'Occitane. The company acts as a data intermediary/processor for customer relationship management services.
caseDescription: CPR Vision Management, a CRM system vendor, suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted personal data of over 118,000 customers from L'Oreal and L'Occitane. The attack exploited a compromised VPN account and affected systems that lacked endpoint security protection. The company also retained legacy customer data beyond its retention obligations for over 18 months after deletion instructions.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to maintain reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, allowing unauthorised access and encryption via an unprotected network lacking endpoint security solutions that could have prevented the attack.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: CPR Vision Management failed to deploy its endpoint security solution to an office network despite having it available.
whyTheyWereWrong: The failure to secure the network and delete unnecessary data caused a ransomware attack that encrypted personal information for 118,719 customers including names, addresses, NRIC numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: CPR Vision Management provided a Certificate of Destruction dated 17 May 2021 stating that L'Oreal's customer data had been deleted on 6 May 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: The personal data was not actually deleted and remained on NAS devices in the office network, where it was subsequently encrypted by ransomware on or about 15 October 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: The affected office network was set up for temporary business continuity purposes during the COVID-19 circuit breaker in April 2020.
claimsVsReality.reality: The network remained unprotected and unmonitored for over 18 months until the ransomware attack in October 2021, making the temporary setup rationale inexcusable by that time.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, and loss of storage media.
regulatoryFindings.description: CPR Vision Management failed to deploy its available endpoint security solution to the office network, leaving it vulnerable to ransomware attack via compromised VPN credentials.
violations: CPR Vision Management failed to deploy its available endpoint security solution to the office network, leaving it vulnerable to ransomware attack via compromised VPN credentials.
The organisation maintained inadequate firewall and VPN logging, preventing forensic determination of how the threat actor gained initial access.
No inventory of data assets was maintained, resulting in an entire office network being excluded from security protections.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 of the PDPA: An organisation must cease to retain documents containing personal data as soon as it is reasonable to assume the purpose for collection is no longer being served and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: CPR Vision Management retained legacy customer data for L'Oreal for over 18 months after L'Oreal's explicit deletion instruction on 26 March 2021, despite furnishing a purported Certificate of Destruction dated 17 May 2021.
violations: CPR Vision Management retained legacy customer data for L'Oreal for over 18 months after L'Oreal's explicit deletion instruction on 26 March 2021, despite furnishing a purported Certificate of Destruction dated 17 May 2021.
The organisation failed to delete personal data that should have been removed when the domain controller server was earmarked for decommissioning, contrary to its own data retention policy.

outcome: The Commission directed CPR Vision Management to: (a) conduct a thorough security audit of its technical and administrative arrangements for personal data protection; (b) rectify any security gaps identified; (c) conduct a comprehensive review of all databases containing personal data to ensure compliance with retention obligations; (d) review and update personal data policies within 60 days of audit delivery; and (e) inform the Commission within 1 week of completion. No monetary penalty was imposed in lieu of these compliance actions, considering the organisation's upfront admission of liability and the absence of evidence of data exfiltration or modification. L'Oreal and L'Occitane were found to have complied with their PDPA obligations.
companyNow: Unknown. The case decision does not indicate current operational status of CPR Vision Management Pte Ltd.
dataType: Name, address, email, mobile number, NRIC number, date of birth, age, gender, race, nationality, loyalty points, amount spent

companyDescription: Fashion Nova, LLC is a California-based e-commerce retailer specializing in fast fashion apparel sold primarily through fashionnova.com. The company designs and manufactures trendy clothing quickly and inexpensively, adding 1,000+ new designs weekly, with most items priced under $49.99.
companyLongDescription: Fashion Nova, LLC is a California-based e-commerce retailer specializing in fast fashion apparel sold primarily through fashionnova.com. The company designs and manufactures trendy clothing quickly and inexpensively, adding 1,000+ new designs weekly, with most items priced under $49.99.
caseDescription: Fashion Nova systematically suppressed hundreds of thousands of negative product reviews (1-3 stars) while automatically publishing positive reviews (4-5 stars) on its website from late 2015 through November 2019. This created a false impression that displayed reviews accurately represented all customer feedback, deceiving consumers about product quality and popularity.
