The ICO noted it may revisit the matter with further formal action if additional incidents or complaints emerge. The matter is now closed.
companyNow: The Crown Prosecution Service continues to operate as the primary prosecuting authority for England and Wales. The organisation has implemented recommended logging and records management improvements.
dataType: Sensitive personal data including victim interview recordings (audio/video), case files relating to sexual assault and rape allegations
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018 Section 40 (sixth data protection principle)

companyDescription: Allied Health Professionals (AHP) is a healthcare provider organisation that processes patient health data. The incident involved unauthorized data exposure through system misconfigurations by its IT service provider.
companyLongDescription: Allied Health Professionals (AHP) is a healthcare provider organisation that processes patient health data. The incident involved unauthorized data exposure through system misconfigurations by its IT service provider.
caseDescription: AHP's IT provider Infotex made unexpected, undocumented system changes that exposed patient data to unauthorized healthcare providers without consent. The incident affected 2,573 patients and was not caught during testing due to inadequate change management processes and insufficient data processor contracts. The ICO issued a reprimand for failure to ensure lawful processing under Article 6(1)(a) of the UK GDPR.
violationSummary: Patient health data was made accessible to third parties (healthcare providers) beyond the scope of patient consent due to organizational failures in access control and change management processes.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Allied Health Professionals failed to implement adequate change management processes and processor contracts.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2,573 patients' sensitive health information became accessible to healthcare providers without their consent, directly violating patients' privacy expectations.

claimsVsReality.claim: AHP's systems had routine testing procedures to catch errors and unintended changes
claimsVsReality.reality: Unexpected system changes made by Infotex were not documented or agreed, and therefore were not identified during testing, indicating routine testing was insufficient without proper change management

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 6(1)(a) UK GDPR requires that processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: AHP did not have suitable policies or contracts in place to ensure patients could give or withhold consent to data sharing
violations: AHP did not have suitable policies or contracts in place to ensure patients could give or withhold consent to data sharing
Inadequate change management contracts with Infotex allowed undocumented system changes to go undetected
Patient health data was made accessible to healthcare providers without patient consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 28 UK GDPR requires a data controller to ensure that any natural person acting under the authority of the controller who has access to personal data does not process them except on instructions from the controller, and ensure data processor obligations are contractually documented.
regulatoryFindings.description: AHP did not have a sufficient contract in place with data processor Infotex outlining necessary data protection clauses and requirements
violations: AHP did not have a sufficient contract in place with data processor Infotex outlining necessary data protection clauses and requirements

outcome: ICO issued a formal reprimand under Article 58 UK GDPR. AHP must: (1) continue checking all data processor contracts for legal compliance; (2) ensure future change management documents are clear and specific; (3) maintain staff awareness and implementation of remedial measures. All 2,573 affected data subjects were informed. AHP introduced a processing contract with Infotex and reviewed contracts to prevent recurrence. The matter is closed but subject to reopening if further incidents emerge.
dataType: Health data, patient records

companyDescription: A Hungarian telecommunications company operating customer service with telephone support. The company processes customer data including voice recordings during service calls.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian telecommunications company operating customer service with telephone support. The company processes customer data including voice recordings during service calls.
caseDescription: A telecommunications company failed to provide prior notice to customers before recording their telephone calls with customer service. The company did not inform customers at the start of calls that conversations were being recorded, violating GDPR transparency requirements. The authority found systemic failures in the company's general notification practices and issued a substantial fine.
violationSummary: The company systematically recorded customer communications without adequate prior transparency, preventing subjects from knowing they were being monitored or understanding the scope and purpose of the surveillance.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The telecommunications company recorded customer service calls without providing clear prior notification at the beginning of calls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers had no meaningful opportunity to consent or refuse recording before disclosing sensitive personal information like account details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers were informed of call recording in accordance with legal requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers received no clear, prior notification or delayed/vague notification mid-call, depriving them of knowledge before consenting to recording.

claimsVsReality.claim: Call recording was mandatory under consumer protection law.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumer protection law only mandates recording for complaint handling, not for general network information calls, making the claimed legal basis false for most calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recordings were retained for 5 years as permitted by law.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company later changed the retention period and legal basis, admitting the 5-year period was not justified; the new script (from March 10, 2022) ties retention to civil law statute of limitations or 1 year post-contract.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(1): Data controller must provide information to the data subject in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, clearly and plainly worded.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company provided no notification at all on the September 17 call, and delayed notification until mid-conversation on September 30 with vague language ('this rögzített vonalon') that did not clearly state the call was being recorded.
violations: The company provided no notification at all on the September 17 call, and delayed notification until mid-conversation on September 30 with vague language ('this rögzített vonalon') that did not clearly state the call was being recorded.
Notification was not provided at the start of the call as required, preventing customers from making informed decisions before conversation began.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(1) and (2): At the time of obtaining personal data, the controller must provide the data subject with information including the controller's identity, the purpose of processing, the legal basis, retention period, and the subject's rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company failed to disclose any of the required information (identity, purpose, legal basis, retention period, rights) on September 17.
violations: The company failed to disclose any of the required information (identity, purpose, legal basis, retention period, rights) on September 17.

On September 30, notification was provided mid-call without explaining the legal basis (initially claimed consumer protection law, later changed to legitimate interest), data retention (initially 5 years, later changed), or subject rights.

The general script applied to all customers from June 2021 to March 2022 cited a false legal basis (consumer protection statute) for mandatory recording when no complaint was involved, and kept recordings for 5 years without justification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 4(1): 'Personal data' is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.
regulatoryFindings.description: Voice recordings of customers constitute personal data, requiring full GDPR compliance including prior notification and lawful basis before processing.
violations: Voice recordings of customers constitute personal data, requiring full GDPR compliance including prior notification and lawful basis before processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: Hungarian Consumer Protection Law (Fgytv.) § 17/B(3): Call recordings are mandatory only for handling complaints, not for general customer service calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company recorded all customer calls with uniform scripts citing consumer protection law as the basis, but most calls involved network information, not complaints, making the legal basis false.
violations: The company recorded all customer calls with uniform scripts citing consumer protection law as the basis, but most calls involved network information, not complaints, making the legal basis false.

outcome: The authority found the company violated GDPR Arts. 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) by failing to provide adequate prior notification of call recording. The company was ordered to pay 5,000,000 HUF (approximately €16.8M) in administrative fines within 30 days. The authority also noted that the company's general data processing notice used from June 2021 to March 2022 was inadequate. The company acknowledged the violations and modified its practices effective March 10, 2022, moving notification to the start of calls and changing the legal basis from consumer protection law to legitimate interest with corrected retention periods. The applicant also received 10,000 HUF compensation for the authority's delay in processing. The decision is subject to judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown. The company made internal changes to its call recording notification practices in March 2022, but current status is not disclosed in the decision.
dataType: Voice recordings, personal identifiers (phone numbers, subscriber information)

companyDescription: Drizly operated an e-commerce platform enabling local retailers to sell alcohol online to consumers of legal drinking age across 1,600+ urban and suburban markets in over 33 US states. The company served as North America's largest online alcohol marketplace, partnering with 4,000+ retailers and processing thousands of orders monthly before being acquired by Uber in 2021.
companyLongDescription: Drizly operated an e-commerce platform enabling local retailers to sell alcohol online to consumers of legal drinking age across 1,600+ urban and suburban markets in over 33 US states. The company served as North America's largest online alcohol marketplace, partnering with 4,000+ retailers and processing thousands of orders monthly before being acquired by Uber in 2021.
caseDescription: Drizly failed to implement reasonable information security practices, allowing a malicious actor to access and exfiltrate personal data of 2.5 million consumers via compromised GitHub credentials in July 2020. The company stored AWS credentials insecurely in GitHub repositories and failed to require multifactor authentication or unique passwords for employee accounts. Drizly only discovered the breach through media reports, not its own security monitoring.
companyWorth: Unknown (subsidiary of Uber; Uber market cap ~$95B as of 2024)
violationSummary: Drizly's failures to implement reasonable information security practices directly enabled the breach and exposure of consumer personal information, constituting a core insecurity violation under Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Drizly failed to implement reasonable security practices, storing AWS credentials in GitHub repositories, not requiring multifactor authentication for employee access.
whyTheyWereWrong: A malicious actor compromised 2.5 million consumers' personal data including names, addresses, payment information.

claimsVsReality.claim: All information is 'securely stored within our database' and 'we use standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices such as 128-bit encryption, firewalls and SSL'
claimsVsReality.reality: Credentials were stored unencrypted in GitHub repositories, no multifactor authentication was required, employee access was never revoked, no vulnerability scanning or monitoring systems existed, and passwords were hashed using broken MD5 algorithm.

claimsVsReality.claim: We use 'standard security practices such as encryption and firewalls'
claimsVsReality.reality: No formal security program, no intrusion detection, no data loss prevention monitoring, no regular security audits or penetration testing, and no incident response capabilities (only learned of breach from media reports).

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to employ reasonable security measures to protect consumer personal information, causing substantial injury not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: Failed to employ reasonable security measures to protect consumer personal information, causing substantial injury not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

Made explicit representations in Privacy Policy claiming use of 'standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices' and '128-bit encryption, firewalls and SSL,' which were false or misleading given the company's actual security failures.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging both unfair information security practices (Count I) and deceptive security statements (Count II). As a complaint document, this represents the initiation of enforcement proceedings. The complaint establishes that Respondents' failures to implement reasonable security measures violated Section 5(a), and that their Privacy Policy representations were misleading. Typical outcomes for such FTC actions include consent orders requiring implementation of comprehensive information security programs, independent security audits, board-level security oversight, and ongoing monitoring and reporting obligations.
companyNow: Drizly, LLC became a wholly-owned subsidiary of Uber Technologies, Inc. on October 13, 2021, prior to the breach discovery. As of 2024, Drizly's operational status is unclear, as Uber discontinued the Drizly service in 2024 as part of organizational restructuring.
dataType: Names, email addresses, postal addresses, phone numbers, device identifiers, order histories, partial payment information, geolocation, consumer demographics (income, marital status, gender, ethnicity, children, home value), passwords
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Practices
Implied promise in Privacy Policy regarding 'standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices'

companyDescription: London Borough of Croydon is a local authority in Greater London, England, providing public services including education, social care, planning, and leisure services to approximately 390,000 residents.
companyLongDescription: London Borough of Croydon is a local authority in Greater London, England, providing public services including education, social care, planning, and leisure services to approximately 390,000 residents.
caseDescription: The London Borough of Croydon failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory timescales required under UK GDPR. Only 49.85% of SARs received between April 2020 and April 2021 were answered on time, leaving 155 requests unanswered. The council had not improved compliance during the investigation and maintained a moderate backlog of SAR cases.
violationSummary: The council excluded data subjects from accessing their personal data within the legal timeframe, violating their fundamental right of access under GDPR Article 15.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: London Borough of Croydon failed to respond to 155 of 310 Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory deadline between April 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens seeking their own personal data faced prolonged delays of months beyond legal limits, preventing them from accessing records needed for employment disputes, medical decisions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The council implemented a Subject Access Request improvement plan to address SAR processing delays.
claimsVsReality.reality: The improvement plan lacked detail on ownership, contingencies, and timeframes and had not achieved full implementation by the time of the ICO investigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The council was processing Subject Access Requests in compliance with UK GDPR requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only 49.85% of SARs were answered within the one-month statutory deadline; 155 of 310 requests failed to meet legal timescales.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) requires that 'the data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed, and, where that is the case, access to the personal data'.
regulatoryFindings.description: London Borough of Croydon failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal data for 155 SARs.
violations: London Borough of Croydon failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal data for 155 SARs.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(3) requires that 'The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The council did not provide copies of personal data within statutory timeframes for 50.15% of requests received.
violations: The council did not provide copies of personal data within statutory timeframes for 50.15% of requests received.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to 'provide information on action taken on a request from the data subject without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receipt of the request.'
regulatoryFindings.description: Only 49.85% of SARs were responded to within one month; the remaining 155 requests exceeded the statutory deadline.
violations: Only 49.85% of SARs were responded to within one month; the remaining 155 requests exceeded the statutory deadline.

outcome: The ICO issued London Borough of Croydon a formal reprimand under Article 58 of UK GDPR. The council is required to: (1) ensure all Subject Access Requests are responded to within statutory deadlines; (2) complete a policy and procedure review for SARs; (3) ensure adequate staff resourcing; (4) improve SAR recording and monitoring; (5) develop a detailed improvement plan addressing the SAR backlog. The council must provide updates to the ICO after 3 months (26 October 2022) and 6 months (26 January 2023). The ICO warned that further non-compliance or incidents could result in additional formal regulatory action. The matter is now closed pending receipt of progress updates.
companyNow: London Borough of Croydon continues to operate as a local government authority in England, responsible for providing public services to residents in Croydon.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (type not specified in document)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 15(1) – Right to confirmation and access to personal data
GDPR Article 15(3) – Obligation to provide copy of personal data
GDPR Article 12(3) – Obligation to respond to requests without undue delay and at latest within one month

companyDescription: Regionstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is the governing body of Region Uppsala, a regional healthcare authority in Sweden responsible for administering hospitals, clinics, and healthcare services across the Uppsala region.
companyLongDescription: Regionstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is the governing body of Region Uppsala, a regional healthcare authority in Sweden responsible for administering hospitals, clinics, and healthcare services across the Uppsala region.
caseDescription: Region Uppsala transmitted sensitive patient health data and personal identification numbers via unencrypted email over nearly four years. Although the email transport was encrypted (TLS 1.2), the actual patient information in Excel files was sent in plaintext, exposing 100,000 to 500,000 individuals to potential unauthorized access. The practice violated the organization's own internal guidelines prohibiting sensitive data transmission via email.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures (encryption at rest) to protect sensitive health data against unauthorized access and disclosure, despite knowing the risks and having internal guidelines prohibiting email transmission of such data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Region Uppsala transmitted unencrypted patient health records, diagnosis codes, and personal ID numbers via email approximately 25 times monthly (automated).
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 100,000 and 500,000 patients' sensitive health data and identification numbers were accessible in plaintext to email recipients despite transport encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Uppsala's internal guidelines stated that sensitive personal data must not be communicated via email.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this explicit policy, the organization transmitted approximately 25–250 emails per month containing unencrypted sensitive patient health data and identification numbers via email for nearly four years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Email transport was encrypted using TLS 1.2 protocol, providing secure transmission.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although transport encryption prevented interception during transmission, the data within Excel files was not encrypted and remained readable in plaintext once received, exposing it to unauthorized access by recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32.1 requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Uppsala transmitted sensitive health data and personal identification numbers via email in unencrypted Excel files, accessible in plaintext to all recipients despite encrypted transport.
violations: Region Uppsala transmitted sensitive health data and personal identification numbers via email in unencrypted Excel files, accessible in plaintext to all recipients despite encrypted transport.
No technical measures (e.g., file-level encryption) were implemented to prevent unauthorized reading or modification of patient data by recipients.
The treatment was systematic and prolonged over multiple years despite the organization's own internal guidelines explicitly prohibiting transmission of sensitive personal data via email.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24.1 requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the regulation, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing and the risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Uppsala identified risks inherent in transmitting sensitive health data via email but failed to implement adequate security measures to mitigate those risks.
violations: Region Uppsala identified risks inherent in transmitting sensitive health data via email but failed to implement adequate security measures to mitigate those risks.
Internal guidelines existed prohibiting email transmission of sensitive data, but the organization did not enforce them through technical controls such as encryption.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Patient data containing health information and personal identification numbers was maintained in cleartext within email files, exposing it to unauthorized reading by both authorized and unauthorized personnel.
violations: Patient data containing health information and personal identification numbers was maintained in cleartext within email files, exposing it to unauthorized reading by both authorized and unauthorized personnel.

outcome: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (IMY, Swedish Data Protection Authority) determined that Region Uppsala violated GDPR Article 32.1 by transmitting unencrypted sensitive patient data. IMY imposed an administrative fine of 300,000 SEK (approximately €32,000) as the primary enforcement action. The decision noted mitigating factors (transport-layer encryption via TLS 1.2, internal-only transmission, and cessation upon incident discovery) but emphasized aggravating factors (systematic multi-year violation, large volume of data, high-risk health information, breach of internal policy). Region Uppsala stopped the practices upon incident notification on 7 May 2019 and initiated work to implement email encryption solutions. The decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Region Uppsala is a regional health authority in Sweden responsible for healthcare delivery and administration in the Uppsala region. It continues to operate as a public regional healthcare organization under Swedish governance.
dataType: Health data, patient records, personal identification numbers, diagnosis codes, contact dates

companyDescription: The Home Office is a UK government department responsible for immigration enforcement, border security, and law enforcement. It was subject to an ICO Assessment Notice regarding data protection compliance concerns in Immigration Enforcement prior to this incident.
companyLongDescription: The Home Office is a UK government department responsible for immigration enforcement, border security, and law enforcement. It was subject to an ICO Assessment Notice regarding data protection compliance concerns in Immigration Enforcement prior to this incident.
caseDescription: A Home Office employee recorded interviews with Windrush scandal survivors on her personal phone without proper authorization or consent protocols, then uploaded them to her personal YouTube account and shared them with 26 colleagues. The Home Office failed to implement adequate data protection safeguards, training, oversight, or impact assessments despite prior ICO concerns about their Immigration Enforcement division.
violationSummary: The Home Office failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures to protect personal data from unauthorized processing and unauthorized disclosure. Recording on personal devices and uploading to uncontrolled public platforms without encryption or access controls exemplifies failure of Article 32 duties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A Home Office employee recorded three face-to-face interviews with Windrush scandal survivors on her personal mobile phone.
whyTheyWereWrong: Three vulnerable Windrush survivors had their deeply personal stories and sensitive data exposed on an unsecured personal YouTube account accessible to 26 employees, with no formal consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Home Office stated the interviews were conducted with willing data subjects who gave consent and had a support person present.
claimsVsReality.reality: No officially recorded consent documentation was maintained; no privacy information was provided to interviewees; no terms of reference or legal basis was documented.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Home Office believed the interviews had been officially recorded within organizational systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: Interviews were recorded on personal mobile phone; neither manager questioned how recordings were made despite one manager refusing to provide an official mobile phone.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach was merely individual human error by the employee.
claimsVsReality.reality: No employees who viewed the YouTube videos raised concerns; no managers considered data protection implications; this represented organizational failure in awareness and oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office recorded interviews on employee's personal mobile phone without security measures
violations: Home Office recorded interviews on employee's personal mobile phone without security measures
Recordings were uploaded to personal YouTube account without encryption or access controls
Links to videos shared with 26 individuals via personal platforms, exposing data to unauthorized access
No guidance on use of personal IT equipment for processing personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(1) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with the Regulation, reviewed and updated where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: No data protection instructions issued by secondment department
violations: No data protection instructions issued by secondment department
No specific data protection training provided to the employee
No checks undertaken to ensure compliance with training requirements
No adequate managerial oversight of the employee's work
No Data Protection Impact Assessment conducted
No Terms of Reference completed for the project

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(1)(a) requires implementation of appropriate technical and organisational measures including pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data as appropriate to risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Interview recordings stored in unencrypted format on personal device
violations: Interview recordings stored in unencrypted format on personal device
No pseudonymization of data subjects in recordings
No consent documentation maintained for processing

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires implementation of measures to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal YouTube account used for business data storage lacks confidentiality controls
violations: Personal YouTube account used for business data storage lacks confidentiality controls
No system resilience or data backup mechanisms employed
Personal mobile phone used for processing without organizational security infrastructure

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to the Home Office in accordance with Article 58 of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner recommended five remedial actions: (1) mandatory rollout of additional data protection training across all departments with annual refreshment; (2) maintenance of adequate records of training completion with clear accountability; (3) routine monitoring of compliance; (4) review of guidance on identifying data protection incidents; (5) re-circulation of guidance with department-specific awareness sessions. The case is now closed, but the ICO warned that if further information emerges or additional incidents are reported, further formal regulatory action may be considered.
companyNow: The Home Office remains a UK government department responsible for immigration, policing, and security. It continues to implement remedial data protection measures following this incident and prior Assessment Notice from the ICO.
dataType: Personal interview recordings, identity information, immigration case details, sensitive life histories
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 24(1) – Responsibility of Controller
UK GDPR Article 32(1)(a) – Encryption and Pseudonymization
UK GDPR Article 32(1)(b) – Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability

companyDescription: The National Crime Agency (NCA) is the UK's federal law enforcement agency established in 2006, responsible for leading the fight against serious and organized crime, and operating international law enforcement cooperation functions including management of Interpol circulations.
companyLongDescription: The National Crime Agency (NCA) is the UK's federal law enforcement agency established in 2006, responsible for leading the fight against serious and organized crime, and operating international law enforcement cooperation functions including management of Interpol circulations.
caseDescription: The NCA failed to process exception reports generated by its Robotic Process Automation system between December 2020 and April 2021, resulting in inaccurate Interpol records. A data subject's extradition order cancellation was not actioned, leading to their unlawful arrest and 18 hours of unnecessary detention. The ICO found the NCA lacked adequate policies, training, and oversight for managing the critical exception-handling process.
violationSummary: The NCA maintained inaccurate law enforcement data due to systematic failure in process oversight and exception handling, resulting in harm to an individual's fundamental right to liberty.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: The NCA failed to process exception reports generated by its Robotic Process Automation system between December 2020 and April 2021, leaving critical manual tasks unactionable.
whyTheyWereWrong: A person was wrongfully arrested and detained in custody for 18 hours longer than necessary because the NCA's failure to process exception reports meant an extradition cancellation was never.

claimsVsReality.claim: The RPA system was functioning effectively to manage Interpol circulations and updates
claimsVsReality.reality: Exception reports indicating where the RPA could not complete tasks and manual intervention was required went unprocessed for 4 months, causing extradition records to remain inaccurate

claimsVsReality.claim: The NCA had adequate processes for managing critical data accuracy tasks
claimsVsReality.reality: No policy, guidance, training, or oversight mechanism existed for handling exception reports, and no records tracked how often manual cancellations were processed

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 38 of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date.
regulatoryFindings.description: NCA held inaccurate Interpol circulation records by failing to action cancellation of extradition order, resulting in unlawful arrest of data subject
violations: NCA held inaccurate Interpol circulation records by failing to action cancellation of extradition order, resulting in unlawful arrest of data subject
No suitable policy, process, or training existed to action exception reports that flagged records requiring manual updates
Lack of oversight demonstrated by absence of records showing how often manual cancellations were processed

outcome: ICO issued a formal reprimand under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018. The NCA is required to: (1) continue to prioritise and manage exception reports to ensure RPA effectiveness and accuracy; (2) ensure all staff complete annual data protection and information governance training; (3) action any outstanding exception reports. The ICO noted the NCA's remedial steps (establishment of daily priority task, new policy on exception report handling) but warned that further information or complaints may trigger additional regulatory action. The matter is now closed.
companyNow: The National Crime Agency continues to operate as the UK's primary law enforcement agency for serious and organised crime, having implemented remedial measures including formalized exception report handling procedures and enhanced staff training protocols.
dataType: Interpol circulation records, extradition orders, personal identification data
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 38 (accuracy principle for law enforcement processing)

companyDescription: MyRepublic Limited is a Singapore-incorporated telecommunications operator licensed to provide facilities-based mobile services. The company accepts customer orders for mobile services through an online portal requiring customer identity verification documents (NRIC, work passes, residential proof).
companyLongDescription: MyRepublic Limited is a Singapore-incorporated telecommunications operator licensed to provide facilities-based mobile services. The company accepts customer orders for mobile services through an online portal requiring customer identity verification documents (NRIC, work passes, residential proof).
caseDescription: MyRepublic Limited, a Singapore telecom operator, failed to protect sensitive customer data stored in an AWS cloud bucket. An attacker exploited multiple security vulnerabilities to access and exfiltrate personal data of 79,388 customers, including full NRIC numbers, photographs, and thumbprints. The company stored critical AWS access credentials in plaintext in source code and exposed them via a public-facing PHP information page.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (Protection Obligation under s.24 PDPA) to protect against unauthorised access, collection, and disclosure of sensitive personal data. Multiple critical vulnerabilities enabled compromise of credentials and subsequent data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MyRepublic stored AWS access credentials in plaintext source code and exposed them through a public PHP info page.
whyTheyWereWrong: Threat actors accessed and exfiltrated 79,388 customers' full NRIC numbers, photographs, thumbprints.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to the bucket was restricted through use of an access key (Access Key) in Amazon Identity and Access Management feature, which could only be used to access the Bucket and no other AWS resources.
claimsVsReality.reality: The access key was exposed in plaintext in publicly accessible source code, in a public-facing PHP info page, and in unencrypted log files, allowing any external attacker to obtain it and access all data in the bucket.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bucket was secured by an access key restriction mechanism.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bucket was publicly accessible on the internet without IP-based restrictions, fundamental encryption, or layered security controls, making it discoverable and exploitable by external actors once the access key was compromised.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage AWS access keys: stored credentials in plaintext source code accessible to all developers; disclosed credentials in publicly accessible PHP info functionality; exposed credentials in unencrypted log files.
violations: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage AWS access keys: stored credentials in plaintext source code accessible to all developers; disclosed credentials in publicly accessible PHP info functionality; exposed credentials in unencrypted log files.

Failed to implement reasonable security controls for AWS environment: made the S3 bucket containing 79,388 customers' sensitive ID documents publicly accessible instead of restricting to authorised users only; did not implement layered defences such as IP-based access restrictions.

outcome: MyRepublic Limited was found in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA s.24. The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 60,000 payable within 30 days, with interest accruing on any outstanding amount at the Rules of Court rate for judgment debts. No further directions were issued as the company had already undertaken comprehensive remedial actions including revoking compromised credentials, removing exposed configuration files, enabling version control, restricting bucket access by IP address, rotating all access keys, consolidating AWS accounts with central monitoring, notifying affected customers with credit monitoring services, and commissioning security improvement programme.
companyNow: MyRepublic Limited remains operational as a Singapore telecommunications operator holding an FBO licence under the Telecommunications Act 1999. The company has implemented enhanced security measures and commissioned ongoing security improvement programmes.
dataType: National ID numbers (NRIC), photographs, thumbprints, work pass information, residential address documents, mobile phone numbers

companyDescription: Former Mayor of Municipality X, acting in capacity as municipal official and subsequently as municipal councilor, involved in employment evaluation procedures and personnel management.
companyLongDescription: Former Mayor of Municipality X, acting in capacity as municipal official and subsequently as municipal councilor, involved in employment evaluation procedures and personnel management.
caseDescription: A former municipal mayor disclosed a municipal employee's personal data (name, position, employment status) in multiple letters sent to trade unions and government agencies without lawful basis. The employee had chosen to be evaluated by the incoming mayor rather than the departing mayor, and the former mayor disseminated her details widely while seeking to compel her compliance with evaluation procedures.
violationSummary: The respondent disclosed personal data of the employee to third parties (trade unions, labor federations) without consent or lawful basis, violating GDPR Article 5(1)(a) principles of lawfulness and transparency. The disclosure was not necessary for any legitimate purpose and targeted entities with no involvement in the evaluation process.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A former mayor disseminated a municipal employee's personal data including name, job title, and employment status in letters sent to trade unions, government ministries.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's personal information was distributed to organizations with no role in the evaluation process, exposing her identity.

claimsVsReality.claim: The respondent claimed the disclosure was necessary to verify the lawfulness of the employee's refusal to be evaluated by him and to seek guidance from proper authorities about the evaluation process.
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosure was not limited to authorities involved in the evaluation process; letters were sent to trade unions and labor federations uninvolved in any evaluation, contradicting necessity claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: The respondent argued the employee's personal data was already publicly available on government websites and through 'Diavgeia' (transparency portal), so disclosure caused no additional harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: Public availability for specific purposes (transparency portal) does not permit redissemination for unrelated purposes to unrelated third parties; each processing must satisfy GDPR requirements independently.

claimsVsReality.claim: The respondent contended his actions were justified as exercise of public authority and lawful legitimate interests under GDPR Article 6(1)(e) and (f).
claimsVsReality.reality: Even if a lawful basis existed for some communication, the actual disclosure to trade unions and federations was disproportionate, unnecessary, and violated principles of data minimization and transparency.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) establishes that personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The respondent disclosed employee personal data (name, position, employment status) to trade unions and government agencies without consent or lawful basis, violating transparency and lawfulness requirements.
violations: The respondent disclosed employee personal data (name, position, employment status) to trade unions and government agencies without consent or lawful basis, violating transparency and lawfulness requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) further requires that processing must serve specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and be limited to what is necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure to entities uninvolved in employment evaluation (trade unions, labor federations) was not necessary for any legitimate purpose and exceeded the scope of the evaluation process.
violations: Disclosure to entities uninvolved in employment evaluation (trade unions, labor federations) was not necessary for any legitimate purpose and exceeded the scope of the evaluation process.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 4624/2019 Article 38(2) criminalizes unauthorized disclosure of personal data by persons holding or possessing such data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The respondent, in his former capacity as mayor, knowingly and arbitrarily disclosed the employee's personal data to third parties without legal basis or authorization.
violations: The respondent, in his former capacity as mayor, knowingly and arbitrarily disclosed the employee's personal data to third parties without legal basis or authorization.

outcome: The Data Protection Authority found a violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(a) regarding lawful and transparent processing. The respondent was ordered to cease unlawful disclosure of personal data and fined €5,000. The case was referred to the competent prosecutor for criminal proceedings under Article 38 of Law 4624/2019. The Authority rejected the respondent's arguments that the data was publicly available or that disclosure was necessary for legitimate purposes, emphasizing that neither public availability nor the respondent's claimed legitimate interests override the fundamental requirement to process data lawfully and fairly.
dataType: Personal data of public employee (name, position, employment status, payroll information)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
Greek Law 4624/2019 Article 38(2) – Unlawful disclosure of personal data

companyDescription: Lovebonito Singapore Pte. Ltd. operates an e-commerce platform retailing clothing and accessories, utilizing Magento Cloud for website hosting and Adyen for payment processing.
companyLongDescription: Lovebonito Singapore Pte. Ltd. operates an e-commerce platform retailing clothing and accessories, utilizing Magento Cloud for website hosting and Adyen for payment processing.
caseDescription: Lovebonito's e-commerce platform suffered a data breach affecting 5,561 customers after a Magento CMS administrator account was compromised. Unauthorized JavaScript code intercepted and exfiltrated credit card data and order information. The company failed to implement adequate security measures including robust password policies, two-factor authentication, network monitoring, and system hardening.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security arrangements (adequate passwords, 2FA, network controls, system patching, access restrictions) for systems containing and controlling sensitive financial and personal data allowed unauthorized access and data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Failed to implement a robust password policy, two-factor authentication, network monitoring, system patching.
whyTheyWereWrong: 5,561 customers' credit card data and personal information were compromised when an administrator account with the easily-guessable password 'ilovebonito88' was hacked.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security measures for Magento CMS were commensurate with risks because Credit Card Data was collected directly by Adyen via frame on checkout page without transmission to Lovebonito
claimsVsReality.reality: Lovebonito controlled the Website including checkout page via Magento CMS, creating foreseeable risk that unauthorized access could modify checkout page and intercept credit card data through malicious code injection

claimsVsReality.claim: Two-factor authentication was not an out-of-the-box feature in Magento CMS version 2.3.2
claimsVsReality.reality: Publicly available Magento version 2.3.x user guides show 2FA was already available in version 2.3.2, though not enabled by default

claimsVsReality.claim: 2FA would not have prevented the incident because attacker used API calls rather than GUI access
claimsVsReality.reality: Benefit of doubt given on this point, but fundamental password policy failures (guessable passwords, no periodic changes) were the underlying vulnerability that enabled the breach

claimsVsReality.claim: Number of affected individuals should be limited to 4,474 in Singapore only
claimsVsReality.reality: PDPA protects all personal data in organization's possession or control; 5,561 total customers affected regardless of geographic location

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement a robust password policy for Magento CMS accounts; relied on default settings without mandatory periodic password changes or prohibition on easily-guessable passwords
violations: Failed to implement a robust password policy for Magento CMS accounts; relied on default settings without mandatory periodic password changes or prohibition on easily-guessable passwords
Administrator account password 'ilovebonito88' incorporated the organisation's name, making it vulnerable to brute force attacks
Failed to implement two-factor authentication (2FA) despite availability as out-of-the-box feature in Magento CMS version 2.3.2
Allowed insecure remote access with no/limited system logging and hardening
System was not patched/maintained; failed to upgrade vulnerable Magento CMS version
Lacked security monitoring for network, network ingress/egress filtering, and remote access connection logging
Had improper access control for Magento CMS with excessive administrator privileges

outcome: Lovebonito was found in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The Commission imposed a financial penalty of SGD 24,000 (reduced from preliminary penalty of SGD 29,000 after representations regarding 2FA effectiveness). The company must pay within 30 days or accrue interest at Rules of Court judgment debt rate. No further directions issued as the company implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: unauthorized code removal, customer notification with complimentary credit monitoring, password resets for all Magento CMS accounts, new password policy with 2FA for all accounts, session management, refined access permissions, remote access VPN, endpoint protection, JavaScript injection monitoring, API whitelisting, non-trusted domain alert monitoring, external penetration tests, Magento CMS version upgrade, and CAPTCHA implementation.
companyNow: Lovebonito is a Singapore-based e-commerce retailer specializing in fashion and accessories. The company has implemented extensive security remediation measures following the incident.
dataType: Order data (names, addresses, phone, email, date of birth), Credit card data (last 4 digits, expiry date, billing address)

companyDescription: RedMart Limited was an online grocery and fresh produce retailer operating in Southeast Asia. Following acquisition by Lazada Group in 2016, it was integrated into Lazada's e-commerce platform.
companyLongDescription: RedMart Limited was an online grocery and fresh produce retailer operating in Southeast Asia. Following acquisition by Lazada Group in 2016, it was integrated into Lazada's e-commerce platform.
caseDescription: RedMart failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect a MongoDB database containing ~898,791 customer and seller records. An attacker compromised a GitHub user account, discovered unencrypted API keys in source code, gained access to AWS infrastructure, and exfiltrated the entire customer database. The organisation did not encrypt the database, require authentication, limit API key access, or implement defence-in-depth controls despite handling highly sensitive personal and financial data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorised access, violating section 24 of the PDPA. Multiple layers of security failures (weak access controls, unencrypted keys, no database authentication) demonstrate systemic insecurity in data protection.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: RedMart embedded sensitive API keys in plain text in GitHub repositories and AWS storage, failed to encrypt its MongoDB database.
whyTheyWereWrong: A threat actor exploited these vulnerabilities to exfiltrate personal data of 898,791 customers including names, addresses, contact numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Technical issues prevented implementation of password protection or encryption for API keys
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigations revealed the organisation did not make sufficient efforts to resolve technical issues in a timely manner; all these security measures were successfully implemented post-incident, proving they were feasible

claimsVsReality.claim: Complex IT architecture with layered defence-in-depth strategy protected the database
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple access points presented clear vulnerabilities at every layer; simple errors in access control and key management defeated the entire system

claimsVsReality.claim: Data was out of date and no longer linked to current Lazada systems
claimsVsReality.reality: Back-end systems (order fulfilment, inventory, warehousing, seller portal) continued to be linked to the Affected Database throughout the interim period

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement reasonable access control on GitHub user accounts by not requiring 2FA for accounts accessing sensitive data (Chef key)
violations: Failed to implement reasonable access control on GitHub user accounts by not requiring 2FA for accounts accessing sensitive data (Chef key)
Did not implement sufficient access controls to limit access to Chef and Hubot API keys; keys were accessible to large developer groups without periodic review or removal of unnecessary access
Stored Chef key in plain text hardcoded in source code and GitHub repositories accessible to multiple developers; stored Hubot key in plain text in AWS S3 bucket
Did not encrypt the MongoDB database or implement any password authentication requirement to access it
Failed to implement separate authentication requirements for the Affected Database; only general RedMart Cloud environment access controls existed
Did not conduct periodic management reviews to ensure API key access was limited to accounts requiring it or to remove unnecessary accounts

outcome: The Personal Data Protection Commission determined that RedMart breached section 24 of the PDPA by failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. The organisation was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD 72,000 within 30 days. No further directions were issued as RedMart had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: database authentication for all databases with personal data, 2FA for all GitHub accounts, restricted IP-based access to sensitive databases, security architecture reviews, removal of hardcoded keys from source code, network traffic logging, endpoint detection and response systems, security monitoring for cloud instances, VPC logging, and mandatory employee privacy training.
companyNow: RedMart was acquired by Lazada Group in 2016 and its customer-facing operations were integrated into Lazada's platform. The organisation ceased independent operations with its website and mobile application shut down on 15 March 2019.
dataType: Names, email addresses, contact numbers, residential addresses, partial credit card details, hashed passwords, call recording URLs

companyDescription: A small HVAC (plumbing and heating) installation and repair service operating in Hungary with approximately 31 employees (15 of whom are technicians), processing roughly 140–150 service jobs per month.
companyLongDescription: A small HVAC (plumbing and heating) installation and repair service operating in Hungary with approximately 31 employees (15 of whom are technicians), processing roughly 140–150 service jobs per month.
caseDescription: A plumbing and heating installation company recorded audio of customers and workers during service calls without proper legal basis, adequate transparency, or documented justification. The company made audio recordings on an ad-hoc basis decided by management, stored them on an offline laptop for up to 6 months, and provided only vague consent language on work orders.
violationSummary: The company systematically recorded audio in customer premises and involved workers without explicit, informed consent and proper legal justification. This falls under surveillance—collection of data about individuals' conversations without transparent notice and lawful basis.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The company recorded customers' and employees' voices during heating and plumbing installation work using a dictaphone on the manager's instruction.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers and employees were exposed to covert audio surveillance of private conversations during home visits without understanding why their voices were being captured.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated audio recording was done 'on an ad-hoc basis' and 'only in exceptional cases' based on manager discretion.
claimsVsReality.reality: The work order template included blanket consent language for 'audio, video, and image recording,' indicating audio recording was treated as a standard practice, not an exception; the company later admitted two recordings were made in practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed the purpose was 'customer protection' and to document conversations to prove workers provided proper service information.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented interest-balancing test, purpose statement, or necessity assessment was completed before recordings were made; recording workers' conversations exceeded what was needed and constituted workplace surveillance without proper justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserted that consent was provided on the work order and verbally on-site.
claimsVsReality.reality: The work-order consent was vague and did not meet GDPR transparency requirements (no mention of purpose, legal basis, retention period, rights, etc.); alleged verbal consent is unverifiable and lacks the written documentation required by the accountability principle.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated it had a documented procedure and rules for handling recordings.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had only informal oral instructions from management; no written data protection policy, no interest-balancing procedure, no formal rules, and no systematic documentation of the processing activity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(b) requires personal data to be collected only for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company recorded audio for purposes stated vaguely as 'customer protection' and 'documentation' on work orders, without a clear, predetermined, documented purpose that would satisfy GDPR's purpose-limitation requirement.
violations: The company recorded audio for purposes stated vaguely as 'customer protection' and 'documentation' on work orders, without a clear, predetermined, documented purpose that would satisfy GDPR's purpose-limitation requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data to be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary (data minimisation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Recording full conversations during service calls captures information unrelated to the stated purpose; workers' background conversations and customer personal information incidental to the work were unnecessarily recorded.
violations: Recording full conversations during service calls captures information unrelated to the stated purpose; workers' background conversations and customer personal information incidental to the work were unnecessarily recorded.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing be lawful based on at least one of six legal bases (e.g. consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interest).
regulatoryFindings.description: The company claimed consent via work order but the language was insufficient and unclear. When it later claimed 'legitimate interest' (Art. 6(1)(f)), it had performed no documented interest-balancing test beforehand, and the purported interest (proving customer information provision/monitoring workers) could be achieved through less intrusive means.
violations: The company claimed consent via work order but the language was insufficient and unclear. When it later claimed 'legitimate interest' (Art. 6(1)(f)), it had performed no documented interest-balancing test beforehand, and the purported interest (proving customer information provision/monitoring workers) could be achieved through less intrusive means.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) establishes accountability: the controller must be responsible for compliance and able to demonstrate it.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company maintained no written procedures, no interest-balancing documentation, no clear data-handling protocols beyond manager's ad-hoc decisions; it could not demonstrate why recording was necessary or how it balanced against individuals' privacy rights.
violations: The company maintained no written procedures, no interest-balancing documentation, no clear data-handling protocols beyond manager's ad-hoc decisions; it could not demonstrate why recording was necessary or how it balanced against individuals' privacy rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13(1)-(2) requires that when data is collected directly from individuals, the controller must provide specified information (identity, purpose, legal basis, retention period, rights, etc.) at the time of collection.
regulatoryFindings.description: The work order's brief mention ('agrees to audio/video recording') lacked all required information: no explanation of purpose, legal basis, data retention, rights, or how recording would be used; no reference to a data protection officer; insufficient transparency.
violations: The work order's brief mention ('agrees to audio/video recording') lacked all required information: no explanation of purpose, legal basis, data retention, rights, or how recording would be used; no reference to a data protection officer; insufficient transparency.

outcome: The Hungarian Data Protection Authority (NAIH) found the company violated GDPR Articles 5, 6, and 13. The authority imposed a fine of 300,000 HUF. The company had already discontinued the recording practice following the authority's initial inquiry. The authority ordered the seizure of recordings to be lifted. No further corrective action was mandated because the practice had been discontinued, but the company must ensure future processing is GDPR-compliant, including documented interest balancing and proper transparency for any lawful surveillance activity.
companyNow: The company voluntarily discontinued audio recording during service calls after the authority's investigation inquiry. Current compliance status and operational details are not disclosed in the decision.
dataType: Voice recordings, audio data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13(1)-(2) – Transparency/information to be provided

companyDescription: Power Leisure Bookmakers Limited is a UK-based sports betting and gambling operator located in London.
companyLongDescription: Power Leisure Bookmakers Limited is a UK-based sports betting and gambling operator located in London.
caseDescription: Power Leisure Bookmakers failed to implement robust security procedures to protect customer personal data, resulting in multiple breaches reported between August 2021 and July 2022. The company had inadequate technical and organisational measures, failed to regularly test security effectiveness, and did not properly assess required security levels. Staff also failed to follow established security procedures despite completing data protection training.
violationSummary: The core failure was inadequate security measures and lack of regular testing/assessment to ensure data protection, directly exposing personal data to breach risks.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Power Leisure Bookmakers Limited failed to implement robust security procedures to protect customer personal data, did not regularly test the effectiveness of its security measures.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal data including betting records and financial information was exposed through preventable security flaws.

claimsVsReality.claim: 95% of staff completed data protection training within the last 12 months; all staff involved in breaches had completed training
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite training completion, staff involved in breaches failed to follow security procedures and had poor understanding of data protection implications, indicating ineffective training content and guidance

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: PLB failed to implement robust security procedures to protect personal data, allowing multiple breaches to occur
violations: PLB failed to implement robust security procedures to protect personal data, allowing multiple breaches to occur

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 24(1) of the UK GDPR requires that the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and to be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with the Regulation, with measures reviewed and updated where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: PLB failed to implement and review appropriate technical and organisational measures, and did not update security measures as necessary
violations: PLB failed to implement and review appropriate technical and organisational measures, and did not update security measures as necessary

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of the UK GDPR requires organisations to have a process for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: PLB failed to regularly test and assess security effectiveness, meaning a critical security flaw was not identified earlier and breaches continued to occur
violations: PLB failed to regularly test and assess security effectiveness, meaning a critical security flaw was not identified earlier and breaches continued to occur

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(2) of the UK GDPR requires that in assessing the appropriate level of security, account shall be taken of the risks presented by processing, in particular from accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: PLB failed to assess the appropriate level of security required, taking into account risks from accidental loss or unauthorised disclosure
violations: PLB failed to assess the appropriate level of security required, taking into account risks from accidental loss or unauthorised disclosure

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to Power Leisure Bookmakers Limited under Schedule 13(2) of the Data Protection Act 2018. The company was required to: (1) implement a new robust security process; (2) test integrity of new processes in breach-prone areas; (3) communicate security changes to staff; (4) conduct regular assurance testing and auditing; (5) review internal security procedures regularly; (6) include PLB breach examples in training materials; (7) enhance data protection training with practical guidance tailored to specific roles; (8) send more frequent reminders about secure data handling; (9) regularly review ICO guidance; (10) ensure incidents are reported within 72 hours. PLB was required to provide a progress update by 6 June 2023. The ICO warned that further incidents or information would trigger reassessment and potential formal regulatory action. The matter is now closed.
companyNow: Unknown current status. The company was required to implement comprehensive remedial measures and provide progress updates to the ICO as of June 2023.
dataType: Customer personal data including names, addresses, financial information, account credentials

company: Εθνική Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος Α.Ε. (National Bank of Greece)
companyDescription: National Bank of Greece (Εθνική Τράπεζα) is the oldest and largest commercial bank in Greece, founded in 1841. It provides banking, investment, and financial services to retail and corporate customers.
companyLongDescription: National Bank of Greece (Εθνική Τράπεζα) is the oldest and largest commercial bank in Greece, founded in 1841. It provides banking, investment, and financial services to retail and corporate customers.
caseDescription: National Bank of Greece enabled transaction history storage on Mastercard chip cards without customer consent and failed to notify cardholders of this processing for years. The bank stored details of the last 10 transactions (date, amount, currency) on card chips in violation of GDPR Article 13 transparency requirements, despite prior DPA recommendations to cease the practice.
violationSummary: Transaction history data was stored on card chips and could be read wirelessly without physical card possession, creating exposure risk. Data was collected and retained without transparent disclosure to data subjects, violating Article 13 GDPR.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: National Bank of Greece embedded transaction history (date, amount, currency) for the last 10 purchases on Mastercard chip cards without customers' explicit consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of cardholders unknowingly carried detailed spending records accessible via contactless reading, exposing intimate financial patterns to anyone with a smartphone nearby.

claimsVsReality.claim: The transaction history feature presented no significant security risk because it stored only date, amount and currency; required special equipment to read; and was protected by card possession requirement.
claimsVsReality.reality: Any smartphone with NFC capability and freely available software could wirelessly read the data without possessing the card. Transaction details could be linked to cardholders via the name printed on card front. Feature was never actually used by the bank despite being enabled.

claimsVsReality.claim: Notifying all cardholders would create excessive cost and customer confusion/anxiety without corresponding risk reduction.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR transparency obligations are non-negotiable regardless of cost. Email and digital banking notification methods were already used by the bank. Customer confusion risk does not justify withholding mandatory disclosures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The feature was optional per Mastercard specifications and the bank did not mandate its use.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank actively enabled and implemented the feature on issued cards without obtaining customer consent, making the optional nature of Mastercard's specification irrelevant to customer expectations and GDPR compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to provide specified information to data subjects when personal data are collected from them, including the controller's identity, processing purposes, and legal basis.
regulatoryFindings.description: National Bank of Greece stored transaction history on card chips without informing cardholders of this processing
violations: National Bank of Greece stored transaction history on card chips without informing cardholders of this processing
No transparency provided regarding the legal basis for storing last 10 transaction details
Bank failed to offer cardholders the ability to object to this specific processing despite it being optional functionality

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Transaction data processing lacked transparency — cardholders unaware their transaction details were being retained on chips
violations: Transaction data processing lacked transparency — cardholders unaware their transaction details were being retained on chips
Processing continued despite 2018 DPA recommendation to cease or provide notice

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires processing to be based on at least one lawful basis — consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests with appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: No valid legal basis established for storing transaction history on chips — not required for card function, not consented to, not contractually necessary
violations: No valid legal basis established for storing transaction history on chips — not required for card function, not consented to, not contractually necessary
Bank claimed potential legitimate interest in dispute resolution but this was merely speculative and not disclosed to customers

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (DPA) found National Bank of Greece in breach of GDPR Article 13 and the transparency principle. The bank was ordered to cease the undisclosed processing and comply with transparency requirements. A fine of €20,000 was imposed. The bank had already begun phasing out the functionality through gradual card replacement, with 78.8% of affected cards (3.1 million of 3.96 million Mastercard cards) replaced by the time of decision. New cards issued no longer contained the transaction history feature.
companyNow: National Bank of Greece remains Greece's largest financial institution. The transaction history feature on card chips has been fully disabled in all newly issued cards; remaining cards with the feature are being replaced at renewal.
dataType: Financial transaction data, payment card history, date and amount of transactions
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 13 (information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject)
GDPR Article 5(1)(a) (lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle)

companyDescription: Accor SA is a French multinational hospitality company and one of the world's largest hotel groups, managing and franchising over 5,600 hotels under brands including Sofitel, Novotel, Ibis, and Raffles.
companyLongDescription: Accor SA is a French multinational hospitality company and one of the world's largest hotel groups, managing and franchising over 5,600 hotels under brands including Sofitel, Novotel, Ibis, and Raffles.
caseDescription: Accor SA failed to provide easily accessible information about marketing processing and made it difficult for individuals to exercise their right to object to marketing emails and access their data. The French supervisory authority proposed a €100,000 fine, but Poland's authority objected that the fine was too low relative to Accor's substantial turnover and infringements, arguing it would not be dissuasive.
fineDisplay: €100,000 (Draft Decision amount; binding decision requires reassessment)
violationSummary: The violations involved inadequate transparency, security defects, and failures to respect data subject rights of access and objection, making this a processing insecurity issue.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Accor failed to provide accessible information about how it processed marketing data and created barriers preventing customers from objecting to marketing emails or accessing their personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over one million customers received marketing emails without being able to understand or control how their data was used.

claimsVsReality.claim: Accor cooperated fully with the French supervisory authority investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: While Accor did provide information and cooperate, it failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to prevent marketing violations and data subject access difficulties that resulted in 11 formal complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: The €100,000 fine is effective and proportionate given Accor's financial situation and the non-structural nature of the breaches.
claimsVsReality.reality: The fine represented only 0.02% of Accor's 2020 turnover and was negligible for a company with over €1.6 billion in annual turnover, failing to deter similar infringements by Accor or other large hospitality companies.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(1) requires that administrative fines be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive in each individual case.
regulatoryFindings.description: Accor failed to provide adequate information on its marketing data processing to over 1 million newsletter subscribers.
violations: Accor failed to provide adequate information on its marketing data processing to over 1 million newsletter subscribers.
