violations: Egnatia Odos treated the complainant as a third party seeking access to toll system records, when he was the actual subject of the toll violation allegation and thus the data subject with respect to his own passage and charge.

outcome: The Greek DPA (Αρχή Προστασίας Δεδομένων Προσωπικού Χαρακτήρα) imposed a fine of €1,000 for violation of GDPR Article 12(3) due to delayed and initially refused response to the data access request. The decision found that Egnatia Odos had received prior guidance from the DPA (in 2017) on its obligations to honor subject access requests for video evidence, yet the company persisted in denying access based on a misinterpretation of law enforcement exceptions. After the DPA's intervention, the company eventually provided a one-page excerpt from its incident log but no video footage, claiming a technical malfunction prevented recording on the day in question. The DPA emphasized that the company's negligence in satisfying the right of access, combined with knowledge of its obligations, warranted an administrative penalty, even though the company ultimately complied.
companyNow: Egnatia Odos A.E. continues to operate as Greece's toll highway operator. The company has reportedly commenced compliance procedures with GDPR following the enforcement action.
dataType: Vehicle registration data, license plate information, personal identification data, video surveillance recordings
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 4(1) – definition of data subject vs. third party

companyDescription: Wakefield Council is a local government authority in West Yorkshire, England, responsible for public services including children's social care and legal proceedings.
companyLongDescription: Wakefield Council is a local government authority in West Yorkshire, England, responsible for public services including children's social care and legal proceedings.
caseDescription: Wakefield Council disclosed a mother's home address and her two children's details in court protection documents sent to the father, despite the mother's documented fear of domestic violence. The breach occurred due to failure to redact confidential information and lack of documented procedures for handling sensitive court documents.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of personal data (home address) to third party (father) not authorized to receive it, resulting in breach of confidentiality and integrity of sensitive personal information in child protection context.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Wakefield Council sent a Child Protection Medical Report containing the home address of a domestic violence victim.
whyTheyWereWrong: The mother, who feared the father due to ongoing domestic violence and a previous break-in, was forced to move herself.

claimsVsReality.claim: Court documents were prepared and sent as standard legal proceeding bundles to parents
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents contained unredacted sensitive home address of abuse victim and children despite available 'hide' function and clear need to protect from perpetrator

claimsVsReality.claim: Social Worker identified documents were ready for filing
claimsVsReality.reality: Social Worker failed to identify that mother's confidential address was included in the Child Protection Medical Report

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Wakefield Council failed to ensure appropriate security by allowing unredacted home address of mother (fleeing domestic violence) to be disclosed to father in court documents without identification and redaction controls
violations: Wakefield Council failed to ensure appropriate security by allowing unredacted home address of mother (fleeing domestic violence) to be disclosed to father in court documents without identification and redaction controls

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing complies with regulation, reviewed and updated where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council had no documented policies, procedures or guidance for Social Workers on redacting confidential addresses from court documents or using available 'hide' function on Children's Services system prior to breach
violations: Council had no documented policies, procedures or guidance for Social Workers on redacting confidential addresses from court documents or using available 'hide' function on Children's Services system prior to breach

outcome: ICO issued formal reprimand under Article 58 of UK GDPR. Council required to implement remedial measures including updated Data Protection training, reviewed policies/procedures for redacting confidential information, accountability monitoring through assurance testing/auditing, and organisational sharing of breach lessons learned. Follow-up ICO audit planned for November 2022. Matter closed pending any future incidents.
companyNow: Wakefield Council continues to operate as local government authority. As of May 2022, Council implemented guidance on redaction procedures and mandatory review questions for Team Managers to verify sensitive information redaction.
dataType: Home address, child protection medical information, family circumstances

companyDescription: A small retail fuel station (gas station/petrol station) operator in Greece engaged in the provision of fuel and related services. The operator installed video surveillance equipment to protect the premises and its assets.
companyLongDescription: A small retail fuel station (gas station/petrol station) operator in Greece engaged in the provision of fuel and related services. The operator installed video surveillance equipment to protect the premises and its assets.
caseDescription: A gas station operator recorded surveillance footage capturing a minor picking up a lost item and subsequently shared this recording with police and disclosed it to the alleged victim without proper legal basis or notice. The operator failed to respond to the minor's parent's access request and did not inform the data subject that their personal data had been further processed and transmitted to authorities.
violationSummary: The operator disclosed the personal data (video imagery of a minor) to third parties (police and alleged victim) without adequate legal basis or consent, and failed to provide transparency about this disclosure to the data subject.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A gas station operator installed a surveillance system that recorded a minor, shared the footage with police and an alleged victim without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The minor's image was displayed to a third party and transmitted to authorities without parental consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed she did not have the technical knowledge to edit and transmit only the portion of footage showing the minor.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of technical capability does not excuse non-compliance with GDPR rights. The operator should either have not transmitted the footage at all without consent, or obtained the data subject's permission and only then transmitted necessary portions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed she was unaware that the complainant's son was accused of a crime and that no one had informed her of the allegations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ignorance of criminal proceedings against an individual does not eliminate the requirement to seek consent before disclosing that individual's image or to respond to data access requests from the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator transmitted video imagery of a minor to police and disclosed it to the alleged victim without prior consent or transparent notification to the data subject.
violations: The operator transmitted video imagery of a minor to police and disclosed it to the alleged victim without prior consent or transparent notification to the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12 requires the controller to take action on a data subject's access request and, if not acting, to inform the data subject without undue delay (maximum one month) of the reasons and the right to lodge a complaint.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator failed to respond to the parent's repeated access requests via phone, personal visits, and through their attorney, and did not provide any explanation for the refusal or notification of the right to complain.
violations: The operator failed to respond to the parent's repeated access requests via phone, personal visits, and through their attorney, and did not provide any explanation for the refusal or notification of the right to complain.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 14(4) requires that when a controller intends to further process personal data for a purpose other than the original collection, the controller must provide information about the new purpose prior to processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator did not inform the data subject that the surveillance footage would be processed further and transmitted to police or shown to third parties.
violations: The operator did not inform the data subject that the surveillance footage would be processed further and transmitted to police or shown to third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Guideline 1/2011 Article 9 permits transmission of surveillance data to third parties only upon prior consent of the data subject, or in specified legal circumstances such as legitimate requests from law enforcement, provided the transmission is necessary and proportionate.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator transmitted the minor's image without first establishing whether a legal basis existed and without confirming the proportionality of disclosing a minor's image to resolve a property dispute.
violations: The operator transmitted the minor's image without first establishing whether a legal basis existed and without confirming the proportionality of disclosing a minor's image to resolve a property dispute.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority imposed an effective, proportionate and deterrent administrative monetary penalty of €3,000 on the gas station operator for failing to respond to the data subject's access request, failing to provide notice of the refusal with reasons, failing to inform the data subject about further processing and transmission of their personal data to law enforcement and third parties, and failing to establish proper legal basis and transparency for the disclosure of surveillance footage containing a minor's image.
companyNow: Unknown — the entity is a sole proprietorship (gas station) in Greece; current operational status not specified in the decision.
dataType: Video surveillance imagery of a minor
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 12 - Right of access and duty to respond
GDPR Article 14(4) - Obligation to provide information when processing for different purpose
Guideline 1/2011 Article 9 - Transmission of surveillance data to third parties
GDPR Article 6 - Legal basis for processing

companyDescription: HM Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS) is an executive agency of the UK Ministry of Justice responsible for operating the courts and tribunal system in England and Wales.
companyLongDescription: HM Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS) is an executive agency of the UK Ministry of Justice responsible for operating the courts and tribunal system in England and Wales.
caseDescription: HMCTS staff used a bulk amendment tool (ATM) to adjourn court cases during COVID-19 lockdowns, causing guilty/not guilty plea records to be incorrectly recorded and automatically cascaded to the Police National Computer. The organisation failed to provide adequate staff guidance, conduct risk assessments, or implement additional safeguards for remote processing, and missed opportunities to identify and stop the ongoing breach.
companyWorth: Part of UK Ministry of Justice (UK government agency)
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate security measures (technical and organisational) to protect personal data processed for law enforcement purposes, particularly when processing shifted to remote work during the pandemic.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: HMCTS used a bulk amendment tool to adjourn court cases during COVID without proper staff instructions or safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of people had their criminal court records wrongly recorded and transmitted to law enforcement databases, exposing them to reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bulk amendment tool (ATM) was introduced in February 2019 with guidance stating it could not be used for adjournments.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff were not adequately re-trained or reminded of this restriction when the COVID-19 emergency required mass adjournments in April-May 2020, and the original guidance was buried and not re-issued.

claimsVsReality.claim: HMCTS issued a staff bulletin on 25 June 2020 informing staff of 'a number of incidents' and errors.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bulletin did not issue a clear directive to cease using the problematic function; it merely repeated old guidance saying 'If you do not want to copy the plea over to other cases, please do not use the ATM functionality,' leaving the flawed tool enabled and allowing the breach to continue.

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident was an unforeseeable emergency response to COVID-19 closures.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the pandemic was unpredictable, the organisation's failure to implement risk assessments, additional safeguards, proper guidance, or adequate training compounded an avoidable breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40: Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: HMCTS did not provide adequate instruction or re-issue critical safety warnings when bulk adjournment functionality was introduced during COVID-19, despite the tool being marked as unsuitable for adjournments in earlier guidance issued over one year prior.
violations: HMCTS did not provide adequate instruction or re-issue critical safety warnings when bulk adjournment functionality was introduced during COVID-19, despite the tool being marked as unsuitable for adjournments in earlier guidance issued over one year prior.
No central directive was issued to staff on how to properly adjourn cases; staff had discretion but lacked clear guidance on risks and proper procedures.
The IT helpdesk failed to recognise reports of errors as indicating a wider data breach, and simply re-issued existing guidance rather than escalating the issue.
No additional safeguards were implemented to ensure security of personal information being processed remotely during the pandemic, despite functionality existing for adequate checks.
Data protection training was inadequate and lacked specific detail on law enforcement processing, risk assessments, DPIAs, and special category data considerations.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018. The organisation was required to take remedial steps including: correcting all affected records; disabling the problematic functionality; implementing a review of guidance available to staff; conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments; establishing a central repository for current guidance and procedures; requiring staff to confirm acceptance of new/updated policies; and reviewing and enhancing data protection training. The matter is now closed pending any further information or incidents.
companyNow: HMCTS remains an executive agency of the UK Ministry of Justice. The enforcement decision and recommendations have been implemented to improve data protection compliance and safeguards.
dataType: Court case data, guilty/not guilty plea records, verdict information
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 (sixth data protection principle – security of personal data)
Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 13(2) (power to issue reprimand)

companyDescription: The Department for Education (DfE) is a UK government department established in 1964 responsible for policy and oversight of education services in England, including administration of the Learning Records Service (LRS) database.
companyLongDescription: The Department for Education (DfE) is a UK government department established in 1964 responsible for policy and oversight of education services in England, including administration of the Learning Records Service (LRS) database.
caseDescription: The DfE permitted unauthorized third-party access to the Learning Records Service (LRS) database containing 28 million records, including children's data, for age verification without appropriate controls, oversight, or transparency. Personal data was processed insecurely and for unintended purposes without data subject awareness.
violationSummary: The DfE disclosed personal data stored on the LRS database to third parties who then processed it without appropriate authorization or the knowledge of data subjects. This represents unauthorized disclosure and subsequent secondary use of sensitive educational data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Department for Education permitted third-party access to the Learning Records Service database containing 28 million personal records.
whyTheyWereWrong: 28 million individuals, including children aged 14 and over, had their educational records shared with external organizations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Third-party organizations accessing the LRS database were processing data for educational service provision purposes as authorized.
claimsVsReality.reality: Third parties processed data for age verification—a purpose not initially intended and not authorized by data subjects, performed without appropriate controls or oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data on the LRS database was being processed securely with appropriate safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: No regular checks were conducted on user activities; the database lacked adequate technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized access or misuse.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data subjects were aware of and had consented to third-party processing of their educational records.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data subjects were unaware of the processing and could not object or withdraw consent, as no transparency information was provided.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: DfE shared LRS database records with third parties and permitted further processing without appropriate lawful basis.
violations: DfE shared LRS database records with third parties and permitted further processing without appropriate lawful basis.
Data subjects were unaware of the processing and could not exercise their rights to object or withdraw consent.
Processing occurred for age verification purposes not disclosed to or authorized by data subjects.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: DfE failed to have adequate measures in place to prevent unauthorised access to the LRS database.
violations: DfE failed to have adequate measures in place to prevent unauthorised access to the LRS database.
No regular checks were carried out on user activities, leaving the database vulnerable to misuse.
Insufficient oversight of third-party processing exposed 28 million records to unauthorized secondary use.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand (rather than a monetary fine due to revised approach to public sector enforcement). The DfE was required to implement five compliance measures: (1) improve transparency around LRS processing so data subjects can exercise rights; (2) regularly review internal security procedures to prevent recurrence; (3) communicate process changes to all staff; (4) conduct thorough Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing; (5) continue data protection training. The DfE had already permanently removed the third-party's access to the database and implemented enhanced registration controls including verification steps, accreditation checks, and routine monitoring for excessive use. Updates were to be provided to the ICO's Assurance Department. The matter is now closed, but the ICO reserved the right to revisit if further incidents are reported.
companyNow: The Department for Education continues to operate as the UK government agency responsible for education policy and services. Following this enforcement action, it has implemented enhanced data protection measures and continues ongoing engagement with the ICO's Assurance Department.
dataType: Educational records, personal data, special category data, children's data (aged 14+)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
GDPR Art. 35 – Data Protection Impact Assessment

company: Kuuhubb Inc., Kuu Hubb Oy, Recolor Oy
companyDescription: Kuuhubb Inc. is a Canadian company with Finnish subsidiaries (Kuu Hubb Oy and Recolor Oy) that developed and marketed the Recolor coloring book mobile application, which was popular with 1–5 million active monthly users in the United States during 2017–2019.
companyLongDescription: Kuuhubb Inc. is a Canadian company with Finnish subsidiaries (Kuu Hubb Oy and Recolor Oy) that developed and marketed the Recolor coloring book mobile application, which was popular with 1–5 million active monthly users in the United States during 2017–2019.
caseDescription: Defendants operated the Recolor coloring app with a 'Kids' category explicitly targeted at children under 13, yet collected personal information including names, emails, photos, and comments without parental consent. The app contained hidden social media features allowing children to publicly post content, interact with strangers, and be tracked for behavioral advertising without any notice to parents.
violationSummary: Defendants allowed persistent identifiers (device IDs) to be collected and shared with behavioral advertising networks (AdMob, AppLovin, Facebook Audience Network, etc.) without parental consent or notice. The Kids category was explicitly designed to attract children, creating a surveillance mechanism targeting minors.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Operated the Recolor coloring app with a 'Kids' category targeting children under 13, collected their names, emails, photos, and comments through social media features.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children under 13 unknowingly posted personal photos, selfies, and comments publicly accessible on the internet, with their data shared to advertisers for targeting.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recolor is a coloring book app for adults.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app contained a Kids category with content explicitly designed to appeal to children (simplified outlines, cartoon animals, licensed characters like My Little Pony), which attracted significant numbers of actual children to the app.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app is a passive coloring activity with no social features.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app incorporated extensive social media features including account creation, public profile pages, ability to post user-generated content (photos, selfies, comments), follow other users, and comment on their work — all without parental knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: User information is secure and not shared with third parties.
claimsVsReality.reality: Children's personal information (names, emails, photos, device IDs, behavioral data) was shared with six advertising networks for behavioral targeting without parental notice or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app is safe for families and all ages.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between August 2017 and June 2019, Defendants received over 120 reports from parents and users that children were using the app as social media; dozens described children posting selfies, graphic images, using graphic language, engaging in bullying, and interacting with adults.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants engaged in deceptive practices by marketing Recolor as a coloring book for adults while operating a Kids category explicitly targeted at children; parents were unaware the app contained social media features enabling public sharing of children's personal information.
violations: Defendants engaged in deceptive practices by marketing Recolor as a coloring book for adults while operating a Kids category explicitly targeted at children; parents were unaware the app contained social media features enabling public sharing of children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 1303(c) and the COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.2 define 'operator' and require operators of websites/services directed to children under 13 to comply with specific requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants were operators of a service directed to children (the Kids category contained cartoon animals, My Little Pony characters, and simplified drawings appealing to minors) but failed to treat the service as subject to COPPA.
violations: Defendants were operators of a service directed to children (the Kids category contained cartoon animals, My Little Pony characters, and simplified drawings appealing to minors) but failed to treat the service as subject to COPPA.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b)–(d) requires operators to provide clear, understandable notice of information practices to parents and to post privacy policies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants failed to provide any parental notice of their collection of children's personal information, including names, emails, photos, comments, and device identifiers; no privacy policy was presented to parents prior to collection.
violations: Defendants failed to provide any parental notice of their collection of children's personal information, including names, emails, photos, comments, and device identifiers; no privacy policy was presented to parents prior to collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5 requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants collected personal information from children with no parental consent mechanism whatsoever; parents were unaware children were creating accounts and posting content.
violations: Defendants collected personal information from children with no parental consent mechanism whatsoever; parents were unaware children were creating accounts and posting content.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(c)(7) prohibits collection of persistent identifiers for behavioral advertising absent notice and verifiable parental consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants allowed six third-party advertising networks (AdMob, AppLovin, Facebook Audience Network, HyprMX, Vungle, Unity Ads) to collect device identifiers for behavioral/targeted advertising to users of the app, including children, without any notice or parental consent.
violations: Defendants allowed six third-party advertising networks (AdMob, AppLovin, Facebook Audience Network, HyprMX, Vungle, Unity Ads) to collect device identifiers for behavioral/targeted advertising to users of the app, including children, without any notice or parental consent.

outcome: The FTC filed a civil complaint seeking monetary penalties of up to $43,792 per violation (adjusted for inflation as of January 13, 2021), a permanent injunction against future COPPA violations, and other equitable relief including rescission or reformation of contracts and refunds. The complaint alleges separate violations for each collection, use, or disclosure of a child's personal information, potentially resulting in massive statutory damages. Defendants are required to cease all violations and comply with COPPA requirements going forward.
dataType: Name, email address, profile photos, user-generated content (comments, selfies), persistent device identifiers, location/behavioral tracking
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) — unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) 15 U.S.C. § 6502(c)
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.2 — definition of personal information and operators
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b)–(d) — privacy notice requirements
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5 — verifiable parental consent requirement
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(c)(7) — prohibition on behavioral advertising without consent

companyDescription: Terra Systems Pte. Ltd. is a communication solutions and call centre services provider operating in Singapore and the region. In June 2020, it was contracted by Singapore's Immigration and Checkpoints Authority to operate a call centre verifying the whereabouts of persons serving Stay-Home Notices during the COVID-19 pandemic.
companyLongDescription: Terra Systems Pte. Ltd. is a communication solutions and call centre services provider operating in Singapore and the region. In June 2020, it was contracted by Singapore's Immigration and Checkpoints Authority to operate a call centre verifying the whereabouts of persons serving Stay-Home Notices during the COVID-19 pandemic.
caseDescription: Terra Systems operated a customer relationship management portal for Singapore's Stay-Home Notice verification programme. On 14 and 21 July 2020, a disgruntled ex-employee accessed and modified personal data of SHN subjects by exploiting weak access controls: generic user IDs, shared common passwords, and unsecured password distribution via Zoom and WhatsApp. The incident exposed 125 individuals' data and modified records of 4 persons.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to take reasonable security steps to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, modification, and disclosure of personal data, breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Terra Systems created a customer relationship management portal for COVID-19 quarantine verification that used generic user IDs (like 'D03').
whyTheyWereWrong: A disgruntled ex-employee obtained the shared password and accessed sensitive data of 125 quarantined individuals including names, contact numbers, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only 4 individuals' personal data were affected by the incident
claimsVsReality.reality: While only 4 records were modified, the weak access controls exposed the data of 125 individuals to risk of unauthorised access; the ex-employee could have accessed all of them

claimsVsReality.claim: The SHN Data was not sensitive and disclosure would not cause discrimination or social stigma
claimsVsReality.reality: In July 2020, during early pandemic uncertainty with high public health concerns and just after circuit breaker measures, SHN data denoted risk of COVID-19 exposure and was sensitive in context

claimsVsReality.claim: The case was less egregious than precedent cases where warnings were issued
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation's negligence was higher than precedent cases because it employed very poor, easily-circumvented access controls (generic IDs, shared passwords, no audit trail) handling critical pandemic health data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement unique user IDs and passwords for agents; instead used generic team-based IDs known to all staff and a common daily password
violations: Failed to implement unique user IDs and passwords for agents; instead used generic team-based IDs known to all staff and a common daily password
Distributed common password via unsecured Zoom briefing attended by ex-employees, and later via WhatsApp
Did not implement web server logging or audit trail functionality to track data access until after first incident on 14 July 2020
Failed to implement policies restricting password sharing or requiring verified identity when agents requested credentials
Did not implement two-factor authentication, unique IDs for individual agents, or other baseline access controls despite handling sensitive pandemic-related data

outcome: The Personal Data Protection Commission found Terra Systems Pte. Ltd. in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. The organisation was ordered to pay SGD 12,000 within 30 days. No additional directions were imposed because the company had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures: ceasing common passwords, assigning unique user IDs and passwords, implementing two-factor authentication, and performing security scanning. The organisation cooperated throughout the investigation.
dataType: Name, last 4 digits of NRIC (national ID), gender, contact number, residential address, COVID-19 test appointment dates

companyDescription: Individual political candidate running for national office in July 2019 Greek elections who engaged in direct telephone-based political campaigning.
companyLongDescription: Individual political candidate running for national office in July 2019 Greek elections who engaged in direct telephone-based political campaigning.
caseDescription: A political candidate made unsolicited political telephone calls to voters without proper consent verification or compliance with the Greek electronic communications law's opt-out registry requirements. The candidate failed to check the national do-not-call list before calling and did not provide adequate information about data subject rights.
violationSummary: The candidate engaged in systematic collection of personal contact data and direct targeting of individuals via telephone without lawful basis under opt-out framework, constituting surveillance of electoral preferences.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A political candidate made unsolicited telephone calls to voters' mobile phones for campaign purposes without obtaining or checking telecommunications providers' opt-out registries to exclude.
whyTheyWereWrong: Recipients received unwanted political calls without their prior consent, and the candidate failed to verify she had permission to contact them, exposing voters to harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The candidate maintained an accurate electoral contact list that was verified and updated months before the campaign.
claimsVsReality.reality: The candidate did not obtain or check the mandatory opt-out registries from telecom providers, failed to verify current consent status, and could not document which specific sources provided the phone numbers or when consent was obtained.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant's data were in lists provided by the political party.
claimsVsReality.reality: When the complainant contacted the party, they were told they were not a party member and their name did not appear on party-distributed lists, contradicting the candidate's claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: The candidate provided proper notice and options for the complainant to opt out.
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence was provided that the candidate informed the recipient about their right to access data, to decline future contact, or other data subject rights during the calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 requires controllers to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights and provide information about the action taken without undue delay, and in any case within one month of receipt of the request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Candidate failed to properly satisfy the complainant's right of access request by not providing an adequate response regarding whether the caller's data were in their electoral lists.
violations: Candidate failed to properly satisfy the complainant's right of access request by not providing an adequate response regarding whether the caller's data were in their electoral lists.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 11(2) prohibits unsolicited promotional calls with human intervention unless the subscriber has declared to the service provider that they do not wish to receive such calls, and requires operators to maintain a free do-not-call registry available to all interested parties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Candidate made political telephone calls without obtaining and checking current opt-out registries from telecom providers before calling, failed to exclude phone numbers registered in do-not-call lists within the required 30-day window.
violations: Candidate made political telephone calls without obtaining and checking current opt-out registries from telecom providers before calling, failed to exclude phone numbers registered in do-not-call lists within the required 30-day window.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 13 requires callers to inform recipients about their rights and the identity of the caller during marketing communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: Candidate did not inform the recipient about the right to access their personal data during the political telephone calls.
violations: Candidate did not inform the recipient about the right to access their personal data during the political telephone calls.

outcome: The Hellenic Authority for the Protection of Personal Data (DPA) found violations of GDPR Art. 15 (right of access), Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 11(2) (unsolicited calls/do-not-call compliance), and Art. 13 (information provision). The candidate was ordered to cease unlawful processing and impose an administrative fine of €2,000. The decision is final and the candidate must comply with data protection requirements in future political communications.
companyNow: The political candidate was subject to enforcement action by the Greek DPA and is bound by compliance obligations in future political communications.
dataType: Contact information (mobile phone numbers)

companyDescription: Belden Singapore Private Limited is a subsidiary of Belden Incorporated, a multinational manufacturing group involved in the production of networking, connectivity and cable products. It conducts cross-border operations with its parent company and other group entities across multiple jurisdictions.
companyLongDescription: Belden Singapore Private Limited is a subsidiary of Belden Incorporated, a multinational manufacturing group involved in the production of networking, connectivity and cable products. It conducts cross-border operations with its parent company and other group entities across multiple jurisdictions.
caseDescription: Belden Singapore transferred personal data of 126 individuals to its US parent company but failed to execute a legally binding data transfer agreement before doing so. When Belden Inc.'s servers were breached by a threat actor in September-November 2020, personal data of both Belden Singapore and formerly-acquired Grass Valley employees were exfiltrated. The organisation lacked the required legal safeguards to ensure comparable protection under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures and legal safeguards for cross-border data transfers. The breach exposed personal data due to inadequate security protections at the receiving end and lack of enforceable contractual obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Belden Singapore transferred personal data of 189 employees and vendors to its US parent company without executing a legally binding deed of accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement,.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data of 189 individuals including names, addresses, identification numbers, salary information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Belden Singapore had a Global Data Transfer Agreement in place that required Belden Inc. to provide comparable data protection standards under the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The GDTA was not legally binding on Belden Singapore because the company had not executed the required Deed of Accession, meaning Belden Singapore could not enforce the agreement's protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Belden Group had implemented comprehensive policies and technical measures to protect personal data transferred overseas.
claimsVsReality.reality: While policies and measures existed and were operationally applied, they lacked legal enforceability against the overseas recipient due to the missing deed of accession.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 26(1) of the PDPA requires that an organisation shall not transfer any personal data to a country or territory outside Singapore except in accordance with requirements prescribed under the PDPA to ensure that organisations provide a standard of protection to personal data so transferred that is comparable to the protection under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Belden Singapore transferred personal data to Belden Inc. in the USA without having executed a legally binding deed of accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement, rendering the contract non-binding on Belden Singapore.
violations: Belden Singapore transferred personal data to Belden Inc. in the USA without having executed a legally binding deed of accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement, rendering the contract non-binding on Belden Singapore.
Although Belden Inc. agreed contractually to provide comparable protection under the PDPA, Belden Singapore could not enforce these obligations against Belden Inc. due to lack of privity of contract.
Belden Singapore failed to establish legally enforceable obligations from the overseas recipient to provide comparable protection standards before transferring the data.

outcome: Belden Singapore was issued a warning for breach of the Transfer Limitation Obligation under section 26 of the PDPA. No monetary penalty was imposed. The Commission noted that the breach was technical and a failure of legal formalities rather than substantive non-compliance. In practice, all relevant Belden group policies, practices and technical measures were implemented to ensure transferred data received comparable protection. Belden Singapore subsequently rectified the oversight by executing a Deed of Accession to the GDTA on 18 June 2021. No further directions were deemed necessary given the remedial actions already taken.
companyNow: Belden Singapore remains part of the Belden Group (parent company Belden Incorporated, headquartered in St Louis, Missouri, USA). The company has since complied with the PDPA Transfer Limitation Obligation by executing the required deed of accession.
dataType: Name, address, email, telephone, date of birth, identification number, marital status, photographs, salary information, tax information

companyDescription: Flying Cape Pte Ltd is a data intermediary and web hosting/management service provider based in Singapore that managed the ACCA Singapore website and its associated user database.
companyLongDescription: Flying Cape Pte Ltd is a data intermediary and web hosting/management service provider based in Singapore that managed the ACCA Singapore website and its associated user database.
caseDescription: Flying Cape Pte Ltd (FCPL), acting as a data intermediary, failed to adequately protect personal data extracted from ACCA Singapore's website. An employee improperly stored an unencrypted Excel file containing 191 users' personal data in a publicly accessible cloud storage bucket, leading to unauthorized exfiltration between September-October 2020. FCPL lacked supervisory arrangements to verify employee compliance with its own IT security policies.
violationSummary: FCPL's failure to encrypt data, use password protection, store data securely, and supervise employee compliance with security policies resulted in unauthorized data exfiltration. This falls squarely within Information Processing – Insecurity under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Flying Cape Pte Ltd extracted personal data into an unencrypted Excel file and stored it in a publicly accessible cloud storage bucket instead of a secured one.
whyTheyWereWrong: 191 individuals' names, email addresses, and phone numbers were exfiltrated by unauthorized attackers because Flying Cape Pte Ltd did not implement oversight mechanisms to detect or prevent.

claimsVsReality.claim: FCPL had IT policies in place requiring encryption and password protection of sensitive data files
claimsVsReality.reality: An FCPL employee violated these policies by failing to encrypt or password-protect the Excel file containing personal data

claimsVsReality.claim: FCPL maintained secure storage procedures for sensitive files
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee incorrectly stored the data file in a publicly accessible cloud storage bucket rather than the designated secure repository

claimsVsReality.claim: FCPL implemented supervisory controls over employee compliance with data protection policies
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commission's investigation found no arrangements to supervise, verify, or detect employee non-compliance with internal policies

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 imposes a Protection Obligation requiring organisations to make reasonable efforts to protect personal data against unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: FCPL failed to encrypt the extracted Excel file as required by its own IT policy
violations: FCPL failed to encrypt the extracted Excel file as required by its own IT policy
FCPL failed to password-protect the sensitive data file
FCPL stored personal data in a publicly accessible cloud storage bucket instead of a secured repository
FCPL implemented no supervisory arrangements to verify or detect employee non-compliance with its internal data protection policies

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 53(1) of the PDPA establishes that an organisation is liable for acts done by its employees in the course of their employment.
regulatoryFindings.description: FCPL is liable for the employee's failure to follow security protocols, and it is liable for FCPL's own failure to implement oversight mechanisms to prevent or detect such failures
violations: FCPL is liable for the employee's failure to follow security protocols, and it is liable for FCPL's own failure to implement oversight mechanisms to prevent or detect such failures

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found FCPL in breach of the Protection Obligation under s.24 of the PDPA. A formal Warning was issued to FCPL. No monetary penalty was imposed and no directions were issued, taking into account: (1) the small number of affected individuals (191), (2) low sensitivity of exfiltrated data (names, emails, phone numbers), (3) FCPL's immediate remedial actions to prevent recurrence, and (4) FCPL's voluntary notification to the Commission. ACCA Singapore was found not in breach because it discharged its Protection Obligation through due diligence assessment of FCPL's policies and contractual data protection requirements.
dataType: Names, email addresses, contact numbers

companyDescription: SAP Asia Pte. Ltd. is a subsidiary of SAP SE, the German multinational software corporation. It provides enterprise resource planning (ERP), human resources, and IT system solutions to businesses across Asia.
companyLongDescription: SAP Asia Pte. Ltd. is a subsidiary of SAP SE, the German multinational software corporation. It provides enterprise resource planning (ERP), human resources, and IT system solutions to businesses across Asia.
caseDescription: SAP Asia failed to properly communicate requirements for an automated payslip system to its external vendor, resulting in a design defect. When the programme was first executed on 31 March 2020, 29 out of 43 former employees received not only their own payslips but also those of other employees, disclosing sensitive payroll and financial information.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements by not ensuring specifications accurately reflected intended use and pre-launch testing adequately simulated real-world deployment of the feature processing personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SAP Asia failed to clearly specify to its vendor that the automated payslip system must issue multiple payslips simultaneously, and then deployed it without testing that capability.
whyTheyWereWrong: 43 former employees' sensitive personal data including names, ID numbers, bank accounts, and detailed salary information were exposed to each other when each employee received all other.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation intended the Programme to generate and email multiple payslips to multiple former employees simultaneously in one execution.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Programme was designed to handle only single payslip issuance to a single employee at a time, a misunderstanding never caught during testing or before deployment.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide the vendor with accurate specifications reflecting the intended Multiple Payslip Issuance functionality, resulting in the vendor designing the system for Single Payslip Issuance only
violations: Failed to provide the vendor with accurate specifications reflecting the intended Multiple Payslip Issuance functionality, resulting in the vendor designing the system for Single Payslip Issuance only
Conducted inadequate user acceptance testing by only testing Single Payslip Issuance scenarios, failing to simulate the intended real-world use of the system
Did not exercise reasonable oversight to ensure the vendor understood the business requirements and implemented them correctly

outcome: SAP Asia was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 13,500 within 30 days. The organisation took remedial actions including notifying all affected former employees, obtaining deletion confirmations from 39 of 43 employees, disabling the flawed programme, reverting to manual processing, and agreeing on continuous process improvements with the vendor. No further directions were deemed necessary based on these remedial measures.
companyNow: SAP Asia Pte. Ltd. continues operations as a subsidiary of SAP SE, providing enterprise resource planning and IT solutions in the Asia-Pacific region.
dataType: Payroll information, name, NRIC/FIN number, employment number, bank account number, salary, earnings, deductions

companyDescription: Crawfort Pte. Ltd. is a fintech/lending company based in Singapore that provides loan application and management services to customers.
companyLongDescription: Crawfort Pte. Ltd. is a fintech/lending company based in Singapore that provides loan application and management services to customers.
caseDescription: Crawfort Pte. Ltd. exposed 5,421 customers' sensitive personal data on the dark web due to an opened S3 server port during a rapid data migration exercise. The company failed to conduct a risk assessment and misconfigured access controls on AWS, allowing unauthorized threat actors to access NRIC images, loan contracts, and income documents. No monetary penalty was imposed due to the company's voluntary admission, prompt remediation, and mitigating circumstances during COVID-19.
violationSummary: The company failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data in its possession, resulting in a data breach where sensitive financial and identity information was publicly accessible and subsequently sold on the dark web.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Opened an S3 server port for one week during emergency data migration in April 2020 without conducting a risk assessment.
whyTheyWereWrong: 5,421 customers' highly sensitive personal data including NRIC images, loan contracts, income statements, and financial information were exposed to threat actors and sold on the dark web.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company opened the S3 server port for only one week for legitimate data migration business continuity purposes during COVID-19 lockdown.
claimsVsReality.reality: The port remained open and unsecured, with no access controls on the S3 bucket, allowing threat actors to access and steal 5,421 customers' most sensitive financial and identity data including NRIC images and loan contracts within that same week.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company operated under emergency circumstances (COVID-19 Circuit Breaker) that necessitated rapid pivot to remote operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Emergency circumstances do not exempt organizations from conducting reasonable risk assessments and implementing basic security controls; the speed of implementation does not justify leaving critical infrastructure publicly accessible.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks, and to prevent the loss of any storage medium or device on which personal data is stored.
regulatoryFindings.description: Crawfort failed to conduct a reasonable risk assessment before carrying out the data migration exercise
violations: Crawfort failed to conduct a reasonable risk assessment before carrying out the data migration exercise
No access control was implemented on the S3 bucket containing affected personal data during the week-long migration
S3 bucket was publicly accessible due to misconfiguration, allowing threat actors to gain unauthorized access

outcome: The Commission accepted Crawfort's request for expedited breach decision procedure following the company's voluntary admission of liability and breach of section 24 of the PDPA. In lieu of a monetary penalty, the Commission directed the company to: (1) engage a qualified security service provider to conduct a thorough security audit of its AWS S3 environment containing personal data; (2) provide the full audit report within 60 days; (3) rectify identified security gaps and update personal data protection policies within 60 days of receiving the audit; and (4) inform the Commission within 1 week of completion of rectification. The company undertook remedial measures including resetting whitelisted IPs, reconfiguring VPNs, conducting penetration testing, monitoring the dark web, engaging independent cyber security consultants, and notifying affected individuals.
dataType: NRIC images, loan contracts, income documents, email addresses, contact numbers, loan amounts

companyDescription: Irish Credit Bureau DAC is a credit reference agency that maintains a database of credit performance data from approximately 280 financial institutions, processing data on approximately 2.8 million individuals. The ICB provides credit reports and credit scores to assist lenders in making credit decisions.
companyLongDescription: Irish Credit Bureau DAC is a credit reference agency that maintains a database of credit performance data from approximately 280 financial institutions, processing data on approximately 2.8 million individuals. The ICB provides credit reports and credit scores to assist lenders in making credit decisions.
caseDescription: Irish Credit Bureau failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure accuracy of personal data in its credit database. A code change on 28 June 2018 unintentionally removed a filter protecting closed loan accounts from updates, resulting in 15,120 inaccurate records being processed and 1,062 disclosed to lenders and data subjects. The ICB also failed to maintain documented records of testing for code changes and lacked a formal approval procedure for system modifications.
violationSummary: The ICB's failure to implement appropriate technical safeguards (filter protection, comprehensive change management, documented testing procedures) directly resulted in inaccurate data being processed and disclosed, causing loss of data subject control and potential economic harm in credit decisions.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: On 28 June 2018, Irish Credit Bureau implemented a code change that unintentionally removed a filter protecting closed loan accounts from updates.
whyTheyWereWrong: The inaccurate records were disclosed to lenders and 118 data subjects, causing one mortgage applicant's credit card closure date to be incorrectly shown as February 2018 instead of February.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ICB submitted that its change management process complied with ISO27001 standard and included appropriate safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: The process lacked any provision for testing proposed coding changes or a formal approval procedure, both recommended by ISO guidance and essential for protecting sensitive financial data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ICB stated it carried out testing of the code change per ISO requirements by technical staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented record of testing was maintained; the actual testing failed to identify that the change would remove the filter protecting closed accounts, indicating inadequate test coverage.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ICB claimed the inaccuracies caused minimal impact on data subjects, limited to changed closure dates.
claimsVsReality.reality: Inaccurate closure dates were disclosed to lenders considering credit applications, influencing lending decisions (evidenced by complaint C-18-10-11 where a mortgage applicant was questioned due to the inaccuracy); data subjects lost control over financial data for up to 9 weeks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 25(1) GDPR requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data protection principles, including accuracy, both at the determination of processing means and during processing itself.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain a technical filter preventing payment profile updates to closed accounts; filter was unintentionally removed 28 June 2018 and not restored until 30 August 2018
violations: Failed to maintain a technical filter preventing payment profile updates to closed accounts; filter was unintentionally removed 28 June 2018 and not restored until 30 August 2018
Failed to implement a comprehensive documented change management process with testing requirements and formal approval procedures for code changes

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR require controllers to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles and processing requirements through appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain documented records of testing undertaken for the 28 June 2018 code change, preventing demonstration of compliance with Article 25(1) testing obligations
violations: Failed to maintain documented records of testing undertaken for the 28 June 2018 code change, preventing demonstration of compliance with Article 25(1) testing obligations
Submitted blank DPIA template and change control form with no analysis of risks or testing measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 26(1) GDPR requires joint controllers to determine their respective responsibilities for compliance by means of an arrangement.
regulatoryFindings.description: No infringement found; ICB determined all means of processing alone; ICB members are not joint controllers
violations: No infringement found; ICB determined all means of processing alone; ICB members are not joint controllers

outcome: Irish Credit Bureau DAC is subject to: (1) a reprimand for infringements of Articles 25(1), 5(2), and 24(1) GDPR; (2) an administrative fine of €90,000 for the Article 25(1) infringement; (3) no requirement for an order to implement formal approval procedures, as the ICB has since implemented comprehensive change management policies (dated 17 February 2021) including formal approval requirements and testing documentation. The ICB must continue to maintain compliance through ongoing assessment of technical and organisational measures. No order under Article 58(2)(d) was necessary given remediation undertaken.
companyNow: Irish Credit Bureau DAC operates as a credit reference agency in Ireland with approximately 280 financial institution members. Following this decision, the ICB has implemented comprehensive remediation measures including new change management, testing, and DPIA policies (as of February 2021).
dataType: Credit performance data, financial history, personal identifiers (name, address, date of birth, occupation, gender)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 25(1) – Data protection by design

companyDescription: Iapps Pte Ltd is a financial technology company specializing in mobile application development and marketing. The company was engaged by Sport Singapore to develop, deploy, and operate the Super Sports Club Membership Management System (SSCMMS) and the ActiveSG mobile application.
companyLongDescription: Iapps Pte Ltd is a financial technology company specializing in mobile application development and marketing. The company was engaged by Sport Singapore to develop, deploy, and operate the Super Sports Club Membership Management System (SSCMMS) and the ActiveSG mobile application.
caseDescription: Iapps Pte Ltd deployed a security code fix to the live ActiveSG mobile app instead of the test environment due to human error, exposing 108 individuals' personal data (including 9 minors' NRIC numbers) to 84 unauthorized users. The company lacked adequate supervisory controls and second-level approval checks in its code deployment process to prevent such errors. Despite prompt remedial action within 2 hours, the Commission found the company in breach of reasonable security obligations under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The company's weak internal work process controls and absence of supervisory checks for code deployment constituted inadequate security arrangements under PDPA s.24, allowing unauthorized disclosure of personal data through deployment error.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Iapps deployed a security code fix directly to the production environment instead of the test environment due to human error.
whyTheyWereWrong: The data breach exposed 108 people's sensitive personal information including NRIC numbers of 9 minors, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Iapps claimed it had second-level checks for code deployment and referenced its Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for the SSCMMS.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the SOP described multi-level checks at the User Acceptance Testing stage, it contained no second-level checks for deployment into the enterprise or production environments. Iapps provided no evidence of second-level checks after UAT and before production deployment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Iapps argued the incident resulted from human error 'in the rush of the moment' and would not have been prevented by a second-level check.
claimsVsReality.reality: A second-level check or automated code deployment software would have prevented the error by requiring an additional approval before production deployment, particularly necessary given time pressures engineers often work under.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Iapps failed to implement second-level approvals or supervisory checks in its code deployment process after User Acceptance Testing, allowing a security code fix to be deployed directly to production instead of the test environment
violations: Iapps failed to implement second-level approvals or supervisory checks in its code deployment process after User Acceptance Testing, allowing a security code fix to be deployed directly to production instead of the test environment
The absence of second-level checks or automated deployment safeguards amounted to weak internal work process controls, inadequate for protecting personal data from security risks

outcome: Iapps Pte Ltd was ordered to pay a financial penalty of S$9,000 within 30 days. The Commission noted that the company's prompt remedial actions (fixing the issue within 2 hours of discovery, implementing environment separation, introducing 2-factor authentication, monitoring affected users, and implementing dynamic QR codes) mitigated the penalty. No further directions were issued. The company cooperated fully with the Commission's investigation. The decision clarifies that data intermediaries acting on behalf of public agencies are now subject to PDPA obligations following amendments effective 1 February 2021, though the previous exclusion still applied to this pre-amendment incident.
companyNow: Iapps Pte Ltd continues to operate as a financial technology company specializing in mobile application development and marketing. The company implemented significant security improvements following the incident, including environment separation and 2-factor authentication controls.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, email addresses, mobile telephone numbers, home telephone numbers, addresses, gender, date of birth, race, employment status, sports interests

company: North London Collegiate School (Singapore) Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: North London Collegiate School (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is an educational institution operating in Singapore, part of a corporate group that includes related entities providing IT and web management services.
companyLongDescription: North London Collegiate School (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is an educational institution operating in Singapore, part of a corporate group that includes related entities providing IT and web management services.
caseDescription: North London Collegiate School failed to adequately secure student admission documents stored on its website, relying only on a robots.txt file to prevent search engine indexing. The documents—containing sensitive personal data of minors—were indexed by search engines and became accessible to the public via internet searches from December 2019 to July 2021. The school admitted to breaching its legal obligation to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data.
violationSummary: The organization's failure to implement adequate technical safeguards resulted in sensitive personal data—particularly of minors—being exposed and indexed by search engines, making it publicly discoverable and accessible without authorization.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The school stored admission application documents containing passports, identity cards, and personal information in an unprotected website directory.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1,700 individuals including minors had their sensitive personal data such as passports, identity card numbers, photographs.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had implemented security measures through its reliance on a related group company to manage website security and make necessary data protection arrangements.
claimsVsReality.reality: There were no clear written agreements, contractual stipulations, or binding corporate rules requiring the group company to implement or recommend security arrangements, leaving full responsibility with the organisation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The robots.txt file would prevent search engines from indexing sensitive admission documents stored in the website directory.
claimsVsReality.reality: Robots.txt is a non-mandatory protocol relying on voluntary compliance by web crawlers with no enforcement mechanism, and the documents were successfully indexed by search engines and appeared in public search results.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks, and to prevent loss of storage media.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation relied solely on robots.txt file, a non-mandatory protocol with no enforcement mechanism, to prevent search engine indexing of sensitive personal data
violations: Organisation relied solely on robots.txt file, a non-mandatory protocol with no enforcement mechanism, to prevent search engine indexing of sensitive personal data
Organisation failed to implement proper folder/directory permissions and access controls to prevent automated indexing by web crawlers
Organisation provided no clear contractual or written requirements to related group company managing the website regarding personal data security arrangements
Sensitive personal data of minors including passports, identity cards, photographs, birth certificates, academic and immunization records remained publicly accessible via search engines for 19 months

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD 10,000 within 30 days. Following the incident, the organisation ceased collecting documents via its website and implemented a specialized school admission software with appropriate security. The organisation committed to implementing binding corporate rules governing data protection and cybersecurity across its corporate group. No other directions were necessary given the remedial actions taken.
companyNow: The organisation has ceased web-based document collection and implemented a specialized admission software system with enhanced security measures. It has committed to establishing binding corporate rules for data protection and cybersecurity governance within its group.
dataType: Passport numbers, Identity card numbers (NRICs), Digital photographs, Birth certificates, Academic reports, Immunization records, Name, Address, Date of birth

companyDescription: Aviva Financial Advisers Pte Ltd is a financial advisory firm in Singapore providing insurance and investment services. It engages independent contractor representatives to serve clients.
companyLongDescription: Aviva Financial Advisers Pte Ltd is a financial advisory firm in Singapore providing insurance and investment services. It engages independent contractor representatives to serve clients.
caseDescription: Three insurance financial advisers, including a former Aviva representative, collected and sold approximately 1,000 client leads without consent. Dennis sold the list to Melissa and Winarto for $1,000 each, disclosing personal data including names, addresses, and insurance details. Melissa and Winarto purchased the list without verifying that proper notification and consent had been obtained from the affected individuals.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of personal data (names, addresses, contact numbers, insurance information) to third parties without individual consent. The sale and transfer of client lists without notification constitutes a breach of confidentiality and unauthorized secondary use.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Aviva Financial Advisers' representative Dennis disclosed approximately 1,000 clients' names, mailing addresses, contact numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,000 individuals' personal financial and contact data was sold for profit and transferred between advisers without their knowledge, exposing them to unsolicited solicitation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dennis claimed he had obtained necessary consent and notified clients regarding disclosure of their personal data to other insurance financial advisers.
claimsVsReality.reality: None of the affected clients verified that Dennis had contacted them to seek consent or notified them of the disclosure; no corroborating evidence was found.

claimsVsReality.claim: Melissa and Winarto claimed they relied on Dennis's verbal assurances that he had informed clients about the change in insurance financial adviser.
claimsVsReality.reality: Neither Melissa nor Winarto obtained written evidence such as sample notifications or consent documents; they failed to undertake proper due diligence before purchasing the list.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 13 of the PDPA requires organisations to obtain consent of individuals before collecting, using and/or disclosing personal data, unless an exception applies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Dennis failed to obtain consent from 1,000 clients before disclosing their personal data to Melissa and Winarto.
violations: Dennis failed to obtain consent from 1,000 clients before disclosing their personal data to Melissa and Winarto.
Melissa and Winarto failed to verify consent had been obtained before collecting/purchasing the client list.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 20 of the PDPA requires organisations to notify individuals of purposes for collection, use or disclosure of personal data on or before collecting such data to obtain consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Dennis did not notify clients that their data would be disclosed to other insurance financial advisers.
violations: Dennis did not notify clients that their data would be disclosed to other insurance financial advisers.
Melissa and Winarto relied on verbal assurances without obtaining written evidence of proper notification to clients.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: AFA had reasonable policies in place and was found not to have breached the Act; Dennis compiled the list independently during his tenure as an independent contractor.
violations: AFA had reasonable policies in place and was found not to have breached the Act; Dennis compiled the list independently during his tenure as an independent contractor.

outcome: Dennis received a warning (no monetary penalty) due to poor health, unemployment since 2018, minimal savings, dependence on aged father, and full refund of proceeds. Melissa and Winarto each received warnings, as they did not sell the data for profit, cooperated fully, and did not use the data without consent. AFA was found to have no breach, with reasonable data protection policies and controls in place. All three individuals were found to be 'organisations' under the PDPA for acting in commercial capacity as independent contractors.
companyNow: Aviva Financial Advisers Pte Ltd is a licensed financial advisory firm in Singapore; no evidence of closure or material change to operations following this decision.
dataType: Names, mailing addresses, contact numbers, insurance plan information

companyDescription: TIGERS MARKET, S.L. (CIF B67245209) is a Spanish telemarketing services company that conducted unsolicited commercial calls for electricity provider switching campaigns.
companyLongDescription: TIGERS MARKET, S.L. (CIF B67245209) is a Spanish telemarketing services company that conducted unsolicited commercial calls for electricity provider switching campaigns.
caseDescription: TIGERS MARKET conducted unsolicited commercial telemarketing calls to a consumer registered on Spain's Robinson List (opt-out registry), requesting they switch electricity providers. The company made multiple calls despite the complainant's explicit preference not to receive such communications. TIGERS operated the calling lines and violated the recipient's right to object to direct marketing.
violationSummary: The company conducted targeted telemarketing surveillance of a consumer who had explicitly opted out via the Robinson List. This constitutes surveillance without consent despite clear prior objection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: TIGERS MARKET made unsolicited commercial telemarketing calls on November 5-6, 2020 to a mobile line registered on Spain's Robinson List opt-out registry to promote electricity provider.
whyTheyWereWrong: The recipient had explicitly registered to block direct marketing calls; TIGERS ignored this opt-out preference.

claimsVsReality.claim: TIGERS claimed in its response to the AEPD that it had no knowledge of the phone line holders and had not processed any personal data of the complainant.
claimsVsReality.reality: NEOTEL (the telecom operator) confirmed TIGERS held the calling line numbers and was conducting telemarketing activities; TIGERS was the confirmed data controller for the personal processing involved in the calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: Spanish LGT Art. 48.1(b) requires users to have the right to object to unwanted direct marketing calls and to be informed of this right.
regulatoryFindings.description: TIGERS made multiple commercial telemarketing calls to a number registered on the Robinson List without consent or proper opt-out compliance.
violations: TIGERS made multiple commercial telemarketing calls to a number registered on the Robinson List without consent or proper opt-out compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 21 grants data subjects the right to object to processing of personal data for direct marketing purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: TIGERS processed the complainant's telephone number for direct marketing despite their registration on the Robinson List opt-out registry.
violations: TIGERS processed the complainant's telephone number for direct marketing despite their registration on the Robinson List opt-out registry.
