Fine justified by: systematic, multi-year practice affecting tens of thousands of vehicle owners; importer's market dominance as sole distributor; lack of transparent identification in customer communications; and failure to implement data minimization despite scale of operation. Decision affirmed by authority with no monetary reduction despite importer's COVID-19 hardship claims, as legal violations and public interest in privacy protection required penalty.
companyNow: Unknown current status. As automotive importer with exclusive distribution rights for a major vehicle brand in Hungary, company likely continues operations under new compliance requirements.
dataType: Email address, home address, phone number, vehicle technical identifiers (chassis number, registration), service details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1) – No valid legal basis
GDPR Art. 12(1) – Information to be provided

companyDescription: ACL Construction (S) Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based construction company providing pre-fabricated structures, structural steel products, and construction services to corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: ACL Construction (S) Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based construction company providing pre-fabricated structures, structural steel products, and construction services to corporate clients.
caseDescription: ACL Construction experienced a ransomware attack in June 2021 where hackers encrypted files and offered data for sale on the darkweb. While the exposed data primarily consisted of business contact information (outside PDPA scope), investigations revealed the company had failed to designate a Data Protection Officer and had no data protection policies in place, violating accountability obligations under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The company's failure to establish accountability mechanisms (DPO designation and data protection policies) meant inadequate safeguards for personal data it held, manifesting in vulnerability to ransomware encryption and exposure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: ACL Construction failed to designate a Data Protection Officer and implement any data protection policies, leaving employee personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The absence of data protection policies and oversight meant the company could not adequately protect employee personal data or respond to security incidents.

claimsVsReality.claim: No personal data affected by the data breach (only business contact information compromised).
claimsVsReality.reality: While exposed files contained primarily business contact information outside PDPA scope, the company also held and failed to adequately protect employee personal data and other incidentally-processed personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company operates primarily with business contact data from corporate clients.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of primary business activities, company still processes employee personal data and other personal information requiring PDPA compliance governance, which was absent.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 11(3) of the PDPA requires an organisation to designate one or more individuals responsible for ensuring the organisation complies with the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACL Construction failed to designate any Data Protection Officer or responsible individual to oversee PDPA compliance.
violations: ACL Construction failed to designate any Data Protection Officer or responsible individual to oversee PDPA compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12(a) of the PDPA requires an organisation to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet its obligations under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACL Construction had no data protection policies or practices in place to govern handling of personal data, including employee data.
violations: ACL Construction had no data protection policies or practices in place to govern handling of personal data, including employee data.

outcome: The Commission refrained from imposing a financial penalty due to the organisation's low level of awareness of PDPA obligations and prompt remedial actions taken after the incident (appointment of a DPO). Instead, the Commission issued a Compliance Order directing ACL Construction to: (a) develop and implement policies and practices complying with PDPA provisions; and (b) establish a compulsory employee training programme on PDPA compliance when handling personal data.
companyNow: ACL Construction appointed a staff member as Data Protection Officer following the incident and is subject to ongoing compliance requirements under the Commission's order.
dataType: Business contact information (names, business phone numbers, business emails), employee personal data, project documents, CAD drawings

companyDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a membership-based recreational club in Singapore offering facilities and services to club members.
companyLongDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a membership-based recreational club in Singapore offering facilities and services to club members.
caseDescription: An employee's email account was compromised via password spraying attack, exposing personal data of 467 individuals. The organisation failed to implement a documented password policy and did not provide structured staff training on data protection obligations, violating the Protection Obligation under PDPA section 24.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (written password policy, staff training, policy enforcement) required under PDPA s.24, resulting in unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to document its password policy in writing and did not provide structured staff training on data protection.
whyTheyWereWrong: The compromise exposed personal data of 467 individuals including names, NRIC numbers, and email addresses, with 600 phishing emails sent to club members.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation claimed it had password requirements in place and disseminated them via IT newsletters (August 2018, September 2019)
claimsVsReality.reality: No written documented password policy existed until 23 February 2021 (after the incident); requirements were ineffective when passed informally without written reference or system enforcement

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation's IT newsletters cited 'TMCC_Password_123' as an example of a good password
claimsVsReality.reality: This password example was weak and easily guessable because it incorporated the organisation's name (TMCC), making it vulnerable to password attacks despite meeting technical complexity requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or loss.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to document password policy in writing, only disseminating requirements via informal newsletters
violations: Organisation failed to document password policy in writing, only disseminating requirements via informal newsletters
Organisation did not provide structured and organised training to staff on PDPA compliance and personal data handling—only ad-hoc informal training
Employee's password was not changed for nearly 5 years (2016–2021) and system-enforced domain password policy was not pushed to her system due to domain controller disruption
These failures created vulnerability to password spraying attack, enabling unauthorised access to employee email account and exposure of 467 individuals' personal data

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation). Monetary penalty of SGD 4,000 imposed, payable within 30 days. No other directions issued due to remedial actions undertaken: organisation engaged IT forensic vendor, implemented recommended cybersecurity measures, documented password policy, implemented regular updates, conducted user awareness training, and provided PDPA training. Organisation cooperated with investigation and admitted breach under expedited procedure.
companyNow: Tanah Merah Country Club remains operational. Following the incident and enforcement action, the organisation has implemented comprehensive remedial measures including documented policies, regular cybersecurity updates, and staff training programmes.
dataType: Email addresses, names, NRIC numbers

company: Everalbum, Inc. (also d/b/a Ever and Paravision)
companyDescription: Everalbum, Inc. provided Ever, a cloud-based photo storage and organization application available on iOS, Android, web, and desktop platforms. The company developed facial recognition technology to automatically group and organize user photos by face. It also offered enterprise facial recognition services through its Paravision brand.
companyLongDescription: Everalbum, Inc. provided Ever, a cloud-based photo storage and organization application available on iOS, Android, web, and desktop platforms. The company developed facial recognition technology to automatically group and organize user photos by face. It also offered enterprise facial recognition services through its Paravision brand.
caseDescription: Everalbum enabled facial recognition on users' photos by default without affirmative consent, then misrepresented users' control over the feature. The company also extracted millions of facial images from user photos to train its own facial recognition technology without proper authorization. Additionally, Everalbum falsely claimed it would delete photos upon account deactivation but retained them indefinitely.
violationSummary: The unauthorized application of facial recognition technology to user photos constitutes systematic surveillance of biometric data without affirmative consent. Additionally, the extraction and use of facial images for training proprietary technology represents secondary use without authorization.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Everalbum enabled facial recognition by default for millions of users without consent, extracted facial images from user photos to train its proprietary face recognition technology.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 12 million users uploaded intimate family photos to cloud storage believing they controlled facial recognition.

claimsVsReality.claim: Face recognition will only be used if users enable or turn it on (stated in Help article and privacy documentation).
claimsVsReality.reality: For approximately 75% of users (those outside Texas, Illinois, Washington, and EU), face recognition was enabled by default from February 2017 to April 2019, with no option to disable it.

claimsVsReality.claim: When face recognition is turned on, you are letting us know that it's ok for us to use the face embeddings of people in your photos (Help article, July 2018).
claimsVsReality.reality: Most users could not 'turn on' face recognition because it was already on by default and uncontrollable; the statement implied affirmative user consent where none existed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Photos and videos will be permanently deleted upon account deactivation (account deactivation messages and customer support).
claimsVsReality.reality: Until October 2019, Everalbum retained all photos and videos from deactivated accounts indefinitely and only began deleting them if accounts had been deactivated for more than three months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facial images extracted from user photos were used only for the Friends feature.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between September 2017 and August 2019, Everalbum extracted millions of facial images from user photos and combined them with public datasets to create four new datasets for developing proprietary facial recognition technology, some of which was sold to enterprise customers via Paravision.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent represented that face recognition would only be used if users enabled or turned it on, but in fact enabled it by default for approximately 75% of users until April 2019 without providing a means to disable it.
violations: Respondent represented that face recognition would only be used if users enabled or turned it on, but in fact enabled it by default for approximately 75% of users until April 2019 without providing a means to disable it.

Respondent represented in its Help article that 'when face recognition is turned on, you are letting us know that it's ok for us to use the face embeddings,' but users outside Texas, Illinois, Washington, and EU could not take any affirmative action to enable or disable the feature.

Respondent represented through account deactivation messages and customer support responses that photos and videos would be permanently deleted upon account deactivation, but retained them indefinitely until October 2019.

outcome: FTC issued a Complaint alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document does not specify the final resolution, but the complaint alleges that Everalbum engaged in deceptive practices regarding (1) user control over facial recognition and (2) deletion of photos upon account deactivation. Respondent was required to cease these practices and comply with specified remedies.
companyNow: Everalbum rebranded its enterprise facial recognition division as Paravision and continued operating. The company implemented corrective measures including opt-in consent for facial recognition and delayed deletion of deactivated account photos. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Biometric data (facial images, face embeddings), photos, videos, location data, IP addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a Norwegian public enterprise that provides financing, grants, and business development services to support innovation and entrepreneurship. The agency operates under state ownership and serves as a key instrument of Norwegian industrial and innovation policy.
companyLongDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a Norwegian public enterprise that provides financing, grants, and business development services to support innovation and entrepreneurship. The agency operates under state ownership and serves as a key instrument of Norwegian industrial and innovation policy.
caseDescription: Innovasjon Norge, a Norwegian government agency, failed to implement adequate safeguards for credit report handling and allowed multiple unauthorized credit inquiries on behalf of customers. The agency mishandled credit worthiness checks without proper legal basis and failed to establish required internal controls, exposing customers' sensitive financial data and credit histories to unnecessary risk.
violationSummary: The agency failed to implement adequate technical and organisational safeguards for personal data processing, particularly credit information. The lack of internal controls and authorization procedures for credit inquiries constitutes a security failure under GDPR Article 32.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Innovasjon Norge performed at least four credit inquiries on customer accounts without proper authorization between January and April 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive credit and financial data were accessed without documented consent or legal basis, exposing them to unauthorized scrutiny of their creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Innovasjon Norge claimed it had proper legal grounds to conduct multiple credit inquiries on customers' accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency failed to document any lawful basis for the credit checks and could not show customer authorization or valid contractual or statutory justification for the inquiries.

claimsVsReality.claim: The agency stated it followed proper procedures for credit information handling.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal controls for credit inquiries were entirely absent; there were no documented authorization requirements, no audit trails, and no verification of legitimate business purpose prior to credit checks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Innovasjon Norge indicated it had implemented adequate safeguards for personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency lacked mandatory technical and organisational measures, including access restrictions, logging systems, and supervisory controls required under GDPR Article 32.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires all processing of personal data to have a lawful basis such as explicit consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge processed credit information without establishing a valid lawful basis. The agency could not document that customers had authorized credit inquiries or that processing fell under an explicit legal exemption.
violations: Innovasjon Norge processed credit information without establishing a valid lawful basis. The agency could not document that customers had authorized credit inquiries or that processing fell under an explicit legal exemption.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including internal controls and access restrictions.
regulatoryFindings.description: The agency failed to implement mandatory internal control procedures for credit inquiries. There were no documented authorization requirements, no verification of legitimate business purpose, and no audit trails for multiple credit checks made in early 2020.
violations: The agency failed to implement mandatory internal control procedures for credit inquiries. There were no documented authorization requirements, no verification of legitimate business purpose, and no audit trails for multiple credit checks made in early 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and in any case not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge failed to timely notify Datatilsynet of the credit inquiry breaches. Notification delays occurred for the first three credit inquiries made in January–February 2020, which were not reported until May 2020.
violations: Innovasjon Norge failed to timely notify Datatilsynet of the credit inquiry breaches. Notification delays occurred for the first three credit inquiries made in January–February 2020, which were not reported until May 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: Norwegian Personal Data Protection Act Article 6 nr. 1 and Article 4 nr. 12 require lawful basis and justified purpose for handling credit information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit inquiries were made without documented lawful basis under Norwegian law. The agency failed to establish that customers had consented to or authorized these inquiries, violating requirements for handling sensitive credit data.
violations: Credit inquiries were made without documented lawful basis under Norwegian law. The agency failed to establish that customers had consented to or authorized these inquiries, violating requirements for handling sensitive credit data.

outcome: Datatilsynet issued a fine of NOK 1,000,000 and issued a compliance order requiring Innovasjon Norge to: (1) immediately cease unauthorized credit inquiries; (2) implement written internal control procedures governing all credit handling; (3) establish clear authorization protocols and audit trails; (4) conduct mandatory data protection training for staff; (5) undergo regular monitoring by Datatilsynet. The agency was required to document implementation within specified timeframes. The decision was enforceable and no appeal was recorded.
companyNow: Innovasjon Norge is a Norwegian government agency under the Ministry of Trade, Fisheries and Food Policy. The agency continues to operate with mandated enhanced data protection oversight following the 2021 enforcement action.
dataType: Credit information, personal identification data, financial records
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1) – lawful basis for processing
Norwegian Personal Data Protection Act Art. 4 nr. 12, Art. 6 nr. 1

companyDescription: VODAFONE ESPAÑA, S.A.U. is a major Spanish telecommunications operator providing mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services. It is a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc, one of the world's largest mobile network operators.
companyLongDescription: VODAFONE ESPAÑA, S.A.U. is a major Spanish telecommunications operator providing mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services. It is a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc, one of the world's largest mobile network operators.
caseDescription: VODAFONE ESPAÑA failed to respond to investigative information requests from the Spanish data protection authority (AEPD), obstructing the authority's investigation into a data handling complaint. The company received a formal information request in February 2021 and provided no response within the required timeframe, violating Article 58(1) of the GDPR.
companyWorth: €46B (Vodafone Group plc market cap as of 2021)
violationSummary: The violation is classified as insecurity because the company's obstruction of investigation prevented authorities from assessing the security and lawfulness of its personal data processing. Non-cooperation with regulators creates risk that undiscovered data handling violations continue unaddressed.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Vodafone España received a formal information request from Spain's data protection authority on 8 February 2021 but failed to provide any response within the required 10 business days or at any.
whyTheyWereWrong: Vodafone's non-cooperation prevented authorities from investigating potential data handling violations affecting its millions of customers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Compliance with data protection obligations, including cooperation with regulatory authorities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company failed to respond to mandatory investigative information request within required timeframe, demonstrating systemic failure in procedures for regulatory cooperation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) grants supervisory authorities the power to order data controllers and processors to provide any information required for performance of their supervisory functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone España failed to comply with AEPD's formal information request (O00007128s2100006950) issued 4 February 2021, despite receipt on 8 February 2021 and a 10 business day response deadline.
violations: Vodafone España failed to comply with AEPD's formal information request (O00007128s2100006950) issued 4 February 2021, despite receipt on 8 February 2021 and a 10 business day response deadline.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(e) defines as a very serious infraction the failure to facilitate access in breach of Article 58(1), punishable by fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: Non-response to regulatory information request constitutes obstruction of supervisory authority's investigation powers, falling under Article 83(5)(e).
violations: Non-response to regulatory information request constitutes obstruction of supervisory authority's investigation powers, falling under Article 83(5)(e).

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72.1 classifies as very serious: (ñ) failure to provide access to personal data, information, premises, equipment and data processing means required by supervisory authority; (o) resistance or obstruction of supervisory authority's inspection function.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone España's failure to respond to information request constitutes obstruction under Article 72.1(o) of LOPDGDD.
violations: Vodafone España's failure to respond to information request constitutes obstruction under Article 72.1(o) of LOPDGDD.

outcome: AEPD initiated sanctioning procedure PS/00155/2021 on 16 April 2021. Initial proposed sanction was €5,000. Vodafone España paid €3,000 on 17 May 2021, utilizing two 20% reductions: (1) recognition of responsibility within the allegations deadline, and (2) voluntary payment before resolution. Payment within the allegations deadline period triggered immediate termination of procedure under LPACAP Article 85. Company waived all administrative appeals and remedies.
companyNow: VODAFONE ESPAÑA, S.A.U. remains an active telecommunications provider in Spain, a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc. The 2021 penalty was a minor enforcement action compared to its overall operations.
dataType: Telecommunications customer data, call records, subscription information

companyDescription: The National Kidney Foundation is one of Singapore's most prominent non-profit health organisations, providing subsidised kidney dialysis treatment and healthcare services. It serves a significant patient population in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: The National Kidney Foundation is one of Singapore's most prominent non-profit health organisations, providing subsidised kidney dialysis treatment and healthcare services. It serves a significant patient population in Singapore.
caseDescription: The National Kidney Foundation failed to implement adequate access controls on employee webmail accounts containing sensitive personal data of approximately 500 patients and staff. A hacker gained access to an employee's email account via phishing, exfiltrating 23,145 emails containing health records, financial information, and identification documents. The organisation had not implemented two-factor authentication despite handling highly sensitive medical and financial data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security measures (specifically two-factor authentication) proportionate to the sensitivity of personal data held, resulting in unauthorised access and data exfiltration. This is classified as insecurity in the Solove taxonomy because the breach occurred due to inadequate technical safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The National Kidney Foundation failed to implement two-factor authentication or robust access controls on employee webmail accounts, leaving 23,145 emails containing sensitive patient.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker accessed Employee A's email account and exfiltrated personal data of approximately 500 individuals including patients' medical conditions, financial arrears.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had implemented extensive security measures including Microsoft ATP email filtering, SPF/DKIM authentication, password policies, employee training, and phishing simulation exercises.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, the basic access controls (password-only authentication) proved insufficient to protect web-accessible email accounts handling sensitive health and financial data. A single successful phishing attack compromised 500 individuals' records.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct risk-based assessment to identify employees handling sensitive personal data and strengthen their access controls accordingly
violations: Failed to conduct risk-based assessment to identify employees handling sensitive personal data and strengthen their access controls accordingly

Did not implement two-factor authentication for webmail accounts containing sensitive health and financial data, despite guidance that such measures should be considered for accounts with sensitive personal data
Relied only on basic password policy (8+ alphanumeric characters) and account lockout after 3 failed attempts, which are insufficient for web-accessible accounts handling health and financial data

outcome: The National Kidney Foundation was issued a warning for breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. No additional directions were imposed given the organisation's full cooperation, prompt remedial actions (implementing 2FA on 22 May 2020, notifying affected individuals on 24 July 2020, offering identity theft monitoring), and extensive pre-existing data protection measures. The organisation must maintain compliance with strengthened access controls going forward.
companyNow: The National Kidney Foundation continues to operate as a prominent non-profit health organisation in Singapore providing dialysis and kidney health services. Post-incident, it has implemented two-factor authentication on all webmail accounts and enhanced security monitoring.
dataType: Health data, financial data (arrears, subsidies), medical conditions, dialysis readings, bank account numbers, identification numbers, education certificates, curriculum vitae, photographs, psycho-social information

company: ΚΑΠΑ ΛΑΜΔΑ ΩΜΕΓΑ ΔΙΑΦΗΜΙΣΤΙΚΗ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΚΗ ΜΟΝΟΠΡΟΣΩΠΗ ΕΤΑΙΡΕΙΑ ΠΕΡΙΟΡΙΣΜΕΝΗΣ ΕΥΘΥΝΗΣ (ΚΛΩ)
companyDescription: ΚΛΩ is a Greek limited liability advertising and telemarketing company specializing in telephone sales (telesales) of cosmetic and personal care products. The company maintains customer records for 5 years for tax compliance and has historically conducted direct marketing campaigns via unsolicited calls.
companyLongDescription: ΚΛΩ is a Greek limited liability advertising and telemarketing company specializing in telephone sales (telesales) of cosmetic and personal care products. The company maintains customer records for 5 years for tax compliance and has historically conducted direct marketing campaigns via unsolicited calls.
caseDescription: ΚΛΩ, a telemarketing firm, made unsolicited promotional calls to individuals based on personal data collected during previous purchases, without valid legal basis or explicit consent. The company continued calls despite customer objections and failed to respect opt-out requests under Greek electronic communications law. Three complainants filed multiple complaints over extended periods regarding repeated unwanted marketing calls.
violationSummary: Company repurposed personal data (phone numbers) collected for transaction completion into marketing use without explicit consent or transparency, and then processed that data for a fundamentally different purpose (promotional calls) than originally stated.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Made repeated unsolicited telemarketing calls promoting cosmetic products to customers over 12+ months using phone numbers from prior purchases.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers received dozens of unwanted sales calls targeting their personal phone numbers without clear consent, leaving them harassed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed all customers were existing clients who gave 'verbal consent' during initial purchase transactions to remain on file for future marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documentary evidence of any consent, written or oral, was ever produced. In at least one case (Complainant C), the complainant denied ever making a purchase from the company; his father had made a single purchase years earlier. In others, objections were explicitly stated but calls continued.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated that calls were made for 'customer satisfaction surveys' to assess whether customers were satisfied with prior purchases.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainants consistently reported that calls were explicitly for product promotion and sales, not satisfaction surveys. Calls often occurred long after purchases and to individuals who had not made purchases themselves.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated customers were informed of their right to request deletion and that no one contacted the company to withdraw consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainants testified that they repeatedly objected verbally during calls, and company records showed continued outreach. No written policy regarding objection procedures was ever provided to customers, and company failed to respect verbal objections in real time.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it engaged a GDPR compliance consultant in August 2019 and was implementing compliance measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Nearly two years after the claimed engagement (through at least September 2020), no compliance documentation was produced, and violations continued. The contract was referenced but no evidence of actual implementation was ever submitted.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires processing to be lawful only if at least one specified condition is met, including explicit prior consent or legitimate interests balancing.
regulatoryFindings.description: ΚΛΩ claimed 'verbal consent' from phone calls without documentary evidence; no written record or demonstrable proof of consent existed
violations: ΚΛΩ claimed 'verbal consent' from phone calls without documentary evidence; no written record or demonstrable proof of consent existed
Company reused customer phone numbers obtained for purchase transactions as basis for marketing calls without separate informed consent
No transparency provided to customers that their data would be used for ongoing promotional purposes distinct from the original transaction

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21(2) gives data subjects the absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing at any time, and the controller must cease processing immediately.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customers verbally objected during calls; company continued placing calls despite stated objections
violations: Customers verbally objected during calls; company continued placing calls despite stated objections
In one case (Complainant A), objections persisted for over one year; company made 11 separate calls across 13+ months despite repeated refusals
Company provided no written procedure for customers to formally exercise objection rights and did not facilitate the right under Article 12(2)

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 3471/2006 Article 11(2) prohibits unsolicited calls with human intervention for commercial promotion unless the called party previously consented or is registered in the opt-out registry.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company made calls to phone numbers registered in the national Do Not Call registry prior to the calls
violations: Company made calls to phone numbers registered in the national Do Not Call registry prior to the calls
No evidence that customers were informed of their right to register objections or how to exercise it
Company failed to obtain updated opt-out lists from telecommunications providers before initiating campaigns

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (APDPD) found ΚΛΩ in violation of GDPR Articles 6, 12(2), and 21, and Law 3471/2006. The Authority determined that the company lacked valid legal basis for processing customer phone numbers for marketing, failed to facilitate customer objection rights, and continued harassment despite stated refusals. The company was ordered to pay an administrative fine of €20,000 and must cease all unlawful processing. ΚΛΩ represented that it has deleted the phone numbers of complainants and discontinued contact; however, the Authority emphasized that this remedial action occurred only after regulatory intervention, not voluntarily. The Authority also noted that while ΚΛΩ claimed engagement of a GDPR compliance consultant in mid-2019, no documentary evidence of implementation was provided and violations continued into 2021.
dataType: Telephone numbers, customer contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1) – Lawfulness of processing (lack of valid legal basis)
GDPR Article 12(2) – Facilitating exercise of data subject rights
Law 3471/2006 Article 11(1)-(2) – Restrictions on unsolicited electronic communications

companyDescription: Asker Kommune is a municipality in Akershus, Norway, providing local government services including education, social services, and public administration to approximately 31,000 residents.
companyLongDescription: Asker Kommune is a municipality in Akershus, Norway, providing local government services including education, social services, and public administration to approximately 31,000 residents.
caseDescription: Asker municipality published 127 complete national identification numbers and names of individuals on its public website via document title listings from 2004–2020, exposing confidential information about children receiving special education, disability support, and housing assistance. The municipality failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures and lacked proper procedures to detect and prevent such breaches, which was only discovered when a private citizen reported it.
violationSummary: Confidential personal data was made publicly accessible on the internet without legal basis or security safeguards. The data exposure was continuous over 16 years and only discovered by a third party, not through internal monitoring.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Asker Kommune published 127 citizens' complete national ID numbers and confidential document titles involving children, special education.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 120 residents, including children, had their full national ID numbers and sensitive personal information about disability services.

claimsVsReality.claim: Asker Kommune stated it had robust procedures with daily manual proofreading of postlists by two employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: These procedures failed entirely; the breach persisted for 16 years undetected and was only discovered when a citizen reported it.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality asserted that confidential information was adequately protected on its systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive data about children's special education, disability status, and housing support was publicly accessible on the internet without any access controls or logging.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality indicated a commitment to data protection (per follow-up letter of 22 May 2020).
claimsVsReality.reality: The municipality lacked even basic audit procedures (sampling) for legacy data and had not detected the 16-year-old breach itself.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Asker Kommune failed to establish adequate security measures to prevent confidential information from being publicly accessible on its website for 16 years.
violations: Asker Kommune failed to establish adequate security measures to prevent confidential information from being publicly accessible on its website for 16 years.
No monitoring or audit procedures were in place to detect the ongoing exposure; a private citizen, not the municipality, discovered the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis for processing personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The publication of 127 citizens' national ID numbers and confidential information on the municipality's website had no lawful basis. No individual consented; no legal authority permitted such publication.
violations: The publication of 127 citizens' national ID numbers and confidential information on the municipality's website had no lawful basis. No individual consented; no legal authority permitted such publication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed securely with integrity and confidentiality.
regulatoryFindings.description: Confidential data about vulnerable individuals (children, those with special needs, recipients of housing support) was exposed publicly without protection, violating the confidentiality principle.
violations: Confidential data about vulnerable individuals (children, those with special needs, recipients of housing support) was exposed publicly without protection, violating the confidentiality principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires controllers to implement accountability measures and adequate procedures to ensure compliance with GDPR.
regulatoryFindings.description: Asker Kommune had no procedures for sampling or auditing old postlists. Daily proofreading by two staff was inadequate and failed to prevent the 16-year breach.
violations: Asker Kommune had no procedures for sampling or auditing old postlists. Daily proofreading by two staff was inadequate and failed to prevent the 16-year breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: Offentlegforskrifta § 7 (Norwegian Public Disclosure Regulation) prohibits publishing national ID numbers and confidential personal information online.
regulatoryFindings.description: The municipality violated the specific Norwegian prohibition by exposing complete national ID numbers and confidential administrative records on the public internet.
violations: The municipality violated the specific Norwegian prohibition by exposing complete national ID numbers and confidential administrative records on the public internet.

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian DPA) imposed a fine of NOK 1,000,000 (approximately USD 104,000) on Asker Kommune, payable to the state treasury. The municipality is required to: (1) immediately cease publication of protected personal data; (2) implement adequate technical and organisational security controls to prevent future breaches; (3) establish mandatory sampling and audit procedures for legacy postlists; (4) contact affected individuals. The decision is subject to appeal to Datatilsynet within three weeks, with further appeal to Personvernemnda (Privacy Board). The municipality acknowledged the breach, took down offending documents, and stated willingness to implement remedial measures.
companyNow: Asker Kommune remains a local government authority in Akershus county, Norway. Following the 2021 decision, the municipality has implemented enhanced data protection procedures and digital governance standards, though specific post-decision improvements are not detailed in this document.
dataType: Personal identification numbers (national ID/fødselsnummer), names, confidential administrative documents (special educational needs, housing benefits), family status information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of valid processing basis
GDPR Art. 32 – Inadequate technical and organisational measures
Offentleglova § 10 and Offentlegforskrifta § 7 – Prohibition on publishing national ID numbers and confidential information online

companyDescription: Storstockholms Lokaltrafik (SL) is the publicly owned operator of public transportation (subway, commuter rail, bus, tram) across Stockholm region and surrounding areas, serving millions of daily commuters.
companyLongDescription: Storstockholms Lokaltrafik (SL) is the publicly owned operator of public transportation (subway, commuter rail, bus, tram) across Stockholm region and surrounding areas, serving millions of daily commuters.
caseDescription: SL deployed body-worn cameras on ticket inspectors to record passengers with both video and audio without adequate legal basis, transparency, or consent. The continuous pre-recording function (1 minute buffer) captured all transit users indiscriminately, including children, even when no violation or incident occurred. SL failed to provide meaningful information to the public before deployment.
companyWorth: Unknown (public authority/state-owned enterprise; not traded on stock exchange)
violationSummary: Systematic, continuous surveillance of identifiable persons in a public place they depend on (transit) with audio capture, a particularly sensitive form of monitoring. The pre-recording technique meant all-comers were monitored even before any wrongdoing occurred.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: SL equipped ticket inspectors with body cameras that continuously recorded video and audio with a one-minute buffer across Stockholm's entire transit network.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of transit-dependent commuters, including children, were secretly audio and video recorded in environments they could not avoid, with no legal basis.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pre-recording for 1 minute is necessary to capture events that arise suddenly during ticket control or hotfoul/violent situations, ensuring inspectors can preserve evidence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vast majority of 1-minute buffers capture innocent passengers unrelated to any incident; IMY found 15 seconds maximally necessary and that this still captured excessive irrelevant persons.

claimsVsReality.claim: Audio recording is essential to understand what was said during disputes and threats, improving evidence quality.
claimsVsReality.reality: Audio was continuously captured in public transit spaces where passengers have no reasonable expectation of being recorded; IMY deemed audio particularly sensitive and inadequately disclosed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Badge on inspector uniforms constitutes adequate notice of video recording under Article 12.7 (standardized symbols).
claimsVsReality.reality: Badge did not clearly convey audio capture (marked as especially sensitive); it did not inform all passengers before they entered the surveillance zone; only those already approached by inspector would see it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fare-evasion prevention and inspector safety are compelling interests justifying continuous surveillance of millions of transit-dependent users.
claimsVsReality.reality: ~30,000 fare violations annually from millions of trips; SL's own data showed ticket inspectors report fewer serious assaults post-camera, but balancing test showed commuters' privacy interest in exercising right to travel outweighed SL's administrative convenience.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: SL processed video and audio of millions of transit users without legal basis; pre-recording occurred before information was given to passengers
violations: SL processed video and audio of millions of transit users without legal basis; pre-recording occurred before information was given to passengers
Continuous 1-minute buffer capture of all persons in camera range violated transparency principle—passengers had no meaningful notice before being filmed

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data be adequate, relevant, and not excessive in relation to the purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Pre-recording for 60 seconds captured vast numbers of uninvolved passengers, far exceeding what was necessary to identify fare evaders or document incidents
violations: Pre-recording for 60 seconds captured vast numbers of uninvolved passengers, far exceeding what was necessary to identify fare evaders or document incidents
All-day continuous recording with 1-minute buffer collected excessive data from innocent commuters unrelated to any violation

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) allows processing based on legitimate interest only if the data subject's fundamental rights and freedoms do not override the controller's interest, assessed through a balancing test.
regulatoryFindings.description: SL's interest in identifying fare evaders (≈30,000 annually from millions of trips) did not outweigh the massive intrusion on privacy of entire transit-dependent population including children
violations: SL's interest in identifying fare evaders (≈30,000 annually from millions of trips) did not outweigh the massive intrusion on privacy of entire transit-dependent population including children
Active recording during fare disputes and audio capture of intimate moments (confessions, anxiety, distress) in confined public spaces created severe privacy invasion disproportionate to SL's aims

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires data controller provide specified information to data subjects when personal data are obtained from them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Only passengers receiving a ticket fine received brief written notice; millions of other recorded passengers received zero information
violations: Only passengers receiving a ticket fine received brief written notice; millions of other recorded passengers received zero information
Badge on inspector uniforms inadequate—it did not inform that audio was being recorded (marked as particularly sensitive in Swedish law)
No clear notice before entering surveillance zone; passengers could not make informed choice to avoid transit system

outcome: IMY imposed a total administrative penalty of 16,000,000 SEK (€1.7M) divided as: 4M SEK for unlawful pre-recording and audio capture for assault prevention (overly excessive under Article 6.1(f) and 5.1(c)); 8M SEK for identity verification recordings (not necessary when ID shown, and audio capture unjustified); 4M SEK for failure to provide transparency information. IMY required SL to cease using pre-recording exceeding 15 seconds and to provide clear notice (signage) before surveillance zones. SL must modify badge and disseminate comprehensive information to all passengers. Decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within 3 weeks.
companyNow: SL (Storstockholms Lokaltrafik) continues as the primary public transport operator for Stockholm region, owned by Region Stockholm. Following the decision, SL has begun implementing mandatory compliance measures including badge modifications and signage.
dataType: Video/image data, audio recordings, biometric identifiers (facial recognition), personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) – Legitimate Interest Test (failed balancing)
GDPR Article 13 – Information to Data Subject (failure to provide)

companyDescription: Support King, LLC (formerly SpyFone.com) is a Puerto Rico-based company that develops and sells mobile device monitoring software. The company marketed its products as tools for parental and employee monitoring but actively enabled stalking and domestic abuse through surreptitious surveillance capabilities.
companyLongDescription: Support King, LLC (formerly SpyFone.com) is a Puerto Rico-based company that develops and sells mobile device monitoring software. The company marketed its products as tools for parental and employee monitoring but actively enabled stalking and domestic abuse through surreptitious surveillance capabilities.
caseDescription: Support King sold surreptitious mobile device monitoring software (SpyFone) marketed for parental and employee monitoring, but actively enabled stalking and domestic abuse. The company failed to implement reasonable data security, resulting in a 2018 breach exposing approximately 2,200 consumers' sensitive data, and falsely claimed to have partnered with security firms and law enforcement to investigate.
violationSummary: SpyFone enabled systematic, surreptitious surveillance of device users without their knowledge or consent. The software was deliberately designed to hide from the monitored person, making it an intrusion into private communications and location data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Support King sold SpyFone monitoring apps that secretly captured SMS messages, GPS locations, emails, photos.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 2,200 consumers' sensitive data including photos and GPS locations were exposed in an August 2018 breach, and stalkers.

claimsVsReality.claim: SpyFone cares about the integrity and security of your personal information. We will take all reasonable precautions to safeguard customer information, including encrypted personal information storage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information including photos, text messages, web histories, and GPS locations were stored unencrypted on accessible servers. In August 2018, an unauthorized third party accessed the server, exposing data from approximately 2,200 consumers.

claimsVsReality.claim: SpyFone products are designed for monitoring children and employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: The products enabled surreptitious monitoring specifically designed to hide from the device user, with instructions to disable security warnings and hide the application. Stalkers and domestic abusers used SpyFone to monitor victims without consent, causing physical, emotional, financial, and social harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondents partnered with leading data security firms to assist in the investigation of the data breach and coordinated with law enforcement authorities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Respondents did not partner with any data security firms and did not work with or coordinate with law enforcement on any aspect of the unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents sold monitoring products enabling surreptitious surveillance without reasonable safeguards to prevent use for stalking and domestic abuse.
violations: Respondents sold monitoring products enabling surreptitious surveillance without reasonable safeguards to prevent use for stalking and domestic abuse.

Respondents represented they would take all reasonable precautions to safeguard customer information and encrypt personal data, but failed to encrypt data, restrict API access, or implement basic security controls.
Respondents represented they partnered with leading data security firms and coordinated with law enforcement following the August 2018 breach, but did neither.

outcome: On December 20, 2021, the FTC issued a complaint against Support King, LLC and Scott Zuckerman alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act based on unfair and deceptive practices. The complaint asserts that the company sold surreptitious monitoring software without adequate safeguards against misuse for stalking and abuse, failed to implement reasonable data security resulting in a breach, and made false representations about data encryption and breach response. The document does not indicate a settlement or final order, but represents the FTC's formal charges initiating enforcement proceedings.
companyNow: Support King, LLC operating as SpyFone.com remained active as of the complaint date (December 2021). No information is provided regarding current operational status, settlement, or closure following the complaint.
dataType: SMS messages, call history, GPS location, web history, contacts, photos, calendar, files, emails, video chats, social media activity, financial information, biometric data (microphone recordings)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices

company: HMI Institute of Health Sciences Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: HMI Institute of Health Sciences Pte. Ltd. is a private provider of healthcare training courses to individuals in Singapore. The organisation collects personal data from employees and trainees for employment management and course registration purposes.
companyLongDescription: HMI Institute of Health Sciences Pte. Ltd. is a private provider of healthcare training courses to individuals in Singapore. The organisation collects personal data from employees and trainees for employment management and course registration purposes.
caseDescription: On 4 December 2019, HMI Institute's file server was hit by ransomware, exposing personal data of approximately 110,080 trainees and 253 employees. The attack succeeded because the organisation failed to implement reasonable security measures: it kept the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) port open for over four years without additional protections, failed to enforce strong password policies, and did not adequately stipulate data protection requirements to its IT vendor.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security steps and arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, modification, and disposal of personal data. Specifically: inadequate remote access controls (RDP port open unprotected), weak password management, shared admin credentials, and lack of contractual data protection requirements with the IT vendor.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: HMI Institute kept a critical remote access port open for over four years without security protections, used weak passwords incorporating the company name.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed systems enabled attackers to encrypt and deny access to personal data of 110,080 participants and 253 employees, including financial information, NRIC numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had a Password Policy consistent with the Commission's recommendations (minimum 8 characters, alphabetical and numeric components).
claimsVsReality.reality: None of the passwords actually used for the administrator account or files met the Password Policy's recommended complexity rules; they incorporated the organisation's name acronym.

claimsVsReality.claim: Keeping the RDP Port permanently closed was not practicable; half a day of downtime would be required to open or close it.
claimsVsReality.reality: For a server storing approximately 110,333 individuals' personal data, including financial information and NRICs, the minor inconvenience of some downtime should have been measured against the significant risk of exposing such data for over four years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation relied on the Vendor's technical expertise for security of the Server.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation did not stipulate clear data protection requirements in the contract, nor did it obtain recommendations from the Vendor about how to protect the data; thus, it could not legitimately delegate its Protection Obligation to the Vendor.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to adequately regulate remote access: kept RDP Port open from 2014–2019 without sufficient protective measures such as IP whitelisting, non-default ports, RDP gateways, or activity logging.
violations: Failed to adequately regulate remote access: kept RDP Port open from 2014–2019 without sufficient protective measures such as IP whitelisting, non-default ports, RDP gateways, or activity logging.

Failed to implement proper password management: passwords used for the administrator account and files did not meet the organisation's own Password Policy (minimum 8 characters, alphabetical and numeric); passwords incorporated the organisation's name acronym, making them guessable via brute force attacks.

Failed to take reasonable steps to ensure Vendor compliance: did not specify clear data protection requirements in the contract with the IT service provider, nor verify that the Vendor understood its role in protecting personal data.

Shared administrator account credentials between the organisation's IT administrator and at least three Vendor employees, creating accountability and audit trail problems, without additional controls like 2FA or anti-hammering.

outcome: The Commissioner found the organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 35,000 within 30 days. No other directions were deemed necessary given the remedial actions already taken. The organisation decommissioned the Server, notified affected parties, disconnected remote access, implemented Internet separation measures, adopted password management policies, engaged IT security consultants to establish an ISO 27001 framework, and conducted cybersecurity training for staff.
companyNow: HMI Institute of Health Sciences Pte. Ltd. remains in operation as a private healthcare training provider in Singapore. Post-incident, it has significantly strengthened its information security posture, including ISO 27001 certification efforts and ongoing staff cybersecurity awareness.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, address, date of birth, contact number, email address, course details, nationality, employer details, employment history, financial information, salary/payment information, CPF information, bank account numbers, race, gender, age, vehicle licence plate

companyDescription: Audio House Marketing Pte Ltd is a retail/marketing company that operated an e-commerce website for customer engagement, including shopping cart and payment functionalities.
companyLongDescription: Audio House Marketing Pte Ltd is a retail/marketing company that operated an e-commerce website for customer engagement, including shopping cart and payment functionalities.
caseDescription: Audio House Marketing Pte Ltd suffered a ransomware attack affecting approximately 98,000 customers' contact information. The breach resulted from SQL injection vulnerabilities in the company's website PHP files that had existed since April 2017. The organisation failed to conduct vulnerability scanning, security assessments, or periodic security reviews, and lacked data protection requirements in its vendor contracts.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure, specifically by not conducting vulnerability assessments, periodic security reviews, or implementing vendor oversight requirements despite handling personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Audio House Marketing failed to conduct vulnerability scanning or periodic security reviews of its website, leaving SQL injection vulnerabilities unpatched since April 2017.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 98,000 customers' names, addresses, emails, and phone numbers were exposed to a ransomware attack because the company ignored well-known SQL injection risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Conducted pre-launch tests prior to website launch in April 2017
claimsVsReality.reality: Pre-launch testing only covered functionality (shopping cart, payment) and failed to identify existing SQL injection vulnerabilities in PHP files

claimsVsReality.claim: Website developer and IT vendor engagement handled security
claimsVsReality.reality: No contracts with website developer stipulated data protection requirements; main IT vendor contract lacked data protection obligations; no adequate oversight of technical security responsibilities

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24(a) of the PDPA: An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Operated website for 4+ years with undetected SQL injection vulnerabilities without conducting vulnerability scanning or assessments
violations: Operated website for 4+ years with undetected SQL injection vulnerabilities without conducting vulnerability scanning or assessments
Failed to perform periodic security reviews or ICT security audits despite Commission guidance
Did not stipulate data protection requirements or security maintenance obligations in contracts with website developer or IT vendor
Lacked adequate oversight mechanisms over subcontractors responsible for technical capabilities

outcome: Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of section 24(a) of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of S$10,000 within 30 days. No additional directions under section 48I were deemed necessary given the organisation's prompt remediation actions: disabling the website on the day of the incident, reformatting the webserver, implementing SQL injection security, and conducting vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. All affected personal data was restored without loss.
dataType: Contact information (names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers)

companyDescription: The Executive Office is the Northern Ireland government department. The Interim Advocate's Office was a temporary body established in August 2019 to support survivors of Historical Institutional Abuse pending establishment of a statutory commissioner.
companyLongDescription: The Executive Office is the Northern Ireland government department. The Interim Advocate's Office was a temporary body established in August 2019 to support survivors of Historical Institutional Abuse pending establishment of a statutory commissioner.
caseDescription: The Executive Office (via the Interim Advocate's Office) sent a newsletter email to 251 subscribers on 22 May 2020 with recipient email addresses visible to all recipients instead of using blind carbon copy. This exposed 209 email addresses, 110 of which contained individuals' full names, to unintended disclosure. The organisation lacked appropriate security measures, documented processes, staff training, and data protection policies to prevent the breach.
violationSummary: The incident involved unintended exposure of personal data (email addresses and names) to a wider audience than intended, making it a classic disclosure/exposure violation rather than a breach of confidentiality with intent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Interim Advocate's Office sent a newsletter email to 251 subscribers with all recipient email addresses visible to every recipient by placing them in the 'To' field instead of using blind.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposure of 209 email addresses to all recipients breached the privacy of survivors of institutional childhood abuse, with 110 addresses containing full names.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IAO described itself at the time of reporting as an arm's length organisation, independent of the Executive Office
claimsVsReality.reality: Following legal advice on 11 December 2020, the Executive Office clarified that the IAO was a constituent part of the Executive Office with no separate legal basis, making the Executive Office the actual data controller

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed with appropriate security including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to ensure appropriate security resulting in inappropriate disclosure of 209 email addresses to all newsletter recipients
violations: Failed to ensure appropriate security resulting in inappropriate disclosure of 209 email addresses to all newsletter recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24(1) and (2) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing complies with the Regulation, with measures reviewed and updated where necessary, and data protection policies implemented where proportionate.
regulatoryFindings.description: No technical solution for group email sending (such as mail merge), no documented process for sending newsletters, no staff training on secure email procedures, inadequate data protection policies (only guidance in telephone induction pack)
violations: No technical solution for group email sending (such as mail merge), no documented process for sending newsletters, no staff training on secure email procedures, inadequate data protection policies (only guidance in telephone induction pack)

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) and (2) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, considering state of the art, costs, nature and scope of processing, and risks of destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or access.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement security measures appropriate to the high-risk context of Historical Institutional Abuse data requiring maximum confidentiality, demonstrating insufficient consideration of data security and risks to data subject rights
violations: Failed to implement security measures appropriate to the high-risk context of Historical Institutional Abuse data requiring maximum confidentiality, demonstrating insufficient consideration of data security and risks to data subject rights

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to the Executive Office under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The organisation took immediate remedial steps including: notifying all affected individuals, providing emotional support, creating Newsletter Desk Instructions (8 July 2020), placing data protection responsibility under Executive Office's Data Protection Officer (1 July 2020), developing comprehensive data protection and information management policies, reviewing and updating the Data Protection Impact Assessment (July 2020), and sharing lessons learned across the Northern Ireland Civil Service (20 July 2020).
companyNow: The Interim Advocate's Office ceased to exist on 11 December 2020 when the Commissioner for Survivors of Institutional Childhood Abuse (COSICA) was established. The Executive Office remains the responsible data controller.
dataType: Email addresses, personal identifiers (names, initials)

companyDescription: HSBC Bank (Singapore) Limited is a full-service banking subsidiary of UK-based HSBC Holdings, offering personal and business banking, credit facilities, and financial services in Singapore with advanced algorithmic credit assessment systems.
companyLongDescription: HSBC Bank (Singapore) Limited is a full-service banking subsidiary of UK-based HSBC Holdings, offering personal and business banking, credit facilities, and financial services in Singapore with advanced algorithmic credit assessment systems.
caseDescription: HSBC rejected a data subject access request for an internal credit evaluation report, withholding redacted opinion data generated by its proprietary algorithm. The applicant challenged the bank's reliance on the 'Evaluative Purpose Exception' to exclude algorithmic scoring and assessments from the report. The Deputy Commissioner upheld HSBC's refusal, finding the withheld data constituted opinion data kept solely for evaluative purposes under Singapore's PDPA.
violationSummary: HSBC excluded algorithmically-generated opinion data from access rights, preventing the data subject from understanding or challenging automated decision-making about his creditworthiness despite PDPA Access and Accuracy Obligations requiring transparency for data used in consequential decisions.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: HSBC redacted five fields from an internal credit evaluation report provided to an applicant, including algorithmic scores and assessments that determined his credit card application decision.
whyTheyWereWrong: The applicant received no explanation for his credit denial and could not review the bank's algorithmic evaluation of his creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: HSBC claimed the redacted data constituted confidential commercial information whose disclosure would harm competitive position and allow reverse-engineering of its proprietary algorithm.
claimsVsReality.reality: HSBC had already publicly disclosed its Credit Decisioning Policy Statement describing the majority of the algorithmic opinions, undermining claims that disclosure would compromise competitive advantage.

claimsVsReality.claim: HSBC argued disclosing the redacted data would reveal information collected for ongoing investigation and regulatory compliance purposes under anti-money laundering rules.
claimsVsReality.reality: Routine client due diligence and information checks for credit application processing do not constitute 'investigations' under PDPA s.2(1), and MAS Notice 626 on anti-money laundering was found irrelevant to the withheld algorithmic assessments.

claimsVsReality.claim: HSBC contended the applicant's request was frivolous because he already knew the personal data he had provided in his application two weeks earlier.
claimsVsReality.reality: The applicant had never had access to HSBC's proprietary algorithmic opinions and assessments—he requested data about how the bank evaluated him, not reproduction of data he himself had provided.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 21(1) of the PDPA grants a data subject the right to access personal data about him in an organisation's possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: HSBC withheld algorithmically-generated opinion data used to evaluate the applicant's creditworthiness, preventing access to personal data directly relevant to a consequential decision about his credit application.
violations: HSBC withheld algorithmically-generated opinion data used to evaluate the applicant's creditworthiness, preventing access to personal data directly relevant to a consequential decision about his credit application.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 23(a) of the PDPA requires an organisation to ensure that personal data it uses when making decisions affecting an individual is accurate and complete.
regulatoryFindings.description: By withholding the algorithmic assessments used to deny credit, HSBC prevented the applicant from verifying the accuracy, completeness, or potential bias in the data underlying the decision that directly harmed him.
violations: By withholding the algorithmic assessments used to deny credit, HSBC prevented the applicant from verifying the accuracy, completeness, or potential bias in the data underlying the decision that directly harmed him.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fifth Schedule para 1(a) of the PDPA allows refusal to provide access to opinion data kept solely for an evaluative purpose, defined as data for determining suitability or eligibility for enumerated purposes including awarding contracts.
regulatoryFindings.description: HSBC lawfully applied the evaluative purpose exception; the Deputy Commissioner found the redacted algorithmic scores were opinion data used to evaluate the applicant's suitability for credit facilities (a form of contract award), justifying non-disclosure.
violations: HSBC lawfully applied the evaluative purpose exception; the Deputy Commissioner found the redacted algorithmic scores were opinion data used to evaluate the applicant's suitability for credit facilities (a form of contract award), justifying non-disclosure.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner upheld HSBC's refusal to disclose the redacted opinion data, confirming that algorithmic creditworthiness assessments qualify as opinion data protected under the Evaluative Purpose Exception. However, the Deputy Commissioner noted HSBC had acted reasonably by providing its Credit Decisioning Policy Statement describing how it uses AI and Big Data for credit assessment. HSBC was found to have acquitted itself from an accountability and transparency perspective despite the legally justified refusal to disclose individual algorithmic opinions.
companyNow: HSBC Bank (Singapore) Limited remains a major full-service banking subsidiary of HSBC Holdings, operating retail and commercial banking services in Singapore with a significant digital and algorithmic credit decisioning infrastructure.
dataType: Financial data, credit application information, employment history, income, education level, algorithmic creditworthiness assessments
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Fifth Schedule para 1(a) – Evaluative Purpose Exception

companyDescription: Zoom Video Communications is a Delaware corporation founded in 2011 that provides cloud-based videoconferencing and collaboration services. As of early 2020, Zoom experienced explosive growth due to COVID-19 pandemic-driven demand for remote communication tools.
companyLongDescription: Zoom Video Communications is a Delaware corporation founded in 2011 that provides cloud-based videoconferencing and collaboration services. As of early 2020, Zoom experienced explosive growth due to COVID-19 pandemic-driven demand for remote communication tools.
caseDescription: Zoom made false and misleading claims about end-to-end encryption for video meetings when it actually lacked this capability. The company also used AES 128-bit encryption instead of the advertised 256-bit encryption, and stored meeting recordings unencrypted for up to 60 days. Additionally, Zoom secretly deployed software to bypass Safari browser security safeguards without user consent.
violationSummary: Zoom's failure to implement adequate security measures (weak encryption, unencrypted storage, secret surveillance bypass) directly enabled potential compromise of sensitive communications and personal data. The deception about encryption strength and end-to-end encryption compounded the insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Zoom falsely claimed to offer end-to-end encryption and 256-bit AES encryption for video meetings while actually using weaker 128-bit encryption.
whyTheyWereWrong: 3.8 million Mac users had a hidden web server secretly installed that bypassed Safari's security protections, exposing them to remote webcam surveillance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Zoom offers end-to-end encryption for all Zoom Meetings
claimsVsReality.reality: Zoom servers, including some in China, maintain cryptographic keys that allow Zoom to decrypt meeting content. Only Connector product (on-premises) supported true end-to-end encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Meetings use AES 256-bit encryption
claimsVsReality.reality: Zoom actually used AES 128-bit encryption in ECB mode, which provides significantly less protection than 256-bit encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cloud Recordings are stored encrypted immediately after meetings end
claimsVsReality.reality: Recorded meetings remained unencrypted on Zoom servers for up to 60 days before being transferred to encrypted cloud storage.

claimsVsReality.claim: July 2018 Mac App update would fix minor bugs
claimsVsReality.reality: Update secretly deployed ZoomOpener web server that bypassed Safari browser protections, persisted after app deletion, and exposed users to RCE and DoS attacks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Deceptively represented that Zoom Meetings used end-to-end encryption when Zoom servers maintained cryptographic keys allowing Zoom to access meeting content
violations: Deceptively represented that Zoom Meetings used end-to-end encryption when Zoom servers maintained cryptographic keys allowing Zoom to access meeting content
