claimsVsReality.reality: No additional information was provided by the 4 November 2020 deadline.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 31 requires controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities on request in the performance of their tasks.
regulatoryFindings.description: CML failed to respond to the Commissioner's cooperation request of 27 August 2020 until 14 September 2020 and provided only partial, non-responsive information.
violations: CML failed to respond to the Commissioner's cooperation request of 27 August 2020 until 14 September 2020 and provided only partial, non-responsive information.
CML provided information relating to events before the SAR was received rather than information about SAR compliance.
CML gave assurances that information would be provided but failed to deliver within the specified timeframe and beyond.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 101 (Information Notices) empowers the Commissioner to order controllers to provide information required for the performance of tasks.
regulatoryFindings.description: An Information Notice was issued on 29 September 2020 requiring compliance by 29 October 2020; CML did not respond until 30 October 2020.
violations: An Information Notice was issued on 29 September 2020 requiring compliance by 29 October 2020; CML did not respond until 30 October 2020.
CML provided only partial information on 30 October 2020 and provided no additional information by the 4 November 2020 deadline despite assurances of action.
CML demonstrated a pattern of non-compliance with formal information requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Articles 12 and 15 require controllers to respond to Subject Access Requests in compliance with prescribed timeframes and provide access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: CML failed to properly comply with the SAR submitted on 7 July 2020, triggering the investigation.
violations: CML failed to properly comply with the SAR submitted on 7 July 2020, triggering the investigation.

outcome: The Information Commissioner imposed an administrative fine of £3,250.00 on Cosmetic Medical Limited, payable by 22 January 2021 via BACS transfer or cheque. The fine addresses failures to cooperate with the Commissioner's investigation and non-compliance with an Information Notice. CML has a right of appeal to the Isle of Man Data Protection Tribunal under Regulation 120. The Commissioner decided not to certify the failure to comply with the Information Notice to the High Court in addition to the penalty.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Request (SAR)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR and LED Implementing Regulations 2018, Regulation 101 (Information notices)
GDPR Articles 12 and 15 (Subject Access Request compliance)

companyDescription: The Central Depository (Pte) Limited is a Singapore-based financial infrastructure company providing integrated clearing, settlement and depository facilities for account holders in the Singapore securities market.
companyLongDescription: The Central Depository (Pte) Limited is a Singapore-based financial infrastructure company providing integrated clearing, settlement and depository facilities for account holders in the Singapore securities market.
caseDescription: The Central Depository failed to conduct adequate software testing when migrating from an old trading system (PTS) to a new one (NPTS). A bug in the dividend cheque printing module caused it to mail cheques containing sensitive personal data to outdated addresses instead of current ones. 211 individuals had their financial and identity information disclosed to unauthorised recipients.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security steps to protect sensitive personal data (NRIC, financial information) by conducting inadequate testing before deploying a system change, resulting in unauthorised disclosure of personal data to third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Central Depository migrated from its Post Trade System to a New Post Trade System without adequately testing whether the Dividend Cheque Module would extract updated addresses when account.
whyTheyWereWrong: 211 account holders' personal data including NRIC numbers, CDP account numbers, and dividend amounts were mailed to outdated addresses, exposing them to fraud risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation expended its best efforts in testing and both the Notification Letters Test and Dividend Cheque Module Test did not return errors, so further targeted testing was not contemplated.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Dividend Cheque Module Test had too narrow a scope and did not include the change-of-address scenario, which was a known scenario tested in other modules. The test results from the independently-coded Notification Letters module could not provide assurance that the Dividend Cheque Module would work correctly.

claimsVsReality.claim: There was no risk of actual financial loss because cheques were made out to the names of affected individuals and could only be encashed into matching accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unauthorised recipients could have fraudulently altered cheque names or presented them for deposit. Additionally, affected individuals were deprived of access to their funds during the period before replacement cheques were issued. The disclosure itself created fraud and identity theft risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Disclosed Data was disclosed only to single recipients and was insufficient to be used for impersonation or executing transactions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The combination of NRIC number, name, account number, and security holdings information disclosed to unauthorised individuals created a material fraud and identity theft risk, and the sending of cheques to wrong addresses meant data was accessible to multiple unknown persons at each address.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct adequate testing before migrating systems to verify the dividend cheque module would extract updated addresses when customers changed address
violations: Failed to conduct adequate testing before migrating systems to verify the dividend cheque module would extract updated addresses when customers changed address
Test scope for the dividend cheque module did not include the change-of-address scenario despite it being a known scenario tested in other modules
Did not test with sufficient test cases to simulate real-world usage of the system
Relied on independent test results from another module (Notification Letters Test) without verifying the Dividend Cheque Module would work correctly

outcome: The Commissioner found the Organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. The Organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 32,000 within 30 days. The Organisation had already implemented remedial actions including: deploying a code fix on 20 April 2019 to ensure updated addresses are consistently extracted, re-issuing replacement cheques and explanation letters to affected individuals, and committing to refresher training on issue reporting procedures. No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures already in place.
companyNow: The Central Depository (Pte) Limited continues to operate as the securities depository and clearing house for Singapore's financial markets. The company has strengthened its testing and code review processes following this enforcement action.
dataType: NRIC number, name, CDP account number, security holdings, dividend amount

companyDescription: University College Dublin is a public research university and constituent university of the National University of Ireland, founded in 1854. It is one of Ireland's leading academic institutions.
companyLongDescription: University College Dublin is a public research university and constituent university of the National University of Ireland, founded in 1854. It is one of Ireland's leading academic institutions.
caseDescription: University College Dublin failed to implement adequate security measures on its email service, resulting in 7 data breaches where unauthorised parties accessed UCD email accounts. The university also stored personal data longer than necessary and failed to notify one breach to the DPC within the required timeframe.
violationSummary: UCD failed to implement appropriate security measures (technical and organisational) required by GDPR Article 32, directly resulting in multiple breaches where unauthorised parties accessed email accounts containing personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: University College Dublin failed to implement appropriate security measures on its email service, stored personal data longer than necessary.
whyTheyWereWrong: Unauthorised third parties accessed thousands of UCD staff and student email accounts containing sensitive personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security using appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data on its email service, allowing unauthorised third parties to access email accounts
violations: UCD failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data on its email service, allowing unauthorised third parties to access email accounts

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure appropriate security of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD did not implement adequate security measures to protect email accounts from unauthorised access
violations: UCD did not implement adequate security measures to protect email accounts from unauthorised access

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) requires personal data be stored in a form which permits identification of data subjects no longer than necessary for processing purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD stored certain personal data in email accounts for longer than necessary
violations: UCD stored certain personal data in email accounts for longer than necessary

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires data controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD notified one personal data breach 13 days after becoming aware of it, exceeding the 'without undue delay' requirement
violations: UCD notified one personal data breach 13 days after becoming aware of it, exceeding the 'without undue delay' requirement

outcome: The Data Protection Commission imposed an administrative fine of €70,000 on UCD, issued a reprimand, and ordered UCD to bring its email service processing operations into full compliance with GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) through implementation of appropriate technical and organisational security measures.
companyNow: University College Dublin continues to operate as Ireland's largest university. The institution has implemented enhanced cybersecurity measures and data protection protocols following the DPC enforcement action.
dataType: Email account credentials, email content, personal identifiers

companyDescription: A Hungarian warehouse and logistics operator managing dry goods storage (telecommunications equipment, hardware, cables) with approximately 37 employees at the monitored facility.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian warehouse and logistics operator managing dry goods storage (telecommunications equipment, hardware, cables) with approximately 37 employees at the monitored facility.
caseDescription: A warehouse operator installed surveillance cameras ostensibly for asset protection but positioned them to monitor employees' work intensity and break-room usage. The company failed to provide adequate, timely notice about the camera system to employees for months after deployment began. Camera angles captured both protected valuables and employee workstations, enabling unauthorized workplace monitoring.
violationSummary: The company deployed electronic surveillance systems with camera angles that were capable of monitoring employees' work activity and break-room usage, not limited to asset protection as claimed. This constitutes unauthorized workplace surveillance—a classic privacy invasion through persistent monitoring.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed warehouse surveillance cameras with viewing angles capturing both high-value assets and employee workstations.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees had no clear understanding that their administrative work areas and break patterns were being monitored, enabling managers to track work intensity.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cameras were installed solely for asset protection and building security (vagyonvédelem és épületek biztonsága).
claimsVsReality.reality: Camera angles were configured to capture employee workstations and break areas, making them equally capable of monitoring work intensity and employee presence during non-working periods.

claimsVsReality.claim: The storeroom area was not designated as a break-room and only involved brief administrative tasks with no continuous employee presence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Employees used the storeroom during breaks; supervisors explicitly instructed employees (including the complainant) to limit their time there, indicating the system was being used to monitor employee behavior during non-work periods.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees were informed about camera operations through a data protection notice provided at hire and through a general policy available on the internal network.
claimsVsReality.reality: The initial notice was generic and non-specific; the detailed operational policy was not issued until April 3, 2020—more than 4.5 months after cameras began recording on November 18, 2019. No location-specific warnings were posted at the monitored areas during the gap period.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires that personal data shall be 'collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes.'
regulatoryFindings.description: Camera in the warehouse storeroom was configured to capture both high-value tools/parts (the stated purpose) and the administrative workstation where employees performed brief clerical tasks, rendering it capable of monitoring work intensity contrary to the stated asset-protection purpose.
violations: Camera in the warehouse storeroom was configured to capture both high-value tools/parts (the stated purpose) and the administrative workstation where employees performed brief clerical tasks, rendering it capable of monitoring work intensity contrary to the stated asset-protection purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed' (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: The camera's field of view encompassed far more than the protected assets—it captured the entire workstation area and employee movements, going beyond what was necessary for asset protection.
violations: The camera's field of view encompassed far more than the protected assets—it captured the entire workstation area and employee movements, going beyond what was necessary for asset protection.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(1) requires the controller to provide data subjects with specified information at the time personal data are obtained from them, including the identity of the controller, the purpose of processing, the legal basis, and other details enabling fair and transparent processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: For approximately 5.5 months (November 18, 2019 – April 3, 2020), employees received no specific notice about the camera system's operation at their worksite. A generic one-page statement provided at hire mentioned cameras only in passing; the detailed operational policy was not issued until months after recording began. No location-specific signage was posted at the monitored areas during this period.
violations: For approximately 5.5 months (November 18, 2019 – April 3, 2020), employees received no specific notice about the camera system's operation at their worksite. A generic one-page statement provided at hire mentioned cameras only in passing; the detailed operational policy was not issued until months after recording began. No location-specific signage was posted at the monitored areas during this period.

outcome: The Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (National Data Protection Authority) found two substantive violations: (1) violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(c) for improper camera positioning enabling unauthorized employee monitoring, and (2) violation of GDPR Art. 13(1) for failure to provide timely, specific notice to affected employees. The Authority ordered the company to: (a) reposition the storeroom camera to eliminate its capability to monitor employee work activity and restrict its field of view to protected assets only, and (b) pay a fine of 700,000 HUF (approximately €2,360 / $2,600 USD). The decision was also ordered to be published in anonymized form. The company was required to comply within 30 days of the decision becoming final. The decision is subject to administrative court review within 30 days of service.
companyNow: Unknown – company identity redacted in published decision. Likely still operating warehouse/logistics operations in Hungary.
dataType: Biometric data (facial recognition/video surveillance), location data, work activity patterns
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13(1) – Transparency/Information to be Provided to Data Subject

companyDescription: A debt collection agency operating in Hungary that specializes in pursuing outstanding debts through payment demands and collection activities.
companyLongDescription: A debt collection agency operating in Hungary that specializes in pursuing outstanding debts through payment demands and collection activities.
caseDescription: A debt collection agency unlawfully processed a complainant's phone number by recording it under a different person's account without consent. The agency failed to adhere to data accuracy principles and could not demonstrate lawful basis for the data processing. The phone number was subsequently deleted after the authority's intervention.
violationSummary: The agency collected and recorded the complainant's phone number during a call without consent or notification, treating contact information as belonging to the debtor. This constitutes surveillance-like collection of personal data without proper legal basis or individual awareness.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A collection agency recorded a person's phone number in another person's debt file without consent, then sent repeated SMS payment demands to that number.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant received multiple threatening SMS messages about a debt that was not theirs, had their phone number tied to another person's file without permission.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agency claimed it did not process the complainant's personal data, only stored the phone number as a contact number for reaching the debtor.
claimsVsReality.reality: The phone number unequivocally belonged to and identified the complainant, constituting personal data under GDPR; it was stored under the debtor's account without consent, making it unlawfully processed personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agency stated the phone number was provided voluntarily by the complainant during a telephone conversation as a means to contact the debtor.
claimsVsReality.reality: No explicit consent or notification was given during the call regarding data processing, retention, or storage; the agency failed to provide transparency about how the data would be used or kept.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires that personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; reasonable measures must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency recorded complainant's phone number under debtor's account despite knowing it was the complainant's contact number, not the debtor's, creating inaccurate records.
violations: Agency recorded complainant's phone number under debtor's account despite knowing it was the complainant's contact number, not the debtor's, creating inaccurate records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing is lawful only if it has a valid legal basis, such as explicit consent from the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency processed complainant's phone number without demonstrating valid legal basis or obtaining explicit consent from the complainant, only implicit agreement to facilitate debt communication.
violations: Agency processed complainant's phone number without demonstrating valid legal basis or obtaining explicit consent from the complainant, only implicit agreement to facilitate debt communication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires data controllers to facilitate individuals' rights under Articles 15–22 and provide responses within one month of request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency initially denied access to data claimed to be under a different person's account, violating transparency obligations despite the data being the complainant's personal information.
violations: Agency initially denied access to data claimed to be under a different person's account, violating transparency obligations despite the data being the complainant's personal information.

outcome: The authority found the collection agency violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(d) and 6(1) through unlawful and inaccurate processing of the complainant's phone number. The agency was ordered to pay 300,000 HUF in administrative fines. The phone number was already deleted from the agency's system prior to the authority's intervention. The complainant's request to delete address and email data was rejected as those data were not unlawfully processed. The authority also awarded 10,000 HUF to the complainant for exceeding processing deadlines. The decision is subject to judicial review at the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
dataType: Telephone number, residential address, email address

companyDescription: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre is a religious non-profit organisation that maintains records of approximately 4,500 members and 4,000 non-members. The organisation collects and manages personal data including contact information, identification numbers, and donation records.
companyLongDescription: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre is a religious non-profit organisation that maintains records of approximately 4,500 members and 4,000 non-members. The organisation collects and manages personal data including contact information, identification numbers, and donation records.
caseDescription: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre suffered a ransomware attack on 31 March 2020 that encrypted personal data of 8,500 individuals. The organisation admitted it failed to implement adequate procedural and technical security measures, including security software and protocols, to protect personal data in its possession. The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA and imposed a $5,000 financial penalty.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to maintain adequate security measures (both procedural and technical) to protect personal data from ransomware attack, directly resulting in encryption of 8,500 individuals' sensitive personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre failed to implement procedural and technical security arrangements, leaving its data management system vulnerable to ransomware infection that encrypted personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: 8,500 members and non-members had their names, addresses, contact numbers, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, and donation details encrypted.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate data protection measures in place
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation had no security software, no relevant protocols, and failed to implement either procedural or technical security arrangements

claimsVsReality.claim: The data management system was properly secured
claimsVsReality.reality: The system was vulnerable to ransomware attack, which successfully encrypted personal data of 8,500 individuals on 31 March 2020

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 imposes a Protection Obligation requiring organisations to make reasonable efforts to protect personal data in their possession or under their control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre did not implement procedural security arrangements to protect personal data
violations: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre did not implement procedural security arrangements to protect personal data
Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre did not implement technical security arrangements to protect personal data
The organisation did not have security software or protocols in place to prevent ransomware from entering its data management system
This negligence resulted in ransomware encrypting personal data of 8,500 individuals

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre to pay a financial penalty of $5,000 within 30 days. The organisation was not issued other directions due to remedial actions already taken, including: setting up a new server with backup, installing a firewall, cleaning and reinstalling all connected computers, and committing to engage consultants to produce a data protection manual and train staff in cyber hygiene and incident response. No evidence of data misuse was found, and the organisation retained a backup copy preventing data loss.
companyNow: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre remains operational. Following the incident, the organisation has implemented enhanced security measures including new server infrastructure, firewall protection, and committed to ongoing staff training in data protection and incident response.
dataType: Name, address, contact number, NRIC number, date of birth, donation details

companyDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a public enterprise owned by the Norwegian Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, established to promote innovation, entrepreneurship, and business development in Norway. The agency provides financing, advisory services, and support to businesses and entrepreneurs.
companyLongDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a public enterprise owned by the Norwegian Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, established to promote innovation, entrepreneurship, and business development in Norway. The agency provides financing, advisory services, and support to businesses and entrepreneurs.
caseDescription: Innovasjon Norge processed credit application data for individuals without a lawful basis under GDPR Article 6. The company obtained and stored personal and financial information from multiple credit inquiries between January and April 2020, failing to document legal grounds for processing and mishandling sensitive credit data internally.
violationSummary: The company processed sensitive personal data (credit inquiries) without establishing a valid legal basis under GDPR Article 6, compounded by inadequate security measures and internal data handling protocols, creating systemic insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Innovasjon Norge processed personal credit application data for multiple individuals without a documented legal basis.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' sensitive financial and credit information was handled internally by Innovasjon Norge without lawful authorization, exposing their creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Innovasjon Norge claimed that credit inquiries were necessary to evaluate customer financing applications.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no documented lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 to process the data. No consent was obtained, no legitimate interest was established, and the processing was not linked to an actual contractual relationship with the individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that it had functional safeguards for handling sensitive financial data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Passwords and access credentials were shared among employees, there was no audit trail, and data was retained without clear deletion policies or access controls—indicating inadequate security measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if it is based on one of six enumerated legal bases (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge processed credit application data of 4-6 individuals from January–April 2020 without documenting a lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained, no contractual relationship existed, and no other legal basis was established or recorded.
violations: Innovasjon Norge processed credit application data of 4-6 individuals from January–April 2020 without documenting a lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained, no contractual relationship existed, and no other legal basis was established or recorded.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit inquiries were stored and handled internally without adequate security safeguards or access controls. Data was shared among Innovasjon Norge staff without documented authorization or need-to-know restrictions, creating risk of unauthorized disclosure.
violations: Credit inquiries were stored and handled internally without adequate security safeguards or access controls. Data was shared among Innovasjon Norge staff without documented authorization or need-to-know restrictions, creating risk of unauthorized disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires that controllers implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge failed to maintain secure routines for handling credit data. Passwords and access credentials were shared among employees; there was no documented audit trail or monitoring of data access; and credit inquiries were retained without clear retention or deletion policies.
violations: Innovasjon Norge failed to maintain secure routines for handling credit data. Passwords and access credentials were shared among employees; there was no documented audit trail or monitoring of data access; and credit inquiries were retained without clear retention or deletion policies.

regulatoryFindings.act: Norwegian Personal Data Act § 6 requires that any processing of personal data by a public body must have a documented lawful basis under the applicable regulations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge, as a public institution, processed credit data without documented legal basis or treatment ground (behandlingsgrunnlag) as required by domestic law.
violations: Innovasjon Norge, as a public institution, processed credit data without documented legal basis or treatment ground (behandlingsgrunnlag) as required by domestic law.

outcome: Datatilsynet issued an administrative penalty of NOK 1,000,000 under GDPR Article 83. Innovasjon Norge was ordered to cease processing of the affected individuals' credit data and to document lawful basis for any future personal data processing. The company must implement enhanced security measures, including restricted access controls, audit logging, and employee training on data protection obligations. Compliance must be demonstrated by 25 January 2021. The penalty reflects the systematic nature of the violation, involving multiple individuals and extended duration (January–April 2020), but was moderated due to lack of evidence that damage was caused and absence of intentional misconduct.
companyNow: Innovasjon Norge remains a Norwegian government development agency. As of 2020, it has been required to strengthen data protection practices and implement documented consent and lawful-basis frameworks for all personal data processing.
dataType: Financial data, personal identifiers, credit information

companyDescription: Tripartite Alliance Limited is an organisation in Singapore that promotes fair and progressive employment practices and provides mediation and advice in employment-related disputes.
companyLongDescription: Tripartite Alliance Limited is an organisation in Singapore that promotes fair and progressive employment practices and provides mediation and advice in employment-related disputes.
caseDescription: Tripartite Alliance's CRM system was infected with ransomware in February 2020, affecting approximately 20,000 individuals and 8,000 companies. The organisation failed to properly oversee its vendor's security monitoring services and did not implement encryption on the database. The organisation admitted to breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA by failing to ensure the vendor met required information security standards.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures (lack of encryption, inadequate vendor oversight, failure to monitor security alerts) that exposed personal data to ransomware attack. This constitutes insecurity in information processing under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Tripartite Alliance Limited failed to adequately monitor its software vendor's security performance, did not encrypt its customer database.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 20,000 individuals' sensitive employment complaint records, salaries, identification numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed it had expanded IT services from the vendor since June 2019 to include security monitoring services, such as blocking cyber-attacks based on alerts.
claimsVsReality.reality: There was inadequate process in place to ensure the vendor proactively monitored alerts and took actions to block malicious activities in a timely manner. Hacking attempts occurred between 7-14 February 2020 without being blocked.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had security monitoring services contracted with the vendor.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor failed to respond to security alerts, and the ransomware attack succeeded because monitoring processes were inadequate and lacked clear vendor instructions and regular reporting requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA (Protection Obligation) requires organisations to protect personal data and ensure that vendors contracted to process or store such data discharge their data protection obligations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to monitor the vendor's performance to ensure the vendor met required information security standards.
violations: Organisation failed to monitor the vendor's performance to ensure the vendor met required information security standards.
Organisation did not implement encryption on the CRM database, making it vulnerable to exposure.
Organisation failed to ensure adequate processes were in place for the vendor to proactively monitor security alerts and block malicious activities in a timely manner.
Organisation did not exercise reasonable oversight over the vendor through clear instructions on regular reporting and updates.

outcome: The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 29,000 within 30 days. Following the incident, the organisation implemented remedial measures including: weekly monitoring of the vendor's IT services; organisation-wide review to strengthen third-party IT provider management; cybersecurity audits, vulnerability assessments and penetration testing for existing IT systems; and migration to a new CRM system. No additional directions were issued in view of these remedial actions.
companyNow: Tripartite Alliance Limited is migrating to a new CRM system and working to terminate the existing CRM system. The organisation has strengthened its vendor management practices and security monitoring procedures.
dataType: name, identification number, contact number, email address, age, race, marital status, salary, compensation amount, employment-related complaints and disputes

companyDescription: Novelship Pte. Ltd. operates an e-commerce platform facilitating peer-to-peer transactions in luxury streetwear brands. The platform connects registered buyers and sellers while handling payment processing through external payment processors.
companyLongDescription: Novelship Pte. Ltd. operates an e-commerce platform facilitating peer-to-peer transactions in luxury streetwear brands. The platform connects registered buyers and sellers while handling payment processing through external payment processors.
caseDescription: Novelship operated an e-commerce website for luxury streetwear trading but failed to conduct adequate security testing before launch. A registered seller exploited URL manipulation vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to personal data of six other sellers for eight months. The company had not performed vulnerability scanning for OWASP Top Ten security flaws, which would have detected the URL manipulation vulnerability.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement adequate technical safeguards to protect personal data against unauthorized access. URL manipulation vulnerability was within OWASP Top 10 and preventable through proper security testing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Novelship launched an e-commerce platform without conducting adequate security testing, skipping vulnerability scanning for OWASP Top Ten vulnerabilities before allowing sellers to upload.
whyTheyWereWrong: Six sellers' names, email addresses, shipping addresses, hashed passwords, and bank account numbers were exposed to unauthorized access for eight months because the company failed to test.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization protected seller personal data through its standard business practices
claimsVsReality.reality: For eight months, seller data including names, addresses, emails, passwords, and bank details were accessible to any registered user who manipulated public listing URLs

claimsVsReality.claim: Website was tested and ready for launch
claimsVsReality.reality: Website had only undergone design and functionality testing; no vulnerability scanning or OWASP Top 10 assessment was performed

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organizations to protect personal data using reasonable security measures appropriate to the type of data collected and processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Novelship failed to conduct vulnerability scanning before website launch despite collecting sensitive personal data including financial information
violations: Novelship failed to conduct vulnerability scanning before website launch despite collecting sensitive personal data including financial information
Organization did not engage qualified competent parties to conduct adequate security testing despite lacking in-house cybersecurity expertise
URL manipulation vulnerability within OWASP Top 10 was undetected, allowing unauthorized access to six sellers' complete personal data sets for eight months

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found Novelship in breach of Protection Obligation under s.24 PDPA. Monetary penalty of S$4,000 imposed, payable within 30 days with interest accruing on default per Rules of Court. No additional remedial directions required as organization had implemented fixes including: correcting URL vulnerability, redacting all bank information, and committing to develop new website. Company must pay within 30 days or face accruing interest.
companyNow: Novelship committed to developing a new website with improved security following the enforcement action. The company implemented remedial measures including removing accessible bank information and fixing the URL vulnerability.
dataType: Names, email addresses, shipping addresses, hashed passwords, bank account numbers

companyDescription: LotaData, Inc. is a Delaware-based company located in San Francisco that provides analysis and insights derived from mobile users' location data.
companyLongDescription: LotaData, Inc. is a Delaware-based company located in San Francisco that provides analysis and insights derived from mobile users' location data.
caseDescription: LotaData falsely claimed on its privacy policy that it was certified and compliant with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks. The company initiated an application in November 2017 but never completed certification, yet continued to represent itself as a Privacy Shield participant. This deceptive practice violated FTC Act Section 5.
violationSummary: LotaData deliberately misrepresented its Privacy Shield compliance status on its publicly accessible privacy policy, creating false impressions about legal certifications and data protection safeguards.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: LotaData falsely claimed on its privacy policy that it was certified and compliant with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, despite never completing certification with the U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European users and customers relied on LotaData's false Privacy Shield claims when deciding to transfer their personal location data to the United States.

claimsVsReality.claim: LotaData complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and the Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
claimsVsReality.reality: LotaData initiated an application to Commerce for Privacy Shield certification in November 2017 but never completed the necessary steps to participate in either framework and was never certified.

claimsVsReality.claim: LotaData has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: LotaData was not certified to participate in either the EU-U.S. or the Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: LotaData represented itself as certified under EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
violations: LotaData represented itself as certified under EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
The company continued making false Privacy Shield compliance statements in its privacy policy despite only initiating an application in November 2017 without completing required certification steps.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint (January 13, 2020) against LotaData alleging deceptive acts in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint seeks to compel removal of false Privacy Shield certification claims and require compliance with applicable data protection frameworks. No monetary penalty is specified in the complaint.
dataType: Location data, mobile user data

companyDescription: The Civil Service Club is a social club for Public Service officers in Singapore, also welcoming staff of Social Service Organisations and the general public as associate members. Members enjoy benefits including sports facility bookings, function room rentals, chalets, and discounted rates for club events.
companyLongDescription: The Civil Service Club is a social club for Public Service officers in Singapore, also welcoming staff of Social Service Organisations and the general public as associate members. Members enjoy benefits including sports facility bookings, function room rentals, chalets, and discounted rates for club events.
caseDescription: The Civil Service Club's membership portal temporarily stored members' profile photographs in a publicly accessible directory on its gateway server. Due to vendor error during troubleshooting, public access to the directory containing approximately 1,770 members' profile photographs and NRIC/FIN numbers was not disabled on 24 June 2019, remaining exposed until 2 July 2019 when the incident was reported. The organisation failed for five years (2014–2019) to implement adequate security arrangements or contractual protections with its IT vendor.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to implement reasonable security arrangements resulted in members' sensitive personal data (identity numbers and photographs) being exposed to public access without authorisation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Civil Service Club stored approximately 1,770 members' profile photographs and NRIC/FIN identity numbers in a publicly accessible web directory for 8 days after its vendor failed to disable.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' sensitive personal identification numbers and photographs were exposed to anyone with the URL, allowing potential identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation stated it was not aware that Members Data had been stored temporarily in the Directory, nor that the vendor's troubleshooting involved enabling public access to the Directory.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the organisation's awareness, it had an obligation under section 24 of the PDPA (in force since 2 July 2014) to take proactive steps to ensure reasonable security arrangements were in place. The organisation failed to do so for five years, until the incident occurred on 2 July 2019.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Gateway Server was specifically deployed to isolate the rest of the Organisation's network from the public, with files designed such that they could not be accessed by the public.
claimsVsReality.reality: The technical controls intended to prevent public access failed when the vendor enabled public access for troubleshooting and then failed to disable it, leaving approximately 1,770 members' personal data publicly accessible for 8 days.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect the Members Data for a period of approximately five years (2 July 2014 to 2 July 2019).
violations: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect the Members Data for a period of approximately five years (2 July 2014 to 2 July 2019).
The organisation did not review or update its contract with the vendor to include data protection clauses or requirements after the PDPA came into force on 2 July 2014.
The organisation did not establish a personal data asset inventory or ensure that its data protection policies covered personal data held in the Club Management System.

The organisation did not communicate sufficient clarity and specifications to the vendor regarding the protection of personal data when the vendor was developing and troubleshooting systems that handled members' personal data.
The organisation's failure to identify these gaps and articulate business requirements for data protection was the gravamen of the breach.

outcome: The Commissioner found that the Civil Service Club breached section 24 of the PDPA by failing to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect members' personal data. Mitigating factors included cooperation with investigations, limited risk (only one complaint, incident would have been discovered during a scheduled 9 July 2019 security audit), and prompt remedial action. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 20,000 within 30 days. Remediation measures already implemented by the organisation (immediate disabling of public access, enhanced housekeeping processes for immediate deletion of photos after display, discontinuation of NRIC/FIN numbers as membership identifiers) satisfied the Commissioner that no further directions were necessary.
companyNow: The Civil Service Club continues to operate as a membership club for Singapore's public service officers and associated members. It has implemented enhanced security measures following the enforcement action.
dataType: Profile photographs, NRIC/FIN numbers (national identity numbers)

companyDescription: SCAL Academy Pte. Ltd. provides courses, seminars and workshops for individuals and collects participant personal data through its website for registration purposes.
companyLongDescription: SCAL Academy Pte. Ltd. provides courses, seminars and workshops for individuals and collects participant personal data through its website for registration purposes.
caseDescription: SCAL Academy's website allowed unauthorized access to 3,628 participants' sensitive personal documents including identity numbers and addresses. A vendor failed to implement required security controls, leaving documents indexed by search engines and accessible without authentication. The organisation failed to verify security measures despite identifying the data protection risk.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in its possession and control.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SCAL Academy failed to verify security measures before deploying a document upload feature on its website.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed personal data of 3,628 individuals—including NRIC numbers, dates of birth, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation instructed the vendor to prevent documents from being leaked online
claimsVsReality.reality: No verification or agreement on specific security measures was made; vendor implemented neither access authentication nor search engine blocking, leaving data fully exposed

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: SCAL Academy instructed the vendor to prevent documents from being 'leaked' online but did not check what security arrangements had been implemented
violations: SCAL Academy instructed the vendor to prevent documents from being 'leaked' online but did not check what security arrangements had been implemented
No agreement on specific technical measures between organisation and vendor
No testing or verification conducted to ensure security arrangements were effective
Vendor omitted to programme access verification, leaving documents accessible without login credentials
Vendor failed to implement Google's recommendations to prevent bot crawlers from indexing website content

outcome: The Commissioner found SCAL Academy in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $15,000 within 30 days. No further directions were issued in light of the remedial actions already taken: implementing indexing prevention measures, requesting Google removal of records, disabling the upload function, removing documents, and notifying 27 affected individuals believed to have suffered significant harm.
dataType: Name, race, nationality, date of birth, gender, country of birth, NRIC or work permit number, address, occupation, employer name

companyDescription: MASMOVIL is a Spanish telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and converged services to residential and business customers.
companyLongDescription: MASMOVIL is a Spanish telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and converged services to residential and business customers.
caseDescription: MASMOVIL failed to properly cancel a customer's telephone service after she exercised her contractual right to terminate. The company continued billing her account for 4 months and sent a payment demand threatening inclusion in credit blacklists, treating her personal data without legitimate basis after the contract ended.
violationSummary: The company's operational failure to properly execute contract termination resulted in unlawful continued processing of personal data (billing, payment demands, credit file threats) lacking any lawful basis under GDPR Article 6.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MASMOVIL continued processing a customer's personal data for billing and debt collection four months after the customer terminated her contract, culminating in a threatening payment demand.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer received a payment demand for €197.01 in January 2019 with threats of credit blacklisting inclusion, despite her contract having ended in September 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed the service of fixed-line telephony was given de alta (activated) and functioning normally, with evidence of traffic shown in invoices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer had made four complaints between May and July 2017 that the line was non-functional; a government regulator (SESIAD) confirmed the service was never effectively activated, estimating damages in the customer's favor.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it processed the customer's data legitimately under Article 6(1)(b) based on an active contract and Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest in debt collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: By September 21, 2018, the company had acknowledged contract termination and paid refunds; processing from that date onward—particularly billing and credit threats in January 2019—lacked any lawful ground.

claimsVsReality.claim: MASMOVIL claimed the data was merely 'blocked' for legal obligations and caused no harm since the customer was never actually reported to credit files.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer received an explicit threat of credit blacklist inclusion on January 28, 2019, causing distress; the threat itself was unlawful processing regardless of whether it was executed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires that personal data processing be lawful and based on one of six specified grounds (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: MASMOVIL processed the customer's personal data for billing and debt collection from September 21, 2018 to January 31, 2019 without any lawful basis, as the contract had terminated and no other ground existed.
violations: MASMOVIL processed the customer's personal data for billing and debt collection from September 21, 2018 to January 31, 2019 without any lawful basis, as the contract had terminated and no other ground existed.
The company sent a payment demand on January 28, 2019 threatening credit blacklist inclusion while processing personal data unlawfully after contract termination.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Continuing to bill and threaten credit file inclusion for a service the company admitted had not been properly deactivated violated transparency and fairness principles.
violations: Continuing to bill and threaten credit file inclusion for a service the company admitted had not been properly deactivated violated transparency and fairness principles.

outcome: MASMOVIL was ordered to pay €60,000. The company was required to cease unlawful processing, block the customer's data (which occurred January 31, 2019), cancel all illegitimate invoices, and implement proper contract termination procedures. The customer was informed that no debt remained and her data had been blocked.
companyNow: MASMOVIL (XFERA MÓVILES, S.A.) remains a major Spanish mobile operator. The company acknowledged the error, cancelled the disputed debt on January 31, 2019 within 48 hours of the customer's complaint, and blocked the customer's data.
dataType: Identification data, contact information

companyDescription: TDARX, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing IT management and security services through the websites tdarx.com and nocdoc.com, with principal office in Winston Salem, North Carolina.
companyLongDescription: TDARX, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing IT management and security services through the websites tdarx.com and nocdoc.com, with principal office in Winston Salem, North Carolina.
caseDescription: TDARX, Inc. falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework after its certification lapsed in 2018. The company failed to comply with mandatory annual verification requirements while participating in the program and failed to affirm continued data protection commitments to Commerce after its certification expired.
violationSummary: TDARX made false and misleading representations about Privacy Shield compliance, creating risk of unauthorized or inadequately protected disclosure of personal data to third parties who relied on those false certifications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: TDARX claimed on its website that it participated in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and complied with its principles, even after its certification lapsed in 2018.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU individuals who transferred personal data to TDARX relied on false claims of Privacy Shield protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: TDARX represented that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and complied with Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: TDARX's Privacy Shield certification lapsed in 2018, one year after initial certification in 2017, and the company was no longer a valid participant.

claimsVsReality.claim: TDARX represented that it would cooperate with EU data protection authorities regarding Privacy Shield complaints and resolve complaints in compliance with Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: TDARX failed to obtain the mandatory annual verification statement required by Supplemental Principle 7 during its 2017-18 certification period and did not affirm continuing data protection obligations after certification lapsed.

claimsVsReality.claim: TDARX maintained on its website statements committing to Privacy Shield compliance and recourse mechanisms.
claimsVsReality.reality: After being warned by Commerce to remove Privacy Shield claims, TDARX continued disseminating the false statements without timely withdrawal or affirmation of continuing protection obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: TDARX represented it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield when its certification had lapsed in 2018, making the representation false or misleading.
violations: TDARX represented it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield when its certification had lapsed in 2018, making the representation false or misleading.
TDARX represented compliance with Privacy Shield principles while failing to obtain required annual verification statements signed by a corporate officer or outside reviewer.
TDARX represented compliance with Privacy Shield continuing obligations while failing to affirm to Commerce that it would continue protecting personal data received during program participation.

regulatoryFindings.act: EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7 requires participating companies to verify annually through self-assessment or outside compliance review that Privacy Shield practice assertions are true and implemented.
regulatoryFindings.description: During 2017-18 certification period, TDARX failed to obtain any attested verification statement required by Supplemental Principle 7.
violations: During 2017-18 certification period, TDARX failed to obtain any attested verification statement required by Supplemental Principle 7.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield framework requires companies that cease participation to affirm to Commerce they will continue applying Privacy Shield principles to personal data received during program participation.
regulatoryFindings.description: TDARX failed to affirm continuing data protection commitments to Commerce when its certification lapsed in 2018, despite retaining personal data collected during participation.
violations: TDARX failed to affirm continuing data protection commitments to Commerce when its certification lapsed in 2018, despite retaining personal data collected during participation.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against TDARX alleging three counts: misrepresentation regarding current Privacy Shield participation, misrepresentation regarding verification compliance, and misrepresentation regarding continuing obligations. The document is a complaint issued January 23, 2020; no settlement or final order terms are included in this document. Typical FTC outcomes in such cases include cease-and-desist orders and compliance directives to remove false claims and implement adequate data protection measures.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types); EU personal data subject to GDPR
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive Acts or Practices
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles – Supplemental Principle 7 (Verification Requirement)
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles – Continuing Obligations

company: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 4375 (MCST 4375)
companyDescription: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 4375, also known as Alexandra Central Mall, is a property management entity overseeing a commercial shopping mall in Singapore. It employs managing agents and security contractors to operate the facility.
companyLongDescription: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 4375, also known as Alexandra Central Mall, is a property management entity overseeing a commercial shopping mall in Singapore. It employs managing agents and security contractors to operate the facility.
caseDescription: A woman was injured when a glass door fell on her at Alexandra Central Mall. CCTV footage of the accident was recorded on an employee's phone and circulated via WhatsApp to multiple staff members and management council members without authorization. The footage eventually reached YouTube and other internet platforms. MCST 4375 failed to implement data protection policies and security procedures to govern CCTV footage handling.
violationSummary: The CCTV footage—containing video of an identifiable person in distress—was exposed to the public internet without consent, safeguards, or authorization procedures. This is a classic case of exposure: personal data made accessible to the general public in an uncontrolled manner.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: MCST 4375 failed to develop data protection policies or provide written instructions to security staff on how to handle CCTV footage, allowing a security supervisor to record.
whyTheyWereWrong: The CCTV footage showing a woman injured by a falling glass door was shared among staff without restrictions and eventually posted to YouTube, exposing her injury.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 4375 expected its managing agent SPMS to put in place necessary data protection policies and practices for PDPA compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: SPMS was never contractually required or instructed to do so, and MCST 4375 itself had zero data protection policies in place.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security arrangements existed at the Fire Control Centre to restrict access to CCTV footage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Physical access controls existed, but there were no procedures governing what employees could do with footage once accessed—no restrictions on recording, copying, or sharing it.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the PDPA requires organizations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet their obligations under the Act.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 4375 had not developed or implemented any data protection policies whatsoever. It delegated this responsibility to its managing agent (SPMS) but provided no contractual requirements or written instructions to do so.
violations: MCST 4375 had not developed or implemented any data protection policies whatsoever. It delegated this responsibility to its managing agent (SPMS) but provided no contractual requirements or written instructions to do so.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organizations to put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 4375 had security to restrict access to the Fire Control Centre but provided no instructions to ABSM or SPMS on handling requests for CCTV footage access or disclosure.
violations: MCST 4375 had security to restrict access to the Fire Control Centre but provided no instructions to ABSM or SPMS on handling requests for CCTV footage access or disclosure.
No written procedures existed for employees to follow when receiving requests for or disclosing CCTV footage containing personal data.

outcome: Deputy Commissioner directed MCST 4375 to: (1) develop and implement data protection policies within 60 days; (2) put in place reasonable security arrangements within 60 days; (3) conduct staff training on PDPA compliance within 60 days; (4) report implementation to the Commission within 1 week of each step. ABSM was directed to put in place security arrangements and policies for CCTV footage handling within 60 days and report implementation. SPMS was found not in breach. MCST 4375 replaced SPMS as managing agent on 18 March 2019 and issued internal memorandum requiring approval for distribution of media materials.
companyNow: MCST 4375 is an ongoing management corporation responsible for Alexandra Central Mall in Singapore. The organization replaced its managing agent (SPMS) following the incident and implemented mandatory approval procedures for media and document distribution.
dataType: CCTV footage, biometric/video recordings
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.12 (develop and implement necessary data protection policies and practices)
PDPA s.24 (reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data)

companyDescription: Singapore Red Cross Society is a non-profit humanitarian organization that operates blood donation services, disaster relief programs, and community welfare initiatives for vulnerable populations in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Red Cross Society is a non-profit humanitarian organization that operates blood donation services, disaster relief programs, and community welfare initiatives for vulnerable populations in Singapore.
caseDescription: Singapore Red Cross Society's blood donor appointment database was breached, exposing personal data of approximately 4,297 individuals. The breach resulted from inadequate security measures: a phpMyAdmin tool with a weak password ('12345') was left accessible on the website, and no regular security reviews were conducted. Additionally, the organization failed to properly delete unnecessary retained data of approximately 900 individuals.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (Section 24 PDPA) to protect personal data, resulting in unauthorized access and data exfiltration. Additionally, failure to delete unnecessary retained data (Section 25 PDPA) violated retention limitation obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Singapore Red Cross Society left a phpMyAdmin database administration tool with a weak password ('12345') publicly accessible on its blood donor website.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 4,297 blood donors had their names, contact numbers, email addresses, and blood types exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had in place various IT security measures and had embarked on a consultancy to ensure PDPA compliance even before the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claimed security measures, critical vulnerabilities existed: a database administration tool with a trivial password ('12345') was left accessible, no regular security reviews were conducted to identify unnecessary applications, and vendor work lacked adequate supervision.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Tool was never used by the organization's staff and was likely created during the development stage.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Tool remained connected to the live website after development was complete, providing attackers an entry point that would not have existed if post-deployment security reviews had been conducted.

claimsVsReality.claim: The attackers were skilled hackers who exploited sophisticated attack methods.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach succeeded due to basic security failures: a weak password '12345' provided trivial access to the database management tool that should never have been accessible on a production website.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization failed to supervise vendor development, resulting in phpMyAdmin tool with weak password ('12345') being left accessible
violations: Organization failed to supervise vendor development, resulting in phpMyAdmin tool with weak password ('12345') being left accessible
No password management policy requiring strong passwords during development phase
No regular security reviews or vulnerability assessments conducted to identify unnecessary applications
Tool remained connected to website after development completion, allowing unauthorized access to database

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 of the PDPA requires an organisation to cease retaining documents containing personal data or remove the means by which personal data can be associated with individuals as soon as reasonable, when the purpose for collection is no longer served and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization provided wrong purging instructions to vendor, instructing removal of only some data elements instead of entire records for 900 individuals
violations: Organization provided wrong purging instructions to vendor, instructing removal of only some data elements instead of entire records for 900 individuals
No verification checks conducted to ensure purging exercise was properly completed
Database still retained records of 900 individuals' personal data unnecessarily

outcome: The Commissioner found the organization in breach of PDPA Sections 24 and 25. A financial penalty of SGD 5,000 was imposed (reduced from a higher initially intended amount due to the organization's upfront voluntary admission of liability and comprehensive remedial actions). The organization was required to pay within 30 days, with interest accruing at the Rules of Court rate on any unpaid balance. No additional directions were imposed given the organization's remedial measures, which included removing the database from the website, implementing layered and restricted access controls, isolating sensitive systems at network level, password training for staff, review and strengthening of standard operating procedures, increased vendor oversight, and implementation of vulnerability assessment and penetration testing regimes for critical systems before deployment and annually thereafter.
companyNow: Singapore Red Cross Society continues to operate as a major humanitarian organization in Singapore, providing blood donation services, disaster relief, and community support programs. The organization has strengthened its data protection and cybersecurity practices following this enforcement action.
dataType: Names, contact numbers, email addresses, blood types
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 (Protection Obligation — reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Medable, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing technology solutions to business customers in pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and research industries, headquartered in Palo Alto, California.
companyLongDescription: Medable, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing technology solutions to business customers in pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and research industries, headquartered in Palo Alto, California.
caseDescription: Medable falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework in its privacy policy from December 2017 to October 2018, despite never completing the certification process. The company represented to users transferring personal data from the EEA that it adhered to Privacy Shield Principles, when in fact it had no such certification. This deceptive practice violated Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violationSummary: Company made deceptive claims about how personal data would be protected, misleading individuals about the legal framework governing their information transfer.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Medable falsely stated in its privacy policy from December 2017 to October 2018 that it was EU/US Privacy Shield certified.
whyTheyWereWrong: European users transferred personal data to Medable based on false Privacy Shield certification claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: Medable is EU/US Privacy Shield certified
claimsVsReality.reality: Medable was never certified; it only initiated an application in December 2017 but did not complete the steps necessary to participate

claimsVsReality.claim: Medable adheres to Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: Without certification, Medable could not legally claim adherence to Privacy Shield Principles

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Medable represented in its privacy policy that it was EU/US Privacy Shield certified when it had never completed certification
violations: Medable represented in its privacy policy that it was EU/US Privacy Shield certified when it had never completed certification
Company claimed adherence to Privacy Shield Principles while lacking actual certification
Misrepresentations continued from December 2017 to October 2018 despite only initiating the application process

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Medable for deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was issued on January 6, 2020. Respondent was required to cease the deceptive practices and comply with FTC directives regarding accurate privacy representations.
dataType: Personal data from European Economic Area residents, including health/research data

companyDescription: T&M Protection Resources, LLC is a Delaware limited liability corporation based in New York that provides background check, security, and investigative services. The company obtained EU resident personal data in connection with its background check services.
companyLongDescription: T&M Protection Resources, LLC is a Delaware limited liability corporation based in New York that provides background check, security, and investigative services. The company obtained EU resident personal data in connection with its background check services.
caseDescription: T&M Protection Resources claimed to comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website but failed to renew its certification in 2018. After certification lapsed, the company continued making false claims about Privacy Shield participation and failed to obtain required annual verification statements. The company also did not affirm its commitment to protect personal data previously collected under the framework.
violationSummary: The company made deceptive representations about Privacy Shield participation when marketing background check services to EU residents, misrepresenting the legal safeguards protecting their personal data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: T&M Protection Resources claimed on its website that it complied with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents whose personal data T&M collected for background checks lost legal protections they believed they had.

claimsVsReality.claim: T&M Protection Resources, LLC complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
claimsVsReality.reality: T&M's Privacy Shield certification expired in 2018 and was never renewed; the company was not a current Privacy Shield participant when making this claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: T&M Protection Resources, LLC has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: T&M obtained certification in 2017 but did not complete renewal steps when certification expired in 2018, and did not affirm its commitment to protect previously collected data.

claimsVsReality.claim: If there is any conflict between the terms in this privacy policy and the Privacy Shield Principles, the Privacy Shield Principles shall govern.
claimsVsReality.reality: T&M made no effort to ensure Privacy Shield Principle compliance, failing annual verification requirements and failing to affirm continuing obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: T&M made express representations on its privacy policy that it complied with EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and had certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed in 2018 and it did not complete renewal steps.
