regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or under their control against risks of unauthorised access, use, disclosure, loss, alteration or destruction.
regulatoryFindings.description: Security Masters failed to implement any standard operating procedures or guidelines for the retrieval and use of visitors' personal data prior to the incident, creating a gap in security arrangements that allowed a security employee to access and misuse eight visitors' mobile phone numbers.
violations: Security Masters failed to implement any standard operating procedures or guidelines for the retrieval and use of visitors' personal data prior to the incident, creating a gap in security arrangements that allowed a security employee to access and misuse eight visitors' mobile phone numbers.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed Security Masters to: (1) within 60 days, revise its training curriculum to ensure security personnel understand the rationale for personal data protection, the importance of consent and authorisation in handling personal data, and appropriate circumstances for using and disclosing personal data on social media for work-related purposes; and (2) inform the Commission within 1 week of implementation. The company also restricted access to personal data to senior personnel and required all security personnel to sign undertakings not to contact visitors in their personal capacity.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, National Registration Identification Card numbers, photographs, closed-circuit television footage

companyDescription: Water + Plants Lab Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based laboratory or research organisation involved in research related to water and plants. The organisation employed at least 28 staff members at the time of the incident.
companyLongDescription: Water + Plants Lab Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based laboratory or research organisation involved in research related to water and plants. The organisation employed at least 28 staff members at the time of the incident.
caseDescription: Water + Plants Lab suffered a ransomware infection on 30 March 2020 that encrypted personal data of 28 employees. The organisation had failed to perform any system patching or security scanning for 12 months before the incident, leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched that attackers could exploit. Although most data was recovered from backup and there was no evidence of data exfiltration, the Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of its security obligations.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures, specifically the absence of regular patching and security scanning, which allowed a known vulnerability vector (malware via email) to compromise personal data systems.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Water + Plants Lab failed to perform any patching and security scanning of its server for 12 months before a ransomware attack.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's negligent security practices exposed 28 employees' sensitive personal data including NRIC/FIN numbers, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to protect personal data by not conducting any patching and security scanning of the server for 12 months before the incident, leaving vulnerabilities that attackers exploited via malware-laden email attachment
violations: Organisation failed to protect personal data by not conducting any patching and security scanning of the server for 12 months before the incident, leaving vulnerabilities that attackers exploited via malware-laden email attachment

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to the organisation. Following the incident, Water + Plants Lab installed a firewall with enhanced capabilities including deeper content inspection for malware detection, and conducted staff training on personal data protection and security threat identification. No monetary penalty was imposed due to minimal actual data loss from successful backup recovery, no evidence of data exfiltration, and remediation measures taken.
dataType: Name, NRIC/FIN/Work Permit number, address, date of birth, mobile number, photograph

companyDescription: AOK Baden-Württemberg is a statutory health insurance company (Krankenkasse) and major component of Germany's public health insurance system, providing health coverage to millions of members in the Baden-Württemberg region.
companyLongDescription: AOK Baden-Württemberg is a statutory health insurance company (Krankenkasse) and major component of Germany's public health insurance system, providing health coverage to millions of members in the Baden-Württemberg region.
caseDescription: AOK Baden-Württemberg conducted sweepstakes from 2015-2019 collecting personal data from participants. The company's technical and organizational measures failed to prevent personal data from over 500 sweepstakes participants being used for marketing purposes without their consent. The breach violated Article 32 GDPR requirements for secure data processing.
violationSummary: The company collected data with consent for sweepstakes but then used it for marketing purposes without valid consent, representing unauthorized secondary use of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: AOK Baden-Württemberg conducted sweepstakes from 2015-2019 collecting personal data including contact details and insurance membership, then used inadequate technical.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data from more than 500 sweepstakes participants was used for marketing communications without their consent, exposing them to unwanted advertising and compromising their privacy rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: AOK's internal guidelines and data protection training would ensure only consented sweepstakes participants' data was used for marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The measures were inadequate; over 500 participants' data was actually used for marketing without their consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including inter alia protection against unauthorised processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: AOK's technical and organizational measures (internal guidelines and data protection training) were insufficient to prevent unauthorized marketing use of personal data from sweepstakes participants who had not consented to such use.
violations: AOK's technical and organizational measures (internal guidelines and data protection training) were insufficient to prevent unauthorized marketing use of personal data from sweepstakes participants who had not consented to such use.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner.
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal data from 500+ individuals was processed for marketing purposes without valid consent, violating the lawfulness principle.
violations: Personal data from 500+ individuals was processed for marketing purposes without valid consent, violating the lawfulness principle.

outcome: LfDI imposed a fine of €1,240,000 on 25 June 2020. AOK immediately ceased all marketing activities upon notification, established a Data Protection Task Force for sales operations, reviewed and revised consent declarations, updated internal processes and control structures, and committed to continuing improvements under LfDI supervision. Fine was reduced within the GDPR Article 83(4) range due to AOK's prompt remediation, cooperative compliance efforts, its critical role as statutory health insurer, and COVID-19 pandemic impacts.
companyNow: AOK Baden-Württemberg remains one of the largest health insurance providers in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The company has implemented enhanced data protection measures and ongoing monitoring as per LfDI requirements.
dataType: Contact data, health insurance membership information

companyDescription: COURTS (Singapore) Pte Ltd is a well-known consumer electronics and furniture retailer operating multiple stores across Singapore. The company operates a membership programme called 'homeclub by COURTS' that provides members with exclusive access to events and discounts.
companyLongDescription: COURTS (Singapore) Pte Ltd is a well-known consumer electronics and furniture retailer operating multiple stores across Singapore. The company operates a membership programme called 'homeclub by COURTS' that provides members with exclusive access to events and discounts.
caseDescription: COURTS (Singapore) sent an eDM to 76,844 members with a flawed link that embedded session identifiers, allowing members to access other members' accounts without authentication. The organization failed to conduct adequate testing before implementation and used inappropriate default system settings without assessment. While the incident lasted less than 24 hours and no actual unauthorized modification was proven, 128 members' personal data was exposed to unauthorized access and modification risks.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access. The embedded session identifier in the eDM URL combined with inadequate testing and failure to assess system defaults created a direct path for unauthorized account access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: COURTS (Singapore) Pte Ltd sent an eDM with an embedded session identifier in the URL and used default system settings that allowed members to automatically access other members' accounts within.
whyTheyWereWrong: 128 members' accounts were exposed to unauthorized access, allowing other members to view and modify their names, addresses, phone numbers, birthdates.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization conducted appropriate testing of the New eDM Link before sending it to 76,844 members.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only one employee performed a single self-test by sending the eDM to himself; no multi-user concurrent login testing was conducted despite the large recipient base.

claimsVsReality.claim: The default system settings were appropriate for the New eDM Link directing members to the login page.
claimsVsReality.reality: The default settings (SID embedded in URL, 60-minute cookie refresh) were designed for non-login marketing links and created session confusion when used for a login-required link, allowing session hijacking.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Platform tool was being used correctly to generate secure eDM links.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Platform had a built-in feature to generate eDM links without SID in the URL, but the employee manually copied a SID-embedded link from the browser instead, unaware of the safer alternative.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct adequate testing before implementation—only single-employee self-testing rather than multi-user concurrent login scenarios despite sending to 76,844 members
violations: Failed to conduct adequate testing before implementation—only single-employee self-testing rather than multi-user concurrent login scenarios despite sending to 76,844 members
Failed to assess appropriateness of default system settings (SID in URL, 60-minute cookie refresh) for the new eDM link use case
Did not understand or utilize the Platform's alternative feature to generate eDM links without SID in URL, instead manually copying SID-embedded link
Existing second-level content checks were insufficient to catch technical security issues

outcome: COURTS (Singapore) Pte Ltd found in breach of PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation). Commissioner directed organization to pay financial penalty of S$9,000 within 30 days. Organization had already implemented remedial actions: (1) fixed the system setting by changing 'Use SID on Storefront' to 'No' on 1 September 2019; (2) implemented password verification for account information and address book changes (effective 6 January 2020); (3) established standard operating procedure for eDM link insertion with multiple concurrent user testing; (4) engaged external vendor for security matters; (5) notified all 128 affected members. No further directions imposed given remediation measures already undertaken. Penalty reduced from initial amount due to COVID-19 pandemic impact on retail business, though Commissioner noted this reduction should not set precedent.
companyNow: COURTS (Singapore) Pte Ltd continues to operate as a consumer electronics and furniture retailer in Singapore. As of the decision date (August 2020), the company was navigating pandemic-related challenges including temporary store closures and operational constraints.
dataType: Name, email address, mobile number, date of birth, residential address, password, transactional information (purchase history)

companyDescription: Click Labs, Inc. is a Florida corporation providing website and mobile app development and support services through the domain jungleworks.com, operating from Seattle, Washington.
companyLongDescription: Click Labs, Inc. is a Florida corporation providing website and mobile app development and support services through the domain jungleworks.com, operating from Seattle, Washington.
caseDescription: Click Labs falsely claimed in its privacy policy to be certified under both the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks. The company initiated a Privacy Shield certification application but never completed it, yet continued representing itself as certified, misleading users about the legal protections for their data.
violationSummary: The company misrepresented the status and legal framework governing personal data transfers, distorting users' understanding of how their data would be protected.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Click Labs falsely claimed in its privacy policy that it had certified to and complied with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, when it had never completed certification.
whyTheyWereWrong: European users transferred personal data to Click Labs based on false Privacy Shield compliance claims, exposing their data to unauthorized collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: We agree to adhere to the Privacy Shield Principles and have certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: Click Labs initiated an application for Privacy Shield certification but never completed the required steps and was never certified by the U.S. Department of Commerce.

claimsVsReality.claim: We shall comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework regarding collection, use, and retention of personal information transferred from the European Union and Switzerland.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was not a participant in either Privacy Shield framework and lacked the legal status to make this claim.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Click Labs represented that it was certified under the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed the certification process with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
violations: Click Labs represented that it was certified under the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed the certification process with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
The company continued making false Privacy Shield claims in its publicly available privacy policy despite only initiating but not completing the required application steps.

outcome: Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on January 23, 2020, alleging deceptive practices. The case proceeded on Count 1 for Privacy Misrepresentation in violation of FTC Act Section 5(a). The complaint sought compliance order requiring the company to cease making false Privacy Shield representations and implement accurate privacy disclosures.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU and Switzerland

companyDescription: Miniclip S.A. is a Swiss mobile and online gaming developer and publisher founded in 2009. As of August 2019, it operated approximately 100 games available on Apple App Store and Google Play, with a significant user base among children and casual gamers.
companyLongDescription: Miniclip S.A. is a Swiss mobile and online gaming developer and publisher founded in 2009. As of August 2019, it operated approximately 100 games available on Apple App Store and Google Play, with a significant user base among children and casual gamers.
caseDescription: Miniclip falsely claimed to be a current participant in the CARU COPPA safe harbor program after being terminated from it in July 2015. The company continued to disseminate compliance certifications on multiple websites and in-app disclosures for years after termination, deceiving consumers about its actual privacy protection status.
violationSummary: Miniclip made materially false representations about its privacy compliance status, creating a false impression about the safety and oversight of children's data in its games. This constitutes distortion under the Solove taxonomy as false certifications misrepresented the actual state of privacy protections.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Miniclip continued claiming on its website, terms, and Facebook policy from 2015-2019 that it was a certified COPPA-compliant participant in the CARU safe harbor program.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents and children relied on Miniclip's false COPPA compliance claims when deciding whether to use its games.

claimsVsReality.claim: Miniclip claimed: 'we have been accepted to join the CARU Kids Privacy Safe Harbor Program and have been certified as COPPA compliant' (stated 2012-2019)
claimsVsReality.reality: CARU terminated Miniclip's participation in the COPPA safe harbor program on July 6, 2015, making it no longer a current participant or certified compliant thereafter

claimsVsReality.claim: Miniclip claimed: 'The information practices of Miniclip.com have been reviewed and meet the standards of the Children's Advertising Review Unit's Kids Privacy Safe Harbor Program'
claimsVsReality.reality: After termination in 2015, Miniclip's practices were no longer reviewed by CARU nor deemed to meet CARU standards, yet these claims continued on company websites and apps through June/July 2019

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Miniclip represented it was a current participant in the CARU COPPA safe harbor program when it was not, having been terminated in July 2015
violations: Miniclip represented it was a current participant in the CARU COPPA safe harbor program when it was not, having been terminated in July 2015
Miniclip disseminated false COPPA compliance certifications on its website, Terms and Conditions, and Facebook pages from 2012-2019
The false representations were material because they misled consumers about the actual privacy protections for children's data

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA safe harbor programs, approved by the FTC, allow operators complying with program guidelines to be deemed in compliance with COPPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Miniclip falsely claimed CARU COPPA safe harbor program participation after termination, fraudulently implying COPPA compliance status it no longer held
violations: Miniclip falsely claimed CARU COPPA safe harbor program participation after termination, fraudulently implying COPPA compliance status it no longer held

outcome: FTC issued Complaint alleging deceptive acts in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was issued June 29, 2020, initiating formal enforcement proceedings against Miniclip for false COPPA compliance claims. Settlement and specific remedies were subject to resolution through adjudication or settlement proceedings.
companyNow: Miniclip remains an active gaming publisher under Chinese ownership (acquired by Tencent in 2020 for approximately $860 million), though the FTC enforcement action and COPPA violations significantly impacted its reputation in the children's gaming space.
dataType: Children's personal information (as covered under COPPA)

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is a multinational telecommunications conglomerate headquartered in Singapore. Through its MySingtel mobile application and other platforms, the company provides mobile, broadband internet, and TV services to customers across multiple markets.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is a multinational telecommunications conglomerate headquartered in Singapore. Through its MySingtel mobile application and other platforms, the company provides mobile, broadband internet, and TV services to customers across multiple markets.
caseDescription: A code update to Singapore Telecommunications' MySingtel mobile app removed a protective condition, causing the API to retrieve and display previously assigned recycled phone numbers and related usage information of current users to 384 former customers. The vendor failed to report the critical code change, and the organization's testing was limited to documented changes only.
violationSummary: The incident resulted from inadequate code review and change management practices that allowed an undisclosed code removal to reach production, exposing personal data of current users of recycled numbers to unauthorized access by previous account holders.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: A vendor removed code that prevented recycled phone numbers from being displayed to previous users, failed to report this removal in the change request.
whyTheyWereWrong: 384 customers could view other customers' recycled service numbers, installation addresses, detailed usage information, service plans, and billing cycles through the mobile app.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vendor would follow industry standard data protection measures and exercise appropriate care in code development
claimsVsReality.reality: Vendor removed critical protective code, failed to document the change, and provided incomplete technical change request to organization

claimsVsReality.claim: Pre-launch testing would catch errors and flaws before deployment
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing was limited to documented changes only; undisclosed code removal went undetected because it was not reported in technical change request

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization failed to implement comprehensive code review procedures to catch undisclosed code changes before production deployment
violations: Organization failed to implement comprehensive code review procedures to catch undisclosed code changes before production deployment
Testing scope was limited to documented changes despite handling sensitive personal data through API calls
Vendor's removal of critical protective condition was not detected due to inadequate change management and communication protocols

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found no contravention of PDPA s.24. The security arrangements were deemed reasonable: (1) organization had contractual data protection clauses with vendor, conducted audits, and provided mandatory PDPA briefings; (2) pre-launch testing was reasonably scoped to documented changes; (3) incident was a one-off, difficult to foresee. Organization implemented remediation: blocked app access within hours, deployed fix next day, reversed erroneous transactions, and added regression testing for recycled numbers and enhanced app to display only active services.
companyNow: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (operating as Singtel) remains a major multinational telecommunications conglomerate headquartered in Singapore, providing mobile, broadband, and TV services across multiple markets.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, user IDs, service numbers, installation addresses, usage details (talk time, SMS, mobile data), value-added services, price plans, billing cycles

companyDescription: Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 is a housing cooperative located in Kohtla-Järve, Estonia, responsible for managing a residential building and services for its member-residents.
companyLongDescription: Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 is a housing cooperative located in Kohtla-Järve, Estonia, responsible for managing a residential building and services for its member-residents.
caseDescription: A housing cooperative in Estonia publicly displayed residents' personal data (names, signatures, apartment numbers) in building stairwells without their consent. The Data Protection Inspectorate ordered immediate cessation of this practice and warned of €500 fines for non-compliance.
violationSummary: The cooperative exposed personal data in physically accessible common areas (stairwells) to anyone entering the building, including third parties and unauthorized individuals.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 posted residents' names, signatures, apartment numbers, and heating system consent lists in building stairwells without obtaining prior written consent from.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents' personal information became visible to third parties and the general public in common areas, exposing at least some residents to identification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The cooperative did not formally respond to or contest the initial enforcement request.
claimsVsReality.reality: The cooperative continued to display personal data in stairwells despite the inspectorate's 16 April 2020 proposal and follow-up complaint on 24 April 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires that processing of personal data shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of a specified basis applies, such as explicit consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The cooperative processed and disclosed residents' personal data without any lawful basis; explicit prior consent was neither sought nor obtained.
violations: The cooperative processed and disclosed residents' personal data without any lawful basis; explicit prior consent was neither sought nor obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Publishing resident names, signatures, and apartment numbers in stairwells lacked transparency and fairness; no resident was informed or consented.
violations: Publishing resident names, signatures, and apartment numbers in stairwells lacked transparency and fairness; no resident was informed or consented.

regulatoryFindings.act: Estonian Personal Data Protection Act §58(1) establishes the authority of the Data Protection Inspectorate to issue binding orders to cease unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The cooperative continued publishing personal data in common areas after being requested to cease the practice.
violations: The cooperative continued publishing personal data in common areas after being requested to cease the practice.

outcome: The Data Protection Inspectorate issued a binding enforcement order (ettekirjutus) requiring the cooperative to cease all further disclosure of residents' personal data without consent by 13 May 2020. Failure to comply will result in repeated fines of €500 per violation, enforceable through the court. The cooperative did not exercise its right to object and must comply or face escalation to enforcement proceedings.
companyNow: The status of Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 is unknown. As a housing cooperative (ühistu), it likely remains operational but was required to implement immediate changes to data handling practices.
dataType: Names, signatures, apartment numbers, contact information

companyDescription: HyperBeard, Inc. is a mobile game developer based in Fremont, California that created and distributed free-to-play mobile apps featuring cute animated characters (cats, dogs, monkeys, axolotls) directed to children, monetized through in-app advertising and in-app purchases.
companyLongDescription: HyperBeard, Inc. is a mobile game developer based in Fremont, California that created and distributed free-to-play mobile apps featuring cute animated characters (cats, dogs, monkeys, axolotls) directed to children, monetized through in-app advertising and in-app purchases.
caseDescription: HyperBeard developed and distributed mobile apps directed to children under 13 that collected personal information through third-party advertising networks without providing privacy notices, disclosing data practices, or obtaining verifiable parental consent. The company allowed advertisers including AdMob, Facebook Audience Network, and others to collect persistent identifiers for behavioral targeting without informing these networks that the apps were directed to children. This violated the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and the COPPA Rule.
violationSummary: The company conducted covert surveillance of children's online activity through persistent identifiers and behavioral tracking via third-party ad networks, without disclosure to parents or obtaining verifiable parental consent required by COPPA.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: HyperBeard operated nine mobile apps with cute animated characters directed to children under 13.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's location data and activity patterns were tracked and sold to advertisers without parents' knowledge, enabling targeted advertising to minors and creating privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apps are 'recommended for children as well as adults' and are innocent entertainment with adorable characters.
claimsVsReality.reality: Apps were deliberately designed, marketed, and promoted exclusively to children via kids' websites, children's books through Scholastic, and licensed merchandise, while collecting their behavioral data without parental knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apps collect minimal data; children simply tap characters and play simple games.
claimsVsReality.reality: Third-party ad networks continuously collected persistent identifiers and tracked user behavior across the apps for behavioral advertising purposes without any disclosure mechanism or parental consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(d) requires operators to post a privacy policy on their website or online service providing clear, understandable, and complete notice of information practices, including what information is collected from children, how it is used, and disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard failed to provide privacy policy notices within the Kids Apps disclosing that third-party advertising networks were collecting persistent identifiers for behavioral advertising.
violations: HyperBeard failed to provide privacy policy notices within the Kids Apps disclosing that third-party advertising networks were collecting persistent identifiers for behavioral advertising.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) requires operators to provide direct, clear, understandable, and complete notice of information practices to parents, including specific disclosures about data collection, use, and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard did not inform parents that their children's apps collected personal information through advertising networks or how that data was used for behavioral targeting.
violations: HyperBeard did not inform parents that their children's apps collected personal information through advertising networks or how that data was used for behavioral targeting.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard allowed third-party ad networks to collect persistent identifiers from children without any parental consent mechanism in place.
violations: HyperBeard allowed third-party ad networks to collect persistent identifiers from children without any parental consent mechanism in place.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard's failure to disclose data collection and practices to parents constituted deceptive conduct; the covert behavioral tracking of children was unfair under FTC standards.
violations: HyperBeard's failure to disclose data collection and practices to parents constituted deceptive conduct; the covert behavioral tracking of children was unfair under FTC standards.

outcome: This is a complaint for civil penalties, permanent injunction, and equitable relief filed June 3, 2020. The complaint seeks (A) a permanent injunction preventing future COPPA violations; (B) monetary civil penalties of up to $41,484 per violation for all Rule violations from January 22, 2018 forward; and (C) other equitable relief the Court deems just and proper. The case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. Final settlement terms are not specified in this complaint document, which is the initial filing.
companyNow: HyperBeard, Inc. was a California-based mobile game developer founded circa 2016. As of the complaint filing in June 2020, the company was actively distributing apps through Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Persistent identifiers, behavioral/advertising tracking data, user activity data
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b), 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b) — failure to provide direct notice to parents
COPPA Rule Section 312.4(d), 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(d) — failure to post privacy policy
COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1), 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) — failure to obtain verifiable parental consent
FTC Act Section 5(a), 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) — unfair and deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(m)(1)(A), 15 U.S.C. § 45(m)(1)(A) — knowing violation

companyDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd. is the Asia-Pacific subsidiary of Royal Caribbean Group, one of the world's largest cruise line operators offering cruises, holidays, and vacation packages.
companyLongDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd. is the Asia-Pacific subsidiary of Royal Caribbean Group, one of the world's largest cruise line operators offering cruises, holidays, and vacation packages.
caseDescription: Royal Caribbean's electronic receipt system hosted on AWS was breached due to unpatched security vulnerabilities and publicly accessible administrative credentials. Customer and employee personal data of over 6,000 individuals was exposed to unauthorized access. The company failed to implement basic security measures including software patches and access controls despite owning and controlling the system.
violationSummary: The organization failed to take reasonable security steps to prevent unauthorized access to personal data in its possession, resulting in a cyber-attack that exposed sensitive customer and employee information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Royal Caribbean failed to patch known security vulnerabilities in its Receipt System and stored administrative credentials in publicly accessible files without access controls on an AWS server.
whyTheyWereWrong: 6,004 customers and 25 employees had sensitive personal data including credit card details, passport information, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Royal Caribbean asserted it was the IT Vendor's responsibility to implement appropriate security measures for the Receipt System.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commission's investigation revealed Royal Caribbean had not engaged the IT Vendor to provide security maintenance or patching services, and Royal Caribbean could not produce written documentation supporting its assertion. As the data controller, Royal Caribbean was ultimately responsible for security.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT Vendor claimed it was Royal Caribbean's network security team that was in charge of security.
claimsVsReality.reality: Royal Caribbean had no documented agreement allocating security responsibilities to the IT Vendor, and the IT Vendor was not engaged to provide security services. Royal Caribbean bore ultimate responsibility as data controller.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Royal Caribbean failed to implement security patches for the phpMyAdmin tool despite known vulnerabilities being publicly listed in Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures
violations: Royal Caribbean failed to implement security patches for the phpMyAdmin tool despite known vulnerabilities being publicly listed in Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures
Royal Caribbean stored administrative credentials (username and password) in files within the same server with no access controls, making them publicly accessible
Royal Caribbean had no documented process in place to ensure regular security maintenance and patching of the Receipt System
Royal Caribbean failed to clarify the scope of services with its IT Vendor regarding security responsibilities, resulting in inadequate security measures

outcome: The Commissioner found Royal Caribbean in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for failing to implement reasonable security measures. The organization was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $16,000 within 30 days. Mitigating factors included the organization's cooperation with the Commission's investigations and prompt remedial actions taken upon discovery of the incident (system taken offline, cybersecurity consultant engaged, affected customers notified). No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures already implemented.
companyNow: Royal Caribbean Cruises continues to operate globally as a major cruise line operator. The company has presumably enhanced its data security practices following this enforcement action and public decision.
dataType: Payment information (credit/debit card numbers, cheque numbers), personal identifiers (name, booking ID), travel booking details, passport information, contact information (email, phone, address), date of birth, nationality, marital status, employee credentials

companyDescription: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited is a Singapore-incorporated engineering company with a network of subsidiaries across Asia, Europe, USA, and the Middle East. The company operates in aerospace, defense, and engineering sectors.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited is a Singapore-incorporated engineering company with a network of subsidiaries across Asia, Europe, USA, and the Middle East. The company operates in aerospace, defense, and engineering sectors.
caseDescription: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited's USA-based subsidiary VT San Antonio Aerospace Inc. suffered a ransomware attack that exposed personal data of 287 Singapore-based individuals to unauthorized access. The organization had transferred this sensitive data from Singapore to the USA to support regulatory filings, employee transfers, and security clearances. The Commission investigation found the organization complied with Singapore's Transfer Limitation Obligation by maintaining binding corporate rules requiring equivalent data protection standards.
violationSummary: The organization's subsidiary failed to maintain adequate security measures to protect transferred personal data, resulting in unauthorized access through a ransomware attack. This demonstrates insecurity in processing and safeguarding transferred personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited transferred personal data of 287 individuals from Singapore to USA-based subsidiaries VT SAA.
whyTheyWereWrong: VT SAA's subsidiary network suffered a ransomware attack that exposed 287 individuals' sensitive data including NRIC numbers, passport details, photographs.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organization had implemented binding corporate rules requiring Group Companies to maintain security measures and provide comparable protection under PDPA or applicable data protection laws.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these rules, the subsidiary VT SAA's inadequate security controls (insufficient endpoint security, limited network monitoring) allowed a ransomware attack to compromise personal data of 287 individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The personal data transferred to the USA was protected by legally enforceable obligations on the receiving companies.
claimsVsReality.reality: 49 individuals' personal data was likely exfiltrated and 238 individuals' data was at risk of exfiltration due to the cybersecurity incident, demonstrating the practical inadequacy of the subsidiary's security posture.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 26(1) of the PDPA provides that an organisation shall not transfer any personal data to a country or territory outside Singapore except in accordance with requirements prescribed under the PDPA to ensure that organisations provide a standard of protection to personal data so transferred that is comparable to the protection under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: While the Organization maintained binding corporate rules that met the Transfer Limitation Obligation requirements in principle, the subsidiary's inadequate cybersecurity architecture allowed unauthorized access to transferred personal data through a ransomware attack, undermining the practical effectiveness of the required comparable protection standard.
violations: While the Organization maintained binding corporate rules that met the Transfer Limitation Obligation requirements in principle, the subsidiary's inadequate cybersecurity architecture allowed unauthorized access to transferred personal data through a ransomware attack, undermining the practical effectiveness of the required comparable protection standard.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 9(1)(b) of the PDPR requires an organisation that transfers personal data to a country or territory outside of Singapore to take appropriate steps to ensure that the recipient of personal data is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide to the transferred personal data a standard of protection that is at least comparable to that under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Organization ensured legal binding through corporate rules, but VT SAA's failure to implement adequate endpoint security controls, network monitoring, and security hardening measures prior to the incident demonstrated that the receiving entity did not maintain a comparable standard of protection in practice.
violations: The Organization ensured legal binding through corporate rules, but VT SAA's failure to implement adequate endpoint security controls, network monitoring, and security hardening measures prior to the incident demonstrated that the receiving entity did not maintain a comparable standard of protection in practice.

outcome: The Commission found that Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited complied with the Transfer Limitation Obligation under Section 26 of the PDPA because it had established binding corporate rules (St Engineering's Group Binding Corporate Rules for Transfers of Personal Data) that met regulatory requirements. The rules bound all subsidiaries worldwide, specified the USA as a permitted transfer destination, and required comparable data protection standards. However, the ransomware incident at VT SAA exposed the subsidiary's cybersecurity deficiencies. Upon discovery, the Organization and VT SAA implemented comprehensive remedial actions including forensic investigation, enhanced cybersecurity architecture, 24/7 Security Operations Centre, and accelerated IT harmonization plans across all entities. The Commission deferred to ongoing US federal law enforcement investigations regarding the subsidiary's conduct.
companyNow: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited continues to operate as a major Singapore-incorporated aerospace and defense engineering company with global operations. The company has since prioritized and accelerated IT security initiatives across all subsidiaries following the incident.
dataType: Name, address, email, telephone, NRIC, passport details, photograph, date of birth, citizenship, country of residence, place of birth, USA Social Security number, USA visa information, government/military service details, CV information, foreign identification numbers, government-issued ID information, information about minors, employee status
legalBasisViolated: PDPR Regulation 9(1)(b) — Ensuring comparable protection standards
PDPR Regulation 10(1)(c) — Legally enforceable obligations on recipients
PDPR Regulation 10(3) — Binding corporate rules requirements

company: SLP Scotia Pte. Ltd. and SLP International Property Consultants Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: SLP Scotia Pte. Ltd. is a real estate brokerage firm operating as a subsidiary of SLP International Property Consultants Pte. Ltd. Both companies operate in the property agency sector and were involved in a merger at the time of this investigation.
companyLongDescription: SLP Scotia Pte. Ltd. is a real estate brokerage firm operating as a subsidiary of SLP International Property Consultants Pte. Ltd. Both companies operate in the property agency sector and were involved in a merger at the time of this investigation.
caseDescription: Four property agents registered with SLP Scotia complained that their personal data (NRIC, date of birth, home address) was improperly disclosed to the parent company SLP International Property Consultants and then to the Council of Estate Agencies without explicit consent during a merger registration process. The Commission found no breach because the disclosure fell within the scope of consent previously granted in the Associate's Agreement for related corporate purposes.
violationSummary: The case centres on whether disclosure of personal data to related corporations during a merger constituted an improper disclosure in breach of consent obligations. While the company disclosed the data without seeking fresh consent, the Commission found existing consent covered the purpose.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: SLP Scotia and SLP International Property Consultants disclosed personal data of property agents including NRIC numbers, dates of birth, and home addresses to the parent company.
whyTheyWereWrong: Property agents who had registered with SLP Scotia faced unexpected contact from the Council of Estate Agencies requesting they initiate applications with the parent company.

claimsVsReality.claim: Complainants alleged they had not consented to disclosure of their personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainants had signed Associate's Agreements containing Clause 24, which explicitly consented to disclosure of personal data to related corporations for Company Purposes, including merger-related facilitation of real estate services.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 13 of the PDPA requires that an organisation must not collect, use or disclose personal data unless the individual gives consent or the collection/use/disclosure is required or authorised under the PDPA or other written law.
regulatoryFindings.description: SLP Scotia and SLP International Property Consultants disclosed agents' personal data (NRIC, DOB, home address) to the parent company and Council of Estate Agencies for merger registration. The Commission found this did not violate s.13 because: (1) agents had signed Associate's Agreements containing Clause 24 which gave consent for disclosure to related corporations for 'Company Purposes'; (2) 'Company Purposes' included facilitating and administering real estate services, which encompassed the merger scenario; (3) both companies were 'related corporations' under the agreement; and (4) disclosure to CEA was mandated by the Estate Agents Act 2010, taking precedence under PDPA s.4(6).
violations: SLP Scotia and SLP International Property Consultants disclosed agents' personal data (NRIC, DOB, home address) to the parent company and Council of Estate Agencies for merger registration. The Commission found this did not violate s.13 because: (1) agents had signed Associate's Agreements containing Clause 24 which gave consent for disclosure to related corporations for 'Company Purposes'; (2) 'Company Purposes' included facilitating and administering real estate services, which encompassed the merger scenario; (3) both companies were 'related corporations' under the agreement; and (4) disclosure to CEA was mandated by the Estate Agents Act 2010, taking precedence under PDPA s.4(6).

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found that SLP Scotia Pte. Ltd. and SLP International Property Consultants Pte. Ltd. did not breach the Consent Obligation under section 13 of the PDPA. The disclosure of personal data to the parent company was covered by prior consent given in the Associate's Agreement, which explicitly authorised disclosure to related corporations for Company Purposes. The subsequent disclosure to the Council of Estate Agencies was mandated by the Estate Agents Act 2010, which takes precedence over PDPA obligations under section 4(6). No penalty was imposed.
dataType: NRIC number, date of birth, home address

companyDescription: Singapore Medical Association is a professional organization representing medical doctors in Singapore, established to promote professional standards and interests of the medical profession.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Medical Association is a professional organization representing medical doctors in Singapore, established to promote professional standards and interests of the medical profession.
caseDescription: An unauthorized user gained access to the Singapore Medical Association's Microsoft Office 365 email account via brute force attack and forwarded 137 emails containing personal data of 68 individuals to an external address between 28-30 January 2020. The organization failed to conduct periodic security reviews, maintain password rotation, implement anti-brute force measures, or encrypt sensitive financial data, violating the Protection Obligation under the Personal Data Protection Act 2012.
violationSummary: The organization failed to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data against unauthorized access risk, resulting in a data breach due to inadequate security measures including lack of password rotation, absence of anti-brute force mechanisms, and failure to encrypt sensitive financial data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Medical Association failed to conduct periodic security reviews of its IT systems, never changed email account passwords since November 2013.
whyTheyWereWrong: 68 individuals had their personal data including National Registration Identification Card numbers, dates of birth, bank account details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization believed an unauthorized user gained entry via brute force attack
claimsVsReality.reality: Organization could not confirm the attack method due to lack of system logs, but the unauthorized entry and email forwarding rule creation were confirmed

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization had reasonable security measures in place
claimsVsReality.reality: No periodic password changes in 7 years, no anti-brute force protections, no encryption of sensitive financial data, and no periodic security reviews

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control against unauthorized access risk through reasonable security steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization failed to conduct periodic security reviews of IT systems
violations: Organization failed to conduct periodic security reviews of IT systems
Email account password unchanged since first use in November 2013 (approximately 7 years)
No anti-brute force measures such as login attempt limits or account lockouts were implemented
No encryption of emails or attachments containing sensitive financial data like bank account details and swift codes
Lack of system logs prevented confirmation of the breach mechanism

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organization in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. A warning was issued to the organization. No formal directions were required as the organization had already taken actions to address the gaps in its security arrangements, including implementation of periodic security reviews, password management, anti-brute force measures, and data encryption policies.
companyNow: Singapore Medical Association continues to operate as a professional body representing physicians in Singapore. Following the enforcement action, the organization implemented corrective measures to strengthen its data protection and cybersecurity practices.
dataType: National Registration Identification Card numbers, dates of birth, indemnity coverage, educational information, financial transaction information (bank account details, swift codes)

companyDescription: Midwest Recovery Systems, LLC is a third-party debt collection company based in Earth City, Missouri, that collects debts on behalf of medical providers, payday lenders, and other creditors.
companyLongDescription: Midwest Recovery Systems, LLC is a third-party debt collection company based in Earth City, Missouri, that collects debts on behalf of medical providers, payday lenders, and other creditors.
caseDescription: Midwest Recovery operated a third-party debt collection business that pursued consumers for phantom, counterfeit, and unauthorized payday loans and medical debts that consumers did not owe or that the company could not verify. The company employed 'debt parking'—reporting debts to credit bureaus before contacting consumers—resulting in 80-97% of disputed debts being found inaccurate. Over $98 million in fraudulent debts were reported since 2015.
violationSummary: The company exposed consumers to harm by placing inaccurate negative information on credit reports without prior notification or verification, damaging their creditworthiness and ability to access credit, housing, and employment.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Midwest Recovery Systems collected phantom payday loans, counterfeit debts, and unverifiable medical debts from consumers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers suffered 35+ point credit score drops, lost mortgage approvals, denied employment, and were coerced into paying debts they never owed; 80-97% of disputed debts were found inaccurate.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserts debts are valid and owed by consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: 80-97% of disputed debts were determined to be inaccurate or invalid upon investigation; $98M+ consisted of unauthorized, counterfeit, or unverifiable debts.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company represents consumers' debts to credit bureaus with accuracy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company furnishes information knowing or with reasonable cause to believe it is inaccurate; receives 24,000+ disputes on notoriously fraudulent Joel Tucker portfolios yet continues collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company investigates consumer disputes properly.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company fails to request validation documents for direct disputes and fails to notify consumers of investigation results or deletions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company collects only legitimate debts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company collects phantom payday loans, counterfeit debts, debts subject to unresolved fraud claims, debts in bankruptcy, and debts already paid by consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Midwest Recovery represented that consumers owed medical, payday loan, or other debts that were false, misleading, or unsubstantiated at the time of collection.
violations: Midwest Recovery represented that consumers owed medical, payday loan, or other debts that were false, misleading, or unsubstantiated at the time of collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807 prohibits debt collectors from using false, deceptive, or misleading representations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company falsely represented the character, amount, and legal status of debts while knowing or should have known they were unauthorized, counterfeit, or unverifiable.
violations: Company falsely represented the character, amount, and legal status of debts while knowing or should have known they were unauthorized, counterfeit, or unverifiable.
Company communicated credit information to CRAs that was known or should have been known to be false.
Company used false representations and deceptive means to collect debts and obtain consumer information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 808 prohibits unfair or unconscionable means to collect debts.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company furnished debt information to CRAs before communicating with consumers, preventing them from disputing debts before credit damage occurred.
violations: Company furnished debt information to CRAs before communicating with consumers, preventing them from disputing debts before credit damage occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 809(a) requires written validation notice within five days of initial communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to send required validation notices containing debt amount, creditor name, dispute rights, and original creditor information to numerous consumers.
violations: Company failed to send required validation notices containing debt amount, creditor name, dispute rights, and original creditor information to numerous consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(1)(A) prohibits furnishing information known or believed to be inaccurate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company furnished $98M+ in unauthorized, counterfeit, and unverifiable debts to CRAs while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe the information was inaccurate.
violations: Company furnished $98M+ in unauthorized, counterfeit, and unverifiable debts to CRAs while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe the information was inaccurate.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(8)(E) and Furnisher Rule 12 C.F.R. § 1022.43(e) require reasonable investigation of consumer disputes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to conduct reasonable investigations of thousands of direct disputes from consumers and did not request validation documents in numerous cases.
violations: Company failed to conduct reasonable investigations of thousands of direct disputes from consumers and did not request validation documents in numerous cases.
Company failed to report investigation results to consumers within the required 30-day period in numerous instances.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri on November 25, 2020. The case seeks permanent injunction to halt violations, rescission or reformation of contracts, restitution, refund of monies paid, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies ($24.3 million in estimated gross revenues), and monitoring requirements. As of the complaint filing date, no settlement or final judgment has been reached.
companyNow: Midwest Recovery Systems, LLC remains operational as of the complaint filing in November 2020. The outcome of the FTC litigation is not specified in this document.
dataType: Financial data, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, personal identifying information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807(2)(A) – false representation of debt character/amount
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807(8) – communicating false credit information
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807(10) – false representations to collect debt
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 808 – unfair collection practices
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 809(a) – failure to provide validation notice
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(1)(A) – furnishing inaccurate information
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(8)(E)(i) – failure to conduct reasonable investigation
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(8)(E)(iii) – failure to report investigation results

companyDescription: Posti Oy is the state-owned Finnish postal service operator, established in the 1890s. It maintains a mandatory address register (osoiterekisteri) under postal law to ensure reliable mail delivery and offers address update services to businesses.
companyLongDescription: Posti Oy is the state-owned Finnish postal service operator, established in the 1890s. It maintains a mandatory address register (osoiterekisteri) under postal law to ensure reliable mail delivery and offers address update services to businesses.
caseDescription: Posti failed to transparently inform address change notification users that their personal data would be disclosed to third-party direct marketers. Information about this processing and data subjects' right to object was buried in terms of service documents and inaccessible during the notification process. Over 161,000–201,000 individuals per year made address change notifications without receiving proper advance notice of data sharing practices.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data to third parties without proper transparency. Data subjects were not informed clearly or at the right time that their address information would be shared for direct marketing, and their right to object was not made apparent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Posti collected address change notifications and automatically shared updated address data with third-party companies for direct marketing without clearly disclosing this practice or users'.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 161,518 and 201,627 people per year made address changes unaware their data would be shared for marketing; they received no transparent notice of sharing or their right to block it,.

claimsVsReality.claim: Posti claimed that information about data sharing and the right to object was available on its website, in privacy notices, and in service terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: While documents existed, they were not actively presented to users at the moment of address notification; 161,518–201,627 users per year never accepted terms or received transparent notice before disclosure occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Posti stated it had informed users about the opt-out right through its privacy statement and product terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy statement buried the mention of the right to object in an isolated sentence under a different section heading; users had to navigate away from the notification form to discover this critical information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Posti asserted that the low number of opt-out requests (under 0.5%) showed users understood and accepted data sharing.
claimsVsReality.reality: Low opt-out rates reflected lack of awareness of the option and lack of transparency, not genuine acceptance; when Posti improved visibility in early 2020, opt-outs increased by approximately 100 immediately.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed transparently with respect to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Posti did not make transparent, at the time of collection, that address data would be disclosed to third parties for direct marketing.
violations: Posti did not make transparent, at the time of collection, that address data would be disclosed to third parties for direct marketing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12 requires the controller to take appropriate measures to provide information in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form using clear and plain language.
regulatoryFindings.description: Information about data sharing and the right to object was scattered across product terms and privacy notice rather than presented clearly during the notification process itself.
violations: Information about data sharing and the right to object was scattered across product terms and privacy notice rather than presented clearly during the notification process itself.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(1)(d) and 13(2)(b) require the controller to provide information about recipients and the right to object when data are collected from the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Posti did not timely provide these required details to users making address notifications; 161,518–201,627 notifications per year lacked terms acceptance.
violations: Posti did not timely provide these required details to users making address notifications; 161,518–201,627 notifications per year lacked terms acceptance.

regulatoryFindings.act: Postal Act 38 § 5 (Finland) states data subjects may prohibit disclosure of their data in address update services.
regulatoryFindings.description: The right to prohibit was not communicated effectively or at the right moment, making it difficult for users to exercise this right.
violations: The right to prohibit was not communicated effectively or at the right moment, making it difficult for users to exercise this right.

outcome: Posti received a €100,000 administrative fine for lack of transparency in personal data handling. The company was ordered to ensure future address notifications clearly and actively inform users at the moment of collection about data sharing for direct marketing and their right to object. Posti committed to updating its service process to present terms for acceptance in all digital notifications, improving data subject rights documentation, and enhancing visibility of opt-out mechanisms. No criminal referral was made. The decision is subject to appeal to Finnish administrative court.
companyNow: Posti remains the primary postal operator in Finland, operating under the name Posti Group and providing mail, parcel, and logistics services across Nordics and beyond. Following this enforcement action, the company has updated its transparency and consent practices for address change notifications.
dataType: Name, address, contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13(1)(d) – Information about recipients/categories of recipients
GDPR Art. 13(2)(b) – Information about right to object
Postal Act (Finland) 38 § 5 – Right to prohibit disclosure

companyDescription: DCR Workforce, Inc. is a Florida-based company providing workforce management software. It operates at 7795 NW Beacon Square Boulevard, Suite 201, Boca Raton, FL 33487.
companyLongDescription: DCR Workforce, Inc. is a Florida-based company providing workforce management software. It operates at 7795 NW Beacon Square Boulevard, Suite 201, Boca Raton, FL 33487.
caseDescription: DCR Workforce falsely claimed compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website while its certification had lapsed in February 2018. The company obtained Privacy Shield certification in January 2017 but continued making false representations about current participation after the certification expired, violating FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibition on deceptive practices.
violationSummary: Company disclosed false representations about Privacy Shield compliance status to the public, misleading individuals and regulatory bodies about its data protection practices and certification status.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: DCR Workforce falsely claimed on its website that it complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents whose employment data was transferred to DCR Workforce believed their personal information received legal privacy protections under Privacy Shield.

claimsVsReality.claim: DCR Workforce complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce and has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: DCR Workforce obtained Privacy Shield certification in January 2017, but that certification lapsed by February 2018. The company was not a current participant in the Privacy Shield framework at the time it made these claims.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: DCR Workforce represented on its privacy policy website that it complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed by February 2018 and it was not a current participant in the framework.
violations: DCR Workforce represented on its privacy policy website that it complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed by February 2018 and it was not a current participant in the framework.
Company continued to make false statements claiming current Privacy Shield participation after certification expiration, violating the FTC's deception authority.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on January 13, 2020 alleging deceptive practices. The case alleges one count of Privacy Misrepresentation under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. Complaint seeks cessation of deceptive representations and compliance with Privacy Shield requirements or alternative compliance mechanisms.
companyNow: Unknown. Document is a complaint issued January 13, 2020; outcome of enforcement action not available in document.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU to US (specific types not detailed)

company: BLS International Services Singapore Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: BLS International Services Singapore Pte. Ltd. is a service provider that handles government-to-citizen services for the High Commission of India in Singapore, including visa and consular services.
companyLongDescription: BLS International Services Singapore Pte. Ltd. is a service provider that handles government-to-citizen services for the High Commission of India in Singapore, including visa and consular services.
caseDescription: BLS International Services failed to properly implement URL encryption in a new booking system for the High Commission of India, resulting in a 39-day vulnerability where URLs could be manipulated to expose 3,357 individuals' personal data. The organisation had intended encryption but due to a coding error and inadequate testing, the vulnerability went undetected until reported by the Personal Data Protection Commission.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement adequate security measures (proper encryption) and failed to detect vulnerabilities through inadequate testing, resulting in unauthorized access risk to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: BLS International implemented a new booking system with URLs that were supposed to be encrypted but contained a critical coding error that went undetected due to inadequate pre-launch testing.
whyTheyWereWrong: The coding error exposed the sensitive personal data of 3,357 individuals including passport numbers, contact details, and email addresses to unauthorized access through URL manipulation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had intended for the booking system URLs to be encrypted to prevent manipulation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The encryption was not implemented properly due to a coding error, and the error went undetected because the organisation conducted only limited testing before deploying the system.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 imposes a Protection Obligation requiring organisations to implement and maintain reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or loss.
regulatoryFindings.description: BLS failed to conduct adequate testing of the booking system before deployment, which resulted in an undetected coding error in URL encryption implementation.
violations: BLS failed to conduct adequate testing of the booking system before deployment, which resulted in an undetected coding error in URL encryption implementation.
The inadequate testing meant the organisation could not identify the vulnerability that allowed manipulation of URLs to access other individuals' personal data.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found BLS International Services in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for failing to conduct adequate testing. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 5,000 within 30 days. Interest accrues at the rate specified in the Rules of Court if payment is not made. No further directions were required as the organisation had already taken remedial actions, including removing the vulnerable URL feature and implementing email delivery of confirmations instead.
companyNow: BLS International Services Singapore Pte. Ltd. continues to operate as a service provider for the High Commission of India in Singapore, having remediated the security vulnerabilities identified in this case.
dataType: Name, passport number, contact number, email address, service request type, booking date/time, appointment date/time

companyDescription: SPH Magazines Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based media and publishing company that operates the HardwareZone forum, a popular online community for technology discussions.
companyLongDescription: SPH Magazines Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based media and publishing company that operates the HardwareZone forum, a popular online community for technology discussions.
caseDescription: SPH Magazines' HardwareZone forum was breached when a senior moderator's compromised credentials were used to access 685,393 user profiles. The company failed to implement password security requirements for senior moderators and did not detect the breach for nearly 2 years, allowing 704,764 attempted profile views between September 2017 and September 2017.
violationSummary: The organization failed to make reasonable security arrangements under PDPA s.24 by omitting password security requirements for privileged accounts and neglecting security testing, directly enabling unauthorized data access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SPH Magazines failed to enforce password security requirements for senior moderators and did not conduct security testing, allowing a hacker to access moderator credentials.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 700,000 forum members had their usernames, email addresses, full names, and optional profile data exposed because moderators were not required to change passwords—one moderator's password.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation's systems and applications had not been compromised during the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: While internal systems were not directly breached, the organisation's failure to secure moderator accounts and conduct security testing created the vulnerability exploited in the attack.

claimsVsReality.claim: Password policy was in place requiring certain length, complexity, and expiration.
claimsVsReality.reality: This policy applied only to employees and did not apply to senior moderators, who had no requirement to change passwords regularly or maintain acceptable complexity standards.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: SPH Magazines failed to implement reasonable password security requirements for senior moderator accounts—no mandatory password changes, length, or complexity standards were applied to these privileged users
violations: SPH Magazines failed to implement reasonable password security requirements for senior moderator accounts—no mandatory password changes, length, or complexity standards were applied to these privileged users
The organisation did not conduct any security testing of the HardwareZone forum website, leaving it without knowledge of overall security gaps
A senior moderator's password was not changed for 10 years and did not meet the length and complexity standards the company required for employees

outcome: The Commissioner directed SPH Magazines Pte Ltd to pay a financial penalty of SGD 26,000 within 30 days. The organisation had already implemented remedial measures including temporary suspension of senior moderator access rights, revised password policy (8 characters, alphanumeric, upper/lower case, 3-month expiry), two-factor authentication for moderators (April 2018), CAPTCHA implementation, and removal/purging of full names and optional profile fields from the database.
companyNow: SPH Magazines Pte Ltd remains operational as part of Singapore Press Holdings, a major media conglomerate. The company has implemented enhanced security protocols following this enforcement action.
dataType: Usernames, email addresses, full names, passwords, year of birth, gender, country, education, job scope, occupation, industry, company size, monthly income, area of interest

companyDescription: Webcada Pte Ltd is a Singapore-registered company operating in the e-commerce/retail sector, providing database and ordering services to customers.
