companyLongDescription: Webcada Pte Ltd is a Singapore-registered company operating in the e-commerce/retail sector, providing database and ordering services to customers.
caseDescription: Webcada's database servers were compromised by ransomware on 29 August 2020 through improperly configured IPMI access, affecting 522,722 individuals. The company lacked a written data protection policy and failed to scan IPMI ports during vulnerability assessments, enabling the attack. While no data exfiltration occurred and all data was restored from backups, Webcada admitted breaches of accountability and protection obligations under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data, particularly by misconfiguring IPMI access settings, omitting security scanning, and lacking documented data protection policies—core failures in data security under section 24 of the PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Webcada Pte Ltd failed to document data protection policies in writing, enabled unnecessary public internet access to server management interfaces.
whyTheyWereWrong: 522,722 customers' names, phone numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and order histories were encrypted by ransomware because Webcada left management interfaces publicly exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Webcada had security measures in place
claimsVsReality.reality: IPMI was publicly accessible and not included in vulnerability scanning; ransomware was successfully deployed via undetected IPMI vulnerabilities

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the PDPA requires organisations to document their data protection policies and practices in writing to increase awareness and ensure accountability.
regulatoryFindings.description: Webcada did not have a written data protection policy prior to the Incident
violations: Webcada did not have a written data protection policy prior to the Incident

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: IPMI access was enabled from the public internet without necessity
violations: IPMI access was enabled from the public internet without necessity
IPMI was omitted from monthly vulnerability scans, preventing detection of exploitable vulnerabilities that were subsequently used to deploy ransomware

outcome: Webcada admitted liability and requested expedited decision treatment. The PDPC imposed a financial penalty of SGD 25,000 (approximately USD 18,390), payable within 30 days with interest accruing on unpaid amounts. No additional directions were issued under section 48I of the PDPA given the organisation's prompt remedial actions: permanent IPMI disablement, removal of public IP addresses, configuration of trusted IP access only, installation of endpoint protection with threat hunting, and implementation of a written data protection policy. The Commission credited the organisation's voluntary admission of liability and swift remediation.
companyNow: Unknown. No public information available regarding Webcada Pte Ltd's current operational status.
dataType: Names, phone numbers, dates of birth, addresses, order histories

company: The Future of Cooking Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: The Future of Cooking Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce retailer specialising in kitchen appliances and accessories, operating an online store at thermomix.com.sg.
companyLongDescription: The Future of Cooking Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce retailer specialising in kitchen appliances and accessories, operating an online store at thermomix.com.sg.
caseDescription: TFC's e-commerce website exposed personal data of 178 customers for over three months due to a buggy WordPress plugin that created a publicly accessible temporary file. TFC failed to implement adequate security measures, including pre-launch vulnerability testing and data protection requirements in its vendor contract with website designer Hachi.
violationSummary: TFC failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically: no pre-launch vulnerability assessments, no contractual data protection requirements with vendors, and failure to monitor for publicly accessible sensitive files.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Installed a WordPress plugin with a bug that generated and publicly exposed a CSV file containing 178 customers' personal data on a web-accessible directory folder for over three months.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' names, billing and shipping addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and payment information were accessible to anyone on the internet, exposing them to identity theft.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: TFC did not specify any data protection requirements for vendor Hachi in contracts or project documentation
violations: TFC did not specify any data protection requirements for vendor Hachi in contracts or project documentation
TFC did not conduct pre-launch security testing or vulnerability assessments on the website
A temporary CSV file containing personal data was generated by a buggy plugin and left accessible to the public without detection or remediation for over 3 months

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found TFC in breach of section 24 of the PDPA Protection Obligation. TFC directed to pay financial penalty of $9,000 within 30 days. No further directions required as TFC took remedial actions: removed the buggy plugin, disabled public access to directory folder, engaged vendor for penetration testing and security enhancements. Hachi Web Solutions was not found in breach as the cause related to website design, not data processing activities.
companyNow: Unknown – likely continues e-commerce operations under thermomix.com.sg domain following remediation.
dataType: Name, email address, billing address, shipping address, customer notes, payment status, transaction ID, product ID, order quantity, telephone number

companyDescription: Digi Távközlési és Szolgáltató Kft is a major Hungarian telecommunications and service provider offering internet, TV, and mobile services to residential and business customers. As of the 2018–2019 fiscal years covered in the enforcement action, the company reported approximately 47–51 billion HUF (roughly €125–140M) in annual net revenue.
companyLongDescription: Digi Távközlési és Szolgáltató Kft is a major Hungarian telecommunications and service provider offering internet, TV, and mobile services to residential and business customers. As of the 2018–2019 fiscal years covered in the enforcement action, the company reported approximately 47–51 billion HUF (roughly €125–140M) in annual net revenue.
caseDescription: Digi, a major Hungarian telecom provider, failed to delete a test database containing sensitive customer data after fixing a system error, leaving 700,000+ individuals' records exposed. When an ethical hacker discovered a known 9-year-old vulnerability in their content management system, the unencrypted data became accessible. The company also failed to patch the vulnerability and conduct regular security scans of their public website.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures (encryption, timely patching, vulnerability scanning) proportionate to the risks posed by processing large volumes of sensitive customer data, directly enabling the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Digi created a test database containing 700,000+ customer records for troubleshooting, failed to delete it after repairs were complete, stored the data unencrypted.
whyTheyWereWrong: An attacker exploited the unpatched vulnerability to access 700,000+ customers' highly sensitive data including names, ID numbers, addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Digi claimed access control through user permissions and proper authorization was sufficient to protect customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: A known, easily-detected 9-year-old vulnerability made the unencrypted database publicly accessible via the website, rendering access controls meaningless; 700,000+ customer records were at risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: Digi claimed the test database required no encryption because it was secured by permission-based access control.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vulnerability bypassed all access controls; the data was stored in plain text and became fully readable to anyone who exploited the known CMS flaw.

claimsVsReality.claim: Digi claimed it was impossible to monitor non-official patches for its open-source CMS due to the volume of patches available.
claimsVsReality.reality: A core security patch for a 9-year-old, widely-known vulnerability was publicly available and easily detectable via automated tools; the company's own internal policies required regular vulnerability scanning, which was not performed on the website.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data to be processed only for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digi retained a test database containing 700,000+ customer records (names, IDs, addresses, banking data) long after the debugging purpose was completed, storing the data purposelessly for months until the security breach.
violations: Digi retained a test database containing 700,000+ customer records (names, IDs, addresses, banking data) long after the debugging purpose was completed, storing the data purposelessly for months until the security breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) requires personal data to be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects only for as long as necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digi stored identifiable customer data in the test database in readable form well beyond the time needed to fix the system error, making individuals' identities permanently at risk.
violations: Digi stored identifiable customer data in the test database in readable form well beyond the time needed to fix the system error, making individuals' identities permanently at risk.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1)–(2) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security proportionate to risks, including encryption where appropriate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digi failed to encrypt sensitive customer data in the database, did not install a known security patch for a 9-year-old vulnerability in their CMS system, and did not perform regular vulnerability scanning of their public website, leaving 700,000+ records directly accessible to attackers.
violations: Digi failed to encrypt sensitive customer data in the database, did not install a known security patch for a 9-year-old vulnerability in their CMS system, and did not perform regular vulnerability scanning of their public website, leaving 700,000+ records directly accessible to attackers.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) found Digi violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(b), 5(1)(e), and 32(1)–(2) and imposed a fine of 100,000,000 HUF (approximately €268,000 / $293,000). The authority ordered Digi to review all databases containing personal data to determine whether encryption is justified and report findings to NAIH within a specified timeframe. The decision is final and non-appealable administratively; judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court is available within 30 days. Digi must pay the fine within 30 days or face enforcement and late-payment interest.
companyNow: Digi Telecom remains one of Hungary's major telecommunications providers. Following this enforcement action, the company has stated it intends to enhance security practices, including consideration of higher-level firewalls and expanded vulnerability scanning.
dataType: Names, birth names, parents' names, birth place and date, address, ID card numbers, personal numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, bank account numbers, payment data, service contracts

company: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 3593 (MCST 3593); New-E Security Pte Ltd
companyDescription: MCST 3593 is a management corporation that manages a residential condominium (Marina Bay Residences) in Singapore. New-E Security Pte Ltd was a contracted security services provider responsible for CCTV surveillance and facility security.
companyLongDescription: MCST 3593 is a management corporation that manages a residential condominium (Marina Bay Residences) in Singapore. New-E Security Pte Ltd was a contracted security services provider responsible for CCTV surveillance and facility security.
caseDescription: MCST 3593 failed to establish data protection obligations in its contract with security vendor New-E. A security supervisor unauthorized disclosed CCTV footage containing images of identifiable individuals to a resident and Facebook. MCST 3593 and New-E lacked written data protection policies, employee training, and contractual safeguards.
violationSummary: CCTV footage containing identifiable individuals was made accessible to unauthorized parties (a resident and Facebook users) due to absence of security arrangements, written policies, and access controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: MCST 3593 engaged New-E Security to manage CCTV systems without contractual data protection clauses, written policies, or formal communication of PDPA obligations.
whyTheyWereWrong: Multiple unidentified residents captured in lobby CCTV footage had their identifiable personal data disclosed to a third party.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 3593 and ETCPM had put in place measures and safeguards to ensure compliance with PDPA regarding data collection, use, disclosure, protection, and retention.
claimsVsReality.reality: MCST 3593 had appointed no DPO, developed no data protection policy, included no data protection clauses in the New-E contract, and communicated no data protection requirements to vendors or agents.

claimsVsReality.claim: New-E had a practice of only releasing CCTV footage to ETCPM representatives.
claimsVsReality.reality: This practice was communicated only verbally; New-E had no written policies, employee training, or access control procedures, resulting in a security supervisor recording and transmitting CCTV footage on a personal mobile phone.

claimsVsReality.claim: No measures could have prevented the Security Supervisor's willful disclosure of CCTV footage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Documented written data protection policies, access control procedures, and employee training would have provided clear guidance, accountability mechanisms, and deterrents to prevent unauthorized disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 11(3) PDPA — An organisation must appoint a Data Protection Officer to ensure compliance with the Act.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 3593 had not appointed any Data Protection Officer at the time of the incident or during investigations.
violations: MCST 3593 had not appointed any Data Protection Officer at the time of the incident or during investigations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 PDPA — An organisation must develop and put in place a personal data protection policy.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 3593 had not developed or implemented any data protection policy governing the handling of CCTV footage or other personal data.
violations: MCST 3593 had not developed or implemented any data protection policy governing the handling of CCTV footage or other personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 PDPA — An organisation must put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 3593 failed to establish contractual data protection clauses with New-E and did not communicate any data protection requirements, leaving CCTV footage unprotected by written guidelines or access controls.
violations: MCST 3593 failed to establish contractual data protection clauses with New-E and did not communicate any data protection requirements, leaving CCTV footage unprotected by written guidelines or access controls.

New-E failed to implement written data protection policies, employee training, or access control procedures for CCTV footage management, permitting unauthorized disclosure by a security supervisor using personal mobile devices.

outcome: Deputy Commissioner directed MCST 3593 to pay SGD 5,000 within 30 days. New-E was directed to implement a data protection policy and internal guidelines with procedures for CCTV management and access control within 30 days, and to report completion within 7 days. MCST 3593 subsequently appointed a Data Protection Officer, implemented a data protection policy and standard operating procedure, and committed to adding data processing provisions in contract addenda. New-E developed employee data protection training and operational procedures.
companyNow: MCST 3593 is an active management corporation overseeing Marina Bay Residences condominium. It has since implemented remedial compliance measures including appointing a DPO and establishing data protection policies.
dataType: CCTV footage (video biometric data), identifiable individuals in common areas
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.11(3) — Failure to appoint Data Protection Officer
PDPA s.12 — Failure to develop and implement personal data protection policy
PDPA s.24 — Failure to put in place reasonable security arrangements

companyDescription: Times Software Pte Ltd is an information technology services vendor that provides payroll software applications and related services to corporate clients, including law firms, professional services companies, and technology companies. The company had been in operation for at least 21 years prior to the 2020 decision.
companyLongDescription: Times Software Pte Ltd is an information technology services vendor that provides payroll software applications and related services to corporate clients, including law firms, professional services companies, and technology companies. The company had been in operation for at least 21 years prior to the 2020 decision.
caseDescription: Times Software's payroll software server suffered a hard disk failure in December 2017. During remediation, an employee failed to re-enable password protection, and the server was reset to default settings. The exposed Employee Data (616 employees across three organizations) was indexed by Google and searchable online from December 2017 to February 2018. Times also retained Employee Data beyond the purpose for which it was collected, in breach of data retention obligations.
violationSummary: Employee data was exposed to the public via the Internet and indexed by search engines due to inadequate security measures (disabled password protection) and poor data handling practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Times Software failed to enable password protection after restoring servers from backup, retained customer employee data after development projects ended.
whyTheyWereWrong: 616 employees' sensitive personal data including bank account numbers, salaries, NRIC numbers, and addresses were exposed online.

claimsVsReality.claim: Times claimed TMF provided Employee Data for a one-time data migration and development exercise
claimsVsReality.reality: TMF disputed this, claiming it had authorized only the data migration and was unaware of or did not consent to use for functionality development

claimsVsReality.claim: Dentons represented that a July 2014 Statement from Times sufficed as a written contract with adequate data protection commitments
claimsVsReality.reality: The Statement only covered staff conduct, physical document security, and encryption during transmission—it completely omitted requirements for electronic storage security, which was the actual context of the data breach

claimsVsReality.claim: TMF asserted it had conducted annual vendor assessments and Times had confirmed a formal data disposal policy
claimsVsReality.reality: Times had retained Employee Data for years after project completion despite the stated policy, and the assessments were insufficient to detect the retention

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Times failed to ensure server restoration procedures included supervisory checks to verify password protection was enabled
violations: Times failed to ensure server restoration procedures included supervisory checks to verify password protection was enabled
Times had poor password management policies, reusing identical passwords across server restorations
Times did not encrypt sensitive financial data (bank account numbers, salaries) when storing in file server system
Times used live customer data for testing instead of anonymized or synthetic data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 of the PDPA requires organisations to cease retaining documents containing personal data or remove means of association as soon as it is reasonable to assume the purpose for collection is no longer served and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Times retained Employee Data of Red Hat and LIU after December 2015 implementation of the development tool, despite SOP requiring deletion upon project sign-off
violations: Times retained Employee Data of Red Hat and LIU after December 2015 implementation of the development tool, despite SOP requiring deletion upon project sign-off
No checks were conducted to ensure the retention limitation SOP was followed

outcome: Times Software was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 20,000 within 30 days. The Commissioner also found Dentons and TMF breached Section 24 (Protection Obligation) by failing to put in place adequate written contractual provisions with their data intermediaries. Dentons and TMF received warnings in lieu of financial penalties. Red Hat and LIU were found not in breach as their contracts, read together with Master Services Agreements, adequately specified data protection obligations. All organizations implemented remedial actions including enhanced security policies, vendor assessments, audit procedures, and removal of exposed data.
companyNow: Times Software continues operations. The company has implemented significant remedial measures including enhanced SOPs for data handling, weekly audits by department heads, monthly cross-department audits, bi-monthly random IT audits, and a requirement that servers published online no longer accept unencrypted files.
dataType: Employee personal data including name, NRIC, residential address, contact details, work designation, employment duration, base salary, date of birth, marital status, nationality, race, bank account information, income tax account number

company: Everlast Projects Pte Ltd, Everlast Industries (S) Pte Ltd, ELG Specialist Pte Ltd
companyDescription: Three related companies specialising in the supply and installation of architectural metal works, glass, and aluminium products. They operated as a corporate group with centralised HR and payroll functions but lacked formal data governance structures.
companyLongDescription: Three related companies specialising in the supply and installation of architectural metal works, glass, and aluminium products. They operated as a corporate group with centralised HR and payroll functions but lacked formal data governance structures.
caseDescription: Three related construction companies operating as a group failed to establish written data protection policies and adequate security measures. A ransomware attack encrypted all files on a centralised server containing 384 employees' sensitive personal data, including financial information. The companies lacked basic security controls like firewalls and periodic security reviews.
violationSummary: The organisations failed to implement reasonable security arrangements under PDPA s.24, resulting in unauthorised encryption of personal data. Lack of firewalls, security reviews, and written policies constitutes systematic insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Three related construction companies centralized employee payroll processing without written data protection policies, written security agreements between entities.
whyTheyWereWrong: 384 employees' sensitive personal data including names, national ID numbers, dates of birth, bank account details, and salary information were encrypted by ransomware.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisations operated efficiently by centralising payroll processing in EPPL's HR department.
claimsVsReality.reality: Centralisation without written contracts, intra-group agreements, or security oversight exposed all 384 employees' sensitive data to ransomware encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Verbal instructions to employees were sufficient for data protection compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of written policies meant no clear reference for employees, no effective training, and no enforceable standards — employees had no way to know what was required.

claimsVsReality.claim: The server and backup systems were adequate for protecting employee payroll data.
claimsVsReality.reality: No firewall, no security reviews, and no IT policies meant basic vulnerabilities went undetected. Ransomware encrypted both primary and physical backup, leaving no usable data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.12 requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations, and communicate these to staff.
regulatoryFindings.description: EPPL, EIPL, and ESPL admitted they had no written data protection policies and relied only on verbal instructions
violations: EPPL, EIPL, and ESPL admitted they had no written data protection policies and relied only on verbal instructions
As a group of companies centralising payroll processing, they failed to establish binding group-level written policies or intra-group agreements setting common standards for data protection

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, modification, and similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: EPPL did not install a firewall for the server, leaving it vulnerable to web-based security threats
violations: EPPL did not install a firewall for the server, leaving it vulnerable to web-based security threats
EPPL did not conduct periodic security reviews or vulnerability scans of its IT infrastructure
EPPL had no written IT security policies (password policy, patching policy, etc.)
EIPL and ESPL failed to implement operational processes to supervise or control EPPL's handling of their employees' data despite EPPL acting as their data intermediary

outcome: Deputy Commissioner Yeong Zee Kin found all three organisations in breach of s.12 (Accountability Obligation) and s.24 (Protection Obligation). No monetary penalty was imposed due to: voluntary notification of the incident, no complaints of misuse, no evidence of data exfiltration, and financial hardship that would result from a penalty. Instead, the Commission directed the organisations to: (1) develop and implement intra-group agreements or binding corporate rules setting common data protection standards within 90 days; (2) review internal policies to align with the new standards within 90 days; and (3) inform the Commission of completion within one week. Monitoring compliance is ongoing.
companyNow: Unknown. The companies remain subject to compliance monitoring and must implement the remedial directives issued by the Commission.
dataType: Employee personal data: name, NRIC/FIN, date of birth, bank account details, salary information

companyDescription: Kohl's is a large national department store chain offering clothing, accessories, beauty goods, and home products through physical retail locations and significant online presence.
companyLongDescription: Kohl's is a large national department store chain offering clothing, accessories, beauty goods, and home products through physical retail locations and significant online presence.
caseDescription: Kohl's violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by refusing to provide identity theft victims with application and business transaction records they requested. The company implemented policies in February 2017 and August 2018 that restricted disclosure of detailed order information to victims, offering it only to law enforcement. Kohl's also failed to respond to many requests within the required 30-day period.
violationSummary: Kohl's wrongfully withheld personal data and transaction records that belonged to identity theft victims, preventing them from accessing information necessary to remedy fraud. This constitutes a breach of confidentiality duty to provide records upon legitimate request.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Kohl's implemented policies from February 2017 through March 2019 that refused to provide identity theft victims with their requested application.
whyTheyWereWrong: Identity theft victims were unable to obtain critical information like fraudulent shipping addresses and phone numbers needed to resolve identity theft cases, recover funds.

claimsVsReality.claim: Kohl's was not permitted to share detailed identity theft transaction information with victims
claimsVsReality.reality: FCRA Section 609(e) explicitly requires business entities to provide such records to victims upon request within 30 days

claimsVsReality.claim: Victims must obtain fraud information only through law enforcement requests
claimsVsReality.reality: The law gives victims themselves the right to request and receive their own transaction records directly from the business

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 609(e)(1) of the FCRA requires a 'business entity' to provide an identity theft 'victim' with 'application and business transaction records' evidencing any transaction that the victim alleges to be the result of identity theft within 30 days of receipt of a request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kohl's refused to provide detailed order information directly to identity theft victims, limiting disclosure to law enforcement only under the February 2017 and August 2018 policies
violations: Kohl's refused to provide detailed order information directly to identity theft victims, limiting disclosure to law enforcement only under the February 2017 and August 2018 policies
Kohl's failed to respond to multiple 609(e) requests within the required 30-day timeframe

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kohl's engaged in unfair practices by preventing identity theft victims from accessing records they were legally entitled to receive
violations: Kohl's engaged in unfair practices by preventing identity theft victims from accessing records they were legally entitled to receive

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint on June 8, 2020 seeking permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleged knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice, with potential penalties of up to $3,993 per violation. Kohl's implemented a compliant policy in April 2019 that provides victims with requested application and transaction records. The case pursued injunctive relief and damages for all violations occurring between February 2017 and March 2019.
companyNow: Kohl's Department Stores, Inc. continues to operate as a major national department store chain with physical stores and online retail presence at www.kohls.com as of the complaint date. The company implemented the required policy changes in April 2019.
dataType: Identity information, financial information, application records, transaction records, shipping address, phone number

companyDescription: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer is a religious organization that maintains member records and communication channels. As a faith-based organization, it holds personal data of its 815+ members for administrative and pastoral purposes.
companyLongDescription: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer is a religious organization that maintains member records and communication channels. As a faith-based organization, it holds personal data of its 815+ members for administrative and pastoral purposes.
caseDescription: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer inadvertently uploaded a file containing personal data of 815 members to a publicly accessible subdirectory on 24 November 2019. The file was indexed by search engines and remained discoverable online for nearly 10 months until a member found it via Google search on 8 September 2020. The organization lacked data protection policies, access controls, and file upload verification systems.
violationSummary: The personal data was inadvertently exposed publicly through upload to an unprotected directory and indexed by search engines, making it accessible to any internet user. This constitutes exposure under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: A staff member accidentally uploaded a file containing 815 members' personal data including names, national ID numbers, addresses, dates of birth, marital status, emails.
whyTheyWereWrong: 815 members' sensitive personal data including national ID numbers and contact information remained exposed online.

claimsVsReality.claim: The subdirectory was intended to be publicly accessible
claimsVsReality.reality: Public accessibility should not have included files containing personal member data without encryption or access controls

claimsVsReality.claim: The upload was accidental (staff mistake)
claimsVsReality.reality: The file remained indexed and accessible for 9.5 months due to systemic lack of upload verification and security controls, not merely human error

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.12 requires organisations to develop and implement data protection policies and practices to ensure compliance with the Act.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization had not developed any internal data protection policies or practices at the time of the incident
violations: Organization had not developed any internal data protection policies or practices at the time of the incident
No system of checks existed for uploading files to the organization's website

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: No access controls existed on the public subdirectory where member data was uploaded
violations: No access controls existed on the public subdirectory where member data was uploaded
No reasonable security measures prevented the file from being indexed by search engines
File remained accessible online for approximately 9.5 months without detection or restriction

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found the organization in breach of PDPA s.12 and s.24. No financial penalty was imposed due to: (1) voluntary notification to Commission; (2) full cooperation with investigation; (3) prompt remedial measures implemented; and (4) minimal actual access to the file with no evidence of misuse. Organization directed to: (a) develop and implement internal data protection policies and practices within 90 days; (b) inform Commission within 1 week of implementation. Organization has since disabled search engine indexing, password-protected member data files, implemented weekly file upload audits, established 3-month file retention limit, and engaged consultant for PDPA staff training.
companyNow: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer continues to operate. Following the enforcement action, the organization has implemented comprehensive data protection improvements including search engine indexing controls, access restrictions, file auditing procedures, and staff training.
dataType: Name, NRIC (national identification number), address, date of birth, marital status, email address, mobile phone number, residential phone number
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.12 (obligation to develop and implement data protection policies and practices)
PDPA s.24 (obligation to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Coop Finnmark SA is a Norwegian grocery retail chain that operates supermarkets in Finnmark region. The company employs store managers responsible for security, including surveillance system oversight.
companyLongDescription: Coop Finnmark SA is a Norwegian grocery retail chain that operates supermarkets in Finnmark region. The company employs store managers responsible for security, including surveillance system oversight.
caseDescription: A store manager at Coop Finnmark filmed surveillance camera footage of minors suspected of shoplifting using his personal mobile phone and shared it with a third party to identify them. The video was subsequently shared further until it reached the minors themselves. The company failed to establish a lawful legal basis for processing and disclosing personal data of children, violating fundamental GDPR principles.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of personal data (video footage) of identifiable minors to third parties without legal basis. The data controller lost control over the information after initial disclosure, and it reached the data subjects themselves.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A store manager filmed surveillance footage of children on their personal phone and shared it with a third party to identify theft suspects.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's personal data in video form was disseminated without legal consent or lawful basis, exposing minors to identification, potential public humiliation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The store manager sent a brief 3-second video clip and the company has internal rules prohibiting unauthorized disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite internal rules explicitly requiring written consent for disclosure, the store manager unilaterally shared the footage via personal phone, which was then distributed further to the identified minors themselves, demonstrating the rules were not effectively enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: The video did not show faces, so identification was limited to clothing, hair, and footwear.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of facial imagery does not make individuals non-identifiable; they remained clearly distinguishable and identifiable by their appearance, clothing, and other visible characteristics—sufficient for privacy harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company acted in good faith to identify shoplifters and took remedial steps by contacting parties and asking them to delete the footage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Once shared via mobile phone, the company lost control and could not prevent further distribution. The minors received the footage showing themselves accused of theft, causing reputational harm and psychological harm to children.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Coop Finnmark disclosed video footage of minors without a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1)
violations: Coop Finnmark disclosed video footage of minors without a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1)

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) permits processing based on legitimate interests only if the controller's interest weighs heavier than the data subject's privacy rights, with heightened protection for children.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's legitimate interest in identifying shoplifters did not outweigh children's fundamental right to privacy, especially given that the same outcome could be achieved by reporting to police
violations: The company's legitimate interest in identifying shoplifters did not outweigh children's fundamental right to privacy, especially given that the same outcome could be achieved by reporting to police

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner ensuring integrity and confidentiality through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Use of an uncontrolled personal mobile phone to film and share footage resulted in loss of control and unintended further dissemination to the data subjects themselves
violations: Use of an uncontrolled personal mobile phone to film and share footage resulted in loss of control and unintended further dissemination to the data subjects themselves

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian Data Protection Authority) issued a final enforcement decision on 22 December 2020 imposing an administrative fine of NOK 400,000 (approximately USD 42,000). The decision found Coop Finnmark violated GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a) and 6 by disclosing video footage of minors without lawful basis. The company is required to pay the fine within four weeks. The decision is enforceable and collection will be handled by the State Collection Agency (Statens innkrevingssentral). The company may appeal within 28 days.
companyNow: Coop Finnmark is a Norwegian grocery retailer operating as part of the Coop group. Following the 2020 enforcement action, the company implemented internal training on data protection rules and reviewed surveillance footage handling procedures.
dataType: Video footage of minors, biometric data (appearance, clothing, gait)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, transparency principle
GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of lawful basis for processing

companyDescription: Hello Travel Pte. Ltd. operated a travel website (www.havehalalwilltravel.com) that maintained user account databases from February 2015 onward.
companyLongDescription: Hello Travel Pte. Ltd. operated a travel website (www.havehalalwilltravel.com) that maintained user account databases from February 2015 onward.
caseDescription: Hello Travel's database containing 71,002 user accounts was posted publicly on an internet forum after a security breach in 2018. The breach resulted from installation of a vulnerable free WordPress plugin, which the company failed to monitor or patch. The organization had not implemented basic security measures, policies for system patching, or security assessments before making changes to its ICT systems.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement basic security measures (system patching, security assessments, testing protocols) resulted in unauthorized access and exfiltration of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Hello Travel failed to implement basic security measures, installed a vulnerable WordPress plugin without assessment.
whyTheyWereWrong: 71,002 users' personal data including names, emails, phone numbers, dates of birth, and nationalities were publicly exposed on internet forums.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's internal investigation suggested unknown parties exploited plugin vulnerabilities
claimsVsReality.reality: The company installed a free open-source WordPress plugin without conducting any security assessment, testing, or establishing patching protocols, making the breach preventable with basic security practices

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 imposes a Protection Obligation requiring organisations to protect personal data in their possession against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Hello Travel failed to implement basic procedural and technical security arrangements to protect personal data
violations: Hello Travel failed to implement basic procedural and technical security arrangements to protect personal data
Did not establish policies or protocols for regular system patching
Did not conduct security assessments or testing when making changes to ICT systems
Failed to secure a vulnerable free WordPress plugin, resulting in database exfiltration

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found Hello Travel in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The organization was directed to pay a financial penalty of $8,000 SGD in 10 monthly instalments of $800 each from January to October 2021. The reduced penalty reflected the organization's cooperation, voluntary admission of liability, prompt remedial actions (encryption of data, engagement to take down database, notification of affected individuals), financial hardship from COVID-19 pandemic, and absence of evidence of data misuse. No further directions were issued given the remedial actions undertaken.
companyNow: Unknown. The company's current operational status is not disclosed in the decision.
dataType: Name, email address, phone number, date of birth, nationality

companyDescription: Grabcar Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based company offering ride-hailing transport services, food delivery, and digital payment solutions through its Grab mobile application, including a carpooling service called GrabHitch.
companyLongDescription: Grabcar Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based company offering ride-hailing transport services, food delivery, and digital payment solutions through its Grab mobile application, including a carpooling service called GrabHitch.
caseDescription: Grabcar deployed a software update to fix an API vulnerability on 30 August 2019, but failed to account for an existing URL-based caching mechanism. This caused the app to serve the same cached profile data to all GrabHitch drivers for 10-second intervals, exposing 21,541 drivers' and passengers' personal data to unauthorised access. The company lacked robust change management processes and failed to conduct properly scoped testing before deployment.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data by making changes to an IT system without understanding interactions with existing systems or conducting proper pre-deployment testing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Grabcar deployed a security update to its mobile app that removed a userID variable from an API endpoint without testing how the change would interact with the app's URL-based caching mechanism.
whyTheyWereWrong: The caching system could not differentiate between drivers without the userID, exposing profile pictures, names, vehicle plate numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The update was deployed to fix a potential API vulnerability allowing GrabHitch drivers to manipulate a userID to access other drivers' data.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the update attempted to address the vulnerability by removing the userID variable, it failed to account for the URL-based caching mechanism, which then served identical cached data to all drivers simultaneously for 10-second intervals.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grabcar's internal investigation initially indicated only 5,651 GrabHitch drivers' data was exposed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Further investigation revealed the actual exposure affected 21,541 GrabHitch drivers' and passengers' personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Grabcar failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage changes to IT systems that process personal data, particularly regarding understanding how updates interact with existing features like caching mechanisms.
violations: Grabcar failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage changes to IT systems that process personal data, particularly regarding understanding how updates interact with existing features like caching mechanisms.

Grabcar did not conduct properly scoped testing before deployment, specifically failing to simulate multiple concurrent or consecutive user scenarios or test how the caching mechanism would operate with the update.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Grabcar in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for the fourth time. The company was directed to pay a financial penalty of S$10,000 within 30 days and to implement a data protection by design policy for its mobile applications within 120 days. The Deputy Commissioner noted this was a particularly grave error as it represented the second similar mistake by Grabcar with respect to different systems, and expressed significant concern given the company's daily processing of large volumes of personal data.
companyNow: Grab remains one of Southeast Asia's leading ride-hailing and super-app platforms. The company has faced multiple regulatory enforcement actions and has undertaken remediation measures including enhanced security procedures and governance reforms.
dataType: Profile pictures, passenger names, vehicle plate numbers, wallet balance/payment history, booking details (addresses, pickup/drop-off times), driver details (total rides, vehicle model/make)
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24 (obligation to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Tapplock, Inc. is a Canadian Internet of Things company that designed and sold Internet-connected, fingerprint-enabled smart padlocks to U.S. consumers through its website and crowdfunding platforms, with fulfillment via a U.S.-based third-party warehouse.
companyLongDescription: Tapplock, Inc. is a Canadian Internet of Things company that designed and sold Internet-connected, fingerprint-enabled smart padlocks to U.S. consumers through its website and crowdfunding platforms, with fulfillment via a U.S.-based third-party warehouse.
caseDescription: Tapplock sold Internet-connected fingerprint-enabled smart locks to U.S. consumers while falsely advertising them as secure and claiming to follow industry best practices for data protection. Security researchers discovered multiple critical vulnerabilities allowing unauthorized access to user accounts and physical locks, exposing personal information and putting property at risk. Tapplock had no security program in place and failed to implement basic protective measures.
violationSummary: The core violation stems from Tapplock's failure to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data and device functionality, resulting in foreseeable vulnerabilities that exposed consumer information and physical property to unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Tapplock advertised fingerprint smart locks as secure with anti-shim and anti-pry technologies, claiming to follow industry best practices protecting personal information including usernames,.
whyTheyWereWrong: Security researchers discovered the locks could be opened by unscrewing the back panel in seconds.

claimsVsReality.claim: Smart locks are 'Bold. Sturdy. Secure.' with 'unbreakable' design incorporating double-layered lock design and anti-shim/anti-pry technologies.
claimsVsReality.reality: Locks could be opened in seconds by unscrewing the back panel, defeating all claimed physical security features.

claimsVsReality.claim: We take 'reasonable precautions' and follow 'industry best practices' to protect personal information from loss, misuse, unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, or destruction.
claimsVsReality.reality: Tapplock had no security program prior to June 2018, no vulnerability testing, no written security policies, failed to encrypt Bluetooth communications, and had authentication mechanisms that could be bypassed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users can share access to their locks with unlimited people and subsequently revoke such access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users could not effectively revoke access; researchers could 'sniff' data packets and continue accessing locks even after revocation due to unencrypted authentication tokens.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Tapplock represented its smart locks were 'secure' and incorporated anti-shim, anti-pry, and double-layered design, when in reality researchers could unlock them by unscrewing the back panel in seconds.
violations: Tapplock represented its smart locks were 'secure' and incorporated anti-shim, anti-pry, and double-layered design, when in reality researchers could unlock them by unscrewing the back panel in seconds.

Tapplock claimed in its privacy policy to take 'reasonable precautions' and follow 'industry best practices' to protect personal information, when it had no security program, no vulnerability testing, no written security policies, and no employee training.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on May 18, 2020, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges two counts: (Count I) deceptive representation regarding security of the smart locks, and (Count II) deceptive representation regarding protection of personal information. The document establishes that Tapplock failed to identify foreseeable risks, employ adequate authentication controls, adopt written security standards, or provide employee training. This is the initial complaint; final resolution pending.
companyNow: Tapplock faced significant reputational damage following public disclosure of vulnerabilities by security researchers in June 2018. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: usernames, email addresses, profile photos, location history, precise geolocation of smart locks
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: AppFolio, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Goleta, California, that provides property management software and tenant screening services to thousands of client property management companies throughout the United States.
companyLongDescription: AppFolio, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Goleta, California, that provides property management software and tenant screening services to thousands of client property management companies throughout the United States.
caseDescription: AppFolio, a tenant background screening service, violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by reporting obsolete criminal records and eviction records over seven years old in tenant screening reports. The company also failed to implement reasonable accuracy procedures, resulting in reports containing mismatched identities, multiple individuals' records, and inaccurate disposition or offense information that likely caused housing denials.
violationSummary: AppFolio's failure to implement reasonable accuracy procedures for criminal records and eviction records, combined with over-reliance on unvetted third-party data without verification, created systematic insecurity in the consumer reporting process.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: AppFolio furnished tenant screening reports containing obsolete eviction and criminal records more than seven years old.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective tenants were denied housing based on inaccurate or outdated criminal and eviction records.

claimsVsReality.claim: AppFolio's contracts with CoreLogic acknowledged that due to the organization of criminal records, there may be instances where identifying information appears to match the applicant but does not pertain to them.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this acknowledgment, AppFolio failed to implement commercially reasonable verification procedures and continued to furnish inaccurate reports with mismatched identities to thousands of property managers.

claimsVsReality.claim: CoreLogic's service disclaimer stated the service was 'AS IS' without warranty of accuracy, timeliness, or completeness.
claimsVsReality.reality: As a Consumer Reporting Agency under the FCRA, AppFolio had independent obligations to ensure accuracy regardless of vendor disclaimers. These contractual disclaimers do not relieve a CRA of its statutory duty to follow reasonable accuracy procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 605(a) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681c(a), generally prohibits Consumer Reporting Agencies from making any Consumer Report that includes Eviction Records and non-conviction criminal records that are more than seven years old.
regulatoryFindings.description: Until at least June 2019, AppFolio reported Eviction Records and non-conviction criminal records that were more than seven years old in multiple instances.
violations: Until at least June 2019, AppFolio reported Eviction Records and non-conviction criminal records that were more than seven years old in multiple instances.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(b) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(b), requires that whenever a Consumer Reporting Agency prepares a Consumer Report it shall follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.
regulatoryFindings.description: Until at least April 2019, AppFolio failed to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of criminal record and Eviction Record information in Tenant Screening Reports.
violations: Until at least April 2019, AppFolio failed to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of criminal record and Eviction Record information in Tenant Screening Reports.
AppFolio implemented insufficient procedures to assess accuracy of information obtained from CoreLogic vendor before including it in reports.
AppFolio failed to assess whether identifiers in records reasonably matched applicants.
AppFolio failed to assess whether results contained information on multiple individuals.
AppFolio failed to assure accurate reflection of disposition, offense name, and offense type.
AppFolio failed to prevent multiple entries for the same criminal or eviction action.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 621(a)(1), 15 U.S.C. § 1681s(a)(1), provides that violations of FCRA also constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a).
regulatoryFindings.description: AppFolio's reporting of obsolete records and failure to ensure accuracy constitute unfair and deceptive practices affecting commerce.
violations: AppFolio's reporting of obsolete records and failure to ensure accuracy constitute unfair and deceptive practices affecting commerce.

outcome: This is a complaint filed on December 8, 2020, seeking monetary civil penalties (up to $4,063 per violation as of January 2020), a permanent injunction to prevent future FCRA violations, compliance orders, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleged knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice, with each instance of non-compliance treated as a separate violation. The case seeks damages for thousands of inaccurate Tenant Screening Reports furnished to property management companies.
companyNow: AppFolio is a publicly traded software company (NASDAQ: APPF) providing property management and tenant screening solutions. The company continues to operate in the property management technology space.
dataType: Criminal records, eviction records, rental payment history, credit information, personal identifying information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 605(a) – Exclusion of obsolete information
Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 607(b) – Reasonable procedures for accuracy
Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 621(a) – Enforcement authority
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: MDIS Corporation Pte Ltd is a not-for-profit professional institute offering lifelong learning and training courses. The organization engaged external vendors to develop and maintain its website including online course registration forms.
companyLongDescription: MDIS Corporation Pte Ltd is a not-for-profit professional institute offering lifelong learning and training courses. The organization engaged external vendors to develop and maintain its website including online course registration forms.
caseDescription: MDIS Corporation failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data of 304 course participants collected through an online registration form. A Microsoft Excel spreadsheet containing the data was inadvertently exposed and accessible via Google search, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive personal information including NRIC numbers and contact details.
violationSummary: Organization failed to take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorized access to personal data by not implementing adequate security measures, conducting security testing, or communicating data protection requirements to service providers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Failed to secure an online course registration form and administrative backend, allowing a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet containing 304 individuals' personal data to be indexed by Google.
whyTheyWereWrong: 304 course participants' NRIC numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, names, billing addresses, and employment details were publicly discoverable via Google search for approximately 6 months,.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization claimed it verbally communicated data protection requirements to the Vendor and Developer
claimsVsReality.reality: Vendor asserted there was no such communication; Organization could not produce any written corroboration and investigation found no evidence of such communication

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization believed password protection to the administrative panel was 'secure enough'
claimsVsReality.reality: Password protection was inadequate; the backend remained accessible to Google search crawlers and could be indexed and exposed publicly, compromising 304 individuals' personal data

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization stated it was not an IT services provider and therefore relied on Vendor to identify risks and implement security
claimsVsReality.reality: As data controller and website owner, Organization retained legal responsibility for data protection that cannot be delegated; failure to provide instructions or exercise oversight violated statutory obligations

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to communicate any data protection requirements to vendor or freelance developer in writing or verifiable form
violations: Failed to communicate any data protection requirements to vendor or freelance developer in writing or verifiable form
Failed to scope pre-launch security testing to identify risks, relying only on password protection without verification it operated as intended
Did not inform vendor of requirement to secure personal data collected through the Form
Did not exercise reasonable oversight of security arrangements despite owning the system and knowing personal data would be collected
Website allowed Google search engines to crawl and index spreadsheet containing disclosed data through unprotected administrative backend

outcome: MDIS Corporation directed to pay financial penalty of S$10,000 within 30 days. No further directions given as remediation measures were already implemented: CMS backend blocking, robot.txt file insertion to prevent search engine crawling, Google removal requests, and security patches deployed by new vendor as of 19 June 2019. New backend system for website to be deployed.
companyNow: MDIS Corporation is a not-for-profit professional institute for lifelong learning in Singapore. Current status unknown, but remediation actions were completed by June 2019.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, email address, mobile phone number, citizenship, company name, contact number, billing address, course information

companyDescription: The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) is the police force for Northern Ireland, with headquarters in Belfast. It provides law enforcement services across Northern Ireland and is accountable to the Northern Ireland Police Authority.
companyLongDescription: The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) is the police force for Northern Ireland, with headquarters in Belfast. It provides law enforcement services across Northern Ireland and is accountable to the Northern Ireland Police Authority.
caseDescription: PSNI's Extradition Unit unlawfully shared personal data including criminal records and biometric information with the US Department of Homeland Security from 2016 to October 2020, affecting 174 individuals. Staff bypassed formal data-sharing protocols and sent sensitive data via unencrypted email. The organization lacked adequate oversight, security measures, and documented lawful basis for the proactive sharing that disrupted travel arrangements and led to entry refusals.
violationSummary: PSNI failed to maintain confidentiality of sensitive personal data through unauthorized disclosure to a third country (US DHS) without proper safeguards, consent, or lawful basis. The systematic, unregulated sharing of criminal records and biometric data outside formal channels constitutes breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: PSNI's Extradition Unit staff proactively shared 174 individuals' criminal conviction data, biometric data.
whyTheyWereWrong: 174 data subjects' sensitive personal data including criminal records and biometrics were transferred to a foreign government without their consent or knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSNI had formal data-sharing arrangements and policies regulating Extradition Unit staff access to systems and data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff bypassed these formal processes and engaged in informal, proactive sharing of personal data outside documented protocols without clear understanding that practices violated policy.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSNI has appropriate security measures in place for handling sensitive personal data in law enforcement contexts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive criminal conviction and biometric data were routinely transmitted to the US via unencrypted email without password protection, exposing data to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data sharing with DHS serves documented law enforcement purposes with appropriate safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: The sharing was proactive and intended merely to alert DHS to possible future travel, not to prevent/detect crime; no documented lawful basis, safeguards, or Schedule 8 conditions supported the processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 34(3) DPA 2018: The controller is responsible for and must be able to demonstrate compliance with data protection legislation.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI lacked effective managerial oversight and governance structures to demonstrate accountability; a culture evolved where staff shared data outside established policies without clear evidence they understood those practices violated policy.
violations: PSNI lacked effective managerial oversight and governance structures to demonstrate accountability; a culture evolved where staff shared data outside established policies without clear evidence they understood those practices violated policy.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 35(1) DPA 2018: Processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes must be lawful and fair.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI engaged in proactive, informal sharing of criminal conviction data outside formal arrangements; no documented lawful reason or formal request justified the sharing; data subjects could not reasonably expect their data to be used to disrupt travel arrangements.
violations: PSNI engaged in proactive, informal sharing of criminal conviction data outside formal arrangements; no documented lawful reason or formal request justified the sharing; data subjects could not reasonably expect their data to be used to disrupt travel arrangements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40 DPA 2018: Personal data for law enforcement must be processed with appropriate security using technical/organizational measures protecting against unauthorized processing and accidental loss/destruction/damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI routinely transmitted sensitive personal data to the US via unencrypted email without password protection, despite having policies/guidance on secure handling; data was processed without appropriate security safeguards.
violations: PSNI routinely transmitted sensitive personal data to the US via unencrypted email without password protection, despite having policies/guidance on secure handling; data was processed without appropriate security safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 42(1) DPA 2018: When processing sensitive personal data, a controller must have an appropriate policy document and either consent or satisfy a Schedule 8 condition.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI shared biometric data (sensitive processing) without data subject consent or awareness; lacked appropriate policy documents; processing was for disrupting travel (not law enforcement crime prevention); failed to satisfy Schedule 8 conditions.
violations: PSNI shared biometric data (sensitive processing) without data subject consent or awareness; lacked appropriate policy documents; processing was for disrupting travel (not law enforcement crime prevention); failed to satisfy Schedule 8 conditions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 73(1) DPA 2018: A controller may not transfer personal data to a third country unless specified conditions and safeguards are met.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI lacked appropriate safeguards and did not establish a lawful basis prior to proactive sharing with US DHS; transfer was not necessary for law enforcement purposes and was not for specified special circumstances.
violations: PSNI lacked appropriate safeguards and did not establish a lawful basis prior to proactive sharing with US DHS; transfer was not necessary for law enforcement purposes and was not for specified special circumstances.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to PSNI. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps already taken by PSNI, including stricter controls requiring future data sharing within formal arrangements, revised guidance/policies, and standard operating procedures for data transfers. PSNI was recommended to: (1) establish clear lawful basis documented prior to sharing via formal arrangements only; (2) review access controls and increase managerial oversight through regular audits; (3) implement higher security levels and management checks; (4) ensure consent or Schedule 8 conditions for sensitive processing with appropriate policy documents; (5) identify lawful bases for third-country transfers within appropriate data protection frameworks. PSNI informed the ICO it had already taken steps to address all recommendations.
companyNow: The Police Service of Northern Ireland remains the primary law enforcement agency for Northern Ireland. Following this enforcement action, PSNI implemented stricter data governance controls and continues to operate under enhanced data protection oversight.
dataType: Criminal conviction data, biometric data, basic personal identifiers (name, contact details), travel authorization data (ESTA/VISA), missing persons information

companyDescription: EmpiriStat, Inc. is a Delaware corporation located in Mount Airy, Maryland that provides statistical analysis and clinical trial support services.
companyLongDescription: EmpiriStat, Inc. is a Delaware corporation located in Mount Airy, Maryland that provides statistical analysis and clinical trial support services.
caseDescription: EmpiriStat falsely claimed to be a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework after its certification lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed. The company failed to obtain required annual verification statements and did not affirm its commitment to continue protecting personal data received during its participation. These misrepresentations violated FTC Act Section 5.
violationSummary: Company made false public statements about Privacy Shield participation and compliance, misleading individuals and regulators about the protection of their personal data transferred internationally.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: EmpiriStat claimed on its website that it currently participated in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework even though its certification lapsed in 2018 and was never renewed.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU individuals and organizations transferred personal data to EmpiriStat believing it met Privacy Shield adequacy standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: EmpiriStat has certified to the Department of Commerce and complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework.
claimsVsReality.reality: Certification was obtained in February 2017 but lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed. Company continued making Privacy Shield claims after certification lapsed.

claimsVsReality.claim: EmpiriStat's practices comply with the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: EmpiriStat failed to obtain required annual verification statements for 2017-18 period and failed to provide them to FTC as mandated by Supplemental Principle 7.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data received from EU is protected under Privacy Shield framework standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: After allowing certification to lapse, EmpiriStat did not affirm to Commerce its commitment to continue protecting personal data previously received, as required by Privacy Shield framework.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: EmpiriStat represented it was a current Privacy Shield participant when certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed.
violations: EmpiriStat represented it was a current Privacy Shield participant when certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed.
EmpiriStat claimed compliance with Privacy Shield Principles without obtaining required annual verification statements during 2017-18 certification period.
EmpiriStat did not affirm to Commerce its commitment to continue protecting personal data received during Privacy Shield participation after allowing certification to lapse.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7 requires annual verification through self-assessment or outside compliance review that Privacy Shield assertions are true and practices implemented.
regulatoryFindings.description: EmpiriStat failed to obtain attested verification statement for 2017-18 certification period.
violations: EmpiriStat failed to obtain attested verification statement for 2017-18 certification period.
EmpiriStat failed to provide verification statement to FTC as required.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield framework requires companies withdrawing from program to affirm to Commerce they will continue applying principles to personal data received during participation.
regulatoryFindings.description: EmpiriStat did not affirm continuing obligations after allowing certification to lapse in 2018.
violations: EmpiriStat did not affirm continuing obligations after allowing certification to lapse in 2018.
EmpiriStat did not take down Privacy Shield claims despite Commerce warning.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on January 13, 2020, alleging three counts of deceptive practices under Section 5 of the FTC Act. Case resolved through enforcement action; document indicates complaint issued but does not specify settlement terms or final order details beyond the charges.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU to US under Privacy Shield framework
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive Acts or Practices
Privacy Shield Principles – Supplemental Principle 7 (Verification requirement)
Privacy Shield Framework – Continuing Obligations (post-withdrawal affirmation requirement)

company: Aman Group S.a.r.l and/or Amanresort International Pte Ltd
companyDescription: Aman Group operates luxury resort properties globally, with the breach affecting both UK-based and Singapore-based systems. Amanresort International Pte Ltd operates as a regional office in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Aman Group operates luxury resort properties globally, with the breach affecting both UK-based and Singapore-based systems. Amanresort International Pte Ltd operates as a regional office in Singapore.
caseDescription: Aman Group suffered a cybersecurity breach on 5 December 2020 affecting approximately 2,500 individuals. Threat actors gained unauthorised access to 11 systems (9 in London, 2 in Singapore) and exfiltrated personal data. The Deputy Commissioner found Aman Group met its Protection obligation under PDPA s.24 and took no enforcement action due to encryption of exfiltrated data and prompt remedial measures.
violationSummary: The breach involved unauthorised access to personal data systems and exfiltration of encrypted personal information, constituting a breach of confidentiality despite mitigating encryption measures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Aman Group's systems were compromised by threat actors who gained unauthorised access to 11 systems across London.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2,500 individuals had their names, dates of birth, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers and professions exposed through inadequate system security that allowed unauthorised access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Threat actors could access and recreate exfiltrated data in plaintext
claimsVsReality.reality: Aman Group's assessment found encryption and proprietary format made it unlikely threat actors could access and recreate data in plaintext; extracts obtained did not resemble current database
