regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks, and the loss of storage media.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aman Group's systems were compromised allowing unauthorised access and exfiltration of personal data, however the Deputy Commissioner found the organisation had met its protection obligation through reasonable security measures and that encrypted exfiltrated data was unlikely to be compromised
violations: Aman Group's systems were compromised allowing unauthorised access and exfiltration of personal data, however the Deputy Commissioner found the organisation had met its protection obligation through reasonable security measures and that encrypted exfiltrated data was unlikely to be compromised

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that Aman Group had met its Protection obligation under PDPA s.24 and that no enforcement action needed to be taken. The decision noted that: (1) exfiltrated data was encrypted in proprietary format making decryption unlikely; (2) analysis of threat actor extracts showed no conclusive links to current databases; (3) Aman Group took prompt and extensive remedial actions to mitigate effects and enhance security; and (4) Aman SG could not be held accountable as it did not hold the data protection role and was not in possession or control of the affected personal data.
dataType: Name, date of birth, address, email address, phone number, profession

companyDescription: Giordano Originals (S) Pte Ltd is a fashion and apparel retail company operating in Singapore with a membership base of approximately 790,000 members and significant employee workforce.
companyLongDescription: Giordano Originals (S) Pte Ltd is a fashion and apparel retail company operating in Singapore with a membership base of approximately 790,000 members and significant employee workforce.
caseDescription: Giordano Originals suffered a ransomware attack and unauthorized network entry on 12 July 2020 affecting 790,000 members and 184 employees. Personal data was encrypted but not exfiltrated. The Commission found the organization had implemented reasonable security measures consistent with regulatory guidance, including encryption, regular backups, endpoint security, monitoring, and phishing prevention.
violationSummary: While the organization experienced a security incident (ransomware and unauthorized entry), the Commission determined that the organization had implemented reasonable security measures consistent with PDPA requirements and regulatory guidance, including encryption, backups, endpoint security, and monitoring. This case illustrates when a security incident does NOT constitute a violation if protective measures are demonstrably reasonable and industry-standard.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Giordano Originals experienced unauthorized network entry and ransomware infection on July 12, 2020, affecting systems storing personal data of 790,000 members.
whyTheyWereWrong: The incident exposed members' names, contact numbers, and partial dates of birth, plus employees' NRICs, addresses, salaries.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization's investigation found no sign of suspicious activity beyond the Singapore network.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unauthorized network entry and ransomware infection occurred; however, the breach was limited to Singapore systems with no impact on other networks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was protected through encryption.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal data was encrypted using industry-standard RSA algorithm and passphrase, making it non-legible without decryption; no evidence of decryption or exfiltration was discovered.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data against unauthorised or accidental access, processing, alteration, loss, destruction or disclosure, by implementing reasonable security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Giordano Originals was investigated for potential breach of section 24 following the ransomware incident and unauthorized network entry. However, the Commission found that the organization had implemented reasonable security measures consistent with PDPA requirements and Commission guidance, including endpoint security solutions, real-time system monitoring, regular vulnerability scanning and patching, encryption using industry-standard RSA algorithm, and automated regular backups. The Commission concluded the organization had met its Protection Obligation and found no breach.
violations: Giordano Originals was investigated for potential breach of section 24 following the ransomware incident and unauthorized network entry. However, the Commission found that the organization had implemented reasonable security measures consistent with PDPA requirements and Commission guidance, including endpoint security solutions, real-time system monitoring, regular vulnerability scanning and patching, encryption using industry-standard RSA algorithm, and automated regular backups. The Commission concluded the organization had met its Protection Obligation and found no breach.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that Giordano Originals had met its Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. No directions or enforcement action were issued against the organisation. The Commission endorsed the organization's implementation of industry-standard encryption and adherence to Commission recommendations. Post-incident, the organization enhanced security measures including increased phishing simulation training, security reviews, and additional monitoring. Personal data was fully restored from backups with no evidence of exfiltration or decryption.
companyNow: Giordano Originals continues to operate as a fashion retail company. Following the 2020 incident, the organization implemented enhanced security measures and has complied with data protection obligations.
dataType: Names, contact numbers, dates of birth, NRIC (national identification), addresses, gender, age, email addresses, educational information, salary information
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation) — assessed and found compliant

companyDescription: Worksmartly Pte. Ltd. was a finance and payroll processing service provider engaged by Roche Singapore in 2017. The company's contract ended on 31 December 2018.
companyLongDescription: Worksmartly Pte. Ltd. was a finance and payroll processing service provider engaged by Roche Singapore in 2017. The company's contract ended on 31 December 2018.
caseDescription: Worksmartly, a finance and payroll processor for Roche, failed to delete sensitive employee and dependent data from a GitHub repository after the contract ended in December 2018. An employee mistakenly changed the repository from private to public in February 2020, exposing personal data of 308 individuals for five days. The organisation lacked security controls and file housekeeping procedures.
violationSummary: The personal data of 308 individuals was publicly exposed on GitHub due to inadequate security settings and file retention practices, directly matching the Exposure category under Information Dissemination.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Worksmartly failed to delete a file containing 308 individuals' personal data after its contract ended.
whyTheyWereWrong: 308 Roche employees and their dependents had highly sensitive data exposed for five days including names, identity numbers, salaries, bank account details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee believed changing the GitHub account setting to public would only make the file accessible to other members of the Organisation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Changing the setting to public made the file accessible to the entire internet, resulting in 23 accesses and 11 downloads in five days.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had conducted file deletion procedures before the contract ended on 31 December 2018.
claimsVsReality.reality: The sensitive data file was inadvertently retained because it was stored in a different folder and not included in the housekeeping process.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 (Protection Obligation) requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession against unauthorised access, collection, use, or disclosure through reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation lacked checks to manage correct security settings on GitHub and relied solely on employees without proper controls or oversight.
violations: Organisation lacked checks to manage correct security settings on GitHub and relied solely on employees without proper controls or oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 (Retention Obligation) requires organisations to not retain personal data longer than necessary for business or legal purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation retained personal data file from 2017 data migration despite contract ending Dec 2018. File should have been deleted but was stored in a different folder and inadvertently omitted during housekeeping.
violations: Organisation retained personal data file from 2017 data migration despite contract ending Dec 2018. File should have been deleted but was stored in a different folder and inadvertently omitted during housekeeping.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Worksmartly in breach of PDPA sections 24 and 25. The organisation was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD $5,000 within 30 days. No further directions were issued due to the organisation's prompt remedial actions: immediately setting GitHub to private and deleting the file, resetting database/server passwords, conducting file housekeeping, and implementing a disciplinary framework for GitHub account management.
companyNow: Unknown. No current information available on the operational status of Worksmartly Pte. Ltd. following this enforcement action.
dataType: Employment data, financial data (salary, bank account details), identity data (NRIC/FIN/Passport), contact information, dependent information

companyDescription: A bar operator in Budapest VII district operating an establishment with security cameras. The operator manages camera surveillance and handles personal data of patrons and others captured on video.
companyLongDescription: A bar operator in Budapest VII district operating an establishment with security cameras. The operator manages camera surveillance and handles personal data of patrons and others captured on video.
caseDescription: A bar operator failed to properly inform a data subject about their right to restrict data processing after the subject requested camera footage be locked for a police investigation. The operator deleted the locked footage after 30 days without notifying the subject, and subsequently ignored multiple requests for access to the footage and information about its deletion.
violationSummary: The operator failed to provide adequate transparency about data restriction and deletion, and failed to respond to data subject requests, undermining the security and proper handling of personal data (video footage).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The bar operator locked camera footage per a patron's request but failed to notify them of the lock, then deleted the locked footage after 30 days without advance notice or explanation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The patron lost permanent access to critical evidence of their assault by security guards because the operator destroyed their restricted data without warning.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed camera footage was locked upon request and would be managed according to law.
claimsVsReality.reality: The operator locked footage but never informed the subject, then deleted it after 30 days without notice, violating the subject's right to restrict processing.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator stated only official police requests could result in footage release.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under GDPR Article 15(3), data subjects have a right to copies of their own personal data; the operator's policy was overly restrictive and not aligned with GDPR.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed earlier legislation (Szvtv.) permitted deletion after 30 days of no authority request.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR, applicable from May 25, 2018, permits restriction of processing for legal proceedings duration; old Hungarian law did not override GDPR subject rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) requires that the controller be responsible for and able to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles (Accountability Principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator failed to maintain dated records of data processing policies and could not prove that camera monitoring complied with GDPR requirements during the relevant period.
violations: The operator failed to maintain dated records of data processing policies and could not prove that camera monitoring complied with GDPR requirements during the relevant period.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(1)-(4) requires controllers to provide clear, transparent communication about data processing in response to data subject requests within one month.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator did not respond to four separate requests from the subject between November 2018 and April 2019, providing information only on April 23, 2019—months after some requests.
violations: The operator did not respond to four separate requests from the subject between November 2018 and April 2019, providing information only on April 23, 2019—months after some requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to access personal data held by controllers.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator failed to fulfill the subject's March 1, 2019 access request and provided no explanation for the omission until April 23, 2019.
violations: The operator failed to fulfill the subject's March 1, 2019 access request and provided no explanation for the omission until April 23, 2019.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 18(1)(c) permits subjects to restrict processing when the controller no longer needs the data but the subject requires it for legal proceedings.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator deleted the locked footage after 30 days despite the subject's ongoing need for it in a criminal investigation, violating the restriction right.
violations: The operator deleted the locked footage after 30 days despite the subject's ongoing need for it in a criminal investigation, violating the restriction right.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 18(3) requires controllers to inform subjects before lifting a processing restriction.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator deleted the restricted footage without prior notice to the subject, preventing them from being aware of the action.
violations: The operator deleted the restricted footage without prior notice to the subject, preventing them from being aware of the action.

outcome: The NAIH (Hungarian National Data Protection Authority) partially upheld the complainant's request. The authority established that the operator failed to provide adequate information about the restriction of processing, the lifting of that restriction, and deletion of footage. The operator was ordered to fulfill the subject's outstanding access request within 30 days and provide written proof. A data protection fine of 2,000,000 Hungarian Forint was imposed by the authority ex officio. The operator was found to have violated the accountability principle regarding the general camera surveillance practice. Appeal is possible to the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
dataType: Video surveillance footage, personal data of individuals captured on camera
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 18 – Right to restrict processing
GDPR Art. 18(3) – Obligation to inform about lifting of restriction

companyDescription: Retina-X Studios, LLC, a Florida-based software company, developed and sold mobile device monitoring applications marketed ostensibly for parental control and employee monitoring. The company operated from 2007 to 2018 and sold over 15,000 licenses across three main products before discontinuing sales.
companyLongDescription: Retina-X Studios, LLC, a Florida-based software company, developed and sold mobile device monitoring applications marketed ostensibly for parental control and employee monitoring. The company operated from 2007 to 2018 and sold over 15,000 licenses across three main products before discontinuing sales.
caseDescription: Retina-X Studios sold mobile device monitoring software (MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, TeenShield) marketed for child/employee monitoring but enabled surreptitious surveillance of unsuspecting victims without their knowledge or consent. The company failed to implement reasonable security measures, resulting in at least two data breaches that exposed sensitive personal information including messages, locations, and photos. The software was heavily marketed as a tool for stalking and abuse, and the company collected personal data from children under 13 without proper safeguards.
violationSummary: The primary harm stems from enabling large-scale surreptitious surveillance of unwitting individuals. Secondary violations include data insecurity and breach of confidentiality. The surveillance capability is foundational to all other harms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Retina-X Studios sold mobile monitoring software (MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, TeenShield) allowing purchasers to secretly track another person's texts, locations, photos.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 15,000 licenses enabled stalkers and domestic abusers to obtain victims' intimate communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Monitoring products are designed for legitimate purposes such as monitoring children and employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: The products were heavily marketed and used by domestic abusers and stalkers to surreptitiously track victims without knowledge or consent. The requirement to jailbreak/root devices to install the software is atypical of legitimate parental control tools, which have non-invasive alternatives.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer databases remain confidential and private. 'Your private information is safe with us.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Unencrypted credentials were stored in the application code, allowing hackers to access databases in both February 2017 and February 2018. Respondents were unaware of the first breach for two months until a journalist contacted them. Collected data including login credentials, text messages, GPS locations, contact lists, browser history, photos, and children's personal information was exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Products are installed with physical access but operate transparently with visible monitoring icons.
claimsVsReality.reality: Respondents provided customers with explicit instructions on how to hide the monitoring icon, enabling surreptitious monitoring of device users who had no knowledge they were being tracked and no way to remove the software.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents sold surveillance software without reasonable safeguards against misuse by abusers and stalkers, causing substantial, unavoidable consumer injury.
violations: Respondents sold surveillance software without reasonable safeguards against misuse by abusers and stalkers, causing substantial, unavoidable consumer injury.
Respondents falsely represented that customer data was 'confidential, private, and safe' while maintaining inadequate security controls that permitted unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.8 requires operators with actual knowledge of collecting children's personal information to establish and maintain reasonable procedures to protect the confidentiality, security, and integrity of that information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents collected approximately 950 dates of birth through TeenShield, approximately one-third identifying children under 13, with actual knowledge that children were being monitored. Respondents failed to implement security standards, policies, or procedures and did not adequately oversee third-party service providers handling children's data.
violations: Respondents collected approximately 950 dates of birth through TeenShield, approximately one-third identifying children under 13, with actual knowledge that children were being monitored. Respondents failed to implement security standards, policies, or procedures and did not adequately oversee third-party service providers handling children's data.

outcome: FTC filed a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5(a) and violations of COPPA Rule. The complaint identifies five counts: (I) Unfairness for selling surveillance tools without safeguards; (II–IV) Deception regarding data security and privacy for MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, and TeenShield; and (V) COPPA violation for failing to protect children's personal information. MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, and TeenShield have not been available for purchase since April 2018, though product websites remain online. The case was filed March 26, 2020. Final consent order or settlement terms would be determined in subsequent proceedings.
companyNow: Retina-X Studios' monitoring products (MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, TeenShield) have been unavailable for purchase since April 2018. The company's websites remain online. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Text messages, email, GPS location, photos, browser history, contact lists, call history, keystroke logs, financial account information, children's personal information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.8 – Failure to establish and maintain reasonable procedures to protect confidentiality, security, and integrity of children's personal information

companyDescription: Google Ireland Ltd is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. and serves as the European contracting entity for Google advertising and digital services, including Google AdWords (now Google Ads), the primary global advertising platform for search, display, and video advertising.
companyLongDescription: Google Ireland Ltd is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. and serves as the European contracting entity for Google advertising and digital services, including Google AdWords (now Google Ads), the primary global advertising platform for search, display, and video advertising.
caseDescription: Google Ireland Ltd failed to respond within the statutory one-month deadline to a data subject's access request under GDPR Article 15 regarding how their name was processed in Google AdWords. The company did not provide substantive information about the lawful basis for processing, algorithmic decision-making, or how the data was used for ad targeting, violating the controller's obligation to respond to access requests promptly and completely.
violationSummary: Google excluded the data subject from access to information about their personal data processing by failing to provide required transparency and access disclosures within statutory deadlines, effectively denying the controller's information obligations.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Google Ireland Ltd failed to respond substantively within one month to a data subject's request for information about how their name was processed in Google AdWords.
whyTheyWereWrong: The data subject was left in the dark for months about whether their name was being used as an advertising keyword, which ads appeared when searching their name.

claimsVsReality.claim: Google's internal processes would route access requests submitted through the correct AdWords contact channels to the appropriate team
claimsVsReality.reality: An access request submitted through the AdWords web form was misdirected and not forwarded to the competent department for over three months, despite multiple follow-ups

claimsVsReality.claim: Google does not use the data subject's name as an advertising keyword or target for automated decision-making in AdWords
claimsVsReality.reality: Google's actual practices regarding how personal names are processed, profiled, and used algorithmically in ad targeting decisions were not transparently disclosed until compelled by the regulator

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken on a request without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt of the request, extendable by two months in complex cases with notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google failed to respond within the one-month deadline to the data subject's access request submitted in 2018
violations: Google failed to respond within the one-month deadline to the data subject's access request submitted in 2018
No extension notice was issued indicating the need for additional time
Response was not provided until after the extended three-month period had passed

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing, access to personal data, and detailed information including processing purposes, data categories, recipients, storage duration, and information about automated decision-making.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google did not provide substantive information about how the data subject's name was processed in AdWords
violations: Google did not provide substantive information about how the data subject's name was processed in AdWords
No explanation of algorithmic logic or search-triggered ad targeting mechanisms was disclosed
Information regarding profiling and automated decision-making related to the data subject was not provided

outcome: The Hungarian Data Protection Authority (NAIH) found that Google Ireland Ltd violated GDPR Articles 12(3) and 15(1) by failing to respond timely and substantively to the data subject's access request regarding name processing in Google AdWords. The authority terminated the own-initiative investigation into general AdWords practices due to lack of systemic evidence. The authority did not impose an administrative fine, finding the violation did not warrant further enforcement beyond the finding of non-compliance. Google did subsequently provide the requested information. The authority compensated the requester 10,000 HUF for exceeding the processing deadline and ordered Google to bear 6,100 HUF in procedural costs for document access. The decision is subject to judicial review at the Budapest Metropolitan Court.
companyNow: Google Ireland Ltd remains the primary EMEA contracting entity for Google services including Google Ads. The company continues to be subject to GDPR enforcement by EU data protection authorities.
dataType: Name, search history, behavioral data, advertising profile

companyDescription: Thru, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Irving, Texas that provides cloud-based file transfer software for enterprises.
companyLongDescription: Thru, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Irving, Texas that provides cloud-based file transfer software for enterprises.
caseDescription: Thru, Inc. falsely claimed on its website that it was certified to participate in the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, while never actually completing certification. The company initiated a Privacy Shield application in June 2017 but failed to finalize the process, yet continued making false compliance statements in its privacy policy.
violationSummary: The company made deceptive public disclosures about Privacy Shield participation that misrepresented the legal status and protection level of personal data transfers, violating FTC deception authority.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Thru, Inc. falsely claimed on its website that it complied with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, despite never completing certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
whyTheyWereWrong: European and Swiss users who transferred personal data to Thru believed their information was legally protected under Privacy Shield adequacy standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Thru Inc. complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
claimsVsReality.reality: Thru never completed Privacy Shield certification steps with the U.S. Department of Commerce, despite initiating an application in June 2017.

claimsVsReality.claim: Thru is a participant in both EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Thru was never certified to participate in either framework and did not appear on the Department of Commerce's public list of certified companies.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Thru represented directly and by implication that it was a certified participant in both EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks on its privacy policy website.
violations: Thru represented directly and by implication that it was a certified participant in both EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks on its privacy policy website.
Thru had not been certified to participate in either framework despite initiating an application in June 2017 and not completing the certification steps.
Thru continued to disseminate false Privacy Shield compliance statements in its privacy policy despite the absence of certification.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Thru, Inc. on January 13, 2020, for deceptive practices. The complaint alleges violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act based on false Privacy Shield certification claims. The document represents the initial complaint; final settlement or consent order terms are not provided in this document.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU and Switzerland (unspecified types)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Creative Technology Ltd is a technology company that developed and sold audio equipment, sound cards, and peripherals. The company operated an online support forum starting in 2004 to help users discuss its products.
companyLongDescription: Creative Technology Ltd is a technology company that developed and sold audio equipment, sound cards, and peripherals. The company operated an online support forum starting in 2004 to help users discuss its products.
caseDescription: Creative Technology Ltd operated an online support forum that was hacked in May 2018 via SQL injection attacks exploiting an unpatched vulnerability in vBulletin software. The company failed to install security patches released in 2016, and used outdated MD5 password hashing. Account data for 484,512 users was exfiltrated; the company then deleted the database within 2 weeks, obstructing the Commission's investigation.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically by not patching known vulnerabilities and using insecure password hashing algorithms, directly enabling the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Creative Technology Ltd operated an online forum using vBulletin software with a known SQL vulnerability for three years without installing available security patches.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unpatched vulnerability allowed hackers to extract personal data from 484,512 user accounts in May 2018, exposing usernames, hashed passwords, email addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company deleted the database to comply with section 25 of the PDPA, which requires cessation of data retention once collection purpose is met.
claimsVsReality.reality: Section 25 of the PDPA allows retention of personal data for legal purposes including Commission investigations. The company should have anticipated a Commission investigation given the scale of the breach (484,512 accounts) and external notification from a security researcher.

claimsVsReality.claim: The personal data disclosed had low sensitivity and was unlikely to cause serious or substantial harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosed data included usernames, hashed passwords, email addresses, IP addresses, and optional personal data (age, date of birth, contact details, location, occupation). MD5-hashed passwords are vulnerable to cracking, putting users at risk if they reused credentials elsewhere, and ~2,600 users had names in their email addresses enabling direct identification.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to patch or update vBulletin software for 3 years despite patches being available since 2016, leaving a known SQL vulnerability unaddressed
violations: Organisation failed to patch or update vBulletin software for 3 years despite patches being available since 2016, leaving a known SQL vulnerability unaddressed
Organisation used MD5 algorithm for password hashing, which is no longer sufficiently secure and susceptible to attack, whereas vBulletin developers themselves had switched to bcrypt in March 2014
These failures collectively prevented reasonable security arrangements from being in place

outcome: The Commissioner found Creative Technology Ltd in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The company was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $15,000 within 30 days, with interest accruing on any outstanding amount at the Rules of Court rate. No other directions were imposed as the company had already ceased operating the forum and deleted the user database. The Commission noted the company's cooperation and remedial actions (notifying affected users, shutting down the forum) as mitigating factors, but treated the hasty deletion of the database as an aggravating factor that prejudiced the investigation.
companyNow: Creative Technology Ltd ceased operating the online support forum. The company is known primarily for audio and sound card products and continues to operate in the technology sector.
dataType: username, hashed password, email address, IP address, age, date of birth, contact details, location, occupation

companyDescription: Majestic Debt Recovery Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based debt collection company engaged by creditors to recover debts on their behalf. Prior to the incident, the company had minimal data protection infrastructure or compliance awareness.
companyLongDescription: Majestic Debt Recovery Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based debt collection company engaged by creditors to recover debts on their behalf. Prior to the incident, the company had minimal data protection infrastructure or compliance awareness.
caseDescription: A debt collection company recorded video footage of exchanges between its representatives and debtor company staff during debt recovery visits, then posted the recordings on its public Facebook page without consent to shame the debtor. The company had no data protection policies, no DPO, and no knowledge of the PDPA. Despite the complainant's explicit objection, the company posted the video anyway.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data (video recordings containing images and audio) of identifiable individuals to the public without consent or lawful basis, causing direct harm through unauthorized exposure and public shaming.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Majestic Debt Recovery recorded video of company staff and a managing director during debt collection visits.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individuals' identifiable images and voices were publicly exposed to shame debtors, causing reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed prior consent from the Company on previous occasions and had 'video proof' of the Complainant consenting to posting videos on Facebook.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation was unable to provide any evidence of prior consent or the 'video proof' referenced. Even if consent existed previously, the Complainant expressly objected at the material time, thereby withdrawing any prior consent under PDPA s.16(1).

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation asserted it would obtain written consent in future before recording and uploading personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Deputy Commissioner found this unconceivable for debtors and noted consent obtained ex ante for shaming purposes would likely be vitiated as obtained through unfair/deceptive practices violating PDPA s.14(2) and s.14(3).

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.13 prohibits organisations from collecting, using or disclosing personal data about an individual unless the individual's consent is obtained (either actual or deemed) or such collection, use or disclosure is required or authorised under the PDPA or any written law.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation recorded and posted video footage containing identifiable images and audio of individuals without consent
violations: Organisation recorded and posted video footage containing identifiable images and audio of individuals without consent
Complainant expressly objected to recording and posting, making consent unavailable
Even if prior consent existed, it was withdrawn by express objection under PDPA s.16(1)
Consent to post on social media for shaming purposes would violate PDPA s.14(2) and s.14(3) as obtained through unfair/deceptive practices

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.11(3) requires organisations to designate one or more individuals responsible for ensuring the organisation's compliance with the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation had not designated a data protection officer prior to the incident
violations: Organisation had not designated a data protection officer prior to the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.12 requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary for the organisation to meet its obligations under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation admitted it had no knowledge of PDPA, no data protection policies or practices prior to the incident
violations: Organisation admitted it had no knowledge of PDPA, no data protection policies or practices prior to the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s.18 requires that use of personal data be appropriate having regard to the reasonable expectations of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: Posting video to shame debtors is not a use any reasonable person would consider appropriate
violations: Posting video to shame debtors is not a use any reasonable person would consider appropriate

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found breaches of PDPA ss.13, 11(3), and 12. Organisation was directed to: (1) pay financial penalty of SGD 7,500 within 30 days; (2) develop and implement data protection policies and practices; (3) establish compulsory PDPA compliance training program for employees. Organisation took remedial action before decision: removed all videos from Facebook, designated a DPO, and committed to obtaining written consent before recording.
companyNow: Unknown. The organisation was cooperative and took prompt remedial action including appointing a DPO and implementing data protection policies following the Commission's notification.
dataType: Biometric data (images and audio recordings), personal identifiers

companyDescription: CALLESGARCIA S.C. is a photography/event services business (likely a wedding photography enterprise) that operated in Spain. The company was engaged to provide wedding reportage photography services.
companyLongDescription: CALLESGARCIA S.C. is a photography/event services business (likely a wedding photography enterprise) that operated in Spain. The company was engaged to provide wedding reportage photography services.
caseDescription: A wedding photography business used a photograph from a client's wedding reportage for commercial advertising without the client's consent. The Spanish Data Protection Authority found this violated GDPR Article 6 by processing personal data (the client's image) without a lawful basis. The company was fined €4,000 and ordered to notify the complainant and comply with privacy regulations.
violationSummary: The company collected personal data (photograph) for a specific purpose (wedding photography) but reused it for a materially different secondary purpose (commercial advertising) without consent, which is a classic secondary use violation.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: CALLESGARCIA S.C. used wedding photographs featuring the complainant's image for commercial advertising and business promotion without obtaining the complainant's consent or authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's facial image was publicly displayed in advertising materials without permission, exposing their likeness to commercial use.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company implied it had the right to use wedding photographs for its own commercial advertising and business promotion.
claimsVsReality.reality: Without explicit consent from the individuals pictured, the company had no lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 to process and reuse the photographs for secondary commercial purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if at least one of the specified conditions applies, including explicit consent of the data subject for specific purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: CALLESGARCIA S.C. processed the complainant's facial image (personal data) for commercial advertising without obtaining prior consent, thereby failing to satisfy any lawful basis under Article 6.
violations: CALLESGARCIA S.C. processed the complainant's facial image (personal data) for commercial advertising without obtaining prior consent, thereby failing to satisfy any lawful basis under Article 6.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72.1(c) classifies as very serious the processing of personal data without any of the lawfulness conditions in GDPR Article 6.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's use of the wedding photograph for business promotion lacked any lawful basis and constituted a serious violation of the framework.
violations: The company's use of the wedding photograph for business promotion lacked any lawful basis and constituted a serious violation of the framework.

outcome: The Director of the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of €4,000 on CALLESGARCIA S.C. (NIF J10460640) and ordered notification to the complainant. The company was instructed to adapt its privacy practices to GDPR Article 13 and cease unlawful processing. The fine is enforceable via bank transfer to the AEPD's account. The respondent may file a repositioning appeal within one month or seek judicial review before the National Court within two months.
companyNow: Unknown. The company's current status and operations cannot be determined from the document.
dataType: Biometric data (facial image/photograph)

companyDescription: R.I.S.E Aerospace Pte. Ltd. is an aerospace company based in Singapore that holds employee personal data including identity documents and financial information.
companyLongDescription: R.I.S.E Aerospace Pte. Ltd. is an aerospace company based in Singapore that holds employee personal data including identity documents and financial information.
caseDescription: R.I.S.E Aerospace suffered a ransomware infection on 23 August 2020 that encrypted personal data of 21 employees. The organisation had failed to implement adequate technical security measures, including no security scans, firmware updates, or documented IT security policies despite manufacturer prompts. The Deputy Commissioner found the company in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA and issued a warning.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures directly enabled the ransomware attack, resulting in unauthorised encryption of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: R.I.S.E Aerospace failed to implement adequate technical security measures, including skipping security scans and firmware updates despite manufacturer prompts.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organization's security negligence exposed 21 employees' sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, passport details, work permit information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to implement technical and organisational measures to protect personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation did not carry out security scans or perform server firmware updates despite being prompted by the device manufacturer
violations: Organisation did not carry out security scans or perform server firmware updates despite being prompted by the device manufacturer
No documented IT security policies were in place for password management, server patching, or system updates
These security failings created exploitable vulnerabilities that allowed ransomware to be injected into the server and encrypt personal data of 21 employees

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found R.I.S.E Aerospace in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA and issued a Warning. The Commission did not issue any additional directions in view of the organisation's remedial actions: discontinuing the network storage server in favour of cloud storage, encrypting all sensitive data, and storing it only on offline devices. No monetary penalty was imposed. The organisation voluntarily notified the Commission of the incident, maintained a backup copy of encrypted data (avoiding total loss), and no evidence emerged of misuse of the affected personal data.
dataType: Name, address, contact number, NRIC number, work permit details, passport details, bank account numbers, child's date of birth

companyDescription: A Hungarian bookkeeping and accounting firm that serves clients by managing their government-related financial transactions and compliance, including handling their ügyfélkapu (centralized government citizen portal) access credentials for online filing and communication.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian bookkeeping and accounting firm that serves clients by managing their government-related financial transactions and compliance, including handling their ügyfélkapu (centralized government citizen portal) access credentials for online filing and communication.
caseDescription: A bookkeeping firm stored client ügyfélkapu (Hungarian government portal) credentials—including usernames and plaintext passwords—in both electronic and paper formats without adequate security safeguards. The paper-based file was blown away and found by a third party, exposing approximately 100 individuals' sensitive government access credentials and personal identification data. The firm failed to implement proper technical and organizational security measures and lacked procedures for reporting data breaches to the supervisory authority.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures (GDPR Art. 32) to protect sensitive personal data, particularly government portal credentials. Storing plaintext passwords and printing sensitive data to paper that could be easily lost constitutes inadequate safeguarding of data integrity and confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: An accounting firm stored unencrypted ügyfélkapu (Hungarian government portal) login credentials along with citizens' full names, tax IDs, social security numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 100 citizens' unencrypted government portal passwords and personal identity data were exposed when a printed list blew away in the wind, enabling identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed that only 9 employees and an authorized IT person could access the server and client data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claims of password protection and authorized access controls, a printed copy containing unencrypted credentials and sensitive personal data was lost and found by a third party, demonstrating that security controls were inadequate and the paper-based storage practice created an uncontrolled exposure risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it had put appropriate security measures in place by encrypting server access and maintaining locked folders for paper documents.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's security was insufficient because plaintext passwords were stored and repeatedly printed, and paper documents were stored in an unlocked folder that allowed a copy to be blown away and lost, proving the claimed measures were inadequate.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, considering the state of the art, implementation costs, and the nature and scope of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company stored ügyfélkapu access credentials (usernames and unencrypted passwords) on a server and routinely printed sensitive data to paper, stored in unlocked folders, enabling unauthorized access and loss of approximately 100 individuals' credentials.
violations: Company stored ügyfélkapu access credentials (usernames and unencrypted passwords) on a server and routinely printed sensitive data to paper, stored in unlocked folders, enabling unauthorized access and loss of approximately 100 individuals' credentials.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24(1)-(2) requires controllers to implement appropriate internal data protection policies, including procedures for incident handling and reporting obligations to supervisory authorities.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company's internal data protection incident handling policy failed to address when breaches must be reported to the supervisory authority, leaving no clear obligation to notify authorities of data incidents.
violations: Company's internal data protection incident handling policy failed to address when breaches must be reported to the supervisory authority, leaving no clear obligation to notify authorities of data incidents.

outcome: The Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (NAIH) found the company violated GDPR Articles 32 and 24. The company was ordered to: (1) cease paper-based storage of client government portal credentials and maintain only electronic copies with electronic backups; (2) amend its internal incident handling policy to include clear procedures for notifying the supervisory authority when required by GDPR Art. 33. The company was fined 500,000 HUF (approximately €1,685 or $1,848 USD at 2020 rates) payable within 30 days of finality. The decision was ordered published without the company's identifying details. The company may appeal to the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown; the company's identity was withheld from public disclosure per the authority's order.
dataType: National ID numbers, tax identification numbers, social security numbers, birth dates, parental names, ügyfélkapu (government portal) usernames and unencrypted passwords
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32(1) – Inadequate technical and organizational security measures
GDPR Art. 24(1)-(2) – Inadequate internal data protection incident handling policy

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a leading telecommunications service provider offering mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and digital services across Singapore and the Asia-Pacific region.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a leading telecommunications service provider offering mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and digital services across Singapore and the Asia-Pacific region.
caseDescription: On 13 July 2020, threat actors used social engineering to compromise staff accounts at Singapore Telecommunications Limited, gaining unauthorized access to 17 subscriber accounts to request SIM card issuance and service changes. The organization reported no data exfiltration and had implemented reasonable security measures. The Deputy Commissioner found the organization met its Protection Obligation and took no enforcement action.
violationSummary: The incident resulted from inadequate resilience against social engineering tactics targeting staff, exposing subscriber account access to unauthorized third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Threat actors gained access to 17 subscriber accounts through coordinated social engineering attacks targeting staff, enabling unauthorized SIM card issuance and service changes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Affected subscribers lost access to their own accounts and could not control their telecommunications services, exposing them to identity theft, fraud, and loss of critical communications access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organization had implemented reasonable security arrangements aligned to industry best practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, threat actors successfully compromised staff accounts through social engineering tactics, gaining unauthorized access to subscriber accounts.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Threat actors gained unauthorized access to 17 subscriber accounts through compromised staff credentials obtained via social engineering, temporarily denying legitimate subscribers access to their own accounts.
violations: Threat actors gained unauthorized access to 17 subscriber accounts through compromised staff credentials obtained via social engineering, temporarily denying legitimate subscribers access to their own accounts.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found that Singapore Telecommunications Limited had met its Protection Obligation under the PDPA despite the incident. The organization had in place reasonable security arrangements including industry-standard password requirements, continuous systems and network enhancements, mandatory annual PDPA training for staff, and reasonable security measures for work environments. The organization took prompt remedial action by suspending compromised accounts and conducting password resets. No enforcement action was taken. Remedial measures to prevent recurrence remain confidential for security reasons.
companyNow: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) remains a major telecommunications service provider in Singapore and the Asia-Pacific region as of 2024.
dataType: Telecommunications service subscriber accounts, SIM card information, voice call records

companyDescription: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. is a medical device and in vitro diagnostics company headquartered in Raritan, New Jersey. It provides diagnostic testing services and products for clinical laboratories and healthcare providers.
companyLongDescription: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. is a medical device and in vitro diagnostics company headquartered in Raritan, New Jersey. It provides diagnostic testing services and products for clinical laboratories and healthcare providers.
caseDescription: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics claimed to comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework in its privacy policy, but allowed its Privacy Shield certification to lapse in 2018. After Commerce warned the company to remove Privacy Shield claims in August 2018, the company continued to falsely represent on its website that it participated in Privacy Shield and complied with the framework's principles, including a verification requirement it never satisfied.
violationSummary: The company disclosed false claims about Privacy Shield participation and compliance on its public-facing privacy policy, misleading consumers and data subjects about the legal basis and protections for their personal data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics falsely claimed on its website that it participated in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework even after its certification lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU and Swiss residents whose personal data was transferred to the United States relied on Ortho-Clinical's false Privacy Shield certification claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. (and its parent/subsidiary company, Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics Bermuda Co. Ltd.) participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework
claimsVsReality.reality: The company obtained Privacy Shield certification in April 2017, but that certification lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed. By 2018 and 2019, the company was not a current participant in Privacy Shield.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. is committed to subjecting all personal data received from the European Union (EU) member countries and Switzerland, respectively, in reliance on each Privacy Shield Framework, to the Framework's applicable Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to comply with Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7, which requires annual verification through self-assessment or outside compliance review. During the 2017-18 period when certified, the company failed to obtain any attested verification statement and did not provide it to the FTC as required.

claimsVsReality.claim: To learn more about the Privacy Shield Frameworks, and to view our certification visit the U.S. Department of Commerce's Privacy Shield List
claimsVsReality.reality: When individuals consulted the Commerce Privacy Shield list after the company's August 2018 certification lapse, they would not find Ortho-Clinical listed as a current participant, contradicting the company's ongoing claims.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ortho-Clinical represented on its privacy policy website that it 'participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework' when its certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed
violations: Ortho-Clinical represented on its privacy policy website that it 'participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework' when its certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed

Ortho-Clinical represented that it 'subjecting[s] all personal data received from the European Union (EU) member countries and Switzerland...to the Framework's applicable Principles' despite not being a current participant
Ortho-Clinical failed to comply with Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7 by not obtaining annual attested verification statements during 2017-18 that it was certified
Ortho-Clinical failed to affirm to Commerce its commitment to continue protecting personal information it received during participation after its certification lapsed

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging three counts of deceptive practices: (1) Privacy Misrepresentation – claiming current Privacy Shield participation when certification had lapsed; (2) Misrepresentation Regarding Verification – representing compliance with Privacy Shield principles while failing to obtain required annual verification statements; (3) Misrepresentation Regarding Continuing Obligations – representing compliance while failing to affirm continuing protection obligations to Commerce. As a complaint, this initiated formal enforcement proceedings under FTC authority; the document does not contain final settlement terms, but FTC enforcement typically results in cease-and-desist orders and compliance monitoring.
companyNow: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. continues to operate as a medical device and in vitro diagnostics provider. The company is owned by Carlyle Group and remains active in clinical diagnostics.
dataType: Personal data from EU and Swiss residents (types not specified but potentially health-related given medical device/diagnostics services)
legalBasisViolated: EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework (Supplemental Principle 7 – Verification requirement)

companyDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is the Spanish subsidiary of Vodafone Group, one of Europe's largest multinational telecommunications companies providing mobile, broadband, and digital services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is the Spanish subsidiary of Vodafone Group, one of Europe's largest multinational telecommunications companies providing mobile, broadband, and digital services to millions of customers.
caseDescription: Vodafone sent customer invoices containing one person's personal data to a neighbor's address, with the envelope addressed to the neighbor but the invoice containing the customer's full details. The company failed to respond to the data protection authority's initial investigation request. Although Vodafone later corrected the error, the initial security lapse and lack of cooperation resulted in a €50,000 fine for violation of GDPR data security principles.
violationSummary: The company's failure to maintain adequate security measures resulted in unauthorized exposure of personal data (customer invoice details) to third parties (the neighbor), meeting the definition of Information Dissemination – Exposure under Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Vodafone sent customer invoices containing full personal data including name, DNI, and address to a neighbor's address.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's sensitive personal data was exposed to an unauthorized third party due to a data migration error and lack of adequate security controls, compromising confidentiality.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone claimed the data duplication and delivery error were the result of a 'punto error' (one-time mistake) and a data migration problem between systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The error exposed customer personal data to a third party for an extended period, demonstrating systemic failures in data quality control and security management, not a minor isolated incident.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone argued that no culpability or negligence could be proven and therefore no sanction should be imposed, citing principles of 'nullum poena sine culpa'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement adequate security measures, controls, and verification procedures required by GDPR Article 5(1)(f), demonstrating significant negligence in data protection practices, regardless of intent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone contended the error was immediately corrected once discovered, mitigating any harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to respond to the data protection authority's initial investigation request for one month, delaying identification of systemic issues and extending the period during which personal data remained at risk.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated with integrity and confidentiality, ensuring adequate security of personal data including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone failed to implement adequate technical or organisational measures to prevent personal data (customer invoice details) from being sent to an unauthorized third party (neighbor's address)
violations: Vodafone failed to implement adequate technical or organisational measures to prevent personal data (customer invoice details) from being sent to an unauthorized third party (neighbor's address)
The company's data management systems contained a data duplication error linking the customer's data to the neighbor's contact information, demonstrating insufficient data processing controls
No preventive measures were in place to verify envelope recipient against invoice data before mailing

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(a) establishes that violations of basic treatment principles (Article 5) are sanctionable with administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone's violation of Article 5(1)(f) regarding data security and confidentiality triggered liability for administrative sanctions as a 'very grave' infraction
violations: Vodafone's violation of Article 5(1)(f) regarding data security and confidentiality triggered liability for administrative sanctions as a 'very grave' infraction

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72(1)(a) classifies as 'very grave' any treatment of personal data that violates the principles and guarantees established in GDPR Article 5.
regulatoryFindings.description: The data exposure incident constituted a substantive violation of GDPR Article 5, classified as a very grave infraction under Spanish data protection law
violations: The data exposure incident constituted a substantive violation of GDPR Article 5, classified as a very grave infraction under Spanish data protection law

outcome: AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €50,000 on Vodafone España, S.A.U. for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The company must pay the fine within the voluntary payment period established by Spanish administrative procedures. The fine is classified as 'very grave' with a prescription period of three years. Vodafone confirmed during the proceedings that the error has been corrected and the neighbor's data has been de-linked from the customer's account. The resolution is final at the administrative level; Vodafone may file a motion for reconsideration within one month or pursue contentious-administrative appeal before the National Court within two months.
companyNow: Vodafone España remains a major telecommunications provider in Spain as part of the Vodafone Group, a multinational telecom company. The company continues operating under enhanced data security scrutiny following this enforcement action.
dataType: Name, address, DNI (national ID number), invoice/billing information

companyDescription: Delivery Hero Germany GmbH operated online food delivery platforms (Lieferheld, Pizza.de) before acquisition by Takeaway.com. The company processes customer data including contact information, account credentials, and order history.
companyLongDescription: Delivery Hero Germany GmbH operated online food delivery platforms (Lieferheld, Pizza.de) before acquisition by Takeaway.com. The company processes customer data including contact information, account credentials, and order history.
caseDescription: Delivery Hero failed to delete inactive customer accounts for years, including one dormant since 2008, and ignored data subject rights requests for account information and deletion. The company also continued sending marketing emails to customers who explicitly objected, with one individual receiving 15 unwanted emails after opting out. These failures reflected systemic organizational problems despite repeated warnings from the regulator.
violationSummary: Delivery Hero systematically failed to honor data subject rights to deletion, access, and objection, excluding individuals from meaningful control over their personal data processing in violation of GDPR Chapter III.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Delivery Hero Germany GmbH failed to delete 10 inactive customer accounts despite years of inactivity, ignored 5 data subject access requests.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal data was retained indefinitely without consent and used for marketing against their explicit wishes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Delivery Hero claimed technical errors and staff oversights caused the data handling failures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The high volume and repetition of violations across multiple categories revealed systemic organizational problems, not isolated technical errors. Despite repeated regulatory warnings over an extended period, the company failed to implement adequate safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) requires that personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than necessary (Storage Limitation Principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Delivery Hero retained 10 inactive customer accounts without justification, including one dormant since 2008, failing to delete data when retention was no longer necessary.
violations: Delivery Hero retained 10 inactive customer accounts without justification, including one dormant since 2008, failing to delete data when retention was no longer necessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and access to their personal data without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: In 5 cases, Delivery Hero failed to provide data subject access requests or only complied after regulatory intervention by Berlin DPA.
violations: In 5 cases, Delivery Hero failed to provide data subject access requests or only complied after regulatory intervention by Berlin DPA.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17 grants data subjects the right to erasure when data is no longer necessary or consent is withdrawn.
regulatoryFindings.description: Delivery Hero did not delete accounts of former customers who had not used the platform for years, violating the right to erasure.
violations: Delivery Hero did not delete accounts of former customers who had not used the platform for years, violating the right to erasure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 21 grants data subjects the right to object to direct marketing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: One customer who explicitly objected to marketing received 15 additional promotional emails; 8 customers complained about unsolicited marketing that continued unabated.
violations: One customer who explicitly objected to marketing received 15 additional promotional emails; 8 customers complained about unsolicited marketing that continued unabated.

outcome: Berlin DPA issued fines totaling €195,407 in August 2019 in two administrative decisions (covering violations under pre-GDPR law and GDPR proper). The decision is final. On 1 April 2019, Takeaway.com acquired Delivery Hero's German brands (Lieferheld, Pizza.de, foodora). The new owner accepted the fines without legal challenge and committed to comprehensive process reviews and data protection improvements.
companyNow: Delivery Hero's German operations were acquired by Dutch-based Takeaway.com in April 2019. Takeaway accepted the fines and implemented data protection remediation measures including staff training and process reviews.
dataType: Email addresses, customer account data, personal identifiers

companyDescription: Financial services company offering vehicle financing, leasing, and credit products. Inherited customer base through a 2010 merger/absorption of predecessor company.
companyLongDescription: Financial services company offering vehicle financing, leasing, and credit products. Inherited customer base through a 2010 merger/absorption of predecessor company.
caseDescription: A financial services company refused to delete a customer's phone number after the customer withdrew consent and requested deletion. The company claimed a 'legitimate interest' in debt collection via phone calls, but performed an inadequate and legally deficient balancing test. The authority found the data processing had no proper legal basis and violated GDPR principles on data minimisation and purpose limitation.
violationSummary: Company processed phone number for debt collection (secondary purpose beyond original contract) without demonstrating compatibility with original collection purpose, and without valid legal basis under GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The company refused to delete a customer's phone number after the customer withdrew consent, claiming a legitimate interest in contacting the customer about overdue debt collection.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer lost the ability to control unwanted telephone contact about a resolved financial matter.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it performed a proper GDPR balancing test and that legitimate interest in debt collection via phone superseded customer's right to erasure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority found the balancing test legally deficient in six critical respects: failed to separate processing purposes, weighted company convenience over data subject rights, provided no evidence phone contact was necessary, ignored alternative communication methods, and did not address data subject expectations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated it needed phone number for 'debt recovery via telephone contact' and 'customer service development,' citing financial efficiency and consent-independent processing rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: Phone contact was not necessary for debt recovery (postal address sufficed); customer service development was never formally identified as a processing purpose; no valid interest balancing supported either use; and customer had withdrawn consent, terminating the only lawful basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b): Personal data shall be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company processed phone number for debt collection via phone calls without demonstrating the secondary purpose was compatible with the original contract purpose (vehicle financing), and without prior notification to customer of this different use.
violations: Company processed phone number for debt collection via phone calls without demonstrating the secondary purpose was compatible with the original contract purpose (vehicle financing), and without prior notification to customer of this different use.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c): Personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimisation').
regulatoryFindings.description: Company retained phone number despite customer's explicit request for deletion and withdrawal of consent. Retention was not necessary as customer's postal address provided sufficient alternative for debt communications.
violations: Company retained phone number despite customer's explicit request for deletion and withdrawal of consent. Retention was not necessary as customer's postal address provided sufficient alternative for debt communications.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f): Processing is lawful only if necessary for the purposes of legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company claimed legitimate interest in debt collection via phone but failed to conduct a proper balancing test. Balancing was defective: weighted company cost-saving and convenience above customer's explicit rejection of phone contact; failed to consider that written communication sufficed; and did not evidence that phone contact was necessary for debt recovery.
violations: Company claimed legitimate interest in debt collection via phone but failed to conduct a proper balancing test. Balancing was defective: weighted company cost-saving and convenience above customer's explicit rejection of phone contact; failed to consider that written communication sufficed; and did not evidence that phone contact was necessary for debt recovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(4): If processing for a purpose different from that for which the personal data were collected, the controller shall determine compatibility by reference to multiple factors including the relationship between original and new purposes, expectations of the data subject, and whether appropriate safeguards exist.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company did not perform a proper compatibility assessment for the secondary purpose (debt collection calls). The assessment omitted goal-by-goal balancing, failed to identify debt collection as a separate processing purpose, and did not address whether customer could have reasonably expected phone-based collection efforts.
violations: Company did not perform a proper compatibility assessment for the secondary purpose (debt collection calls). The assessment omitted goal-by-goal balancing, failed to identify debt collection as a separate processing purpose, and did not address whether customer could have reasonably expected phone-based collection efforts.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(3): Where personal data are processed for a purpose different from that for which they were collected, the controller shall inform the data subject before such processing about that different purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customer was never informed that their phone number would be used for unsolicited debt collection calls, only for original financing contract purposes.
violations: Customer was never informed that their phone number would be used for unsolicited debt collection calls, only for original financing contract purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17(1)(b): The data subject has the right to obtain erasure of personal data without undue delay where the data subject withdraws consent on which processing is based and there is no other legal basis for the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customer withdrew consent and requested deletion. Company refused, claiming legitimate interest, but that interest was not legally established via valid balancing. Company therefore violated the erasure right by refusing deletion.
