violations: Customer withdrew consent and requested deletion. Company refused, claiming legitimate interest, but that interest was not legally established via valid balancing. Company therefore violated the erasure right by refusing deletion.

outcome: Authority partially granted customer's complaint. Found violation of right to erasure, purpose limitation, data minimisation, and failure to conduct valid legitimate interest balancing. Ordered company to delete phone number from all records and notify customer of deletion. Imposed 1,000,000 HUF administrative fine for the processing violations. Company must provide proof of deletion within 30 days. Decision is final subject to administrative court review within 30 days.
dataType: Telephone number, address/residential data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(4) – Compatibility Test for Secondary Purpose
GDPR Art. 13(3) – Information for Secondary Processing

companyDescription: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank is Hungary's central bank and primary financial regulatory authority, responsible for monetary policy, payment system oversight, and banking supervision. It maintains extensive customer financial records and transactional data from its banking operations and regulatory functions.
companyLongDescription: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank is Hungary's central bank and primary financial regulatory authority, responsible for monetary policy, payment system oversight, and banking supervision. It maintains extensive customer financial records and transactional data from its banking operations and regulatory functions.
caseDescription: The Hungarian National Bank failed to respond timely to multiple data subject access requests submitted between June–November 2018, and unlawfully deleted camera footage after the data subject requested processing restrictions. The bank also denied access to camera footage copies, failed to provide statutory legal references, and did not provide copies of internal circulars.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to implement processing restrictions and subsequent deletion of personal data (camera footage) demonstrates insecurity in data handling. The delayed responses and withholding of mandatory information also constitute failures to provide transparency and access as required.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Magyar Nemzeti Bank failed to respond within one month to three data subject access requests submitted in June, August.
whyTheyWereWrong: A bank customer lost irreplaceable evidence of her interactions at bank branches because the bank destroyed video.

claimsVsReality.claim: MNB stated it was implementing a court-ordered interim measure restricting all communications with the subject regarding contractual disputes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The interim measure applied only to communications about prior contractual matters, not to data protection access requests, which MNB should have treated separately and answered on time.

claimsVsReality.claim: MNB claimed camera footage deletion followed standard security industry practice under the then-applicable Hungarian law (Szvtv.), requiring deletion 30 days after a restriction request without authority action.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR (effective May 2018) imposed no such automatic deletion requirement; controllers must maintain restricted data until the legal claim is resolved, and national law cannot override this fundamental GDPR obligation.

claimsVsReality.claim: MNB stated it could not provide redacted camera footage because footage contained both third-party images and business secrets.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR explicitly permits redaction of third-party personal data and legitimate trade secrets; the subject's presence in footage and general bank operations are not protected secrets, and redaction was both lawful and feasible.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(3) requires data controllers to provide information on actions taken in response to subject rights requests within one month of receipt, or extend by two months with notice of reasons.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB failed to respond to requests submitted 14 June 2018, 22 August 2018, and 5 November 2018 until 8 February 2019 (more than three months for the last request), without timely notification of extension or reasons.
violations: MNB failed to respond to requests submitted 14 June 2018, 22 August 2018, and 5 November 2018 until 8 February 2019 (more than three months for the last request), without timely notification of extension or reasons.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(4) requires controllers to inform subjects of reasons when denying action on a request.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB's 18 December 2018 response did not identify which specific requests were denied or why, merely stating some requests were repetitive without clear designation.
violations: MNB's 18 December 2018 response did not identify which specific requests were denied or why, merely stating some requests were repetitive without clear designation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15(1) and (3) grant subjects the right to access personal data and obtain a copy thereof, with exceptions only for third-party confidentiality and trade secrets that can be redacted.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB refused to provide redacted copies of camera footage containing third persons and business secrets, despite the clear lawfulness of redaction; withheld precise statutory citations for data retention; failed to disclose whether personal data processing was ongoing with security services.
violations: MNB refused to provide redacted copies of camera footage containing third persons and business secrets, despite the clear lawfulness of redaction; withheld precise statutory citations for data retention; failed to disclose whether personal data processing was ongoing with security services.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 18(1)(c) permits subjects to request restriction of processing when data is no longer needed for processing purposes but is required for legal claims.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB deleted at least three camera recordings within the necessary timeframe for legal proceedings despite the subject's explicit restriction request, destroying evidence the subject needed for potential litigation.
violations: MNB deleted at least three camera recordings within the necessary timeframe for legal proceedings despite the subject's explicit restriction request, destroying evidence the subject needed for potential litigation.

outcome: The authority partially granted the subject's complaint. MNB was ordered to: (1) provide redacted copies of camera footage with third-party and trade secret information masked within 30 days; (2) provide a copy of the 2017 June 30 internal circular (or redacted version) within 30 days; (3) pay a administrative penalty of 700,000 HUF (approximately USD 1.96 million). The authority found MNB violated Articles 12, 15, and 18 of the GDPR. The decision became final upon service and is subject to judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank (National Bank of Hungary) continues to operate as Hungary's central bank and financial supervisory authority. It remains responsible for monetary policy, banking regulation, and data protection compliance.
dataType: Financial records, contract details, personal identification data, biometric data (signature samples), camera footage, audio recordings of calls

companyDescription: The Singapore Accountancy Commission is the national professional body that regulates accountants and administers accounting qualifications in Singapore, including the Singapore Chartered Accountant Qualification programme.
companyLongDescription: The Singapore Accountancy Commission is the national professional body that regulates accountants and administers accounting qualifications in Singapore, including the Singapore Chartered Accountant Qualification programme.
caseDescription: The Singapore Accountancy Commission mistakenly enclosed a folder containing personal data of 6,541 individuals in emails sent to 41 unintended recipients between June and October 2019. The organisation lacked robust processes, supervisory checks, and technical measures to protect personal data during email transmission. Staff were not trained on data protection policies, resulting in a breach of the Protection Obligation under the PDPA.
violationSummary: Personal data was disclosed to unintended recipients due to inadequate security arrangements and lack of protective measures, constituting a breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Singapore Accountancy Commission mistakenly enclosed a folder with personal data of 6,541 accountancy programme personnel.
whyTheyWereWrong: 6,541 individuals' sensitive personal data including National Registration ID numbers, dates of birth, contact details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had data protection policies and procedures in place
claimsVsReality.reality: These policies were not translated into actual security arrangements, supervisory checks, or technical measures to protect data

claimsVsReality.claim: Staff understood data protection requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff involved in sending emails were not informed of the organisation's personal data policies during induction training

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or control against unauthorised access.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organisation failed to implement supervisory checks or second-tier review processes for emails containing personal data
violations: The organisation failed to implement supervisory checks or second-tier review processes for emails containing personal data
No technical measures were in place to prevent sending personal data to unintended recipients
Staff involved in data handling were not trained on the organisation's personal data protection policies as part of induction
Data protection policies were not translated into practical security arrangements

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 5,000 within 30 days. The Commission did not issue additional directions, citing the organisation's admission of breach, cooperation with the investigation, and prompt remedial actions including cybersecurity training for all employees and revision of data handling policies and procedures.
companyNow: The Singapore Accountancy Commission continues to operate as Singapore's professional accounting body. Following the 2019 incident, the organisation implemented enhanced data protection measures and employee training programmes.
dataType: Names, National Registration Identification Card numbers, dates of birth, contact details, education and employment information, examination results

companyDescription: LightYear Dealer Technologies is a Missouri-based software company founded in 1996 with approximately 80 employees. It develops and operates a dealer management system (DMS) that tracks sales, finance, inventory, payroll, and customer information for automotive dealerships nationwide.
companyLongDescription: LightYear Dealer Technologies is a Missouri-based software company founded in 1996 with approximately 80 employees. It develops and operates a dealer management system (DMS) that tracks sales, finance, inventory, payroll, and customer information for automotive dealerships nationwide.
caseDescription: LightYear Dealer Technologies operated a dealer management system that stored highly sensitive personal information about 14+ million consumers and 39,000 employees in unencrypted clear text with no access controls. An unsecured storage device attached to the backup network in April 2015 created an open port that remained undetected for 18 months, enabling a hacker to breach and download personal information of 12.5 million consumers between October and November 2016. The company failed to develop written security policies, conduct risk assessments, monitor systems, or implement basic safeguards required by law.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable data security safeguards (encryption, access controls, monitoring, risk assessment) required under the Safeguards Rule, resulting in a massive breach. This is a core insecurity violation — the data was collected but not adequately protected.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: DealerBuilt stored personal data for 14+ million consumers and 39,000 employees in unencrypted clear text without access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker exploited the unsecured device and stole personal information including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: LightYear's backup service was secure and appropriately protected customer data
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer data was stored in unencrypted clear text with no access controls; a storage device with an open port remained undetected for 18 months, exposing 12.5 million consumers' data to breach

claimsVsReality.claim: The company maintained adequate security monitoring and device management procedures
claimsVsReality.reality: LightYear performed no vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, device inventory, or system monitoring; the open port was discovered only when a customer called about publicly accessible data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: LightYear's failure to employ reasonable security measures to protect personal information caused substantial injury to consumers (identity theft, fraud, financial loss) not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.
violations: LightYear's failure to employ reasonable security measures to protect personal information caused substantial injury to consumers (identity theft, fraud, financial loss) not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314), implementing GLB Act Section 501(b), requires financial institutions to protect security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing, implementing, and maintaining a comprehensive information security program.
regulatoryFindings.description: LightYear failed to develop, implement, and maintain a written organizational information security policy.
violations: LightYear failed to develop, implement, and maintain a written organizational information security policy.
LightYear failed to designate employees to coordinate the information security program.
LightYear failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks through periodic risk assessments or vulnerability testing.
LightYear failed to design and implement basic safeguards (encryption, access controls, authentication, monitoring) to control identified risks.
LightYear failed to regularly test or monitor the effectiveness of safeguards' key controls, systems, and procedures.
LightYear stored consumers' personal information in clear text without access controls or authentication protections.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against LightYear Dealer Technologies alleging violations of the FTC Act and the Safeguards Rule. The complaint seeks a compliance order requiring the company to implement reasonable security safeguards. No monetary penalty is specified in the complaint document; enforcement would proceed through settlement negotiations or administrative proceedings.
companyNow: LightYear Dealer Technologies (DealerBuilt) continues to operate its dealer management system software. The company has approximately 180 customers comprising nearly 320 dealership locations. Status following this enforcement action is not disclosed in the complaint.
dataType: Consumer personal information (name, address, phone, email, SSN, driver's license, DOB, credit card numbers, vehicle identifiers), employee payroll data (name, address, phone, email, SSN, wages, bank account information)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(1) - Section 5(a) prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information Rule (Safeguards Rule), 16 C.F.R. Part 314

companyDescription: The Budapest Police Headquarters is Hungary's largest regional police authority, responsible for law enforcement operations, crime prevention, and public safety across Budapest and surrounding areas. It maintains large databases of sensitive law enforcement and personnel data.
companyLongDescription: The Budapest Police Headquarters is Hungary's largest regional police authority, responsible for law enforcement operations, crime prevention, and public safety across Budapest and surrounding areas. It maintains large databases of sensitive law enforcement and personnel data.
caseDescription: Budapest Police Headquarters lost a 4GB USB drive containing unencrypted personnel data for 1,733 employees during an off-site management meeting. The drive included sensitive employment records and personal identifiers. The organization failed to report the incident to the National Data Protection Authority within the mandatory 72-hour window, instead waiting 45 days, citing the need for internal investigation and risk assessment.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement basic technical and organizational measures to protect personal data (encryption, access controls), creating vulnerability to unauthorized access and disclosure. Additionally, they failed the mandatory incident notification obligation under GDPR Article 33(1).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Budapest Police Headquarters lost an unencrypted USB drive containing 1,733 employees' full personnel records with birth dates, mothers' names.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,733 police officers' sensitive personal data including birth dates, mothers' names, and TAJ numbers remained exposed on unencrypted media indefinitely, enabling identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed delay was necessary to complete internal investigation and obtain risk assessment from parent organization (ORFK) before reporting.
claimsVsReality.reality: All material facts regarding the incident, affected data, and personal identifiers were known to management on January 11, 2019, and the mandatory 72-hour reporting window was 15 times longer than the actual 45-day delay. Risk assessment could have been conducted in parallel with notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization stated personnel data lacked sensitive information and were primarily publicly accessible.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data included birth dates, mother's names, and TAJ identification numbers—highly sensitive personal identifiers enabling identity theft—stored on an unencrypted device creating ongoing confidentiality breach risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed proper internal incident procedures were followed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal procedures (ORFK Directive 15/2018) required immediate notification of the data protection officer within 72 hours. The officer was not notified until January 28 at 07:30—well outside the mandatory window.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires data controllers to notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach that risks the rights and freedoms of individuals.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization delayed notification for 45 days (until February 25, 2019) despite becoming aware of the incident on January 11, 2019, exceeding the 72-hour deadline by fifteen times.
violations: The organization delayed notification for 45 days (until February 25, 2019) despite becoming aware of the incident on January 11, 2019, exceeding the 72-hour deadline by fifteen times.
Justifications for delay (completion of internal investigation, awaiting risk assessment from parent organization) were rejected as insufficient under GDPR requirements.
The data protection officer was not notified until January 28 at 07:30, well beyond the 72-hour window from incident discovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorized access and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: The USB drive was stored on a private device without any password protection, encryption, or access controls.
violations: The USB drive was stored on a private device without any password protection, encryption, or access controls.
Personnel data including sensitive identifiers (TAJ numbers, birth dates) were copied to an unencrypted portable storage device in violation of internal IT security policies.
No data loss prevention or centralized encryption management systems were implemented despite availability of such technology.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (Integrity and Confidentiality) requires personal data be processed securely, with appropriate protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: 1,733 employees' birth data, mother's names, and TAJ identification numbers were exposed to ongoing confidentiality breach risk through an unencrypted, uncontrolled storage device.
violations: 1,733 employees' birth data, mother's names, and TAJ identification numbers were exposed to ongoing confidentiality breach risk through an unencrypted, uncontrolled storage device.
The organization created conditions enabling identity theft and misuse of sensitive personal identifiers through inadequate safeguarding.

outcome: The Hungarian National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) issued a decision on June 25, 2019, finding the Budapest Police Headquarters violated GDPR Article 33(1) by failing to report the data breach within 72 hours. The Authority imposed a 5,000,000 HUF fine and ordered the organization to implement necessary measures to ensure future incidents are reported within the required timeframe, with compliance documentation required within 30 days. The decision has been ordered published with the organization's identifying information. The fine is enforceable unless challenged through administrative court proceedings within 30 days.
companyNow: The Budapest Police Headquarters (Budapesti Rendőr-főkapitányság) continues to operate as Hungary's primary law enforcement authority for Budapest. The authority has since implemented enhanced data protection procedures and incident reporting protocols as required by the enforcement order.
dataType: Personnel data (full names, birth dates, mother's names, TAJ numbers, job titles, employment records)

companyDescription: AXA Insurance Pte. Ltd. is an insurance company operating in Singapore, providing insurance products and services to policyholders. The company employs customer care specialists and maintains records of policyholder information including NRIC numbers and policy details.
companyLongDescription: AXA Insurance Pte. Ltd. is an insurance company operating in Singapore, providing insurance products and services to policyholders. The company employs customer care specialists and maintains records of policyholder information including NRIC numbers and policy details.
caseDescription: AXA Insurance failed to implement adequate document segregation processes during scanning operations, causing personal data of 87 policyholders to be inadvertently attached to an email sent to an unintended recipient. A customer care specialist compounded the failure by not reviewing the attachment before sending. The Commission found AXA breached its obligation to make reasonable security arrangements under PDPA section 24.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement segregation processes and review procedures resulted in unauthorised disclosure of personal data of 87 individuals to a recipient not authorised to receive it.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: AXA Insurance failed to segregate internal documents from customer documents during scanning.
whyTheyWereWrong: Eighty-seven policyholders' names, NRIC numbers, insurance policy numbers, and servicing agent details were disclosed to an unauthorized person due to AXA's absence of basic document segregation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Documents were being properly processed and secured during scanning operations
claimsVsReality.reality: No process existed to segregate internal documents from customer documents, allowing sensitive personal data to be mixed and sent to unintended recipients

claimsVsReality.claim: Communications with attachments were being reviewed before sending
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer care specialist who sent the email failed to check the attachment before transmission, allowing 87 individuals' personal data to reach an unintended recipient

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control from misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: AXA failed to implement a process to segregate documents intended for internal record purposes from documents for customers during document scanning operations
violations: AXA failed to implement a process to segregate documents intended for internal record purposes from documents for customers during document scanning operations
AXA's customer care specialist failed to check the attachment before sending the email containing personal data of 87 policyholders to an unintended recipient

outcome: The Commission issued a warning to AXA Insurance after considering the organisation's admission of liability, the impact of the breach on 87 affected individuals, and the corrective measures taken by the organisation.
companyNow: AXA Insurance Pte. Ltd. continues to operate as a major insurance provider in Singapore. The warning and subsequent corrective measures have been implemented to prevent future breaches.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, insurance policy numbers, servicing agent details

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a leading telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services in Singapore and across the Asia-Pacific region.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a leading telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services in Singapore and across the Asia-Pacific region.
caseDescription: During a database migration, Singapore Telecommunications' MySingTel app exposed the personal data of 750 mobile subscribers to unauthorised access due to a technical issue. The flaw allowed subscribers to view account details and usage information of other subscribers through the app. The company failed to conduct adequate testing of the migration process, particularly for scenarios involving timeout events and historical mobile numbers.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data through inadequate testing and design flaws during a critical system migration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Telecommunications Limited failed to adequately test its database migration system for timeout scenarios.
whyTheyWereWrong: 750 subscribers' sensitive personal data including mobile numbers, plans, usage details, and account numbers were exposed to unauthorised access by other subscribers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation intended for error messages to be displayed when MRD queries timed out, not for queries to be routed to the Existing System.
claimsVsReality.reality: When timeouts occurred, the system defaulted to routing queries to the Existing System despite the stated intention, and when combined with reassigned historical numbers, exposed other subscribers' data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data breach 'happened only where there was an obscure combination of factors'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Deputy Commissioner found the combination of factors (foreseeable timeout + known dummy number reassignment mechanism + historical number queries) was not obscure and should have been anticipated in testing.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to conduct thoroughly scoped testing to ensure dummy numbers in migration scenarios did not produce unintended effects
violations: Organisation failed to conduct thoroughly scoped testing to ensure dummy numbers in migration scenarios did not produce unintended effects
Test plan did not anticipate likely scenarios such as session timeout despite the organisation's own intention to display error messages on timeout

Inadequate testing allowed foreseeable combination of factors (timeout + historical number + reassignment) to expose 750 subscribers' data and enable actual unauthorised access to 39 subscribers' accounts

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $9,000 within 30 days. No further directions were made as the organisation completed its migration on 19 August 2018 and the remedial actions (displaying error messages for migrated subscribers encountering timeouts) sufficiently addressed the risks. The temporary fix was implemented within 11 hours of the incident.
companyNow: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) remains a major telecommunications provider in Singapore and the region, owned by Temasek Holdings. The company has since completed its database migration and implemented error handling for timeout scenarios.
dataType: Mobile numbers, mobile plans, usage details, account numbers, add-on services

companyDescription: L'Oreal Singapore Pte. Ltd. is the Singapore subsidiary of L'Oreal SA, a global cosmetics and beauty products manufacturer and retailer operating e-commerce platforms and customer engagement systems.
companyLongDescription: L'Oreal Singapore Pte. Ltd. is the Singapore subsidiary of L'Oreal SA, a global cosmetics and beauty products manufacturer and retailer operating e-commerce platforms and customer engagement systems.
caseDescription: L'Oreal's website had a critical caching defect that exposed customer profile data. When website code changes were made in November 2018, insufficient testing failed to detect that subsequent logins would display previous customers' personal data. The company disabled the login page upon discovery.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement adequate security measures (testing and safeguards) to protect personal data, resulting in unauthorized disclosure through a preventable technical vulnerability.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: L'Oreal instructed its vendor to modify website code for speed improvements in November 2018 but failed to scope User Acceptance Tests to include normal operating conditions.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data of 7 customers including names, emails, addresses, phone numbers and dates of birth were exposed to unauthorized disclosure when subsequent users could view cached data.

claimsVsReality.claim: L'Oreal stated it had completed all necessary and appropriate User Acceptance Tests based on the reasonably foreseeable impact of the requested code changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The UATs were inadequately scoped; they only tested single-user login scenarios and failed to include the foreseeable scenario of multiple sequential users logging in, which would have revealed the caching vulnerability.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorized disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: L'Oreal failed to ensure appropriate testing of website changes, specifically by not simulating normal operating conditions with multiple sequential user logins
violations: L'Oreal failed to ensure appropriate testing of website changes, specifically by not simulating normal operating conditions with multiple sequential user logins
The organisation did not implement adequate security measures to prevent the foreseeable risk of data caching and unauthorized disclosure to subsequent users
Testing scope was inadequate, covering only single-user login scenarios rather than the realistic multi-user environment

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found L'Oreal in breach of section 24 of the PDPA and issued a formal warning. The organisation disabled the Customer Login Page upon discovery of the vulnerability, engaged a consultant to investigate the matter, and was directed to implement recommendations to prevent similar incidents in the future.
companyNow: L'Oreal Singapore continues to operate as a subsidiary of L'Oreal SA, the multinational cosmetics company. The incident prompted implementation of enhanced testing and security protocols for website changes.
dataType: Name, email address, postal address, mobile number, date of birth

companyDescription: SAFRA National Service Association is a Singapore-based membership organisation that operates recreational facilities including a shooting club. It provides services and programs to its members.
companyLongDescription: SAFRA National Service Association is a Singapore-based membership organisation that operates recreational facilities including a shooting club. It provides services and programs to its members.
caseDescription: An employee of SAFRA's shooting club sent two batches of mass emails with an Excel spreadsheet attached containing personal data of 780 members to 491 members. The employee followed a manual, undocumented process of drafting emails with spreadsheets then attempting to delete them before sending, but failed to remove the attachment. SAFRA's lack of documented procedures, process automation, and adequate staff training led to the breach.
violationSummary: SAFRA failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised disclosure of personal data. The manual email process with multiple hand-off points and reliance on employee error prevention, without automation or documented procedures, created unnecessary risk of accidental disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SAFRA's employee sent mass emails with an attached Excel spreadsheet containing 780 shooting club members' personal data to 491 members, disclosing names, NRIC numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 780 members' sensitive personal data including national identification numbers, birth dates, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee claimed the spreadsheet disappeared from the email draft after trying to delete it due to a webmail software glitch, and he proceeded to send the emails believing the attachment had been removed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Deputy Commissioner found on balance of probabilities that there was no software glitch. The webmail service provider confirmed no such issue had been encountered or reported by any users. The employee simply failed to delete the attached spreadsheet prior to sending the emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: SAFRA claimed it had replicated the employee's steps and encountered the same attachment removal issue, witnessing the test although no screenshots or video were made.
claimsVsReality.reality: The screenshots provided by SAFRA were inconclusive in demonstrating the attachment issue. When the Commission contacted the webmail provider, they confirmed no such issue existed in their software.

claimsVsReality.claim: SAFRA claimed it had given verbal instructions to staff on data protection practices including using bcc function and checking for unnecessary attachments.
claimsVsReality.reality: Verbal instructions were insufficient; the employee was unaware of any SOPs, and the organisation had no documented process for the monthly mass email task performed since at least September 2016.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: SAFRA failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by using a manual, undocumented process for sending mass emails with personal data spreadsheets
violations: SAFRA failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by using a manual, undocumented process for sending mass emails with personal data spreadsheets
No written standard operating procedures existed despite the task being performed at least monthly since September 2016
Reliance on verbal instructions and human error prevention rather than process automation or documented safeguards
No documented process to verify attachments were removed before sending emails containing sensitive personal data

outcome: Deputy Commissioner found SAFRA contravened section 24 of the PDPA. Directions imposed: (a) pay financial penalty of $10,000 within 30 days; (b) conduct review of email system and processes to implement process safeguards and written standard operating procedures within 120 days. SAFRA subsequently implemented multiple remedial measures including restricting mass email sending to designated personnel, reducing download data categories, implementing access controls, masking NRIC numbers, updating IT policy for database encryption, providing staff training, and beginning system automation enhancement.
companyNow: SAFRA National Service Association continues operations as a membership organisation. Following the enforcement action, it has implemented enhanced data protection measures including automated email systems, restricted database access, staff training programs, and updated IT policies for data handling.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, date of birth, address, telephone number, email address

companyDescription: A non-profit professional association working with the Singapore Tourism Board to promote the professionalism and standards of tourist guides as tourism ambassadors of Singapore. Members are registered tourist guides who can access networking and professional development services through the organisation.
companyLongDescription: A non-profit professional association working with the Singapore Tourism Board to promote the professionalism and standards of tourist guides as tourism ambassadors of Singapore. Members are registered tourist guides who can access networking and professional development services through the organisation.
caseDescription: A non-profit tourism organisation failed to implement reasonable security measures on its website, leaving 111 members' sensitive identification documents—including NRICs, driving licences, and biometric data—publicly accessible through web directories. The organisation had not appointed a data protection officer, specified security requirements to its vendor, or conducted any security testing since launching the site in October 2018. Upon discovery, the organisation disabled access and notified members, but the data had already been exposed.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to implement basic access controls resulted in sensitive identification documents being directly accessible to the public and web crawlers, increasing accessibility and risk of misuse of highly sensitive biometric and identity data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Organisation collected members' identification document images including NRICs, driving licences.
whyTheyWereWrong: 111 members' highly sensitive identity data including NRIC numbers, fingerprints, photographs, thumbprints, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation engaged a professional IT vendor to develop a secure website for member management
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor was given no specifications regarding data protection, security requirements, or access controls; the organisation then took full management responsibility without implementing security testing or policies

claimsVsReality.claim: Member identification documents were collected for legitimate administrative purposes (training grants, secure location access verification, driving licence verification)
claimsVsReality.reality: These sensitive documents were stored without any separation of access controls, placing them in the same public directories as member profile pages intended for public discovery

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation lacked technical expertise to handle security
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of expertise does not excuse failure to give clear business requirements to the vendor regarding what data should be publicly accessible versus restricted

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to specify data protection and storage requirements to its vendor when commissioning website development
violations: Organisation failed to specify data protection and storage requirements to its vendor when commissioning website development
No security testing was conducted after the website launched in October 2018
Identification document images were stored in publicly accessible directories without any access controls such as folder permissions, password protection, or IP restrictions
ID Data intended only for administrative purposes (grants, secure location access, licence verification) was not segregated from public profile directories

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 11(3) requires organisations to designate one or more individuals (data protection officers) responsible for ensuring compliance with the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation had not appointed any data protection officer at the time of the incident and during operations
violations: Organisation had not appointed any data protection officer at the time of the incident and during operations

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 12 requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations, and communicate such policies to staff.
regulatoryFindings.description: No data protection policies or practices were developed or implemented prior to the incident
violations: No data protection policies or practices were developed or implemented prior to the incident
No written policies existed to guide handling of personal data collected via the website

outcome: The Commissioner found contraventions of PDPA sections 24, 11(3), and 12. The organisation was directed to: (1) pay SGD 20,000 in 8 monthly instalments from February to September 2020; (2) review website security and implement appropriate security arrangements within 60 days; (3) put in place written internal data protection policies within 60 days; (4) develop and implement employee training policy on PDPA compliance within 60 days; and (5) require all existing employees to complete such training. The organisation appointed two DPOs, disabled public access to web directories, contacted Google to remove cached images, and developed a data protection policy in response.
companyNow: The Society of Tourist Guides (Singapore) continues to operate as a non-profit organisation promoting tourist guide professionalism in Singapore, now with enhanced data protection governance following enforcement action.
dataType: NRIC numbers, photographs, driving licence details, employment pass information, biometric data (thumbprints, fingerprints), addresses, date of birth, race, gender, military rank, blood group, occupation, religious affiliation
legalBasisViolated: PDPA section 11(3) (Designation of data protection officer)
PDPA section 12 (Personal data protection policies and practices)

companyDescription: EU Holidays Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based travel agency that specialises in holiday packages and tour reservations. The company operates an e-commerce website allowing customers to book tours directly or through partner agents.
companyLongDescription: EU Holidays Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based travel agency that specialises in holiday packages and tour reservations. The company operates an e-commerce website allowing customers to book tours directly or through partner agents.
caseDescription: EU Holidays failed to implement basic security controls on its website, leaving customer tax invoices containing sensitive personal data publicly accessible for over 13 months. The company did not specify data protection requirements in its vendor contract, did not review website security, and had no internal data protection policies despite regularly collecting customer data for tour reservations.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to take reasonable security steps to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data, contrary to section 24 of the PDPA. Personal data containing sensitive information was stored in publicly accessible directories without technical safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: EU Holidays stored customer tax invoices containing sensitive personal data in publicly accessible web directories without password protection or access controls for over one year.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,077 customers' personal data including passport details, dates of birth, addresses, contact numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: EU Holidays intended for tax invoices from direct reservations to be stored in a backend Content Management System accessible only to authorised staff
claimsVsReality.reality: Tax invoices were actually stored in a publicly accessible web directory (Web Directory 1) without any authentication or access controls, contradicting the company's stated intention

claimsVsReality.claim: EU Holidays intended for Web Directory 2 to be accessible only to partner agents using email addresses and passwords
claimsVsReality.reality: Web Directory 2 was publicly accessible because the organisation provided no access control instructions to the vendor, resulting in no authentication mechanisms being implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: EU Holidays failed to assess risks to personal data collected through its website
violations: EU Holidays failed to assess risks to personal data collected through its website
Did not include data protection requirements in vendor contract for website development
Did not review or specify security arrangements for storage of customer data in web directories
Tax invoices containing sensitive personal data were stored in publicly accessible web directories without access controls, folder permissions, or authentication mechanisms
Failed to implement any of the reasonable technical security measures such as non-public folders, access controls via web applications, or .htaccess file restrictions

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 12 requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations and communicate such policies to staff.
regulatoryFindings.description: EU Holidays had not developed or implemented any internal data protection policies
violations: EU Holidays had not developed or implemented any internal data protection policies
Despite regularly collecting customer personal data as part of its travel agency business, the company provided no guidance to employees on handling such data
No policies in place to ensure compliance with PDPA obligations

outcome: The Commissioner found EU Holidays in breach of PDPA sections 12 and 24. The organisation was ordered to: (1) pay a financial penalty of $15,000 SGD within 30 days; (2) within 60 days, review website security and implement appropriate security arrangements; (3) put in place a data protection policy with written internal policies; and (4) develop and deliver mandatory PDPA training for all employees. The organisation had taken prompt remedial action by deleting invoices from Web Directory 1 and disabling public access to Web Directory 2 upon notification.
companyNow: EU Holidays Pte. Ltd. remains in operation as a Singapore-based travel agency. Following the PDPC enforcement action, the company was required to implement comprehensive data protection measures and employee training by end of 2019.
dataType: Name, email address, physical address, contact number, date of birth, passport details, travel destination, departure date, gender, rooming arrangement, booking date, amount payable

companyDescription: MRI Diagnostics Pte Ltd (NovenaMRI) is a medical centre providing magnetic resonance imaging and X-Ray diagnostic services to patients in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: MRI Diagnostics Pte Ltd (NovenaMRI) is a medical centre providing magnetic resonance imaging and X-Ray diagnostic services to patients in Singapore.
caseDescription: MRI Diagnostics failed to implement adequate security controls when engaging a cloud service provider, resulting in approximately 4,099 patients' personal data including health records being exposed via the internet. An overseas IT vendor removed access restrictions during system maintenance and failed to reinstate them, allowing Excel spreadsheets containing sensitive data to be indexed by Google and accessible to unauthorized parties.
violationSummary: The company failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access to personal data in its possession and control, allowing a vendor's negligence to result in exposure of sensitive health information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MRI Diagnostics subscribed to a cloud-based teleradiology system without conducting due diligence on the vendor's security standards, failed to establish a written agreement.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 4,099 patients' names, NRIC numbers, and sensitive radiology scan information were exposed to public internet access because MRI Diagnostics failed to require vendors to maintain.

claimsVsReality.claim: MRI Diagnostics claimed it had a written agreement with Clarity regarding data protection
claimsVsReality.reality: MRI Diagnostics could not produce supporting evidence of any written agreement; Clarity disputed the claim and admitted no written agreement existed

claimsVsReality.claim: The system was secure as it was provided by a contracted cloud service provider
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor removed access restrictions during maintenance and omitted to reinstate them, allowing Excel spreadsheets with sensitive data to be indexed by Google and exposed to unauthorized access

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: MRI Diagnostics failed to provide vendors with clear specifications on data protection requirements
violations: MRI Diagnostics failed to provide vendors with clear specifications on data protection requirements
Failed to conduct proper due diligence of vendor security standards (e.g., ISO 27001 compliance)
Could not produce evidence of a written agreement with Clarity despite claiming one existed
Did not verify or oversee data protection arrangements after engaging the vendor
Failed to implement adequate access controls for systems storing sensitive health data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 11(3) of the Personal Data Protection Act requires organisations to appoint a data protection officer.
regulatoryFindings.description: Clarity failed to appoint a data protection officer as required
violations: Clarity failed to appoint a data protection officer as required

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act requires organisations to develop and implement data protection policies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Clarity failed to develop or implement any data protection policies
violations: Clarity failed to develop or implement any data protection policies

outcome: MRI Diagnostics received a warning for breach of the Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the PDPA. No further directions were imposed as the company ceased its business relationship with Clarity. Clarity (the service provider) was directed to appoint a data protection officer, develop and implement a data protection policy, and inform the Commission within 7 days of completion of each directive, all within 30 days from the decision date.
companyNow: MRI Diagnostics has ceased its business relationship with Clarity as of the decision date. Current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Health data (radiology scans, X-Rays), names, NRIC numbers

company: Office Depot, Inc. and Support.com, Inc.
companyDescription: Office Depot is a nationwide office supply retailer operating over 1,000 stores selling office supplies, furniture, print services, and technical support services. Support.com is a technology services company providing cloud-based software and technical support services directly and indirectly to consumers through retail partners.
companyLongDescription: Office Depot is a nationwide office supply retailer operating over 1,000 stores selling office supplies, furniture, print services, and technical support services. Support.com is a technology services company providing cloud-based software and technical support services directly and indirectly to consumers through retail partners.
caseDescription: Office Depot and Support.com deceived millions of consumers by using a deceptive software tool (PC Health Check Program) that falsely reported malware infections and security problems on computers, regardless of actual system status. The program was deliberately configured to show 'malware found' whenever employees checked initial symptom boxes, not based on actual scans. This deception was used to convince consumers to purchase expensive diagnostic and repair services costing $300+.
violationSummary: The deception involved misrepresenting the results of security diagnostics through deliberately flawed software logic, constituting insecurity in information processing by providing false threat assessments designed to manipulate consumer purchasing decisions.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Office Depot and Support.com programmed the PC Health Check software to automatically report false malware infections whenever store employees checked initial problem checkboxes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Tens of millions of consumers were deceived into purchasing expensive computer repair services costing over $300 each based on fabricated malware findings, causing financial harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The PC Health Check Program is a free diagnostic service that scans computers for viruses and security problems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The program did not perform genuine scans; results were predetermined based solely on whether initial checkbox statements were selected, not on actual system conditions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Results showed 'Malware Symptoms Found' and 'infections detected' based on scan findings.
claimsVsReality.reality: These results were automatically generated whenever any of four initial symptom checkboxes were checked, regardless of actual malware presence or the results of the actual 'Quick Malware Scan'.

claimsVsReality.claim: Store employees run 'complete diagnostics' and the program will 'check for viruses' and make PCs 'run faster'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The program ran brief, limited scans that had no connection to the malware findings displayed. Results were triggered by checkbox selection, not diagnostic logic.

claimsVsReality.claim: Support.com presented the tool as using 'heuristic questions to identify likely malware infestations' running in 'a few minutes'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tool assumed infection based on symptom questions asked, not on actual malware detection, and the questions themselves were the sole trigger for malware findings.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Office Depot falsely represented that the PC Health Check Program detected actual malware infections and security problems on consumers' computers when results were predetermined solely by checkbox selection.
violations: Office Depot falsely represented that the PC Health Check Program detected actual malware infections and security problems on consumers' computers when results were predetermined solely by checkbox selection.
Support.com provided the deceptive software as a means and instrumentality for Office Depot to commit these deceptive practices, knowing it would be used to deceive consumers.
The companies knew since 2012 that checking any initial symptom box would automatically trigger malware findings regardless of actual system status, yet continued the practice.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief. The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, restitution and refund of monies paid, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies, rescission or reformation of contracts, and other equitable remedies. As of the complaint filing (March 2019), the case was pending in the Southern District of Florida. Office Depot suspended use of the PC Health Check Program in November 2016 following media investigation by KIRO 7.
companyNow: Office Depot continues operations as a major office supply retailer with over 1,000 stores. The company severed its relationship with Support.com around 2017 and acquired its own tech-support services company to continue offering computer diagnostic and repair services.
dataType: Computer system information, security diagnostics
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce
FTC Act Section 13(b) – authority to seek injunctive relief

companyDescription: InfoTrax Systems, L.C. is a technology company founded in 1998 that provides backend operations systems and online distributor tools for the direct sales and multi-level marketing industry. The company manages critical business functions including compensation, inventory, orders, accounting, and data security for major clients like dōTERRA, XanGo, and LifeVantage.
companyLongDescription: InfoTrax Systems, L.C. is a technology company founded in 1998 that provides backend operations systems and online distributor tools for the direct sales and multi-level marketing industry. The company manages critical business functions including compensation, inventory, orders, accounting, and data security for major clients like dōTERRA, XanGo, and LifeVantage.
caseDescription: InfoTrax Systems failed to implement reasonable data security measures to protect approximately 11.8 million consumers' personal information. Attackers exploited vulnerabilities over nearly two years (May 2014–February 2016), accessing sensitive data including SSNs, payment card numbers, and credentials. The company stored unencrypted sensitive data and lacked intrusion detection systems, code review processes, and network segmentation.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security safeguards and encryption for sensitive personal data directly enabled unauthorized access and exposure of consumer information on a massive scale.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: InfoTrax operated backend systems for multi-level marketers while failing to implement code reviews, penetration testing, input validation, network segmentation, intrusion detection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Intruders accessed personal information of approximately 11.8 million consumers undetected for 21 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: InfoTrax purported to ensure that all personal information was adequately protected by contract.
claimsVsReality.reality: InfoTrax stored 11.8 million consumers' SSNs, payment cards, bank details, and passwords in unencrypted text, lacked intrusion detection, and remained unaware of attacker access for 21 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondents assumed responsibility for the security and confidentiality of consumers' personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Respondents failed to conduct code reviews, penetration testing, implement network segmentation, or maintain inventory of stored data, leaving systems vulnerable to compromise.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents failed to employ reasonable data security practices to protect personal information (names, addresses, SSNs, financial account information) from unauthorized access and exfiltration.
violations: Respondents failed to employ reasonable data security practices to protect personal information (names, addresses, SSNs, financial account information) from unauthorized access and exfiltration.
Respondents failed to conduct adequate code reviews and penetration testing to assess cybersecurity risks.
Respondents failed to implement input validation, malicious file upload protections, and network segmentation.
Respondents failed to implement intrusion detection/prevention systems, file integrity monitoring, or data loss prevention tools.
Respondents failed to maintain a systematic inventory and deletion process for unnecessary consumer personal information.
Respondents stored sensitive personal information (SSNs, payment card data, bank account information, authentication credentials) in clear, readable text without encryption.

As a result, attackers accessed the systems undetected for 21 months (May 2014–February 2016), compromising data of approximately 1 million consumers on March 2, 2016 alone, and over 2,300 unique payment card numbers on subsequent intrusions.

Breached information was used to commit identity theft and fraud, resulting in 238 unauthorized credit card charges, 34 new fraudulent credit lines, 15 tax fraud cases, and ongoing financial harm to distributors and consumers.

outcome: On December 30, 2019, the FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the initial complaint, not a final settlement. Respondents were required to cease the alleged practices and implement comprehensive data security measures, subject to FTC monitoring and compliance reviews. The case initiated enforcement action against both the company and CEO Mark Rawlins individually.
companyNow: InfoTrax Systems continues to operate as a technology service provider for multi-level marketers. The company was required to implement extensive data security improvements and remediation measures under FTC oversight.
dataType: Full names, dates of birth, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, Social Security numbers, government identification numbers, payment card information (credit/debit card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates), bank account information (account and routing numbers), user IDs and passwords
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Deutsche Wohnen SE is one of Germany's largest residential real estate companies, managing hundreds of thousands of apartments across the country. The company provides residential rental housing and related property management services.
companyLongDescription: Deutsche Wohnen SE is one of Germany's largest residential real estate companies, managing hundreds of thousands of apartments across the country. The company provides residential rental housing and related property management services.
caseDescription: Deutsche Wohnen SE maintained an archive system that stored tenant personal data indefinitely without ability to delete obsolete records. Data including salary statements, tax records, and financial information from years past remained accessible despite no longer serving their original purpose. Despite a 2017 regulatory warning, the company failed to remediate the unlawful storage system for over 18 months.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures (Art. 32 equivalent) to manage data retention and deletion. The archive system's design prevented lawful data management, creating ongoing exposure of sensitive tenant financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Deutsche Wohnen SE used an archive system that stored tenant personal data including salary statements, tax records, and bank details without any capability to delete outdated information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of tenants had years-old sensitive financial and personal information left accessible in company systems indefinitely.

claimsVsReality.claim: Deutsche Wohnen claimed to have made preparations to remedy the identified data storage deficiencies after the 2017 regulatory warning.
claimsVsReality.reality: By March 2019 (18+ months later), no actual data cleanup had occurred and no lawful justification for continued storage could be demonstrated; preparatory measures had not resulted in legal compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: The archive system was a neutral storage mechanism for tenant records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system was deliberately designed without any deletion capability, embedding non-compliance into its core architecture and making lawful data management structurally impossible.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) requires that personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than necessary (Storage Limitation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Deutsche Wohnen retained tenant salary statements, tax records, insurance data, and bank statements for years beyond their original collection purpose, with no mechanism to delete obsolete records.
violations: Deutsche Wohnen retained tenant salary statements, tax records, insurance data, and bank statements for years beyond their original collection purpose, with no mechanism to delete obsolete records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing (Integrity and Confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: The archive system offered no controls to prevent unauthorized viewing of years-old sensitive financial data; multiple archived records were accessible to staff without legitimate need.
violations: The archive system offered no controls to prevent unauthorized viewing of years-old sensitive financial data; multiple archived records were accessible to staff without legitimate need.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 25(1) requires data protection by design and by default, including technical and organizational measures to implement data protection principles effectively.
regulatoryFindings.description: Deutsche Wohnen deliberately designed an archive structure incapable of data deletion, embedding non-compliance into its system architecture from inception.
violations: Deutsche Wohnen deliberately designed an archive structure incapable of data deletion, embedding non-compliance into its system architecture from inception.

outcome: Fine of €14.5 million imposed on 30 October 2019 for violations between May 2018 and March 2019. Additional fines of €6,000–€17,000 imposed for 15 individual cases of unlawful data retention. Decision not yet final as of press release date; Deutsche Wohnen SE entitled to appeal. Regulatory expectation that company will restructure archive systems and implement proper data deletion protocols. Berlin DPA publicly recommended all data processors review archive compliance with GDPR.
companyNow: Deutsche Wohnen SE remains a major German residential property manager, operating hundreds of thousands of rental units across Germany. The company is subject to ongoing regulatory scrutiny regarding data protection compliance.
dataType: Financial data, employment records, salary information, tax records, social insurance data, bank account information, personal identification documents
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
GDPR Art. 25 Abs. 1 – Data Protection by Design and by Default

companyDescription: FWD Singapore Pte Ltd is an insurance and financial services company operating in Singapore, providing various insurance and investment products to customers.
companyLongDescription: FWD Singapore Pte Ltd is an insurance and financial services company operating in Singapore, providing various insurance and investment products to customers.
caseDescription: FWD Singapore failed to adequately test code fixes for its payment advice letter generation system, resulting in a logic error that sent 42 payment advice letters containing 71 individuals' names and identification numbers to incorrect recipients between June and July 2019. The organisation breached its Protection Obligation by failing to conduct manual code review and unit testing to a reasonable standard. The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning after finding the organisation had retrieved 67 of 71 affected letters and voluntarily notified the Commission.
violationSummary: The unintended disclosure of personal data (names and identification numbers) to incorrect recipients constitutes a breach of confidentiality and improper dissemination of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: FWD Singapore deployed a code fix that inadvertently introduced a logic error in its payment advice letter system.
whyTheyWereWrong: Seventy-one individuals' names and identification numbers were sent to wrong addresses, exposing their sensitive financial information to strangers because FWD failed to conduct adequate code.

claimsVsReality.claim: The code fix would resolve the earlier logic error in the payment advice letter generation system.
claimsVsReality.reality: The fix introduced a second logic error that caused incorrect mailing addresses to be extracted, sending personal data to wrong recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: FWD failed to take reasonable care in conducting manual code review and unit testing before deploying the fix, allowing a second logic error to go undetected and cause disclosure of personal data to incorrect recipients.
violations: FWD failed to take reasonable care in conducting manual code review and unit testing before deploying the fix, allowing a second logic error to go undetected and cause disclosure of personal data to incorrect recipients.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to FWD Singapore Pte Ltd for breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. No directions were required as the organisation took steps to improve its development processes to prevent recurrence. The organisation had successfully retrieved letters containing personal data of 67 out of 71 affected individuals and voluntarily notified the Commission of the incident.
companyNow: FWD Singapore Pte Ltd is an active financial services provider operating in Singapore, part of the FWD Group which provides insurance and financial products across Asia.
dataType: Names, identification numbers

companyDescription: National Healthcare Group Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based healthcare organisation that operates clinics and engages with partner doctors through its NHG Partners programme to provide healthcare services.
companyLongDescription: National Healthcare Group Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based healthcare organisation that operates clinics and engages with partner doctors through its NHG Partners programme to provide healthcare services.
caseDescription: National Healthcare Group failed to restrict internet access to a list containing personal information of 129 partner doctors and 5 members of the public. A penetration test in 2016 identified the vulnerability, but the organisation did not remediate it. The list remained publicly accessible via Google search until February 2018, when a doctor discovered it and notified the organisation.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to protect personal data from unauthorised exposure to the internet, making sensitive personal information of doctors and members of the public accessible via public search engines.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: National Healthcare Group failed to implement access restrictions in a web configuration file before launching its website in December 2015.
whyTheyWereWrong: 134 individuals' sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, dates of birth, photographs, and contact information remained exposed online for over 14 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vulnerability was not sufficiently highlighted by the vendor in the Penetration Test Report and the organisation was not aware of its significance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The penetration test findings were the first item in the report and expressed in non-technical terms requiring no technical expertise to understand. The recommendation to restrict internet access was clear and actionable.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation relied on the IT Services Provider and Website Developer to act on issues identified in the Penetration Test Report, delegating responsibility to vendors.
claimsVsReality.reality: While organisations may delegate work to vendors, they cannot delegate their statutory responsibility for data protection compliance. The organisation failed to exercise reasonable oversight of remediation efforts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT Services Provider was a data intermediary responsible for the vulnerability and should bear responsibility.
claimsVsReality.reality: The IT Services Provider provided technical support but did not process the disclosed personal data through the website. The root cause was a missing access restriction in the web configuration file, and the organisation had sole responsibility for security arrangements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: National Healthcare Group failed to implement access restrictions in the web configuration file before deploying the website in December 2015
violations: National Healthcare Group failed to implement access restrictions in the web configuration file before deploying the website in December 2015
The organisation did not remediate a vulnerability identified in the June/July 2016 penetration test report, despite clear recommendations to reconfigure authorisation rules
The organisation failed to exercise reasonable oversight of the penetration test findings and did not ensure vendors remediated the identified vulnerabilities
Personal data including NRIC numbers, dates of birth, and photographs remained publicly accessible via internet for over 14 months due to the unremediated vulnerability

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found that National Healthcare Group breached the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA by failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 6,000 within 30 days. No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures already implemented, which included taking the website offline immediately upon notification, removing cached copies from Google, notifying affected individuals, and adopting additional security checks for future website deployments including performing penetration tests prior to going live.
companyNow: National Healthcare Group remains a major healthcare provider in Singapore, operating multiple clinics and healthcare services through its network of partner doctors and medical facilities.
dataType: Names, mobile numbers, email addresses, mailing addresses, clinic addresses, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, photographs, Singapore Medical Council registration numbers

company: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association
companyDescription: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association is a registered volunteer society comprising parent members of Henry Park Primary School. The organisation operated a website to allow members to access their account information.
companyLongDescription: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association is a registered volunteer society comprising parent members of Henry Park Primary School. The organisation operated a website to allow members to access their account information.
caseDescription: A parent-run school association's website exposed member personal data through inadequate access controls. Personal data intended for registered members only was indexed by Google and discoverable via search, revealing names, contact numbers, and children's information. The organisation failed to conduct security testing and had no data protection policies.
violationSummary: Personal data was unintentionally exposed to the public through inadequate access controls and indexing by search engines, making it accessible to anyone performing a web search.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association developed a WordPress website to manage member accounts containing names, contact numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' personal data including names, contact numbers, and children's identities became publicly searchable on Google, exposing families to potential privacy violations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation conducted tests verifying that only logged-in members could view account particulars and public users could not.
