claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these manual tests, personal data was crawled, indexed and publicly searchable by Google, indicating the access controls were ineffective against automated search engine indexing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was restricted to registered members only.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal data was publicly discoverable through Google search results, accessible to anyone searching by name.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 11(3) PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct adequate security testing such as vulnerability scans before launching the website
violations: Failed to conduct adequate security testing such as vulnerability scans before launching the website
Did not implement proper access controls to restrict unauthorised access to member data
Conducted only rudimentary manual tests that failed to identify access control weaknesses

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 PDPA requires organisations to implement policies and practices to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not develop or implement any data protection policies
violations: Did not develop or implement any data protection policies
Did not establish practices necessary to comply with PDPA obligations
Had no data protection notice or framework in place

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 PDPA requires organisations to appoint a person responsible for compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint any individual responsible for ensuring PDPA compliance
violations: Failed to appoint any individual responsible for ensuring PDPA compliance
Lacked accountability framework and compliance oversight

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of PDPA sections 11(3), 12, and 24. Within 60 days, the organisation was directed to: (1) appoint one or more individuals responsible for PDPA compliance; (2) develop and implement internal data protection and training policies; (3) provide data protection training to all volunteers handling personal data. The organisation had already taken remedial steps by taking the original website offline (15 March 2019) and launching a new website (14 November 2019) that removed online database access and included a data protection notice.
companyNow: The organisation replaced its compromised website with a new version that removed online member database access and implemented data protection notice. Status as of current date unknown, but mandatory compliance directions were issued.
dataType: names, contact numbers, child names, child class information

companyDescription: SearchAsia Consulting Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based recruitment company that matches job seekers with employers looking to hire. The company operated a website allowing job seekers to upload résumés for recruitment matching purposes.
companyLongDescription: SearchAsia Consulting Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based recruitment company that matches job seekers with employers looking to hire. The company operated a website allowing job seekers to upload résumés for recruitment matching purposes.
caseDescription: SearchAsia Consulting, a recruitment company, failed to implement basic access controls on a folder containing job seekers' résumés uploaded to its website. The unsecured folder was indexed by search engine crawlers, making résumés publicly accessible to anyone searching for individuals by name or email. The company did not document security instructions to contractors, conduct security tests, or verify that promised protections were actually implemented.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession from unauthorised access and disclosure. The core failure was lack of access controls and failure to test or verify security implementation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SearchAsia stored job seekers' uploaded résumés in an unsecured folder without access controls, allowing search engine bots to index and publicly expose them via Internet searches.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job seekers' sensitive personal data including names, phone numbers, employment history, educational qualifications, and in some cases nationality, date of birth, marital status.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation asserted it had instructed the web developer to restrict folder access to only one employee
claimsVsReality.reality: The web developer denied receiving any security specifications and no documentary evidence was provided to support the claim

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation relied on the web hosting provider to ensure adequate security features on the website
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation never informed the web host that the folder contents needed to be protected, so no specific security measures were implemented for the résumé folder

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation asked the developer whether résumés would be encrypted and the developer responded saying it was 'safe'
claimsVsReality.reality: No written security specifications were provided, and no testing or verification was conducted to confirm that any protective measures were actually implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or under their control from unauthorised access, disclosure and similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to implement access controls on the folder storing résumés
violations: Organisation failed to implement access controls on the folder storing résumés
Organisation did not provide written security specifications to the web developer
Organisation did not conduct any checks or tests to verify that access controls were implemented or that data was encrypted
Organisation did not inform the web hosting provider that the folder contents required protection
Folder was left publicly accessible without restrictions and was indexed by search engine crawlers

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found SearchAsia Consulting in breach of section 24 of the PDPA and directed the organisation to pay a financial penalty of SGD 7,000 within 30 days. No other enforcement directions were issued given the organisation's post-incident remediation actions, which included disabling directory listing, adding search engine crawler prevention mechanisms, removing public access permissions from sensitive file directories, and requesting Google to remove cached résumés from search results.
companyNow: SearchAsia Consulting Pte. Ltd. appears to remain operational. Following the enforcement action, the company implemented remedial security measures including access control improvements and search engine blocking mechanisms.
dataType: Names, phone numbers, employment history, educational qualifications, achievements, skillset, nationality, date of birth, marital status, current salary

companyDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a private data analytics and consulting company that provided voter-profiling, microtargeting, and political marketing services. The company operated as part of the SCL Group family of companies and was based in New York. It described itself as 'politically neutral' on its website.
companyLongDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a private data analytics and consulting company that provided voter-profiling, microtargeting, and political marketing services. The company operated as part of the SCL Group family of companies and was based in New York. It described itself as 'politically neutral' on its website.
caseDescription: Cambridge Analytica and its executives harvested Facebook profile data from approximately 250,000–270,000 app users and 50–65 million of their friends through a deceptive app (GSRApp). They falsely represented that the app would not collect any identifiable information, but actually collected persistent Facebook User IDs and other identifiable data. The data was used for political microtargeting and voter profiling.
violationSummary: The company made false representations about what data would be collected (claiming no identifiable information) when in fact persistent User IDs and other identifiable information were harvested and used to identify and profile individuals for political purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Cambridge Analytica and its executives developed and operated the GSRApp that secretly harvested Facebook profile data including persistent user IDs from approximately 250,000–270,000 direct.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company falsely told users the app would not collect identifiable information, but it harvested Facebook User IDs and personal details from at least 30 million identifiable U.S.

claimsVsReality.claim: The GSRApp will NOT download your name or any other identifiable information—we are interested in your demographics and likes
claimsVsReality.reality: The GSRApp collected Facebook User IDs (persistent, unique identifiers linking users to their profiles) along with demographics, birthdate, location, friends list, and likes data

claimsVsReality.claim: Cambridge Analytica was politically neutral
claimsVsReality.reality: The company actively provided voter-profiling and microtargeting services to U.S. political campaigns and clients, with specific interest in questions about national security and political orientation

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents represented that GSRApp did not collect any identifiable information from Facebook users who authorized it, when in fact it collected Facebook User IDs and other identifiable profile data
violations: Respondents represented that GSRApp did not collect any identifiable information from Facebook users who authorized it, when in fact it collected Facebook User IDs and other identifiable profile data
They made this false representation knowing that approximately half of survey participants initially refused to grant permission, and only after the false claim was added did participation increase

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Aleksandr Kogan and Alexander Nix on December 18, 2019, alleging deceptive practices. The complaint seeks to hold respondents responsible for their deceptive acts in harvesting personal information from Facebook users through false representations about data collection. The proceedings indicate compliance orders and monitoring were the enforcement mechanism rather than a monetary fine.
companyNow: Cambridge Analytica filed for bankruptcy in May 2018 and proceedings were ongoing at time of complaint. The company is now defunct. SCL Elections, the related U.K. entity, was placed into liquidation on April 17, 2019.
dataType: Facebook profile data including User IDs, name, gender, birthdate, location, friends list, public page likes
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5 – Deceptive acts or practices involving foreign commerce

companyDescription: Unrollme was an email management service offering two features: unsubscribing users from unwanted emails and consolidating wanted subscription emails into a daily 'Rollup' digest. It operated via website, iOS app, and Android app.
companyLongDescription: Unrollme was an email management service offering two features: unsubscribing users from unwanted emails and consolidating wanted subscription emails into a daily 'Rollup' digest. It operated via website, iOS app, and Android app.
caseDescription: Unrollme, an email management service, obtained full access to users' email accounts under the guise of removing unwanted subscription emails. However, its parent company Slice secretly accessed and harvested e-receipts and personal data from those inboxes for market research and sale to third parties. Unrollme deceived users through misleading messages claiming it would 'not touch personal stuff' and failed to disclose the secondary data collection.
violationSummary: Unrollme collected email data ostensibly for subscription management but secretly repurposed it for market research and commercial sale without user knowledge or consent, constituting prohibited secondary use.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Unrollme granted its parent company Slice full access to users' email accounts and failed to disclose that Slice would extract entire e-receipts containing names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 55,000 consumers granted email access after Unrollme falsely promised their personal data would not be touched, exposing their credit card numbers, billing addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Unrollme stated 'we won't touch your personal stuff' and required email access only to monitor and manage subscription emails.
claimsVsReality.reality: Parent company Slice used automated crawlers to capture and store entire e-receipt bodies (including full personal data, credit card info, health product purchases) for market research and commercial sale.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer support represented: 'we are not reading your personal emails' and 'our algorithm only looks at subscription emails and does not touch your private emails.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Slice accessed and preserved all e-receipts without removing personal or sensitive information before storage in its Data Warehouse for analytics and sale to third parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to email was necessary for core service delivery (unsubscribing and creating Rollup consolidation).
claimsVsReality.reality: Access enabled Slice to conduct undisclosed secondary data collection and monetization of user purchase history and sensitive financial/health information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unrollme represented it would not touch users' personal emails (Paragraphs 11–12) but granted Slice access to harvest entire e-receipts containing personal financial and health data.
violations: Unrollme represented it would not touch users' personal emails (Paragraphs 11–12) but granted Slice access to harvest entire e-receipts containing personal financial and health data.
Unrollme represented access was required only to scan for subscriptions (Paragraph 13) but failed to disclose it also enabled Slice to collect and sell personal purchase data to third parties.

Customer support provided false assurances that Unrollme only accessed subscription emails and did not see personal content, despite knowing Slice was capturing full e-receipt bodies with sensitive information.

outcome: FTC issued Complaint against Unrollme alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges two counts: (1) false representation that Unrollme would not touch personal emails, and (2) failure to disclose material information about secondary data use by Slice. The case alleges that over 20,000 consumers were deceived by early messages and over 35,000 by later messages into granting email access. Unrollme was required to comply with FTC orders; final settlement details are not included in this complaint document.
companyNow: Unrollme remained operational under Slice Technologies ownership following the FTC complaint. The company made privacy disclosures more explicit after May 2017 in response to FTC concerns.
dataType: Email content, e-receipts, billing addresses, shipping addresses, credit card information, health-related product/service purchases
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three major nationwide consumer reporting agencies in the United States, operating since 1899. It collects, processes, and maintains credit and personal information on over 200 million U.S. consumers, providing credit reports, credit scores, and related services to businesses and direct consumers.
companyLongDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three major nationwide consumer reporting agencies in the United States, operating since 1899. It collects, processes, and maintains credit and personal information on over 200 million U.S. consumers, providing credit reports, credit scores, and related services to businesses and direct consumers.
caseDescription: Equifax failed to patch a known critical vulnerability in its ACIS Dispute Portal system for over four months, allowing attackers to steal personal information from approximately 147 million consumers. The company's security practices were inadequate across patch management, network segmentation, access controls, encryption, and intrusion detection. Equifax also made false claims about its security safeguards in privacy policies.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security safeguards—including patch management, encryption, access controls, network segmentation, and intrusion detection—resulted in unauthorized access and massive personal data breach, fitting the Solove category of inadequate information security controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Equifax failed to patch a critical Apache Struts vulnerability for over four months despite receiving alerts.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers exploited the unpatched vulnerability to steal personal information from 147 million consumers including SSNs, names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax maintains privacy policies stating 'We are committed to protecting the security of your information through procedures and technologies designed for this purpose' and 'We limit access to your personal information to employees having a reasonable need to access this information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax failed to patch known critical vulnerabilities for months, stored sensitive data in plain text, did not segment databases, left credentials unencrypted in accessible file shares, and allowed widespread employee and contractor access to sensitive data without business justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax maintains 'reasonable physical, technical, and procedural safeguards to help protect your personal information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax lacked patch management enforcement, relied on misconfigured vulnerability scanners, had no network segmentation, no encryption for SSNs, minimal intrusion detection on legacy systems, and no file integrity monitoring—enabling a 4-month undetected breach affecting 147 million consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. Acts are unfair if they cause or are likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security measures (patch management, encryption, network segmentation, access controls, intrusion detection) to protect 147 million consumers' sensitive personal information, causing substantial injury through identity theft risk.
violations: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security measures (patch management, encryption, network segmentation, access controls, intrusion detection) to protect 147 million consumers' sensitive personal information, causing substantial injury through identity theft risk.

Equifax represented in privacy policies that it limits access to personal information to employees with reasonable need and maintains reasonable physical, technical, and procedural safeguards, when in fact it did neither.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including identifying risks, designing safeguards to control risks, and regularly testing/monitoring effectiveness.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to implement reasonable patch management procedures, resulting in a critical vulnerability remaining unpatched for 4+ months despite receiving government alerts.
violations: Equifax failed to implement reasonable patch management procedures, resulting in a critical vulnerability remaining unpatched for 4+ months despite receiving government alerts.
Equifax failed to implement network segmentation, allowing attackers who breached ACIS to easily access dozens of unrelated databases.
Equifax stored 145+ million SSNs and other sensitive data in plain text instead of encrypted form, contrary to its own policies.
Equifax failed to implement intrusion detection controls on legacy ACIS systems, preventing discovery of attackers on the network for months.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Relief against Equifax Inc., alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act and the Safeguards Rule. The complaint sought permanent injunctive relief, restitution, refund of monies paid, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The document filed on July 22, 2019, initiates the enforcement action; the final settlement and specific remedial requirements would be determined through subsequent proceedings.
companyNow: Equifax remains one of the three major consumer reporting agencies in the United States. Following the 2017 breach and subsequent enforcement actions, the company has implemented significant remediation and security improvements, though it continues to face litigation and regulatory oversight.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, physical addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses, payment card numbers and expiration dates
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act, Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices

company: Zala Megyei Kormányhivatal Keszthelyi Járási Földhivatall (Keszthely Land Registry Office)
companyDescription: The Keszthely Land Registry Office is a government agency responsible for managing property registrations and land records in Keszthely, Hungary, operating under the Zala County Government Administration.
companyLongDescription: The Keszthely Land Registry Office is a government agency responsible for managing property registrations and land records in Keszthely, Hungary, operating under the Zala County Government Administration.
caseDescription: A Hungarian land registry office distributed a single property registration decision to 41 property owners, each containing the full decision with personal data of all others affected. This exposed sensitive financial and personal data of property owners to unauthorized third parties, violating data minimization and transparency principles.
violationSummary: The defendant unlawfully increased the accessibility of personal data by sending comprehensive decision documents containing third-party personal data to unrelated property owners, violating data minimization and transparency principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Keszthely Land Registry Office distributed a single decision document to all 41 affected property owners containing the full personal.
whyTheyWereWrong: Forty property owners' sensitive personal and financial information—including names, addresses, birth years, borrowed amounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office claimed that applicable regulations contained no detailed requirements for delivery of decisions ('a vonatkozó jogszabályok nem tartalmaznak részlet-rendelkezéseket').
claimsVsReality.reality: FVM Regulation §99 explicitly required excerpt-based delivery when a decision contained multiple measures not affecting all parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office claimed it could not extract excerpts from the computerized decision ('a számítógép generálja, így az ilyen formátumú döntésből nem lehet kivonatos határozatot nyomtatni').
claimsVsReality.reality: The system manual made no provision for automated excerpt generation in multi-property decisions, but the regulation explicitly required excerpt delivery regardless of technical constraints.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently with respect to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The land registry provided misleading information to complainants, stating that regulations contained no detailed delivery requirements when FVM Regulation §99 explicitly required excerpt delivery.
violations: The land registry provided misleading information to complainants, stating that regulations contained no detailed delivery requirements when FVM Regulation §99 explicitly required excerpt delivery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: The office sent complete decisions containing all 41 property owners' personal data to each recipient when only individual excerpts were necessary and legally required.
violations: The office sent complete decisions containing all 41 property owners' personal data to each recipient when only individual excerpts were necessary and legally required.

regulatoryFindings.act: FVM Regulation §99 requires that when a decision contains multiple measures not affecting all parties, only the relevant excerpt must be delivered to each affected party.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office delivered the complete 41-property decision to all recipients instead of extracting and sending individual property excerpts as required.
violations: The office delivered the complete 41-property decision to all recipients instead of extracting and sending individual property excerpts as required.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) upheld the complainants' request, finding the land registry violated data minimization and transparency principles under GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(c). The office was ordered to pay a 600,000 HUF administrative fine and 10,000 HUF compensation for exceeding the 120-day processing deadline. The authority found the violation resulted from negligent staff error and improper software use rather than systemic policy, but mandated compliance with excerpt delivery requirements going forward. The decision is subject to administrative review before the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
companyNow: The Keszthely Land Registry Office remains part of Hungary's Zala County Government Administration, operating under land registration oversight. The office has acknowledged the violation and modified practices to comply with excerpt-based delivery requirements.
dataType: Names, birth years, mothers' names, addresses, loan amounts, loan currency, loan purpose
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
GDPR Art. 58(2)(b) – Corrective power to admonish

companyDescription: XFERA MÓVILES, S.A., operating under the brand MASMOVIL, is a Spanish virtual mobile network operator and broadband service provider offering combined telecommunications services including landline, mobile, and internet access to residential and business customers.
companyLongDescription: XFERA MÓVILES, S.A., operating under the brand MASMOVIL, is a Spanish virtual mobile network operator and broadband service provider offering combined telecommunications services including landline, mobile, and internet access to residential and business customers.
caseDescription: XFERA modified a customer's service contract without consent, replacing her personal details with those of an unknown third party while retaining her bank account for billing. The unauthorized change disabled her landline and internet access. The company failed to verify identity during the modification process, indicating lax security procedures.
violationSummary: Company failed to implement reasonable security measures to verify identity before altering personal data in customer contracts. Lack of procedural safeguards allowed unauthorized modification of sensitive personal information linked to financial accounts.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: XFERA modified a customer's contract without consent, changing the account holder's name and address to a third party while keeping her bank account.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer lost access to essential services for months, experienced unauthorized charges to her bank account, and suffered financial.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that a third party acting with fraudulent intent caused the identity change, making the infraction attributable to external bad faith rather than company negligence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal incident documentation showed the operator directly modified customer data in the system without verifying identity, despite receiving different information from the customer during the call—indicating company operational failure, not external fraud alone.

claimsVsReality.claim: XFERA invoked pendency of criminal proceedings as grounds to suspend the administrative procedure due to 'prejudicial' penal jurisdiction.
claimsVsReality.reality: The administrative violation (unlawful data processing without consent) and potential criminal charges (fraud, forgery) involve different legal goods, different actors, and different standards—no true identity of subject, fact, and legal ground exists to require suspension.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1(a) requires that personal data treatment be lawful and based on at least one legal ground, including explicit informed consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: XFERA processed and modified the complainant's personal data (name, address, DNI, bank details) without her knowledge or consent, associating her financial account with a third party's identity.
violations: XFERA processed and modified the complainant's personal data (name, address, DNI, bank details) without her knowledge or consent, associating her financial account with a third party's identity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: XFERA altered contract terms and personal data without any transparent communication or authorization from the customer, creating a substantial imbalance in the contractual relationship.
violations: XFERA altered contract terms and personal data without any transparent communication or authorization from the customer, creating a substantial imbalance in the contractual relationship.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires implementation of appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company operator made direct changes to customer records based on unverified telephone information, failing to implement identity verification procedures before processing modifications to sensitive personal data.
violations: Company operator made direct changes to customer records based on unverified telephone information, failing to implement identity verification procedures before processing modifications to sensitive personal data.

outcome: AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €60,000 on XFERA for violation of GDPR Article 6.1(a). The decision became final and executable. The company was required to make payment within the prescribed voluntary payment period. The decision is subject to appeal before the National Court (Audiencia Nacional) within two months.
companyNow: MASMOVIL/XFERA continues operating as a Spanish telecommunications provider. The 2019 enforcement action prompted internal implementation of training measures and external advisory services for staff involved in commercial processes.
dataType: Personal identifiers, financial data, address, email, phone number, DNI, bank account details

companyDescription: ClixSense was a crowdsourced task and survey platform owned by James V. Grago Jr. and operating as a sole proprietorship in Hampstead, North Carolina. Users earned money by viewing advertisements, completing online surveys, and performing microtasks. The company generated $6.7 million in revenue in 2015 and $9.1 million in 2016.
companyLongDescription: ClixSense was a crowdsourced task and survey platform owned by James V. Grago Jr. and operating as a sole proprietorship in Hampstead, North Carolina. Users earned money by viewing advertisements, completing online surveys, and performing microtasks. The company generated $6.7 million in revenue in 2015 and $9.1 million in 2016.
caseDescription: ClixSense operated a platform where users earned money viewing ads and completing surveys. The company publicly promised to use 'latest security and encryption techniques' but actually stored 6.6 million consumers' personal data—including Social Security numbers—in clear text with no encryption. A 2016 data breach exposed 2.7 million users' records after hackers exploited unreasonable security practices.
violationSummary: ClixSense failed to implement reasonable and necessary security measures to protect personal data at rest and in transit. Data was stored unencrypted despite promises of encryption. This constitutes insecurity under the Solove taxonomy because the company's negligent security practices created unreasonable risk of unauthorised access and exposure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: ClixSense stored 6.6 million users' personal data including Social Security numbers in unencrypted clear text, lacked network segregation, access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers accessed and publicly posted personal information for 2.7 million consumers including 500,000 U.S.

claimsVsReality.claim: ClixSense utilizes the latest security and encryption techniques to ensure the security of your account information.
claimsVsReality.reality: ClixSense stored all personal information—names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, passwords—in clear text with zero encryption from at least 2011 through 2016.

claimsVsReality.claim: We view protection of users' privacy as a very important community principle.
claimsVsReality.reality: ClixSense failed to perform basic security measures, did not test for vulnerabilities, lacked intrusion detection, did not segregate networks, and allowed employees to store credentials in plain text on personal devices.

claimsVsReality.claim: You and your information are one of our most important assets.
claimsVsReality.reality: 6.6 million consumers' sensitive personal information was exposed in a data breach; approximately 2.7 million records including Social Security numbers were publicly posted on a hacking forum.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ClixSense represented it utilized 'latest security and encryption techniques' but stored all personal data in clear text with zero encryption
violations: ClixSense represented it utilized 'latest security and encryption techniques' but stored all personal data in clear text with zero encryption
ClixSense failed to implement vulnerability testing, intrusion detection, access controls, or network segregation—basic industry standards since 2013

ClixSense engaged in unreasonable security practices including storing plain-text credentials in employee email, failing to change default credentials, and downloading untrusted software without isolation

outcome: On June 19, 2019, the FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive and unfair practices. The document is the initial complaint filed; no final settlement or order is shown in this complaint document itself. Typical FTC outcomes in such cases involve consent orders requiring reasonable security safeguards, data minimisation, privacy policy updates, and ongoing compliance monitoring. Final resolution would be documented in a separate order.
companyNow: ClixSense was operational as of the complaint date (June 2019). No public information provided in this document regarding current status post-enforcement.
dataType: Full names, physical addresses, dates of birth, gender, email addresses, usernames, passwords, security question answers, Social Security numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Count I: Deception – Misrepresentation about encryption
Count II: Deception – Misrepresentation about latest security techniques
Count III: Unfairness – Failure to employ reasonable security practices

companyDescription: The Travel Corporation (2011) Pte. Ltd. is a travel services company based in Singapore that offers travel packages both directly to Singapore customers and through third-party travel agencies.
companyLongDescription: The Travel Corporation (2011) Pte. Ltd. is a travel services company based in Singapore that offers travel packages both directly to Singapore customers and through third-party travel agencies.
caseDescription: A new employee of The Travel Corporation lost an unencrypted portable hard disk containing personal data of 18,630 customers, employees, and suppliers. The organisation had failed to implement adequate security measures for portable storage devices and had not appointed a data protection officer as required by law.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by not implementing password protection or encryption for portable storage devices, and by failing to establish operational frameworks to enforce written policies. This represents a systemic failure in data security practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: An employee took an unencrypted portable hard disk containing personal data of 18,630 customers, employees, and suppliers out of the office on 25 July 2018.
whyTheyWereWrong: 18,630 individuals' sensitive personal data including names, contact details, passport numbers, and NRIC numbers were exposed to potential identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation had a Portable Computer and Storage Devices Policy stipulating that portable devices must have designated custodians
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy existed on paper only; no operational frameworks, procedures, or enforcement mechanisms were in place to actually implement the policy in business units. Employees received only verbal instructions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organisation had guidelines in its Acceptable User Policy and Information Sensitivity Policy requiring password protection and data encryption
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite clear guidelines, the organisation did not implement any password protection or encryption policies for its portable storage devices, including the hard disk that was lost.

claimsVsReality.claim: The hard disk was misplaced by a new employee who should have understood security requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation had failed to establish adequate systems, training, or supervision to ensure compliance; the employee was not provided with documented procedures or enforcement mechanisms to follow.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to implement password protection or data encryption for portable storage devices despite having guidelines in its Acceptable User Policy and Information Sensitivity Policy requiring such measures
violations: Organisation failed to implement password protection or data encryption for portable storage devices despite having guidelines in its Acceptable User Policy and Information Sensitivity Policy requiring such measures

Organisation had a Portable Computer and Storage Devices Policy requiring designated custodians but failed to establish operational frameworks or procedures to effectively implement this policy in business units
Organisation relied solely on verbal instructions rather than enforced documented procedures to prevent employees from removing portable storage devices containing personal data from office premises

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 11(3) of the PDPA requires organisations to designate one or more individuals responsible for ensuring compliance with the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the data breach incident on 25 July 2018, only appointing one on 22 October 2018 after notification to the Commission
violations: Organisation failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the data breach incident on 25 July 2018, only appointing one on 22 October 2018 after notification to the Commission

outcome: The Commissioner found the organisation in breach of PDPA s.24 and s.11(3). The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $12,000 SGD within 30 days. The Commissioner considered mitigating factors including: prompt notification and cooperation with investigations, timely remediation measures (ceasing portable device use and implementing cloud-based storage), active implementation of external auditor recommendations, and absence of complaints. The organisation was not subject to additional directions due to remedial measures taken.
companyNow: The Travel Corporation (2011) Pte. Ltd. continues to operate as a travel package provider in Singapore, having remediated its data protection practices post-incident by implementing cloud-based storage systems and appointing a data protection officer.
dataType: Names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, postal addresses, passport numbers, NRIC numbers, office contact information

companyDescription: SecurTest, Inc. is a Florida-based background screening services company that processes personal data for employment and HR purposes, including transfers from European jurisdictions.
companyLongDescription: SecurTest, Inc. is a Florida-based background screening services company that processes personal data for employment and HR purposes, including transfers from European jurisdictions.
caseDescription: SecurTest falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks on its website from September 2017 to July 2018, despite not having completed the certification process. The company initiated an application in September 2017 but did not finish the required steps until August 2018, after FTC staff contacted them about the deceptive statements.
violationSummary: The misrepresentation disclosed false information about Privacy Shield certification, directly affecting how consumers understood the protections for their cross-border data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: SecurTest falsely claimed on its website from September 2017 to July 2018 that it was certified under the EU-U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union and Swiss residents transferred their personal data to SecurTest under the mistaken belief their information would receive legally-mandated privacy protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: SecurTest, Inc. has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: SecurTest had not completed the certification process and did not self-certify to Commerce until August 31, 2018, despite these claims made from September 2017 to July 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: SecurTest complies with the EU-US Privacy Shield Framework and the Swiss-US Privacy Shield Framework.
claimsVsReality.reality: SecurTest was not a participant in either framework during the period it made these claims, though it had initiated an application in September 2017.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SecurTest represented that it had self-certified to the Privacy Shield frameworks when it had not completed certification, making material misrepresentations about the legal framework protecting personal data transfers from the EU and Switzerland.
violations: SecurTest represented that it had self-certified to the Privacy Shield frameworks when it had not completed certification, making material misrepresentations about the legal framework protecting personal data transfers from the EU and Switzerland.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. SecurTest corrected its website statements and completed Privacy Shield certification on August 31, 2018, after FTC staff intervention. The complaint was issued on August 12, 2019.
companyNow: Unknown current status; company achieved Privacy Shield certification in August 2018 and appears to continue offering background screening services.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU and Switzerland (unspecified types)

company: Tan Tock Seng Hospital Pte. Ltd.
companyDescription: Tan Tock Seng Hospital Pte. Ltd. is a public hospital in Singapore providing inpatient, outpatient, and emergency medical services.
companyLongDescription: Tan Tock Seng Hospital Pte. Ltd. is a public hospital in Singapore providing inpatient, outpatient, and emergency medical services.
caseDescription: Tan Tock Seng Hospital sent appointment reschedule letters containing patient personal data to wrong addresses due to staff error in a mail merge operation. The staff only sorted the address field in a spreadsheet without sorting corresponding patient records, causing misalignment. The organisation failed to conduct any quality checks on the generated letters before sending.
violationSummary: Patient personal data was exposed to unintended recipients due to misdirected mail, resulting from inadequate security controls and lack of verification procedures.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Staff manually generated appointment reschedule letters using mail merge in Microsoft Word by sorting only the address field in a spreadsheet.
whyTheyWereWrong: 85 patients' sensitive personal data including names, NRIC numbers, and appointment details were mailed to wrong addresses, exposing this information to unintended recipients.

claimsVsReality.claim: Letters were generated using standard automatic processes with data extraction from a spreadsheet
claimsVsReality.reality: On 12 February 2019, staff manually generated letters using mail merge but only sorted the address field without sorting corresponding patient records, breaking the data alignment

claimsVsReality.claim: Quality assurance was part of standard procedures for sensitive correspondence
claimsVsReality.reality: No checks were conducted on generation and printing; no verification occurred before dispatch to patients

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data through reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Hospital failed to conduct any checks or verification on letter generation and printing despite the manual processing being prone to error
violations: Hospital failed to conduct any checks or verification on letter generation and printing despite the manual processing being prone to error
No quality assurance procedures were in place despite staff handling sensitive patient data through a manual mail merge process
Simple random sampling of letters would have detected the misalignment and prevented or greatly reduced the number of affected individuals

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. The Commission issued a warning to the organisation. No compliance directions were required as the organisation has already implemented corrective measures addressing the security gap.
companyNow: Tan Tock Seng Hospital remains a major public hospital in Singapore. It has implemented corrective measures to address the security gaps identified in this case.
dataType: Patient names, NRIC numbers, appointment details

companyDescription: Learnaholic Pte. Ltd. was an IT vendor providing attendance-taking and e-learning systems to schools under contract with Singapore's Ministry of Education. The company also offered data upload and system maintenance services.
companyLongDescription: Learnaholic Pte. Ltd. was an IT vendor providing attendance-taking and e-learning systems to schools under contract with Singapore's Ministry of Education. The company also offered data upload and system maintenance services.
caseDescription: Learnaholic, an IT vendor providing attendance and e-learning systems to schools, failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect approximately 47,802 students, parents, and staff records. Multiple security lapses—including opening a firewall port without closing it, disabling password protection on remote access, and storing unencrypted personal data in employee email—created a vulnerability that was exploited by a hacker, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data including 372 minors' medical records.
violationSummary: The company failed to make reasonable security arrangements as required by PDPA s.24. Multiple independent and compounded security lapses created an easily exploitable vulnerability that resulted in unauthorised access and data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Installed remote desktop software without password protection, left a firewall port open for over a month.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 47,802 students, parents, and staff had their names, NRIC numbers, addresses, contact information, and medical records of 372 minors exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed it had disabled the input feature at the client side when using VNC Viewer software, preventing unauthorised changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disabling input at the client side only affected the organisation's own ability to make changes; a hacker connecting to the server could still make changes. Only disabling input at the server side would have prevented exploitation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation represented that the total number of affected individuals was 35,000 and that the vulnerability was discovered and fixed in end-April 2016.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PDPC determined the actual number of unique affected individuals was 47,802. Uncertainty exists about when the vulnerability was truly remediated; the Commissioner gave benefit of the doubt but initially based the penalty on February 2017 (when SPF notified the company).

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation stated it had requested schools to upload data themselves, password-protect attachments, and that the preferred school practice was to comply with security guidelines.
claimsVsReality.reality: Evidence showed the preferred practice of many schools was to send unencrypted personal data to the organisation, and the organisation's own policy requiring password protection was observed only in breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed emails with personal data were deleted when no longer required and that the hacker accessed many attachments only because he had access to the email account for 3 months.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation admitted that emails with personal data were retained for months to address school enquiries. The data was stored unencrypted and without time-limited retention, facilitating extended hacker access once credentials were compromised.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation represented that medical data of minors was non-sensitive in nature, consisting only of conditions like colour vision and allergies.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under PDPA and PDPC guidance, medical data and personal data of minors (persons under 21) are treated as sensitive in nature, requiring higher standards of protection regardless of the type of medical condition.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to secure remote access: opened a firewall port and disabled password protection on VNC Server, creating an easily exploitable vulnerability
violations: Failed to secure remote access: opened a firewall port and disabled password protection on VNC Server, creating an easily exploitable vulnerability
Left the vulnerability exposed for over one month (March to end-April 2016) without notification to the school or remediation
Placed configuration files containing login credentials in an accessible folder that was synced across multiple network clusters
Stored sensitive personal data in unencrypted form in an employee's email account without deletion protocols or encryption
Did not inform the school of critical firewall configuration changes made during troubleshooting
Failed to implement basic data retention controls: kept bulk personal data in email indefinitely rather than securely archiving or deleting after use

outcome: The Commissioner found Learnaholic in breach of PDPA s.24 and imposed a financial penalty of SGD 60,000 payable within 30 days. The company was directed to implement comprehensive remediation: change all passwords, activate two-factor authentication, delete personal data from email accounts, implement automatic deletion scripts in the Update Folder to prevent sensitive files from being synced to clusters, and establish new protocols requiring deletion of emails containing personal data once action is taken. The Commissioner gave the company credit for swift remedial actions taken after discovery by the Singapore Police Force, including activation of 2FA, deletion of stored data, and implementation of automated security controls.
companyNow: Unknown current operational status. The company implemented significant remedial measures following the breach, including two-factor authentication, automated file deletion scripts, and revised data retention practices.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, contact numbers, email addresses, home addresses, medical information (minors)
legalBasisViolated: PDPA s.24 (Protection Obligation – reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: NHS Highland is a territorial health authority in Scotland providing healthcare services to the Highland region. It operates multiple clinical services including specialist and community health provision.
companyLongDescription: NHS Highland is a territorial health authority in Scotland providing healthcare services to the Highland region. It operates multiple clinical services including specialist and community health provision.
caseDescription: NHS Highland sent an email to 37 patients without using BCC, exposing all email addresses to all recipients. The email list revealed individuals connected to HIV services, allowing recipients to infer sensitive health status. The organisation lacked adequate technical and organisational measures to prevent such disclosure and had not obtained proper consent for sending emails on behalf of patient groups.
violationSummary: Email addresses were exposed to unintended recipients through failure to use adequate security measures (BCC), resulting in unauthorised disclosure of personal data linked to sensitive health information.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: NHS Highland sent a group email to 37 patients without using the Blind Carbon Copy option, revealing all recipients' email addresses (which included names) to every recipient.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' email addresses and names were exposed to all other recipients, allowing them to identify which individuals were accessing HIV services.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCC is accepted best practice for group communications
claimsVsReality.reality: BCC provided insufficient security; email recall failed, exposing 37 recipients' addresses and enabling identification of individuals accessing HIV services

claimsVsReality.claim: Standard email policy adequately addressed group communication security
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy was insufficient for sensitive patient communications; no consent was in place, and the sensitivity of health-related email exposure was not considered

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) UK GDPR requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised processing and accidental loss or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: NHS Highland relied on BCC for group communications without considering it the most secure method; email recall attempts failed, leaving data permanently exposed
violations: NHS Highland relied on BCC for group communications without considering it the most secure method; email recall attempts failed, leaving data permanently exposed

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) UK GDPR requires controllers and processors implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCC was standard practice in induction materials but not the most appropriate way to manage emails to sensitive patient groups; no alternative secure methods were implemented
violations: BCC was standard practice in induction materials but not the most appropriate way to manage emails to sensitive patient groups; no alternative secure methods were implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 25 UK GDPR requires controllers implement appropriate technical and organisational measures at determination and time of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent for NHS Highland to send emails on behalf of patient groups was not in place and did not explicitly cover non-medical communications; sensitivity of HIV-related email addresses was not considered when arrangement was established
violations: Consent for NHS Highland to send emails on behalf of patient groups was not in place and did not explicitly cover non-medical communications; sensitivity of HIV-related email addresses was not considered when arrangement was established

outcome: ICO issued a reprimand to NHS Highland for violations of Articles 5(1)(f), 25, and 32(1) of UK GDPR. No administrative penalty was imposed under the ICO's revised public sector enforcement approach (June 2022). NHS Highland was required to provide progress updates within three months on recommendations including: reviewing data protection and email policies; conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments for group emails containing special category data; and implementing regular UK GDPR training. NHS Highland has ceased sending group emails to patients and added recommendations to its Information Governance action plan.
companyNow: NHS Highland continues to operate as a territorial health authority in the Scottish NHS. Following the incident, it has ceased the practice of sending group emails to patients and implemented enhanced information governance measures.
dataType: email addresses, special category data (health data relating to HIV services)
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 25 – Data Protection by Design and Default
UK GDPR Article 32(1) – Security of Processing

companyDescription: Ninja Logistics Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based logistics company providing packaging, delivery, and tracking services to retailers and their end customers. The company operates a web-based parcel tracking system.
companyLongDescription: Ninja Logistics Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based logistics company providing packaging, delivery, and tracking services to retailers and their end customers. The company operates a web-based parcel tracking system.
caseDescription: Ninja Logistics operated a parcel tracking webpage with sequential Tracking IDs that could be easily guessed or manipulated. The company was aware of this security vulnerability from launch in 2014 but failed to implement effective authentication controls for nearly 2 years. Over 1.2 million customers' names, addresses, and signatures were exposed to unauthorized access.
violationSummary: The Tracking IDs, especially sequential ones, were easily manipulated to expose customer personal data. The vulnerability allowed unauthorized access and disclosure of identifying information (names, addresses, signatures) to an indefinite audience without authentication.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Operated a parcel tracking website for approximately 2 years using only sequential Tracking IDs as sole authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1.26 million customers' names, delivery addresses, and signatures were exposed to unauthorized access for nearly 2 years because the company knew Tracking IDs could be easily manipulated.

claimsVsReality.claim: Keeping personal data accessible was 'well-meaning and intended to be an additional feature to differentiate from competitors' and allowed retailers/customers to access information without contacting the company
claimsVsReality.reality: The feature lacked basic security controls; personal data remained accessible to anyone who could guess sequential Tracking IDs, exposing 1.26 million individuals to unauthorized access for ~2 years

claimsVsReality.claim: Some retailers require longer Tracking ID validity periods to respond to customer feedback and conduct investigations
claimsVsReality.reality: Delivery information typically needed for weeks post-delivery, not years; company had accumulated data from 1.26 million individuals over ~2 years, demonstrating unreasonable retention

claimsVsReality.claim: Names in exposed data are 'considerably less sensitive and complete than other published cases' and no actual unauthorized access occurred
claimsVsReality.reality: Combined with addresses and signatures, names enabled identity theft and fraud; vulnerability persisted without controls, making actual exfiltration technically easy

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement effective second-layer authentication despite knowing Tracking IDs could be manipulated from system launch
violations: Failed to implement effective second-layer authentication despite knowing Tracking IDs could be manipulated from system launch
Did not remove completed delivery records containing customer names, addresses, and signatures after delivery completion
Allowed 1,262,861 customers' personal data to remain accessible through guessable sequential Tracking IDs for approximately 2 years

outcome: Commissioner found breach of PDPA s.24. Ninja Logistics directed to: (1) Pay SGD 90,000 financial penalty within 30 days; (2) Implement reasonable validity period for Tracking IDs (14 days post-delivery, potentially extending to 45 days) within 30 days; (3) Engaged Crest-certified security firm for security framework and PDPA training; (4) Removed customer addresses from 'Pending Pickup' and 'On Vehicle for Delivery' statuses; (5) Engaged law firm to improve data protection policies. No evidence of actual data exfiltration found, but vulnerability exposed significant number of individuals to risk.
companyNow: Ninja Logistics continues operations as a logistics provider in Singapore. The company implemented the directed security measures including Tracking ID expiration (14 days) and is considering extension to 45 days based on retailer feedback.
dataType: Names, addresses, signatures, delivery tracking information

companyDescription: i-vic International Pte. Ltd. is an IT services and business process outsourcing company that was contracted by the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) to manage IT infrastructure and customer relationship management systems for a government work trial programme administered on behalf of Workforce Singapore.
companyLongDescription: i-vic International Pte. Ltd. is an IT services and business process outsourcing company that was contracted by the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) to manage IT infrastructure and customer relationship management systems for a government work trial programme administered on behalf of Workforce Singapore.
caseDescription: i-vic International, a data processor managing a work trial programme's IT infrastructure, failed to adequately test its automated email system. On 1 April 2019, a code error caused the system to attach confidential documents containing personal data of three individuals to emails sent to nine unintended recipients. The organisation had not tested how its email generation system would behave when queued during concurrent batch processes, despite knowing that concurrent processing occurred monthly.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (testing and code validation) to prevent unauthorised disclosure of personal data, resulting in a direct breach of confidentiality and exposure of sensitive information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: i-vic failed to test how its automated email system would behave when processing queued emails during concurrent batch operations.
whyTheyWereWrong: Three individuals' highly sensitive personal data—including names, NRIC numbers, signatures, residential addresses, bank accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: i-vic International tested the code of the Automated Email Generation Process
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation only tested the basic code but did not test how the code behaved when email generation instructions were queued during the concurrent Reward Programme Process that ran on the 1st of each month, which was when the actual incident occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Emails would be processed and sent individually and not queued during the Reward Programme Process
claimsVsReality.reality: Due to a code error in the batch processing logic, emails were queued and then processed as a batch with incorrect file attachment logic, causing confidential documents to be attached to wrong recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: i-vic International failed to put in place diligent and properly scoped testing of the Automated Email Generation Process, specifically failing to test how the code behaved when instructions were queued during the concurrent Reward Programme Process that ran monthly on the 1st of each month.
violations: i-vic International failed to put in place diligent and properly scoped testing of the Automated Email Generation Process, specifically failing to test how the code behaved when instructions were queued during the concurrent Reward Programme Process that ran monthly on the 1st of each month.

The organisation knew the Automated Email Generation Process could not run while the Reward Programme Process was executing, but did not test the impact of this constraint on email queueing and attachment logic.
This testing failure resulted in a code error that caused wrong documents containing personal data of three individuals to be attached to emails sent to nine unintended recipients.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found that i-vic International contravened section 24 of the PDPA by failing to implement reasonable security arrangements through inadequate testing. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $6,000 within 30 days. No further directions were issued as the organisation had already remediated the code error and rewrote relevant code to enable automated encryption of attachments and prevent incorrect file attachment. Interest would accrue at the Rules of Court rate on any unpaid balance.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, signatures, residential addresses, mobile numbers, email addresses, age, race, bank account numbers, academic qualifications, work trial company details, work experience

companyDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry Pte. Ltd. is a ferry service operator in Singapore providing passenger transportation services.
companyLongDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry Pte. Ltd. is a ferry service operator in Singapore providing passenger transportation services.
caseDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry's email account was compromised by malware due to poor password management practices. An email account password was shared by 11 employees and not changed for 3 years, enabling the malware infection to send phishing emails to customers. Although only individual customer data was disclosed to each recipient, the organisation failed to implement reasonable security measures required under data protection law.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically inadequate password management and access controls that fell below what is reasonably required under the Protection Obligation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Horizon Fast Ferry shared a single email account password among 11 employees and failed to change it for nearly 3 years, allowing a malware-infected computer to send phishing emails to customers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Three customers received phishing emails impersonating the company due to weak password management, exposing their personal booking information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation implemented various security measures prior to the incident such as regularly updating antivirus software
claimsVsReality.reality: While antivirus was updated regularly, the organisation had critically failed to manage password security—the email account password was shared among 11 employees and unchanged for 3 years

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or under their control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Password to the email account was shared by 11 employees and had not been changed for almost 3 years, falling short of reasonable security standards
violations: Password to the email account was shared by 11 employees and had not been changed for almost 3 years, falling short of reasonable security standards
Despite regular antivirus updates, the organisation failed to implement adequate access controls and password management practices

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA for failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. A warning was issued to the organisation. No monetary penalty was imposed given the limited scope of harm (3 customers affected, no cross-customer data disclosure), but the organisation must implement improved password management and access controls going forward.
dataType: Customer contact information and booking data

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is a major telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services in Singapore. The company developed the 'My Singtel' mobile application to enable customers to manage their accounts and service plans.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is a major telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services in Singapore. The company developed the 'My Singtel' mobile application to enable customers to manage their accounts and service plans.
caseDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited's mobile app contained a design vulnerability (Direct Object Reference Vulnerability) in its API that allowed unauthorized access to customer account details and billing information. An anonymous informant discovered the flaw, which exposed approximately 330,000 customers' personal data to potential unauthorized disclosure. The company failed to implement proper input validation despite having commissioned security penetration tests and receiving professional advice on such vulnerabilities.
violationSummary: The company failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, and disclosure of personal data. The Direct Object Reference Vulnerability was a known, well-documented security risk that should have been detected and prevented during the design phase.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Telecommunications failed to validate API parameters in its Mobile App, allowing attackers to intercept and modify customer identifiers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 330,000 customers' names, billing addresses, account numbers, phone numbers, and service usage information were exposed to unauthorized access because the company did not implement.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that exploiting the Direct Object Reference Vulnerability was 'not something that a normal user of the App would attempt' and required the attacker to be 'technically competent'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commissioner found that anyone with basic working knowledge of how mobile apps communicate with servers through APIs could have exploited the vulnerability, and the necessary tools and software were freely available online.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company represented that the 2015 penetration test vulnerabilities were specific to input fields only, not non-input fields.
claimsVsReality.reality: A review of the 2015 Penetration Test Report showed that both input and non-input fields were affected by Direct Object Reference vulnerabilities, and the company should have conducted a comprehensive code review.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that not all 330,000 customers' data was put at risk, since the attacker would need the correct combination of mobile number, billing account number, ID, and billing cycle date.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commissioner found that any technically competent attacker could have systematically accessed all 330,000 customer records, as the vulnerability allowed parameter manipulation during authenticated sessions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Singapore Telecommunications Limited failed to implement input validation on API parameters in its Mobile App design, allowing the Direct Object Reference Vulnerability to exist
violations: Singapore Telecommunications Limited failed to implement input validation on API parameters in its Mobile App design, allowing the Direct Object Reference Vulnerability to exist
The company did not validate parameters against login credentials before performing requested operations, despite this being a well-known OWASP Top 10 security risk
Despite commissioning security penetration tests that identified similar vulnerabilities in October 2015, the company failed to conduct a comprehensive code review of all input and non-input fields
The company did not implement validation controls that could have prevented unauthorised access to personal data of approximately 330,000 customers

outcome: The Commissioner found Singapore Telecommunications Limited in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The company was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 25,000 within 30 days. The Commissioner did not impose additional remediation directions given that the company had already enhanced the API to tightly couple Mobile App user identifiers to authenticated sessions and implemented error message logging. The vulnerability has been fixed in the current version of the Mobile App.
companyNow: Singapore Telecommunications Limited continues to operate as a major telecommunications provider in Singapore. The company has remediated the API vulnerability and implemented enhanced security controls on its Mobile App.
dataType: Mobile phone number, billing address, billing account number, customer name, service plan information, data/talktime/SMS usage

companyDescription: NTUC Income Insurance Co-Operative Limited is an insurance cooperative in Singapore providing various insurance products to members and the general public.
companyLongDescription: NTUC Income Insurance Co-Operative Limited is an insurance cooperative in Singapore providing various insurance products to members and the general public.
caseDescription: NTUC Income's website enhancement on 10 July 2019 contained a coding error that caused personal data from 17 users' uploaded documents to be sent to 123 other users via automated acknowledgement emails. The error occurred because the application failed to properly reset file identifiers between users, causing documents from one user to be associated with subsequent users who did not upload files.
violationSummary: Personal data of one user group was disclosed to another group without consent due to inadequate security controls and code quality assurance processes, representing a breach of confidentiality.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Enhanced its website enquiry system on 10 July 2019 to allow users to upload supporting documents, but deployed the feature with a coding error that associated uploaded files with wrong users.
whyTheyWereWrong: 123 individuals received automated acknowledgement emails containing personal data of 17 other users, including names, policy numbers, premium amounts, sum assured, coverage periods.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website enhancement was ready for live deployment after manual code review
claimsVsReality.reality: A coding error in the variable assignment logic was not detected during manual code review and caused a significant data breach affecting 140 individuals

claimsVsReality.claim: Testing procedures adequately validated the file upload functionality
claimsVsReality.reality: Test scenarios did not include realistic situations where consecutive users had different file upload patterns, leaving the vulnerability undetected

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data against loss, unauthorised or accidental access, processing, use, modification, disclosure or other misuse.
