regulatoryFindings.description: NTUC Income failed to implement adequate code review processes to detect the variable assignment error in the website enhancement before deployment
violations: NTUC Income failed to implement adequate code review processes to detect the variable assignment error in the website enhancement before deployment
The organisation's testing procedures did not simulate the realistic scenarios where some users would upload files while others would not, allowing the flaw to reach production

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found NTUC Income in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA and issued a formal warning. No further directions were required as the organisation implemented corrective measures including replacing manual code review with automated tools (Crucible and SonarQube), establishing adequate test scenarios, and implementing test plans and reviews before IT system changes are deployed.
companyNow: NTUC Income Insurance Co-Operative Limited continues to operate as a major insurance provider in Singapore. The organisation has implemented enhanced code quality and testing procedures following this enforcement action.
dataType: Names, policy numbers, premium amounts, sum assured, period of coverage, email addresses, mailing addresses

companyDescription: The Baden-Württemberg Police Department is a state law enforcement agency responsible for policing in the German state of Baden-Württemberg. It operates under the Data Protection Authority (LfDI) of the state.
companyLongDescription: The Baden-Württemberg Police Department is a state law enforcement agency responsible for policing in the German state of Baden-Württemberg. It operates under the Data Protection Authority (LfDI) of the state.
caseDescription: A police officer unlawfully accessed vehicle registration data and telecommunications contact information from government databases using his official credentials for private purposes—to locate and contact a casual acquaintance without authorization. The LfDI imposed a fine on the officer personally, establishing that public sector employees are not immune from data protection sanctions when abusing access for private gain.
violationSummary: The officer obtained personal data through authorized government systems but repurposed it for an entirely unauthorized private purpose (locating and contacting a casual acquaintance), constituting secondary use without any valid legal basis or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A police officer used his official credentials to query government databases (ZEVIS and SARS) to obtain a private acquaintance's vehicle registration, personal details.
whyTheyWereWrong: The officer obtained and used personal data from government databases for private contact purposes without consent, exposing the victim to unsolicited contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Public sector employees are exempt from GDPR sanctions under LDSG §28.
claimsVsReality.reality: The exemption applies only to the employer authority itself; individual employees remain personally liable when acting outside official duties for purely private purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer processed personal data without any lawful basis or transparency, purely for private purposes unrelated to police duties.
violations: Officer processed personal data without any lawful basis or transparency, purely for private purposes unrelated to police duties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data collected for specified purposes to be processed only in ways compatible with those original purposes (purpose limitation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Data obtained through official police access was repurposed for private contact without any connection to law enforcement objectives.
violations: Data obtained through official police access was repurposed for private contact without any connection to law enforcement objectives.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6 requires a valid legal basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests) for any processing of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer had no legal basis; the private contact was neither authorized nor consented to by the data subject.
violations: Officer had no legal basis; the private contact was neither authorized nor consented to by the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: LDSG §28 establishes that sanctions under GDPR may not be applied to public authorities themselves, but this exemption does not protect individual employees acting outside their official duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer acted in purely personal capacity, not as an agent of the police authority, so the exemption for public authorities did not apply and personal liability was appropriate.
violations: Officer acted in purely personal capacity, not as an agent of the police authority, so the exemption for public authorities did not apply and personal liability was appropriate.

outcome: The LfDI imposed a fine of €1,400 on the police officer on 9 May 2019. The decision is legally final. The case establishes precedent that public sector employees cannot claim immunity when they abuse official data access for purely private purposes. The fine was calculated as a first offense affecting only one individual, within the maximum penalty framework of GDPR Art. 83(5). No remediation or monitoring was specified beyond the fine itself.
companyNow: The Baden-Württemberg Police Department continues as an operating law enforcement agency in Germany. This enforcement action prompted internal policy review regarding data access controls and employee training on data protection obligations.
dataType: Vehicle registration data, personal contact information, phone numbers (landline and mobile)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of valid legal basis
LDSG §28 – Prohibition on unauthorized processing by public sector employees

companyDescription: Aetna Inc. is a major health care insurance company headquartered in Hartford, Connecticut, providing health care services across the United States. The company was acquired by CVS Health Corporation in 2018 for approximately $70 billion.
companyLongDescription: Aetna Inc. is a major health care insurance company headquartered in Hartford, Connecticut, providing health care services across the United States. The company was acquired by CVS Health Corporation in 2018 for approximately $70 billion.
caseDescription: Aetna mailed settlement letters to approximately 1,991 California residents revealing HIV medication status through a transparent envelope window. The company failed to adequately protect the confidentiality of sensitive health information when transmitting it to a settlement administrator, causing unlawful disclosure of protected medical data.
violationSummary: The company breached its duty to maintain confidentiality of protected health information by disclosing HIV status through transparent envelope windows, directly compromising patient privacy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Aetna mailed settlement letters to 1,991 Californians in envelopes with enlarged, clear windows that visibly revealed through the window that recipients were taking HIV-related medication.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,991 individuals had their sensitive HIV medication status involuntarily exposed to postal workers, mail handlers, family members.

claimsVsReality.claim: Aetna's settlement letters would inform members about alternative pharmacy options for HIV medications in a manner consistent with legal compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The envelopes used transparent windows that exposed recipients' HIV medication use to anyone handling the mail, violating California's medical privacy laws.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 56.101(a) requires health care service plans to preserve the confidentiality of medical information they create, maintain, preserve, store, abandon, destroy, or dispose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna failed to maintain and preserve medical information in a manner that preserved confidentiality by providing HIV medication information without adequate protective measures to the settlement administrator
violations: Aetna failed to maintain and preserve medical information in a manner that preserved confidentiality by providing HIV medication information without adequate protective measures to the settlement administrator

regulatoryFindings.act: California Health & Safety Code § 120980 penalizes any person who negligently discloses results of an HIV test in a way that identifies the taker of the test.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna negligently disclosed HIV test results and medication information through transparent envelope windows in a manner that identified recipients to postal workers and others handling the mail
violations: Aetna negligently disclosed HIV test results and medication information through transparent envelope windows in a manner that identified recipients to postal workers and others handling the mail

regulatoryFindings.act: California Constitution Article 1 § 1 provides for a fundamental right of privacy, including protection of a person's HIV status.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna violated individuals' constitutional privacy rights by exposing HIV medication status through envelope design
violations: Aetna violated individuals' constitutional privacy rights by exposing HIV medication status through envelope design

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent business practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna engaged in unfair business practices by failing to implement basic confidentiality measures when mailing sensitive health information
violations: Aetna engaged in unfair business practices by failing to implement basic confidentiality measures when mailing sensitive health information

outcome: The complaint seeks injunctive relief to prevent future violations, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation of Civil Code § 56.101 and § 17200, recovery of investigation costs, and other equitable relief. The case was filed January 28, 2019 in San Bernardino Superior Court seeking to establish liability and obtain remedies for the privacy breach.
companyNow: Aetna Inc. continues to operate as a major health insurance provider and subsidiary of CVS Health Corporation (acquired 2018). The company remains subject to HIPAA and state privacy law compliance requirements.
dataType: HIV medication status, health data

companyDescription: SSA Group International Pte Ltd is an education and training organization offering course registration services.
companyLongDescription: SSA Group International Pte Ltd is an education and training organization offering course registration services.
caseDescription: SSA Group International Pte Ltd maintained a publicly accessible webpage containing 53 individuals' course registration information without authentication or security controls. The webpage was indexed by search engines and remained exposed for over a year without detection or security review.
violationSummary: The organization failed to adopt reasonable security safeguards (authentication, security reviews, vulnerability scanning) against unauthorized access, directly enabling public exposure of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SSA Group International Pte Ltd created and maintained a webpage containing 53 individuals' course registration information without authentication mechanisms.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed individuals' names, course titles, sponsorship types, and transaction dates were publicly searchable online for 18+ months, allowing anyone to discover.

claimsVsReality.claim: The webpage had not been easy to locate
claimsVsReality.reality: Online search of the 53 affected individuals' names produced the webpage's URL directly

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to adopt reasonable security measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access.
regulatoryFindings.description: SSA Group failed to implement authentication mechanisms to restrict access to the webpage
violations: SSA Group failed to implement authentication mechanisms to restrict access to the webpage
No formal security instructions were provided to the webpage developer during creation in April 2018
No security reviews, vulnerability scanning, or ongoing monitoring were conducted for the webpage since its creation

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to SSA Group International Pte Ltd for breach of section 24 PDPA. No monetary penalty was imposed. The organization has implemented corrective measures addressing security gaps, including authentication controls. No further directions were required as remediation was already completed.
dataType: Names, course titles, sponsorship type, referral source, transaction dates

company: Kecskemét Megyei Jogú Város Polgármesteri Hivatala (Mayor's Office of Kecskemét)
companyDescription: Kecskemét Megyei Jogú Város Polgármesteri Hivatala is the mayor's office and primary administrative authority for Kecskemét, a major Hungarian city. It handles government functions, whistleblower complaints, and public administration duties for the local municipality.
companyLongDescription: Kecskemét Megyei Jogú Város Polgármesteri Hivatala is the mayor's office and primary administrative authority for Kecskemét, a major Hungarian city. It handles government functions, whistleblower complaints, and public administration duties for the local municipality.
caseDescription: A Hungarian local government office illegally disclosed a whistleblower's personal data to the institution being reported, without legal basis or consent. The disclosure resulted in the whistleblower's wrongful termination from employment. The authority failed to protect the confidentiality of the whistleblower report as required by law.
violationSummary: The government office disclosed confidential whistleblower personal data to an unauthorized third party (the institution under investigation), violating explicit statutory protections for whistleblower anonymity and the requirement for legal basis under GDPR Article 6.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Shared a confidential whistleblower report containing the reporter's full personal data (name, email, phone) with the institution being reported, without anonymization or legal justification.
whyTheyWereWrong: The whistleblower lost their job after the employer learned of the complaint through this illegal disclosure, suffering severe financial.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office claimed the report could be shared under the Whistleblower Protection Act §3(4)(b) because information validity had not been questioned.
claimsVsReality.reality: The statute's exception for demonstrably malicious or false reports applies only when bad faith and falsity have been established through proper investigation—not merely when they have not been questioned. No such determination was made.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office stated the whistleblower's personal data were already known to the institution as the whistleblower's employer, so no unauthorized disclosure occurred.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the employer knew the individual, it did not previously know that person was the source of the confidential whistleblower complaint, nor did it have authorization to receive that sensitive report.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office unlawfully disclosed whistleblower personal data without legal basis (Article 6 grounds missing) and without transparency to the data subject.
violations: The office unlawfully disclosed whistleblower personal data without legal basis (Article 6 grounds missing) and without transparency to the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public task, or legitimate interest) for any data processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office had no lawful basis to share the whistleblower's name, email, and phone with the investigated institution. The exception for demonstrably malicious or false reports was not applicable here.
violations: The office had no lawful basis to share the whistleblower's name, email, and phone with the investigated institution. The exception for demonstrably malicious or false reports was not applicable here.

regulatoryFindings.act: Hungarian Whistleblower Protection Act §3(2)-(3) restricts sharing whistleblower personal data only to authorities with legal jurisdiction and duty of care, with explicit consent exception.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office shared the report with the institution under investigation (the whistleblower's own employer), which had no statutory authorization to receive it and was the subject of the complaint.
violations: The office shared the report with the institution under investigation (the whistleblower's own employer), which had no statutory authorization to receive it and was the subject of the complaint.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Articles 33-34 require notification of high-risk incidents and timely notice to affected individuals.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office complied with incident reporting to authorities but initially failed to understand and properly manage the severity of the breach until the employee inquired about data exposure.
violations: The office complied with incident reporting to authorities but initially failed to understand and properly manage the severity of the breach until the employee inquired about data exposure.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) found the office unlawfully disclosed whistleblower personal data without legal basis, breaching GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 6, as well as Hungarian whistleblower protection laws. The authority imposed a 1,000,000 HUF fine payable within 30 days, ordered compliance measures, and mandated public disclosure of the decision with the office's identifying information. The office must ensure proper handling of future whistleblower reports and implement training and internal controls. Administrative appeal available to Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: The Mayor's Office of Kecskemét continues to function as the local government administrative body for the city. Following this decision, it is required to implement revised internal procedures for handling whistleblower reports and protect such data from further unauthorized disclosure.
dataType: Personal data from whistleblower report: name, email address, phone number, identification of whistleblower status

companyDescription: Chizzle Pte. Ltd. provides a mobile application designed to connect learners and teachers in Singapore, Australia, and India. The company operates a L.A.M.P. stack IT infrastructure to support its mobile learning platform.
companyLongDescription: Chizzle Pte. Ltd. provides a mobile application designed to connect learners and teachers in Singapore, Australia, and India. The company operates a L.A.M.P. stack IT infrastructure to support its mobile learning platform.
caseDescription: Chizzle's mobile learning application suffered a cyberattack on 30 July 2018 that deleted its database and compromised personal data of 2,213 users. The attack occurred through an unsecured phpMyAdmin tool that the organization was unaware it possessed and had configured to allow remote internet access. The company failed to conduct any security review of its IT infrastructure, missing the opportunity to identify and remediate this critical vulnerability.
violationSummary: The organization failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, directly resulting in unauthorized access, data deletion, and compromise of 2,213 individuals' personal information through an exposed database administration tool.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Chizzle Pte. Ltd. failed to conduct any security review of its mobile application and IT system, leaving a phpMyAdmin database administration tool configured for remote internet access despite.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unauthorized attacker exploited the exposed phpMyAdmin tool to gain full database control and permanently delete personal data of 2,213 users including names, dates of birth, genders.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization believed an unauthorized party gained entry through phpMyAdmin via a brute force attack.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization had no logs to prove a brute force attack occurred. Regardless, the phpMyAdmin tool was remotely accessible from the internet and allowed full database control (read, write, delete) once accessed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization was not aware that phpMyAdmin was part of its system and had no need for the tool.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tool was installed as part of the standard L.A.M.P. stack in 2016 and remained unconfigured and unreviewed for over two years, indicating a lack of any security governance or system inventory practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Chizzle failed to conduct any security review of its L.A.M.P. stack IT infrastructure despite past regulatory guidance emphasizing the need for such reviews.
violations: Chizzle failed to conduct any security review of its L.A.M.P. stack IT infrastructure despite past regulatory guidance emphasizing the need for such reviews.
The phpMyAdmin tool was installed and configured to allow remote internet access without the organization's awareness or understanding of its presence.
No security arrangements were implemented to prevent web-based threats or unauthorized access to the database through the exposed phpMyAdmin tool.
The organization failed to identify that the tool was unnecessary and should have been removed or secured during a basic security review.

outcome: The Commissioner found Chizzle in breach of PDPA s.24 for failure to make reasonable security arrangements. The organization was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD 8,000 (reduced from a higher amount due to the organization's dire financial position) within 30 days. Additionally, Chizzle was directed to: (a) engage qualified personnel to conduct a security audit of its mobile application and IT systems; (b) provide a schedule and scope within 30 days; (c) rectify identified security gaps; (d) develop an IT security policy within 60 days of audit completion; (e) review and revise developmental processes to adopt data protection by design within 120 days; and (f) report completion of each direction within 1 week. Interest accrues on unpaid penalty at Rules of Court rates.
companyNow: Unknown. The organization was in dire financial standing at the time of the decision, with the Commissioner noting the penalty was reduced to avoid a crushing burden that could force closure.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, genders, email addresses, mobile numbers, residential addresses

companyDescription: iClick Media Pte. Ltd. is an IT vendor providing services to organisations handling personal data in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: iClick Media Pte. Ltd. is an IT vendor providing services to organisations handling personal data in Singapore.
caseDescription: iClick Media, an IT vendor for EU Holidays, failed to develop any internal policies and practices required under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012. The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of section 12 of the PDPA for lacking fundamental data protection governance, including written policies, employee training, and compliance frameworks.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to establish policies and practices constitutes systemic insecurity—the lack of governance, training, and documented procedures for personal data handling creates vulnerability to unauthorised access, misuse, and breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: iClick Media failed to develop any internal policies, written procedures, or data protection governance frameworks despite serving as an IT vendor handling personal data for EU Holidays.
whyTheyWereWrong: The absence of data protection policies and employee training left personal data vulnerable to mishandling, unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to ensure compliance with PDPA obligations.
regulatoryFindings.description: iClick Media failed to put in place any internal policies and practices to meet PDPA obligations
violations: iClick Media failed to put in place any internal policies and practices to meet PDPA obligations
Organisation lacked written data protection policy
No employee training programme existed regarding PDPA obligations

outcome: Deputy Commissioner directed iClick Media to, within 60 days: (1) Put in place a data protection policy including written internal policies compliant with PDPA; (2) Develop and deliver mandatory employee training on PDPA obligations when handling personal data; (3) Submit written update to Commission within 7 days of completing the above actions.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a membership-based leisure and hospitality organization that operates an electronic direct mail system for member communications.
companyLongDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a membership-based leisure and hospitality organization that operates an electronic direct mail system for member communications.
caseDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club's electronic direct mail system was accessed without authorization on 9 June 2019, resulting in unauthorised spam emails being sent. The breach was caused by weak password controls: the common login password comprised the organization's initials and year 2010, was shared by at least 3 people, and had never been changed. The organization lacked arrangements to enforce password strength, expiry, and protection.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data stored in the EDM system, specifically weak access controls and password management, resulting in unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Tanah Merah Country Club maintained a weak, shared password (organization initials plus 2010) for its email system that was never changed since setup, with no password strength.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' personal data and email accounts were exposed to unauthorized access and exploitation, allowing attackers to hijack the system.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organisation failed to implement password strength requirements, password expiry policies, or password protection mechanisms
violations: The organisation failed to implement password strength requirements, password expiry policies, or password protection mechanisms
A common password was used and shared among at least 3 persons without change for 9 years
No technical or organizational controls existed to prevent unauthorized access to the EDM system containing personal data

outcome: The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $8,000, later reduced to $4,000 on reconsideration, within 30 days. No other directions were issued in view of remedial measures taken by the organisation. The organisation's prompt cooperation with the investigation and swift remediation actions were taken into consideration in penalty determination.
dataType: Email addresses, member contact information

companyDescription: Interauct! Pte Ltd was a web hosting and auction platform operator that managed an online mobile number auction service for a telecommunications provider from 2000 to 2018.
companyLongDescription: Interauct! Pte Ltd was a web hosting and auction platform operator that managed an online mobile number auction service for a telecommunications provider from 2000 to 2018.
caseDescription: Interauct! Pte Ltd operated a mobile number auction for a telecommunications provider from 2000–2018. The company created backup files of participant personal data during server migrations in 2012 and 2016 but failed to delete them afterward. In April 2019, a vendor's server misconfiguration exposed these files on the internet, potentially affecting 3,380 individuals. Although no actual unauthorized access occurred, the company violated data retention obligations.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to delete personal data after it was no longer needed, breaching data retention obligations. The unnecessary retention left data vulnerable to exposure when server misconfiguration occurred, exemplifying insecurity in data handling practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Interauct! Pte Ltd created backup files containing 8,750 individuals' personal data during server migrations in 2012 and 2016, then failed to delete these files after migrations were completed.
whyTheyWereWrong: 3,380 customers' sensitive personal data including ID numbers, addresses, dates of birth, and contact details remained unnecessarily stored on vendor servers for up to 7 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed reasonable security arrangements were in place via the vendor to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: While security arrangements did prevent direct unauthorized access (files required exact complex URLs; only the Telco accessed them), the organisation failed to delete unnecessary backup files, creating long-term retention risk.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to not retain personal data longer than necessary for the purposes for which it was collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: Interauct! Pte Ltd retained backup files containing 3,380 individuals' personal data for 3–7 years after server migrations were completed, with no legitimate business reason to retain them.
violations: Interauct! Pte Ltd retained backup files containing 3,380 individuals' personal data for 3–7 years after server migrations were completed, with no legitimate business reason to retain them.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Interauct! Pte Ltd in breach of the Retention Limitation Obligation under section 25 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. The organisation was issued a warning. No additional directions were imposed because the breach has been remedied: the organisation deleted the files within 3 hours of discovery and ensured the vendor fixed the server misconfiguration within 6 hours.
dataType: Name, ID (passport/NRIC), mobile number, address, date of birth, email address

companyDescription: Saturday Club Pte Ltd is a membership-based club organisation in Singapore that collects and processes member personal data.
companyLongDescription: Saturday Club Pte Ltd is a membership-based club organisation in Singapore that collects and processes member personal data.
caseDescription: Saturday Club Pte Ltd failed to develop any internal policies and practices necessary to comply with the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. Following investigation into a suspected data breach, the Deputy Commissioner found the organisation in breach of section 12 of the PDPA and issued compliance directions.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to establish internal policies and practices constitutes inadequate data security and governance measures, directly enabling the suspected data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Saturday Club Pte Ltd failed to develop any internal policies and practices necessary to protect personal data collected from its members, resulting in a suspected data breach.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' personal data was exposed to unauthorized access and compromise because the club had no security policies, procedures, or safeguards in place to protect it.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet their obligations under the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Saturday Club Pte Ltd had not developed any internal policies and practices necessary to meet its obligations under the PDPA, leaving personal data exposed to breach risk.
violations: Saturday Club Pte Ltd had not developed any internal policies and practices necessary to meet its obligations under the PDPA, leaving personal data exposed to breach risk.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found Saturday Club Pte Ltd in breach of section 12 of the PDPA and issued directions (compliance orders) requiring the organisation to develop appropriate internal policies and practices to protect personal data.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting and data analytics firm founded in 2013 that specialized in voter profiling and targeted political advertising using personal data harvested from millions of social media users.
companyLongDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting and data analytics firm founded in 2013 that specialized in voter profiling and targeted political advertising using personal data harvested from millions of social media users.
caseDescription: Cambridge Analytica, a political data firm, engaged in the unauthorized collection and misuse of Facebook user data without informed consent. The company weaponized psychological profiling and behavioral targeting of millions of users for political campaigns. The FTC moved for summary judgment after Cambridge Analytica failed to oppose the complaint during bankruptcy proceedings.
violationSummary: Cambridge Analytica covertly harvested vast quantities of personal data through third-party apps and without clear disclosure of collection scope or political targeting purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Cambridge Analytica collected and retained personal data from millions of Facebook users without authorization and used psychological profiling to manipulate political behavior.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Facebook users had their personal data harvested and weaponized for political manipulation without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed to provide legitimate political consulting and voter targeting services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cambridge Analytica harvested personal data without authorization, used psychological profiling to manipulate voters, and engaged in deceptive data practices that violated user privacy and election integrity.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users consented to data collection through Facebook app terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users were not informed that third-party apps shared their data with Cambridge Analytica or how their data would be used for voter manipulation and political targeting.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Cambridge Analytica deceived millions of users by collecting personal and psychological data without informed consent or clear disclosure of political targeting purposes.
violations: Cambridge Analytica deceived millions of users by collecting personal and psychological data without informed consent or clear disclosure of political targeting purposes.
The company engaged in unfair practices by weaponizing personal data for voter manipulation without user knowledge or authorization.

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint for summary decision against Cambridge Analytica. Cambridge Analytica, then in bankruptcy, did not file opposition within the 14-day period required under FTC Rules of Practice 3.24(a)(2). The FTC found no material facts in dispute and sought final judgment and order. The company ceased operations in 2018 and entered bankruptcy, with assets liquidated.
companyNow: Cambridge Analytica shut down in May 2018 following the data privacy scandal. The company is now defunct, with remaining assets handled through bankruptcy proceedings.
dataType: Personal data, behavioral data, political preferences, psychological profiles
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Privacy violations through unauthorized data collection and use

companyDescription: Globalsign.in Pte Ltd (GSI) is a Singapore-based email marketing service provider that operates the Global2Mail (G2M) online marketing web application, which sends mass marketing emails on behalf of client organisations.
companyLongDescription: Globalsign.in Pte Ltd (GSI) is a Singapore-based email marketing service provider that operates the Global2Mail (G2M) online marketing web application, which sends mass marketing emails on behalf of client organisations.
caseDescription: GSI's email marketing platform (G2M) was compromised when an unauthorized intruder accessed the administrator account on 18 August 2017, leading to spam emails sent to 359,364 email addresses. The breach exposed personal data of 149,172 MSIG customers and 201,192 customers of other GSI clients. GSI failed to implement adequate security controls including password rotation, strong password enforcement, two-factor authentication, and regular security scans.
violationSummary: GSI failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (Section 24 of PDPA) to prevent unauthorized access to personal data. Multiple technical and administrative security failures enabled the breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Globalsign.in operated an email marketing platform with critical security failures: no mandatory password changes, shared administrator credentials across staff.
whyTheyWereWrong: 149,172 MSIG customer email addresses and personal names were exposed when attackers accessed the unprotected administrator account.

claimsVsReality.claim: GSI claimed it had complied with MSIG's express instructions to 'delete and purge the data after each marketing campaign'
claimsVsReality.reality: The G2M platform still retained 149,172 email addresses provided by MSIG when the breach occurred, contradicting the claim of deletion

claimsVsReality.claim: GSI represented that MSIG had platform access and could delete content, implying GSI was not responsible for data retention
claimsVsReality.reality: MSIG explicitly instructed GSI to delete data, and GSI remained contractually and legally obligated to protect and timely delete the personal data

claimsVsReality.claim: GSI claimed it was in the midst of purging data (5 June 2017 email: 'Yes, we are in the midst of purging the most recent campaigns')
claimsVsReality.reality: This email showed delays in purging and that some recently concluded campaigns' data had not yet been removed

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by preventing unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: GSI failed to implement mandatory password expiry for administrator and client accounts
violations: GSI failed to implement mandatory password expiry for administrator and client accounts
No logs recorded when administrator account passwords were changed
Users were encouraged but not required to use strong passwords
Multiple staff shared identical administrator account credentials, preventing identification of who accessed the system
No security scans were conducted during the 12 months prior to the incident
The administrator account was successfully accessed without authorization on 18 August 2017

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 of the PDPA requires organisations to cease retaining personal data once the purpose for collection is no longer served and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: GSI retained 149,172 email addresses provided by MSIG after marketing campaigns concluded, despite contractual obligation to delete them
violations: GSI retained 149,172 email addresses provided by MSIG after marketing campaigns concluded, despite contractual obligation to delete them
MSIG sent at least three emails (9 December 2016, 30 May 2017, 5 June 2017) requesting deletion, which GSI did not fully comply with

outcome: The Commissioner found GSI in breach of sections 24 and 25 of the PDPA and imposed a financial penalty of SGD 34,000, payable within 30 days. MSIG was found to have complied with its obligations under section 24 by imposing contractual security requirements on GSI and monitoring compliance. Post-incident remediation by both organisations was acknowledged but considered baseline compliance rather than mitigation. GSI implemented 2FA, encrypted databases, HTTPS enforcement, improved access logging, and engaged consultants for ISO 27001 compliance.
companyNow: Globalsign.in Pte Ltd remains a service provider operating the Global2Mail email marketing platform, with enhanced security measures implemented following the 2017 incident.
dataType: Email addresses, first and last names
legalBasisViolated: PDPA section 25 (Accuracy and protection of personal data)

companyDescription: The Budapest Regional Court is the appellate court serving the Budapest metropolitan region in Hungary's judicial system, overseeing cases from district courts and handling judicial administration for subordinate courts.
companyLongDescription: The Budapest Regional Court is the appellate court serving the Budapest metropolitan region in Hungary's judicial system, overseeing cases from district courts and handling judicial administration for subordinate courts.
caseDescription: The Budapest Regional Court illegally extracted a list of 51 judges who were members of the Hungarian Judges' Association (MABIE) from payroll records, compiled them for a different purpose than salary deduction, and distributed the list to court leaders without consent. The data included tax identification numbers and membership details. The court violated GDPR principles by processing special category data without legal basis and sharing it with unauthorized recipients.
violationSummary: The core harm was unauthorized disclosure of special category data (union membership) to third parties (court supervisors) without legal basis, combined with purpose creep from legitimate payroll processing to political organizing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The court president compiled a list of 51 judges' union membership data including names, tax identification numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Fifty-one judges had their sensitive union membership and tax identification data exposed to their supervisors without authorization, chilling their freedom of association.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data extraction was necessary for administrative purposes to determine how many MABIE members served at the court.
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual purpose was to encourage judges to withdraw from the union by distributing the membership list to supervisory staff for political persuasion, a purpose incompatible with the original payroll deduction authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: The court only distributed the list to inquiring leaders seeking confirmation of their own membership.
claimsVsReality.reality: The court distributed detailed membership data on 51 judges to 18 court leaders during a mandatory meeting, including members not present and data beyond what any individual leader could legitimately need.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tax identification numbers appeared in the list accidentally.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tax IDs were extracted from payroll records alongside union data, demonstrating systematic data aggregation beyond the stated purpose, and their inclusion in the distributed list served no legitimate administrative function.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: The court extracted union membership data from payroll systems originally authorized only for salary deduction, then used it to identify members for political persuasion purposes without consent or lawful basis.
violations: The court extracted union membership data from payroll systems originally authorized only for salary deduction, then used it to identify members for political persuasion purposes without consent or lawful basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1) provides lawful processing requires consent, contractual necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests; for public authorities, legitimate interests are excluded.
regulatoryFindings.description: The court had no consent, no legal obligation, and no valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) for extracting and compiling the membership list for the stated political purpose.
violations: The court had no consent, no legal obligation, and no valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) for extracting and compiling the membership list for the stated political purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 9(1) prohibits processing special category data including data revealing trade union membership.
regulatoryFindings.description: Union membership is a special category; the court processed it outside the narrow exceptions in Art. 9(2), particularly 9(2)(d) which requires organization activity and does not apply to employer use.
violations: Union membership is a special category; the court processed it outside the narrow exceptions in Art. 9(2), particularly 9(2)(d) which requires organization activity and does not apply to employer use.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(3) requires data controllers to inform data subjects of processing for new purposes before processing occurs.
regulatoryFindings.description: The court disclosed data for political persuasion without informing the 51 judges of this secondary use or obtaining new consent.
violations: The court disclosed data for political persuasion without informing the 51 judges of this secondary use or obtaining new consent.

outcome: The Hungarian National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) found the court violated GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) and Art. 6(1) by processing union membership data outside its original purpose without lawful basis and sharing it with unauthorized recipients. The authority ordered the court to: (1) notify all 18 meeting attendees within 15 days about the unlawful disclosure and demand deletion of the list; (2) ensure deletion is documented and reported within 15 days; and (3) pay 3,000,000 HUF administrative fine within 30 days. The authority also ordered public disclosure of the court's identity on its website. The decision is final and enforceable; the court may appeal to the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days. Data deletion remains prohibited until appeal deadlines expire.
companyNow: The Budapest Regional Court (Fővárosi Törvényszék) continues to operate as Hungary's primary appellate court. Following this 2019 decision, the court would have been required to implement data protection compliance measures and delete the unlawfully processed membership list.
dataType: Trade union/interest representation membership, tax identification numbers, employment data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 9(1) – Prohibition on Processing Special Category Data
GDPR Art. 9(2)(d) – Exception for Associations (not applicable)

companyDescription: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. is a Spanish mobile phone retailer that operated an e-commerce website collecting customer data through registration, contact, and newsletter subscription forms.
companyLongDescription: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. is a Spanish mobile phone retailer that operated an e-commerce website collecting customer data through registration, contact, and newsletter subscription forms.
caseDescription: A Spanish mobile phone retailer collected personal data through website registration, contact, and newsletter subscription forms without providing the mandatory privacy information required by GDPR Article 13. The company failed to identify itself in the legal notice and lacked a privacy policy, leaving users in the dark about how their data would be handled.
violationSummary: The company excluded data subjects from essential information required by law, preventing them from understanding their rights and the processing of their personal data.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000 operated a website collecting users' names, email addresses, and passwords through registration.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users submitting personal data through the website had no way to learn who controlled their information, why it was being collected, how long it would be kept.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company operated a website with legitimate data collection mechanisms (registration forms, contact forms, newsletter signup)
claimsVsReality.reality: No privacy policy existed and the company failed to identify itself or disclose any information about data processing to users, violating fundamental GDPR transparency requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data is obtained from a data subject, the controller must provide at the moment of collection the identity and contact details of the controller, purposes of processing, legal basis, recipients, data retention period, and rights of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000 failed to provide any privacy policy on its website
violations: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000 failed to provide any privacy policy on its website
The company did not identify itself as the data controller in its legal notice
Users collecting data had no access to mandatory information about processing purposes, retention, or their rights
No information was provided about the legal basis, recipients, or data retention criteria

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 11 permits satisfaction of Article 13 duties by providing basic information and directing users to additional information via an electronic address, but basic information must include controller identity, processing purpose, and rights information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Website lacked even basic privacy information in accessible format
violations: Website lacked even basic privacy information in accessible format
No electronic direction to privacy policy or additional information was provided

outcome: The Director of AEPD imposed a fine of €1,500 on MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. for violation of GDPR Article 13. The company was ordered to make the sanction effective within the payment term specified by Spanish administrative procedure law. The resolution is executable and subject to administrative and judicial appeal within the specified timeframes. No evidence of post-decision compliance improvements was documented.
companyNow: Unknown. No information regarding the current operational status of MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. is provided in the document.
dataType: Name, surname, email address, password, contact information

companyDescription: Actstitude Pte Ltd is a social media platform marketing agency that operated a web-based recruitment portal allowing job applicants to upload their resumes.
companyLongDescription: Actstitude Pte Ltd is a social media platform marketing agency that operated a web-based recruitment portal allowing job applicants to upload their resumes.
caseDescription: Actstitude Pte Ltd operated a resume upload webpage for job applicants without implementing access controls or security testing. Over 160 resumes were stored with manipulable URLs that were indexed by Google, allowing unauthorized access to personal data. The company failed to conduct vulnerability scanning or periodic security reviews despite collecting sensitive employment information.
violationSummary: Resumes were exposed through the company's failure to implement basic access controls, making personal data vulnerable to unauthorized disclosure and search engine indexing. This constitutes a direct exposure of personal data to the public.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Actstitude Pte Ltd created a resume upload webpage without access controls, failed to conduct vulnerability scanning before launch or periodic security reviews.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 160 job applicants' resumes containing personal information, names, and contact details were indexed by Google.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or control against unauthorised disclosure and other misuse.
regulatoryFindings.description: Actstitude did not implement access controls to restrict access to resume files
violations: Actstitude did not implement access controls to restrict access to resume files
No vulnerability scanning was conducted at pre-launch (5 July 2018) or periodically thereafter
The organisation failed to detect or prevent URL manipulation that enabled unauthorised access to resume data
Lack of security measures resulted in Google indexing URLs containing sensitive personal information

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. A warning was issued to Actstitude Pte Ltd. No further directions were required as the organisation had already taken action to address the security gaps in its systems.
dataType: Resume data (personal information, employment history, contact details)

companyDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three largest consumer reporting agencies in the United States. It owns, licenses, and maintains personal information on hundreds of millions of consumers and businesses globally, generating credit reports and analytics sold to financial institutions, retailers, insurers, and government agencies.
companyLongDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three largest consumer reporting agencies in the United States. It owns, licenses, and maintains personal information on hundreds of millions of consumers and businesses globally, generating credit reports and analytics sold to financial institutions, retailers, insurers, and government agencies.
caseDescription: Equifax failed to patch a known critical vulnerability in Apache Struts software for months, allowing intruders to access and exfiltrate personal information on over 147 million U.S. consumers (15.8 million California residents) from May-July 2017. The company's inadequate security infrastructure, outdated asset inventories, misconfigured scanning tools, and poor breach notification practices violated California data protection laws.
violationSummary: Equifax failed to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures to protect personal information from unauthorized access, and failed to detect and remediate a known, critical vulnerability in timely fashion, allowing massive data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Equifax failed to patch a critical Apache Struts vulnerability in its public-facing dispute portal for months after being alerted on March 8, 2017, despite having a documented patching process.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 147 million consumers, including 15.8 million California residents, had their Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses, driver's license numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax represents via its website that it takes reasonable steps to protect the security of consumers' personal information and uses technical, administrative, and physical security measures that comply with applicable federal and state laws.
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax failed to patch a known critical vulnerability for 4+ months, lacked comprehensive IT asset inventory, used outdated employee contact lists, misconfigured security scanning tools, and allowed intruders to access and exfiltrate 147+ million consumers' sensitive personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) requires entities to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information owned, licensed, or maintained, to protect personal information from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security procedures by not patching a known critical vulnerability in Apache Struts for over 4 months after notification.
violations: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security procedures by not patching a known critical vulnerability in Apache Struts for over 4 months after notification.
Equifax lacked a comprehensive inventory of its IT assets, preventing timely identification and patching of vulnerable systems.
Equifax misconfigured its vulnerability scanning tools, which failed to detect or alert staff that the Apache Struts vulnerability had not been patched.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.82 requires entities to disclose a breach of security of unencrypted personal information of California residents in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax discovered suspicious activity on July 29, 2017, but delayed public announcement until September 7, 2017 (over one month later).
violations: Equifax discovered suspicious activity on July 29, 2017, but delayed public announcement until September 7, 2017 (over one month later).
The delayed announcement caused widespread confusion and burdened consumers with identity protection costs and time.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by publicly representing that it takes reasonable steps to protect consumer personal information while maintaining inadequate security infrastructure.
violations: Equifax engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by publicly representing that it takes reasonable steps to protect consumer personal information while maintaining inadequate security infrastructure.
Equifax made unfair, deceptive, untrue, and misleading statements regarding its data security practices at the time of the breach.

outcome: Complaint for injunction, civil penalties, and other equitable relief filed July 22, 2019. Plaintiff seeks court orders to prevent further unfair competition violations, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under Business & Professions Code § 17206, recovery of investigation costs, and such other relief as the court deems just and proper. The complaint alleges violations of California Civil Code §§ 1798.81.5(b) and 1798.82, as well as § 17200 UCL.
companyNow: Equifax remains one of the three largest consumer reporting agencies in the United States as of the complaint filing. The company continues to collect and maintain personal information on over 820 million consumers and 91 million businesses worldwide.
dataType: Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses, driver's license numbers, credit card numbers, credit history, financial account information, credit inquiry records, public records (bankruptcies, tax liens, civil judgments)
legalBasisViolated: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law)

companyDescription: Honestbee Pte Ltd is an online food and grocery delivery service that connects third-party merchants with customers for logistics and delivery services.
companyLongDescription: Honestbee Pte Ltd is an online food and grocery delivery service that connects third-party merchants with customers for logistics and delivery services.
caseDescription: Honestbee stored customer personal data provided by third-party merchants in an unsecured AWS S3 bucket without access restrictions, exposing approximately 8,000 individuals' data publicly. The company failed to implement basic security measures to protect the data. After notification, Honestbee blocked public access and implemented remedial measures including code reviews and security audits.
violationSummary: The company exposed personal data of thousands of individuals to public access through misconfigured cloud storage, failing to protect sensitive personal information from unauthorized disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Stored personal data of approximately 8,000 customers in an unsecured Amazon Web Services bucket without access restrictions.
whyTheyWereWrong: 8,000 individuals had their sensitive personal information including names, residential addresses, email addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data used for testing was properly secured
claimsVsReality.reality: Data was stored in an unsecured, publicly accessible AWS bucket without access restrictions

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Honestbee failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by storing personal data in an AWS bucket without access restrictions, allowing public access to the data.
violations: Honestbee failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by storing personal data in an AWS bucket without access restrictions, allowing public access to the data.

outcome: Honestbee Pte Ltd was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $8,000 within 30 days. The organisation has blocked public access to the personal data, circulated a report to its engineering team to prevent similar mistakes in code reviews, and is in discussions with cybersecurity companies to perform regular security audits. The Commission did not impose other directions given the remedial measures taken.
companyNow: Honestbee has implemented remedial measures including access restrictions, internal code review protocols, and engaged cybersecurity firms for security audits to prevent future breaches.
dataType: Names, email addresses, residential addresses, mobile numbers

company: Zero1 Pte. Ltd. and IP Tribe Pte Ltd
companyDescription: Zero1 Pte. Ltd. was a Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) providing mobile services, partnering with Singtel Mobile Singapore. The company relied on third-party platforms (IP Tribe Pte Ltd, Openet, and 6D Technologies) for billing system development and data migration.
companyLongDescription: Zero1 Pte. Ltd. was a Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) providing mobile services, partnering with Singtel Mobile Singapore. The company relied on third-party platforms (IP Tribe Pte Ltd, Openet, and 6D Technologies) for billing system development and data migration.
caseDescription: Zero1 Pte. Ltd., a Mobile Virtual Network Operator, experienced a data breach where 118 subscriber invoices containing personal data were emailed to unintended recipients due to Batch ID duplication during platform migration. The root cause was inadequate pre-launch testing that failed to simulate the staggered migration scenario, and insufficient processes to ensure unique Batch ID generation.
violationSummary: Personal data was exposed to unintended third parties (other subscribers) due to inadequate security testing and lack of safeguards to ensure unique identifiers in the system.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Zero1 Pte. Ltd. and IP Tribe Pte Ltd deployed a new billing platform without adequately testing it against realistic migration scenarios, relying instead on only two test accounts.
whyTheyWereWrong: 118 subscribers received invoices containing their names, addresses, mobile numbers, charges, and international call details sent to other subscribers' email addresses due to undetected batch ID.

claimsVsReality.claim: IP Tribe Pte Ltd represented that it had proper oversight of the data migration and system development process.
claimsVsReality.reality: IPT retained key responsibility for pre-launch testing scope but failed to design adequate test scenarios, relying on insufficient two-account testing despite knowing 12,000-15,000 subscribers would be migrated.

claimsVsReality.claim: The billing system would reliably generate and send invoices to correct subscribers via the new platform.
claimsVsReality.reality: Batch ID duplication caused 118 invoices to be sent to wrong subscriber email addresses due to undeleted data from prior migration attempts and missing date/time stamp safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data by implementing and maintaining reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Zero1 and IPT failed to scope pre-launch testing to include the Migration Scenario (staggered migration with high volume of email assignments), using only two test accounts instead.
violations: Zero1 and IPT failed to scope pre-launch testing to include the Migration Scenario (staggered migration with high volume of email assignments), using only two test accounts instead.
IPT failed to ensure adequate processes to generate unique Batch IDs, allowing duplication which resulted in invoices being sent to wrong subscribers.
Neither party implemented safeguards such as date/time stamps in Batch ID generation before the incident occurred.

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Zero1 Pte. Ltd. and IP Tribe Pte Ltd in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA s.24 and issued a Warning to each party. No monetary penalty was imposed. Both organisations had already taken remedial actions to address gaps in security arrangements, including implementation of date/time stamps in Batch ID generation and improved testing procedures. No further directions were required.
companyNow: Zero1 Pte. Ltd. was a licensed Mobile Virtual Network Operator providing mobile services in Singapore. Current operational status unknown from document.
dataType: Name, address, subscriber ID, mobile number, mobile charges, international call details

companyDescription: Marshall Cavendish Education Pte. Ltd. is an educational technology company that provides learning management systems and hosting services to Ministry of Education schools in Singapore. The company operated the www.mconline.com.sg platform serving over 250,000 student and staff users.
companyLongDescription: Marshall Cavendish Education Pte. Ltd. is an educational technology company that provides learning management systems and hosting services to Ministry of Education schools in Singapore. The company operated the www.mconline.com.sg platform serving over 250,000 student and staff users.
caseDescription: MCE's learning management system was hit by ransomware on 1 February 2017 after a senior system engineer changed a firewall rule to allow internet access without reinstating it, and then installed remote access software on the backup server. The ransomware encrypted databases containing personal data of over 250,000 users, including minors. MCE failed to implement adequate supervisory controls and security procedures to prevent or detect these critical configuration changes.
violationSummary: MCE failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorised access and modification. The organisation did not implement adequate supervisory controls, change management procedures, or monitoring to prevent or detect critical system changes that exposed data to ransomware attacks.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Marshall Cavendish Education failed to implement adequate supervisory controls over firewall changes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 250,000 individuals—including minors—had their personal data encrypted by ransomware attackers.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCE claimed it had adequate supervisory measures and that the incident was discovered through routine monitoring, demonstrating effective oversight.
claimsVsReality.reality: MCE's own general manager admitted there were no measures to prevent unauthorised software installation, no standard operating procedures for firewall changes, and no documentation requirements. A senior system engineer was able to install remote access software and make critical firewall changes multiple times over an extended period without detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCE asserted that the senior system engineer wilfully disregarded company policy, and that no practicable steps could prevent such wilful misconduct.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even if an employee acts wilfully, the organisation's failure to implement basic supervisory controls, approval processes, audit logs, and monitoring mechanisms demonstrates inadequate organisational security arrangements. The Commissioner found that while wilful disregard cannot be completely prevented, the lack of implementation mechanisms deprived MCE of credible claims to reasonable security measures.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCE claimed there was no loss of personal data because no exfiltration occurred and network logs would have detected database downloads.
claimsVsReality.reality: The encryption of personal data by ransomware constituted unauthorised modification and loss of access/control. MCE was forced to delete encrypted files per its data protection policy, resulting in loss of new incremental data created between the last backup and the attack. The perpetrator had access and could have exfiltrated data if chosen.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: MCE failed to make reasonable security arrangements by not reinstating firewall restrictions after a temporary change intended to diagnose an antivirus issue, leaving the backup server continuously exposed to internet access.
violations: MCE failed to make reasonable security arrangements by not reinstating firewall restrictions after a temporary change intended to diagnose an antivirus issue, leaving the backup server continuously exposed to internet access.
MCE did not implement supervisory oversight or approval processes for installation of remote access software on servers holding personal data.
MCE lacked standard operating procedures to document firewall configuration changes, and the IT Manager did not exercise competent supervision over the senior system engineer.
MCE maintained 15 unnecessary remote access accounts to critical systems, demonstrating inadequate risk appreciation and access controls.

Ransomware exploited these weaknesses via brute-force attacks, encrypting personal data of 250,928 individuals (206,240 active and 44,688 inactive users) and causing unauthorised modification and loss of access to that data.

outcome: The Commissioner found MCE in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. MCE was directed to pay a financial penalty of S$40,000 within 30 days. The Commissioner noted that MCE had already taken extensive remedial measures including: implementing security assessments for remote internet access, reviewing firewall rules, engaging external auditors, strengthening controls over program deployment and source code access, implementing monthly user access reviews, improving user account management, defining clearer system engineering duties, hiring an IT security officer, and establishing formal approval and documentation procedures for system changes. No further directions were issued given these remedial steps, but MCE must maintain ongoing compliance with PDPA obligations.
companyNow: Marshall Cavendish Education continues to operate as an educational technology provider in Singapore. Following the 2017 incident, the company implemented substantial security improvements including hiring dedicated cybersecurity personnel and establishing formal IT governance procedures.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, birth certificate numbers, school names, schooling levels, class information, email addresses, home addresses, mobile numbers, parent/guardian contact information and identification numbers

companyDescription: GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN, S.L. is a real estate management company (gestora inmobiliaria) based in Spain that handles property transactions and sales.
companyLongDescription: GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN, S.L. is a real estate management company (gestora inmobiliaria) based in Spain that handles property transactions and sales.
caseDescription: A real estate management company disclosed personal data of third parties (names, surnames, addresses) in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers. The company failed to maintain the integrity and confidentiality of personal data and did not respond to the data protection authority's investigation request.
violationSummary: The company breached the confidentiality of personal data by disclosing third parties' identifiers to unauthorized recipients (prospective buyers). This constitutes a breach of confidentiality under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN disclosed personal data of third parties including names, surnames, and home addresses in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two individuals' complete personal identifiers were exposed to an unauthorized third party during a real estate transaction, compromising their privacy.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that guarantees adequate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures ('integrity and confidentiality').
regulatoryFindings.description: The company facilitated disclosure of personal identifiers (names, surnames, addresses) in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers without authorization, violating the integrity and confidentiality principle.
violations: The company facilitated disclosure of personal identifiers (names, surnames, addresses) in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers without authorization, violating the integrity and confidentiality principle.
The company failed to demonstrate proactive responsibility for compliance with data protection obligations when required to respond to the data protection authority's investigation request.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5 establishes that violations of Article 5(1)(f) constitute very serious infringements subject to administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: The breach of Article 5(1)(f) triggered enforcement action under Article 83.5, making the company subject to administrative fines.
violations: The breach of Article 5(1)(f) triggered enforcement action under Article 83.5, making the company subject to administrative fines.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) Director imposed an administrative fine of €2,500 on GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN, S.L. for violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f) regarding integrity and confidentiality of personal data. The company must pay the fine within the specified voluntary payment period. The decision is final but subject to administrative review or contentious-administrative appeal before the National Court within two months of notification.
dataType: Personal identifiers (names, surnames, home address)

company: Landesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit (LfDI) Baden-Württemberg
companyDescription: The LfDI Baden-Württemberg is the state data protection authority responsible for enforcing GDPR and data protection legislation in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It investigates complaints, enforces compliance, and issues guidance on data protection matters.
companyLongDescription: The LfDI Baden-Württemberg is the state data protection authority responsible for enforcing GDPR and data protection legislation in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It investigates complaints, enforces compliance, and issues guidance on data protection matters.
caseDescription: This is a press release by the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority reporting a ten-fold increase in data breach notifications since GDPR came into effect. The authority highlights pervasive failures in data handling, particularly in medical practices, caused by negligence, ransomware attacks, and misdirected communications.
violationSummary: The violations stem from inadequate security measures, lack of internal controls, and organisational failures to properly safeguard personal data. Both technical insecurity (ransomware) and process failures (misdirection) fall under insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Multiple organizations across Baden-Württemberg reported nearly 1,000 data breaches in 2019, including postal misdirection, hacking attacks, email misdirection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' extremely sensitive health records including medical reports, prescriptions, and X-rays were exposed to unauthorized recipients or encrypted by ransomware.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed with integrity and confidentiality, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Multiple organisations failed to maintain confidentiality by misdirecting sensitive health data via post, email and fax to unauthorised recipients
violations: Multiple organisations failed to maintain confidentiality by misdirecting sensitive health data via post, email and fax to unauthorised recipients
Organisations lacked adequate encryption and ransomware protections, allowing hackers to access personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security of processing.
