regulatoryFindings.description: Medical practices lacked adequate internal control mechanisms to prevent accidental disclosure of health data
violations: Medical practices lacked adequate internal control mechanisms to prevent accidental disclosure of health data
Organisations failed to implement encryption, employee training, and data security procedures
No adequate measures to protect against ransomware attacks

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires notification of data breaches to the supervisory authority without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Nearly 1,000 breach notifications received in 2019 alone, with 177 in May, indicating widespread organisational failure to prevent breaches in the first instance
violations: Nearly 1,000 breach notifications received in 2019 alone, with 177 in May, indicating widespread organisational failure to prevent breaches in the first instance

outcome: The LfDI issued monetary penalties totalling €207,140 for data handling failures. The highest penalties were two fines of €80,000 each: one for a digital publication that published health data due to inadequate internal controls, and one for a financial company that improperly disposed of personal data. The authority issued compliance guidance and emphasised mandatory notification of affected individuals for health data breaches, in addition to authority notification.
companyNow: The Landesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit (LfDI) Baden-Württemberg continues to function as the state-level data protection authority in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, overseeing GDPR compliance and investigating data protection violations.
dataType: Health data, patient records, prescriptions, X-ray images, general personal data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 - Notification of a personal data breach

companyDescription: Chan Brothers Travel Pte Ltd is a travel and tourism company that operated a website powered by Salesforce Community Cloud to collect customer enquiries and feedback through online forms.
companyLongDescription: Chan Brothers Travel Pte Ltd is a travel and tourism company that operated a website powered by Salesforce Community Cloud to collect customer enquiries and feedback through online forms.
caseDescription: Chan Brothers Travel's website automatically indexed personal data through a Salesforce SEO feature after a March 2018 software update. The company failed to understand the security implications of the 'Public' access setting and the new SEO feature, leaving 5,593 individuals' data searchable via web engines. The organisation did not provide clear instructions to its maintenance vendor to review security configurations.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal data stored in its IT system, resulting in unauthorised indexing and searchability of data through web search engines.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Chan Brothers Travel failed to review security implications of a Salesforce software update, did not understand the SEO feature functionality.
whyTheyWereWrong: The personal data of 5,593 individuals including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and approximately 50 NRIC numbers became indexed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation claimed not to have received notification from Salesforce of the SEO feature release
claimsVsReality.reality: Salesforce published release notes on its website; Aodigy received information about the release in its capacity as vendor for another project; the release occurred in March 2018 when Chan Brothers was still maintaining the website internally

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, processing, use or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Chan Brothers failed to acquire knowledge of security settings for the Salesforce platform and was unaware of security implications of the SEO feature
violations: Chan Brothers failed to acquire knowledge of security settings for the Salesforce platform and was unaware of security implications of the SEO feature
Organisation did not configure security settings to protect personal data collected by the Forms
Failed to assess implications of the 'Public' access setting on data security
Did not provide clear instructions to outsourced vendor to review security configurations including new software features

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found Chan Brothers Travel in breach of section 24 of the PDPA and issued a Warning. No monetary fine was imposed due to mitigating factors: limited data types at risk (excluding most NRIC numbers), voluntary notification of the incident, and prompt cooperation during investigation. No directions were required as the organisation took immediate steps to prevent recurrence.
dataType: Names, email addresses, mobile phone numbers, NRIC numbers (national identity)

company: Budapesti Műszaki és Gazdaságtudományi Egyetem (Budapest University of Technology and Economics)
companyDescription: Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) is Hungary's oldest and largest technical university, founded in 1782, providing engineering and technical education and research.
companyLongDescription: Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) is Hungary's oldest and largest technical university, founded in 1782, providing engineering and technical education and research.
caseDescription: A university failed to provide an employee access to their personal data and employment records within the legally required one-month deadline. The university delayed responding to the access request for over three months and did not provide complete information even after regulatory intervention. This violated the employee's right to access their own personal data under GDPR.
violationSummary: The university denied the data subject effective access to their own personal data for an extended period without valid grounds, violating the right to access guaranteed under GDPR Article 15.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Budapest University of Technology and Economics failed to provide an employee's requested personal data within the required one-month deadline.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee was denied timely access to their own employment records, including tax withholding details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The university stated it would respond to the data request and requested the employee's patience (November 20, 2018 email).
claimsVsReality.reality: The university did not respond substantively for over three months until after regulatory intervention; the response was incomplete.

claimsVsReality.claim: The university claimed the employee already had certain information like M30 tax documents, so this satisfied the access request.
claimsVsReality.reality: Receiving information through employment processes does not discharge GDPR obligations; the university must provide complete personal data files upon request.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken on a data subject's request without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt, extendable by two months for complex or numerous requests if the controller notifies the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: University failed to respond to the data access request within one month of receipt (October 10, 2018) without providing notice of extension or justification
violations: University failed to respond to the data access request within one month of receipt (October 10, 2018) without providing notice of extension or justification
First substantive response only provided after regulatory intervention, in January 2019, over three months later
Response was incomplete and the data subject had to request additional clarification

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and access to a copy of their personal data along with specified metadata.
regulatoryFindings.description: University did not provide complete personal data copies and supporting documents as required, including employment records and work descriptions
violations: University did not provide complete personal data copies and supporting documents as required, including employment records and work descriptions
University claimed certain information had already been provided to the employee, but this does not satisfy the GDPR access right obligation to provide complete records on demand

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(3) requires the controller to provide a copy of personal data being processed in a commonly used electronic format when requested electronically.
regulatoryFindings.description: University did not provide data in accessible format within required timeframe
violations: University did not provide data in accessible format within required timeframe
Incidentally transmitted M30 tax form containing personal data of another individual (data breach/additional violation)

outcome: The Hungarian Data Protection Authority (NAIH) found the university violated GDPR Articles 12(3)-(4) and 15(1)-(3). The authority ordered the university to: (1) fulfill the employee's data access request within 8 days of the decision; (2) prove compliance within 8 days after fulfillment; (3) pay 600,000 HUF administrative fine; (4) allow publication of the decision with the university's identifying data on the authority's website. The decision is subject to judicial review within 30 days. The case highlights institutional failures in handling data subject rights even at an academic institution.
companyNow: The Budapest University of Technology and Economics remains a leading Hungarian technical university and continues its operations as a public higher education institution.
dataType: Employment records, social security registration details, tax information, work-related documentation

companyDescription: An unnamed private entity engaged in unauthorized debt claim purchasing and collection without Magyar Nemzeti Bank licensing. It processed personal data of bank loan borrowers in connection with unlicensed financial services.
companyLongDescription: An unnamed private entity engaged in unauthorized debt claim purchasing and collection without Magyar Nemzeti Bank licensing. It processed personal data of bank loan borrowers in connection with unlicensed financial services.
caseDescription: An unlicensed financial entity engaged in unauthorized debt claim purchasing activity without Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) approval and unlawfully processed personal data of loan borrowers. The entity obtained personal data through an assignment agreement and continued processing it for debt collection purposes without proper legal basis, in violation of GDPR principles of lawful processing, purpose limitation, and data minimization.
violationSummary: The entity processed personal data pursuant to an activity (unlicensed debt purchasing) that was itself unauthorized under financial services law, violating GDPR Article 5(1)(a) lawfulness requirement and Article 6 legal basis requirements. The processing was insecure in the sense of lacking proper legal authority.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Purchased bank loan debt claims without Magyar Nemzeti Bank authorization and processed borrowers' personal data including names, birth details, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Borrowers had their personal data illegally processed and shared to an unauthorized debt collector.

claimsVsReality.claim: The entity claimed it had a valid legal basis to process personal data under the contract performance provision and prior consent, and that it could continue processing even after consent withdrawal due to legal obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The underlying loan contract had terminated and been assigned; no valid legal basis existed under GDPR Article 6. The entity was unlicensed to purchase claims, making the processing itself illegal. Prior consent obtained under the loan contract did not transfer to the debt purchaser.

claimsVsReality.claim: The entity claimed it implemented a data protection policy as of 25 May 2018 and was compliant thereafter.
claimsVsReality.reality: A policy does not create legal basis or lawfulness; the entity continued to process data without proper GDPR Article 6 grounds and in violation of Article 5 principles, regardless of internal procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: The entity processed personal data in connection with unlicensed debt purchasing activity, which itself violated Hungarian financial services law (MNB authorization requirement), making the processing inherently unlawful.
violations: The entity processed personal data in connection with unlicensed debt purchasing activity, which itself violated Hungarian financial services law (MNB authorization requirement), making the processing inherently unlawful.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(b) requires that personal data be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Data collected under an original loan contract with the bank was processed for debt collection purposes after the underlying contract terminated and was assigned to an unlicensed third party, violating purpose limitation and the incompatibility of purposes.
violations: Data collected under an original loan contract with the bank was processed for debt collection purposes after the underlying contract terminated and was assigned to an unlicensed third party, violating purpose limitation and the incompatibility of purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) provides that processing is lawful only if one of six legal bases is satisfied (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: The entity relied on contract performance (Article 6(1)(b)), but the underlying contract (the bank loan) had terminated before assignment; it also incorrectly relied on prior consent and a legal obligation basis that did not apply under GDPR.
violations: The entity relied on contract performance (Article 6(1)(b)), but the underlying contract (the bank loan) had terminated before assignment; it also incorrectly relied on prior consent and a legal obligation basis that did not apply under GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(2) empowers supervisory authorities to censure and restrict processing where violations occur.
regulatoryFindings.description: The authority found violations of Articles 5 and 6 and exercised its authority to restrict and prohibit debt-related processing of the individuals' data.
violations: The authority found violations of Articles 5 and 6 and exercised its authority to restrict and prohibit debt-related processing of the individuals' data.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) partially upheld the individuals' complaint. The Authority found the entity unlawfully processed the individuals' personal data in connection with unauthorized debt claim purchasing. The Authority: (1) censured the entity for violating GDPR Articles 5(1)(a)–(b) and 6(1); (2) ordered restriction of the individuals' personal data processing and prohibited their use for debt claim collection purposes; (3) rejected the individuals' request for a specific fine amount but imposed an administrative fine of 1,000,000 HUF (approximately €3,400) on the entity due diligence grounds. The Authority noted that data stored in connection with proceedings before other authorities (tax, central bank, bankruptcy, police, land registry) may be retained for purposes of defending legal claims, consistent with GDPR Article 17(3)(e). The decision is final subject to judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown. The entity was unlicensed and operating illegally; no information provided on current operational status. The MNB prohibited it from engaging in debt claim purchasing activity as of January 2019.
dataType: Personal identification data (name, birth name, birthplace, date of birth, mother's name, address), financial data (loan amounts, collateral information)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1) – Legal basis for processing
GDPR Article 58(2)(b) – Supervisory authority power to censure
GDPR Article 83(5)(a) – Administrative fines for principles violations

companyDescription: Jean Yip Salon Pte Ltd is a salon business operating in Singapore that provides hair and beauty services with an online appointment booking system.
companyLongDescription: Jean Yip Salon Pte Ltd is a salon business operating in Singapore that provides hair and beauty services with an online appointment booking system.
caseDescription: Jean Yip Salon Pte Ltd inadvertently exposed an internal employee system to public internet access by failing to ascertain server contents when enabling public access to its appointment booking system. The exposed system contained personal data of 28 employees accessible via default credentials with no password policy enforcement.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to adopt reasonable security measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access, directly resulting in exposure of sensitive employee information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Jean Yip Salon opened public server access without verifying what systems it hosted, failed to deactivate old user accounts.
whyTheyWereWrong: The personal data of 28 employees including their NRIC numbers, residence status, dates of birth, nationalities.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to adopt reasonable measures to protect personal data in their possession against risks of unauthorised access.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation opened public server access without ascertaining what systems it hosted
violations: Organisation opened public server access without ascertaining what systems it hosted
Employee system intended for internal use only became publicly accessible
No processes existed to remove or deactivate unnecessary user accounts
No password policy was enforced, allowing access via well-known default credentials

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the Organisation in breach of section 24 of the PDPA and issued a formal warning. No directions were issued as the Organisation had already implemented corrective measures addressing the security gaps.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, residence status, date of birth, nationality, gender, mobile number, job designation

companyDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company engaged in credit recovery and vehicle repossession services, processing personal data including contact information for enforcement purposes.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company engaged in credit recovery and vehicle repossession services, processing personal data including contact information for enforcement purposes.
caseDescription: A debt collection company continued to process a debtor's telephone numbers after the debtor withdrew consent and requested deletion. The company claimed a legitimate interest basis under GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) for debt collection, but the interest assessment was flawed and did not override the data subject's right to erasure. The authority found the processing unlawful and imposed a fine.
violationSummary: The company repurposed telephone numbers originally collected with consent for debt collection under an asserted but inadequately justified legitimate interest, continuing processing after withdrawal of the original legal basis.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The debt collection company retained and processed a customer's telephone numbers after the customer explicitly withdrew consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer lost the ability to control contact with the company and faced continued unwanted phone calls for debt collection purposes after clearly requesting all communications cease,.

claimsVsReality.claim: We must retain telephone numbers because processing is necessary for legal proceedings (Art. 17(3)(e)) and for the purposes of legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)).
claimsVsReality.reality: Debt collection is not a legal proceeding—it is a pre-legal settlement effort. No court case had been filed. The company's own interest assessment was contradictory and incomplete, failing to prove telephone contact was necessary when postal contact was available and the data subject had explicitly requested postal-only contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: We have conducted a proper interest balancing test (Érdekmérlegelés) that justifies retention of telephone numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The interest assessment contained multiple fundamental flaws: it was internally contradictory, it focused narrowly only on vehicle withdrawal scenarios while ignoring other debt collection purposes, it generalized about data subject preferences, and it entirely failed to address what happens when an individual objects to or refuses telephone contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: We must notify the data subject about vehicle withdrawal consequences via telephone because the administrative decision does not contain full details.
claimsVsReality.reality: Administrative decisions that comply with statutory requirements and produce legal effect do not require supplementary telephone notification. The data subject is presumed to know traffic law (Road Traffic Act) requirements for vehicle operation, and explanation of legal consequences is not the company's obligation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Processing is restricted to third-party collection and vehicle withdrawal notification only.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's response letter explicitly stated it retained telephone numbers 'as long as the debt remains unpaid' and used them for general debt collection communication—far broader than the narrow restriction it later claimed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires that personal data be 'collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The company collected telephone numbers with consent for loan assessment and contact during the contractual relationship, then continued processing for debt collection purposes after consent was withdrawn, without a valid legal basis.
violations: The company collected telephone numbers with consent for loan assessment and contact during the contractual relationship, then continued processing for debt collection purposes after consent was withdrawn, without a valid legal basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed' (data minimisation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Telephone numbers were retained and processed for debt collection despite the data subject's explicit request for deletion and despite postal address being available for contact, making telephone data unnecessary.
violations: Telephone numbers were retained and processed for debt collection despite the data subject's explicit request for deletion and despite postal address being available for contact, making telephone data unnecessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17(1)(b) grants the data subject the right to erasure when 'the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based, and there is no other legal ground for the processing.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The company refused the erasure request, claiming a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) without conducting a proper, balanced interest assessment that demonstrated necessity or proportionality.
violations: The company refused the erasure request, claiming a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) without conducting a proper, balanced interest assessment that demonstrated necessity or proportionality.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) permits processing only if 'necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's interest assessment was contradictory, incomplete, failed to address the data subject's explicit objection, did not justify why telephone contact was necessary given postal contact availability, and did not properly weigh the company's interest against the data subject's right to erasure.
violations: The company's interest assessment was contradictory, incomplete, failed to address the data subject's explicit objection, did not justify why telephone contact was necessary given postal contact availability, and did not properly weigh the company's interest against the data subject's right to erasure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 47 Recital establishes that when legitimate interest is the legal basis, a balancing test must be conducted beforehand, determining the legitimate interest, the impact on the data subject, necessity, and proportionality.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's interest balancing document contained fundamental gaps: it was contradictory (claiming both equal balance and superiority of the company's interest), narrowly focused only on vehicle withdrawal notifications, generalized about data subject preferences, and failed to address what happens when an individual objects.
violations: The company's interest balancing document contained fundamental gaps: it was contradictory (claiming both equal balance and superiority of the company's interest), narrowly focused only on vehicle withdrawal notifications, generalized about data subject preferences, and failed to address what happens when an individual objects.

outcome: The authority granted the data subject's request, ordering immediate erasure of both telephone numbers from all records and prohibiting further processing. The company was required to confirm deletion and notify the data subject within 30 days. The authority rejected the data subject's request for an administrative fine initially, but then exercised official discretion to impose an administrative fine of 1,000,000 Ft (approximately €1,000,000) for the unlawful processing. The decision is subject to judicial review before the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days. Disputed data may not be deleted or destroyed pending court resolution.
dataType: Telephone numbers (landline and mobile)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) – Purpose Limitation (Purpose Limitation Principle)
GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) – Legitimate Interest (inadequate or absent interest assessment)
GDPR Art. 13(3) – Transparency of purpose changes
GDPR Art. 47 Recital – Necessity of interest balancing

companyDescription: PeopleSearch Pte. Ltd. is a subsidiary of a listed Singapore company specialising in professional recruitment and flexible staffing services across Asia, including outsourced payroll management for corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: PeopleSearch Pte. Ltd. is a subsidiary of a listed Singapore company specialising in professional recruitment and flexible staffing services across Asia, including outsourced payroll management for corporate clients.
caseDescription: PeopleSearch Pte. Ltd. suffered a ransomware attack on 1-2 March 2019 that encrypted personal data of 472 employees and 472 next-of-kin records stored on a virtual machine server. The organisation had failed to conduct security scans, penetration testing, or patching for at least 12 months prior to the incident, leaving the system vulnerable to exploitation.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (regular patching, security testing) to prevent unauthorised access and modification of personal data, directly resulting in a ransomware incident that compromised sensitive financial and identity information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PeopleSearch failed to conduct any security scans, penetration testing, or patching of its payroll server for at least 12 months, leaving the system vulnerable to ransomware attack.
whyTheyWereWrong: 944 individuals including employees and their family members had their NRIC numbers, bank account numbers, salary details, and contact information encrypted.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation's omission of security testing and patching was due to departure of an employee responsible for VM Server oversight
claimsVsReality.reality: The Deputy Commissioner rejected this explanation as insufficient justification for 12 months of neglected security maintenance on a system storing sensitive personal data

claimsVsReality.claim: The ransomware attack posed immaterial risk of data exfiltration
claimsVsReality.reality: While outgoing traffic logs showed no spike suggesting exfiltration, the ransomware still caused unauthorised modification and encryption of 944 individuals' sensitive records including NRIC numbers and financial data, rendering them inaccessible

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: PeopleSearch failed to conduct any security scans, penetration testing, or patching of the VM Server for at least 12 months preceding the incident
violations: PeopleSearch failed to conduct any security scans, penetration testing, or patching of the VM Server for at least 12 months preceding the incident
The organisation attributed its omission to departure of an employee responsible for VM Server oversight, without establishing alternative processes

This failure resulted in unpatched vulnerabilities that were exploited by attackers to plant ransomware and encrypt 944 individuals' sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, financial information, and residential addresses
The VM Server stored personal data of a sensitive nature requiring stronger security measures, but the organisation fell far short of the required protection standard

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found PeopleSearch in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $5,000 within 30 days, with interest accruing at the Rules of Court judgment debt rate if unpaid. The decision noted mitigating factors including the organisation's regular backup practices (which enabled 2-day recovery), prompt remedial actions post-incident, full cooperation with investigations, no evidence of data exfiltration, and absence of complaints or demonstrated harm to affected individuals. The VM Server was subsequently decommissioned on 1 April 2019.
companyNow: PeopleSearch Pte. Ltd. continues to operate as a subsidiary of a listed Singapore company providing recruitment and staffing services. The payroll division was incorporated into a separate legal entity on 1 April 2019, and the vulnerable VM Server was decommissioned.
dataType: NRIC numbers, residential addresses, contact numbers, email addresses, bank account numbers, salary details, next of kin information (name, age, contact number, relationship)

companyDescription: CampVision Ltd. is a youth programme provider that engaged SHINE Children and Youth Services to collect evaluation feedback from programme participants.
companyLongDescription: CampVision Ltd. is a youth programme provider that engaged SHINE Children and Youth Services to collect evaluation feedback from programme participants.
caseDescription: CampVision Ltd. engaged SHINE to collect evaluation feedback from youths using Typeform's online survey platform. In June 2018, Typeform suffered a data breach exposing personal data of 106 individuals. CampVision failed to establish a written contract with SHINE or provide data protection instructions, violating its obligations as a data controller.
violationSummary: CampVision failed to ensure adequate security measures and contractual safeguards were in place with its processor SHINE, resulting in exposure of sensitive personal data to unauthorized access via third-party breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CampVision Ltd. engaged SHINE to collect personal data from youths including names, NRIC numbers, email addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data of 106 youths including their NRIC numbers, email addresses and school information were exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: SHINE was engaged to collect evaluation feedback on CampVision's behalf.
claimsVsReality.reality: SHINE collected sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers without contractual protections or written instructions from CampVision regarding data security.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to ensure their data processors take adequate measures to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: CampVision failed to enter into a written contract with SHINE setting out SHINE's obligations with respect to processing and protection of personal data.
violations: CampVision failed to enter into a written contract with SHINE setting out SHINE's obligations with respect to processing and protection of personal data.
CampVision failed to convey any instructions to SHINE regarding protection of the personal data collected on its behalf.

outcome: Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found CampVision in breach of section 24 of the PDPA and issued a warning to the organisation. The decision establishes that controllers must have written contracts with processors and provide explicit data protection instructions.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, email addresses, school affiliation

companyDescription: ReadyTech Corporation is a California-based company that provides online and instructor-led training services. The company was accused of misrepresenting its EU-U.S. Privacy Shield certification status to European customers.
companyLongDescription: ReadyTech Corporation is a California-based company that provides online and instructor-led training services. The company was accused of misrepresenting its EU-U.S. Privacy Shield certification status to European customers.
caseDescription: ReadyTech falsely represented that it was actively in the process of certifying compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had initiated but never completed the certification process. The company's privacy policy explicitly stated compliance commitments and dispute resolution procedures under Privacy Shield, misleading EU residents about the legal protections for their personal data transfers.
violationSummary: ReadyTech made materially false disclosures in its privacy policy about the legal status of personal data protection, misleading consumers about their data safeguards. This constitutes deceptive disclosure of material facts regarding data handling practices.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: ReadyTech published privacy policies on its website falsely claiming it was actively in the process of certifying compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents who submitted personal data to ReadyTech believed their information would receive Privacy Shield protections, but the company never completed certification.

claimsVsReality.claim: ReadyTech is in the process of certifying that we comply with the U.S. – E.U. Privacy Shield framework
claimsVsReality.reality: ReadyTech initiated an application in October 2016 but never completed the steps necessary to participate in or self-certify to the Privacy Shield framework

claimsVsReality.claim: In compliance with the US-EU Privacy Shield, ReadyTech commits to resolve complaints about your privacy
claimsVsReality.reality: ReadyTech was not certified under Privacy Shield and therefore had no legal obligation or standing to make such commitments under the framework

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ReadyTech falsely represented that it was actively in the process of certifying compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had initiated but never completed the certification process
violations: ReadyTech falsely represented that it was actively in the process of certifying compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had initiated but never completed the certification process
ReadyTech's privacy policy contained explicit statements of Privacy Shield compliance and commitment to dispute resolution procedures that were not supported by actual certification

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on October 17, 2018, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint sought a compliance order to require ReadyTech to cease making false Privacy Shield representations and ensure accurate privacy policy disclosures. The case addresses the FTC's authority to challenge false claims of Privacy Shield certification by companies under its jurisdiction.
dataType: Personal data from EU residents (unspecified types, potentially including names, contact information)

companyDescription: BLU Products, Inc. is a Florida-based mobile device manufacturer that outsources manufacturing to original device manufacturers (ODMs) and sells devices under the BLU brand through major retailers including Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. The company has sold over 50 million devices globally.
companyLongDescription: BLU Products, Inc. is a Florida-based mobile device manufacturer that outsources manufacturing to original device manufacturers (ODMs) and sells devices under the BLU brand through major retailers including Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. The company has sold over 50 million devices globally.
caseDescription: BLU Products preinstalled ADUPS spyware on mobile devices that secretly collected and transmitted sensitive personal data including full text message contents, real-time location, call logs, and contact lists to Chinese servers without user knowledge or consent. BLU's privacy policy falsely claimed it limited data sharing to service providers only as needed for their functions and claimed to implement appropriate security procedures, both materially deceptive.
violationSummary: BLU disclosed consumers' sensitive personal information to ADUPS (a third-party service provider) without adequate notice, consent, or limitation to necessary purposes. This represents unauthorised disclosure beyond the scope consumers would reasonably expect.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: BLU Products licensed and preinstalled ADUPS software on millions of mobile devices that secretly collected.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers unknowingly had their most intimate communications, precise location movements, and contact networks intercepted.

claimsVsReality.claim: BLU limits disclosure of consumer information to third-party service providers only to the extent necessary to perform their services or functions and not for other purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: ADUPS received and transmitted consumers' complete text messages, real-time location data, call and text logs with phone numbers, contact lists, and application inventories—none of which were necessary for firmware updates.

claimsVsReality.claim: BLU implements appropriate physical, electronic, and managerial security procedures to help protect personal information provided by consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: BLU failed to assess ADUPS's privacy and security practices before engagement, lacked written security standards for vendor oversight, did not contractually require data security standards, and failed to identify critical command injection vulnerabilities in preinstalled software.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: BLU represented in its privacy policy that it limits disclosure of consumer information to third-party service providers only to the extent necessary to perform their functions, but in fact ADUPS collected and transmitted text messages, location data, call logs, contacts, and app lists that were not needed for firmware updates.
violations: BLU represented in its privacy policy that it limits disclosure of consumer information to third-party service providers only to the extent necessary to perform their functions, but in fact ADUPS collected and transmitted text messages, location data, call logs, contacts, and app lists that were not needed for firmware updates.

BLU represented that it implements appropriate physical, electronic, and managerial security procedures to protect personal information, but failed to perform due diligence on ADUPS, lacked written security standards for service provider oversight, failed to contractually require data security standards, and failed to assess security risks of third-party software.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on 6 September 2018 alleging two counts of deceptive practices. The complaint alleges violations of FTC Act Section 5 regarding both deceptive disclosure practices and deceptive security claims. Resolution included compliance orders requiring BLU to implement comprehensive information security measures, maintain security controls over third-party vendors, obtain consumer consent for data collection beyond necessary functions, and submit to ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: BLU Products continues to operate as a mobile device manufacturer, but the company faced significant reputational damage from the ADUPS scandal and regulatory enforcement action.
dataType: Text messages, location data, call logs, contact lists, application usage
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair and deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive privacy and security representations

company: Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (Data Protection Authority of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern)
companyDescription: The Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is an independent data protection supervisory authority responsible for monitoring GDPR/privacy law compliance across the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It provides guidance, conducts investigations, mediates complaints, and issues enforcement actions.
companyLongDescription: The Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is an independent data protection supervisory authority responsible for monitoring GDPR/privacy law compliance across the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It provides guidance, conducts investigations, mediates complaints, and issues enforcement actions.
caseDescription: This is the 2018 activity report of the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern data protection authority documenting enforcement actions, consultations, and guidance. The report addresses GDPR implementation challenges, data breach notifications, and privacy violations across multiple sectors including police bodycams, healthcare, education, and municipal administration.
violationSummary: Systemic failures in encryption, access control, secure transmission protocols, and data protection infrastructure across multiple enforced entities. Organizations failed to implement or maintain security standards required by GDPR Art. 32.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Multiple organizations under their oversight failed to implement basic data security measures, including unencrypted email transmission of sensitive personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: A 15-year-old sexual abuse victim had her contact information illegally obtained by a police officer who then solicited her via SMS; another 13-year-old witness was contacted by an investigator.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organizations claimed uncertainty about GDPR encryption requirements and legitimate business justifications for unencrypted transmission
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Art. 32 explicitly requires encryption as a standard technical measure; legitimate business needs do not justify exposing sensitive data to interception. Unencrypted fax transmission to wrong recipient, unencrypted email with health/financial data, and unencrypted smart meter readings all violated established standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Police and justice sector actors claimed lack of awareness about GDPR restrictions on access to personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: Police officers knowingly exploited access to contact databases for sexual coercion of minors and extortion. This constituted deliberate misuse rather than ignorance; discipline and criminal referral were appropriate.

claimsVsReality.claim: Educational institutions claimed uncertainty about photo permissions and media release forms required under GDPR Art. 13
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Art. 13 requires explicit, granular consent for each use (e.g., homepage vs. press vs. distribution to other parents). Silent consent and blanket permissions violate the standard.

claimsVsReality.claim: Health sector entities claimed insufficient time/resources to implement GDPR compliance measures
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR became enforceable May 25, 2018. Organizations had 24 months from adoption (May 2016) to prepare. Late implementation reflects priority failure, not impossibility.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: OLG Rostock sent confidential criminal case documents via unencrypted fax to wrong recipient, exposing defendant and case details to third parties
violations: OLG Rostock sent confidential criminal case documents via unencrypted fax to wrong recipient, exposing defendant and case details to third parties
Public authority transmitted sensitive social data via unencrypted email to employee's work address, visible to colleagues and sent without authorization to mayor
Municipal ratsinformation system was compromised for 6+ years (2012-2018) with unencrypted resident data stored and exposed in procurement documents

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including encryption of personal data and the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: Smart meters transmitted consumption data unencrypted, enabling behavioral profiling through second-by-second granularity instead of monthly consolidated readings
violations: Smart meters transmitted consumption data unencrypted, enabling behavioral profiling through second-by-second granularity instead of monthly consolidated readings
Email communications lacked end-to-end encryption (S/MIME or OpenPGP) despite transport of sensitive health data, financial records, and legal documents
Fax-based transmission of sensitive documents lacked error detection; manual typos in recipient numbers resulted in misdirection to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and in any case within 72 hours.
regulatoryFindings.description: Municipal authority delayed breach notification by 14 days after discovery of ratsinformation system compromise affecting 6 years of council records
violations: Municipal authority delayed breach notification by 14 days after discovery of ratsinformation system compromise affecting 6 years of council records
Organization failed to conduct timely security assessment following system compromise, delaying identification of scope of exposed data

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires measures to prevent unauthorized persons from gaining access to personal data processing systems and data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Police officer misused position to access contact details of minors, using obtained numbers to sexually solicit a 15-year-old witness via SMS
violations: Police officer misused position to access contact details of minors, using obtained numbers to sexually solicit a 15-year-old witness via SMS
Criminal investigator accessed witness contact information and subsequently contacted 13-year-old witness via WhatsApp with sexual advances
Police officer used access to arrest records to identify and contact witness to extort withdrawal of domestic violence complaint against his son

outcome: The authority issued warnings and compliance orders to violating organizations. For police abuses, formal disciplinary proceedings were initiated against officers who misused access. Municipalities were required to cease operation of insecure systems (e.g., ratsinformation platform), notify affected residents, and implement enhanced security protocols. Organizations were directed to implement encryption standards (TLS 1.2+, S/MIME, OpenPGP), conduct data protection impact assessments using Standard-Datenschutzmodell, and appoint data protection officers. Ongoing monitoring and consultation services provided to healthcare, education, and municipal sectors.
companyNow: The Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Data Protection Authority continues operation as an independent regulatory body. In 2018, the authority reported severe personnel constraints (insufficient staff relative to workload following GDPR implementation) and continued advocacy for additional resources to fulfill enforcement mandates.
dataType: Multiple types including health data, financial data, biometric data, personal identifiers, location data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 35 - Data protection impact assessment
GDPR Art. 37 - Data protection officer designation
GDPR Art. 4 Nr. 14 - Biometric data definition

company: Prime Sites, Inc. (doing business as Explore Talent)
companyDescription: Explore Talent (Prime Sites, Inc.) operated an online talent search network allowing aspiring actors, models, and artists to search for auditions and casting calls. The company charged users for premium 'pro' memberships to access and apply for listed opportunities.
companyLongDescription: Explore Talent (Prime Sites, Inc.) operated an online talent search network allowing aspiring actors, models, and artists to search for auditions and casting calls. The company charged users for premium 'pro' memberships to access and apply for listed opportunities.
caseDescription: Explore Talent collected personal information from over 100,000 children under 13 without parental consent or adequate notice, in violation of COPPA. The company made false privacy claims and misrepresented casting opportunities to deceive users into paying for premium memberships.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected and disclosed personal information from children under 13 without parental knowledge or consent, enabling surveillance and exposure of minors' identities and photographs online.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Explore Talent collected personal information from over 100,000 children under 13 without obtaining parental consent, made their profiles publicly visible with names and photographs.
whyTheyWereWrong: More than 100,000 children's names, photos, email addresses, mailing addresses, and phone numbers were made publicly searchable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Explore Talent stated in its Privacy Policy: 'We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13.'
claimsVsReality.reality: More than 100,000 users who registered as under age 13 had their personal information collected, including names, emails, addresses, phone numbers, birthdates, and photographs, which became publicly visible on user profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: Casting directors and agents were interested in specific Explore Talent users for particular roles, as represented by telemarketers in sales calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: When one user directly contacted a casting director for 'Jack Reacher 2,' the director stated the film was not working with Explore Talent and all speaking roles were already cast. Another user promised a role in 'Fast and Furious' received no contact despite paying for pro membership.

claimsVsReality.claim: Explore Talent is the 'world's largest talent resource' with opportunities to connect users with industry professionals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company systematically targeted vulnerable minors with false casting opportunities, charged them money based on unfounded claims, and exposed their personal data and photographs to predatory contact.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(d) requires an operator to provide sufficient notice on its Web site or online services of the information it collects online from children, how it uses such information, and its disclosure practices for such information, among other required content.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent maintained a fine-print Privacy Policy buried at the bottom of the homepage among a dozen other hyperlinks, not prominently displayed or required to be reviewed or agreed to by registrants.
violations: Explore Talent maintained a fine-print Privacy Policy buried at the bottom of the homepage among a dozen other hyperlinks, not prominently displayed or required to be reviewed or agreed to by registrants.
The Policy falsely stated the company did not knowingly collect information from children under 13, despite routinely collecting personal information from 100,000+ child users.
The Policy did not provide adequate substantive notice about what information was collected from children, how it was used, or how it was disclosed.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b) requires an operator to provide direct notice to parents of the information collected online from children, how it is used, and its disclosure practices, among other required content.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent provided no direct notice to parents of the personal information collected from child users.
violations: Explore Talent provided no direct notice to parents of the personal information collected from child users.
Parents were not notified about collection of full names, email addresses, mailing addresses, phone numbers, birthdates, photographs, and physical measurements.
Parents were not informed that children's profiles would be publicly visible to other users and unregistered visitors.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) requires an operator to obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection, use, and/or disclosure of personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent collected personal information from children under 13 without obtaining any verifiable parental consent.
violations: Explore Talent collected personal information from children under 13 without obtaining any verifiable parental consent.
The company did not verify that profiles indicating an age under 13 were created by legal guardians.
Users indicating age 12 or younger were only presented with a confirmation message asking them to verify their birthdate, not blocked from registration or required to provide parental consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) / 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent made false and misleading representations in its Privacy Policy that it 'does not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13,' while knowingly collecting such information from 100,000+ child users.
violations: Explore Talent made false and misleading representations in its Privacy Policy that it 'does not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13,' while knowingly collecting such information from 100,000+ child users.

Defendant's telemarketers made false representations to users that casting directors had chosen them for specific roles in major motion pictures (e.g., 'Jack Reacher' sequel, 'Fast and Furious' films) without any basis in fact.
Users who paid for pro memberships based on these false casting representations received no contact about promised opportunities.

outcome: Complaint filed seeking permanent injunction against future COPPA and FTC Act violations, monetary civil penalties (up to $16,000 per violation), and other equitable relief. The document indicates this is the initial complaint stage; no final settlement or judgment amount is specified in the complaint itself.
companyNow: As of the complaint filing date (February 5, 2018), Explore Talent was operating ExploreTalent.com with over 10 million members. No resolution information is provided in this complaint document.
dataType: Children's personal information including full names, email addresses, telephone numbers, mailing addresses, photographs, birthdates, physical measurements
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) (verifiable parental consent requirement)
FTC Act Section 5(a) / 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) (unfair or deceptive acts)

companyDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd. is a wholly owned subsidiary of USA-based Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd (Liberia). It operates as a data intermediary handling sales, marketing, cruise bookings, loyalty programmes, and payment collection for Singapore-based customers of the Royal Caribbean Group.
companyLongDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd. is a wholly owned subsidiary of USA-based Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd (Liberia). It operates as a data intermediary handling sales, marketing, cruise bookings, loyalty programmes, and payment collection for Singapore-based customers of the Royal Caribbean Group.
caseDescription: Royal Caribbean's payment reminder system sent collated customer lists containing personal data of 526 individuals to unrelated customers instead of the organisation. The data breach resulted from a coding error made by the company's IT support provider in the Philippines when configuring the automated email system. The Deputy Commissioner found the organisation was not in breach of its protection obligations as the error occurred wholly within the vendor's operations.
violationSummary: The confidentiality of customer personal data was breached when sensitive booking and payment information was inadvertently disclosed to unrelated third parties via automated email system malfunction.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) sent automated payment reminder emails containing personal data of 526 customers including names, booking IDs, financial details.
whyTheyWereWrong: 526 customers had their financial information, booking details, and personal names exposed to strangers without their knowledge or consent, creating identity theft and fraud risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The automated payment reminder system was a proven, successfully implemented system used in other countries.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system contained a critical coding error in Singapore's implementation that caused customer data to be sent to wrong recipients, and the organisation and vendor were unaware of the error until the complaint was received.

claimsVsReality.claim: RCL Philippines had a robust testing and sign-off process for new system implementations including test cycles and sample email review.
claimsVsReality.reality: The process failed to detect the SQL parameter coding error, suggesting inadequate testing procedures or insufficient expertise in validating the email recipient logic.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or under their control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Royal Caribbean failed to prevent unauthorised disclosure of customer personal data through inadequate oversight of vendor's system configuration and testing processes, resulting in 526 customers' financial and booking data being sent to unrelated individuals
violations: Royal Caribbean failed to prevent unauthorised disclosure of customer personal data through inadequate oversight of vendor's system configuration and testing processes, resulting in 526 customers' financial and booking data being sent to unrelated individuals

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Royal Caribbean was not in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA because the coding error occurred wholly within RCL Philippines' operations and did not arise from business functions the organisation was conducting as a data intermediary. The organisation had taken remedial actions including employee training on data protection, reviewed supervisory frameworks for new employees, and improved communication protocols with its IT vendor. The case was concluded with no monetary penalty.
companyNow: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd. continues operations as a subsidiary of Royal Caribbean Group, handling Singapore-based cruise bookings, sales, and payment collection for the parent company.
dataType: Financial data, booking information, personal names, payment details

whatTheyDid: Operated NoveltyExcuses.com selling over 50 customizable fake financial, identity, and medical documents including pay stubs, utility bills, insurance cards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Products are novelties and entertainment items for gags, tricks, and fooling friends/family/colleagues
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents were designed to deceive third parties (lenders, landlords, employers) into believing false information, and were actively used for identity theft, loan fraud, and housing fraud

caseDescription: IDmission LLC falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website and privacy policy. violationSummary: IDmission distorted the reality of its data protection status by falsely representing Privacy Shield certification, creating a misleading impression of compliance that was essential to consumer trust in cross-border data transfers.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: IDmission LLC published false statements in its privacy policy claiming it had certified to and complied with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents transferred personal data to IDmission believing their information would receive legal protections equivalent to EU standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: IDmission, LLC complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: IDmission initiated an application for Privacy Shield certification in October 2017 but did not complete the necessary steps to participate in the framework or achieve actual certification

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers can view IDmission's Privacy Shield certification on the official privacyshield.gov website
claimsVsReality.reality: IDmission was not listed on the Privacy Shield registry because it never completed the certification process

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.

violations: IDmission represented that it was a participant in and certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had not completed the certification process and was not actually certified

companyDescription: RealPage, Inc. is a property management software company providing tenant screening, rental management, and business intelligence tools to residential property owners and managers throughout the United States. The company compiled criminal records, eviction histories, and credit information into automated tenant background reports.
companyLongDescription: RealPage, Inc. is a property management software company providing tenant screening, rental management, and business intelligence tools to residential property owners and managers throughout the United States. The company compiled criminal records, eviction histories, and credit information into automated tenant background reports.
caseDescription: RealPage operated tenant screening services that provided inaccurate criminal background reports to landlords and property managers. The company used overly broad matching criteria with insufficient filters, resulting in criminal records belonging to different individuals being included in tenant screening reports. This led to prospective tenants being denied housing based on inaccurate information.
violationSummary: RealPage failed to implement reasonable procedures to ensure accuracy of consumer reports, instead operating an inherently insecure matching system that predictably generated false positives identifying wrong individuals. This constitutes a systemic failure to secure and verify personal data before transmission to third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: RealPage used overly broad matching criteria with soft phonetic matching and partial name matches to compile tenant screening reports without adequate filtering or manual verification.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of applicants were denied housing based on criminal records belonging to other individuals, including people with completely different names, birthdates, genders, and races.

claimsVsReality.claim: RealPage's proprietary matching algorithm provided accurate criminal background information for tenant screening.
claimsVsReality.reality: The algorithm's broad soft-matching criteria produced significant false positives, matching individuals with different names (not nicknames), different birth dates, different genders, and different races to the same search query, with no filtering or manual review to catch these errors.

claimsVsReality.claim: RealPage filtered results to ensure only accurate records were reported.
claimsVsReality.reality: RealPage's filtering was minimal and inconsistent: it only excluded records without exact middle name matches if middle name was available, only partially filtered by state/gender if that data was provided, and had no procedures to identify when multiple different individuals appeared in a single report.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(b) requires that whenever a consumer reporting agency prepares a consumer report, it shall follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.
regulatoryFindings.description: RealPage used broad matching criteria (soft name matches, phonetic matching, flexible date of birth ranges) without adequate filtering to identify correct individuals
violations: RealPage used broad matching criteria (soft name matches, phonetic matching, flexible date of birth ranges) without adequate filtering to identify correct individuals
RealPage did not implement procedures to assess accuracy of results, particularly when records contained internal inconsistencies or clearly referenced multiple individuals
RealPage continued reporting inaccurate criminal records despite receiving disputes throughout the relevant period (2012-2017)

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act defines a consumer reporting agency as any person that regularly engages in assembling or evaluating consumer information for furnishing consumer reports to third parties.
regulatoryFindings.description: RealPage qualified as a consumer reporting agency by regularly selling tenant screening reports containing criminal records, credit information, and other personal data to rental property owners and management companies
violations: RealPage qualified as a consumer reporting agency by regularly selling tenant screening reports containing criminal records, credit information, and other personal data to rental property owners and management companies

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: RealPage's failure to implement reasonable accuracy procedures constituted unfair practices that caused substantial injury to consumers seeking housing
violations: RealPage's failure to implement reasonable accuracy procedures constituted unfair practices that caused substantial injury to consumers seeking housing

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint against RealPage seeking monetary civil penalties (up to $3,500-$3,817 per violation depending on violation date), permanent injunction against future FCRA and FTC Act violations, and other equitable relief. The complaint does not indicate a final settlement amount as this was the initial complaint filing on October 16, 2018.
companyNow: RealPage is owned by Thoma Bravo private equity firm (acquired 2019). The company continues as a leading property management software provider but has undergone regulatory compliance changes following this FTC action.
dataType: Criminal records, eviction history, rental history, credit information, personal identifiers (name, date of birth, address, gender, race), photographs

Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 621(a) (15 U.S.C. § 1681s(a))

companyDescription: SmartStart Employment Screening, Inc. is a Delaware-based background and employment screening services company operating from Clearwater, Florida. The company serves businesses requiring employment verification and background check services.
companyLongDescription: SmartStart Employment Screening, Inc. is a Delaware-based background and employment screening services company operating from Clearwater, Florida. The company serves businesses requiring employment verification and background check services.
caseDescription: SmartStart falsely claimed to participate in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website through at least June 2018, even after its certification expired in September 2017. The company obtained Privacy Shield certification in September 2016 but failed to renew it and did not complete the required steps to affirm continued protection of personal data received during participation.
violationSummary: The company's deceptive claims about Privacy Shield participation constitute disclosure violations because they misrepresented the legal protections and oversight applicable to personal data, undermining individuals' ability to make informed decisions about data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: SmartStart Employment Screening falsely claimed on its website through June 2018 that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU citizens and job applicants submitted sensitive personal background data to SmartStart believing it would receive Privacy Shield protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: SmartStart complies with the EU-US Privacy Shield Framework and has certified adherence to Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: SmartStart obtained Privacy Shield certification in September 2016 but allowed it to expire in September 2017 without renewal and did not complete required steps to affirm continued protection of previously received personal data

claimsVsReality.claim: SmartStart has joined the EU Privacy Shield Program
claimsVsReality.reality: SmartStart is not a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework as of at least June 2018 when false statements were still being disseminated

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SmartStart represented directly and by implication that it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles when in fact its certification had expired in September 2017 and was not renewed.
violations: SmartStart represented directly and by implication that it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles when in fact its certification had expired in September 2017 and was not renewed.

SmartStart represented that it would abide by Privacy Shield framework principles requiring affirmation to Commerce of continued protection of personal data upon ceasing participation, but failed to make such affirmation.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on November 15, 2018 alleging two counts of deceptive practices. The complaint seeks cessation of false Privacy Shield claims and compliance with Privacy Shield requirements or alternative protective measures. companyDescription: Innovative Paycheck Solutions (operating as FakePayStubOnline.com) was a document forgery service operated by Katrina Moore that sold counterfeit financial documents including pay stubs, tax forms, and bank statements, along with services to falsify genuine bank statements.
companyLongDescription: Innovative Paycheck Solutions (operating as FakePayStubOnline.com) was a document forgery service operated by Katrina Moore that sold counterfeit financial documents including pay stubs, tax forms, and bank statements, along with services to falsify genuine bank statements.
caseDescription: Katrina Moore operated a website selling fake pay stubs, tax forms, bank statements, and document falsification services since 2013. The company knew these documents would be presented as genuine to lenders, landlords, and government agencies, facilitating identity theft, tax fraud, and loan fraud. The FTC sued for unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.

violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Sold fake financial documents including pay stubs, W-2s, 1099s, and bank statements, and offered services to edit real bank statements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Purchasers used the fake documents to commit identity theft and loan fraud, causing victims to experience damaged credit, fraudulent loan applications, delayed tax refunds.

claimsVsReality.claim: All items sold on this site are for novelty and entertainment purposes only.
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents were designed to look authentic and were marketed as such, with customers able to populate them with any personal or financial information and used to commit fraud against lenders, landlords, and government agencies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Products are 'fake' but look 'authentic' and contain 'accurate' calculations, and we do not use watermarks.
claimsVsReality.reality: The authentic appearance and lack of watermarks facilitated use of forged documents in fraudulent loan applications, rental agreements, and tax filings, directly enabling identity theft and financial crime.

claimsVsReality.claim: The term 'fake' is used for search engine optimization purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents were sold specifically because they appeared genuine enough to deceive financial institutions and government agencies into processing fraudulent applications based on stolen personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.

violations: Defendant advertised and sold fake financial documents knowing they would be presented as genuine to third parties such as lenders and landlords, deceiving recipients about their authenticity and origin.
Defendant did not clearly mark fake documents as inappropriate for use beyond novelty purposes, instead emphasizing their authentic appearance and accurate tax calculations, facilitating fraud.

Defendant's practices caused substantial injury to consumers (identity theft victims and fraud victims) who could not reasonably avoid the harm, with no countervailing consumer or competitive benefits.

outcome: The FTC obtained a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief against Katrina Moore. The document filed on September 13, 2018 represents the initial complaint; final resolution and remediation requirements would be determined by subsequent court orders.

violationSummary: The company's false claim of Privacy Shield participation masked the true absence of adequate data protection mechanisms, creating insecurity regarding how personal data of EU individuals was actually protected.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: mResource LLC falsely claimed on its website through at least June 2018 that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU job applicants and individuals who submitted personal data to Loop Works believed their information would receive Privacy Shield legal protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: Loop is a participant in the U.S. Department of Commerce's EU-U.S. Privacy Shield and has certified that we adhere to the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's Privacy Shield certification expired in December 2017 and was not renewed; it was not a current participant when making these claims.
