caseDescription: VenPath claimed to participate in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and comply with its principles on its website, but allowed its certification to lapse in October 2017 without renewing it or affirming continued protection of personal data. The company continued making false claims of Privacy Shield participation for at least eight months after certification expired, violating FTC deception authority.
violationSummary: VenPath's deceptive statements about Privacy Shield participation and compliance constitute misrepresentation regarding the safeguards applied to EU residents' personal data, enabling unlawful transfers and inadequate protection.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: VenPath claimed on its website through at least June 2018 that it participates in and is certified to the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework, directing users to the official Privacy Shield list.
whyTheyWereWrong: VenPath's Privacy Shield certification expired in October 2017 and was never renewed, meaning EU residents' personal data lacked the legal protections VenPath falsely promised.

claimsVsReality.claim: VenPath participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework.
claimsVsReality.reality: VenPath's Privacy Shield certification expired in October 2017 and was never renewed; it was not a current participant.

claimsVsReality.claim: VenPath complies with the Privacy Shield Principles for all onward transfers of personal data from the EU.

companyDescription: PayPal is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Jose, California, operating as a leading digital payments platform. The company provides payment and social networking services, including the Venmo peer-to-peer mobile payment application acquired in 2013.
companyLongDescription: PayPal is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Jose, California, operating as a leading digital payments platform. The company provides payment and social networking services, including the Venmo peer-to-peer mobile payment application acquired in 2013.
caseDescription: PayPal's Venmo payment service misrepresented fund availability and transfer timelines, delayed or reversed transactions without disclosure, and failed to implement adequate privacy controls and security safeguards. Millions of consumers relied on misleading claims about overnight fund transfers and private transaction settings, suffering financial losses when funds were frozen or removed without warning.
violationSummary: PayPal made false or misleading representations about fund transfer timelines and privacy settings, withheld material facts about transaction holds/reversals and retroactive sharing capabilities, and failed to implement promised 'bank-grade' security, resulting in unauthorized account access and financial loss.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Venmo represented that funds were credited to accounts and could transfer to bank accounts overnight.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers suffered financial hardship unable to access expected funds for rent and bills; some lost thousands of dollars when Venmo reversed transactions after customers had already.

claimsVsReality.claim: Money credited to your Venmo balance. Transfer to your bank overnight.
claimsVsReality.reality: Funds could be frozen or reversed during hidden fraud reviews; overnight transfers were not guaranteed and often delayed or failed without disclosure to consumers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Use Venmo with anyone and for purchases; cash out to any bank overnight.
claimsVsReality.reality: Transactions were frequently delayed or reversed, particularly involving new users or business transactions, contradicting claims that 'anyone' could transact and receive funds immediately.

claimsVsReality.claim: Setting your default audience to 'Participants Only' will ensure your payments are only visible to you and the other participant.
claimsVsReality.reality: The other transaction participant could retroactively override the privacy setting and publish the transaction publicly at any time without notice to the user.

claimsVsReality.claim: Venmo uses bank-grade security systems and data encryption to protect your financial information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Venmo lacked basic security safeguards; it did not notify users of password changes, email address changes, or new devices added to accounts, enabling unauthorized account takeovers and fund withdrawals without any user notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Venmo represented that money credited to a Venmo account could be transferred to an external bank account overnight, but failed to disclose that funds could be frozen or removed during hidden fraud review processes, in numerous instances causing delays or reversals.
violations: Venmo represented that money credited to a Venmo account could be transferred to an external bank account overnight, but failed to disclose that funds could be frozen or removed during hidden fraud review processes, in numerous instances causing delays or reversals.

Venmo represented that the Default Audience Setting and Individual Audience Setting would restrict transaction visibility to specified groups (e.g., 'Participants Only' or 'Friends'), but failed to disclose that another transaction participant could retroactively override privacy settings and publish previously private transactions without notice.

Venmo represented it used 'bank-grade security systems and data encryption' to protect financial information, but failed to implement basic safeguards including security notifications for account changes, resulting in unauthorized account takeovers where funds were withdrawn without consumer notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) and Regulation P (12 C.F.R. Part 1016) require financial institutions to provide customers with a clear and conspicuous initial privacy notice that accurately reflects the institution's privacy policies and practices, and to deliver the notice so each consumer receives actual notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Venmo failed to provide a clear and conspicuous initial privacy notice; the signup screen displayed the disclosure in grey text on a light grey background, insufficient to call attention to the nature and significance of the information.
violations: Venmo failed to provide a clear and conspicuous initial privacy notice; the signup screen displayed the disclosure in grey text on a light grey background, insufficient to call attention to the nature and significance of the information.

Venmo's privacy notice was not accurate; it claimed information was shared only with a user's 'social web' for 'public' or 'friends-only' transactions, but Venmo actually shared all transactions by default with 'everyone on the Internet,' including non-account holders.

Venmo failed to deliver the initial privacy notice so consumers could reasonably expect to receive actual notice; users could click a link to the Privacy Policy but the company did not require acknowledgement of receipt as a condition of service access.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, safeguard implementation, and regular testing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Until at least August 2014, Venmo failed to maintain a written comprehensive information security program.
violations: Until at least August 2014, Venmo failed to maintain a written comprehensive information security program.
Until at least September 2014, Venmo failed to assess reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information.

Until approximately March 2015, Venmo failed to implement basic safeguards including security notifications to consumers of password/email changes or new device additions to accounts, and failed to maintain adequate customer support to investigate and respond to unauthorized transaction reports, resulting in account takeovers where funds were withdrawn without notification.

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a Complaint on May 23, 2018, alleging violations of FTC Act Section 5, the Privacy Rule, Regulation P, and the Safeguards Rule. The complaint seeks a Consent Order requiring PayPal/Venmo to implement comprehensive remedial measures including: clear and accurate disclosures about fund transfer timing and conditions, accurate privacy notices and settings, implementation of adequate security safeguards including security notifications and customer support, and ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: PayPal remains a major global fintech company and continues to operate Venmo as a peer-to-peer payment service. Following this enforcement action, PayPal implemented corrective measures to its privacy controls and security practices.

companyDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a San Francisco-based transportation network company providing ride-sharing, delivery, and mobility services globally. Founded in 2009, it operates in over 70 countries.
companyLongDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a San Francisco-based transportation network company providing ride-sharing, delivery, and mobility services globally. Founded in 2009, it operates in over 70 countries.
caseDescription: In November 2016, Uber discovered hackers had accessed personal data of millions of customers and over 174,000 California drivers. Rather than notifying affected individuals and regulators as required by law, Uber paid hackers $100,000 for silence and deletion. Notification was only issued over a year later in November 2017.
violationSummary: Hackers breached Uber's cloud storage containing personal data, causing loss of confidentiality. Uber then compounded the breach by intentionally concealing it and suppressing notification to affected individuals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Concealed a data breach affecting millions of users by paying hackers $100,000 to delete stolen data and remain silent, delaying notification to regulators and victims for over 13 months.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 174,000 California drivers' unencrypted names and driver's license numbers were stolen, along with names, emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber maintained reasonable security procedures to protect personal information
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber published cloud storage credentials in plain text, lacked multi-factor authentication, and allowed personal credentials for GitHub access

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber would notify affected individuals of breaches expeditiously
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber concealed the breach for 13+ months, notifying regulators only in November 2017, 11 months after hackers were paid

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber's systems were adequately secured against unauthorized access
claimsVsReality.reality: Hackers easily exploited a 'major vulnerability' in Uber's security system via GitHub access and plaintext credentials

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.82(a) requires disclosure of a breach of security of a system and issuance of security breach notification to affected individuals in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uber failed to notify affected drivers and users until November 2017, more than 13 months after the November 2016 breach, violating the requirement for expedient notification.
violations: Uber failed to notify affected drivers and users until November 2017, more than 13 months after the November 2016 breach, violating the requirement for expedient notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) requires implementation and maintenance of reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information to protect it from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uber failed to implement reasonable security by: (1) allowing employees to use personal usernames/passwords for GitHub access without multi-factor authentication; (2) publishing cloud storage credentials in plain text in computer code; (3) inadequate access controls on its private GitHub workspace.
violations: Uber failed to implement reasonable security by: (1) allowing employees to use personal usernames/passwords for GitHub access without multi-factor authentication; (2) publishing cloud storage credentials in plain text in computer code; (3) inadequate access controls on its private GitHub workspace.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uber engaged in unlawful and fraudulent conduct by deliberately concealing the breach, paying hackers to suppress evidence, and intentionally delaying notification to regulators and victims.
violations: Uber engaged in unlawful and fraudulent conduct by deliberately concealing the breach, paying hackers to suppress evidence, and intentionally delaying notification to regulators and victims.

outcome: The complaint sought permanent injunction preventing Uber from engaging in unfair competition, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation, and recovery of costs of suit. The document is the initial complaint filed September 25, 2018; final resolution and settlement terms are not reflected in this document.
companyNow: Uber Technologies remains a major global ride-sharing platform. The company subsequently settled related investigations and implemented enhanced security and compliance programs following the 2016 breach disclosure.
dataType: Names, driver's license numbers, email addresses, mobile phone numbers

company: EMP Media, Inc. (d/b/a MyEx.com, Post My Ad, T & A Media, Internet Secrets)
companyDescription: EMP Media, Inc. was a Nevada corporation founded in 2008 that operated multiple online properties including MyEx.com, a revenge porn website dedicated to publishing intimate images and personal information without consent.
companyLongDescription: EMP Media, Inc. was a Nevada corporation founded in 2008 that operated multiple online properties including MyEx.com, a revenge porn website dedicated to publishing intimate images and personal information without consent.
caseDescription: EMP Media operated MyEx.com, a revenge porn website that solicited and published intimate images of individuals without consent, along with their personal information. The company charged victims $499–$2,800 to remove their images and data. The FTC and Nevada alleged unfair and deceptive practices causing substantial consumer harm.
violationSummary: The company publicly disclosed intimate images and personal information without consent, enabling identification and contact of individuals. This falls squarely within 'Disclosure' – the unauthorized revelation of sensitive personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: EMP Media operated MyEx.com, a revenge porn website that solicited intimate images without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 12,620 victims had explicit images published without consent, causing job loss, depression, anxiety, unwanted contact from strangers.

claimsVsReality.claim: MyEx.com's 'Removal Policy' stated the site did not permit removal requests and blamed users: 'if you don't want photos of you end up on the internet be more careful who you send them too'
claimsVsReality.reality: The site actively solicited intimate images, demanded $499–$2,800 from victims to remove them, and operated as an extortion scheme

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendant Applegate told GoDaddy that the Netherlands address and 'Eun Kim' contact were fabricated: 'it's a made up name for the address'
claimsVsReality.reality: These false identities were used to evade law enforcement after GoDaddy informed Applegate of child exploitation reports and contact from internet crimes task forces

claimsVsReality.claim: Removal services were presented as 'independent arbitration services' (reputationguard.co, internetreputation.com)
claimsVsReality.reality: These services were controlled or affiliated with EMP and the defendants, routing funds through Western Union to the Philippines in the name of 'Sheila Garcia' – an apparent front

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: EMP solicited intimate images without consent from individuals and published them alongside personal information on a publicly accessible website
violations: EMP solicited intimate images without consent from individuals and published them alongside personal information on a publicly accessible website
EMP charged victims $499–$2,800 to remove non-consensual intimate images and personal data, constituting extortion

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines unfairness as causing substantial consumer injury that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Approximately 12,620 victims suffered job loss, psychological harm, harassment, safety threats, and financial losses
violations: Approximately 12,620 victims suffered job loss, psychological harm, harassment, safety threats, and financial losses
Victims could not avoid the harm as individuals had no control over whether their images were submitted or published

regulatoryFindings.act: Nevada Revised Statutes § 598.0923(4) prohibits deceptive trade practices involving coercion, duress, or intimidation in a transaction.
regulatoryFindings.description: EMP demanded payment from consumers under threat of continued public display of intimate images and personal information
violations: EMP demanded payment from consumers under threat of continued public display of intimate images and personal information

outcome: Complaint filed January 9, 2018, seeking temporary, preliminary, and permanent injunctive relief; rescission or reformation of contracts; restitution; refund of monies paid; disgorgement of ill-gotten gains; and other equitable relief. The court was asked to suspend the website, freeze assets, and enforce compliance monitoring. The complaint documents that EMP took in over $4 million from January 2014 through April 2016 alone, partially through removal fees.
companyNow: EMP Media was dissolved July 7, 2016. MyEx.com continues to operate behind anonymized domain registration through Yeicox Limited (British Virgin Islands), registered via Panama-based privacy services, evading enforcement.
dataType: Personal information (name, age, address, employer, phone number, email, social media accounts); intimate/sexually explicit images and videos
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce
FTC Act Section 5(n) – Substantial consumer injury not outweighed by countervailing benefits
Nevada Revised Statutes § 598.0923(4) – Deceptive trade practice using coercion, duress, or intimidation

companyDescription: Apartment Hunters, Inc. operated prepaid rental listing websites targeting housing-vulnerable populations, including Section 8 voucher recipients. The company charged subscription fees for access to rental property contact information while making deceptive claims about listing accuracy and housing search success rates.
companyLongDescription: Apartment Hunters, Inc. operated prepaid rental listing websites targeting housing-vulnerable populations, including Section 8 voucher recipients. The company charged subscription fees for access to rental property contact information while making deceptive claims about listing accuracy and housing search success rates.
caseDescription: Apartment Hunters operated prepaid rental listing websites (WeTakeSection8.com, ApartmentHunterz.com, FeaturedRentals.com) that charged consumers fees to access contact information for property managers. The company made false and unsubstantiated claims about listing accuracy, availability, exclusivity, and how quickly consumers would find housing. The majority of listings were unavailable or did not accept the vouchers advertised, particularly on the Section 8 site targeting low-income families with strict housing deadlines.
violationSummary: Defendants misrepresented material facts about rental listings (accuracy, availability, exclusivity, and search outcomes), deceiving consumers into purchasing subscriptions under false pretenses.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Apartment Hunters charged consumers $14.99–$49 for access to rental listings on WeTakeSection8.com, ApartmentHunterz.com.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers—particularly vulnerable Section 8 voucher holders with only 60–120 days to secure housing—lost subscription fees.

claimsVsReality.claim: 500,000+ Section 8 approved or low-priced apartments and homes available for rent nationwide with most up-to-date listings updated daily
claimsVsReality.reality: Majority of listings were unavailable for rent; most available units did not accept Section 8 vouchers; company did not verify availability in timely manner

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers find a place within 5–7 business days (WeTakeSection8.com) or 3–5 days (ApartmentHunterz.com)
claimsVsReality.reality: No substantiation provided; company knew claims were inaccurate; actual consumer outcomes differed significantly; defendants received hundreds of complaints about unavailable properties

claimsVsReality.claim: Exclusive rights to list thousands of Section 8 and other rental listings not found on free websites
claimsVsReality.reality: No exclusive rights existed; company did not verify whether listings appeared on free websites; same listings appeared across multiple platforms

claimsVsReality.claim: Listings are validated and phone numbers, email addresses, and availability are confirmed
claimsVsReality.reality: Company did little verification and received listings from third-party data partners with known inaccuracies in description, price, availability, and address

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants represented that rental listings were accurate, up-to-date, and available for rent when in fact the majority were unavailable or did not match advertised criteria (particularly Section 8 acceptance).
violations: Defendants represented that rental listings were accurate, up-to-date, and available for rent when in fact the majority were unavailable or did not match advertised criteria (particularly Section 8 acceptance).
Defendants claimed consumers would find housing within 3–7 business days; in reality, no substantiation supported these claims and complaints showed actual outcomes differed significantly.

Defendants claimed to have exclusive rights to thousands of listings and that consumers could not find these on free websites, when they had no exclusive rights and did not verify whether listings appeared elsewhere.
Defendants claimed to validate listings and update them daily in real-time when they did little verification and received listings from third-party data partners with known inaccuracies.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief seeking temporary, preliminary, and permanent injunctive relief; rescission or reformation of contracts; restitution; refund of monies paid; disgorgement of ill-gotten monies; and costs. The document filed 09/11/18 initiated the case. Final resolution and settlement terms would be determined in subsequent court proceedings or settlement agreements.
companyNow: Apartment Hunters continued operating prepaid rental listing services after its California PRLS license was revoked in 2015 for similar deceptive practices. The company remained subject to FTC enforcement action as of the September 2018 complaint.
dataType: Personal contact information (phone numbers, email addresses), rental history information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Global Outsource Solutions Pte. Ltd. is a warranty service provider that collected and managed product warranty registration data for its clients' customers through an online platform.
companyLongDescription: Global Outsource Solutions Pte. Ltd. is a warranty service provider that collected and managed product warranty registration data for its clients' customers through an online platform.
caseDescription: Global Outsource Solutions operated a warranty registration website that exposed customers' personal data due to inadequate security controls. A user discovered they could access another individual's warranty information on the registration summary page. The company had failed to implement reasonable security arrangements or develop internal data protection policies.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, resulting in unauthorized access to another individual's information. This constitutes a failure of information security controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Global Outsource Solutions operated a warranty registration website that failed to implement security controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: A complaint revealed that customers could view other individuals' complete personal information on the warranty registration page, exposing sensitive contact details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Website was secure and appropriate for handling customer personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: Website lacked basic security controls and allowed unauthorized users to access other customers' personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 12 of the PDPA requires organisations to develop and implement policies to ensure compliance with the Act and to put employees through data protection training.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization failed to develop and implement internal data protection policies for employees handling personal data in relation to warranty registration
violations: Organization failed to develop and implement internal data protection policies for employees handling personal data in relation to warranty registration

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the PDPA requires organisations to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorized access.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization did not provide security requirements to the website vendor, did not review security arrangements, and did not conduct security testing, resulting in unauthorized access to customer personal data
violations: Organization did not provide security requirements to the website vendor, did not review security arrangements, and did not conduct security testing, resulting in unauthorized access to customer personal data

outcome: The organization admitted to the incident but could not identify its cause. The Commission found breaches of sections 12 and 24 of the PDPA. The organization has removed the warranty registration section from its website and is revamping the website with necessary security arrangements. It is directed to develop and implement data protection policies, implement staff training in data protection, and put all employees handling personal data through data protection training.
companyNow: The organization has ceased the warranty registration functionality on its website and is in the process of revamping the website to incorporate necessary security arrangements.
dataType: Name, email address, mailing address, contact number, product purchase details, retailer information, store location

companyDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a multinational transportation and delivery company founded in 2009 that operates a mobile application connecting drivers with riders seeking transportation services. As of the complaint period, Uber had over 160,000 active drivers and more than 1 billion completed rides with over $1.5 billion in annual revenues.
companyLongDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a multinational transportation and delivery company founded in 2009 that operates a mobile application connecting drivers with riders seeking transportation services. As of the complaint period, Uber had over 160,000 active drivers and more than 1 billion completed rides with over $1.5 billion in annual revenues.
caseDescription: Uber falsely represented that it closely monitored and audited employee access to consumer data and provided reasonable security for personal information stored in databases. In reality, Uber failed to implement basic security controls, stored sensitive data unencrypted, and suffered two major breaches exposing millions of riders' and drivers' personal information, which it concealed for over a year.
violationSummary: Two major data breaches resulted directly from Uber's inadequate security practices and deceptive representations. Millions of consumers' confidential personal information was exposed to unauthorized access despite Uber's public promises of strong protections.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Uber falsely promised that internal employee access to riders' and drivers' personal data was continuously monitored.
whyTheyWereWrong: In reality, Uber stored millions of consumers' unencrypted names, phone numbers, driver's license numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber has a strict policy prohibiting all employees from accessing rider or driver data, with close monitoring and auditing by data security specialists on an ongoing basis
claimsVsReality.reality: From August 2015 to May 2016, Uber ceased timely follow-up on automated alerts and only monitored high-profile executive accounts, not general employee access. No continuous monitoring occurred during this period unless employees self-reported.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information is securely stored with standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices such as encryption, firewalls and SSL
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive personal information including names, license numbers, SSNs, and bank account data were stored in plain, unencrypted text in database backups until at least November 2016

claimsVsReality.claim: Information will be kept secure and encrypted to the highest security standards available
claimsVsReality.reality: Engineers posted AWS access keys in plain text to GitHub repositories, and Uber did not require multi-factor authentication for programmatic service account access until November 2016, allowing 2016 breach of 57M+ people

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that internal access to consumer personal information is closely monitored and audited by data security specialists on an ongoing basis, when in fact Uber failed to closely monitor or audit such access from August 2015 to May 2016
violations: Represented that internal access to consumer personal information is closely monitored and audited by data security specialists on an ongoing basis, when in fact Uber failed to closely monitor or audit such access from August 2015 to May 2016

Represented that consumers' personal information would be securely stored with reasonable security practices such as encryption, when in fact Uber stored sensitive personal information in plain text, failed to implement multi-factor authentication until September 2015, and failed to require multi-factor authentication for programmatic access until November 2016

Represented through customer service that information would be kept 'secure and encrypted to the highest security standards available,' when in fact Uber's actual practices left data vulnerable to unauthorized access

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5(a). The case proceeded based on Uber's false claims about data security and access monitoring, combined with actual breaches exposing millions of consumers' sensitive personal information. Uber was required to implement comprehensive information security improvements, including mandatory encryption, multi-factor authentication, access controls, ongoing auditing, and third-party security assessments.
companyNow: Uber Technologies remains a major global ride-sharing and delivery platform operating in hundreds of cities worldwide. The company continues operations while under FTC enforcement oversight and compliance obligations.
dataType: Names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, Social Security numbers, driver's license information, bank account and routing numbers, vehicle registration, insurance information, precise geolocation data, trip records
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Failure to provide reasonable and appropriate data security

companyDescription: Md7, LLC is a Delaware-based limited liability company that assists wireless operators in managing real estate-related issues. The company operates from San Diego, California.
companyLongDescription: Md7, LLC is a Delaware-based limited liability company that assists wireless operators in managing real estate-related issues. The company operates from San Diego, California.
caseDescription: Md7, LLC falsely claimed on its website to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework, which governs compliant transfer of personal data from Europe to the US. The company initiated an application but never completed certification, making deceptive statements about its participation to consumers and business partners.
violationSummary: The company made false representations about certification status that would affect how consumers understood privacy protections for their personal data, constituting deceptive disclosure under FTC standards.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Md7, LLC published privacy policies on its website falsely claiming it was certified and compliant with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had not completed certification with the U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union and Swiss customers transferred personal data to Md7 believing their information would receive Privacy Shield-level legal protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: Md7, LLC complies with the US-EU Privacy Shield Framework and has certified that it adheres to Privacy Shield principles
claimsVsReality.reality: Although Md7 initiated an application for Privacy Shield certification to the U.S. Department of Commerce, it did not complete the necessary steps and is not listed as a certified participant on the Privacy Shield directory maintained by Commerce.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers can view our Privacy Shield certification page at privacyshield.gov
claimsVsReality.reality: No certification page exists for Md7, LLC because the company never completed the certification process and therefore has no listing on the Privacy Shield website.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Md7, LLC represented expressly and by implication that it was a participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework through statements in its privacy policy and website, when in fact it had not completed certification and was not a certified participant.
violations: Md7, LLC represented expressly and by implication that it was a participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework through statements in its privacy policy and website, when in fact it had not completed certification and was not a certified participant.
The company claimed to comply with Privacy Shield principles and directed customers to view its certification page on privacyshield.gov, creating a false impression of regulatory compliance.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on November 20, 2017, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint seeks compliance order to cease false Privacy Shield claims and correct misleading statements. Document indicates this is the initial complaint filing; final resolution terms not yet specified in this document.
dataType: Personal data from EU/EEA individuals and employees

companyDescription: TaxSlayer, LLC is a Georgia-based tax return preparation and electronic filing service founded over 50 years ago. The company developed browser-based software and mobile applications to help consumers prepare and file federal and state income tax returns, serving over 950,000 users in 2016.
companyLongDescription: TaxSlayer, LLC is a Georgia-based tax return preparation and electronic filing service founded over 50 years ago. The company developed browser-based software and mobile applications to help consumers prepare and file federal and state income tax returns, serving over 950,000 users in 2016.
caseDescription: TaxSlayer failed to protect over 950,000 users' sensitive financial and tax data by omitting clear privacy notices and implementing inadequate security controls. A list validation attack from October 2015 to December 2015 compromised 8,882 accounts, enabling attackers to file fraudulent tax returns and divert refunds. Victims suffered identity theft, requiring extensive remediation efforts.
violationSummary: TaxSlayer failed to design and implement adequate safeguards for sensitive financial information entrusted by 950,000+ users. The company did not conduct risk assessments, had no written security program until November 2015, lacked strong authentication controls, and did not notify users when critical account details were altered. This directly enabled credential-based account takeover and tax identity theft.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: TaxSlayer failed to provide clear privacy notices to customers, did not require strong passwords, lacked multi-factor authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers exploited these security gaps to breach 8,882 accounts and commit tax identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: TaxSlayer advertised secure, reliable tax preparation and refund services
claimsVsReality.reality: TaxSlayer had no written security program, weak password policies, and no multi-factor authentication until after the breach, allowing attackers to compromise 8,882 accounts and commit tax identity theft

claimsVsReality.claim: TaxSlayer's privacy policy informed customers of data handling practices
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy policy was buried in a lengthy license agreement without clear presentation, and TaxSlayer did not require customers to acknowledge it before using the service

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) and Regulation P (12 C.F.R. Part 1016) require financial institutions to provide consumers with a clear and conspicuous initial and annual privacy notice that accurately reflects the institution's privacy policies and practices, and deliver the notice so each consumer can reasonably be expected to receive actual notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: TaxSlayer's privacy policy was embedded at the end of a long license agreement without conveying its importance or relevance to customers
violations: TaxSlayer's privacy policy was embedded at the end of a long license agreement without conveying its importance or relevance to customers
TaxSlayer did not require customers to acknowledge receipt of the privacy notice as a necessary step to obtaining the service

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive information security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards appropriate to the institution's size, complexity, and the sensitivity of customer information.
regulatoryFindings.description: TaxSlayer had no written information security program until November 2015, despite collecting highly sensitive tax and financial data from 950,000+ users since the 1990s
violations: TaxSlayer had no written information security program until November 2015, despite collecting highly sensitive tax and financial data from 950,000+ users since the 1990s
TaxSlayer failed to conduct risk assessments identifying reasonably foreseeable threats such as credential-stuffing attacks
TaxSlayer did not require strong passwords (only 8-16 character requirement with no complexity standards), enabling dictionary and brute-force attacks
TaxSlayer failed to implement multi-factor authentication until December 21, 2015, after the breach occurred
TaxSlayer did not require email address validation at account creation to verify accuracy and communicate security issues
TaxSlayer failed to notify users when material changes were made to mailing address, password, security question, bank routing number, or refund method
TaxSlayer did not use rate-limiting or IP/device blocking tools to prevent rapid-succession credential-stuffing attacks

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint against TaxSlayer on October 20, 2017, alleging violations of the FTC Act, Privacy Rule, Regulation P, and Safeguards Rule. The complaint details two counts: Count I (Privacy Rule/Reg. P violations for inadequate privacy notices) and Count II (Safeguards Rule violations for failure to implement comprehensive security controls). The document does not indicate a final settlement or penalty amount; it represents the initial enforcement action. TaxSlayer was required to address the failures and implement compliance measures.
companyNow: TaxSlayer continues to operate as a tax preparation software provider. The company has since implemented multi-factor authentication and enhanced security controls in response to the enforcement action and breach.
dataType: Financial data, tax information, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, payment card numbers, personal identification, income, employment status, government benefits, health insurance information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 313 (Regulation P 12 C.F.R. Part 1016)

companyDescription: VIZIO, Inc. is a television manufacturer founded in 2002 that designs and sells internet-connected televisions in the United States. Since 2010, the company has sold over 11 million smart TVs with built-in streaming and interactive features.
companyLongDescription: VIZIO, Inc. is a television manufacturer founded in 2002 that designs and sells internet-connected televisions in the United States. Since 2010, the company has sold over 11 million smart TVs with built-in streaming and interactive features.
caseDescription: VIZIO manufactured smart TVs with automated content recognition (ACR) software that secretly collected second-by-second viewing data from over 11 million households without informed consent. The company sold this viewing history to third parties for audience measurement, advertising analytics, and targeted advertising. Consumers received inadequate notice and were misled about the extent of data collection and sale.
violationSummary: VIZIO engaged in comprehensive, second-by-second surveillance of consumer television viewing across multiple content sources without consumers' knowledge or informed consent. The default-enabled tracking and surreptitious transmission of pixel-level viewing data to company servers exemplifies unlawful surveillance.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: VIZIO installed automated content recognition (ACR) software by default on smart televisions to continuously track second-by-second viewing habits.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 11 million households had their detailed television viewing behavior harvested and sold to third parties for advertising targeting.

claimsVsReality.claim: Smart Interactivity enables program offers and suggestions about what to watch.
claimsVsReality.reality: Smart Interactivity was primarily used to track viewing habits and monetize viewing data; program offers/suggestions were rarely or never provided.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers received notice of ACR tracking and had the ability to easily disable it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumers received no on-screen notice (post-August 2014) or inadequate notice (February 2014 pop-up with no data collection disclosure). March 2016 notice timed out in 30 seconds without easy menu access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Viewing data was collected for audience measurement and analytics purposes only.
claimsVsReality.reality: Viewing data was sold to third parties for audience measurement, advertising effectiveness analysis, and targeted ad placement across devices based on household IP addresses.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: VIZIO collected second-by-second viewing data from 11+ million TVs via default-enabled ACR software without obtaining informed consumer consent.
violations: VIZIO collected second-by-second viewing data from 11+ million TVs via default-enabled ACR software without obtaining informed consumer consent.
VIZIO represented 'Smart Interactivity' as enabling 'program offers and suggestions' but actually used it for comprehensive viewing surveillance and data monetization.
VIZIO failed to adequately disclose that viewing data was collected, stored indefinitely, and sold to third parties for audience measurement, advertising analytics, and targeted ad placement.
Initial on-screen notices (2014) made no mention of data collection. Later notifications (2016) timed out in 30 seconds and did not provide easy access to disable tracking.

regulatoryFindings.act: New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act § 56:8-2 prohibits unconscionable commercial practices, misrepresentation, and knowing omission of material facts in connection with sale of merchandise.
regulatoryFindings.description: VIZIO marketed televisions with vague descriptions of 'Smart Interactivity' that concealed the extent of tracking and data commercialization.
violations: VIZIO marketed televisions with vague descriptions of 'Smart Interactivity' that concealed the extent of tracking and data commercialization.
VIZIO omitted material facts about viewing data collection and third-party sale despite this information being essential to consumer decision-making.
VIZIO did not provide promised 'program offers or suggestions' for over two years yet continued marketing 'Smart Interactivity' feature.

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint seeking permanent injunctive relief and equitable remedies including rescission, restitution, civil penalties, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. VIZIO was required to obtain affirmative informed consent before collecting and sharing viewing data, provide clear and prominent disclosures, and cease deceptive representations. The company must implement reasonable data security measures and allow consumers to delete viewing data.
companyNow: VIZIO continues to manufacture and sell smart televisions. The company is now owned by LeEco (as of 2016) and later by Walmart (2024), operating under enhanced FTC compliance obligations and privacy requirements.
dataType: Television viewing history, IP addresses, MAC addresses, WiFi data, demographic information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair and deceptive practices
New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act § 56:8-2 – Misrepresentation and omission of material fact

company: Credit Bureau Center, LLC (formerly MyScore LLC)
companyDescription: Credit Bureau Center, LLC (formerly MyScore LLC) operated websites including eFreeScore.com, CreditUpdates.com, and FreeCreditNation.com that advertised free credit scores and reports but enrolled consumers in unauthorized negative option credit monitoring services.
companyLongDescription: Credit Bureau Center, LLC (formerly MyScore LLC) operated websites including eFreeScore.com, CreditUpdates.com, and FreeCreditNation.com that advertised free credit scores and reports but enrolled consumers in unauthorized negative option credit monitoring services.
caseDescription: Defendants operated a scheme using fake rental property ads on Craigslist and fraudulent landlord emails to lure consumers to websites offering 'free' credit reports. Consumers were deceived into enrolling in a negative option credit monitoring service charging $29.94 monthly without clear disclosure or authorization. outcome: On remand from the First Circuit Court of Appeals (Fanning v. FTC, 821 F.3d 164, 1st Cir. 2016), John Fanning challenged the scope of the Compliance Monitoring Provision as overbroad and violating due process. The First Circuit found that the original scope was unreasonable—noting it would require Fanning to report even if he became a waiter at a restaurant, which was unrelated to the actual violations. Fanning argued the monitoring must be limited to business affiliations or employment involving reputational/social media websites where similar content-source misrepresentation could occur. The final resolution required narrowing the compliance monitoring to activities reasonably related to the original violations.

violations: Respondent made representations that VisualDiscovery would enable consumers to discover similar products and best prices but failed to disclose that it would act as a man-in-the-middle intercepting all communications including encrypted HTTPS websites and collecting browsing data transmitted to Superfish servers.

Respondent's preinstallation of software without adequate notice or informed consent that intercepted sensitive encrypted communications and collected browsing data caused substantial injury to consumers not offset by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable.

Respondent failed to implement reasonable security measures to assess and address security risks created by third-party software, resulting in critical vulnerabilities that exposed consumer personal information to unauthorized access including fraudulent certificate issuance and man-in-the-middle attacks.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging three counts of violation: (1) deceptive failure to disclose VisualDiscovery's man-in-the-middle functionality and data collection; (2) unfair preinstallation of man-in-the-middle software without adequate notice or consent; (3) unfair security practices in failing to reasonably assess third-party software risks. The document is the complaint; ultimate resolution through consent order or settlement would follow.
companyNow: Lenovo continues as one of the world's largest PC manufacturers. The company has since implemented enhanced security review procedures for preinstalled software following this enforcement action.

companyDescription: A voluntary industry charter signed by Belgian and Luxembourg media organisations (print, audiovisual, and magazine publishers) establishing procedures for citizens to request rectification, updates, or de-indexing of online publications mentioning them.
companyLongDescription: A voluntary industry charter signed by Belgian and Luxembourg media organisations (print, audiovisual, and magazine publishers) establishing procedures for citizens to request rectification, updates, or de-indexing of online publications mentioning them.
caseDescription: This is a voluntary charter establishing rights for citizens mentioned in online publications. It balances privacy rights against press freedom by allowing citizens to request rectification, judicial information updates, or de-indexing of inaccurate or outdated content from search engines and media archives.
companyWorth: Multiple organizations (combined revenue in hundreds of millions EUR for major signatories like VRT, RTBF, Mediahuis, Rossel)
violationSummary: The charter recognizes that permanent online accessibility of archived content (particularly judicial/criminal information) creates persistent visibility via search engines, increasing accessibility and privacy harm despite original publication being lawful.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Multiple Belgian media organizations signed a voluntary charter establishing procedures for citizens cited in online publications to request rectification of factual errors.
whyTheyWereWrong: This document does not describe wrongdoing by the signatory companies.
outcome: This is a voluntary charter establishing procedures for media organisations to handle citizen requests regarding online publications. It does not constitute an enforcement action or penalty. Signatories commit to: (1) rectifying factual errors upon sufficient proof; (2) updating judicial information when cases conclude (acquittal, dismissal, rehabilitation, pardon, amnesty); (3) de-indexing from search engines only after the search engine has refused the request, via technical means (robots.txt, noindex tag) while keeping content accessible on the media site. Decisions must be made within three months. The charter balances archival preservation and collective memory against individual privacy, maintaining that archived press content should remain accessible as a matter of democratic importance.
companyNow: This charter represents a collective commitment by major Belgian and Luxembourg media organisations (Vlaamse Nieuwsmedia, LA PRESSE.be, The Ppress, Medialaan, RTBF, RTL Belux, VRT, and Fédération des télés Locales) to establish privacy-respecting procedures for handling online publication requests.
dataType: Personal names, judicial information, criminal records, accident details

companyDescription: Henry Schein Practice Solutions, Inc. develops and sells office management and clinical software for dental practices. The company's Dentrix software is widely used in dental practices for patient records, scheduling, billing, and insurance claim processing.
companyLongDescription: Henry Schein Practice Solutions, Inc. develops and sells office management and clinical software for dental practices. The company's Dentrix software is widely used in dental practices for patient records, scheduling, billing, and insurance claim processing.
caseDescription: Henry Schein marketed Dentrix G5 software as providing industry-standard AES encryption to protect sensitive patient dental records, but the software actually used a weak proprietary algorithm. The company knew as early as November 2010 that the data protection was inferior and not suitable for HIPAA compliance, yet continued deceptive marketing for two years until June 2013 when a public vulnerability was disclosed. Dentists purchasing the software believed they were meeting regulatory obligations when they were not.
companyWorth: Unknown (subsidiary of Henry Schein, Inc., parent company market cap approximately $12-15B as of mid-2010s)
violationSummary: The company's misrepresentation about encryption security constituted insecurity in data processing; the weak algorithm left patient data vulnerable to unauthorized access and breach. This also involves deceptive practices regarding security claims.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Henry Schein advertised Dentrix G5 dental software as using industry-standard 'encryption' to protect patient data.
whyTheyWereWrong: Dentists relying on false encryption claims failed to implement additional security measures, leaving thousands of patients' sensitive health records including SSNs, diagnoses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dentrix G5 provides 'encryption' and 'new encryption capabilities' to keep patient records safe and secure
claimsVsReality.reality: Dentrix G5 used a weak, untested proprietary algorithm known as a 'weak obfuscation algorithm' that was less secure than industry-standard AES encryption and vulnerable to attack

claimsVsReality.claim: Dentrix G5 helps dentists comply with HIPAA security standards and meet regulatory obligations
claimsVsReality.reality: The encryption used did not meet NIST Special Publication 800-111 guidance required by HHS, and did not qualify for the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule 'safe harbor' that exempts encrypted data from breach notification requirements

claimsVsReality.claim: The SQL database delivers 'improved data protection by storing customer data in an encrypted format'
claimsVsReality.reality: The protection was a data masking technique using cryptography, not standard encryption, offering minimal protection against sophisticated attackers

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that Dentrix G5 provides industry-standard encryption when it actually used a weak proprietary algorithm not suitable for HIPAA compliance
violations: Represented that Dentrix G5 provides industry-standard encryption when it actually used a weak proprietary algorithm not suitable for HIPAA compliance
Represented that Dentrix G5 helps dentists meet HIPAA regulatory obligations when the encryption used was not compliant with NIST guidance or the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule safe harbor
Continued deceptive marketing for seven months after US-CERT and NIST publicly disclosed the vulnerability in June 2013

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Henry Schein on May 20, 2016 for deceptive claims regarding encryption capabilities and HIPAA compliance. The complaint alleges two counts: (Count I) deceptive claims of industry-standard encryption, and (Count II) deceptive claims that the software helps dentists meet HIPAA regulatory obligations. The document is the initial complaint; final resolution and penalties are not specified in this document.

companyDescription: Practice Fusion is a cloud-based electronic health record (EHR) provider for ambulatory healthcare settings, founded in 2007. The company operated the Patient Fusion patient portal and provider directory service.
companyLongDescription: Practice Fusion is a cloud-based electronic health record (EHR) provider for ambulatory healthcare settings, founded in 2007. The company operated the Patient Fusion patient portal and provider directory service.
caseDescription: Practice Fusion solicited patient satisfaction surveys from April 2012, representing responses would go to healthcare providers. Without adequate disclosure, the company publicly posted approximately 613,000 reviews on its Patient Fusion website in April 2013, exposing highly sensitive health information combined with identifying data that consumers believed was private.
violationSummary: The core violation is the unauthorized disclosure of sensitive health information combined with identifying data to the public, after consumers were led to believe their responses would be confidential communications with their healthcare providers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Practice Fusion sent satisfaction surveys to patients claiming to help improve provider service, collected 613,000 responses over 12 months, then published them publicly without prior disclosure.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients disclosed identifying information combined with sensitive health details (medications, psychiatric conditions, procedures.

claimsVsReality.claim: Survey emails stated feedback would help providers improve service, signed 'Thank you, [Provider Name]' and framed as sent on behalf of the provider's office.
claimsVsReality.reality: Responses were collected to populate a public-facing review website, not for confidential provider use. The framing led patients to believe communication was private.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy stated 'For your protection, do not include any personal information' and offered a 'Keep this review anonymous' checkbox.
claimsVsReality.reality: The anonymity checkbox only changed the display name (Anonymous vs. first name), not whether identifying data in the review text was exposed publicly. Personal information disclosed in reviews was posted publicly.

claimsVsReality.claim: Patient Authorization (shown only to those who clicked through) disclosed that reviews would be published publicly and not protected under HIPAA.
claimsVsReality.reality: Most consumers were not required to view the Patient Authorization (only to check a box acknowledging it) and had no prior indication from the survey emails or initial privacy policy that responses would be publicly posted.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented directly or indirectly that survey responses would be communicated only to the consumer's healthcare provider (April 5, 2012 – April 8, 2013)
violations: Represented directly or indirectly that survey responses would be communicated only to the consumer's healthcare provider (April 5, 2012 – April 8, 2013)
Failed to disclose that responses would be published publicly on the Patient Fusion review website
The 'Keep this review anonymous' checkbox only affected the display name, not whether identifying information in the text would be exposed
Patients had no historical or contextual reference to alert them to public posting, as reviews were not visible until launch
Privacy policy 'Surveys, questionnaires, and polls' section did not mention public posting until April 8, 2013

outcome: FTC issued complaint on August 15, 2016, for deceptive failure to disclose. Document does not specify final settlement terms, but indicates complaint phase initiated alleging violations of Section 5(a). The case alleged that Practice Fusion's deceptive practices harmed consumers by exposing sensitive health information without adequate prior notice or consent.
companyNow: Practice Fusion was acquired by Allscripts Healthcare Solutions in 2016. The company continues to operate as a cloud-based EHR platform, but has implemented enhanced privacy controls following enforcement action.
dataType: Health data, medical conditions, medications, treatments, patient names, phone numbers

companyDescription: Oracle Corporation is a multinational technology company specializing in database software, enterprise resource planning systems, and cloud computing solutions. It acquired Java in 2010 through the purchase of Sun Microsystems.
companyLongDescription: Oracle Corporation is a multinational technology company specializing in database software, enterprise resource planning systems, and cloud computing solutions. It acquired Java in 2010 through the purchase of Sun Microsystems.
caseDescription: Oracle misrepresented that Java SE updates would provide the latest security improvements, but failed to disclose that the update process did not remove all older, insecure versions. Consumers remained vulnerable to exploit kits targeting known vulnerabilities, risking theft of financial and personal data.
violationSummary: Oracle failed to maintain reasonable security for Java SE by not removing vulnerable software versions, and failed to disclose this material limitation to consumers who relied on security representations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Oracle represented that Java SE updates would ensure the latest security improvements but failed to disclose that updates only removed the most recent prior version.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers unknowingly retained multiple insecure Java versions after updating, leaving them vulnerable to attackers using exploit kits to steal PayPal credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: Java SE updates provide 'safe and secure access' with 'the latest security improvements'
claimsVsReality.reality: Updates removed only the most recent prior Java version; older vulnerable versions remained installed, exposing consumers to known exploits

claimsVsReality.claim: The update process ensures Java applications 'run with the most up-to-date security'
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple outdated, vulnerable Java versions could persist on the same computer after updating, enabling targeted attacks

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Oracle represented that updating Java SE would ensure users had the latest security improvements, but failed to disclose that updates did not remove all older, vulnerable Java versions.
violations: Oracle represented that updating Java SE would ensure users had the latest security improvements, but failed to disclose that updates did not remove all older, vulnerable Java versions.
Oracle knew by 2011 that its update mechanism was insufficient to remove legacy versions, yet continued the deceptive practice and failed to inform consumers during the update process.
Consumers were misled into believing their systems were secure after updating, when they remained vulnerable to exploit kits targeting known Java vulnerabilities in unremoved older versions.

outcome: FTC issued complaint alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. Oracle's failure to disclose that Java SE updates did not automatically remove all prior vulnerable versions constituted an unfair or deceptive act, leaving consumers exposed to security risks they were not made aware of.
companyNow: Oracle Corporation remains a leading global software and cloud computing company. The company has continued to develop Java and expanded its enterprise software and cloud infrastructure offerings.
dataType: Financial data (usernames, passwords, PayPal/bank/credit card credentials), sensitive personal information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: ASUSTeK Computer, Inc. is a Taiwanese multinational hardware and electronics company founded in 1989. It designs and manufactures routers, computers, motherboards, graphics cards, and other consumer electronics. ASUS sells routers worldwide through subsidiaries and third-party retailers.
companyLongDescription: ASUSTeK Computer, Inc. is a Taiwanese multinational hardware and electronics company founded in 1989. It designs and manufactures routers, computers, motherboards, graphics cards, and other consumer electronics. ASUS sells routers worldwide through subsidiaries and third-party retailers.
caseDescription: ASUS marketed routers with security features but failed to implement reasonable security protections, leaving over 918,000 routers vulnerable to unauthorized access. Multiple vulnerabilities in AiCloud, AiDisk, and firmware allowed attackers to access consumers' personal files, compromise local networks, and steal login credentials. On or before February 2014, thousands of ASUS routers were breached, exposing sensitive personal information and leading to identity theft.
violationSummary: ASUS failed to implement reasonable security measures (encryption, input validation, secure defaults, vulnerability testing) to protect sensitive personal information, resulting in widespread unauthorized access, data exposure, and identity theft.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: ASUS marketed routers with security features but shipped them with authentication bypass vulnerabilities, unencrypted file transfers, weak default credentials.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers compromised thousands of ASUS routers and accessed consumers' USB storage devices containing SSNs, tax returns, and financial information, leading to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: AiCloud is 'your secure space' and 'the most complete, accessible, and secure cloud platform' for private file sharing with 'indefinite storage and increased privacy.'
claimsVsReality.reality: AiCloud had multiple critical vulnerabilities: authentication bypass allowed attackers to access files without credentials; password disclosure vulnerability exposed login credentials in cleartext; thousands of routers were breached and files were indexed by search engines.

claimsVsReality.claim: AiDisk allows consumers to 'safely secure and access your treasured data through your router.'
claimsVsReality.reality: AiDisk used unencrypted FTP protocol, defaulted to unauthenticated internet access to all files, and recommended weak credentials ('Family'/'Family'). Thousands of routers exposed files searchable online; attackers gained unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Routers include security features like 'SPI intrusion detection' and 'DoS protection' and can 'protect computers from any unauthorized access, hacking, and virus attacks.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Routers had pervasive vulnerabilities (CSRF, buffer overflow, cross-site scripting) that attackers actively exploited. ASUS didn't test for these well-known vulnerabilities or implement low-cost protections like anti-CSRF tokens, leaving networks at risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firmware upgrade tool 'checks the ASUS server for the firmware update' and accurately indicates if your router has the latest version.
claimsVsReality.reality: ASUS repeatedly failed to update its firmware list on the server. The tool inaccurately told consumers their routers were up-to-date when critical security patches were available; this blocked consumers from protecting themselves.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ASUS represented that it took reasonable steps to ensure routers could protect local networks from attack, but failed to implement security architecture reviews, secure protocols (AiDisk used unencrypted FTP), secure defaults, or vulnerability testing.
violations: ASUS represented that it took reasonable steps to ensure routers could protect local networks from attack, but failed to implement security architecture reviews, secure protocols (AiDisk used unencrypted FTP), secure defaults, or vulnerability testing.

ASUS represented AiCloud as a secure means to access personal information, but the application contained authentication bypass and password disclosure vulnerabilities allowing unauthorized access without credentials.
ASUS represented AiDisk as secure, but defaulted to unauthenticated internet access, used unencrypted file transfer, and provided misleading warnings that discouraged security configuration.

ASUS represented the firmware upgrade tool would accurately indicate current firmware status, but failed to maintain its server list, repeatedly notifying consumers their routers were up-to-date when critical security updates were available.

regulatoryFindings.act: Unfair practice standard requires acts causing substantial injury to consumers not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
regulatoryFindings.description: ASUS's failure to implement reasonable security (secure design reviews, code review, penetration testing, low-cost protections like anti-CSRF tokens, secure defaults) caused thousands of routers to be compromised by readily-available attack tools.
violations: ASUS's failure to implement reasonable security (secure design reviews, code review, penetration testing, low-cost protections like anti-CSRF tokens, secure defaults) caused thousands of routers to be compromised by readily-available attack tools.

Consumers had no reasonable way to discover or avoid the risks—vulnerabilities were in default settings and undisclosed to users. A consumer who attempted firmware updates was blocked by the malfunctioning upgrade tool, unable to protect himself despite trying.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging five counts of unfair and deceptive practices (router security misrepresentations, AiCloud security misrepresentations, AiDisk security misrepresentations, firmware upgrade tool misrepresentations, and unfair security practices). The complaint sought to enjoin these practices and require ASUS to implement comprehensive security protections, maintain processes for receiving and addressing vulnerability reports, provide timely notice to consumers of known security risks, and submit to ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: ASUSTeK Computer remains a major global hardware manufacturer specializing in computer components, networking equipment, and consumer electronics. The company has significantly expanded its product lines since 2016 and continues to be a leading router manufacturer.
outcomeSummary: Complaint filed; consent order likely (typical FTC enforcement structure for IoT/security cases)
dataType: Financial information, login credentials, social security numbers, tax returns, medical information, private photos and videos, files on USB storage devices
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – False or Misleading Representations Regarding Security

caseDescription: IOActive falsely claimed compliance with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework on its website from 2009 to 2015, even after allowing its certification to lapse in May 2012. The company displayed the official Safe Harbor certification mark and made explicit statements about compliance while having 'not current' status with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
violationSummary: IOActive misrepresented its Safe Harbor certification status, creating false appearance of compliance with EU data protection adequacy standards. The company's display of the official certification mark and explicit compliance statements while lacking current status constitutes material distortion affecting consumer trust.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: IOActive displayed the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor certification mark and claimed compliance with the Safe Harbor Framework on its website from May 2009 through May 2015.
whyTheyWereWrong: European customers relied on IOActive's false Safe Harbor claims when transferring personal data, believing their information had legal protections it did not actually possess.

claimsVsReality.claim: IOActive stated: 'The company complies with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce regarding the collection, use, and retention of personal information from European Union member countries.'
claimsVsReality.reality: IOActive did not renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in May 2012, resulting in 'not current' status on the Commerce Department's public registry, yet the company continued displaying the certification mark and making compliance claims until May 2015

claimsVsReality.claim: Company displayed the official U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework Certification Mark on its website with accompanying compliance text
claimsVsReality.reality: The mark was only authorized for organizations maintaining 'current' self-certification; IOActive's status was 'not current' for over 3 years while displaying the mark

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: IOActive represented, expressly and by implication, that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework by displaying the official certification mark and publishing compliance statements on its privacy policy
violations: IOActive represented, expressly and by implication, that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework by displaying the official certification mark and publishing compliance statements on its privacy policy
This representation was false and misleading because IOActive's certification became 'not current' in May 2012 when it failed to renew, yet the company continued making these claims until May 2015

regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent represented, expressly or by implication, that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework when it was not, from August 2012 onwards.
violations: Respondent represented, expressly or by implication, that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework when it was not, from August 2012 onwards.
Website privacy policies and statements misrepresented Safe Harbor compliance status to consumers and data subjects for approximately three years after certification lapsed.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on September 29, 2015, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint establishes one count of misrepresentation regarding Safe Harbor participation. Respondent's status was updated to 'not current' on the Commerce Department's public Safe Harbor website, but the company continued making false claims.
