company: Filiquarian Publishing, LLC; Choice Level, LLC
companyDescription: Filiquarian Publishing, LLC and Choice Level, LLC were Minnesota companies operating criminal records mobile applications distributed through iTunes and Google Play. They sold background check apps marketed for employment screening without implementing required Fair Credit Reporting Act compliance safeguards.
companyLongDescription: Filiquarian Publishing, LLC and Choice Level, LLC were Minnesota companies operating criminal records mobile applications distributed through iTunes and Google Play. They sold background check apps marketed for employment screening without implementing required Fair Credit Reporting Act compliance safeguards.
caseDescription: Filiquarian and Choice Level operated mobile apps that provided criminal records for employment screening without complying with Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) requirements. They failed to verify users' permissible purpose, maintain accuracy procedures, or provide required notices, operating unregulated consumer reporting agencies while disclaiming FCRA compliance.
violationSummary: Criminal records were disclosed to unknown third parties without verification of permissible purpose or identity, creating risk of misuse and violation of consumer privacy in sensitive employment decisions.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Operated mobile apps selling criminal record reports to users for $0.99, marketed for employment screening, without verifying user identity, purpose, or legitimate permissible use.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sold thousands of criminal background reports to unvetted buyers with no identity checks, exposing individuals to wrongful employment discrimination, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apps include disclaimer: 'products not to be considered screening products for insurance, employment, loans, and credit applications' and 'not compliant with FCRA'; users assume responsibility for FCRA compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Apps were actively marketed as 'perfect application for you' when 'hiring somebody and wanting to quickly find out if they have a record.' The disclaimer contradicted the marketing and could not exempt respondents from being a consumer reporting agency under FCRA when operating as such.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users could access 'hundreds of thousands of criminal records' for employment purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: No verification procedures existed to confirm users had a legitimate employment-related permissible purpose, enabling misuse by anyone with $0.99.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604(a) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(a), prohibits a consumer reporting agency from furnishing consumer reports to persons unless the CRA has reason to believe they have a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents furnished consumer reports via mobile apps to third parties without any procedures to inquire into the purpose for which the user was purchasing the report.
violations: Respondents furnished consumer reports via mobile apps to third parties without any procedures to inquire into the purpose for which the user was purchasing the report.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(a) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a), requires CRAs to maintain reasonable procedures to limit the furnishing of consumer reports for permissible purposes, including requiring prospective users to identify themselves, certify their purpose, and verifying their identity.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents failed to require prospective users to identify themselves, certify purposes, or certify limited use. They made no reasonable effort to verify user identity or certified purposes.
violations: Respondents failed to require prospective users to identify themselves, certify purposes, or certify limited use. They made no reasonable effort to verify user identity or certified purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(b) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(b), requires CRAs to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of information in consumer reports.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents maintained no procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of information in the reports they provided.
violations: Respondents maintained no procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of information in the reports they provided.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(d) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(d), requires CRAs to provide notices to all users of consumer reports and to all persons who regularly furnish consumer report information to the CRA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents failed to provide any required notices to users or information furnishers.

caseDescription: Citibank failed to fix a known security vulnerability in its Account Online portal for nearly three years, allowing hackers to access customer data for over 360,000 users including 80,454 Californians. The breach exploited a simple URL parameter manipulation technique and exposed unencrypted personal and financial information. Citibank delayed notifying affected customers by over one month after discovering the breach.
violationSummary: Citibank failed to implement adequate access controls and encryption, allowing unauthorized access to customer data through a preventable exploit. This is a classic insecurity violation where inadequate technical safeguards led to breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Citibank left a known technical vulnerability in its Account Online service unpatched for nearly three years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Account Online platform was secure and compliant with federal and state data protection requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The platform contained a simple, exploitable vulnerability that permitted unauthorized account access through basic URL parameter manipulation without re-authentication, violating GLBA, OCC Guidelines, CalOPPA, and state law.

caseDescription: Epic Marketplace engaged in history sniffing—covertly accessing consumers' browsing history outside its ad network—from 2010 to 2011 to build detailed behavioral profiles. caseDescription: Google represented to Safari users that their browser's default privacy setting would block DoubleClick tracking cookies and targeted ads. However, Google secretly circumvented Safari's privacy controls by exploiting a form-submission loophole, placing tracking cookies on millions of Safari users without their knowledge or consent.
violationSummary: Google conducted unauthorized surveillance of Safari users' browsing activity through deceptive circumvention of browser privacy controls. The secret placement of tracking cookies enabled persistent identification and monitoring of user behavior across the web.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance

whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Safari users' web browsing activity was collected and tracked without their knowledge.

claimsVsReality.reality: Google's code exploited Safari's form-submission exception to place DoubleClick cookies on Safari browsers with default settings, circumventing the privacy protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: After opting out, 'Google will not collect interest category information and you will not receive interest-based ads.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Google collected interest-category information from Safari users who did not opt out because Google falsely represented that the Safari default setting provided equivalent protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Google is a member of NAI and adheres to the NAI Code, which requires clear disclosure of data collection practices.

violations: Google represented that Safari's default setting would not place DoubleClick cookies or collect interest-category information, but actually placed these cookies on Safari users' browsers
Google represented that users would not receive targeted advertisements if they did not change Safari's default setting, but served targeted ads based on secretly collected data
Google represented compliance with NAI Code Section III(2)(a) requiring disclosure of data collection practices, but failed to disclose the Safari tracking practices

regulatoryFindings.act: Google Consent Order Part I(A) requires Google not to misrepresent the extent to which consumers may exercise control over collection, use, or disclosure of covered information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google assured Safari users that the browser's default setting would protect them from DoubleClick tracking, implying consumer control, while secretly circumventing that control
violations: Google assured Safari users that the browser's default setting would protect them from DoubleClick tracking, implying consumer control, while secretly circumventing that control

Google's statements that users could 'opt out' and would then not receive targeted ads applied equally to first-party and third-party cookies, but this protection was illusory for Safari users whose cookies were already placed

outcome: The United States filed a complaint for civil penalties and other relief under FTC Act Sections 5(l) and 16(a) seeking monetary penalties (up to $16,000 per violation based on 2012 penalties inflation adjustment) and permanent injunction from violating the Google Consent Order. The case established that circumventing browser privacy controls through deceptive technical means, combined with false statements about user control and privacy protection, constitutes a material violation of prior FTC settlement obligations. Google was required to cease the conduct and comply with the Consent Order's comprehensive privacy program requirements including biennial third-party assessments.

company: Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc., also dba Franklin Toyota/Scion
companyDescription: Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc., doing business as Franklin Toyota/Scion, was a Georgia-based franchise automobile dealership that sold new and used vehicles, provided leasing and repair services, and offered consumer financing.
companyLongDescription: Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc., doing business as Franklin Toyota/Scion, was a Georgia-based franchise automobile dealership that sold new and used vehicles, provided leasing and repair services, and offered consumer financing.
caseDescription: Franklin Toyota failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect customer personal information, resulting in approximately 95,000 consumers' sensitive data being exposed on peer-to-peer networks. The company made deceptive claims about safeguarding customer information while lacking basic security controls. It also failed to provide required privacy notices and opt-out mechanisms under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures required under the Safeguards Rule, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information through a P2P network. This represents systemic insecurity in handling customer data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Franklin Toyota collected sensitive personal information from approximately 95,000 customers including names, Social Security numbers, addresses, dates of birth.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 95,000 customers' complete personal identification data became permanently available for download by anyone globally on peer-to-peer networks.

claimsVsReality.claim: We restrict access to non public personal information about you to only those employees who need to know that information to provide products and services to you.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no implemented access controls; a P2P application on a networked computer exposed files to anyone globally.

claimsVsReality.claim: We maintain physical, electronic, and procedural safe guards that comply with federal regulations to guard non public personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked risk assessments, incident response plans, security monitoring, employee training, and any formal information security program.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Franklin Toyota represented that it implements reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, but failed to implement any such measures, resulting in data exposure via P2P networks.
violations: Franklin Toyota represented that it implements reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, but failed to implement any such measures, resulting in data exposure via P2P networks.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, security design/implementation, testing/monitoring, service provider oversight, and incident response.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to assess risks to consumer personal information collected and stored online
violations: Failed to assess risks to consumer personal information collected and stored online
Failed to adopt policies such as an incident response plan to prevent unauthorized disclosure
Failed to use reasonable methods to prevent, detect, and investigate unauthorized access
Failed to adequately train employees about information security
Failed to employ reasonable measures to respond to unauthorized access or conduct security investigations
Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program
Failed to designate an employee to coordinate the company's information security program

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) requires financial institutions to provide customers annual privacy notices reflecting their policies and practices, and to provide reasonable means and notices for customers to opt out of information sharing with nonaffiliated third parties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to send consumers annual privacy notices as required
violations: Failed to send consumers annual privacy notices as required
Failed to provide a clear and conspicuous opt-out notice explaining customers' rights to opt out of sharing nonpublic information with unaffiliated third parties
Did not provide a mechanism by which consumers could opt out of information sharing with nonaffiliated third parties

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on October 3, 2012 alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, the Safeguards Rule, and the Privacy Rule. The complaint alleges unfair and deceptive practices due to false representations about data security, inadequate safeguards resulting in P2P network exposure of 95,000 consumers' records, failure to provide required privacy notices and opt-out mechanisms. The case was initiated requiring Franklin Toyota to implement comprehensive security measures and comply with privacy notification requirements.
companyNow: Unknown. Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc. was a franchise automobile dealership operating in Statesboro, Georgia. Current status of operations is not documented in this complaint.

company: Blue Cross of California (Anthem Blue Cross)
companyDescription: Blue Cross of California, doing business as Anthem Blue Cross, is a California-based health insurance company offering HMO, PPO, and point-of-service health plans to individuals, employer groups, public entities, and seniors through Medicare supplemental and Medicare Advantage products.
companyLongDescription: Blue Cross of California, doing business as Anthem Blue Cross, is a California-based health insurance company offering HMO, PPO, and point-of-service health plans to individuals, employer groups, public entities, and seniors through Medicare supplemental and Medicare Advantage products.
caseDescription: Anthem Blue Cross publicly exposed and printed Social Security numbers of 31,125 Medicare Supplement members on marketing mailers and 2,631 Medicare Part D members on collection letters, with no legal requirement to do so. The Social Security numbers were visible through envelope windows and printed as member identification numbers without adequate safeguards. This violated California privacy law by unnecessarily disclosing sensitive personally identifiable information.
violationSummary: Anthem's exposure of unencrypted Social Security numbers in mailed documents visible through envelope windows and as member IDs on collection letters constitutes information dissemination through exposure—making sensitive personal identifiers accessible to unintended recipients.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Anthem displayed 31,125 Medicare members' Social Security numbers visibly through envelope windows on marketing mailers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 33,756 members faced identity theft and fraud risks when their full Social Security numbers were exposed in mail without legal requirement, allowing theft from postal systems and mail recipients.

claimsVsReality.claim: Anthem represented that it could safely handle sensitive member information and maintain appropriate privacy protections for Social Security numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Anthem printed and mailed unencrypted Social Security numbers to tens of thousands of members without legal necessity, exposing them through envelope windows and as identification numbers on collection letters.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) prohibits publicly displaying Social Security numbers in a manner that is visible to the public.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem displayed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members in an area visible through the window of envelopes sent via United States mail service.
violations: Anthem displayed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members in an area visible through the window of envelopes sent via United States mail service.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(5) prohibits printing Social Security numbers on documents when neither state nor federal law requires such numbers to be on the documents.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem printed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members on marketing mailer documents mailed to Marketing Mailing Recipients without legal requirement.
violations: Anthem printed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members on marketing mailer documents mailed to Marketing Mailing Recipients without legal requirement.
Anthem printed the Social Security numbers of 2,631 members on collection letters mailed to Collection Letter Recipients without legal requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including any unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business act or practice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem engaged in unfair competition by violating California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) and § 1798.85(a)(5) through the public display and unnecessary printing of Social Security numbers.
violations: Anthem engaged in unfair competition by violating California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) and § 1798.85(a)(5) through the public display and unnecessary printing of Social Security numbers.

outcome: The complaint sought injunctive relief, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under Business and Professions Code § 17206, and recovery of investigation costs. The case sought to permanently enjoin Anthem and related parties from committing further acts of unfair competition involving Social Security number exposure. No settlement amount was disclosed in the complaint document.
companyNow: Anthem Blue Cross remains in operation as part of Anthem, Inc., a major health insurance provider. The company has since implemented enhanced data protection protocols and privacy safeguards for member information.
dataType: Social Security numbers

companyDescription: MySpace was a social networking website founded in 2003 that allowed users to create customizable profiles and connect with friends. At its peak around 2008, it was one of the world's most visited websites before being overtaken by Facebook. By 2012, the company faced significant user decline and competitive pressure.
companyLongDescription: MySpace was a social networking website founded in 2003 that allowed users to create customizable profiles and connect with friends. At its peak around 2008, it was one of the world's most visited websites before being overtaken by Facebook. By 2012, the company faced significant user decline and competitive pressure.
caseDescription: MySpace shared users' Friend IDs (persistent identifiers linked to full names and profile data) with third-party advertisers without explicit user consent, contradicting its privacy policy. The Friend ID enabled advertisers to access users' basic profile information including full names and to link browsing habits to personal details. MySpace also misrepresented compliance with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework principles.
violationSummary: MySpace disclosed personally identifiable information (Friend IDs functioning as persistent identifiers) to third parties (advertisers) without user notice or consent, directly contradicting its privacy policy and Safe Harbor certifications. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure and breach of confidentiality.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: From January 2009 through June 2010, MySpace transmitted users' Friend IDs, ages, and genders to third-party advertisers in unencrypted plain text.
whyTheyWereWrong: MySpace's undisclosed sharing of Friend IDs enabled third-party advertisers to identify individual users by name, combine their identities with tracking cookies.

claimsVsReality.claim: MySpace will not share users' personally identifiable information (PII) with third parties unless users have given permission.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace shared Friend IDs (which provide access to full names and basic profile information) with numerous third-party advertisers without user notice or consent from January 2009 onward.

claimsVsReality.claim: The information used for ad customization does not provide users' PII or identify users as individuals to third parties.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace transmitted Friend IDs to advertisers, which directly enabled identification of users by their full names and linkage to personal profiles for approximately 84% of users.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users' web browsing activity shared with advertisers is anonymized.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace provided Friend IDs to advertisers alongside tracking cookies, enabling complete de-anonymization and linkage of browsing history to named individuals' personal profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: MySpace adheres to the Safe Harbor Privacy Principles of notice and choice.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace collected and shared European users' personal data with advertisers without providing notice of this practice or meaningful choice mechanisms, directly violating Safe Harbor requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: MySpace represented it would not share PII with third parties without user permission, but shared Friend IDs (which give access to full names and basic profile information) with advertisers without consent.
violations: MySpace represented it would not share PII with third parties without user permission, but shared Friend IDs (which give access to full names and basic profile information) with advertisers without consent.

MySpace claimed its ad customization process does not allow advertisers to access PII or individually identify users, but transmitted Friend IDs to advertisers enabling identification of 84% of users by full name.

MySpace represented that users' web browsing activity shared with advertisers is anonymized, but linked Friend IDs to tracking cookies, allowing advertisers to correlate browsing history with personal profile information.

regulatoryFindings.act: The U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework requires organizations to provide clear notice of personal data collection and use purposes and to obtain individuals' choice regarding disclosure to third parties before collection or use begins.
regulatoryFindings.description: MySpace certified compliance with Safe Harbor Notice and Choice principles while actively transmitting European users' Friend IDs to third-party advertisers without notice or consent.
violations: MySpace certified compliance with Safe Harbor Notice and Choice principles while actively transmitting European users' Friend IDs to third-party advertisers without notice or consent.
MySpace provided no mechanism for users to opt out of sharing identifiers with advertisers, despite Safe Harbor requiring clear and conspicuous, readily available, and affordable choice mechanisms.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on August 30, 2012, alleging four counts of deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. A consent order was entered requiring MySpace to implement reasonable data security measures, obtain affirmative express consent before using Friend IDs for advertising targeting, restrict future data sharing to purposes disclosed in privacy policy, provide users with transparent privacy controls, conduct biennial privacy audits by an independent third party, and maintain compliance monitoring for 20 years. MySpace was prohibited from misrepresenting its Safe Harbor status.
companyNow: MySpace ceased major operations around 2015 following loss of users to Facebook and other platforms. The brand is now operated under new ownership as a music and entertainment platform with minimal social networking features. The company's user base and revenue are a fraction of historical levels.
dataType: Personal identifiers (name, email, date of birth, gender), profile information (relationship status, sexual orientation, hobbies, interests), Friend ID, location, photos, videos, messages, browsing activity
legalBasisViolated: U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework – Notice Principle
U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework – Choice Principle

companyDescription: HireRight Solutions, Inc. (formerly USIS Commercial Services, Inc.) is an Oklahoma-based consumer reporting agency that provides background screening reports to thousands of employers throughout the United States to assist in hiring and employment-related decisions.
companyLongDescription: HireRight Solutions, Inc. (formerly USIS Commercial Services, Inc.) is an Oklahoma-based consumer reporting agency that provides background screening reports to thousands of employers throughout the United States to assist in hiring and employment-related decisions.
caseDescription: HireRight Solutions, a background screening company, failed to maintain reasonable accuracy procedures for criminal history reports provided to employers. The company included expunged records, duplicate entries, records from other individuals, and failed to allow consumers to access or dispute inaccurate information in their files.
violationSummary: HireRight failed to implement adequate procedures to ensure accuracy of personal data in consumer reports, resulting in systematic data quality failures that exposed individuals to misidentification and employment discrimination.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: HireRight Solutions furnished inaccurate background screening reports to employers containing expunged criminal records, duplicate entries for the same offense.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job applicants were wrongfully denied employment or other employment benefits based on false criminal history information attributed to them in background reports.

claimsVsReality.claim: HireRight provides accurate background screening reports reflecting current public record status
claimsVsReality.reality: Reports included expunged records, duplicate entries, and records from other individuals; company failed to implement procedures to ensure accuracy or currency

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers can easily access and dispute information in their background reports
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumers faced backlogs, delays, and were required to obtain copies before disputes could be initiated; reinvestigation results were not provided

claimsVsReality.claim: Public record information is reported to employers with proper notification to consumers
claimsVsReality.reality: Notifications occurred days after reporting to employers, well after employment decisions may have been made; company did not maintain strict procedures for accuracy

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA § 607(b) requires consumer reporting agencies to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of consumer report information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to update reports to reflect expungement of criminal records from public records
violations: Failed to update reports to reflect expungement of criminal records from public records
Failed to prevent inclusion of multiple entries for the same criminal offense in single reports
Failed to prevent provision of obviously erroneous information, such as records of different consumers with different names and dates of birth in single reports

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA § 609(a)(1) requires consumer reporting agencies to disclose all information in a consumer's file upon request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Experienced numerous backlogs preventing fulfillment of consumer requests for their own reports
violations: Experienced numerous backlogs preventing fulfillment of consumer requests for their own reports
Delayed or failed to provide consumers access to information in their files due to inadequate staffing and technical problems

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA § 611(a)(1)(A) requires reinvestigation within 30 days of receiving notice that a consumer disputes information completeness or accuracy.
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not conduct reinvestigations of disputed items upon receipt of dispute notice
violations: Did not conduct reinvestigations of disputed items upon receipt of dispute notice
Required consumers to have a copy of their report before initiating reinvestigation, which delayed the process and deterred consumers from disputing inaccurate information

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA § 611(a)(6) requires written notice of reinvestigation results no later than five business days after completion.
regulatoryFindings.description: Closed dispute reinvestigations without providing written notice of results to affected consumers
violations: Closed dispute reinvestigations without providing written notice of results to affected consumers

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA § 613(a)(1)-(2) requires background screeners furnishing public record information for employment to either notify consumers at time of reporting or maintain strict procedures ensuring information is complete and current.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to notify consumers at time public record information was reported to employers
violations: Failed to notify consumers at time public record information was reported to employers
Maintained complex multi-step notification process initiated only after report transmission, typically taking more than one day, so notices were not sent at time of reporting
Failed to maintain strict procedures to ensure public record information was complete and up to date

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act § 5(a) prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by furnishing inaccurate consumer reports that harmed employment prospects of individuals who were denied employment or employment-related benefits
violations: Engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by furnishing inaccurate consumer reports that harmed employment prospects of individuals who were denied employment or employment-related benefits

outcome: This is a complaint for civil penalties and injunctive relief filed by the United States on behalf of the FTC. The complaint alleges five counts of FCRA violations and corresponding FTC Act violations. The case seeks monetary civil penalties, a permanent injunction against further violations, and equitable relief. Penalties authorized under the Federal Civil Penalty Inflation Adjustment Act range from $2,500 per violation (for violations before Feb 10, 2009) to $3,500 per violation (for violations on or after that date). The complaint indicates that each instance of non-compliance constitutes a separate violation.
companyNow: HireRight Solutions continues to operate as a consumer reporting agency and background screening service, now part of larger employment verification and risk management entities. The company remains subject to FCRA compliance requirements.
dataType: Criminal history records, public record information, personal identifiers, employment history

FTC Act § 5(a) (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: EPN, Inc. (also operating as Checknet, Inc.) is a Utah-based debt collection agency that collects debts on behalf of clients in commercial credit, retail, and healthcare sectors. The company processes and stores sensitive consumer personal information as part of its core business operations.
companyLongDescription: EPN, Inc. (also operating as Checknet, Inc.) is a Utah-based debt collection agency that collects debts on behalf of clients in commercial credit, retail, and healthcare sectors. The company processes and stores sensitive consumer personal information as part of its core business operations.
caseDescription: EPN, a debt collection agency, failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive consumer personal information stored on its computer networks. A peer-to-peer file-sharing application installed by an executive exposed approximately 3,800 consumers' highly sensitive data—including Social Security numbers, health insurance information, and diagnosis codes—to public P2P networks. The files remained accessible indefinitely once shared.
violationSummary: The company's pervasive failure to implement reasonable and appropriate information security measures—including lack of incident response plan, employee training, network monitoring, and P2P application detection—directly resulted in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information to the internet.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: EPN failed to implement reasonable security measures including no incident response plan, inadequate employee training, no network scanning for unauthorized applications.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal information for approximately 3,800 consumers including Social Security numbers, health insurance numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: EPN handled clients' sensitive consumer data as part of routine debt collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: EPN had no meaningful security infrastructure to protect this data; a P2P application installed without authorization exposed files to public networks indefinitely.

claimsVsReality.claim: EPN's systems were secure and appropriately managed.
claimsVsReality.reality: EPN lacked an incident response plan, did not assess security risks, provided inadequate employee training, did not scan for unauthorized applications, and had no monitoring of outgoing data transmissions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: EPN failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, causing substantial injury to approximately 3,800 consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: EPN failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, causing substantial injury to approximately 3,800 consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the formal complaint issued October 3, 2012. Resolution terms, including any consent order or remedial requirements, are not detailed in this complaint document; the case proceeded to adjudication or settlement negotiation.
dataType: Personal identification (name, address, date of birth, SSN), employment information, health insurance data, diagnosis codes, medical visit types
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

company: W3 Innovations, LLC (doing business as Broken Thumbs Apps)
companyDescription: W3 Innovations, LLC, doing business as Broken Thumbs Apps, was a software development company based in Cupertino, California that developed and distributed approximately 40 mobile applications for iPhone and iPod touch through Apple's App Store, with several apps specifically targeted at children under 13.
companyLongDescription: W3 Innovations, LLC, doing business as Broken Thumbs Apps, was a software development company based in Cupertino, California that developed and distributed approximately 40 mobile applications for iPhone and iPod touch through Apple's App Store, with several apps specifically targeted at children under 13.
caseDescription: W3 Innovations developed and distributed mobile apps directed to children under 13 that collected over 30,000 email addresses and personal information without parental consent or adequate privacy notices. The company operated online services (Emily's Girl World and Emily Dress-up apps) with built-in features that encouraged children to submit personal information through blogs and direct email to a fictional character 'Emily', but failed to obtain verifiable parental consent or post required privacy policies.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected personal information from children through multiple mechanisms (blogs, email submissions, comment forms) without notice or consent, constituting surveillance of a vulnerable population.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: W3 Innovations operated mobile apps including Emily's Girl World and Emily's Dress Up targeted at children, collecting over 30,000 email addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 30,000 children under age 13 had their email addresses and personal information collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Emily's Girl World app marketing stated: 'a fun story-telling app with charming graphics ... which we thought that younger girls and nostalgic adults in particular might enjoy' and 'Best of all, as if all of that wasn't enough, you can also send an email directly to Emily to say hi! As other fans will tell you, Emily listens and reads all of your emails.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The app actively collected personal information from children including email addresses, names, personal stories, photographs, and embarrassing personal details through multiple submission mechanisms, yet the company maintained no privacy policy, provided no parental notice, and obtained no parental consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The apps were interactive and encouraged user engagement and sharing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The interactive features (blogs, comment forms, direct email) functioned as personal information collection mechanisms that harvested over 30,000 email addresses from children without safeguards, parental awareness, or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) requires operators of online services directed to children to post a clear privacy policy on their website or online service.
regulatoryFindings.description: W3 Innovations failed to maintain or link to any online notice of their information collection, use, and disclosure practices for the Emily's Girl World app and Emily Dress-up apps.
violations: W3 Innovations failed to maintain or link to any online notice of their information collection, use, and disclosure practices for the Emily's Girl World app and Emily Dress-up apps.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide clear, understandable, and complete notice directly to parents of information practices and required disclosures.
regulatoryFindings.description: W3 Innovations did not provide any direct notice to parents regarding collection, use, or disclosure of children's personal information.
violations: W3 Innovations did not provide any direct notice to parents regarding collection, use, or disclosure of children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent prior to collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: W3 Innovations collected over 30,000 email addresses and personal information from children without obtaining any verifiable parental consent before collection.
violations: W3 Innovations collected over 30,000 email addresses and personal information from children without obtaining any verifiable parental consent before collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: A violation of the COPPA Rule constitutes an unfair or deceptive act or practice under Section 5(a)(1) of the FTC Act. W3 Innovations' collection of children's personal information without consent and without required privacy notices was inherently deceptive and unfair.
violations: A violation of the COPPA Rule constitutes an unfair or deceptive act or practice under Section 5(a)(1) of the FTC Act. W3 Innovations' collection of children's personal information without consent and without required privacy notices was inherently deceptive and unfair.

outcome: The United States sought permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation (with violations calculated per collection/use/disclosure instance), and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges over 30,000 separate violations based on individual collections of email addresses and personal information. A permanent injunction would prevent future COPPA violations. The company was required to implement comprehensive compliance measures including privacy policy posting, parental notice, and verifiable consent mechanisms.
companyNow: Unknown. The complaint was filed in 2012 by the U.S. Department of Justice on behalf of the FTC. The current operational status of W3 Innovations, LLC and its app distribution status is not specified in the document.
dataType: Email addresses, names, personal information from children (under 13)
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) – failure to post privacy policy
COPPA Rule Section 312.4(c) – failure to provide direct notice to parents
COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1) – failure to obtain verifiable parental consent
FTC Act Section 5(a)(1), 15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(1) – unfair and deceptive practices

companyDescription: Ceridian Corporation is a Delaware-based service provider that offers payroll processing, payroll-related tax filing, benefits administration, and other human resource services to business customers, operating the Powerpay web-based platform for small businesses.
companyLongDescription: Ceridian Corporation is a Delaware-based service provider that offers payroll processing, payroll-related tax filing, benefits administration, and other human resource services to business customers, operating the Powerpay web-based platform for small businesses.
caseDescription: Ceridian operated Powerpay, a web-based payroll service, while making false claims about security. The company stored sensitive employee data in plain text, failed to fix known SQL injection vulnerabilities, and in December 2009 attackers exploited these failures to steal personal information of over 27,600 employees including Social Security numbers and bank account details.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data, resulting in a data breach of sensitive payroll information. This reflects the Solove category of Insecurity, which concerns inadequate safeguards against unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Ceridian stored employee personal data in plain text, failed to assess web application vulnerabilities to SQL injection attacks, did not implement readily available defenses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these failures to steal personal information of at least 27,673 employees, including Social Security numbers, bank account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ceridian's comprehensive security program is designed in accordance with ISO 27000 series standards, industry best practices and federal, state and local regulatory requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ceridian stored sensitive personal information in plain text, failed to assess vulnerability to SQL injection attacks, did not implement available defenses, and failed to detect unauthorized access until data was stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ceridian shall use the same degree of care as it uses to protect its own confidential information of like nature, but no less than a reasonable degree of care, to maintain in confidence customer information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ceridian failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access, resulting in the theft of 27,673 individuals' sensitive financial and personal data through an easily-exploitable SQL injection vulnerability.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ceridian represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures compliant with ISO 27000 standards and used reasonable care, but in fact stored data in plain text, failed to patch known vulnerabilities, and did not detect unauthorized access.
violations: Ceridian represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures compliant with ISO 27000 standards and used reasonable care, but in fact stored data in plain text, failed to patch known vulnerabilities, and did not detect unauthorized access.

Ceridian's failure to implement reasonable security measures caused substantial injury to consumers when hackers exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to export 27,673 individuals' sensitive personal information.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 8, 2011, alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint resulted in a consent order requiring Ceridian to implement comprehensive information security improvements, including establishing a security program, conducting regular risk assessments, implementing authentication and encryption, maintaining reasonable logging and monitoring, and submitting to ongoing independent security audits for 20 years.
companyNow: Ceridian is now part of Dayforce (formerly HighGround Inc./Dayforce), a leading Human Capital Management platform, following acquisitions and restructurings. The company continues to provide payroll, benefits, and HR services globally.
dataType: Name, address, email, phone number, Social Security number, date of birth, direct deposit account numbers, bank account numbers

companyDescription: Frostwire LLC was a Florida-based software company that designed and distributed file-sharing applications compatible with peer-to-peer networks, particularly the Gnutella network. The company operated from at least 2007 through 2011, offering free downloads of both desktop and mobile file-sharing applications.
companyLongDescription: Frostwire LLC was a Florida-based software company that designed and distributed file-sharing applications compatible with peer-to-peer networks, particularly the Gnutella network. The company operated from at least 2007 through 2011, offering free downloads of both desktop and mobile file-sharing applications.
caseDescription: Frostwire designed and distributed file-sharing applications (FrostWire Desktop and FrostWire for Android) that misled consumers about file-sharing settings and caused them to unwittingly share personal files publicly. The desktop version misrepresented which downloaded files would be shared, while the Android app defaulted to sharing all pre-existing files across multiple categories without adequate consumer disclosure or control.
violationSummary: The application's default configurations and misleading UI exposed consumers' personal files to public access and download on P2P networks without adequate consent or disclosure. This falls squarely within the exposure category of information dissemination—making private information broadly accessible to unknown parties.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Distributed FrostWire Desktop and FrostWire for Android applications with deceptive installation interfaces.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers unwittingly exposed intimate personal files including photographs, voice recordings, and documents to millions of anonymous users worldwide for download.

claimsVsReality.claim: Files downloaded and stored in the 'Save' folder will not be shared with the file-sharing network
claimsVsReality.reality: Downloaded files were automatically designated as 'Individually shared' files and were actively shared on the Gnutella network regardless of folder placement

claimsVsReality.claim: Users can control what's shared through the installation setup screen's checkbox options
claimsVsReality.reality: Pre-checked boxes defaulted to sharing all files in multiple categories (Pictures, Video, Audio/Music, Applications, Documents, Ringtones) with no adequate disclosure; users had to manually unshare individual files one at a time after installation

claimsVsReality.claim: If you uncheck 'Share Finished Downloads' in Options-Sharing, downloads will not be shared
claimsVsReality.reality: Previously downloaded files continued to be shared as 'Individually shared' files even after unchecking the setting; the UI did not disclose this persistent sharing of existing downloads

claimsVsReality.claim: FrostWire for Android provides '[c]ontrol what's shared'
claimsVsReality.reality: The application provided no meaningful control mechanism; it automatically shared broad file categories by default and required tedious one-by-one unsharing of individual files without clear UI instructions

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Misrepresented through the 'Save Folder and Shared Folders' dialog box that files downloaded to the 'Save' folder would not be shared with the Gnutella network, when in fact they were automatically shared as 'Individually shared' files
violations: Misrepresented through the 'Save Folder and Shared Folders' dialog box that files downloaded to the 'Save' folder would not be shared with the Gnutella network, when in fact they were automatically shared as 'Individually shared' files
Failed to disclose that FrostWire Desktop, by default, publicly shared files consumers downloaded from the Gnutella network even when stored in 'unshared' folders

Designed FrostWire for Android with default settings that automatically designated pre-existing files in multiple categories (Pictures, Video, Audio/Music, Applications, Documents, Ringtones) for public sharing immediately upon installation, without adequate consumer notice or ability to control which files would be shared

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines an unfair practice as one that causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that is not reasonably avoidable and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: FrostWire for Android's design caused substantial injury by enabling unwitting public sharing of personal files (photographs, documents, voice recordings) with little or no notice to consumers
violations: FrostWire for Android's design caused substantial injury by enabling unwitting public sharing of personal files (photographs, documents, voice recordings) with little or no notice to consumers

Consumers could not reasonably avoid this injury given the default installation process, lack of adequate disclosure, and burdensome unsharing procedures (requiring manual unsharing of files one at a time)
The unfair practice provided no countervailing benefits to consumers, as standard file-sharing applications (including Frostwire Desktop itself) do not share user-originated files by default

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint seeking permanent injunctive relief under Section 13(b) of the FTC Act and other equitable remedies to halt violations and redress consumer injury. The complaint alleges three counts: (1) false representations about file-sharing in FrostWire Desktop, (2) failure to disclose material information about download sharing in FrostWire Desktop, and (3) unfair design of FrostWire for Android. As this is the original complaint document filed on 10/07/2011, the final resolution and specific remedies are not detailed in this filing. The FTC sought permanent injunction, consumer redress, and case costs.
companyNow: Frostwire ceased active development of its desktop and mobile file-sharing applications following regulatory pressure and has largely faded from public prominence. The company's current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Personal files stored on mobile devices and computers including pictures, videos, documents, audio files, applications, and user-originated content
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce

companyDescription: ScanScout was a video advertising network that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, specializing in online behavioral advertising and targeted video ad placement.
companyLongDescription: ScanScout was a video advertising network that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, specializing in online behavioral advertising and targeted video ad placement.
caseDescription: ScanScout used Flash cookies to track user online behavior for targeted video advertising from April 2007 to September 2009. The company's privacy policy falsely claimed users could prevent tracking by changing browser settings to block cookies, but Flash cookies operated outside browser controls and could not be disabled this way. This deceptive practice violated FTC Act Section 5(a).
violationSummary: ScanScout engaged in systematic collection and storage of users' online activities through Flash cookies to enable behavioral targeting, while deceiving users about their ability to control this surveillance.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ScanScout used Flash cookies to collect and store user online activity data for targeted video advertising while falsely telling users they could prevent tracking by changing browser cookie.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of users could not actually stop ScanScout's data collection because Flash cookies operated outside browser controls, allowing the company to profile.

claimsVsReality.claim: You can opt out of receiving a cookie by changing your browser settings to prevent the receipt of cookies
claimsVsReality.reality: ScanScout used Flash cookies that were not controlled through browser settings; changing browser privacy settings did not prevent Flash cookie tracking

claimsVsReality.claim: General user data is automatically collected through the use of cookies and users can control this via browser settings
claimsVsReality.reality: Flash cookies could not be deleted or blocked through browser settings, making user control claims false for the actual tracking mechanism in use

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ScanScout represented in its privacy policy that consumers could prevent data collection by changing browser settings to block cookies
violations: ScanScout represented in its privacy policy that consumers could prevent data collection by changing browser settings to block cookies
This representation was false or misleading because Flash cookies were not controlled through browser settings and remained active even when HTTP cookies were blocked
Consumers had no actual ability to opt out of ScanScout's tracking by the means suggested in the privacy policy

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on December 14, 2011, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleged that ScanScout's representations about cookie opt-out methods were false and misleading because Flash cookies operated independently of browser controls. This initiated formal enforcement proceedings against the respondent.
dataType: Online behavioral activity, browsing history, IP address, operating system, browser type

companyDescription: SettlementOne Credit Corporation was a consumer credit reporting company that compiled and sold trimerge reports—consolidated credit data from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion—to mortgage brokers and other lenders to assess consumer creditworthiness.
companyLongDescription: SettlementOne Credit Corporation was a consumer credit reporting company that compiled and sold trimerge reports—consolidated credit data from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion—to mortgage brokers and other lenders to assess consumer creditworthiness.
caseDescription: SettlementOne failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive consumer credit reports it compiled and distributed to mortgage brokers. Between February and June 2008, hackers exploited vulnerabilities in end-user client networks and accessed at least 784 consumer reports without authorization. The company did not assess client security risks, implement monitoring systems, or take corrective action after breaches were discovered.
violationSummary: SettlementOne's comprehensive failure to implement, monitor, or maintain reasonable security controls directly led to unauthorized access to sensitive consumer financial data, exemplifying the insecurity category of privacy harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: SettlementOne failed to develop information security policies, assess client security risks, or require basic security measures like firewalls.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least 784 consumers had their highly sensitive financial data including Social Security numbers, addresses, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: SettlementOne issued credentials (username/password) to authorized clients to access consumer reports through a secure online portal.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not verify the security of client computer networks and allowed clients without basic security measures (firewalls, updated antivirus software) to access highly sensitive consumer data, enabling hackers to exploit vulnerabilities in client networks.

claimsVsReality.claim: SettlementOne operated a controlled system for distributing consumer reports to legitimate business users.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between February and June 2008, hackers exploited multiple vulnerabilities in end-user client networks and accessed at least 784 consumer reports. Hackers could also view any report pulled by the client in the previous 90 days, indicating systemic lack of access controls and monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: SettlementOne responded appropriately to security breaches.
claimsVsReality.reality: After discovering breaches, the company terminated some affected end users but did nothing in other cases. In one instance, SettlementOne restored access to an end user whose credentials had been stolen, despite the client providing no documentation that their systems were virus-free or properly secured.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. §§ 314.3, 314.4) requires financial institutions to protect customer information by developing comprehensive written security programs containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, implementation of controls, monitoring effectiveness, and adjustment in light of identified risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne failed to develop and disseminate information security policies for itself and end-user clients.
violations: SettlementOne failed to develop and disseminate information security policies for itself and end-user clients.
SettlementOne failed to assess risks of allowing end users with unverified or inadequate security to access consumer reports.
SettlementOne failed to implement reasonable steps to address identified risks, such as evaluating end-user computer network security or requiring appropriate security measures.
SettlementOne failed to maintain an effective system of monitoring access to consumer reports and detecting suspicious activity.
SettlementOne failed to take corrective action after discovering breaches, and in one instance restored access to an end user despite stolen credentials and lack of documentation of proper security.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604 (15 U.S.C. § 1681b) prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports except for specified permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne furnished consumer reports to unauthorized hackers who had no permissible purpose to obtain such reports.
violations: SettlementOne furnished consumer reports to unauthorized hackers who had no permissible purpose to obtain such reports.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(a) (15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a)) requires consumer reporting agencies to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes and prohibits furnishing reports to any person if the agency has reasonable grounds for believing the report will not be used for a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports when it allowed clients without adequate security safeguards to access them.
violations: SettlementOne failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports when it allowed clients without adequate security safeguards to access them.

SettlementOne furnished consumer reports under circumstances where it had reasonable grounds for believing the reports would not be used for permissible purposes, as evidenced by the multiple breaches.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect consumers' personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: SettlementOne engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect consumers' personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: This is a Complaint issued on August 17, 2011. The document indicates the FTC had reason to believe violations occurred and alleged unfair and deceptive practices. The case would proceed to settlement or adjudication. Typical FTC outcomes for such cases include Consent Orders requiring comprehensive information security program implementation, regular compliance monitoring and reporting, third-party security audits, and corrective measures.
dataType: financial data, credit reports, Social Security numbers, addresses, employer history, account numbers
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604, 15 U.S.C. § 1681b
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a)

company: Playdom, Inc. (subsidiary of Disney Enterprises, Inc.)
companyDescription: Playdom was an online game developer and operator. It was formed as successor to Acclaim Games, Inc. (dissolved), acquiring Acclaim's online virtual world platforms in May 2010. Disney acquired Playdom as a subsidiary on August 27, 2010, consolidating online gaming properties.
companyLongDescription: Playdom was an online game developer and operator. It was formed as successor to Acclaim Games, Inc. (dissolved), acquiring Acclaim's online virtual world platforms in May 2010. Disney acquired Playdom as a subsidiary on August 27, 2010, consolidating online gaming properties.
caseDescription: Playdom (formerly Acclaim Games) operated approximately 20 online games, including Pony Stars directed at children, and collected personal information from approximately 1.224 million children without proper parental consent. The company failed to provide adequate notice to parents, obtain verifiable parental consent before data collection, and falsely represented in its privacy policy that children could not disclose personal information online when in fact the platform enabled such disclosure through user profiles and forums.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected personal information from children across multiple platforms without proper parental consent mechanisms. COPPA surveillance violations occurred through registration systems and profile data collection.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Playdom operated approximately 20 online games that collected personal information from approximately 1.224 million children under 13 without obtaining verifiable parental consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 1.224 million children were exposed to contact and safety risks because their real names, locations, email addresses, and instant messenger IDs were collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: When a child under 13 years of age signs up we not [sic] collect the Email address without the permission of the Parent or Legal Guardian and we will collect the other items listed above. We do not collect anything else.
claimsVsReality.reality: Defendants collected children's email addresses, usernames, passwords, birth years, gender, and enabled children to publicly post real names, locations, website URLs, email addresses, and instant messenger IDs through personal profile pages and community forums.

claimsVsReality.claim: If a child under 13 years of age wants to post information on our website or chat with other players, we will require that they do not disclose any personal information such as the real name, address, phone number and anything that can be used to contact the child.
claimsVsReality.reality: The platform design and personal profile pages included fields for children to enter and publicly disclose real name, location, website, email, and various instant messenger IDs. Children could create profiles, post comments in forums, and upload personal information visible to other users.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 312.4(b) requires operators to post a clear, understandable, and complete privacy policy on their website describing what information they collect from children online, how they use it, and their disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants' privacy policy falsely stated they would prohibit children from posting personal information such as real names, addresses, phone numbers, and contact information, when in fact the personal profile pages and community forums allowed children to enter and publicly post such information.
violations: Defendants' privacy policy falsely stated they would prohibit children from posting personal information such as real names, addresses, phone numbers, and contact information, when in fact the personal profile pages and community forums allowed children to enter and publicly post such information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide direct notice to parents of their information collection, use, and disclosure practices for children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants failed to provide parents with direct notice of information practices prior to collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information.
violations: Defendants failed to provide parents with direct notice of information practices prior to collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent prior to any collection, use, or disclosure of personal information from children under 13.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants collected children's personal information (email, user ID, password, birth year, gender, instant messenger IDs) without obtaining verifiable parental consent. Sending a welcome email to a parent-provided address and automatically granting full account access does not constitute verifiable consent.
violations: Defendants collected children's personal information (email, user ID, password, birth year, gender, instant messenger IDs) without obtaining verifiable parental consent. Sending a welcome email to a parent-provided address and automatically granting full account access does not constitute verifiable consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants made false and misleading representations in their privacy policy that they would prohibit children from disclosing personal information online, while the platform design and features actually enabled and facilitated such disclosures.
violations: Defendants made false and misleading representations in their privacy policy that they would prohibit children from disclosing personal information online, while the platform design and features actually enabled and facilitated such disclosures.

outcome: The United States filed a civil complaint seeking monetary penalties, permanent injunction, and other equitable relief. Each of approximately 1,224,000 instances of COPPA violations constitutes a separate violation subject to civil penalties of up to $11,000 per violation (pre-February 10, 2009) or $16,000 per violation (post-February 10, 2009). The complaint requested injunctive relief to prevent future violations and required compliance with COPPA Rule provisions.
companyNow: Playdom became a subsidiary of Disney Enterprises, Inc. in August 2010. By August 26, 2010, Playdom had permanently shut down most of the online virtual worlds formerly operated by Acclaim Games, though some games were transferred to non-U.S. operators (e.g., Feerik Ltd.). The company remains under Disney ownership.
dataType: Email addresses, usernames, birth year, gender, location data, instant messenger IDs, user activity logs, forum posts
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(c) – insufficient parental notice
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) – lack of verifiable parental consent
FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) – unfair or deceptive acts
FTC Act Section 5(m)(1)(A) – civil penalties authority

companyDescription: ACRAnet, Inc. was a consumer reporting agency based in Spokane, Washington that assembled and sold trimerge reports (merged credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) to mortgage brokers and other entities for credit determination purposes.
companyLongDescription: ACRAnet, Inc. was a consumer reporting agency based in Spokane, Washington that assembled and sold trimerge reports (merged credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) to mortgage brokers and other entities for credit determination purposes.
caseDescription: ACRAnet, a consumer reporting agency, failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect highly sensitive consumer financial data. Between December 2007 and November 2008, hackers exploited vulnerabilities in end-user client networks, accessing at least 694 consumer reports without authorization. The company allowed clients without basic security protections to access trimerge reports containing unverified credentials.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security controls resulted in unauthorized disclosure of consumer reports containing sensitive personal and financial information to third parties (hackers). This constitutes a breach of confidentiality of information in the company's custody.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ACRAnet failed to implement information security safeguards, allowed clients without firewalls or antivirus software to access sensitive consumer credit reports.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited vulnerabilities in end-user networks and accessed at least 694 consumer reports containing Social Security numbers, account numbers, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: ACRAnet issued credentials to authorized end-user clients for secure access to sensitive consumer reports
claimsVsReality.reality: ACRAnet allowed clients with no verified security measures (no firewalls, outdated antivirus) to access reports, and did not evaluate or monitor client network security

claimsVsReality.claim: ACRAnet implemented reasonable safeguards to protect consumer information
claimsVsReality.reality: ACRAnet had no comprehensive written security policies, did not assess risks, did not monitor access patterns, and did not correct known vulnerabilities after multiple breaches

claimsVsReality.claim: ACRAnet protected consumer reports from unauthorized access
claimsVsReality.reality: Hackers accessed at least 694 consumer reports and had ability to view any report pulled by end users in the previous 90 days

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet failed to design and implement information safeguards to control risks to customer information
violations: ACRAnet failed to design and implement information safeguards to control risks to customer information
Failed to regularly test or monitor the effectiveness of existing controls and procedures
Failed to evaluate and adjust the information security program in light of known or identified risks
Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive information security program

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681b) prohibits a consumer reporting agency from furnishing a consumer report except for specified permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet furnished consumer reports to hackers who did not have a permissible purpose to obtain a consumer report
violations: ACRAnet furnished consumer reports to hackers who did not have a permissible purpose to obtain a consumer report

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(a) of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a)) requires every consumer reporting agency to maintain reasonable procedures to limit the furnishing of consumer reports to specified purposes and prohibits furnishing reports if the agency has reasonable grounds for believing the report will not be used for a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes
violations: ACRAnet failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes
ACRAnet furnished consumer reports under circumstances where it had reasonable grounds for believing the reports would not be used for permissible purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures caused or was likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers
violations: ACRAnet's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures caused or was likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers

outcome: FTC issued a formal complaint on August 17, 2011, alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule, FCRA, and FTC Act. The complaint was the basis for enforcement action requiring ACRAnet to implement comprehensive information security improvements and comply with ongoing monitoring and compliance obligations.
dataType: financial data, full name, addresses, Social Security numbers, date of birth, employment history, account numbers
legalBasisViolated: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act § 501(b) / Safeguards Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 314

companyDescription: Chitika was an online behavioral advertising company operating from Massachusetts that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, using cookies to track consumer browsing and serve targeted ads.
companyLongDescription: Chitika was an online behavioral advertising company operating from Massachusetts that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, using cookies to track consumer browsing and serve targeted ads.
caseDescription: Chitika, an online behavioral advertising company, represented to consumers that they could opt out of targeted advertising for a reasonable period. However, the opt-out cookies expired after only 10 days, automatically resuming tracking without consumer knowledge. After FTC contact, Chitika extended the expiration to 10 years but only for future opt-outs, leaving prior opt-outs unprotected.
violationSummary: Chitika misrepresented the duration of consumer opt-out protections, then resumed tracking and secondary use of consumer data (behavioral targeting) without renewed consent after opt-out cookies expired.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Chitika set opt-out cookies that expired after only 10 days (May 2008–February 2010), automatically resuming behavioral tracking.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers who clicked Chitika's opt-out button believed their tracking preferences would persist for a reasonable period.

claimsVsReality.claim: You can opt-out of receiving Chitika cookies, and this opt-out will last for a reasonable period of time. Chitika encourages business practices that protect user privacy.
