claimsVsReality.reality: Opt-out cookies expired after only 10 days (until March 2010), causing automatic resumption of tracking and behavioral targeting without consumer knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Chitika uses cookies to store anonymous activity data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cookies contained unique identification numbers and were linked to specific consumer browsing activities including search terms, enabling persistent identification and tracking.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Chitika represented that opt-out would last for a reasonable period of time, but opt-out cookies actually expired after 10 days, resuming tracking without consumer knowledge
violations: Chitika represented that opt-out would last for a reasonable period of time, but opt-out cookies actually expired after 10 days, resuming tracking without consumer knowledge
Consumers were not informed that opt-out cookies would expire after 10 days, deceiving them about the duration of privacy protection
After opting out, consumers' browsing activities were tracked and used for targeted advertising once the opt-out cookie expired, violating their explicit privacy choice

outcome: Complaint issued June 7, 2011 alleging deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5(a). Chitika modified opt-out cookie expiration to 10 years after FTC staff contact (March 1, 2010), but modification applied only to future opt-outs. Complaint challenged the deceptive representations regarding opt-out duration and effectiveness. Document represents initial complaint filing; final settlement terms not provided in this document.
companyNow: Chitika operated as a significant online advertising intermediary in the late 2000s and early 2010s. The company's current operational status is unknown from available information.
dataType: Search terms, web browsing activity, online activity tracking data
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices in commerce

companyDescription: Teletrack, Inc. was a Georgia-based consumer reporting agency that compiled and sold consumer credit reports and marketing lists to non-traditional credit providers including payday lenders, rental purchase stores, and non-prime auto lenders.
companyLongDescription: Teletrack, Inc. was a Georgia-based consumer reporting agency that compiled and sold consumer credit reports and marketing lists to non-traditional credit providers including payday lenders, rental purchase stores, and non-prime auto lenders.
caseDescription: Teletrack, a consumer reporting agency, furnished marketing lists containing consumer names and addresses to third parties without permissible purposes under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). The company compiled these lists from credit inquiry data without obtaining proper consent, violating FCRA section 604 which restricts the purposes for which consumer reports may be furnished. This constituted knowing violations forming a pattern or practice of FCRA breaches.
violationSummary: Teletrack disclosed consumer personal information and derived marketing lists to third parties (purchasers of mailing lists) without permissible purpose or consumer consent, constituting unauthorized disclosure in violation of FCRA section 604.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Teletrack sold marketing lists containing consumers' names, addresses, and personal details derived from credit inquiries to third parties for marketing purposes without proper legal.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' sensitive personal information was disclosed to marketers without their knowledge or consent, enabling unwanted solicitations and exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Teletrack was operating as a compliant consumer reporting agency furnishing reports only for permissible purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Teletrack was furnishing marketing lists derived from credit inquiry data to third parties for marketing purposes, violating FCRA section 604 which permits furnishing consumer reports only for specific enumerated purposes, not general marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumer data was being used only for the original purpose of credit decisioning.
claimsVsReality.reality: Teletrack added consumer names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employer information, and credit inquiry flags to marketing databases and sold these lists to third parties for direct marketing campaigns.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681b) prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports to third parties except for certain enumerated permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Teletrack furnished consumer reports (marketing lists) to third parties for marketing purposes, which is not a permissible purpose under section 604 of the FCRA.
violations: Teletrack furnished consumer reports (marketing lists) to third parties for marketing purposes, which is not a permissible purpose under section 604 of the FCRA.
Since at least 2007, Teletrack engaged in multiple instances of furnishing consumer reports to persons without permissible purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 621(a)(1) of the FCRA authorizes the FTC to enforce compliance with the FCRA using all FTC Act functions and powers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Teletrack's violations of FCRA section 604 constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in violation of FTC Act section 5(a).
violations: Teletrack's violations of FCRA section 604 constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in violation of FTC Act section 5(a).

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Teletrack's practice of furnishing marketing lists derived from credit inquiries without permissible purposes constitutes unfair and deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.
violations: Teletrack's practice of furnishing marketing lists derived from credit inquiries without permissible purposes constitutes unfair and deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.

outcome: The complaint sought preliminary and permanent injunctive relief, monetary civil penalties of $2,500 per violation (pre-February 2009) and $3,500 per violation (post-February 2009), judgment on each count, and costs of litigation. The complaint alleged knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice. The government requested equitable remedies to halt ongoing violations and prevent future breaches.
companyNow: Teletrack, Inc. (now operating as Clarity Services or similar subsidiary under parent company ownership) continues as a consumer reporting agency serving alternative finance and specialty lending sectors.
outcomeSummary: Complaint filed seeking penalties and injunction
dataType: Name, address, Social Security number, phone number, employer information, date of birth, email address, driver's license number

companyDescription: Lookout Services, Inc. was a Texas-based company providing the I-9 Solution, a web-based platform designed to help employers comply with federal employment eligibility verification requirements by collecting and storing employee identity documents and Social Security numbers.
companyLongDescription: Lookout Services, Inc. was a Texas-based company providing the I-9 Solution, a web-based platform designed to help employers comply with federal employment eligibility verification requirements by collecting and storing employee identity documents and Social Security numbers.
caseDescription: Lookout Services operated the I-9 Solution, a web-based platform storing highly sensitive employment verification data for over 37,000 consumers. Despite marketing claims of secure data protection and perimeter defense, the company failed to implement basic security measures, allowing unauthorized access through weak credentials (including the guessable 'test/test' login) and URL manipulation vulnerabilities. Two separate breaches in October and December 2009 exposed this sensitive personal information.
violationSummary: The company failed to provide reasonable and appropriate security measures for highly sensitive personal information, including weak authentication, lack of intrusion detection, and password storage in clear text. The insecurity directly enabled unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Lookout Services marketed its I-9 Solution as secure while storing passwords in clear text, allowing weak passwords identical to usernames.
whyTheyWereWrong: An employee of a customer company gained unauthorized access to personal information of over 37,000 consumers including Social Security numbers, passport numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Secure Your Data – data will be encoded and transmitted over secured lines and the FTP interface will protect your data from interception and unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lookout stored passwords in clear text, allowed weak credentials like 'test/test', did not require password changes, and allowed URL manipulation to bypass authentication entirely.

claimsVsReality.claim: Perimeter Defense – servers continuously monitor attempted network attacks on a 24x7 basis using sophisticated software tools.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lookout did not deploy an intrusion detection system until October 2009, after the initial breach; inadequate system log monitoring until December 2009; two separate breaches occurred exposing over 37,000 consumers' data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lookout represented, expressly and by implication, that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, when in fact it failed to establish password complexity requirements, enforce credential changes, deploy intrusion detection systems, or prevent URL-based authentication bypass.
violations: Lookout represented, expressly and by implication, that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, when in fact it failed to establish password complexity requirements, enforce credential changes, deploy intrusion detection systems, or prevent URL-based authentication bypass.

Lookout engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers through identity theft risk that was not reasonably avoidable.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 15, 2011 alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint does not specify final settlement terms in the provided document, but enforcement action was initiated requiring Lookout to address security deficiencies and comply with FTC orders regarding reasonable data security practices.
companyNow: Unknown – the company may have been acquired, dissolved, or reformed after the 2009 breaches and FTC enforcement action.
dataType: Social Security numbers, passport numbers, alien registration numbers, driver's license numbers, military identification numbers, names, addresses, dates of birth
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

company: US Search, Inc. and US Search, LLC
companyDescription: US Search, Inc. is a data broker that operates www.ussearch.com, providing online search services to the public that aggregate publicly available personal information. The company offers reverse lookup services and consumer information reports derived from public records and partner sources.
companyLongDescription: US Search, Inc. is a data broker that operates www.ussearch.com, providing online search services to the public that aggregate publicly available personal information. The company offers reverse lookup services and consumer information reports derived from public records and partner sources.
caseDescription: US Search, Inc. and its subsidiary charged consumers $10 for a 'PrivacyLock' service that purported to remove their personal information from search results and affiliated websites. However, the service failed to block information appearing in reverse searches, address-based real estate searches, associate searches, and newly generated records—making the core promise deceptive.
violationSummary: The company made misleading representations about a privacy removal service, implying comprehensive blocking of personal information when the service failed to prevent disclosure across multiple search types and record categories.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Charged consumers $10 for a 'PrivacyLock' service that was marketed as preventing their names and addresses from appearing in US Search's website, advertisements, and search results.
whyTheyWereWrong: The PrivacyLock service failed to prevent personal information from appearing in reverse phone/address searches, real estate records, associate listings.

claimsVsReality.claim: PrivacyLock will prevent your name and address from appearing on the US Search website, US Search advertisements, and US Search reports, guaranteed for 1 year.
claimsVsReality.reality: PrivacyLock did not block information from appearing in reverse searches by phone number or address, in real estate record searches, or when the consumer's name appeared as an associate in searches for other people.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your information will be suppressed from affiliate and advertiser websites as well, backed by our 1 year promise.
claimsVsReality.reality: The service failed to suppress information from all relevant search types and record categories, leaving personal data accessible through multiple search pathways.

claimsVsReality.claim: When consumers change addresses, new records would remain subject to PrivacyLock protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: When consumers changed addresses, new records were generated that were not subject to the PrivacyLock restriction.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made false or misleading representations that the PrivacyLock service would prevent a consumer's name from appearing on the company's website, advertisements, and search results when in fact the service failed to block reverse searches, real estate record searches, associate searches, and newly generated records.
violations: Made false or misleading representations that the PrivacyLock service would prevent a consumer's name from appearing on the company's website, advertisements, and search results when in fact the service failed to block reverse searches, real estate record searches, associate searches, and newly generated records.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 14, 2011, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The company was required to cease the deceptive representations and implement a compliance program. Details of any monetary settlement or additional remediation are not specified in this complaint document.
companyNow: US Search merged with BeenVerified (owned by Blackstone). The data broker service continues to operate under different ownership and regulatory scrutiny has remained a persistent issue for the industry.
dataType: Name, age, address, phone number, aliases, maiden name, death records, address history, relatives, neighbors, marriage/divorce records, associates, property information, bankruptcy, tax liens, civil judgments, criminal records, email address, online profiles

companyDescription: Skid-e-kids was a social networking website marketed as the 'Facebook and MySpace for kids,' targeting children ages 7-14 and their parents, allowing profile creation, photo/video uploads, messaging, and friend connections.
companyLongDescription: Skid-e-kids was a social networking website marketed as the 'Facebook and MySpace for kids,' targeting children ages 7-14 and their parents, allowing profile creation, photo/video uploads, messaging, and friend connections.
caseDescription: Skid-e-kids, a social networking site marketed to children ages 7-14, collected personal information from approximately 5,600 children without obtaining verifiable parental consent. The operator's privacy policy falsely claimed to collect parent email addresses and notify parents before account activation, but in reality never requested parental contact information and automatically registered children without any parental involvement or notification.
violationSummary: The operator systematically collected personal information from children through mandatory registration and profile creation without implementing required parental consent mechanisms, enabling ongoing surveillance-like data collection.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Operated Skid-e-kids, a social network marketed to children ages 7-14, that collected personal information including names, birth dates, email addresses, locations, photos.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 5,600 children's personal information was collected and made publicly accessible through user profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: The privacy policy stated that the Skid-e-kids.com website requires child users to provide a parent's valid email address in order to register, and that parental email would be used to activate the account and notify parents of privacy practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The registration process never requested a parent's email address, accounts were automatically activated immediately upon child registration, and parents were never notified or provided any opportunity to consent before their children's personal information was collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Website marketed as 'the social networking alternative for kids ages 7 to 14' where 'parents are in charge.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Parents had no actual involvement, notification, or control over their children's account creation or data collection; children could independently register and publicly share personal information without parental knowledge or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA prohibits operators of commercial websites or online services directed to children from collecting personal information from children without verifiable parental consent and without providing clear notice of information practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children
violations: Failed to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children
Failed to provide clear, understandable notice on the website of what information is collected from children and how it is used
Failed to provide direct notice to parents of information collection practices before collecting data
Misrepresented in privacy policy that parent email addresses would be collected and parents would be notified, when in fact no parent contact was ever requested or attempted

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made false and misleading representations in privacy policy claiming parental email collection and notification procedures that were never implemented
violations: Made false and misleading representations in privacy policy claiming parental email collection and notification procedures that were never implemented
Deceived parents and guardians about the information collection practices and parental involvement in account activation

outcome: This is a complaint filing seeking permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation (approximately 5,600 instances of personal information collection without consent), and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges violations of COPPA and FTC Act Section 5. Resolution and final penalty amount not specified in this complaint document.
companyNow: The current status of Skid-e-kids and Jones O. Godwin is unknown from this complaint filing dated 2011. The case sought permanent injunction to prevent future violations.
dataType: Children's personal information including name, birth date, gender, email address, location, profile information, photos, videos

companyDescription: Twitter, Inc. operates www.twitter.com, a social networking platform that enables users to post brief messages ('tweets') of 140 characters or less to followers via web, email, and mobile devices. Founded in 2006, Twitter facilitates communication among individuals, media outlets, businesses, and government entities.
companyLongDescription: Twitter, Inc. operates www.twitter.com, a social networking platform that enables users to post brief messages ('tweets') of 140 characters or less to followers via web, email, and mobile devices. Founded in 2006, Twitter facilitates communication among individuals, media outlets, businesses, and government entities.
caseDescription: Twitter failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect nonpublic user information and honor user privacy choices despite making explicit privacy commitments. Between January and May 2009, intruders exploited weak administrative password policies to gain unauthorized access to sensitive user data and send fraudulent tweets from high-profile accounts.
violationSummary: Twitter's inadequate security practices failed to protect nonpublic user information from unauthorized access and compromised the integrity of user privacy controls despite explicit representations regarding security safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Twitter granted nearly all employees unrestricted administrative access to the system, stored admin passwords on public login webpages, failed to enforce strong passwords.
whyTheyWereWrong: Intruders exploited these failures to access millions of users' nonpublic tweets and personal information, reset passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: Twitter is very concerned about safeguarding the confidentiality of personally identifiable information and employs administrative, physical, and electronic measures designed to protect information from unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Twitter granted nearly all employees unrestricted administrative access without password policies, required weak passwords that could be guessed, stored credentials in plain text in personal email accounts, and lacked basic security controls like password expiration or separate admin login pages.

claimsVsReality.claim: Direct messages are not public; only author and recipient can view direct messages.
claimsVsReality.reality: Intruders exploited administrative access failures to view any user's direct messages, and Twitter employees could access direct messages of any user through inadequately secured administrative credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: Protected tweet accounts keep updates private and only approved followers are able to see the profile and tweets.
claimsVsReality.reality: Intruders gained unauthorized administrative control allowing them to view protected tweets of any user, and employees could access protected tweets without adequate access restrictions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Twitter represented in its privacy policy that it employed 'administrative, physical, and electronic measures designed to protect your information from unauthorized access' when in fact it failed to establish basic password security policies, enforce periodic password changes, restrict administrative access, or provide a separate administrative login page.
violations: Twitter represented in its privacy policy that it employed 'administrative, physical, and electronic measures designed to protect your information from unauthorized access' when in fact it failed to establish basic password security policies, enforce periodic password changes, restrict administrative access, or provide a separate administrative login page.

Twitter represented that direct messages were private and viewable 'only by author and recipient' and that protected tweets could be viewed 'only by approved followers', while simultaneously failing to prevent unauthorized administrative access that could expose these messages to intruders.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the complaint initiating proceedings; final settlement terms are not included in this document, but FTC enforcement actions against Twitter typically resulted in consent orders requiring implementation of comprehensive information security improvements, regular third-party audits, and ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: Twitter was acquired by Elon Musk in October 2022 and rebranded as X in 2023. The platform continues operating as a major social media service with billions of users, though under different ownership and management.
dataType: Email addresses, IP addresses, mobile phone numbers, direct messages, protected tweets, user account credentials, personal identifiable information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Directors Desk LLC provided a secure online platform allowing corporate board members to access board meeting materials, minutes, and related documents. The company marketed compliance with U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework to attract corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: Directors Desk LLC provided a secure online platform allowing corporate board members to access board meeting materials, minutes, and related documents. The company marketed compliance with U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework to attract corporate clients.
caseDescription: Directors Desk LLC claimed to be a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework but failed to renew its certification. From February 2008 to August 2009, the company maintained false statements on its website representing current Safe Harbor participation when it had 'not current' status. The FTC charged this as deceptive practice under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violationSummary: The company materially misrepresented its compliance status with an international privacy framework, distorting consumer understanding of data protection commitments through false claims on its privacy policy.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Directors Desk claimed on its website to be a current Safe Harbor participant while its certification lapsed for 18 months from February 2008 to August 2009.
whyTheyWereWrong: Corporate board members using Directors Desk transferred sensitive board meeting materials and personal data across borders relying on false Safe Harbor claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: Directors Desk is a participant in the Safe Harbor program developed by the U.S. Department of Commerce and the European Union. We have certified that we adhere to the Safe Harbor Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: From February 2008 to August 2009, Directors Desk did not renew its Safe Harbor certification and held 'not current' status on the Department of Commerce's public registry.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy effective since June 2004 with current Safe Harbor compliance
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy was never renewed after February 2007 self-certification, and certification lapsed in February 2008 without renewal for 18 months

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company represented expressly and by implication that it was a current Safe Harbor participant when it had not renewed certification and held 'not current' status
violations: Company represented expressly and by implication that it was a current Safe Harbor participant when it had not renewed certification and held 'not current' status
False and misleading privacy policy statements were disseminated on company website to consumers and business partners
Company failed to notify Department of Commerce that its Safe Harbor representation was no longer valid, as required by Safe Harbor rules

outcome: Complaint issued January 12, 2010. Directors Desk was ordered to cease deceptive practices and comply with the Safe Harbor framework if claiming participation. Company required to maintain accurate representations of privacy certification status on all platforms.
companyNow: Unknown. Directors Desk LLC appears to have ceased major operations; website and Safe Harbor certification status are no longer current as of available public records.
dataType: Corporate board member personal data, board meeting materials, board minutes, documents
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: First Advantage SafeRent, Inc. is a consumer reporting agency founded in 2005 that assembles and sells tenant screening reports, including eviction records, payment history, and criminal background information, to multi-family housing businesses for leasing decisions.
companyLongDescription: First Advantage SafeRent, Inc. is a consumer reporting agency founded in 2005 that assembles and sells tenant screening reports, including eviction records, payment history, and criminal background information, to multi-family housing businesses for leasing decisions.
caseDescription: SafeRent, a consumer reporting agency serving the multi-family housing industry, systematically rejected consumer requests for file disclosures and dispute reinvestigations submitted by facsimile, requiring consumers to use mail instead. This violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act's mandatory disclosure and reinvestigation requirements.
violationSummary: SafeRent's rejection of non-mail requests prevented consumers from exercising their statutory right to access and dispute their consumer files, effectively excluding them from FCRA protections.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: SafeRent rejected consumer requests for file disclosures and dispute reinvestigations submitted by facsimile, requiring consumers to submit written requests by U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective renters were locked out of accessing their own consumer reports and correcting false eviction records, causing delays in clearing their names.

claimsVsReality.claim: SafeRent could limit file disclosure and reinvestigation requests to written mail submissions only
claimsVsReality.reality: The FCRA requires consumer reporting agencies to disclose and reinvestigate upon consumer request without imposing unreasonable procedural barriers such as refusing facsimile submissions

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 609(a)(1) requires all consumer reporting agencies to disclose to consumers, upon request, all information maintained in their consumer files.
regulatoryFindings.description: SafeRent rejected multiple file disclosure requests submitted by facsimile and required consumers to submit written requests through U.S. mail instead
violations: SafeRent rejected multiple file disclosure requests submitted by facsimile and required consumers to submit written requests through U.S. mail instead

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 611(a)(1)(A) requires all consumer reporting agencies to reinvestigate the completeness or accuracy of items in a consumer's file upon receipt of a dispute notice from the consumer.
regulatoryFindings.description: SafeRent did not conduct reinvestigations of disputed items when consumers submitted requests by facsimile, instead requiring written reinvestigation requests via U.S. mail
violations: SafeRent did not conduct reinvestigations of disputed items when consumers submitted requests by facsimile, instead requiring written reinvestigation requests via U.S. mail

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SafeRent's systematic rejection of facsimile requests constituted unfair and deceptive practices in violation of Section 5(a)
violations: SafeRent's systematic rejection of facsimile requests constituted unfair and deceptive practices in violation of Section 5(a)

outcome: SafeRent agreed to a Stipulated Final Judgment and Order requiring payment of $100,000 civil penalty. The company was permanently enjoined from failing to disclose consumer file contents upon request and from failing to maintain reasonable procedures to ensure reinvestigation compliance. SafeRent must comply with ongoing monitoring, reporting, and record-keeping requirements for five to eight years, including notification of business changes, annual compliance reports, and distribution of the Order to all relevant personnel.
companyNow: First Advantage SafeRent, Inc. remains a consumer reporting agency in the multi-family housing sector. The 2010 settlement required sustained compliance monitoring through at least 2015-2018.
dataType: Tenant eviction records, lease and payment information, criminal history records, consumer files

companyDescription: Dave & Buster's, Inc. is a Missouri-based corporation operating 53 restaurant/entertainment complexes across the United States under the brands Dave & Buster's, Dave & Buster's Grand Sports Café, and Jillian's. The company accepts payment cards and cash for consumer purchases and operates interconnected networks for transaction processing.
companyLongDescription: Dave & Buster's, Inc. is a Missouri-based corporation operating 53 restaurant/entertainment complexes across the United States under the brands Dave & Buster's, Dave & Buster's Grand Sports Café, and Jillian's. The company accepts payment cards and cash for consumer purchases and operates interconnected networks for transaction processing.
caseDescription: Dave & Buster's failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive payment card data collected from 53 restaurant/entertainment locations. An intruder exploited multiple security vulnerabilities between April and August 2007, compromising approximately 130,000 payment cards and resulting in hundreds of thousands of dollars in fraudulent charges.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures for sensitive personal financial information falls squarely within the Solove category of insecurity — the handling of personal information in a manner that creates substantial risk of unauthorized access or disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Dave & Buster's collected sensitive payment card data including account numbers, expiration dates.
whyTheyWereWrong: An intruder exploited these security gaps between April and August 2007 to intercept 130,000 payment card records.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's networks were secure and protected consumer payment card data appropriately.
claimsVsReality.reality: The networks lacked basic security measures including intrusion detection, firewalls, access controls, and traffic monitoring, allowing an intruder to access systems for four months undetected.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Dave & Buster's engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information, thereby causing or likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: Dave & Buster's engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information, thereby causing or likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on May 20, 2010, alleging violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The respondent's inadequate security practices—specifically the absence of intrusion detection systems, inadequate third-party access restrictions, lack of outbound traffic monitoring, absence of firewalls between payment systems and corporate networks, and unsecured wireless access points—created conditions enabling unauthorized access and interception of 130,000 payment card records between April 30 and August 28, 2007. The company was required to implement comprehensive security reforms and monitoring.
companyNow: Dave & Buster's, Inc. continues to operate as a publicly traded company (PLAY on NASDAQ). The company has subsequently implemented improved security measures and data protection protocols in response to enforcement actions.
dataType: Payment card data (credit/debit card account numbers, expiration dates, security codes)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Direct Marketing Associates was an Arizona-based direct mail marketing company that provided marketing services to automobile dealers throughout the United States, including list acquisition, solicitation printing, and mailing services.
companyLongDescription: Direct Marketing Associates was an Arizona-based direct mail marketing company that provided marketing services to automobile dealers throughout the United States, including list acquisition, solicitation printing, and mailing services.
caseDescription: Direct Marketing Associates obtained consumer credit reports from credit reporting agencies by falsely claiming they would be used to make firm offers of credit. The company then mailed deceptive solicitations claiming consumers were 'pre-approved' for auto financing by fake finance companies that did not exist. Defendants misused consumer credit data and engaged in unfair and deceptive practices under both the FTC Act and Fair Credit Reporting Act.
violationSummary: Consumer reports obtained for stated permissible purpose (firm credit offers) were actually used for deceptive direct marketing solicitations with non-existent lenders unable to honor offers. Data was repurposed beyond authorized scope.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Direct Marketing Associates obtained consumer credit reports from credit agencies by falsely claiming they would facilitate firm credit offers from finance companies like 'Evergreen Automotive.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' sensitive credit data was obtained and misused without legitimate purpose, and they received fraudulent pre-approval letters for automobile financing that no actual lender intended.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers named in solicitations had been 'pre-approved' for automobile financing by entities such as 'Evergreen Automotive Acceptance'
claimsVsReality.reality: No pre-approval had occurred; consumers had not been selected based on genuine creditworthiness assessments; the named finance companies were not functioning financial institutions

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumer reports obtained from credit reporting agencies would be used to make firm offers of credit in accordance with FCRA permissible purpose requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: Reports were obtained without any agreement with actual functioning finance entities to honor offers; defendants simply mailed generic deceptive solicitations to consumers

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendants had arrangements with finance companies to honor pre-approval offers to consumers meeting pre-specified criteria
claimsVsReality.reality: No such arrangements existed; defendants had no agreement or arrangement with any party to ensure consumers would receive actual credit offers

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, including false or misleading statements or representations in advertising or sales solicitations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants represented that consumers had been pre-approved for automobile financing when in fact no pre-approval had occurred and the named finance companies were not functioning entities
violations: Defendants represented that consumers had been pre-approved for automobile financing when in fact no pre-approval had occurred and the named finance companies were not functioning entities

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604(f) prohibits any person from using or obtaining consumer reports unless the reports are obtained for a permissible purpose and that purpose is certified in accordance with FCRA Section 607.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants obtained consumer reports by falsely representing they had a permissible purpose under FCRA Section 604(c) to make firm offers of credit on behalf of finance companies, when they actually intended to send deceptive solicitations without genuine credit offers
violations: Defendants obtained consumer reports by falsely representing they had a permissible purpose under FCRA Section 604(c) to make firm offers of credit on behalf of finance companies, when they actually intended to send deceptive solicitations without genuine credit offers

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604(c) establishes a permissible purpose for obtaining consumer reports in connection with making a 'firm offer of credit or insurance,' which requires the offer will be honored if the consumer meets pre-specified criteria.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants lacked a permissible purpose because the named finance companies were not functioning businesses and did not provide loans; consumers could not actually receive the offers represented in the solicitations
violations: Defendants lacked a permissible purpose because the named finance companies were not functioning businesses and did not provide loans; consumers could not actually receive the offers represented in the solicitations

outcome: The complaint sought civil penalties, permanent injunction against future violations of the FTC Act and FCRA, and other equitable relief. The case was filed March 26, 2010 in U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona. The complaint requests monetary civil penalties of not more than $2,500 per FCRA violation and a permanent injunction to halt violations.
dataType: Credit history, consumer reports, demographic information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604(c) – Permissible purpose requirement
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604(f) – Prohibition on obtaining reports without permissible purpose
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(d)(1) – Consumer report definition
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(l) – Firm offer of credit definition

companyDescription: LifeLock, Inc. is an identity theft protection and monitoring company founded in 2005 based in Tempe, Arizona. The company provides fraud alerts, credit monitoring, and identity restoration services to consumers and has enrolled over one million customers.
companyLongDescription: LifeLock, Inc. is an identity theft protection and monitoring company founded in 2005 based in Tempe, Arizona. The company provides fraud alerts, credit monitoring, and identity restoration services to consumers and has enrolled over one million customers.
caseDescription: LifeLock advertised an identity theft prevention service that claimed to provide complete protection against identity theft and secure customer data with encryption and access controls. In reality, the service did not prevent most types of identity theft, stored sensitive customer information in unencrypted plain text, failed to implement basic security measures, and lacked reasonable access controls.
violationSummary: LifeLock failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information despite representing that they used encryption, secure access controls, and highly secure physical/electronic procedures. The company's inadequate security practices created unnecessary risk of unauthorized access to stored and transmitted sensitive customer data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: LifeLock marketed an identity theft prevention service claiming it prevented all types of identity theft, continuously monitored credit.
whyTheyWereWrong: The service failed to prevent common identity theft types like existing account misuse, stored sensitive customer data including SSNs unencrypted in plain text.

claimsVsReality.claim: LifeLock will make your personal information useless to a criminal
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer SSNs, credit card numbers, and other sensitive data were stored and transmitted in unencrypted plain text, making them accessible to unauthorized persons

claimsVsReality.claim: We prevent identity theft from occurring / First company to prevent identity theft from occurring
claimsVsReality.reality: The service only placed fraud alerts on credit reports; it did not prevent most forms of identity theft including existing account misuse, medical fraud, and employment fraud

claimsVsReality.claim: LifeLock clients are contacted every time someone attempts to open credit in their name or change an address
claimsVsReality.reality: Fraud alerts do not require creditors to contact customers before opening accounts (FCRA permits but does not require phone calls) and do not prevent address changes

claimsVsReality.claim: All stored personal data is electronically encrypted / We work with secure, encrypted channels
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive customer information was stored on corporate networks and transmitted over the internet in clear readable text without encryption until at least September 2007

claimsVsReality.claim: Only authorized employees of LifeLock will have access to the data that you provide to us, and that access is granted only on a 'need to know' basis
claimsVsReality.reality: LifeLock failed to limit access to personal information, did not require strong passwords, allowed remote access from employees' homes without adequate security controls, and did not implement basic access restrictions

claimsVsReality.claim: We constantly monitor what's happening with each person's credit
claimsVsReality.reality: LifeLock did not provide ongoing monitoring or review of customers' credit files

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that the ID theft prevention service provided complete protection against all forms of identity theft when it protected only against fraud alerts and did not cover existing account misuse, medical identity theft, employment fraud, or law enforcement evasion
violations: Represented that the ID theft prevention service provided complete protection against all forms of identity theft when it protected only against fraud alerts and did not cover existing account misuse, medical identity theft, employment fraud, or law enforcement evasion
Represented that the service prevented unauthorized address changes when Initial Alerts do not require creditors to contact customers before changing address information
Represented that the service constantly monitored customers' credit files when it provided no ongoing monitoring or review
Represented that customers would always receive phone calls from creditors before new accounts opened when FCRA permits alternative verification methods

Represented that they employed reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information when they stored sensitive data in unencrypted plain text, failed to require strong passwords, lacked access controls, and did not patch vulnerabilities
Represented that all stored personal data was electronically encrypted when sensitive information was transmitted and stored in clear readable text
Represented that access to sensitive customer information was limited to authorized employees on a need-to-know basis when access was not adequately restricted

outcome: The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, rescission or reformation of contracts, restitution, refund of monies paid, and disgorgement of ill-gotten monies. The case was filed March 8, 2010, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona. LifeLock subsequently entered into a settlement with the FTC involving substantial monetary penalties and compliance obligations.
companyNow: LifeLock remains an identity theft protection company but operates under FTC consent decrees requiring robust security measures, substantiation of claims, and periodic independent assessments. The company's reputation and market position were significantly damaged by the enforcement action.
dataType: Name, address, email, phone number, Social Security number, credit card details

companyDescription: Rite Aid Corporation is a publicly-traded pharmacy retailer operating thousands of retail stores across the United States, providing prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, and general retail merchandise. The company processes sensitive health and financial information from millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Rite Aid Corporation is a publicly-traded pharmacy retailer operating thousands of retail stores across the United States, providing prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, and general retail merchandise. The company processes sensitive health and financial information from millions of customers.
caseDescription: Rite Aid made public commitments to protect customer health information and privacy but failed to implement basic security measures for disposing of personal data. The company discarded pharmacy labels, employment applications, and customer records containing sensitive information in publicly accessible dumpsters, exposing personal data to identity theft and prescription fraud.
violationSummary: Rite Aid failed to implement reasonable security measures for personal information, particularly during disposal, creating substantial risk of unauthorized access and misuse of sensitive health and financial data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Rite Aid discarded materials containing customers' and job applicants' personal information in readable text in unsecured.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive health records, financial data, and Social Security numbers were exposed in public dumpsters where anyone could retrieve them to commit identity theft or fraudulently obtain.

claimsVsReality.claim: Rite Aid takes its responsibility for maintaining protected health information in confidence very seriously (stated in Notice of Privacy Practices since 2003)
claimsVsReality.reality: Rite Aid routinely discarded pharmacy labels, employment applications, and customer records containing sensitive health information in unsecured public dumpsters where anyone could access them

claimsVsReality.claim: Rite Aid would like to assure you that we respect and protect your privacy (stated in customer brochure since 2004)
claimsVsReality.reality: Rite Aid failed to implement basic disposal procedures, employee training, or compliance monitoring to prevent disclosure of customers' prescription information, health insurer details, and financial data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Rite Aid made express and implied representations that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access
violations: Rite Aid made express and implied representations that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access

Rite Aid failed to implement reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers through disclosure of health, financial, and identity data in public dumpsters

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices. The complaint alleges Rite Aid violated Section 5(a) of the FTC Act through false or misleading representations about data security and failure to implement reasonable safeguards for personal information disposal. The case proceeding would typically result in a consent order requiring comprehensive remediation of data security practices, employee training, compliance monitoring, and regular audits.
companyNow: Rite Aid Corporation continues to operate as a major U.S. pharmacy chain with approximately 2,000 stores (reduced from ~4,900 at time of complaint due to Chapter 11 bankruptcy restructuring completed in 2023). The company has implemented enhanced data security and privacy controls.
dataType: Health data, prescription information, payment card data, financial data, Social Security numbers, personal identifiers

companyDescription: World Innovators, Inc. is a Connecticut-based list broker and marketing consulting services provider operating through its website www.worldinnovators.com.
companyLongDescription: World Innovators, Inc. is a Connecticut-based list broker and marketing consulting services provider operating through its website www.worldinnovators.com.
caseDescription: World Innovators, a Connecticut list broker, claimed on its website to be a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework from November 2001 onwards. However, the company failed to renew its Safe Harbor certification in September 2004 and remained in 'not current' status until July 2009, while continuing to make false claims of Safe Harbor compliance on its website. This deceptive practice violated FTC Act Section 5(a).
violationSummary: Company misrepresented its Safe Harbor certification status in privacy policy statements, creating a false impression of compliance and data protection standards that did not actually apply.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: World Innovators falsely claimed on its website from November 2001 through at least December 2008 that it was a current member of the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor program.
whyTheyWereWrong: European customers and business partners relied on World Innovators' false Safe Harbor claims when transferring personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: World Innovators is a member of the U.S. Department of Commerce Safe Harbor program (stated in privacy policies from November 2001 through December 2008)
claimsVsReality.reality: Company's Safe Harbor certification lapsed in September 2004 and remained in 'not current' status until July 2009; it was not a current participant during most of the claimed period

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: World Innovators represented expressly and by implication that it was a current Safe Harbor participant from November 2001 to present
violations: World Innovators represented expressly and by implication that it was a current Safe Harbor participant from November 2001 to present
Company was not a current Safe Harbor participant from September 2004 to July 2009 when its certification lapsed and status became 'not current'
Representations in privacy policies (November 2001, February 2005, September 2006, December 2008) were false or misleading

outcome: FTC issued complaint on January 12, 2010, alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case sought enforcement action based on deceptive representations regarding Safe Harbor compliance. The company was required to cease false claims and implement compliance measures regarding Safe Harbor certification status.
dataType: Personal data subject to EU data protection requirements
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce

companyDescription: Central Credit, LLC is a consumer reporting agency and nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency that has compiled and sold information about consumers' gaming experiences and check-cashing transactions to casinos since at least 1956. The company maintains databases on check-writing history of individuals across the United States.
companyLongDescription: Central Credit, LLC is a consumer reporting agency and nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency that has compiled and sold information about consumers' gaming experiences and check-cashing transactions to casinos since at least 1956. The company maintains databases on check-writing history of individuals across the United States.
caseDescription: Central Credit, a consumer reporting agency that compiled and sold gaming and check-cashing information to casinos for credit decisions, failed to provide required notices to furnishers and users of consumer reports, failed to provide Summary of Rights notices to consumers, and failed to establish a streamlined process for free annual file disclosures as required for nationwide specialty consumer reporting agencies.
violationSummary: Central Credit failed to disclose required notices and information to consumers and furnishers, preventing them from understanding their rights under the FCRA regarding check-writing history and gaming transaction data used for credit decisions.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Central Credit sold gaming and check-cashing data to casinos as consumer reports without providing furnishers and users with required FCRA notices prior to 2008.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers requesting their credit files could not easily access them or learn their rights to dispute inaccurate information, while furnishers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Central Credit's reports improve credit decisions for casinos extending credit to consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumers were never informed of their rights to dispute inaccurate information or understand how gaming and check-cashing data was being used against them in credit decisions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(d) of the FCRA requires consumer reporting agencies to provide Furnisher Notices and User Notices informing furnishers and users of their responsibilities under the FCRA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Central Credit failed to provide Furnisher Notices to furnishers prior to 2008
violations: Central Credit failed to provide Furnisher Notices to furnishers prior to 2008
Central Credit failed to provide User Notices to users prior to 2008

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 609(c)(2) of the FCRA requires that when a consumer reporting agency provides a file disclosure, a Summary of Rights must be provided containing all required information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Central Credit failed to provide Summary of Rights notices containing all required information prior to 2008
violations: Central Credit failed to provide Summary of Rights notices containing all required information prior to 2008

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 612(a)(1)(C) and (a)(2) of the FCRA and the Streamlined Process Rule 16 C.F.R. § 610.3 require nationwide specialty consumer reporting agencies to establish a streamlined process with a clearly and prominently posted toll-free number for free annual file disclosures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Central Credit did not establish the required streamlined process
violations: Central Credit did not establish the required streamlined process
Central Credit did not clearly and prominently post toll-free number on websites
Central Credit did not provide clear instructions for requesting free annual disclosures

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Central Credit's failure to provide required notices constitutes unfair or deceptive practices
violations: Central Credit's failure to provide required notices constitutes unfair or deceptive practices
Central Credit's failure to establish streamlined disclosure process constitutes unfair or deceptive practices

outcome: The case sought monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation for violations before February 10, 2009, and $3,500 per violation thereafter; a permanent injunction prohibiting future FCRA violations; and payment of court costs. Central Credit is a subsidiary of Global Cash Access, Inc., headquartered in Las Vegas, Nevada.
companyNow: Central Credit, LLC remains a wholly owned subsidiary of Global Cash Access, Inc., based in Las Vegas, Nevada. The company continues to provide check verification and check warranty services.
