companyDescription: EchoMetrix, Inc. was a Delaware corporation operating parental control software (Sentry) since 2004 and market research software (Pulse) launched in 2009. Principal place of business was in Syosset, New York.
companyLongDescription: EchoMetrix, Inc. was a Delaware corporation operating parental control software (Sentry) since 2004 and market research software (Pulse) launched in 2009. Principal place of business was in Syosset, New York.
caseDescription: EchoMetrix sold parental monitoring software (Sentry) that collected children's online communications, then secretly fed this data into a commercial market research database (Pulse) sold to marketers without adequate disclosure. Parents purchasing Sentry were unaware their children's conversations and browsing were being shared with third parties for commercial analysis.
violationSummary: EchoMetrix failed to disclose material secondary use of children's personal data collected through Sentry software. The disclosure to Pulse marketers constitutes unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information revealed by minors in private communications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: EchoMetrix collected children's online activity including chat conversations and instant messages through its Sentry parental control software.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents purchased Sentry believing it would only monitor their children's activity for parental supervision, but their children's sensitive communications were instead monetized.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sentry monitors children's computer activities for parents' protective purposes
claimsVsReality.reality: Sentry data was also fed into commercial Pulse database sold to marketers and advertisers without parental knowledge or consent

claimsVsReality.claim: Pulse aggregates publicly available social media content from forums, blogs, chats, and instant messages
claimsVsReality.reality: Pulse database included children's private online conversations captured by Sentry until November 2009, sourced from monitored minors whose parents had no idea their data would be used for commercial research

claimsVsReality.claim: EULA clearly discloses data usage and third-party sharing
claimsVsReality.reality: Disclosure was buried 30 paragraphs deep in multi-page scroll box, with only vague language about 'anonymous reporting for external clients'

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. Misrepresentations or omissions of material fact constitute deceptive acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: EchoMetrix represented that Sentry would monitor children's computer activity but failed to adequately disclose that this data would be shared with third-party marketers through Pulse.
violations: EchoMetrix represented that Sentry would monitor children's computer activity but failed to adequately disclose that this data would be shared with third-party marketers through Pulse.
Material disclosure regarding secondary use of children's sensitive communications was buried in multi-page EULA and required scrolling through approximately 30 paragraphs to locate.

Vague EULA language stating data would be used for 'conduct research and provide anonymous reporting for internal and external clients' did not clearly communicate that children's actual online conversations would be sold to marketers.

outcome: FTC filed complaint on November 30, 2010, seeking permanent injunction and equitable relief. The complaint alleges deceptive omissions under Count One regarding failure to disclose secondary use of children's data. Document does not reflect final settlement or judgment, only initial complaint filing.
companyNow: Unknown. No public information in document regarding current status of EchoMetrix or Sentry/Pulse products post-2010.
dataType: Children's online activity, instant messages, chat conversations, web history, personal information (name, address, email, child age/gender)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 13(b) – Authority to obtain permanent injunction

companyDescription: Genica Corporation and its wholly-owned subsidiary Compgeeks.com operated an e-commerce business selling computer systems, peripherals, and consumer electronics online through the www.geeks.com website, collecting sensitive customer payment information during transactions.
companyLongDescription: Genica Corporation and its wholly-owned subsidiary Compgeeks.com operated an e-commerce business selling computer systems, peripherals, and consumer electronics online through the www.geeks.com website, collecting sensitive customer payment information during transactions.
caseDescription: Genica and Compgeeks.com collected sensitive financial information from customers purchasing computer equipment online but failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect it. From January to June 2007, hackers exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to access and export personal data including credit card information of hundreds of customers. The company's privacy policies promised strong security protections that were never actually implemented.
violationSummary: The core violation is the failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, combined with the storage of sensitive data in unencrypted, plain-text format vulnerable to SQL injection attacks.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Genica Corporation and Compgeeks.com collected sensitive customer credit card information through www.geeks.com but stored it in plain text.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these preventable security failures between January and June 2007, stealing hundreds of customers' complete credit card numbers, expiration dates.

claimsVsReality.claim: We use secure technology, privacy protection controls and restrictions on employee access to safeguard your personal information
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information was stored in clear, readable text on a network accessible through the website with no encryption

claimsVsReality.claim: We use state of the art technology (e.g., Secure Socket Layer, or SSL) encryption to keep customer personal information as secure as possible
claimsVsReality.reality: Information was not encrypted in storage and was vulnerable to SQL injection attacks that went undetected and unpatched for months

claimsVsReality.claim: We have put in place privacy protection control systems designed to ensure that personal Customer data remains safe and private
claimsVsReality.reality: No adequate network monitoring, intrusion detection, access controls, or vulnerability assessment mechanisms were implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents made express and implied representations that they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access through privacy policies stating they use 'state of the art technology' and 'privacy protection control systems' to keep customer data 'safe and private'
violations: Respondents made express and implied representations that they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access through privacy policies stating they use 'state of the art technology' and 'privacy protection control systems' to keep customer data 'safe and private'

In truth, respondents did not implement reasonable and appropriate security measures: they stored personal information in clear, readable text; failed to assess vulnerability to SQL injection attacks; did not implement defenses; lacked network monitoring and access controls; and failed to employ intrusion detection systems
These false or misleading representations regarding data security constituted deceptive acts affecting commerce

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 16, 2009 against Genica Corporation and Compgeeks.com alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act for misrepresentations regarding data security. The case proceeded to enforcement, with respondents required to implement comprehensive information security improvements and ongoing monitoring/compliance obligations.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, expiration dates, security codes), contact information (name, address, email, phone)

companyDescription: ExpatEdge Partners, LLC was a Minnesota-based software and consulting services company providing expatriate payroll and tax management solutions to businesses with international employees.
companyLongDescription: ExpatEdge Partners, LLC was a Minnesota-based software and consulting services company providing expatriate payroll and tax management solutions to businesses with international employees.
caseDescription: ExpatEdge Partners claimed on its website from 2002 to 2009 that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework. However, the company failed to renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in November 2006 and never renewed it thereafter, while continuing to make false claims of current Safe Harbor compliance on its privacy policies.
violationSummary: The company made false public claims about its participation in a privacy framework designed to protect personal data transfers from the EU. This misrepresentation undermined trust in data protection commitments and breached the confidentiality framework consumers relied upon.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: ExpatEdge Partners disseminated privacy policies from December 2002 through July 2009 falsely claiming it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers and business partners who relied on ExpatEdge's false Safe Harbor claims believed their personal data received EU-standard protections when in fact the company had no valid compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: ExpatEdge self-certifies the Policy to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor Privacy Program (stated in privacy policies Dec 2002–Jul 2009).
claimsVsReality.reality: ExpatEdge did not renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in November 2006 and remained in 'not current' status on the Commerce Department's public website from that date forward.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ExpatEdge represented expressly and by implication that it was a current participant in the Safe Harbor framework by stating 'ExpatEdge self-certifies the Policy to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor Privacy Program' in privacy policies posted from December 2002 until July 2009.
violations: ExpatEdge represented expressly and by implication that it was a current participant in the Safe Harbor framework by stating 'ExpatEdge self-certifies the Policy to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor Privacy Program' in privacy policies posted from December 2002 until July 2009.

Since November 2006, ExpatEdge was not a current participant in the Safe Harbor, as it failed to renew its self-certification and remained listed with 'not current' status on the Commerce Department's public Safe Harbor list.
The representations were false or misleading because they misled consumers and business partners about the company's actual privacy compliance status and data protection commitments.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on November 9, 2009, alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The company was required to cease making false Safe Harbor claims and comply with FTC orders regarding accurate privacy representations. The case establishes that companies failing to maintain or renew Safe Harbor certification while claiming current participation are subject to FTC enforcement action.
companyNow: Unknown. The complaint was issued in 2009; current status of ExpatEdge Partners, LLC is not documented in this file.
dataType: Personal data related to expatriate employees (tax, payroll, employment information)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) — Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Progressive Gaitways LLC was a Colorado-based medical equipment company operating two e-commerce websites (theratogs.com and gaitways.com) selling therapeutic and gait-related medical devices.
companyLongDescription: Progressive Gaitways LLC was a Colorado-based medical equipment company operating two e-commerce websites (theratogs.com and gaitways.com) selling therapeutic and gait-related medical devices.
caseDescription: Progressive Gaitways falsely claimed on two websites that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework when it had either never self-certified (gaitways.com) or had allowed its certification to lapse in 2006 (theratogs.com). The company continued displaying these false certifications for years despite knowing its Safe Harbor status was 'not current' or non-existent.
violationSummary: The company distorted its actual Safe Harbor compliance status, falsely representing to consumers that their personal data would receive the privacy protections promised by Safe Harbor participation. This is a material misrepresentation about data handling practices.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Progressive Gaitways posted false statements on its websites claiming it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy program.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers in Europe and elsewhere who shared personal data with the company relied on these false Safe Harbor claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: TheraTogs is a participant in the Safe Harbor program developed by the U.S. Department of Commerce and the European Union. We have certified that we adhere to the Safe Harbor Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: theratogs.com allowed its Safe Harbor self-certification to lapse in November 2006 and was marked 'not current' on the Commerce Department website. The company never renewed certification but continued making these claims from December 2008 through June 2009.

claimsVsReality.claim: PGW [Progressive Gaitways] is a participant in the Safe Harbor program developed by the U.S. Department of Commerce and the European Union. We have certified that we adhere to the Safe Harbor Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: gaitways.com never submitted any self-certification to the Safe Harbor program. The company had never been a Safe Harbor participant for this domain, yet made identical certification claims from at least June 2007 through June 2009.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. A company that self-certifies to the Safe Harbor but fails to comply or maintain certification may be subject to enforcement action.
regulatoryFindings.description: Progressive Gaitways falsely represented that theratogs.com was a current Safe Harbor participant from December 2008 to June 2009, when it had allowed certification to lapse in November 2006 and never renewed.
violations: Progressive Gaitways falsely represented that theratogs.com was a current Safe Harbor participant from December 2008 to June 2009, when it had allowed certification to lapse in November 2006 and never renewed.

Progressive Gaitways falsely represented that gaitways.com was a current Safe Harbor participant from at least June 2007 to June 2009, when it had never submitted any self-certification for that domain.

The company was aware Safe Harbor status required annual re-certification and that theratogs.com status was marked 'not current' on the public Commerce Department list, yet continued making false Safe Harbor claims.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Progressive Gaitways on November 9, 2009, alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges unfair and deceptive acts through false Safe Harbor participation claims on both websites. The document indicates enforcement action was initiated; a compliance order would require cessation of deceptive practices and potential monitoring.
dataType: Personal data of customers (nature not specified in complaint, but implied to include contact/transactional data for EU consumers)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Rail Terminal Services, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company based in Seattle, Washington, provided transportation services on a contract basis to railroads including Burlington Northern Santa Fe, Union Pacific, and Norfolk & Southern, utilizing background checks for employee access to railroad properties.
companyLongDescription: Rail Terminal Services, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company based in Seattle, Washington, provided transportation services on a contract basis to railroads including Burlington Northern Santa Fe, Union Pacific, and Norfolk & Southern, utilizing background checks for employee access to railroad properties.
caseDescription: Rail Terminal Services obtained background checks on job applicants and employees using a consumer reporting agency, but failed to provide required pre-adverse and post-adverse action notices when taking employment decisions based on the reports. From mid-2004 through June 2006, RTS took adverse action against approximately 24 employees by placing them on indefinite unpaid administrative leave without providing the legally mandated notices.
violationSummary: RTS's failure to implement required notice procedures exposed employees to adverse employment decisions without transparency, constituting a security and procedural failure in handling consumer reports used for employment decisions under FCRA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Rail Terminal Services obtained background checks on 24 employees through e-Verifyfile.com's e-RAILSAFE system to determine employment eligibility.
whyTheyWereWrong: Twenty-four employees lost their livelihoods and had no opportunity to correct inaccurate background information before being terminated.

claimsVsReality.claim: RTS could use background check information from e-Verifyfile.com to make employment decisions regarding job applicant access to railroad properties.
claimsVsReality.reality: While RTS was permitted to use consumer reports for employment purposes, it was legally obligated to provide statutory notices both before and after adverse actions; RTS provided neither.

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 604(b)(3) requires that any person using a consumer report for employment purposes must provide a pre-adverse action notice to the individual prior to taking adverse action, including copies of the consumer report and Summary of Consumer Rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: RTS failed to provide pre-adverse action notices to 24 employees before placing them on indefinite unpaid administrative leave based on background check information.
violations: RTS failed to provide pre-adverse action notices to 24 employees before placing them on indefinite unpaid administrative leave based on background check information.

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 615(a) requires that after taking adverse action based on a consumer report, the person must provide an adverse action notice including the CRA's name, address, and telephone number; statement that the CRA did not make the decision; notice of the right to dispute accuracy; and right to obtain a free copy of the report.
regulatoryFindings.description: RTS failed to provide post-adverse action notices containing any of the statutorily required information to the 24 affected employees after taking adverse employment actions.
violations: RTS failed to provide post-adverse action notices containing any of the statutorily required information to the 24 affected employees after taking adverse employment actions.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: RTS's failure to provide required FCRA notices constituted unfair and deceptive practices affecting employment applicants and employees.
violations: RTS's failure to provide required FCRA notices constituted unfair and deceptive practices affecting employment applicants and employees.

outcome: The complaint for civil penalties and injunctive relief was filed on August 5, 2009, seeking monetary penalties under FCRA Section 621(a) (up to $2,500 per knowing violation) and a permanent injunction prohibiting future violations of the FCRA and FTC Act. The court was authorized to award penalties for each separate violation and issue injunctive relief to prevent future non-compliance.
dataType: Criminal background records, employment screening information

companyDescription: TALX Corporation is a for-profit subsidiary of Equifax Inc. headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri. Since 2002, TALX has operated as a nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency selling employment and income history information to lenders, pre-employment screeners, social service agencies, and other entities.
companyLongDescription: TALX Corporation is a for-profit subsidiary of Equifax Inc. headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri. Since 2002, TALX has operated as a nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency selling employment and income history information to lenders, pre-employment screeners, social service agencies, and other entities.
caseDescription: TALX Corporation, a subsidiary of Equifax, failed to provide required notice disclosures to furnishers of employment and income information and to users of consumer reports from 2002 until 2006. As a nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency selling employment and income history reports to lenders, employers, and government agencies, TALX violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by omitting mandatory Furnisher Notices and User Notices disclosing parties' obligations under federal law.
violationSummary: TALX failed to disclose required notices regarding obligations of furnishers and users, preventing proper consumer data handling and transparency.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: TALX Corporation failed to provide mandatory Furnisher Notices and User Notices to employers and lenders using its employment and income history reports from 2002 until 2006.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employers and lenders using TALX reports were unable to comply with Fair Credit Reporting Act requirements because they lacked legally required notices explaining their obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: TALX could operate as a consumer reporting agency providing employment reports to third parties without special compliance obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: As a nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency, TALX was required by FCRA §607(d) to provide Furnisher Notices and User Notices disclosing legal obligations to all furnishers and users of its reports.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(d)(1) of the FCRA requires a consumer reporting agency to provide a Notice To Furnishers of Information disclosing furnishers' obligations under the FCRA.
regulatoryFindings.description: TALX failed to provide Furnisher Notices to employers and other furnishers of employment and income information prior to 2006.
violations: TALX failed to provide Furnisher Notices to employers and other furnishers of employment and income information prior to 2006.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(d)(2) of the FCRA requires a consumer reporting agency to provide a Notice To Users of Consumer Reports disclosing users' obligations under the FCRA.
regulatoryFindings.description: TALX failed to provide User Notices to lenders, employers, and other users of employment and income reports prior to 2006.
violations: TALX failed to provide User Notices to lenders, employers, and other users of employment and income reports prior to 2006.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 603(f) and 603(w) of the FCRA define consumer reporting agencies and nationwide specialty consumer reporting agencies subject to notice requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: TALX, as a nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency maintaining employment and income history files, was obligated to provide notices but did not do so.
violations: TALX, as a nationwide specialty consumer reporting agency maintaining employment and income history files, was obligated to provide notices but did not do so.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 621(a) of the FCRA authorizes the FTC to enforce compliance with FCRA provisions and treat violations as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act.
regulatoryFindings.description: TALX's failure to provide required notices constitutes both FCRA violations and unfair or deceptive practices under FTC Act § 5(a).
violations: TALX's failure to provide required notices constitutes both FCRA violations and unfair or deceptive practices under FTC Act § 5(a).

outcome: Complaint filed seeking monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation of the FCRA, permanent injunction against future violations, costs of action, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice, with each instance of failure to provide notices treated as a separate violation. Final settlement or judgment outcome not specified in this complaint document.
companyNow: TALX Corporation remains a subsidiary of Equifax Inc. as of 2009, operating its employment and income verification business after implementing required compliance measures.
dataType: Employment history, income history

companyDescription: CVS Caremark Corporation (now CVS Health) is a major American pharmacy retailer and healthcare services provider operating approximately 6,300 retail pharmacy stores in the United States, alongside online and mail order pharmacy businesses, serving millions of customers annually.
companyLongDescription: CVS Caremark Corporation (now CVS Health) is a major American pharmacy retailer and healthcare services provider operating approximately 6,300 retail pharmacy stores in the United States, alongside online and mail order pharmacy businesses, serving millions of customers annually.
caseDescription: CVS failed to implement adequate data security measures to protect sensitive customer and employee information. The company discarded materials containing personal information in readable text in publicly-accessible trash dumpsters across at least 15 U.S. cities, exposing data to identity theft and prescription medicine theft. This violated FTC Act Section 5 by being an unfair and deceptive practice.
violationSummary: Personal information was disclosed to the public through improper disposal in accessible trash dumpsters, making it readily available to unauthorized individuals without CVS consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: CVS discarded materials containing customer and employee personal information—including prescriptions, pharmacy labels, credit card receipts.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sensitive health records, payment card numbers, and Social Security numbers were left accessible in publicly searchable trash dumpsters across at least 15 U.S.

claimsVsReality.claim: CVS/pharmacy stated: 'nothing is more central to our operations than maintaining the privacy of your health information' and that 'We take this responsibility very seriously.'
claimsVsReality.reality: CVS failed to implement basic security measures for disposal of personal information, discarding sensitive customer and employee data in readable text in publicly-accessible dumpsters across at least 15 cities, exposing health information, financial data, and government ID numbers to the public.

claimsVsReality.claim: CVS represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: CVS lacked policies and procedures for secure disposal, failed to adequately train employees on secure disposal practices, did not assess compliance with disposal policies, and had no process for discovering and remedying data security risks.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: CVS represented through privacy policies (since 2003) that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information, but failed to do so.
violations: CVS represented through privacy policies (since 2003) that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information, but failed to do so.
CVS discarded sensitive customer and employee personal information in readable text in unsecured public dumpsters, directly contradicting privacy commitments.
Discarded materials contained health information, financial data, government IDs, and Social Security numbers accessible to the public for identity theft and prescription fraud.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(n) provides that an act or practice is unfair if it causes substantial injury to consumers that is not offset by countervailing benefits and is not reasonably avoidable.
regulatoryFindings.description: CVS's failure to implement secure disposal policies, employee training, compliance monitoring, or risk assessment caused substantial injury to millions of pharmacy customers and employees.
violations: CVS's failure to implement secure disposal policies, employee training, compliance monitoring, or risk assessment caused substantial injury to millions of pharmacy customers and employees.
The exposure of personal information in trash dumpsters in at least 15 cities was not reasonably avoidable by consumers who could not control CVS's disposal practices.
No countervailing benefits offset the security failures; CVS had a clear obligation to protect sensitive data given its representations about privacy.

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint against CVS Caremark Corporation on June 18, 2009 (Docket No. C-4259) alleging unfair and deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5. The complaint alleged that CVS made false representations about protecting personal information while failing to implement reasonable security measures, specifically regarding disposal of sensitive documents. The case resulted in a compliance order requiring CVS to implement comprehensive information security improvements, establish policies and procedures for secure disposal, train employees, conduct risk assessments, and submit to ongoing monitoring and reporting to the FTC. While no monetary penalty is specified in the complaint, CVS was required to remediate and implement stringent data protection standards.
companyNow: CVS Health Corporation remains one of the largest pharmacy chains and healthcare companies in the United States, operating thousands of retail pharmacies and providing integrated healthcare services and insurance products.
dataType: Health data, prescription information, financial data (payment cards, bank accounts), government ID numbers, Social Security numbers, employee records
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5(n) – Unfair practices that cause substantial consumer injury

companyLongDescription: James B. Nutter & Company is a mortgage lender that originates and services single-family residential mortgage loans throughout the United States. The company collects extensive sensitive personal and financial information from borrowers in connection with its lending operations.
caseDescription: James B. Nutter & Company, a mortgage lender, failed to implement reasonable security safeguards for sensitive consumer financial data between September 2004 and November 2008. The company stored personal information in unencrypted plain text, lacked a comprehensive security program, and did not properly oversee third-party service providers. An intruder exploited these deficiencies to hijack the company's network and send millions of spam emails, and could have accessed customer data without authorization.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement adequate technical and administrative safeguards to protect stored personal information from unauthorized access, combined with the actual intrusion that demonstrated the vulnerability of their systems, directly exemplifies the Insecurity category in Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: From September 2004 to November 2008, James B. Nutter & Company failed to develop a comprehensive written information security program.
whyTheyWereWrong: An intruder exploited these security failures to direct the company's network to send millions of spam emails undetected.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate security measures in place to protect customer financial information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company stored sensitive data in unencrypted plain text, lacked a comprehensive security program, did not monitor network access or assess security risks, and an intruder successfully hijacked the network to send millions of spam emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's privacy notices accurately informed customers about data sharing practices and opt-out rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy notices did not describe security practices, did not accurately inform customers that data was shared with third parties like credit reporting agencies, and falsely limited opt-out rights to 30 days rather than the entire loan relationship.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company appropriately managed third-party service providers handling customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company provided backup tapes containing unencrypted personal information to service providers without contractual requirements to protect the security and confidentiality of that data.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314), implementing GLB Act Section 501(b), requires financial institutions to develop and maintain a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program
violations: Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program
Failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to security, confidentiality, and integrity of personal information
Failed to design and implement safeguards to control identified risks and failed to regularly test and monitor them
Failed to investigate, evaluate, and adjust the security program in light of known or identified risks
Failed to oversee service providers and require them by contract to implement safeguards to protect personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313), implementing GLB Act Sections 501-509, requires financial institutions to provide customers with privacy notices that set out the institution's security practices, accurately describe disclosures of customer information to third parties, and accurately inform customers of their opt-out rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide privacy notices for several years after the Rule became effective on July 1, 2001
violations: Failed to provide privacy notices for several years after the Rule became effective on July 1, 2001
Provided notices that failed to set out respondent's security practices
Provided notices that did not accurately describe disclosures of customer information to third parties such as credit reporting agencies
Informed customers they had only 30 days to exercise opt-out rights, contrary to the Rule's provision allowing opt-out at any time during the course of loans

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 12, 2009, alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule and Privacy Rule. The complaint does not specify the final settlement terms as it represents the initial enforcement action. Typically, such complaints result in consent orders requiring the company to implement comprehensive security programs, conduct regular risk assessments, encrypt sensitive data, monitor network access, establish employee training programs, and require contractual safeguards from third-party service providers. The company was also required to provide accurate and timely privacy notices to customers with correct opt-out information.
companyNow: James B. Nutter & Company remains a privately-held mortgage lender headquartered in Kansas City, Missouri. The company continues to operate in the single-family residential mortgage market, though it faced significant reputational and operational challenges following the FTC enforcement action.
dataType: Financial data, SSN, driver's license, bank/credit card account numbers, mortgage information, income, debt, employment, credit histories
legalBasisViolated: 16 C.F.R. Part 314 (Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information Rule)
16 C.F.R. Part 313 (Privacy of Customer Financial Information Rule)

companyDescription: Quality Terminal Services, LLC provided transportation services on a contract basis to railroads including Burlington Northern Santa Fe and Union Pacific, requiring background checks on employees and applicants.
companyLongDescription: Quality Terminal Services, LLC provided transportation services on a contract basis to railroads including Burlington Northern Santa Fe and Union Pacific, requiring background checks on employees and applicants.
caseDescription: Quality Terminal Services failed to provide required notices to job applicants before and after denying them employment based on background check reports. The company did not send pre-adverse action notices to 53 applicants or proper adverse action notices to 42 applicants, violating the Fair Credit Reporting Act's notice requirements.
violationSummary: The company failed to disclose adverse action notices and the basis (consumer reports) to individuals affected by employment decisions, violating requirements to inform consumers of decision-making processes using their data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Quality Terminal Services failed to provide 53 job applicants with pre-adverse action notices disclosing their background check reports before denying them employment.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job applicants were denied employment without learning what information triggered their rejection or their rights to dispute inaccurate background check data.

claimsVsReality.claim: QTS obtained background checks through e-Verifile.com using the e-RAILSAFE system to comply with railroad requirements for employee security
claimsVsReality.reality: QTS used these reports to deny employment but systematically failed to provide applicants with legally required notice of adverse action, preventing applicants from understanding decisions or disputing inaccurate information

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 604(b)(3) requires entities using consumer reports for employment purposes to provide pre-adverse action notice including the report and Summary of Consumer Rights before taking adverse action.
regulatoryFindings.description: QTS failed to provide pre-adverse action notices to 53 job applicants before denying them employment based on background checks
violations: QTS failed to provide pre-adverse action notices to 53 job applicants before denying them employment based on background checks

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 615(a) requires entities taking adverse action based on consumer reports to provide notice after the action with specified information including CRA identity, statement that CRA did not make the decision, and notice of dispute rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: QTS failed to provide proper adverse action notices to 42 applicants; notices provided contained none of the required information
violations: QTS failed to provide proper adverse action notices to 42 applicants; notices provided contained none of the required information

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: QTS's failure to provide required FCRA notices constituted unfair and deceptive practices affecting job applicants
violations: QTS's failure to provide required FCRA notices constituted unfair and deceptive practices affecting job applicants

outcome: The complaint seeks monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per knowing violation (up to 53 pre-adverse action violations and 42 adverse action violations), permanent injunctive relief prohibiting future FCRA violations, and payment of costs. The document indicates knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice, allowing the maximum penalty per violation.
companyNow: Unknown current status; the complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado against Quality Terminal Services, LLC, a Colorado limited liability company.
dataType: Criminal background records, consumer reports
legalBasisViolated: FCRA Section 604(b)(3) (15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)) – Pre-adverse action notice requirement
FCRA Section 615(a) (15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)) – Adverse action notice requirement
FTC Act Section 5(a) (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Sears Holdings Management Corporation is a subsidiary of Sears Holdings Corporation, which operates the Sears Roebuck and Kmart retail stores and their associated e-commerce websites (sears.com and kmart.com). The company handles marketing operations for these major retail brands.
companyLongDescription: Sears Holdings Management Corporation is a subsidiary of Sears Holdings Corporation, which operates the Sears Roebuck and Kmart retail stores and their associated e-commerce websites (sears.com and kmart.com). The company handles marketing operations for these major retail brands.
caseDescription: Sears distributed a software application for its "My SHC Community" market research program that tracked nearly all internet activity on users' computers, including secure banking sessions and health records, while misleading consumers about the scope of monitoring. The company represented the software would track "online browsing" but failed to disclose it monitored nearly all internet behavior, transmitted sensitive financial and health data to Sears servers, and persisted without visible indication to users.
violationSummary: The application conducted continuous, comprehensive surveillance of consumer internet activity across all websites and secure sessions without meaningful informed consent. This constitutes surveillance-type privacy violation under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Sears distributed software that monitored nearly all internet activity on consumers' computers, including secure banking sessions, health records.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers unknowingly exposed sensitive financial, health, and personal information to remote servers without understanding the software's true scope.

claimsVsReality.claim: "My SHC Community" is a place where "your voice is heard and your opinion matters" and membership is "absolutely free"
claimsVsReality.reality: Membership required installation of invasive tracking software that monitored all internet activity including secure banking and health records, with consumers receiving only a $10 payment conditional on keeping the software installed for one month

claimsVsReality.claim: The Application would "track your online browsing" and "confidentially track your online browsing"
claimsVsReality.reality: The software monitored nearly all internet behavior on the computer, including secure sessions containing banking statements, prescription records, shopping carts, email headers, and personal financial information across all websites

claimsVsReality.claim: Information collected would be used "to better understand you and your needs, enabling us to create more relevant future offerings"
claimsVsReality.reality: The software transmitted detailed tracking data including secure page content, banking information, and health records to Sears servers without adequate consumer understanding of the surveillance scope

claimsVsReality.claim: "You can uninstall the software at any time through the Add/Remove program utility on your computer"
claimsVsReality.reality: While technically uninstallable, the software ran invisibly in the background with no visible indication (no desktop or system tray icon) that it was monitoring, making users unaware of its persistent presence

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent represented through pop-up messages and email invitations that the Application would track "online browsing" but failed to disclose it monitored nearly all internet behavior on consumers' computers including secure sessions, shopping carts, online banking, health records, and email headers
violations: Respondent represented through pop-up messages and email invitations that the Application would track "online browsing" but failed to disclose it monitored nearly all internet behavior on consumers' computers including secure sessions, shopping carts, online banking, health records, and email headers
Initial recruitment materials made no mention of the software application, and Privacy Policy linked from pop-up box did not mention it

The detailed description of data collection scope was buried approximately 75 lines down in a scroll box containing a multi-page Privacy Statement and User License Agreement that consumers had to scroll through to find
Material facts about monitoring scope, data transmission to remote servers, and collection of sensitive financial and health information were not adequately disclosed in light of representations made

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Sears Holdings Management Corporation alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the complaint filed August 31, 2009. Based on the complaint nature, a consent order with compliance requirements and monitoring obligations was expected to follow.
companyNow: Sears Holdings Corporation filed for bankruptcy in 2018 and went through restructuring. The company continues to operate limited Sears and Kmart stores, though it is significantly reduced from its historical size.
dataType: Web browsing history, shopping cart contents, online banking statements, video rental transactions, library borrowing histories, online drug prescription records, email headers, secure session data, personal financial information, health information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Life is good, Inc. is a Massachusetts-based retail company that designs and distributes apparel and accessories through its website and retail operations, operating from its principal office in Boston.
companyLongDescription: Life is good, Inc. is a Massachusetts-based retail company that designs and distributes apparel and accessories through its website and retail operations, operating from its principal office in Boston.
caseDescription: Life is good failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect customer payment and personal information stored on its website. Between June and August 2006, hackers exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to access thousands of customers' credit card data. The company's privacy policy falsely promised that 'all information is kept in a secure file,' but the company stored sensitive data in plain text, failed to assess known vulnerabilities, and did not deploy readily available defenses.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures (including encryption, vulnerability assessment, simple defenses, and unauthorized access monitoring) for sensitive consumer financial data stored on its network, resulting in a data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Life is good stored thousands of customers' credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes in plain text on an unencrypted network; failed to assess or defend against commonly known.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between June and August 2006, hackers exploited the company's negligent security practices to steal credit card.

claimsVsReality.claim: We are committed to maintaining our customers' privacy. All information is kept in a secure file.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumer information including credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes was stored in plain text without encryption, making it vulnerable to unauthorized access and exploitation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Information collected is used to tailor communications with you.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company stored credit card security codes indefinitely without business justification, creating unnecessary risks of unauthorized access and exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Life is good represented in its privacy policy that 'all information is kept in a secure file,' but actually stored consumer credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes in clear, readable text without encryption or reasonable protections.
violations: Life is good represented in its privacy policy that 'all information is kept in a secure file,' but actually stored consumer credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes in clear, readable text without encryption or reasonable protections.
The company failed to implement simple, free or low-cost security defenses against commonly known SQL injection attacks despite having readily available technical solutions.
The company did not adequately assess the vulnerability of its web application and network to known attacks, and failed to employ reasonable measures to detect unauthorized access.
The company created unnecessary risks by storing credit card security codes and consumer information indefinitely without business justification.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on April 16, 2008, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint challenged Life is good's false claims regarding data security and the company's failure to implement reasonable safeguards. The case was resolved via a settlement requiring compliance with information security standards and ongoing monitoring.
companyNow: Life is good, Inc. remains an active apparel and accessories retailer operating its website at lifeisgood.com. The company operates under compliance obligations resulting from the FTC settlement.
dataType: Name, address, email address, phone number, credit card number, credit card expiration date, credit card security code
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce

companyDescription: Goal Financial, LLC was a California-based financial services company that originated student loans and provided loan-related services, collecting sensitive personal and financial information from consumer loan applications.
companyLongDescription: Goal Financial, LLC was a California-based financial services company that originated student loans and provided loan-related services, collecting sensitive personal and financial information from consumer loan applications.
caseDescription: Goal Financial failed to implement reasonable security safeguards for sensitive consumer financial data. In 2005-2006, employees exploited these security gaps to remove over 7,000 consumer files and sell hard drives containing unencrypted personal information of approximately 34,000 consumers. The company's privacy policy falsely claimed it maintained appropriate security measures.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement, maintain, and monitor basic security safeguards, resulting in unauthorized access, theft, and exposure of sensitive personal information at scale.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Goal Financial failed to implement reasonable security measures for sensitive consumer financial data, allowing employees to steal over 7,000 customer files.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 34,000 consumers had their Social Security numbers, dates of birth, income, and employment information exposed in clear text when an employee sold hard drives containing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Goal Financial maintained physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards that comply with federal regulations to guard nonpublic personal information, with access limited to employees who need it.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to assess risks, restrict access, implement a comprehensive security program, train employees, or require service providers to protect data. Employees freely removed 7,000+ files and sold unencrypted hard drives containing 34,000 consumers' sensitive data.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, access controls, monitoring, service provider oversight, and program adjustment.
regulatoryFindings.description: Goal Financial failed to conduct adequate risk assessments of paper files and computer networks
violations: Goal Financial failed to conduct adequate risk assessments of paper files and computer networks
Failed to restrict access to personal information to authorized employees only
Failed to implement comprehensive information security policies and procedures for collection, handling, and disposal
Failed to provide adequate employee training on data protection and incident response
Failed to require third-party service providers to protect security and confidentiality by contract

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) requires financial institutions to provide customers with clear and conspicuous notices that accurately reflect their privacy policies and security practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Goal Financial disseminated a privacy policy stating it maintained physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards complying with federal regulations, when in fact it did not implement reasonable security measures
violations: Goal Financial disseminated a privacy policy stating it maintained physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards complying with federal regulations, when in fact it did not implement reasonable security measures

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Goal Financial made express and implied representations that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information from unauthorized access, which were false and misleading
violations: Goal Financial made express and implied representations that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information from unauthorized access, which were false and misleading

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on April 9, 2008, alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule, Privacy Rule, and FTC Act. The complaint culminated in a consent order requiring Goal Financial to implement comprehensive information security improvements, including documented risk assessments, access controls, employee training, service provider oversight, and ongoing monitoring and adjustment of the security program. The company was required to maintain compliance with these obligations.
