Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Sections 501-509 – Privacy Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 313
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Premier Capital Lending, Inc. was a Texas-based mortgage lender specializing in loans for combined purchases of real estate and manufactured homes. As a lender, the company routinely obtained and handled sensitive consumer financial information including credit histories and consumer reports.
companyLongDescription: Premier Capital Lending, Inc. was a Texas-based mortgage lender specializing in loans for combined purchases of real estate and manufactured homes. As a lender, the company routinely obtained and handled sensitive consumer financial information including credit histories and consumer reports.
caseDescription: Premier Capital Lending failed to implement adequate security safeguards for sensitive consumer financial data. An unauthorized hacker gained access to a third party's CRA login credentials issued by the company, compromising consumer reports for 400 individuals. The company failed to conduct risk assessments, monitor for unauthorized activity, or timely identify the full scope of the breach.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security safeguards to protect sensitive personal financial information from unauthorized access, directly enabling a data breach affecting hundreds of consumers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Premier Capital Lending issued consumer report access credentials to a third-party seller without auditing their computer network security, allowing a hacker to access.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker breached the seller's computer and accessed 317 unauthorized consumer reports plus 83 existing reports containing full names, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: We maintain physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards that comply with federal standards to store and secure information about you from unauthorized access, alteration and destruction. Our control policies authorize access to customer information only by individuals who need access to do their work.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company issued CRA credentials to a third-party seller without auditing their security, failed to monitor for unauthorized activity, and took over a year to discover that 83 consumer reports had been compromised by a hacker.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. § 314.3, 314.4) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including: identifying reasonably foreseeable risks; designing and implementing safeguards to control those risks; regularly testing or monitoring safeguard effectiveness; overseeing service providers by contract; and evaluating and adjusting the program based on testing results.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security
violations: Failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security
Failed to implement reasonable steps to assess third-party security risks before granting CRA login access
Failed to conduct reasonable reviews of consumer report requests for signs of unauthorized activity using readily available management reports or invoices
Failed to assess the full scope of consumer information stored and compromised by the hacker

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. § 313.4) requires a financial institution to provide a clear and conspicuous notice that accurately reflects its privacy policies and practices to its customers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Disseminated a privacy policy containing false or misleading statements claiming the company maintains safeguards complying with federal standards to protect information from unauthorized access, when in fact the company failed to implement reasonable security measures
violations: Disseminated a privacy policy containing false or misleading statements claiming the company maintains safeguards complying with federal standards to protect information from unauthorized access, when in fact the company failed to implement reasonable security measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made express and implied representations that the company implements reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, which was false or misleading given the company's failure to implement adequate safeguards
violations: Made express and implied representations that the company implements reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, which was false or misleading given the company's failure to implement adequate safeguards

outcome: On December 10, 2008, the FTC issued a complaint against Premier Capital Lending, Inc. and Debra Stiles for violations of the Safeguards Rule, Privacy Rule, and FTC Act Section 5(a). The document represents the initial enforcement action; the complaint alleges violations but does not specify the final settlement terms or remediation requirements, which would be determined in subsequent proceedings.
dataType: Financial data, credit histories, consumer reports, names, addresses, Social Security numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Safeguards Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 314 (implementing Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act § 501(b), 15 U.S.C. § 6801(b))
FTC Privacy Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 313 (implementing Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act § 503(a), 15 U.S.C. § 6803(a))

company: First Interstate Mortgage Corporation (FIM) and Nevada One Corporation
companyDescription: First Interstate Mortgage Corporation and Nevada One Corporation were mortgage brokerage companies providing real estate financing services, including loan processing and mortgage lender placement. Both were owned and operated by Gregory Navone from approximately 2000-2008.
companyLongDescription: First Interstate Mortgage Corporation and Nevada One Corporation were mortgage brokerage companies providing real estate financing services, including loan processing and mortgage lender placement. Both were owned and operated by Gregory Navone from approximately 2000-2008.
caseDescription: Gregory Navone, operating mortgage brokerage companies FIM and Nevada One, collected sensitive consumer financial data but failed to implement reasonable security safeguards or proper disposal procedures. Approximately 40 boxes of intact consumer documents containing at least 230 consumer reports and sensitive financial information were discovered in a public dumpster, exposing thousands of customers to identity theft and financial fraud.
violationSummary: Sensitive consumer information derived from consumer reports was exposed to unauthorized access when discarded in a public dumpster without secure destruction, creating widespread risk of identity theft and financial harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Gregory Navone operated mortgage brokerage firms FIM and Nevada One that collected sensitive consumer data including Social Security numbers, bank account numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 230 intact consumer reports and thousands of pages of sensitive financial documents containing names, addresses, Social Security numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: We maintain physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards that comply with federal standards to store and secure information from unauthorized access, alteration and destruction.
claimsVsReality.reality: No reasonable security safeguards were implemented; sensitive consumer data was stored insecurely in residential garages and ultimately abandoned in a public dumpster

claimsVsReality.claim: Agreements with service providers require them to safeguard customer information and not use it for other purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: No such contractual safeguards requiring service providers to protect information were actually implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made false representations about implementing reasonable security safeguards for consumer information when actual security was inadequate
violations: Made false representations about implementing reasonable security safeguards for consumer information when actual security was inadequate
Represented that service providers would safeguard customer information when no contractual safeguards were in place

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 628 of the FCRA and the Disposal Rule require persons maintaining consumer information derived from consumer reports to take reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access or use in connection with disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement policies and procedures requiring information to be disposed of in a manner preventing it from being read or reconstructed
violations: Failed to implement policies and procedures requiring information to be disposed of in a manner preventing it from being read or reconstructed
Failed to ensure employees or third parties were qualified and trained for secure disposal
Failed to oversee collection and transport of documents for disposal, resulting in intact boxes of sensitive records in a public dumpster

outcome: The complaint sought permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per knowing violation of the FCRA (with each disposal failure constituting a separate violation), compliance orders requiring implementation of information security and disposal policies, and reimbursement of litigation costs. As this is a complaint filing rather than a final judgment, the case outcome and specific penalty amount were not yet determined at the time of document issuance.
companyNow: FIM was dissolved in approximately August 2008. Nevada One ceased operations or was transferred to other operators by at least December 2003. Both companies are no longer operational.
dataType: Consumer financial data, Social Security numbers, bank and credit card account numbers, income and credit histories, mortgage information, tax returns, bank statements

companyDescription: TJX Companies, Inc. is a Delaware-incorporated off-price retailer operating over 2,500 stores worldwide under banners including T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, A.J. Wright, HomeGoods, Winners, and T.K.Maxx, selling apparel, footwear, and home fashions.
companyLongDescription: TJX Companies, Inc. is a Delaware-incorporated off-price retailer operating over 2,500 stores worldwide under banners including T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, A.J. Wright, HomeGoods, Winners, and T.K.Maxx, selling apparel, footwear, and home fashions.
caseDescription: TJX failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive payment card and consumer personal information across its retail networks. Between July 2005 and December 2006, hackers exploited these weaknesses to access and steal data from tens of millions of payment cards and approximately 455,000 consumer records. The company stored sensitive data in clear text, lacked encryption, weak password protocols, and failed to detect or prevent unauthorized access.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational safeguards to protect sensitive personal data. The deliberate storage of data in clear text, absence of encryption, weak access controls, and failure to monitor for breaches directly enabled unauthorized access and data theft.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: TJX stored tens of millions of payment card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes in unencrypted clear text on its networks.
whyTheyWereWrong: Intruders exploited these security gaps to steal tens of millions of payment card numbers between 2005.

claimsVsReality.claim: TJX claimed reasonable and appropriate security measures were in place to protect consumer payment card and personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company stored sensitive data in clear text, transmitted it unencrypted, lacked wireless access controls, used weak passwords, had no firewalls isolating payment systems, and failed to monitor for breach attempts or update security tools.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's networks were secure and properly isolated to prevent unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between July 2005 and December 2006, intruders connected to networks without authorization, installed hacker tools, and extracted tens of millions of payment cards and consumer records undetected.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: TJX failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect tens of millions of payment cards and personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers through data theft and fraudulent charges.
violations: TJX failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect tens of millions of payment cards and personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers through data theft and fraudulent charges.

The company's failure was unfair because it was caused by negligent practices (storing data in clear text, lacking encryption, weak passwords, no firewall protection, insufficient breach detection) that were not offset by countervailing benefits and were not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against TJX for unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. Following the breach disclosure in January 2007, TJX implemented remedial security measures to prevent further unauthorized access and notified law enforcement and affected consumers. The company entered into a consent order requiring comprehensive security improvements, ongoing compliance monitoring, and third-party assessments of its information security practices.
companyNow: TJX Companies remains one of the largest off-price retailers globally, operating T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, HomeGoods, and international banners. The company has since significantly enhanced its data security infrastructure and compliance programs.
dataType: Payment card data (account number, expiration date, security code), banking information (routing, account, check numbers), personal identification numbers, driver's license numbers, Social Security numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) - Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

company: Reed Elsevier Inc. and Seisint, Inc.
companyDescription: Reed Elsevier Inc. is a multinational information and analytics company. Through its LexisNexis division (which acquired Seisint in 2004), it operates consumer and business information databases used by law enforcement, insurers, and creditors.
companyLongDescription: Reed Elsevier Inc. is a multinational information and analytics company. Through its LexisNexis division (which acquired Seisint in 2004), it operates consumer and business information databases used by law enforcement, insurers, and creditors.
caseDescription: Reed Elsevier and its subsidiary Seisint operated Accurint, a verification database containing millions of consumers' sensitive personal information including Social Security numbers. The companies failed to implement adequate security controls on user credentials, allowing attackers to exploit weak passwords and authentication systems to gain unauthorized access to the database. From 2003 to mid-2005, multiple breaches exposed information about over 316,000 consumers, enabling identity theft and fraudulent credit card activation.
violationSummary: The company failed to provide reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive consumer information stored in accessible databases. Weak authentication structures created an unreasonable risk of unauthorized access despite well-publicized warnings since the late 1990s and actual attacks since 2002.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Reed Elsevier and Seisint operated Accurint databases containing millions of consumers' sensitive personal information with inadequate security, including weak passwords.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 316,000 consumers had their names, addresses, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers stolen by attackers, resulting in fraudulent credit accounts opened in their names.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondents implemented procedures to identify customers, limit access, and track searches through user ID and password authentication systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The authentication systems used weak credentials (allowing identical user ID and password, common dictionary words), lacked enforcement, permitted credential sharing, and were vulnerable to known attacks, allowing unauthorized access for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondents provided secure access to sensitive consumer information in Accurint databases.
claimsVsReality.reality: Attackers repeatedly exploited the weak authentication systems since at least 2002 to access over 316,000 consumers' sensitive personal data without authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive consumer information, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: Respondents failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive consumer information, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on July 29, 2008, alleging unfair trade practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document indicates this is a complaint initiating enforcement proceedings; it does not contain a final settlement or consent order. Respondents were required to cease the unfair security practices and implement reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to consumer information.
companyNow: Reed Elsevier Inc. (now RELX PLC) remains a major global information and analytics company. Seisint operates as a LexisNexis subsidiary and continues to provide consumer and business verification services, now with significantly enhanced security protocols.
dataType: Social Security numbers, consumer identification information, motor vehicle records, names, addresses, dates of birth

companyDescription: Ingenix, Inc. is a wholly owned subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group Incorporated, headquartered in Eden Prairie, Minnesota. It operates as a healthcare data aggregation company providing medical profiles and analytics to insurance companies for underwriting and claims purposes.
companyLongDescription: Ingenix, Inc. is a wholly owned subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group Incorporated, headquartered in Eden Prairie, Minnesota. It operates as a healthcare data aggregation company providing medical profiles and analytics to insurance companies for underwriting and claims purposes.
caseDescription: Ingenix, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group, operated MedPoint, a data aggregation service that compiled and sold detailed 5-year prescription drug histories and medical profiles of insurance applicants to insurers. The FTC found that Ingenix was a consumer reporting agency under the Fair Credit Reporting Act but failed to provide required statutory notices to insurance companies purchasing these medical profiles, violating FCRA Section 607(d).
violationSummary: Ingenix disclosed detailed prescription and health information to third parties (insurers) for decision-making purposes without providing required statutory disclosures, failing to notify consumers of the scope, use, and their rights regarding these sensitive medical reports.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Ingenix aggregated five-year prescription drug histories from pharmacy benefit managers and created detailed medical profiles containing specific medications, dosages, refills.
whyTheyWereWrong: Insurance applicants' highly sensitive prescription and health data was compiled into profiles used for underwriting decisions without consumers receiving notice of their rights to dispute.

claimsVsReality.claim: Insurance applicants provided consent authorizing insurers to access their health and medical records through MedPoint
claimsVsReality.reality: While consent forms existed, Ingenix as the consumer reporting agency failed to provide the legally required separate notices to insurers explaining their obligations under FCRA, preventing consumers from understanding the full scope and use of their data

claimsVsReality.claim: MedPoint provides objective prescription history data to support underwriting decisions
claimsVsReality.reality: MedPoint went beyond historical data to generate predictive medical condition scores and risk assessments, making inferences about health status used for insurance eligibility determinations without complying with FCRA disclosure requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(d) requires that any consumer reporting agency provide to any person to whom it provides a consumer report a 'Notice To Users of Consumer Reports: Obligations of Users Under the FCRA' with content specified in 16 CFR 698, Appendix H.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ingenix failed to provide the required FCRA notice to insurance companies that purchased medical profiles generated by MedPoint
violations: Ingenix failed to provide the required FCRA notice to insurance companies that purchased medical profiles generated by MedPoint
Ingenix classified its MedPoint medical profiles as consumer reports but did not comply with mandatory disclosure requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(d) defines a consumer report as information that bears on a consumer's credit worthiness, credit standing, credit capacity, character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living, used or expected to be used for purposes of establishing consumer eligibility for credit or insurance.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ingenix's medical profiles qualified as consumer reports because they contained health and prescription information used by insurers to establish eligibility for insurance
violations: Ingenix's medical profiles qualified as consumer reports because they contained health and prescription information used by insurers to establish eligibility for insurance

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(f) defines a consumer reporting agency as one that regularly engages in assembling or evaluating consumer information for the purpose of furnishing consumer reports to third parties for monetary fees.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ingenix operated as a consumer reporting agency by aggregating prescription and health data and furnishing medical profiles to insurers for compensation
violations: Ingenix operated as a consumer reporting agency by aggregating prescription and health data and furnishing medical profiles to insurers for compensation

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ingenix's violation of FCRA Section 607(d) constituted an unfair and deceptive practice in commerce
violations: Ingenix's violation of FCRA Section 607(d) constituted an unfair and deceptive practice in commerce

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on February 6, 2008, against Ingenix for violating the Fair Credit Reporting Act by failing to provide required consumer notices to users of its medical profiles. The enforcement action required Ingenix to comply with FCRA obligations going forward. This complaint was a precursor to a settlement order requiring compliance modifications.
companyNow: Ingenix remains a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group (now Optum), and continues to provide data analytics and healthcare information services.
dataType: Health data, prescription drug records, medical conditions, pharmacy information, physician information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(d), 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(d)
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(d), 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(d)
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(f), 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(f)
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 621(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1681s

companyDescription: ValueClick operated lead generation websites connecting consumers to advertisers, and e-commerce sites selling products like printer cartridges and consumer goods. The company used misleading free-product offers to generate qualified leads for third-party merchants.
companyLongDescription: ValueClick operated lead generation websites connecting consumers to advertisers, and e-commerce sites selling products like printer cartridges and consumer goods. The company used misleading free-product offers to generate qualified leads for third-party merchants.
caseDescription: ValueClick operated deceptive free merchandise offers requiring consumers to spend money on third-party promotions without clear disclosure, and failed to encrypt sensitive financial data despite promising industry-standard security. Customer databases were vulnerable to SQL injection attacks and stored CVV2 codes in insecure formats.
violationSummary: Primary violation involves inadequate security measures for sensitive financial data. Company falsely represented encryption compliance, stored CVV2 codes without proper protection, and failed to implement defenses against known SQL injection vulnerabilities, exposing customer financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: ValueClick advertised free merchandise like iPods and laptops through misleading emails and websites.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers spent hundreds of dollars on required paid offers and subscriptions only to discover they could never actually obtain the promised free merchandise.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers can get free merchandise (iPods, laptops, Visa gift cards) just by entering their zip code or participating in a survey
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumers had to complete numerous mandatory paid offers from third parties, often costing significant money, and in many cases could not complete all requirements to receive the promised item

claimsVsReality.claim: The ValueClick Network employs industry standard security measures to ensure the security of all data. ValueClick encrypts sensitive information such as passwords and financial data.
claimsVsReality.reality: ValueClick stored credit card data on HSM sites with no encryption at all. E-Babylon sites used only a weak alphabetic substitution cipher, not industry-standard encryption. Both were vulnerable to SQL injection attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your Personally Identifiable Information resides on a secure server. We encrypt your Personally Identifiable Information and thereby prevent unauthorized parties from viewing such information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive customer data including CVV2 codes were stored in databases using insecure methods vulnerable to well-known SQL injection attacks. Solutions to prevent such attacks were readily available and inexpensive but not implemented.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that advertised offers were without cost or obligation while failing to disclose that consumers must complete paid third-party promotions
violations: Represented that advertised offers were without cost or obligation while failing to disclose that consumers must complete paid third-party promotions
Failed to clearly and conspicuously disclose material costs and obligations associated with obtaining promised free merchandise
Represented encryption of sensitive customer information consistent with industry standards while actually storing data without encryption or with weak alphabetic substitution
Represented reasonable and appropriate security measures while leaving databases vulnerable to SQL injection attacks

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a)(2) of CAN-SPAM Act prohibits initiating commercial email with subject headings likely to mislead recipients about material facts.
regulatoryFindings.description: Initiated commercial emails with misleading subject lines such as 'Free PS3 for survey' and 'Free Apple iPhone for Daniel' without disclosing participation requirements and costs
violations: Initiated commercial emails with misleading subject lines such as 'Free PS3 for survey' and 'Free Apple iPhone for Daniel' without disclosing participation requirements and costs

outcome: The complaint sought judgment against all three defendants, monetary civil penalties against ValueClick and Hi-Speed Media for CAN-SPAM violations (up to $11,000 per violation), rescission of contracts, restitution and refund of consumer monies, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, permanent injunction against future violations, and payment of costs of action. The document is the complaint filed in court requesting relief.
companyNow: ValueClick was acquired by System1, Inc. in 2012. The lead generation business model described in this complaint has largely shifted as regulatory pressure increased.
dataType: Credit card numbers, CVV2 codes, billing address, shipping address, phone, fax, email, password, order identification number, credit card expiration date
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
CAN-SPAM Act Section 5(a)(2) – Misleading subject headers in commercial email

companyLongDescription: Milliman, Inc. is a Washington-based actuarial consulting firm that has provided services to insurance and healthcare sectors since 1947. caseDescription: Milliman, Inc. operated IntelliScript, a data aggregation service that compiled 5-year prescription drug histories and medical profiles of insurance applicants. The FTC alleged that Milliman qualified as a consumer reporting agency under the Fair Credit Reporting Act but failed to provide legally required notices to insurance companies purchasing these reports. The company violated Section 607(d) of the FCRA by not furnishing the mandated "Notice To Users of Consumer Reports: Obligations of Users Under the FCRA" to its clients.

violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Milliman compiled five-year prescription drug histories including dosages, refills, pharmacy names.
whyTheyWereWrong: Insurance applicants' sensitive medical and prescription data was aggregated and used to determine eligibility for insurance with no legal safeguards or transparency.

claimsVsReality.claim: IntelliScript medical profiles could be used for insurance underwriting decisions with consumer consent through insurance company consent forms
claimsVsReality.reality: The system operated without providing insurance companies (the actual users of the consumer reports) with mandatory FCRA disclosures about their legal obligations, undermining the protective framework

claimsVsReality.claim: Data was collected from Pharmacy Benefit Managers with appropriate authorization
claimsVsReality.reality: Although applicants consented to health record access, Milliman failed to ensure proper regulatory compliance in furnishing the aggregated reports to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(d) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires consumer reporting agencies to provide to any person to whom they furnish a consumer report a 'Notice To Users of Consumer Reports: Obligations of Users Under the FCRA' with content specified in 16 CFR 698, Appendix H.

violations: Milliman failed to provide this required notice to insurance companies purchasing IntelliScript medical profiles despite qualifying as a consumer reporting agency

violations: Milliman's IntelliScript medical profiles met this definition as they contained detailed health information used for insurance underwriting and claims decisions

regulatoryFindings.description: Milliman engaged in this practice by assembling prescription drug histories and selling medical profiles to insurance companies for fees
violations: Milliman engaged in this practice by assembling prescription drug histories and selling medical profiles to insurance companies for fees

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a)(1) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Milliman's violation of FCRA Section 607(d) constituted an unfair and deceptive practice under FTC Act Section 621(a)
violations: Milliman's violation of FCRA Section 607(d) constituted an unfair and deceptive practice under FTC Act Section 621(a)

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on February 6, 2008, alleging violations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act and FTC Act. The document indicates this is the initial complaint stage; full resolution details are not included in the provided pages. Milliman would have been subject to compliance orders requiring provision of mandated consumer report user notices and potentially ongoing monitoring of FCRA compliance.
companyNow: Milliman, Inc. is a global actuarial and consulting firm still operating today, providing services to insurance and healthcare industries. The company has evolved significantly from its IntelliScript data aggregation service.
dataType: Health data, prescription drug records, medical profiles

Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 603(d), 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(d)

companyDescription: American United Mortgage Company is an Illinois corporation that provides services in connection with financing home purchases and refinancing existing home mortgages, including accepting, receiving, and processing loan applications in person, by mail, and online. The company collects personal information from consumers, consumer reporting agencies, banks, lenders, real estate brokers, and others.
companyLongDescription: American United Mortgage Company is an Illinois corporation that provides services in connection with financing home purchases and refinancing existing home mortgages, including accepting, receiving, and processing loan applications in person, by mail, and online. The company collects personal information from consumers, consumer reporting agencies, banks, lenders, real estate brokers, and others.
caseDescription: American United Mortgage Company failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect consumers' personal information and improperly disposed of sensitive documents containing financial data in unsecured dumpsters accessible to the public. Hundreds of documents containing consumer reports and financial information for 36 individuals were discovered in and around the company's dumpster between December 2005 and March 2006. Additionally, the company failed to provide required privacy notices to customers for approximately five years.
violationSummary: Consumer financial information was exposed through improper disposal practices in unsecured, publicly accessible dumpsters, creating increased accessibility to identity thieves and other unauthorized parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: American United Mortgage Company left hundreds of documents containing consumers' names, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, credit histories.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least 36 consumers' complete financial identities including SSNs, account numbers, and credit reports were publicly accessible in trash, enabling identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: American United maintained secure disposal practices for consumer information
claimsVsReality.reality: Hundreds of intact documents containing SSNs, account numbers, and consumer reports were left in unsecured public dumpsters accessible to anyone

claimsVsReality.claim: American United had comprehensive information security safeguards in place
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards and failed to identify foreseeable risks to customer information

claimsVsReality.claim: American United informed customers of its privacy practices and information sharing
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to provide privacy notices to customers for approximately five years (July 2001 to March 2006)

regulatoryFindings.act: The Disposal Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 682, issued pursuant to FACTA §216) requires any person maintaining or possessing consumer information for a business purpose to take reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access to or use of the information in connection with its disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: American United failed to implement reasonable policies and procedures requiring proper disposal of consumer personal information and consumer reports
violations: American United failed to implement reasonable policies and procedures requiring proper disposal of consumer personal information and consumer reports
American United failed to take reasonable actions in disposing of such information through methods such as burning, pulverizing, or shredding so information could not be read or reconstructed

Hundreds of intact documents containing consumer reports and information derived therefrom were found in unsecured dumpster near office in February 2006, with many documents in open trash bags accessible to the public

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314, §501(b) of the GLB Act) requires financial institutions to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: American United failed to develop or implement reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information
violations: American United failed to develop or implement reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information
American United failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information
American United failed to develop, implement, or maintain a comprehensive written information security program as required by the Rule

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313, §§501-509 of the GLB Act) requires financial institutions to provide consumers, no later than when a customer relationship arises and annually thereafter, a clear and conspicuous notice that accurately reflects the institution's privacy policies and practices including security policies and practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: American United failed to provide its customers with a copy of its privacy policy from July 1, 2001 until March 2006, a period of approximately five years
violations: American United failed to provide its customers with a copy of its privacy policy from July 1, 2001 until March 2006, a period of approximately five years
American United failed to describe its information collection and sharing practices with respect to affiliated and non-affiliated third parties

outcome: The complaint sought monetary civil penalties for violations of the Disposal Rule, Safeguards Rule, and Privacy Rule, as well as injunctive relief. The Court was authorized to award monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation of Section 628 of the FCRA and was authorized to issue a permanent injunction prohibiting the defendant from violating the FCRA. Each instance in which American United failed to comply with the Disposal Rule constitutes a separate violation for assessment of monetary civil penalties. The case requests that the Court enjoin the defendant from violating the Disposal, Safeguards, and Privacy Rules and award such additional relief as the Court deems just and proper.
companyNow: Unknown. American United Mortgage Company's current operational status is not documented in the complaint.
dataType: Financial data, consumer reports, credit histories, bank and credit card account numbers, income histories, social security numbers
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act §621 (Disposal Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 682)

companyDescription: Action Research Group, Inc. was a Florida-based company that, along with affiliated entities Eye in the Sky Investigations, Inc., engaged in obtaining and selling confidential telephone call records and customer proprietary network information from telecommunications carriers without authorization.
companyLongDescription: Action Research Group, Inc. was a Florida-based company that, along with affiliated entities Eye in the Sky Investigations, Inc., engaged in obtaining and selling confidential telephone call records and customer proprietary network information from telecommunications carriers without authorization.
caseDescription: Action Research Group and affiliated companies illegally obtained and sold confidential customer telephone records without authorization. They used deception including impersonating account holders and telecom employees to trick carriers into disclosing call records. The practice violated federal telecommunications law and exposed millions of consumers to privacy invasion and security risks.
violationSummary: The defendants obtained and disclosed confidential customer proprietary network information (telephone call records) without authorization, violating the duty of confidentiality owed to consumers and the strict statutory restrictions under the Telecommunications Act.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Action Research Group obtained and sold confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers by impersonating account holders or carrier employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers had their private call records illegally exposed, enabling identity theft, stalking, harassment, and surveillance without any ability to prevent or detect the breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendants represented themselves as authorized to obtain customer phone records (as account holders, carrier employees, or otherwise authorized persons).
claimsVsReality.reality: Defendants were not account holders, carrier employees, or otherwise authorized to obtain or access customer phone records. They used false pretenses and fraudulent documents to deceive carriers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendants could legitimately provide customer phone records to clients for a fee.
claimsVsReality.reality: Federal law strictly prohibits disclosure of customer proprietary network information without affirmative written customer consent. No legitimate authorization existed for Defendants' business model.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants represented they were authorized account holders, carrier employees, or otherwise authorized to obtain customer phone records when they were not, causing carriers to disclose confidential records.
violations: Defendants represented they were authorized account holders, carrier employees, or otherwise authorized to obtain customer phone records when they were not, causing carriers to disclose confidential records.
Defendants obtained and sold confidential customer phone records without customer knowledge or consent, causing substantial injury to consumers through privacy invasion and security risks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) prohibits carriers from disclosing customer proprietary network information except as required by law or with customer approval.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants induced carriers to disclose customer proprietary network information through fraudulent misrepresentation, circumventing statutory protections.
violations: Defendants induced carriers to disclose customer proprietary network information through fraudulent misrepresentation, circumventing statutory protections.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2) requires customer phone records be disclosed only upon affirmative written customer request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants obtained phone records without any affirmative written customer authorization or approval.
violations: Defendants obtained phone records without any affirmative written customer authorization or approval.

outcome: The FTC sought permanent injunction, rescission of contracts, restitution, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The complaint was filed February 13, 2007 in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida, Orlando Division. The court had authority to grant preliminary injunctive relief, permanent injunctions to prevent future violations, and ancillary relief including contract rescission and restitution to injured consumers.
companyNow: Unknown. Action Research Group, Inc. was a Florida corporation involved in obtaining and selling confidential telecommunications data. The status of the company following this 2007 FTC enforcement action is not documented in the complaint.
dataType: Telephone call records, customer proprietary network information (CPNI)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) - Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) - Restrictions on disclosure of customer proprietary network information
Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2) - Requirement for affirmative written customer consent

companyDescription: Guidance Software, Inc. was a California-based software company that developed computer forensics and incident response tools for investigating data breaches and security incidents. The company served corporate and law enforcement customers through its software products and Professional Services Division.
companyLongDescription: Guidance Software, Inc. was a California-based software company that developed computer forensics and incident response tools for investigating data breaches and security incidents. The company served corporate and law enforcement customers through its software products and Professional Services Division.
caseDescription: Guidance Software collected sensitive customer data including credit card information but failed to implement adequate security measures. Between September and December 2005, hackers exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities in the company's web application to access thousands of credit card records. The company had made explicit privacy claims about protecting customer data but did not implement basic, low-cost security defenses against known attack vectors.
violationSummary: Guidance Software failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive personal information stored on its corporate network, exposing thousands of credit card records to unauthorized access through known attack vectors (SQL injection).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Guidance Software stored thousands of customers' credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes in plain readable text on a web-accessible network.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker exploited these security failures between September and December 2005 to steal credit card information for thousands of customers, exposing them to fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: This website takes every precaution to protect our users' information. When users submit sensitive information via the website, your information is protected both online and off-line.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer data was stored in clear readable text on a web-accessible server, vulnerable to SQL injection attacks that were actively exploited for months before detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sensitive information is encrypted and is protected with the best encryption software in the industry - SSL.
claimsVsReality.reality: While SSL encryption was used for data transmission, the underlying sensitive data was stored in plain text on the corporate network, and the company had not assessed or defended against known web application vulnerabilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: Guidance Software is committed to keeping the data you provide us secure and will take reasonable precautions to protect your information from loss, misuse or alteration.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement basic security controls including vulnerability assessment, defense against SQL injection, monitoring of network connections, and detection of unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Guidance Software represented in privacy policies (2002-2005) that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect sensitive personal information, stating 'This website takes every precaution to protect our users' information' and that information is 'protected with the best encryption software in the industry - SSL.'
violations: Guidance Software represented in privacy policies (2002-2005) that it implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect sensitive personal information, stating 'This website takes every precaution to protect our users' information' and that information is 'protected with the best encryption software in the industry - SSL.'

In fact, Guidance Software did not implement reasonable and appropriate security measures. It: (1) stored customer data in clear readable text despite using SSL encryption; (2) failed to assess web application vulnerabilities to SQL injection attacks; (3) did not implement simple, low-cost, readily available defenses to such attacks; (4) stored network user credentials in plain text; (5) did not use readily available security measures to monitor and control internet connections; (6) failed to employ sufficient measures to detect unauthorized access.

A hacker exploited these failures from September through December 2005, using SQL injection attacks to obtain unauthorized access to thousands of credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 30, 2007, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint charged that Guidance Software's privacy representations were false and misleading given the company's actual security practices. A compliance order requiring implementation of reasonable security measures and periodic assessments was expected to follow (typical FTC settlement outcome for such cases), though the final settlement terms are not included in the complaint document.
companyNow: Guidance Software was acquired by OpenText Corporation in 2012 and operates as part of OpenText's cybersecurity solutions division.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, expiration dates, security codes), contact information (name, address, email, phone)

companyLongDescription: Accusearch, Inc., operating under the domain Abika.com, was a data brokerage service that advertised the ability to obtain and sell confidential telephone call detail records from telecommunications carriers to paying clients worldwide, including records for prepaid calling cards and internet-based phone services.

whatTheyDid: Accusearch obtained and sold confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers without authorization by using false pretenses, fraudulent statements.

violations: Accusearch obtained and sold customer proprietary network information (phone records) without knowledge or authorization, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

violations: Accusearch induced carrier employees to disclose confidential customer phone records through false pretenses and fraudulent statements without customer knowledge or written authorization.

violations: Accusearch obtained customer phone records without any customer authorization and sold them to third parties without designation by the customer.

caseDescription: CEO Group, Inc. and its founder Scott Joseph obtained and sold confidential customer telephone records from telecommunications carriers without customer authorization. The company then sold these records to third parties for profit.

violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: CEO Group, Inc. and founder Scott Joseph obtained confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers using false pretenses, fraudulent statements.

caseDescription: ChoicePoint, a major data broker with billions of consumer records, failed to implement reasonable procedures to verify subscriber identities before furnishing sensitive consumer reports. Fraudsters obtained unauthorized access to 163,000 consumers' personal information including SSNs and credit reports, resulting in at least 800 confirmed identity theft cases. The company made false public claims about its rigorous credentialing and monitoring practices.
violationSummary: ChoicePoint failed to maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to verify subscriber identities and monitor for unauthorized activity, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive consumer information.

Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: ChoicePoint sold consumer reports containing Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and financial data to applicants with false credentials.
whyTheyWereWrong: 163,000 consumers had their sensitive personal information exposed to identity thieves, resulting in at least 800 confirmed cases of identity theft and financial fraud against real people.

claimsVsReality.claim: ChoicePoint uses administrative, technical, personnel, and physical safeguards to protect the confidentiality and security of personally identifiable consumer information

companyDescription: CardSystems Solutions, Inc. was a Delaware corporation based in Tucson, Arizona that provided authorization processing services for credit and debit card purchases. The company processed card purchases totaling at least $15 billion annually for approximately 119,000 merchants.
companyLongDescription: CardSystems Solutions, Inc. was a Delaware corporation based in Tucson, Arizona that provided authorization processing services for credit and debit card purchases. The company processed card purchases totaling at least $15 billion annually for approximately 119,000 merchants.
caseDescription: CardSystems Solutions failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive payment card data stored on its systems. A hacker exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to steal magnetic stripe data for tens of millions of credit and debit cards, resulting in millions of dollars in fraudulent purchases and widespread card cancellations affecting consumers.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures directly resulted in a data breach exposing millions of payment card records, demonstrating inadequate information security practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: CardSystems Solutions stored credit and debit card magnetic stripe data in vulnerable formats for up to 30 days, failed to assess SQL injection vulnerabilities.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker exploited these failures to steal magnetic stripe data for tens of millions of cards, enabling fraudulent purchases that forced banks to cancel.

claimsVsReality.claim: CardSystems provided secure payment authorization processing services to merchants.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company stored sensitive payment card data in vulnerable formats, failed to implement basic security controls, and was compromised by a hacker who exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to exfiltrate tens of millions of payment card records over several months.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: CardSystems failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information it stored, causing substantial injury to consumers through data breach exposing tens of millions of payment card records with complete magnetic stripe data, security codes, and cardholder information.
violations: CardSystems failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information it stored, causing substantial injury to consumers through data breach exposing tens of millions of payment card records with complete magnetic stripe data, security codes, and cardholder information.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against CardSystems on September 5, 2006, alleging violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act for failing to provide reasonable security for personal information. The complaint initiated an enforcement proceeding to address the company's inadequate security practices that led to the massive payment card data breach.
companyNow: CardSystems Solutions was acquired by Global Payments Inc. in 2007, following the breach and regulatory action. The breach became one of the largest payment card data breaches at that time.
dataType: Financial data, credit and debit card information, magnetic stripe data, customer names, card numbers, expiration dates, security codes

companyLongDescription: Nations Title Agency, Inc. was a Kansas-based financial services company specializing in real estate settlement services, residential closings, title abstracts, title commitments, appraisals, foreclosure management, and asset disposition. caseDescription: Nations Title Agency and its parent company failed to implement reasonable security safeguards for sensitive consumer financial information, resulting in a 2004 hacker breach and the discovery of discarded documents containing personal data in an unsecured dumpster in 2005. whatTheyDid: Nations Title Agency failed to implement reasonable security measures for consumer data, including risk assessments, access controls, employee training, secure document disposal.

A hacker gained access to the network in April 2004, and sensitive documents were found discarded in an unsecured dumpster in February 2005.

companyDescription: DSW Inc. is a major footwear retailer operating approximately 190 stores across 32 U.S. states as of 2005-2006, selling men's and women's shoes through physical retail locations. The company processes payment card and check information at point-of-sale terminals across its nationwide store network.
companyLongDescription: DSW Inc. is a major footwear retailer operating approximately 190 stores across 32 U.S. states as of 2005-2006, selling men's and women's shoes through physical retail locations. The company processes payment card and check information at point-of-sale terminals across its nationwide store network.
caseDescription: DSW Inc. stored sensitive payment card and checking account data in unencrypted files on inadequately secured computer networks across 190 stores. The company failed to implement basic security measures such as encryption, access controls, and unauthorized access detection. This resulted in a breach compromising approximately 1.44 million credit/debit cards and 96,000 checking accounts, causing fraudulent charges and financial losses to customers.
companyWorth: Unknown (as private subsidiary of Caleres Inc.; Caleres Inc. market cap approximately $1.5B as of recent data)
violationSummary: The core violation was inadequate security controls over personal financial data. DSW failed to implement readily available technical safeguards (encryption, access restrictions, monitoring) that would have prevented unauthorized access, directly resulting in a large-scale data breach affecting millions of payment cards and banking credentials.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: DSW stored sensitive payment and banking information including credit card numbers, debit card security codes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these security failures to steal data from approximately 1.44 million credit and debit cards.

claimsVsReality.claim: DSW was operating normal retail payment processing systems to authorize credit cards, debit cards, and checks at point-of-sale.
claimsVsReality.reality: DSW's systems stored sensitive payment data in unencrypted files on unsecured networks, allowing hackers to access and steal data from multiple store locations through inadequately protected wireless access points.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: DSW failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information, specifically: storing sensitive data in multiple files without business justification; failing to use encryption or access controls on wireless networks; storing unencrypted files accessible via commonly known credentials; insufficient network segmentation; and inadequate unauthorized access detection; resulting in compromise of 1.44 million credit/debit cards and 96,385 checking accounts
violations: DSW failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information, specifically: storing sensitive data in multiple files without business justification; failing to use encryption or access controls on wireless networks; storing unencrypted files accessible via commonly known credentials; insufficient network segmentation; and inadequate unauthorized access detection; resulting in compromise of 1.44 million credit/debit cards and 96,385 checking accounts

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint on March 7, 2006, alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document indicates the initiation of an enforcement proceeding against DSW. Resolution would typically include a Consent Order requiring DSW to implement comprehensive information security measures, maintain reasonable safeguards for personal information, conduct regular security assessments, and submit to monitoring and compliance reporting.
companyNow: DSW Inc. (now operating as Designer Shoe Warehouse) remains in operation as a subsidiary of Caleres Inc. The company continues retail footwear operations and has since implemented enhanced data security protocols in response to this enforcement action and industry standards evolution.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, debit card numbers, expiration dates, security codes, checking account numbers, routing numbers, account numbers), identification data (driver's license numbers and state)

companyDescription: Petco Animal Supplies, Inc. is a major pet supplies and services retailer operating over 636 stores across the United States and a website at PETCO.com. The company sells pet food, supplies, and veterinary services to consumers.
companyLongDescription: Petco Animal Supplies, Inc. is a major pet supplies and services retailer operating over 636 stores across the United States and a website at PETCO.com. The company sells pet food, supplies, and veterinary services to consumers.
caseDescription: Petco made misleading claims that consumer credit card information was encrypted and secure on its website, but failed to implement reasonable security measures. An SQL injection attack in June 2003 exposed credit card numbers in plain text. The company had ignored well-known vulnerabilities that security experts had warned about since 1997.
violationSummary: Petco failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect sensitive personal financial information stored in its database. Data was maintained in unencrypted form despite representations claiming encryption and protection from unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Petco falsely promised customers that their credit card numbers were fully encrypted and secure, but stored the data in plain readable text in its database where attackers could access it using.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers who trusted Petco's security guarantees had their credit card numbers and personal information exposed to unauthorized access by third parties who exploited the unprotected database.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your information is secure. Customers' data is strictly protected against any unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Credit card numbers were stored in plain readable text in the database and could be accessed by attackers using SQL injection attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Entering your credit card number via our secure server is completely safe. The server encrypts all of your information; no one except you can access it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data was only encrypted during transmission. Once it reached the server, it was decrypted and stored in plain text, accessible to anyone exploiting the SQL injection vulnerability.

claimsVsReality.claim: 100% Safeguard Your Shopping Experience Guarantee means you never have to worry about the safety of your credit card information.
claimsVsReality.reality: An actual SQL injection attack in June 2003 exposed credit card numbers in clear text, directly violating this guarantee.

claimsVsReality.claim: Protecting your information is our number one priority, and your personal data is strictly shielded from unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement basic security procedures to detect application vulnerabilities or prevent exploitation, despite industry warnings since 1997.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Petco represented that personal information was maintained in encrypted format and inaccessible to unauthorized persons, but stored credit card data in plain text in the database
violations: Petco represented that personal information was maintained in encrypted format and inaccessible to unauthorized persons, but stored credit card data in plain text in the database

Petco represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures, but failed to implement simple, readily available defenses against SQL injection attacks despite industry knowledge of the vulnerability since 1997

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on March 4, 2005, alleging unfair or deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case alleged false claims regarding data security and encryption. Resolution likely included compliance orders requiring implementation of reasonable security measures, regular monitoring, and structural reforms to data protection practices.
companyNow: Petco Animal Supplies was acquired by BC Partners in 2017 and went private. The company continues to operate as a major pet supply retailer with both physical stores and e-commerce operations, having presumably implemented enhanced security practices following the FTC enforcement action.
dataType: Credit card numbers, expiration dates, names, addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyLongDescription: Superior Mortgage Corporation was a New Jersey-based residential mortgage lender operating 40 branch offices across 10 states and six websites, collecting sensitive customer financial data during loan applications.

Customer data collected through mortgage applications remained unprotected for over two years.

companyDescription: Sunbelt Lending Services, Inc. was a mortgage company and financial institution operating primarily in Florida with headquarters in Clearwater. companyLongDescription: Sunbelt Lending Services, Inc. was a mortgage company and financial institution operating primarily in Florida with headquarters in Clearwater. Additionally, Sunbelt failed to provide required privacy notices to online customers.

violations: Data Breach & Negligence

claimsVsReality.reality: Sunbelt failed to establish contracts with service providers requiring safeguards or to verify they implemented adequate security measures

companyDescription: Consumerinfo.com offered free credit reports online and bundled credit monitoring services. The company operated under multiple trade names including Experian Consumer Direct, QSpace Inc., and iPlace Inc., and was based in Irvine, California.
companyLongDescription: Consumerinfo.com offered free credit reports online and bundled credit monitoring services. The company operated under multiple trade names including Experian Consumer Direct, QSpace Inc., and iPlace Inc., and was based in Irvine, California.
caseDescription: Consumerinfo.com advertised free credit reports but automatically enrolled consumers in a paid credit monitoring service without adequate disclosure of the $79.95 annual fee. Consumers were charged without express informed consent after a 30-day trial period, with fees automatically renewing and charges appearing on credit cards as 'Credit Report Fee'. The company further misrepresented its free reports as equivalent to statutory free reports required under the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act.
companyWorth: Unknown (subsidiary of Experian plc, valued at approximately $6.5B as of 2005)
violationSummary: The company failed to adequately disclose material terms (automatic charging, annual fees, auto-renewal) despite collecting sensitive financial and identity data. This constitutes inadequate disclosure of information practices affecting how personal data (especially credit card numbers) would be used.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Consumerinfo.com advertised free credit reports with a 30-day free trial membership while concealing an automatic $79.95 annual charge that renewed without explicit consumer consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers were charged hundreds of millions in aggregate fees without understanding their credit card obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: FREE credit report with 30-day FREE trial membership at no obligation, no commitment
claimsVsReality.reality: Automatic enrollment in paid $79.95/year (or $12/month after 2004) credit monitoring service with fees charged if consumer did not actively cancel within 30 days

claimsVsReality.claim: Valid credit card information required only to establish your account; card will not be charged during free trial
claimsVsReality.reality: Credit cards were charged automatically after 30 days without express informed consent, and charges renewed annually without contemporaneous notice

claimsVsReality.claim: Your credit rating will NOT be affected when we pull your free credit report
claimsVsReality.reality: Truthful, but materially misleading when combined with undisclosed paid service enrollment and charges

claimsVsReality.claim: Free reports available through our websites are equivalent to statutory free reports under the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act
claimsVsReality.reality: The free reports offered through consumerinfo.com and freecreditreport.com were commercial promotions requiring enrollment in a paid service, not the statutory free annual reports available through www.annualcreditreport.com established by the FACT Act

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.

violations: Represented consumers could obtain free credit reports and free trial memberships at no obligation while failing to disclose the $79.95 annual fee unless they cancelled within 30 days
Failed to disclose adequately that automatic charges would be assessed to consumers' credit cards without express informed consent

Auto-renewed annual memberships by charging credit cards without contemporaneous notice or consumer action required

outcome: The FTC sought permanent injunction, consumer redress including rescission of contracts, refunds of monies paid, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The complaint was filed August 15, 2005, seeking relief for deceptive marketing and unfair billing practices. The case established precedent for requiring clear, conspicuous disclosure of material terms (especially automatic renewal and fees) before charging consumers for purportedly 'free' services.
